Progress is being made against that goal, with fewer than 160 hotels in operation today compared with a peak of over 400 in 2023. So far, 44 asylum hotels have been closed this year, with more to follow. That is £1 billion saved for the British taxpayer already. As we continue this vital work alongside the wider efforts to restore order and control, we have been working relentlessly upstream to prevent the vile trade of organised immigration crime in the first place. We have reduced the number of small boats from the highs we saw under the previous Government. As Members will know, arrivals are down around 40% when compared with last year. The annual record for crossings remains at 45,700 in 2022. Organised immigration crime arrests and other disruptions are at record levels. Our work with France has prevented more than 50,000 attempted crossings since the general election, and over 60% of small boat events have been prevented this year. We will ensure that our approach reflects the needs of the whole country by building a system that is orderly, controlled and, at long last, fair.

Ministers slipped out their decision to grant planning permission after the House had risen last Thursday, so I am grateful to you for granting this urgent question, Mr Speaker. People across Bicester and the surrounding communities are angry about this decision, and they have every right to be. They took the consultation seriously. The Government recorded 3,177 objections and just one response in support. They raised serious and locally informed questions that deserved answers before planning approval. Instead, the Government pressed ahead, even though they accepted there would be harm to public services, including policing and transport, alongside wider concerns about public safety and community cohesion, even after mitigation. The overwhelming impression is that the Government are hellbent on opening another large asylum centre, and that they simply do not care about the real and specific problems with this site at MOD Bicester. MOD Bicester has never provided residential accommodation. It is a semi-derelict storage depot with asbestos-ridden buildings. Water, power and sewerage infrastructure must be built from the ground up, alongside new accommodation and transport arrangements for an isolated site. That is an extraordinary amount of work simply to make the location usable. I believe it will cost over £1 billion over 10 years to build and operate this centre. What is more, the Government are plain wrong to state that it is a disused military site. The Ministry of Defence spent £100 million establishing an internationally renowned bomb disposal training unit there. On Friday, that unit was training not just at MOD Bicester but on site A, the very place the Government now propose to put an asylum centre. That facility will be lost if this project goes ahead. Will the Minister commit to publishing the full business case and costs of the proposal before it goes ahead? Will the Minister commit to visiting MOD Bicester with me before any final decision, to meet residents and the people running our local services, and to see for herself why this is the wrong plan and the wrong site for local people, asylum seekers and taxpayers?

I appreciate the issues and concerns raised by the hon. Gentleman, and I look forward to meeting him again after this discussion today. The Minister for Housing and Planning, my right hon. Friend the Member for Greenwich and Woolwich (Matthew Pennycook) took public representations regarding this application, which the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government fully considered in taking her decision. The application has been made by an urgent planning route because it is an issue of urgent national importance: responding to the sustained pressure on asylum accommodation and the need to reduce reliance on hotels. There is a reason we have undertaken this urgent planning process. The hon. Gentleman raised the issue of cost. The final per person cost for MOD Bicester will depend on the outcome of the planning and procurement process, so I cannot comment at this point, but for comparison the cost of the existing large sites—the hon. Gentleman knows we already have two—at Wethersfield and Crowborough is £135 and £138 per night respectively, which is significantly cheaper than hotels, at £199 per night. As I have already said, overall asylum costs have fallen by £1 billion since this Government came to office.

I welcome the work the Government are doing to close asylum hotels, including in Banbury town centre. It has to be said that when such accommodation proliferated under the Conservatives, we heard very little from anybody who is now sitting on the Opposition Benches. It was also the case that local authorities such as Cherwell district council, where Piddington is located and which covers my constituency, were often left in the dark about matters relating to them. Will the Minister reassure me that she is in constant conversation with local authorities to ensure that they have the information they need about this site of significant public national interest?

I thank my hon. Friend for his important point. Engagement with local authorities is crucial to everything we are doing. Community impact is embedded throughout the process of site selection, feasibility planning, and, where a site proceeds, mobilisation and operation. I can confirm that we will continue to work closely with local authorities, and also with police, health partners and other key stakeholders, to understand local circumstances, community concerns and any pressures on local services. We will always identify appropriate mitigations.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) on securing this urgent question. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Mid Buckinghamshire (Greg Smith) for all his tireless work advocating for the adjacent village of Marsh Gibbon and for the smaller villages near Piddington. Last week, the Government made a choice. They chose to put women and girls in Piddington at risk—risk they knew would come from the horrific crimes committed by other illegal migrant men against girls as young as 12. They chose to use emergency powers and ignore local opinion. Those chose for not a single Minister to meet residents before that decision was made. They chose to ignore police warnings of an increased risk of crime. They chose to impose 1,250 illegal migrant men on a village of 350 people, knowing that these men pose a direct risk to community safety—men who broke the law in coming here and should be deported. Tomorrow, the Conservatives will give the Government and those on the Liberal Democrat Benches another chance to back our borders plan to leave the European convention on human rights, deport illegal migrants in a week, and control our borders. I have been to Piddington twice, with my right hon. Friend the Leader of the Opposition and the shadow Home Secretary. We listened to residents, so I can say this with certainty: Ministers have got this decision categorically wrong. Their choice will have consequences that they will have to live with. From Piddington to Linton-on-Ouse to Barnham, this Government are choosing to ignore the very people they are supposed to put first—their citizens. Why do Ministers consider that it was appropriate to use emergency powers to bypass local planning scrutiny? Why has no Government Minister visited Piddington or the surrounding villages to hear residents’ concerns directly? Why are the Government approving the site in full knowledge that they cannot ensure the safety of women and girls? It is a decision that the Government will come to regret.

I wonder if the hon. Lady has come to regret the decisions that her Government took when they opened two camps in Wethersfield and Crowborough. The camps provide a much safer and more secure process of accommodating asylum seekers. Indeed, the hon. Lady raised concerns about the local crime rate, but I wonder whether she has been to Wethersfield, which has been operating for a number of years, to hear that there has been no evidence of rising crime in the area. The chief constable of Essex police stated on 11 September that crime linked to the Wethersfield site is “very low” and that there is no reason for the public to be concerned about possible criminality in the area associated with the site. In fact, Braintree is one of the lowest-crime areas in the country and sees fewer incidents now compared to when the site was opened three years ago. I find the brass neck of the Conservatives astonishing—they lost total control of the asylum and immigration system, and we are still dealing with that. The Home Secretary is taking control of our borders. We are reducing people coming here through illegal routes by boat. We are closing the asylum hotels. We are removing those with no right to be here. We are getting a grip on the chaos the Conservatives left behind.

Can the Minister confirm this for me? As far as I am aware no consultation was undertaken and no Ministers visited before hotels were opened in Walsall, Wolverhampton, Dudley or West Bromwich near my constituency. Would the Minister be so kind as to confirm that the use of asylum hotels has fallen by 50% under this Government, and that the move to using disused MOD property is to make sure that the accommodation for asylum seekers is dispersed across the country and does not fall disproportionately on poor areas like my own area of the west midlands or her area in the north-east?

My hon. Friend makes the important point that no consent was sought from our communities when hotels that were insecure were put in the middle of them with no notice. MOD Bicester is controlled accommodation that is self-contained—everything onsite and the impact on local communities minimised. On top of all that, we are already saving £1 billion, with more to come as I look forward to closing the rest of the hotels before the end of the Parliament.

As the Prime Minister conceded, the crisis in asylum accommodation is a direct result of Brexit, when we lost the returns agreement with the EU, which was compounded by the previous Conservative Government’s decision to stop processing asylum claims. Does the Minister share my contempt for the scenes in Piddington last Friday, when the authors of this mess—the Tory shadow Home Secretary and the Reform home affairs spokesperson—entered into an unedifying scrap seeking to blame each other for the problem that both their parties caused? The Liberal Democrats have a plan to clear the asylum backlog within six months, by doubling the number of asylum caseworkers and joining the EU migration and asylum pact. Does the Minister agree, first, that wasting billions on using hotels and military sites, such as MOD Bicester, is no solution to the asylum crisis; secondly, that rather than overriding local planning concerns, money would be better spent employing more asylum caseworkers; and thirdly, that the UK should join the EU migration and asylum pact?

The hon. Gentleman is right that those scenes were unedifying—those who contributed to the mess that we inherited seek to throw stones at one another while we are getting on with solving yet another mess. I am proud of this Government’s record. I enjoyed working with the hon. Gentleman on the Immigration and Asylum Bill Committee, where we went through a number of issues. While we may disagree on the EU pact, we both agree that greater co-operation internationally is key to solving the problem, because patterns of migration move across borders and boundaries. We will continue to bring down the abuses in our system, and I look forward to the hon. Gentleman joining us in voting for the Bill on Report and Third Reading tomorrow.

I welcome the work the Government are doing on closing asylum hotels. Does the Minister agree that former military sites with permanent security and CCTV are much more appropriate and controlled settings for holding those awaiting asylum decisions than the asylum hotels that the Tories not only opened but celebrated opening in working-class communities such as mine?

My hon. Friend makes an important point. These large sites are designed to be self-contained, with basic services provided on site to reduce demand and pressure on local services and minimise the need for anyone to leave. We work with voluntary organisations to ensure that activities are available on site, helping to create an environment that encourages people to remain on site all day and meets their day-to-day needs. As I said, we know that existing sites have operated very successfully with basic on-site services and 24/7 security designed to minimise the impact on local communities.

MOD Bicester site A is just a mile from the Buckinghamshire border, and many of my communities in Mid Buckinghamshire are threatened by its use for 1,256 illegal migrants. I cannot believe that the Minister said earlier that MHCLG had considered all the representations, when 3,177 of those local voices said no and only one said yes—the Government appear to have gone with that one. Equally, I cannot believe that the Minister is trying to say that those 1,256 men will be incentivised not to leave this small camp, built entirely out of portacabins and modular buildings, and sit around playing ping pong, rather than the things we all know they are actually going to do. Given the clear safety risk, and given that it works out at two and a half times the cost of the equivalent asylum hotels, will the Minister at least come and visit, listen to local voices and turn around on this plan?

I am very happy to meet the hon. Gentleman to discuss his representations. As I said, we have listened to the concerns of communities, which are essential to our immigration reforms. That is why we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, including military sites. We are working to house asylum seekers fairly across the country, engaging with local authorities to reduce the impact on communities. We have already saved taxpayers more than a billion pounds on asylum support costs since the election.

I thought that my hon. Friend the Member for Tipton and Wednesbury (Antonia Bance) made a very good point about hypocrisy from the Opposition earlier. I was relieved to hear the Minister talk about the number of asylum hotels being reduced from 400 to 160, I think, which is dramatic. I read earlier that asylum application processing is at its highest rate for 25 years. Will the Minister reassure me that the Government are getting a grip of the asylum system and the mess that they inherited?

I can absolutely assure my hon. Friend of that. I look forward to the debate we will have in this Chamber tomorrow on Report and Third Reading of the Immigration and Asylum Bill, which is further evidence of us ensuring that we remove those who have no right to be in this country, tighten the appeals system against abuse and have a fair system that has public consent while we continue to bring down the illegal misuse of our systems.

If I may say so, it is a bit rich for Government Members to point at Opposition Members when they voted against every single piece of our legislation to reform the illegal migration system and tackle abuse of the asylum system. Specifically, does the Minister recognise that Bicester, Wethersfield and now Tillingham, in the Maldon district, would not be necessary had her Government not scrapped the Rwanda plan, which has now been adopted by five EU countries—

For deportation purposes, it is the same, because these people are illegal and should not be in our country. Rwanda is a safe country. I ask the Minister: if the policy is okay for five EU countries, what will it take for the Government to relook at those plans, which her Department negotiated in the first place?

The right hon. Lady’s Government had a majority, so I am not quite sure how she can blame us for their legislation not passing. I am afraid there were so many flaws in the Rwanda policy that it was torn to pieces by lawyers, and the reality was that for millions of pounds in taxpayers’ money, only four people went over there.

This Government are committed to listening to local people, which is really important when we think about the sites in not only Bicester but Linton-on-Ouse. Local communities and agencies including in York have set out an evidence base showing why Linton-on-Ouse would be the incorrect site to use: not only will the costs be exorbitant compared with using asylum hotels, putting pressure on the taxpayer, but the infrastructure is completely absent. Will the Minister review the model and ensure that the Government come up with a better model by working with communities to find a solution?

I appreciate the points that my hon. Friend makes. She is always a doughty champion for her constituents, and I look forward to continuing to discuss this issue with her. I am afraid, however, that we are confident that the move towards this kind of accommodation not only protects against the impact on local communities that many people have seen across the country, but provides a fairer deal for the taxpayer and ensures that there is less of a burden on local communities than we have seen over the last few years.

Constituents will be appalled that the Government might spend up to a billion pounds of taxpayers’ cash on opening Piddington—and appalled that the Government accept that it will put women and girls in the locality at risk. There is a simple question here, Minister: why not make it a proper detention centre and detain the illegals behind the wire?

The hon. Gentleman knows perfectly well that we have obligations under the 1951 refugee convention and other legislation that was forged to ensure that when we said “Never again” after the second world war, we meant it. Those people have a right to come here to seek asylum, but we have to ensure that we have 24-hour security on the site. Many of those people are incentivised to behave well because they want their claims to be processed. If the hon. Gentleman took the time to look at existing military sites, he would see that there is zero impact on crime.

I commend the great work our Government are doing to reduce small boat arrivals, but the Minister is aware of my view, because I have told her, that large military sites are unlikely to ever be the best solution for the need to accommodate people who are seeking asylum. What consideration have the Government given to the repurposing of the plentiful vacant office accommodation in our larger cities, where there are existing communities and medical, legal and cultural resources?

I appreciate my hon. Friend’s representations. He knows very well that we have moved to a wide range of accommodation. While emptying hotels that were costly and damaging to local communities, we are looking at a dispersal model of small and medium sites as well as military sites around the country. I encourage my hon. Friend and any local authority that has thoughts and ideas about appropriate accommodation to come forward, because we would always be keen to listen to them.

Some of the language that the Minister has used in the last few answers is quite disturbing. When looking back through Hansard tomorrow, it will seem as though some of the decisions have already been made on Linton-on-Ouse, because the Minister just said in response to the hon. Member for York Central (Rachael Maskell) that these are the most appropriate places to house people. The difference with Linton-on-Ouse is that the village is inside the site. The Minister said that sites would be self-contained. That would suggest that they are secure, but they are not. The children’s playground is but yards from where potential accommodation would be, and the school and the nursery are a five-minute walk away. The Home Secretary said that she would not open hotels or asylum centres near primary schools. Is that still the policy, which would rule out Linton-on-Ouse? The children’s playground is, basically, within the site. Is that a factor? Please will the Minister come to Linton-on-Ouse to see it for herself?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his representations. I am very happy to meet him; I hope he has received correspondence from me to say so. To clarify, I am talking about the model. There has been no decision on Linton-on-Ouse; that is under consideration. I want to be absolutely clear on that. As we have made clear, we will take everything into consideration, whether it is local schools, local amenities or local play areas. All of that is taken into account when we make any application. I look forward to meeting him to hear his representations further.

For five years before I was elected, I worked on finding asylum accommodation in Scotland. Time and again, councils and the police would say to us that hotels had been opened by the previous Government without their being informed—they had no clue at all. They would tell us all the time, “If only we knew this was happening, we could put the resources in place and deal with asylum seekers in our communities.” I welcome the Government’s taking a planned approach to asylum accommodation that works with local communities, especially the local police, so that proper resources are in place. Has the Minister been looking at the Home Affairs Committee and National Audit Office inquiries into large sites? Large sites can go well, as they have in Wethersfield, or in Scotland with the Scottish Government’s Ukrainian refugees ships, or they can go badly. Lessons must be learned. Is the Home Office taking steps to look at that?

I thank my hon. Friend for all the work that he and the Home Affairs Committee have done on this issue. We take all the Committee’s recommendations seriously. He is right: the move to military sites and dispersal accommodation is all about having a sustainable and managed approach to the estate, not the chaos that saw the explosion of hotels around the country—often in areas of deprivation because of low cost—that put a huge strain on local communities, with no consent, as he identified, and at great expense to the taxpayer purse.

I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) on securing the UQ. The issue came up when we were serving on the Immigration and Asylum Bill Committee, and the Minister will remember amendments tabled by my hon. Friend that would have seen the Government needing to bring forward impact assessments about site suitability, cost estimates and a financial breakdown. This is a really emotive issue that is becoming a partisan political football. We could cut through that by taking up those amendments on Report tomorrow. Will the Minister take that opportunity?

I appreciate the amendments; it is important that they are debated fully during the Bill’s proceedings tomorrow. The hon. Member will of course understand that while we will undertake all surveys and mitigations, there are commercial sensitivities, so we may not be able to publish everything at every stage. However, we will always do our utmost so that people have before them all the evidence on these issues that we are able to publish.

The debate has become really unfortunate, and some of the language used to describe the people who will be accommodated in places like Bicester has been truly appalling. It is no wonder that people feel anxious about these facilities when the far-right Reform and the Tories characterise whole groups of people as deviant, a threat and a danger to women and girls in their campaign to divide and to scapegoat whole communities. These are people fleeing unimaginable situations—they deserve and require a right to rebuild their lives. I have asked several times: when will the Government get on top of this? When will they present their challenge to the misinformation and disinformation that spreads from the likes of those sat behind me?

The hon. Gentleman makes a really important point. There are people fleeing war and persecution whom we have historic and moral obligations to support and provide sanctuary. But we also know that our asylum system has been abused. That is why we are taking steps through the Immigration and Asylum Bill, which will be back before Parliament tomorrow, to ensure that we not only protect the rights of people fleeing war and persecution to have protection in this country, but maintain that public consent, which is being eroded by so many, as he said, and driving grievance.

The Minister has been wheeled out to defend the indefensible. She talks about the Government’s consultation, but the Government are clearly not listening, as we see time and again, to the views of the 3,177 people who were against her Government’s project. Why will the Government not listen to local people?

The right hon. Lady expresses shock. I express shock at hearing the Conservative party turning 180° on a policy they were quite happy to champion while they were in power. We are not ignoring concerns raised by residents; we are taking them seriously. They are central to our reforms. As I said, we are closing every asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into alternative accommodation, because that is what the British public said to us, and that is what they voted on at the last election.

The Government rightly promised to end the use of asylum hotels in their manifesto, but moving illegal migrants out of hotels and in next door was not what voters had in mind. Now, because of the Government’s failure to stop the boats, residents in Piddington are terrified of what will happen to their community. If the Minister is so adamant that there is nothing to see here, why have the Government once again failed to publish the data showing the scale of illegal migrant crime?

The hon. Lady will know of the huge progress made under the Government to end the abuse of our asylum process and to stop the boats. The numbers of people crossing the Channel are down by over 40% this year. Eighty thousand people who had no right to be here have been returned, which is up over 50%. Immigration enforcement has been increased, with an over 80% rise in illegal working arrests. The last Government allowed net migration of 2.5 million in just four years—around one in 30 people in this country came here under the last few years of her Government—so a bit of contrition from the Conservative party would be good.

This is an appalling and frightening decision, not just because of the effect it will have on the people of this small village but because of what it says about the power of the state to impose life-changing impacts on people because the Government have failed in their policy of stopping the invasion of our country by illegal immigrants. Can the Minister confirm whether those who will be housed in this centre will be issued with the Home Office guidance asking them not to rape, sexually abuse or harass the women and children they come across? What assurance does she think that gives to the women of this village, who will be outnumbered by these people by eight to one? Is it not better to send them back to where they came from when they land on our shores, rather than try to rehouse them?

Anyone who has committed a crime on these shores would now be eligible for removal from point zero of their sentence. As I have said, we are removing more people—80,000 people, up more than 50% on the previous Government—so that action will be taken in relation to anyone committing a crime. We take this extremely seriously and we expect anyone coming to these shores to abide by our laws. The right hon. Gentleman seems to be completely unaware that two of these sites are already in operation and the impact on crime has been completely negligible, as expressed by the local chief constable, so his scaremongering does him no service.

My constituents in Woodhouse, Woodhouse Eaves and the surrounding villages in a similar setting to that of Piddington are really concerned that MOD Garats Hay could be next. Will the Minister rule out the use of MOD Garats Hay today and give my constituents some peace of mind?

The hon. Gentleman would be the first to know if we were considering that option. As I have said, we always ensure that we engage with Members of Parliament on any issues pertaining to their constituency. Those whose constituencies are under consideration are fully aware, and that is why we continue to engage with the Members of Parliament affected.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker; I hope your finger is feeling better. Piddington deserves to be heard, but then so did every working-class town and village that Westminster ignored before placing these overwhelmingly fighting-age Muslim men on their streets. Why is it a national outrage when one Oxfordshire village faces a migrant invasion but an acceptable sacrifice for MPs in this Chamber when hundreds of working-class communities across the country suffer the very same fate?

The hon. Gentleman knows that we are proud to undertake our international obligations to support those genuinely fleeing war and persecution. We do everything we can to ensure that those coming here have the right to be here and will be housed in appropriate accommodation. He is right to say that previously there was no consent sought from the communities who had to manage the impact of asylum accommodation on their local communities, with all the costs and impacts on local services. That is why we are making sure, through the use of these former military sites, that people are contained and have a limited impact on local communities.

The illegal migrants this Government intend to house at great expense in Piddington should be deported. The Minister will know that five EU countries have announced their intention to create a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda using facilities paid for by British taxpayers and abandoned by Labour. Does the Minister accept that the only way to stop small boats is to detain those illegal migrants on arrival and to deport them?

I am not going to take any lessons from the Conservatives on stopping small boats, because we saw the situation explode from 2018 onwards on their watch and we are still dealing with the consequences. We have taken action across continents to bring down the numbers of small boats by over 40%.

Does the Minister accept that going down the road of Crown development opens up a totally unregulated vista of permitted development within this site thereafter, and that there are additional permitted development rights for Crown development, including emergency development, under which no one would have to apply for planning permission at all, including development for national security purposes? By adopting the Crown development approach, is not the Minister abandoning all planning control over this site?

The application has been made via this route because the proposed development is considered urgent and of national importance. We are responding to sustained pressures on the asylum accommodation estate, which many colleagues have raised here in the Chamber today, and the need to reduce reliance on hotels. It will enable relevant planning issues to be considered but it does not predetermine the outcome, so no final decision has been taken on the site’s future use.

Like elsewhere in the United Kingdom, communities and constituents in Strangford tell me that they are already feeling the immense strain of the Government’s asylum dispersal policies on local housing, policing and health services, while former military bases are crying out to be used as homes for our veterans. Some 3,177 local residents objected to housing for 1,200 working-age adult men beside a village of 350. The Government have to take note of that, so why are the Minister and the Government riding roughshod over local democracy by using urgent Crown powers? Will the Minister assure the House that similar fast-track powers will not be used to impose large-scale asylum sites on communities in Northern Ireland without full local consultation?

I want to be clear with the hon. Gentleman: we recognise the strength of feeling in local communities. We listen hard to them, as we listen to the representations of Members of Parliament. The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy, but protest must not cross the line into some of the violent behaviour we have seen, including in areas in his part of the world. It is important that we continue to listen to people, and that is why we are closing every single asylum hotel and moving asylum seekers into safe, contained accommodation, including these military sites. We want to work with all colleagues in the House to ensure that we house asylum seekers fairly across the country.

With permission, I will make a statement on the Microsoft 365 outage. On Thursday 12 and Friday 13 November, an outage affecting Microsoft IT systems caused impacts around the world. Users of Microsoft products were unable to send and receive emails or to use a range of other Microsoft products and services. This was a serious incident that caused disruption for a lot of people and businesses. Microsoft initially explained that the incident was caused by an elevated load on its infrastructure and later provided further details of the three main issues that led to the outage. The company said there is no indication that the incident was caused by malicious activity. In the UK, the incident affected individuals, businesses and the public sector. There were impacts on the health sector and other public services, but key services such as 999 remained operational. There were no major critical service impacts, and public sector resilience plans were in place. The incident could have been more serious if it had lasted longer or affected wider parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure. It reinforces the importance of promoting and improving our digital resilience—something that the Government have already taken significant steps on. There was some organisational disruption in local government, where many organisations rely on Microsoft products. Multiple local resilience forums were stood up to provide support and co-ordination among local services. The incident also caused disruption across businesses of all sizes. Staff were unable to carry out their normal duties, and firms were unable to complete their usual transactions. Members and staff in this place were also affected. We recognise the disruption that it caused to people and organisations, and we are still working to understand the full impact. However, critical and important services remained available and operational across the country. Accident and emergency departments remained open. Transport services were unaffected by this outage. Borders remained operational. There were no known issues with UK mobile, broadband or landline connectivity. Major telecoms providers confirmed that their services were working as normal. We currently have no evidence of wider impacts on UK data centre infrastructure or other cloud operators, and no such impacts have been reported to us by industry at this stage. There were no reported impacts on water or waste water treatment processes. Businesses, including shops and services, remained open right across the United Kingdom. By Friday afternoon, Microsoft systems were back online, and services were returning to normal. The Government take this issue seriously. Public sector organisations and Government Departments have plans in place to mitigate potential impacts and ensure the continuation of their operations in exactly these situations. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport is the lead Department for national digital resilience issues. As soon as we became aware of the problem on Thursday evening, we contacted Microsoft to start discussions on the issue, to assess the impact and to request details of how the problem was to be resolved. The Minister with responsibility for cyber security, who is in the other place, spoke to the chief executive officer of Microsoft UK on Friday. My officials in DCMS led the co-ordination of the response across Departments in collaboration with the Cabinet Office. We expect Microsoft to share the lessons learned from the incident. We will be engaging further on how it will prevent such incidents from happening in the future, and plan for swifter remediation of incidents to limit service disruption. Digital services, such as the cloud computing services that Microsoft provides, are already regulated under the UK’s Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018, which require providers to manage security and resilience risks, prevent and minimise the impact of incidents, and report significant incident

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I do not think I have ever been wished happy birthday like that—an important first for me. I thank the Minister for advance sight of his statement, and all those who worked tirelessly to keep our essential public services running during what was an extremely challenging incident. Last week’s outage should serve as a wake-up call about the resilience of our national digital infrastructure. A technical fault at a single company caused widespread disruption across our NHS, police forces, schools, businesses and Departments. At least 47 NHS trusts reported difficulties, with some NHS services resorting to pen and paper to keep the basics going. The Minister tells us that there were no major impacts on critical services, but acknowledges that the Government are still working to understand the full extent of the disruption. How can he therefore be confident in that assessment? Can the Minister tell the House how many appointments, treatments and operations were delayed? Do we know of any incidents in which patient safety was compromised? Can he provide assurances that no critical communications have been permanently lost? While I welcome the Minister’s assurances regarding the UK’s telecommunications networks, that is a separate issue from the resilience of internet-based telephone systems that depend on the affected platforms. Many public bodies advised people to contact them by telephone instead, but increasingly our telephone systems are integrated with the very same digital platforms that failed last week. What assessment has the Minister made of the impact caused by affected telephone systems, particularly within the NHS? No one disputes that there are immense benefits to digitisation and even standardisation across our public services, but those benefits must be balanced against the risks of over-reliance on individual providers. Indeed, the Government’s own cloud procurement guidance explicitly recognises these risks. Have the Government undertaken a comprehensive audit of our dependence on individual technology suppliers across our critical national infrastructure? The Minister speaks of diversifying the Government’s supply arrangements, yet only last month the Government declined to introduce the supplier diversification targets recommended by the Science and Technology Committee. In light of last week’s events, does he expect to reconsider that decision? When did the Government last conduct a cross-departmental exercise simulating the prolonged failure of a major technology provider? What assessment has been made of the impact of the outage on the functioning of central Government? The Minister assures us that Departments have contingency plans in place for precisely such circumstances. Which Departments activated those plans last week, and how effective did they prove to be? Without asking him to disclose sensitive information, can he confirm that independent back-up systems are in place to ensure that the machinery of government can continue to function in the event of a more prolonged outage? Thankfully, there is no indication that the incident was the result of a cyber-attack, but that makes the scale of disruption all the more alarming. If a technical fault can wreak such havoc, what might be achieved through a sophisticated and co-ordinated attack by a hostile state, backed by artificial intelligence? What if the outage had lasted a week, rather than a day? What if it had coincided with a national emergency? In January, the Government announced their £210 million cyber action plan. Will the Minister say more about the lessons that will be drawn from the incident, and will he consider whether further provisions are needed in the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill to address supplier concentration? The Minister says that he will engage further with Microsoft. Given the £1.9 billion spent on Microsoft licences across the public sector in 2024-25, will th

A very happy birthday to the shadow Minister, and I am sorry that she has had to spend it in the Chamber with me, dealing with these serious issues. She asked a number of questions, and I am grateful for the way that she approached them. The questions she raised are those that the Government have been asking for some time, including through the Government resilience action plan in 2025; the cyber action plan came from the £210 million that we invested in that. I can only re-emphasise that it is very early in the situation, and that there was no real impact on the public sector. When I said that we do not yet fully understand the disruption across the whole economy, that was more about the private sector. Understanding the impact and disruption that the outage had on the economy as a whole will take more time. We are not aware of any delays in the NHS, or of NHS patients who were put in danger, and 999 services remained as they have always been. The hon. Lady asked about the assessment of different telephone systems, and diversification across Government. The cyber action plan is there to ensure exactly that; it looks at legacy systems and diversification. The national cloud infrastructure procurement process is about diversification of cloud services; the Government can use that big procurement to diversify our tech stack, ensure that we are seeding British companies, and ensure that we have some sovereignty here. There are only a few suppliers in the marketplace—the big ones that we all know. More than 90% of the civil service uses some kind of Microsoft product, so diversification must be part of the assessment. A comprehensive audit has been done of our resilience in Government. The hon. Lady asks what might have happened if there was a hostile state involved, or if the outage happened during a national emergency. All our plans are in place for that. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, along with the National Cyber Security Centre, stands up the co-ordination group. It ensures that there is only one point of contact, and ensures co-ordination not just across Government, but between companies. As I understand, this was not a cyber-attack. If we think about the incident as being a five-lane motorway, one of the lanes was already down because Microsoft was working on it. There was a bug in the fourth lane of the motorway, if I can stretch the analogy. That overloaded the capacity; pretty much all the traffic was pushed into one or two lanes, and that caused the system to fall over. It was an incident after an incident. Three things happened that meant that we ended up in this situation. Microsoft resolved this relatively quickly, working in co-ordination with DCMS and the NCSC, and we are not aware at this stage that there is any legacy from that. It seems that the backlog is through, and everyone who sent or was to receive something should have got it. We are pleased that the backlog is now gone, and I encourage Members to determine whether they and their constituents have received the email traffic that they should have got by Friday afternoon; by 2 pm on Friday, the incident had passed.

Our NHS, our police, our schools and our businesses unable to function properly—my Committee’s report on delivering digital government concluded that the UK is overly dependent on a small number of US-based technology providers. Last week, the British people paid the price; next week, it could be our economy, our critical national infrastructure or our transportation. When will the Minister know how much the Government are spending on IT and with which companies? The Government were unable to tell us that in response to our report. He talked about establishing our technology stack, but when will he know where we are spending our IT money and with which companies? The Minister said that there was no impact on the public sector and no costs were incurred. Will he confirm that? Will he find out what costs were incurred by the private sector? Will those companies be entitled to any compensation? There is a lot I could say about this issue, but finally, France and Germany are using open source to move away from the big tech providers. Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the Government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called “commercial accountability”. Will the Minister set out the Government’s approach to open source?

I am grateful to the Chair of the Select Committee for raising those issues, which we have discussed many times in the Committee. She asks about the shape of large and medium-sized managed service providers, like Microsoft. They account for about 97.6% of the total managed service provider marketplace in this country, which is worth about £47 billion, and about 321 large providers account for 86% of that total. We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high. There is not much in the way of diversification in the marketplace for that, but some Departments use Google and some use Microsoft, so there is that sort of diversification. The Government cyber action plan will look at where Government sits within the supply chain and logistics sector, and lay out our vulnerabilities and our vendor lock-in. It is incredibly important that we see that through as quickly as possible, but that is not easy. The sovereign AI fund, brought forward by the former Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leicester West (Liz Kendall), before the summer, provides half a billion pounds to seed our own sovereign AI for the tech stack. As my hon. Friend the Chair of the Select Committee knows, we cannot compete in all parts of the tech stack —it would be wrong for us to try to do so—but we can compete in the parts that we are good at, and the sovereign AI fund is there to invest in those kinds of organisations and areas. In the Budget, we committed half a billion pounds to building the secure foundations for an AI-enabled economy. That is different from the sovereign AI fund that I mentioned. At questions to the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport last Thursday, we talked about ensuring that cyber-security is on the agenda in every single boardroom, so that business people are aware that the NCSC has free cyber-security tools that all businesses should be using. I encourage them to use them, so that our economy, as well as the Government, becomes more resilient.

Microsoft’s failure last week is a wake-up call for the UK. Our public services and economy need to stop relying on a few US firms and back more British tech. The outage knocked out services used by over a million UK businesses and public bodies, with 20 million users. Eleanor in the UK could not send urgent cancer referrals. Hugo could not pay his staff, who live pay cheque to pay cheque. Mohamed, a pharmacist, could not dispense prescriptions. Online police reporting went down. Even this House lost its main communication channel. This is not a surprise. The Institute for Public Policy Research found that the US receives almost twice as much UK public sector tech spend as every other foreign country combined. It found that only £1 in every £6 of Government spending goes to British firms. We found that more than half of central Government keep most of their data with two US companies, and Palantir is still embedded in public services. In July, digital resilience failure was added to the national risk register, so the Government know the risk, but they lack a strategic plan. The Liberal Democrats have spent months calling for a digital sovereign strategy, which has received cross-party support. It would allow us to stay open globally, while building resilience and competition, and would stop that lock-in. We even tabled an amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, but unfortunately the Government rejected it. They might like to consider that the IPPR suggests practical steps. It says that we should build at home, in those areas where Britain can genuinely compete; use the Government’s power as a buyer, regulator and standard setter to shape the market; and partner with other middle powers, including the EU, so that no single country holds the off switch. The Tories attacked our idea, but industry and experts agree with the Lib Dems. TechUK talks about a confident sovereign strategy for supporting growth, security and resilience. UK Research and Innovation calls for a sovereign AI strategy, and the Open Rights Group warns that over-reliance on foreign firms is an urgent national security issue. We do not have digital resilience; we still have digital dependence. Will the Minister back our calls and commit to publishing a digital sovereign strategy to support growth, security and resilience?

I am grateful to the hon. Lady for those comments. It is really important to lay out that this is an isolated incident for Microsoft. It was not a cyber-attack as such; its systems were overloaded, due to a combination of three factors that compounded the problem. The incident affected 74 countries across the world, so it was widespread, not just in the United Kingdom. The hon. Lady asks about investment in sovereign technology. We have put £500 million in the sovereign AI fund, £1 billion into the AI hardware plan and £2 billion into quantum investment, so that the Government can be a first customer for some of these technologies, giving them routes to market. That is a really big commitment, in terms of AI and tech sovereignty of this country’s tech stack. Departments are responsible for contracting services. We recognise that relying on a small number of suppliers can create risks to resilience, competition and value for money. Our aim is resilience through choice; we are not trying to swap one dependency for another. Large global providers bring scale, security and capability, and benefit public services. The Government mean to keep access to the best technology, while building greater choice and stronger UK capability; I think everyone in the House would agree with that. We are moving away from each organisation buying separately, and towards a joined-up approach from Government, to give economies of scale. Procurement decisions are based on value for money for the taxpayer, security, and the effective delivery of services. That is why we are very keen to take forward the Government cyber action plan. We are very keen to ensure that the NCSC and DCMS continue to work together on these issues. We are looking at the national cloud infrastructure project to try to seed and develop those sovereign capabilities here. Until we get to the end of that process, we will not really know where we are in providing competition to the big suppliers, but everyone is aware that it is a problem that we have little choice in this marketplace other than to use some of these global providers, and the Government are actively working to resolve that.

Many of my constituents rely on terrestrial TV and radio, and Friday’s outage showed us what happens when digital goes down. In the light of this morning’s recommendation by the Lords National Resilience Committee, will the Minister rule out switching off terrestrial television—the back-up that keeps working when digital goes down? I am very concerned that not ruling that out would present a very real threat to our national security.

I am very grateful to my hon. Friend for raising the issue of the future of TV distribution, which was raised in our media Green Paper; the consultation on that has finished, and the White Paper will be produced shortly. We took the decision in the Green Paper to turn off digital terrestrial television, but the issue is what date we use. That is examined in the Green Paper; it will be either 2034 or 2044. We have not made a decision as a Government on that date. We have made a decision on what we will do, but not on when we will do it.

We are the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee. The Minister has set out very clearly, as have others, the entrenched position of Microsoft in the UK’s digital ecosystem. Considering the great over-reliance of domestic businesses, consumers, Government and local authorities on its software, can the Minister set out how urgent the diversification and resilience building that he mentioned is? Has that urgency changed in the light of what happened on Friday? In addition, the Competition and Markets Authority is currently looking at whether it should designate Microsoft as having strategic market status, and is due to conclude that work in February. Has the Minister’s readiness to respond to that report also changed in the light of Friday’s events?

I am grateful to the Chair of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee for her questions. It is still DCMS—we need to get that into our minds. The hon. Lady raises two important points. The first, which is about over-reliance on certain suppliers, is well made; that is why the Government have been putting a lot of money into sovereign AI and tech sovereignty in terms of the tech stack. We have the Government cyber action plan that examines the readiness and resilience of individual Government Departments, looking at legacy technology and co-ordination across the piece. We also have the national cloud infrastructure programme, which is about making sure that big, Government-wide procurement can seed UK businesses, looking at cloud sovereignty and making sure that we have a choice of suppliers. We are such a big customer; we need to make sure that we have those suppliers on our shores. We introduced the Government cyber charter to ensure that any strategic suppliers, including Microsoft, are early adopters of Government cyber policy and best practice. That charter sets clear expectations for suppliers, strengthening resilience across Government supply chains and encouraging them to drive the same standards throughout their wider supplier networks. The hon. Lady’s point about Microsoft is well made. The Government contract with Microsoft in a way that is very deep and broad. That gives us an economy of scale with one of the world’s best suppliers in this area and access to new technology, but it also probably gives us vendor lock-in and a lack of choice in what other vendors we might be able to use. However, this was not a cyber-security incident; it was just a technology failure in one of Microsoft’s operations. This problem was caused by a backlog of data going through a very narrow lane, as opposed to the service that Microsoft is normally able to provide.

I thank the Minister for his statement. I am not 100% convinced that we know exactly what happened, but I am pleased that he feels that Microsoft is telling the truth. The Minister said that the first job of Government is to protect their citizens. I completely agree, and my Bill—the Artificial Intelligence (Consent and Misuse) Bill—would go a long way towards ensuring that we protect our citizens as AI advances. As has been mentioned, EU countries are migrating away from Microsoft systems; that was mainly driven by the President of the US claiming that he was going to activate the kill switch for Microsoft, which worried a lot of countries. Can the Minister be clear about how we are planning to migrate away from US-based systems and invest a lot more in British-based systems, so that we can have more data sovereignty?

There are a number of answers to that question, and I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising it. First, let me go through again what this incident involved. We are working very closely with Microsoft, and it has confirmed that this was not an attack on its systems. One of its servers went down due to a defect that had been found; there was a surge in load that brought that bug—that defect—to the fore. There was another completely unrelated issue, which was that a server that accounts for 14% of capacity was also down for maintenance at the time. This outage was caused by the volume of traffic choking the servers that were left, which produced a backlog and brought the servers down. Microsoft resolved the problem relatively quickly. By 2 pm on Friday, services were coming back online. My hon. Friend asked what we are doing to diversify away from US suppliers and the big international suppliers. I have already mentioned the £500 million sovereign AI fund, which is there to back British businesses and promote that sovereignty; the £1.1 billion AI hardware plan; and the £500 million to try to resolve some of these issues that was in this year’s Budget. We have a tech stack that is dominated by US tech companies. We want more AI sovereignty in the United Kingdom; we are willing to fund that, and we are funding it. That is how we will make sure we have the most resilient services, but also the most technologically advanced services, in the UK.

I am grateful to the Minister for making this important statement. Those of us with rural constituencies represent many people who are very worried about the copper switch-off that is coming as we move to fibre. Fibre is an energy-intensive system, unlike the copper system, and it seems to be coming without a delay being considered. Donald Rumsfeld once talked about the known unknowns. We know that an attack will happen somewhere. The Minister has outlined that this outage was a specific issue, but it shows how reliant we are on these systems. The hon. Member for Rotherham (Sarah Champion) talked about the switching off of terrestrial television. These things are of great concern. I urge the Minister to take away what happened on Friday and look at the broader picture. When the known unknown happens and everything gets closed down, the proven and tried systems of copper connections and terrestrial radio and television should be there as a back-up system on which people can rely.

This is an issue for all of us in this Chamber, because we rely on that technology. Similar discussions about whether we are over-reliant on technology probably happened, if we check Hansard , with the invention of the personal computer and the internet. Technology makes us a better economy and makes it easier for businesses to operate. It makes it easier for us all to stay connected and informed. Resilience is a key part of what we are trying to do in government, whether through our cyber action plan or all the other initiatives that I have mentioned from this Dispatch Box. That cyber action plan has £210 million in funding to better utilise cyber-skills and to deliver once and for all, at scale, a co-ordinated approach across Government to tackle all those critical risks that the right hon. Gentleman mentions. The right hon. Gentleman talks about power and national power outages. We know that telecoms networks have substantial power back-ups at core network sites. We have a resilient electricity system, but we cannot plan for every eventuality. It would be wrong for a Minister of any colour to stand at this Dispatch Box and say that we will not have any other cyber-attacks or any other outages such as this. What we need to do is minimise them, minimise the risk and make sure that the Government are in the best place, including in terms of the wider economy.

I declare an interest, as I have a close relative who is working on the regulation of Microsoft. I thank the Minister for his statement. Will he update the House more broadly on how the UK is planning to be more resilient in this field, particularly given that a relatively small number of suppliers have such a critical role in the economy?

As I have said, we recognise that relying on a small number of suppliers can create risks for resilience, competition and value for money. Those suppliers provide us with the very best technology, and we are not trying to swap one dependency for another, but alongside the large global providers, which bring skills, security and capability, we must ensure that we have our own sovereignty in this country in the areas of the tech stack that we are good at. We have put taxpayers’ money where our mouth is to develop that tech stack and that sovereignty, so that we have resilience.

The statement raises the issues of resilience and preparedness in the public and private sectors. Can the Minister and his team do more to support businesses, both small and large—including through the known communication channels, such as the Federation of Small Businesses, Prosper and others—by more widely distributing advice and messages about digital preparedness tools? This has been a significant enough incident to warrant a ministerial statement, but there are rural and remote businesses and public services that tackle digital challenges every single day of the week due to lack of fibre broadband and other issues. Can more be done to roll out fibre broadband even faster?

There was a lot in that question, and I will try to run through it in order. Building Digital UK has Project Gigabit, which is trying to get to 99% of all premises by 2032. Many of those who are most affected and are the hardest to reach will be in the hon. Gentleman’s constituency in the highlands of Scotland. For that 1%, there will be additional technologies—they are evolving all the time—to make sure that everyone is connected. As I have said at the Dispatch Box many times, we cannot have growth in every postcode without connectivity, and the more rural somewhere is, the more difficult it is to have that connection. From the point view of the wider economy and business, the only thing that I can continue to emphasise from this Dispatch Box is that people should use the National Cyber Security Centre’s free tools on cyber-security. That should be on the lips of every board member sitting around the boardroom table. We will have a much more resilient economy with much more resilient businesses only if everybody plays their part.

West London is part of a cluster of data centres where, if there is a problem with one centre, data can be backed up in another. In my constituency, two data centres have recently been agreed by Ealing council, which has taken the position that only data centres with the highest environmental standards will be allowed. Does the Minister agree that clustering data centres in this way is the right approach to digital resilience, along with the Government’s new data centre covenant, which will ensure that we meet our climate commitments?

I could not have put it better myself. We do need data centres for this. If we are talking about AI sovereignty and tech sovereignty, it is best for them to be onshore here in the United Kingdom. That is a big challenge, but we must ensure that it is done correctly, and I pay tribute to Ealing council for the way in which it has done it in its area.

The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill is in its final stages of parliamentary scrutiny, and in this context I particularly note the role of resilience in ensuring our national economic security. What assessment have the Government made of the potential impact in future outages on critical national infrastructure—including communications and supply chains—on which essential services depend, and what further amendments to the Bill might be needed?

The Bill will return to this House relatively soon. It updates the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 to bring some of these companies into scope, including data centres, and contains a provision to extend the scope, if necessary, to include more organisations and more sectors of the economy. It will be back in this House before the end of the year, and we will be able to debate these matters in more detail then, but its purpose is to ensure that we have greater resilience and to update the regulations.

I thank the Minister for coming to the House in such a timely fashion. I know he will have been disappointed to learn today that the new James Bond is not a Scotsman. The Microsoft outage had a huge impact on residents and businesses in my constituency of Harlow, and I was reassured to hear when I contacted my local hospital that it had not been hugely impacted, but will the Minister reassure the House that he will do everything he can to hold Microsoft to account and ensure that there is no spectre of future outages?

I am glad that my hon. Friend managed to talk to his NHS trust and resolve that issue over the weekend. Only two NHS trusts stood up an incident response unit, but it was no longer required so they stood it back down relatively quickly. That shows that the system does work. The co-ordination of the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and the National Cyber Security Centre to bring together the Government Cyber Co-ordination Centre meant that the information was filtered from Microsoft through the Government to trusts and local government so that they could stand up incident responses if they needed to do so, but they did not need to do so in this particular case.

I thank the Minister for his statement, and for his welcome comments about backing more British suppliers that are small and medium-sized enterprises. May I ask him to extend that review and look into not only alternative suppliers of the solutions, but the decision to have software as a service as the default choice every time, so that we can improve the resilience of the services here and possibly even copy the French by developing our own open-source solution?

I can only re-emphasise what I have said already. The Government are backing our work on the tech stack with taxpayers’ money to see how we can seed good businesses in this country that wish to grow and enter these marketplaces. It is difficult for the Government to do that, because the big suppliers are there for us to secure value for money for the taxpayer. However, the current procurement process through the national cloud infrastructure programme is about ensuring that we not only secure the best value for money but have some tech sovereignty on British soil by seeding those companies to make them grow.

Given the Microsoft 365 outage, the Vodafone outage last year and Storm Éowyn, which prevented my constituents from receiving communications, does the Minister agree that sometimes the older ways are the best? In my constituency, we have a 90-year-old transmitter that still transmits analogue. I worry that if the Government go ahead with their plan to switch off analogue, it will cut off people in a way that we know will happen again. What can the Minister tell my constituents to assure them that old technologies will still be considered critical national infrastructure?

The media Green Paper lays out that the Government have already made the choice that we will switch off digital terrestrial television and move to internet protocol television at some point in the future, but the date has not yet been determined—it could be 2034 or 2044. We are examining the consultation to work out the best way forward. The hon. Lady’s constituents can be assured that no decision has been made, and we will take into account the issues that she raises when making that decision.

The Microsoft outage was, of course, a shock—indeed, it was a wake-up call to us all—but it may be that we got away lightly. Imagine if it lasted for a week or a fortnight, enhanced by bad actors. The Minister and other Members have referred to the need for open-source alternatives. Will he commit to coming back within three to six months on plans and progress for such alternatives?

The rhetoric from the hon. Gentleman is not necessarily helpful, because it was an isolated incident at Microsoft. There have been incidents in the past, which he referred to, and there will be incidents in the future. Our job is to make the Government as resilient as possible, and to put in place the tools and legislation to make sure that the economy is as resilient as possible, so that the UK can stand when these kinds of incidents happen.

I am pleased that the Minister has spoken about the steps that this Government will take in relation to digital resilience, because for weeks I have been pointing out a fault in the General Register Office’s new electronic register for births, deaths and stillbirths in England and Wales, which went live earlier this month. Over 70 senior council officials from around 50 local authorities wrote to the Home Office and told it that when the system fails, it is impossible to issue the death certificates needed for the deceased to be repatriated and buried overseas—something that is very important for many religious communities. In response, the Home Office has simply ignored warnings and continued regardless. Does the Minister agree that the lessons of the Microsoft outage should be learned by the Government as well as corporations, and will he agree to raise this matter with his counterparts in the Home Office so that we can prevent a disaster from happening?

I am not aware of that incident, but I will raise it with Ministers in the Home Office to find out what has happened. The hon. Gentleman asks us to learn the lessons from the Microsoft outage, which we and Microsoft will learn, but we were learning lessons before the Microsoft incident, because this Government want to be much more resilient. The Government’s cyber action plan, which was published at the start of this year, is part of that project, and is backed by £210 million of taxpayers’ money. That is about central direction, co-ordination, pace, consistency and clarity when it comes to the resilience of Government, and it is also about making sure that the wider economy has resilience.

I thank the Minister for his very comprehensive answers and for his interest in this matter. When Microsoft goes down, the country grinds to a halt—“IP meltdown” is how we refer to it. In my constituency last week, problems were not only financial. We saw NHS staff forced to use pen and paper, courts forced to adjourn, and councils and schools left scrambling to function. The IT system in my office, and in Government offices, was down until 1.40 pm on Friday, and my constituents and others were disadvantaged as a result. It raises serious questions about our over-reliance on a single system. What steps are being taken to ensure that every Government Department has proper contingency plans and offline back-ups, so that a technical failure never again paralyses our public services?

The hon. Gentleman talks about people reverting to pen and paper and other systems kicking in. The whole point of having a resilience plan is that when things happen across the tech stack or any of the systems, other systems kick in. That is why we did not see widespread disruption across the whole public sector. Yes, it was an inconvenience. My own emails went down until about 2 o’clock on Friday. I know that because the test email I sent myself on Thursday night arrived at about 2 pm on Friday, and the acknowledgment that it had arrived bounced back. The backlog has been cleared, and Microsoft resolved the problem as quickly as it could, but the whole point of the Government’s cyber action plan is to make sure that all Government Departments, local government and our public sector have resilience, and that the private sector also has resilience.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. There are about 300,000 jobs in tech and telecoms in Berkshire—Reading lies in that county and is the county town—and there are many more thousands of those jobs across the country, yet we only occasionally discuss issues related to this very important area of employment. Could there be a debate in the House on the contribution of tech and telecoms to the British economy?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. As he will know, that is not a matter for the Chair, but he has put on record the great extent of businesses in his constituency that are reliant on tech.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. We have lots of tech companies in Harlow, but my point of order refers to a mistake I made, and as a former maths teacher, I apologise for getting my numbers wrong. Last Thursday, when I spoke in the Backbench Business debate about the battle of the Somme, I referred to Private Thomas Lewis—he lived in my constituency and, sadly, died in the Somme—but I stated his age incorrectly. I said he was 19 when, sadly, he was killed at the battle of the Somme, but he was actually 21. I am taking this opportunity to set the record straight. —[ Official Report , 12 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 403.]
I thank the hon. Gentleman for his point of order. He has sought to correct the record at the earliest possible opportunity, although I am far from convinced that that was actually a point of order.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I would like to correct the record of the debate on Friday on the private Member’s Bill promoted by the hon. Member for St Ives (Andrew George). I incorrectly said: “We also build the infrastructure first. We are extending the grid roads, our famous roundabouts and our redways, which means that bicycles and pedestrians do not have to interact with the roads. Those provisions are set out in our council planning.” —[ Official Report , 13 November 2026; Vol. 793, c. 468.] What I meant to say was “in the local plan”, because as you will know, the council plan has everything in it that the council does, whereas the local plan has statutory standing in planning guidance. Thank you for allowing me to correct the record at the earliest opportunity.
I thank the hon. Member for her point of order. She has indeed done well to correct the record about the difference between a local plan and a council plan, and I am sure we thank her for that.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Thank you for allowing me to raise this point of order. In fact, it is the first point of order I have raised, so please bear with me. On 4 November, I spoke in the Adjournment debate on the strategic licensing regulations for London, and I am afraid that, as I am still a newbie to this place, I neglected to state an interest in that my partner is the manager of the trading standards and licensing department at Brent council. I believe I should have raised that at the time. A little time has gone by since then, but I am afraid I did not realise that I should have raised the issue until my partner mentioned it to me over the weekend, having noticed that I had spoken in the debate. I apologise for raising this so late. I hope you can assist me in correcting the record, and I will make sure not to make the same mistake again. —[ Official Report , 4 November 2026; Vol. 792, c. 969.]
I thank the hon. Member for what I think may actually have been a point of order. She has indeed corrected the record, and I thank her for that.

With permission, I would like to make a statement on digital capability for health and care. This Government are determined to give patients access to technology that supports their care while improving productivity. We want to give the health and care system more choice, greater resilience and less dependence on any single supplier, as well as the ability to adapt and evolve as new technologies emerge in future, with better value for taxpayers through time. These objectives require a new approach: one that will stimulate a more diverse and innovative supplier market, including greater use of sovereign AI as well as internationally developed capabilities, building on the shift from analogue to digital set out in the 10-year health plan. As we have just been learning, the global outage of certain Microsoft systems on Friday brought home the importance of avoiding overdependence. Our future capability should avoid being locked into any single technology. We need a new approach—one that will boost competition, demand interoperability and diversify NHS technology within a safe and modern regulatory framework. That approach has three parts: investing in strategic technologies; changing how future technology capabilities are procured; and developing open standards and our safety regime. In the Budget, my right hon. Friend the Chancellor confirmed a further £140 million for sovereign AI. The NHS will work with sovereign AI on speeding up clinical trials, monitoring medicines safety and scaling proven AI products across the NHS, such as cancer cell detection. The Government have committed to using public procurement as a strategic lever to back British industry and ensure communities benefit from growth and good jobs. We will evolve NHS procurement processes in line with that aim. Within a fair and open competition framework, we will use our purchasing power to create routes to market for innovative companies, giving British start-ups a fair crack at NHS contracts. Rather than the NHS simply buying the technology of the future, we want it to help create the market for it. That is where the federated data platform comes in. Fragmented information stops the NHS from providing patients with effective and emotionally intelligent care. A hospital can have beds available, but struggle to match them with patients waiting to be admitted. A clinical team can waste valuable time trying to understand where patients are on a waiting list, rather than treating them. Different parts of the NHS can hold pieces of the same operational jigsaw without being able to see the whole picture. Those are just some of the problems the FDP is helping the NHS to solve. Technology and Government priorities have moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023 and our procurement model needs to move with them, so today I can update the House: we will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract. From January, the NHS will begin this vital work with patients, our partners and the market. Formal procurement will begin in the second half of next year and we expect the full process, from engagement to completion, to take around 18 months. This is about the NHS building on what works, while opening the next generation of FDP to the best technologies. Interoperability, resilience and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, to work with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and to test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability.
