The introduction of this tax, even at £2 a person per night, would increase the cost of a week-long stay for a family of four by £56. That is a lot of money. The Government have acknowledged that the tax could push up the price of a holiday for Britons and force them abroad. The knock-on effect, not only for my local accommodation providers but for the wider hospitality industry in South Shields, will be devastating. We are not comparable to Barcelona, Amsterdam, Venice and other European holiday hotspots. In fact, some of those destinations have introduced a similar tax to curb tourism. They also have much lower VAT than we do. If we are going to introduce European taxes, we should introduce European VAT as well. In Manchester and Liverpool, the tax is operated by the businesses in a defined geographical area, and any revenue spend is agreed by an established board of those businesses. That approach is not as heavy-handed as what the Government are proposing in this Bill, and it puts the industry, which knows its businesses best, at the forefront of decision making. In other areas of the UK where the tax has been introduced, it has been in operation for only a short time. It is at a fixed rate, and there is clear guidance about what the revenue must be spent on. It is also worth noting that so far, the tax has largely been introduced for cities only, but under this Bill, entire regions can have it imposed on them, with no exempt areas.

I represent Tiverton and Minehead, which is the most beautiful constituency in the country, but also one of the most deprived. Within it lies Butlin’s in Minehead, to which some 3,000 or 4,000 people come each week. They are not the most wealthy people. Does the hon. Lady agree that paying an extra £56 a week could put them off coming to visit my constituency?

I agree with the hon. Lady on that, but I do not agree that her constituency is the most beautiful. The north-east economy is spread across cities, towns, countryside and coast. It may well be that the tax will not have much impact in our cities in the north-east, but it will negatively impact our small towns, our countryside and our coastal areas. The tax was not in our manifesto, for good reason. Research by UK Hospitality has found that even at a modest 5%, the tax could lead to 33,000 job losses per year, a £2.24 billion hit to the economy and over 11 million fewer overnight stays. Far from increasing tourism and growth, this tax will lead to a decrease in tourism and more boarded-up accommodation providers. That will be followed by a loss of footfall in my pubs, bars, cafés and restaurants. The north-east of England has the highest number of young people not in employment, education or training in the country. In September, the number of unemployment benefits claimants in my constituency remained above the national average, at 2,735 people. We are a small coastal town that thrives on hospitality, and I cannot stress enough that this really is the wrong tax at the wrong time. I am utterly dismayed that the Government are ploughing ahead with it, but I sincerely hope that they will work with me and the industry to amend this Bill as it passes through the House. As it stands, it is likely to rip the heart out of my home—my beautiful coastal town—and that is not something I will ever countenance.

When we debate legislation such as this, it is easy to make the focus the strategic authorities, the levy rates and the governance structures. That misses the point, because the real impact will be on people. There is the owner of a small hotel wondering how many more costs their business can absorb, and the pub with a handful of rooms trying to stay viable through the winter months.

Some constituents have written to me with concerns that the overnight levy will apply to overnight stays by scouts groups, which could put off scouts groups from staying away, even though we know how vital such visits are to them. The Government have recognised that campsites and hostels are used by these groups, but there is nothing in the Bill to protect them. Does my hon. Friend agree that there should be a national exemption for charity-run hostels, campsites, activity centres and meeting places, so that volunteer groups such as the scouts can keep going on trips?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. It is so important that young people and those who access such charitable groups are able to continue to have time away affordably. I hope that there will be amendments to the Bill to ensure the protection that is needed. This debate is also about the parent staying overnight while their child receives treatment, and the carer accompanying a disabled relative to an appointment far from home. It is they who will feel the effects of this Bill. The Liberal Democrats have long championed Britain’s hospitality industry. We were the first to call for an emergency VAT cut and we have campaigned for business rates reform.

My hon. Friend is making powerful points. We face a doubling of VAT compared with our competitors on the other side of the channel. We have also seen rocketing utility costs and the impact of the jobs tax. Does she agree that now is not the time to force the industry to swallow the bitter pill of an overnight visitor levy?

I completely agree that we need to look at the cumulative impact that this levy will add to, at a time when the hospitality industry is experiencing incredible challenges. As I have said, we as a party have consistently argued that pubs, hotels and tourism businesses should be supported, not treated as an endless source of new taxation. That is why, when the Bill was announced, we approached it with caution.

May I gently suggest to the hon. Lady that her words of support for hospitality, holiday venues and so on would have more force if her party’s Members were not on a one-line Whip tonight? If they are so against this Bill in principle and so concerned about the damage it will do to those sectors, why are they on a one-line Whip?

The hon. Member will understand later why my hon. Friends and I have taken a different approach this evening. We as a party believe strongly in devolution. We believe that local communities should have greater control over their future, including greater freedom over how they raise and spend money. A well-designed visitor levy would help communities invest in the infrastructure and services that make places attractive to residents and visitors alike. However, whether that succeeds depends entirely on one question: will it work for the people who are expected to pay for and administer it? Hospitality businesses are already facing rising employment costs, the Government’s national insurance rise and a tax burden that is higher than for many of our international competitors. The Liberal Democrats have heard repeatedly from hoteliers and accommodation providers that margins are already tight and costs are mounting. Before asking those businesses to collect a levy, Ministers must explain what assessment they have made of the impact—the cumulative impact—or are Ministers simply hoping that hospitality businesses will quietly shoulder yet another burden while council finances continue to deteriorate? That is why it is deeply concerning that, as yet, no national impact assessment appears to have been published alongside this legislation. I know that the Secretary of State referred to this point in her opening remarks, but I must disagree with the idea that the need to do impact assessments should land in the laps of our local authorities and mayoral strategic authorities. It should, in part, be down to the Government to publish one alongside this Bill as it progresses through Parliament. Members should not be asked to grant these powers without understanding what it will mean for the businesses that are expected to make it work. My concern is about not only who pays, but who decides. The Bill is presented as a devolution measure, yet it allows mayors to override constituent councils and proceed with a levy even when those councils object. If Ministers truly trust local communities—and if they truly trust local government—they should trust the elected councils that represent them. Genuine devolution means more power flowing downwards, not simply being transferred from Whitehall to another distant layer of government. If local people are being asked to support a visitor levy, they should be able to see where that money goes. Communities should see cleaner streets, safer public spaces, better transport links and improvements to the visitor experience as a direct result of any levy. Yet the Bill does not guarantee that the revenue will be spent in the communities where it is raised, nor does it guarantee that the Treasury will not quietly reduce central Government funding in response. Every £1 raised through this levy must be an additional £1 for local communities. Businesses and visitors should not be asked to pay more simply so that central Government can contribute less. A key question for the Secretary of State is: can she guarantee that this will not be the case, and that local government settlements will not be reduced where an authority chooses to introduce a visitor levy? We should also remember that not every overnight stay is a holiday. Some people travel because a loved one is seriously ill, some travel to receive treatment and some are carers accompanying a disabled relative. This Bill leaves important questions about those groups unanswered. As drafted, there is no clear protection for many of the people who stay away from home not out of choice or leisure, but because difficult circumstances leave them with no alternative. Finally, there is the question of proportionality. The Government describe this as a modest local levy, yet the Bill introduces extensive enforcement powers and may create offences carrying a maximum sentence of 14 years. Of course, deliberate fraud should be punished, but when introducing a new tax that i

Throughout this debate, many Members have made references to other countries that have such a tax, such as France, Spain and Italy. Does my hon. Friend agree that we should follow the punitive measures for evading such a tax in those countries, which are largely fines, rather than jailing people at the same time as the Government are releasing people from prison early?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. It is important that we look at areas that already have established approaches to find a proportionate and appropriate response. For all those reasons, the Liberal Democrats tabled a reasoned amendment declining to give the Bill a Second Reading. We support the devolution of power, but we cannot support a Bill that asks hospitality businesses, carers, families and local communities to shoulder new burdens while Ministers refuse to answer fundamental questions about local control, local funding, exemptions, administration and proportionality. We on these Benches are willing to work constructively with the Government in Committee to produce a better Bill that really works for areas that choose—and that is really important—to implement it. I do hope that Ministers will listen to our concerns and to that offer, as we tabled a reasoned amendment, but we also make that offer should the Bill go through.

As the chair of the all-party parliamentary group for hospitality and tourism, and the Member of Parliament for a town whose economy has been built on welcoming visitors for generations, I approach this Bill from both a national and a local perspective. Over the years, I have spoken to hoteliers, restaurateurs, attractions, local authorities and tourism businesses right across the UK, and my views have been shaped by what they have told me about the opportunities and challenges facing the sector. For that reason, I commissioned our APPG inquiry that brought together evidence from hospitality and tourism businesses, local authorities, trade bodies and industry experts to examine the potential impact of a visitor levy on the visitor economy, businesses and local communities. From those inquiry meetings, we agreed a number of recommendations. I am pleased that the Government have listened and engaged with me and other colleagues from across the House on those recommendations. Local leaders know their streets, infrastructure gaps and cultural assets far better than Whitehall ever could, so it is right to give them greater fiscal power, particularly for coastal areas like mine. I welcome the confirmation that levy receipts will stay local and support tourism-related priorities. I hope that local areas will see that money, if a mayor decides to implement a levy, reinvested in ways that drive growth and improve visitor experience. Local consultation is vital. Local leaders must work with their communities—the people who keep their local economies going. It is on this point that the sector has raised concerns with me. While local authorities must explain proposed spending, there is no guarantee that receipts will benefit the visitor economy, or that businesses paying the levy will have any influence on how it is spent. The Tourism Alliance, UKHospitality and voices across the sector have proposed a reasonable solution: ringfence a sustainable proportion of receipts to benefit the visitor economy; ensure businesses are represented when spending decisions are made; and require authorities to show that the money is additional to what they have already spent. We should also consider local economic impact assessments to ensure that we take a robust and locally informed approach. A single assessment covering a whole strategic authority could overlook the different circumstances of a city compared with a coastal community. We must also ensure that businesses can recover the cost of administrating the levy. They will need to change their booking systems, train their staff and spend hours collecting and reporting the data. They must not be left out of pocket for doing so. There needs to be a consistent national framework for how the levy is administered. A business operating across different mayoral areas should not have to navigate a patchwork of different processes. Local control over how the money is invested should go hand in hand with clear administrative rules that keep the burden on businesses to a minimum. We must consider the impact on visitors. Blackpool was built as a place of rest and entertainment for working people. Families visiting us often make careful decisions about how long they stay and what they can afford. The Government say that the percentage rate protects affordability, charging less for lower-cost stays and more for higher-cost stays, but I know that even small increases in the cost of accommodation may affect how long a family stay, how many local businesses they spend money in, and whether they come back. Blackpool welcomes huge numbers of day visitors. Locally, we are focused on encouraging them to stay longer. The policy seeks to empower local areas, but I worry that it has the potential to undermine the efforts of towns like mine. Every major regeneration strategy in Blackpool assumes a thriving visitor and tourism sector. It is there in the growth of conferences and business events, in the continued success of

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. I am really upset. I really like the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government and it is deeply upsetting to speak so negatively about her Bill. North Yorkshire hospitality, like so many areas of the UK hospitality sector, is only just recovering from covid. It has been on its knees and it is now being battered by high energy costs, high wage costs, high rates costs, inflation pressure impacting spending, and a welter of employment legislation that is about to come down the track. Not all of that is the Government’s fault. Some of those factors are not within the Government’s control, but many are. It is challenging at the moment for hoteliers or campsite owners anywhere in the UK, but in North Yorkshire and in particular in my constituency which is very rural, those challenges are especially acute. It is more difficult, because venues are less straightforward to get to, impacting visitor footfall, staffing and supply chain costs. Let us take a hotel or a campsite deep in the heart of the Yorkshire Dales. Getting staff and the cost of getting staff is a major challenge. Some hotels have to offer accommodation or bus services. Transport, food and drink supply costs are higher in remote locations. Energy supply, already tough for all providers of accommodation, is more expensive off-grid. Broadband and other services, too, are more expensive. Other considerations need to be added to the cost of running a rural hotel. It might be further away than is reasonable from a hospital, so more healthcare needs to be provided onsite. Planning a hotel expansion in beautiful areas such as North Yorkshire is more difficult, because it takes longer to go through the planning process. The UK hospitality sector is worried about the Government’s plans, but those in North Yorkshire hospitality are really frightened by the additional layer of tax and bureaucracy at a time when they and their businesses are only just surviving. The Tourism Alliance has talked about the seasonal aspect for rural and coastal destinations that compete on price and are more exposed. As we have heard, rural destinations depend much more on domestic and price-sensitive visitors. Communicating the fragility of the current situation in rural hospitality is key, because almost all the hospitality businesses I work with are not making a profit. They are losing money, obviously, but one more hammer blow could tip them over, and that means less revenue and fewer jobs.

I am listening to the right hon. Gentleman’s speech and I agree that the new plan needs to be done in consultation with businesses. Does he at least acknowledge that the visitor levy could be used to supply transport, for instance? He was talking about getting people to and from home and work.

I thank the hon. Lady for that intervention, but the case I am making is that we need lower taxes and less taxation to encourage more visitors, and for the cost of running a business to be less of a stress. More than 6,000 people in my constituency of Skipton and Ripon are employed in accommodation and food services. Often, as we heard earlier, these are jobs for the very young people we are trying to get back into employment. Not just the direct jobs are affected. Local food producers, taxi drivers, electricians, technicians and others who supply the businesses, and the pubs, restaurants, tourist sites and venues all need the footfall. Jobseekers and local suppliers are already worrying about the consultation on shooting. Shoots in constituencies such as mine provide many, many dinners and events at this time of year, so many venues are already worried. We have heard from the Secretary of State about the Mayor of York and North Yorkshire, who has already said that he is going to whack a 5% tax on—it could be more—which means that we will be competing against Lancashire, Northumberland and other attractive counties that may not apply a tax at all. We have also heard about the huge further administrative costs for those businesses, which are really struggling. We want them to invest in their businesses, not in HMRC services. Given the context of the challenges facing the sector, the only responsible thing is to put the Bill on hold. Yes, there are lots of issues around the consultation—rural protections, caps, limits to the duration of the levy and reviews of the policy—but I want the Secretary of State to come to North Yorkshire. I will pay for a night in a hotel, and then she can see how hard those people are working, and she can pause the Bill and bring it back when she is leader of the Labour party in a few Parliaments’ time.

In 2024, London attracted 21 million visitors, and many of those came to the community I represent to visit our world-class museums, parks and hospitality venues, or Portobello Road, Notting Hill, including Notting Hill carnival, and more. I am proud that those people came from all over the world, but we should not be complacent given the fierce international competition for tourism. We must continue to invest in the types of infrastructure that support the visitor experience and benefit local communities such as mine, which is why I support the Bill. The Mayor of London’s position is that the levy will be set at no more than 5% of the cost of accommodation. The priorities that he has set out for spending the visitor levy in London are the right ones: attracting more visitors to London; ensuring that tourism benefits local communities and is managed sustainably; and driving long-term economic growth. I am very encouraged by the path of fiscal devolution that the Government are on, and the visitor levy is a key part of that. Therefore, one of the questions will obviously be about how the money is spent.

On that point, I also welcome many visitors to my constituency, and both councils there spend a lot of money on trying to make the place clean and welcoming—it is not cost free. Does my hon. Friend agree that in London where we do not have a combined authority, part of the visitor levy needs to be given to the local councils, so that the total is shared perhaps equally between councils and the Mayor of London?

I will come on to some suggestions about how the levy could be shared, but my hon. Friend is right to say that London is in a different situation to other mayoral areas, given that we do not have a combined authority and the governance arrangements are different. I am hugely supportive of our mayor and his ambitions for London, and the visitor levy will unlock major London projects that will benefit everyone, but it is also important that communities such as mine and my hon. Friend’s, where the tourist impacts are considerable, feel the benefits directly. Take Portobello Road as an example—one of the world’s most famous street markets. Currently, Ladbroke Grove and Notting Hill Gate stations are both inaccessible, but they are key gateways for millions of tourists to come to the market. The road itself has been subject to controversial plans from the Royal Borough of Kensington and Chelsea to install temporary bollards for security purposes. Obviously, we want to keep the street safe—I have no issue with that—but that has caused major access issues, so the residents are rightly asking how temporary those bollards will be. The visitor levy could help speed up a permanent solution that ensures a safe, well-run market for residents and tourists alike. Take Knightsbridge as another example, where the business improvement district has a plan to increase footfall and unlock an additional £2.8 billion in spending over the next decade. The question is then how those projects will be able to seek support, and what reassurances London MPs can have about the involvement of local authorities in how the revenue is spent. That will require joint working and collaboration, to which I know the mayor and London councils are committed. To give a positive example, this year Notting Hill carnival received considerable additional support from City Hall, above the level that the local authority would have been able to provide, which led to a significantly better experience for everyone attending the carnival and for local residents. That additional funding was hugely welcome, and I hope it will continue in future years, with the visitor levy providing a potential source for the mayor to utilise. That example of joint working is why the proposal for a joint board to provide oversight for a portion of the visitor levy revenue is a step in the right direction, and I hope that Ministers will support it. I know there are strong views as to what percentage could be overseen by a board or the mayor, but for me the key thing is not the number; the mayor should be able to use the revenue stream to power major London projects and be ambitious about London’s international reputation for visitors, while also creating space for meaningful local projects, delivered by local authorities in partnership with the mayor, that will be win-wins for both residents and visitors. That is how we build support for the new levy and ensure that communities such as mine see and feel the difference. I also hope that there will space in the “Rewiring the State” White Paper for a more comprehensive view of London’s governance. London is of course different to the rest of the country. It does not have a combined authority; the London Assembly does scrutiny very well, but that is not the same as delivery. As fiscal devolution gathers speed, I expect we will keep coming back to those questions about the difference of London’s governance model and how we build consensus around what a permanent new deal for London might look like. I am also very pleased that the visitor levy will address some of the issues related to short-term lets. At every community meeting that I hold, residents tell me stories about the impact of poorly managed short-term letting, from antisocial behaviour and fly-tipping, to potential violations of building insurance, illegal subletting and breaches of London’s 90-day cap for whole homes being let unless they have a specific licence. The Bill cannot solve all th

It is a pleasure to follow the hon. Member for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell). I am tempted to ask: when is a tax not a tax? The answer is: when Ministers of the Crown cannot bear to use the word “tax”, so they call it a levy. A levy somehow sounds rather nice and gentle, doesn’t it? But it’s a tax, it’s a tax, it’s a tax. It is easy to dismiss this Bill, which I oppose, as the family holiday tax, because that is usually how we define visitors. As others have mentioned, however, this will also be another tax on working people, such as the tradesmen and women who work out of area; the additional costs of their accommodation are going to be passed on to their customers, and they are therefore likely to find fewer jobs. This will be a tax on those with health concerns or caring responsibilities who travel out of area and have to go up the night before for an appointment or stay overnight after having treatment in order to recuperate.

I thank my hon. Friend for making the point about parents staying overnight when their children are in hospital. I just want to remind the Minister that some of those illnesses are serious—we are talking about not just one or two nights, but potentially months. I have direct experience of this from my own meningitis; I am quite sure that many other families will have experienced something similar. These things can take months.

My hon. Friend is right. She makes the point, as others have and as I hope to be able to do, that the Bill raises so many legitimate expectations for exemptions—common-sense, caring, kind, practical exemptions—that by the time they were all encapsulated in the Bill as it progresses through this place, one would have to ask, “What is the point of the Bill?” If fairness and rationality are to be at the heart of all of this, there will—or should be—legions of exemptions. I am still not convinced as to what particular problem the Government are trying to solve with this Bill. Is it that Britain is too attractive a place for overseas visitors to come, and we think we should knock them back a little bit? Is it that we want to discourage staycations, short breaks and so on? I am not entirely sure—and neither, I would suggest, are those on the Treasury Bench. North Dorset has many businesses. We do not have a coast—we are entirely rural—although the county of Dorset obviously does. [ Interruption. ] The Secretary of State is off to choose the hotel she is going to share with my right hon. Friend the Member for Skipton and Ripon (Sir Julian Smith). I am sure there will be some good pre-Christmas deals that she can have a look at with him—

Indeed—my right hon. Friend makes the obvious point, and I am grateful to her for doing so. North Dorset has a lot of businesses that benefit either directly or indirectly through tourism, which are very often in sectors that are under pressure from the main purpose of their trade. I think of the pubs with rooms in my constituency: the Anvil Inn at Pimperne, the Fox Inn at Ansty, the Crown at Marnhull, the Langton Arms at Tarrant Monkton, the Talbot at Iwerne Minster, and the Swan Inn in Sturminster Newton—all businesses trying to do well and trying to keep their head above water against both myriad switches and changes in customer demand and a burdensome tax and regulatory system. Those pubs often see letting those rooms as a way of helping to break even. I think also of the farmers in my constituency who have diversified into the tourism sector merely to try to keep their heads above water. It will not, I hope, be lost on the Minister how many of these rural campsites have the word “farm” in the title. As I say, many of these farms have diversified into summer tourism to provide vital income. According to the Tourism Alliance, the visitor economy—a cash cow the Government obviously think can be milked further—is worth £147 billion per annum in the UK, sustains 2.4 million jobs and generates £52 billion in tax revenue. If the Government are to plough blindly on down the route of introducing this tax, there are, it seems to me, some obvious amendments that I hope my right hon. and hon. Friends will seek to push. There should be a cap on the levy enshrined in legislation, not left to the discretion of a mayor. A clearer and tighter way must surely be found to enforce ringfencing or hypothecation of the tax in order to ensure that the local tourism economy benefits from it. There should be an exemption from VAT on the levy itself. The Government’s consultation said that there would be, but the Bill is silent, and silent is not good enough. That is particularly true given the point I made in an intervention of the differential in sales taxes between us and the countries the Government have sought to pray in aid. We have Europe’s highest rate of hospitality tax at 20%. Ireland’s is 9%. In France, Italy and Spain, it is 10%, while in Greece it is 13%. If we are going to compare fruits, let us at least compare apples with apples and oranges with oranges. UK tourism and hospitality is already fighting in a dramatically competitive international sector with one hand tied behind its back, and now the Government, through this new tax, would seek to impede their business growth still further. There are, of course, other exemptions that I hope will be considered, such as establishments where accommodation is ancillary to the main business—I mentioned those rural pubs that have rooms—or having a set number of rooms below which an establishment is exempt from the levy. We should also exempt rooms available and provided by religious institutions providing retreat, accommodation in youth hostels and the YMCA and YWCA. I want to mention campsites in particular. I have a number of campsites in my constituency, such as Woodfrys Farm in Melbury Abbas and Redlands Breaks in Hazelbury Bryan. We have them in Blandford; we have Home Farm Camping in Tarrant Gunville and others. All of them are trying to attract people to the area to spend their hard-earned money, not just on the campsite but elsewhere, to support the economy. Every pound in tax that the Government take through this levy will result in either one of two things, or possibly both of them. First, it will reduce the amount of holiday time that hard-working families can actually afford to take. At a time when we are surely supposed to be encouraging family time and everything that goes with it, we should surely be trying to find ways to arrive at the complete opposite landing spot. Secondly, even if that does not happen, the people who are visiting—people who, as the hon. Member for South S

My hon. Friend is raising a very good point. Does he feel that, in the same way that people tried to avoid the landfill tax by fly-tipping, this tax on camping may mean that we see more fly-camping, where people camp at will in the countryside—in an uncontrolled environment without facilities and where they may leave litter or cause wildfires, and similarly damage the countryside?

I agree with my right hon. Friend—perhaps “Carry On Fly-Camping” could be the next film in the series. He is right; this is going to have significantly negative knock-on effects. These are negative effects that the Government are authoring with no particular urging from anybody outside of the Government’s mind so to do. I do not particularly want to see competition between the mayoral authority of Devon and Cornwall and the mayoral authority of Wiltshire, Somerset and Dorset, if we are to be given one, where they are trying to differentiate between the two. UK plc should be promoting itself as a tourism destination; it should not a case of, “Come to this bit of England or that bit of England because this bit charges x and this bit charges y.” I ask the Minister to address this point specifically in summing up. Those who operate campsites or places where people can bring their own motorhome or tourer are not providers of accommodation; they are merely providing a pitch. This is a point that Mr Cooper of Inside Park raised with me.

The hon. Lady is right, but the key word there is “can”! I wonder if the hon. Lady would honestly be able to find me a politician, particularly one who ascribes to her party, who when offered a smorgasbord of tax opportunities suddenly says, “Oh no, no, no—I am on a frightfully strict diet.” Of course not—they will fill their boots. They will tax until the pips squeak, and they will use it for every pet policy that they have. It does not have to be tourism related or local economy related; no, no—we give all the discretion to the mayor. The point that the Opposition is making is that if the Government wish to run forward pell-mell with this, there must be clear parameters beyond which a mayor, were they to choose to use the powers, could not stray.
If the hon. Lady wishes to point me to a Labour politician who wants to not tax, I will of course give way to her again.

The thing is this: I have confidence in the Mayor of London, and I have confidence that the money will be ringfenced to be used locally, as is written in the legislation. I do not disagree with the right hon. Gentleman with regard to ensuring that there is a cap—mayors have already said that there will be a 5% cap—but we should be honest and talk about where there can and should be exemptions. That is what we will work towards.

It is not for me to give the hon. Lady political advice, but I would just say that “I agree with and support the current Mayor of London” is not her best prospectus to get her party’s nomination for that post—a task I wish her well in. I am afraid that the hon. Lady is not correct. This is not ringfenced in the Bill; there is no hypothecation there. The Government effectively rest their argument on a benign use of the discretionary powers of the mayor and then a sensible disbursement of the fees—and, as the hon. Member for South Shields rightly said, without any consultation with anyone involved in the tourism sector, Members of Parliament, council leaders, chambers of commerce, residents associations or anybody else. No, no: the mayor, sitting behind this screen of smoke and mirrors, Wizard of Oz-like, pushing the buttons and pulling the levers, is suddenly going to exercise the omnipotent powers of the Wizard of Oz and arrive at this benign visitor levy, which is going to lead to growth. But growth in what? Youth unemployment figures, one presumes. It is going to lead to growth in the rate of closure of rural hospitality businesses and of rural pubs. That is the only growth that a further tax is going to lead to. Any idea that this is some sort of pump priming or fertile seed bed for tender shoots of economic growth, fostered and encouraged by those on the Treasury Bench, is frankly for the birds. This is a tax that will destroy jobs and family holidays and put pressure on hard-working people, just at a time when they deserve to have a break. If this is the Government’s definition of “Let us give the people of this country hope”, I dread to think what their prospectus of despair would look like. Let me conclude, Madam Deputy Speaker, before I do myself or the House a mischief. The Bill, as many Members have said already, raises far more questions than it does answers, it generates far more problems than it seeks to solve, and it seeks to answer a question that has not been asked. It seems to rely on an entirely imbalanced argument that some European countries have a visitor tax while entirely neglecting the fact that there is a sharp differential in sales taxes between us and most of Europe. It is a tax that will hit hard UK tourism. It will hit hard entrepreneurs and businesses. It will hit harder still working families. Farms, pubs, SMEs and campsites are already struggling with over-regulation and tax obligations. A holiday tax will be a further burden that is neither wanted nor needed. For the sake of UK tourism, I urge with all my heart that the Government think again.

It is a privilege to follow the hon. Member for North Dorset (Simon Hoare), who is undoubtedly the finest Select Committee Chair on the Opposition Benches, though I am afraid to say that on this matter we most profoundly disagree. I am the Member of Parliament for Crawley, and prior to that, I was the leader of Crawley council. Crawley is the finest town in England. Unfortunately, most people still do not know where it is, which is why we always follow up a mention of it with the sentence, “It’s where Gatwick airport is.” It is a privilege that much of the country will, in the course of their lifetime, travel into or through my constituency without knowing its name, and they are very welcome to, but that does have an impact. Before I get to that, I would like to address some of the points made by Opposition Members. During my time as local authority leader, we had to go through Brexit. What many Members ignored at the time, when they were shouting, “No deal is better than any deal,” is the open skies agreement. For those who are not aware, the open skies agreement was the basis on which UK planes flew anywhere in the world. Without it, planes coming to and leaving the UK would need to agree a deal with every single destination. There was a moment, prolonged over three-and-a-half years, when it genuinely looked possible that every plane in this country would be grounded, as the Tories cheered on no deal being better than any deal. We have open skies agreements in place today by virtue of doing a deal with the EU, which many Conservative Members still appear to disagree with, but the reality is that we are still worse off than we were with the previous deal. They are telling us that we are going to destroy the entire hospitality economy over a couple of quid on a night’s stay in a hotel, when they were ready to destroy the entire aviation industry and the inbound tourism economy because of their ideological bent. I have to say to them that the crocodile tears do not impress. I was local authority leader in my constituency during covid, when every plane was grounded for a time. We went from being the town with the densest employment in the entire country outside of London to the worst-affected economy in the country. The then Government said that they were prepared to help, but would do absolutely nothing in practice to help. There was no financial support, and no support or attention from Ministers or civil servants. It was down to the local authority to rebuild that place, brick by brick, back up to that status, without the help of the Government. I do not take Opposition Members seriously when they raise concerns, given how they behaved in the past. Visitors are very welcome to Crawley—it is a privilege to have them, and they are good for our economy—but they do have an impact, including on roads and transportation. We can talk about potholes—apparently it is a concern that the money could be used for potholes. What do Opposition Members think people use to come into and go out of a constituency? A very high proportion use cars, and our roads suffer by virtue of that. I have to say that the argument that more funding for maintaining our roads will be in any way unpopular with local electorates is not very convincing. Just this morning, I was collared by a man in my local Tesco who was boasting about how many roadworks were taking place, and who said how good it was to see the roads being redone, thanks to the Government’s additional funding. We have to deal with housing and the impact of short-term lets on our local economy. We have to deal with the impact of visitors on waste and environmental issues. I accept that commercial waste is dealt with separately, but it still has to be dealt with at the strategic level by strategic authorities. We also have to deal with water— [ Interruption. ] It still has to go somewhere, and at the end of the day, that infrastructure will be overseen by the strategic authority. Having a mechanis
Thank goodness the hon. Member went to a sewage works. He is talking plenty. Is there any chance that during his speech he will mention the visitor levy?

I will get on to the visitor levy—but back to the sewage works. If you want to attract the most fun comments you can on your social media feeds, I recommend taking a video at a sewage works; people’s creativity goes through the roof. The impacts of expansion and of tourism on sewage are significant, and the works is having to plan what will happen in the event of Gatwick’s expansion. I will not completely bore hon. Members again on local authority funding—I went on about it when we debated business rates—but when we look at the history of local authority funding, we see it is grounded in Tudor England. It was brought in to deal with the disbursement of poor relief by parish councils in Tudor times, as back then there was a requirement that everyone earned a minimum wage. The knock-on effect is that everyone in a community who is putting pressure on that infrastructure is expected to pay towards its maintenance. We have council tax. There is a discount for single-person households, to take into account the fact that fewer people live in them. Businesses have gone through various systems, but today they contribute towards their area through business rates. What about communities that see a drastic increase in their size, and on the pressure on their infrastructure, but see no contribution made towards the provision of infrastructure in that area? We could claim that business rates make a difference, but there is the capping and levying on top of business rates. My community collected £120 million of business rates this year and got to keep £4 million to £5 million. If we get more people in, using more local hospitality, that figure will not change. The reality for those communities is that there is no accounting for the fact— [ Interruption. ] The hon. Member for Ashfield (Lee Anderson) seems to be having a fine conversation. Are you discussing the impact that you appear to have on my constituency by taking this line? Are you discussing the impact on my community? No, of course you are not.
Order. I remind the hon. Gentleman that when he says “you”, he is in fact referring to the Chair.
My sincere apologies, Madam Deputy Speaker. I will apologise separately in due course. Regrettably, I forgot the formalities of the Chamber.

The hon. Gentleman may be interested to know that he will enjoy the support of Reform Members. At a recent Local Government Association meeting, Reform councillors voted in favour of the visitor levy, so I have no doubt that he will be making common argument with them.

That is an interesting point. With that foreknowledge, I look forward to hearing the remarks of Reform Members. A levy would not be an imaginary figure; in my area, it would reduce the council tax pressure on my constituents. It would enable the people who use an area’s infrastructure to make a proportional contribution to the community’s infrastructure needs. Overwhelmingly, these are more deprived areas, so the knock-on effect for communities will be positive. That is why I called for a visitor levy for over a decade as a local authority leader. I understand why people worry about the impact of a levy, as the hospitality sector has suffered, but the Government have done much to support it. Significant business rates reform in the form of higher thresholds, better tapering and a permanent reduction overall have supported the sector. For those with licences, there are changes in beer duty for licensed premises and retail premises. That, again, supports the sector. Regulatory changes that support the sector are continuing to go through: just last week, I was on a Delegated Legislation Committee increasing the number of temporary event notices. The Government are working to support the hospitality sector. We completely agree that there should be support for families who are struggling and need to spend time with their loved ones. That is the very reason why, in the summer, the Government introduced the summer of savings programme, designed to support people throughout that period. Constituents of hon. Members across the Chamber will have enjoyed that. As has been discussed, tourist taxes already exist—most people who have visited Europe will know that—so we do not have to guess what the impact will be, and studies have shown repeatedly that in those countries that have implemented those taxes, there has been no impact. We will have paid them, and in most cases, we probably did not notice them. Let us bear in mind that almost two thirds of UK tourists go out of country, so UK tourists are already being charged tourist taxes during their time aboard. Opposition Members are apparently saying that people coming to the UK should not pay to maintain our local infrastructure, in the way that we pay to maintain infrastructure abroad. The point has been made about VAT. It is true that many countries have a lower VAT rate for hotels, but as a whole, the UK has one of the lowest VAT rates in the continent, so over all, it may well be that costs end up roughly equivalent. There is no evidence of risk. Why are my council tax payers being asked to pay the full cost of the impact of tourists travelling through my community, and staying in it? We have been warned about various tax increases in the past. Conservative Members told us that the English school system would entirely collapse if we charged the full rate of VAT on private school fees and, of course, that did not happen; that was utterly predictable. This is a storm in a tea cup. This is Second Reading, which is for talking about the concept of whether we could have a visitor levy—a tourist tax—in some areas. We can discuss every provision imaginable in the Public Bill Committee and on Third Reading. My hon. Friend the Member for Blackpool South (Chris Webb) made important remarks about what should be taken into account, and the Liberal Democrats have indicated that they are prepared to work towards additional provisions to improve the Bill—that is welcome—but this debate is about the concept, rather than the final version. Let us say that there is an impact from the levy. People can say that this is a postcode lottery, but this is democracy, and we have created mayors. People might not like mayors and may have opposed them, but they exist and are voted for by local communities—and if they make bad decisions, they can be voted out by those communities. Elected members occasionally make mistakes. That is to be accepted; it is part of the democratic process. We do not deny that people in

It is a great pleasure to follow the hon. Member for Crawley (Peter Lamb), although I find myself in the unfortunate position of not being able to agree with a single word he has just said. I am also very puzzled about this Bill and why the Government have decided to bring it forward now. It is generally accepted that Governments do not get people to do more of something by taxing it. Taxation is usually quite a persuasive way of trying to get people to do less of something, so my starting point is that I am deeply suspicious of an overnight visitor levy because it will have the unwelcome consequence of encouraging fewer overnight stays. However, on the basis that the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, which I chair, has only in the last couple of months kicked off an inquiry into the UK’s competitiveness as a global visitor destination, and what might attract people or put them off, I decided that I would approach this topic with an open mind. We have received more than 110 written submissions, we have so far held two oral evidence sessions, and we have visited Blackpool and Morecambe. It is safe to say that one issue has been raised consistently throughout all of that: the overnight visitor levy. As a Committee, our focus has been on whether the levy will make our town, cities, coast and countryside more attractive to visitors. Tourism is worth £147 billion to the UK economy—it is about 5% of our GDP—so boosting the number of inbound tourists is vital if we are serious about economic growth. Inbound tourism stimulates investment in new infrastructure, increases business competition, creates jobs and opportunity and is self-perpetuating, in that growth stimulates growth. The Government have set a sensible ambition for overseas visitor numbers to rise from 42.5 million in 2024 to 50 million by 2030, but there are major challenges in the way of that ambition. The UK is the second highest-taxed accommodation market in Europe and ranks 113th out of 119 countries for price competitiveness. That is why the Government should be worried. Domestic overnight tourism fell by 5% in 2025. That is why the Government should be worried. Most English regions outside London have not yet returned to 2019 visit volumes by inbound tourists. That is why the Government should be worried. By 2030, inbound visits to the UK are forecast to be 23% up on 2019, but that is compared with 34% in western Europe overall. The UK is losing out. That is why the Government should be worried. They must not simply add to the pressures on an already struggling hospitality sector with a visitor levy. They must not further weaken the UK’s global competitiveness in this valuable industry. I want to set out a few of the key concerns that the Select Committee has heard so far. First, there is the question of cross-Government co-ordination. A key theme of our inquiry has been that tourism is often overlooked in Whitehall. I have already explained to the House how important it is to our economy. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport may be responsible for tourism within Government, and it may do its best to champion the industry, but its efforts can be undermined by decisions taken in other parts of Government. The visitor levy is primarily a devolution measure led by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, so Ministers have to ensure that the needs of the tourism industry do not get lost in a policy designed primarily to boost mayoral powers, and that it does not become a means of propping up the coffers of cash-strapped local authorities. Secondly, there is the question of how the proceeds are used. Our evidence has stressed that any revenue raised by the levy must be genuinely and visibly additional. If we are asking tourists to cough up, they must be able to see the benefit. Their money must be used to support the visitor economy, even if that is in a wider sense, so I encourage the Minister to consider what safeguards might

Last year, I was delighted but not entirely surprised to see Chester celebrated as the UK’s most welcoming city. Ranked 10th in the world by Booking.com, our city was praised for its “friendly locals and vibrant community spirit” and for exuding “a warm, inviting charm that leaves visitors feeling truly at home.” This accolade, which we received thanks to everyone who works so hard in the sector, has been reflected in our visitor economy growing to £4.4 billion across Cheshire and Warrington, with 1.7 million staying visitors in Cheshire West and Chester alone. For my constituency of Chester North and Neston, tourism is a rapidly growing sector, directly employing local people and empowering local businesses. More than that, this growth allows us to showcase our historic gem of a home as a superb retail, business and leisure destination. This levy therefore has the potential to create a significant positive impact for Chester, and I believe that it could replicate the successes seen abroad in cities such as Milan and Paris. OECD research supports this, suggesting that enhanced fiscal decentralisation is associated with higher economic growth and local investment. At home, case studies from across the UK have shown that such a levy can have a significant economic benefit for businesses, residents and visitors when delivered locally and with transparency. My hon. Friend the Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur) earlier described the positive impact that Edinburgh had felt. Chester’s tourism partners have in the past explored an accommodation business improvement district similar to those in Liverpool and Manchester. Their estimates showed that Chester could raise around £1 million a year through a modest charge of no more than £2 per room per night, plus VAT, which is approximately 2% of the average cost of a hotel room in Chester city centre. Any proposed levy must be delivered with careful consideration and the continued input of key stakeholders, large and small. I welcome the provisions in the Bill that will require extensive local consultation, which are a recognition of the expertise of those on the frontline of our expanding tourism sector. That consultation is key. For this proposal to carry public approval, stakeholders must be confident that money is being properly reinvested in the services they use and value. Where the levy is introduced, that will lead to greater collaboration and engagement, with hoteliers and other stakeholders likely to agree investment plans with local public sector partners to generate further economic uplifts. The Labour mayoral candidate for Cheshire and Warrington, Dan Price, has pledged to implement a modest levy, building on the views of local stakeholders, such as hoteliers, Destination Chester, Marketing Cheshire and visitor attractions such as the fantastic Chester zoo, about the transformative potential of this fund for our visitor economy. Furthermore, Dan has promised that if the proposal for the levy is agreed, he will introduce a visitor economy commissioner, giving the sector a dedicated champion at the combined authority level. Measured and well-informed proposals such as Dan’s will allow investment to drive up business and trade, beautify our streets and improve services for all visitors and residents. The tourism partnership in Chester is keen for a number of key asks to be answered. First, stakeholders want to ensure that any visitor levy is set at a competitive rate. I welcome the Bill’s focus on a locally led approach, which will ensure that this ask is met. Secondly, they want a potential future levy to be straightforward to collect and administer, avoiding unnecessary burdens on tourism businesses, especially those that offer packaged visitor experiences. I refer here to the comments of my hon. Friend the Member for Blackpool South (Chris Webb). We need to explore the issue of packaged experiences that include not just an overnight stay, but an experience, such as pe

The British seaside holiday is part of the fabric of Bognor Regis and Littlehampton. Wherever anyone goes in my constituency in the summer, they will find families enjoying the seaside holiday they have spent all year looking forward to. I could give credit to the West Sussex sunshine, but our local businesses would rightly have something to say about that. An undeniable attraction of the British seaside holiday is that it is fantastic value for money. From the guest houses and hotels that welcome the same families back every year, to the fish and chip shops that stay open late on a summer evening, as well as the seafront attractions that give children so much joy, people choose to holiday in Bognor Regis and Littlehampton not only because it is wonderful, but because it is affordable. Our businesses make that possible. From independents such as the East Beach guest house, the Navigator hotel and Bailiffscourt hotel and spa, to household names such as Butlin’s and Premier Inn, businesses work so hard to ensure that families can enjoy a great British holiday at a price they can afford. However, this Government have so far spent their time in office making it harder for such businesses to survive. They have hiked employer national insurance, pushed up business rates by an average of more than 30% and piled on red tape. As one local business owner put it to me recently: “This Government has made it harder to run a business than ever before.” Not content with adding layer upon layer of cost on businesses, the Government now want to make it more expensive for families to holiday in seaside towns such as Bognor Regis and Littlehampton. Nationally, Oxford Economics estimates that this 5% levy could result in 12 million fewer overnight stays and £1.7 billion less visitor spending, and put 33,000 jobs at risk. In local terms, for a family of four holidaying for a week in Littlehampton, that could add more than £100 to the bill. For many, that is simply unaffordable; even if they could afford it, that is money that will no longer be spent in other local businesses. There are no two ways about it: higher accommodation prices will reduce occupancy rates in hotels and B&Bs in our seaside towns. Some families will cut their holiday short; others will look abroad or decide that they cannot afford to go away at all. That is the real fear for Richard and Mark Groome, the proprietors of East Beach guest house in Littlehampton. They know that people cannot afford to spend any more, and they worry that they will choose to stay away instead. What will that force them to do? They have already cut back on costs, and are desperate not to put up prices for their customers, but they are now worried that the Government are making that decision for them. The levy will deter tourists and lead to less custom for the businesses around their lovely hotel. That means less spending on the locally roasted coffee at Edge by the Sea, Mewsbrook Park café or East Beach café in Littlehampton; on the delicious food at Chez Moi in Aldwick, which has been recommended in The Sunday Times , at Fino in Felpham, or at Lemongrass in Rustington; or on a well deserved holiday beverage at the Waverley in Bognor Regis, the Maypole in Yapton or any number of outstanding venues across my constituency. For businesses that rely on a good summer to get through the winter, the levy will force them to push up prices, cut staff and, in some cases, close their doors for the last time. At a roundtable with local hospitality businesses in July, I heard genuine fear about the impact of this holiday tax. Iain Brown, the director of Sussex Inns, hit the nail on the head when he called it out for what it is: an “absolute killer blow” for our hospitality sector. He is right. There will be a further damaging knock-on effect of this tax. Tomorrow we expect the Milburn review. It will rightly say that we need to get more young people off welfare and into work. Young people deserve the chance to e

I will speak in support of the Bill, but I believe that we need to bring some amendment to it. The quality of York’s tourism offer is exceptional. Right now, the streets are buzzing. We have the Christmas market, the nutcracker trail and numerous attractions, such as the railway museum, the castle museum, Clifford’s tower, the art gallery and Yorkshire museum. The retail offer is exceptional because of its independence, but also because the people in tourism, hospitality and retail work exceptionally hard to make it a success. We are on the tentative list to become a world heritage site, and that in itself incurs a cost. If we invest, we will gain the benefit from that and save, but we need the resource in our city. Occupancy remains high in our city, and yet cuts to our council’s budget have meant that improvements have not been forthcoming at the rate we would want to see. The visitor levy provides an opportunity to invest in that infrastructure and improve the offer we can make to residents and visitors, and therefore see a greater boom in the hospitality sector—not what the naysayers on the Opposition Benches are saying. However, we need to recognise that when people come to our city, they draw on its infrastructure, whether that is street cleaning, bin collections, A&E—especially for those who like to party at night—or the police who ensure that our city is a safe place. We are an incredibly safe city. We have 9.1 million visitors to our small and perfectly formed city and 1.7 million overnight stays, so that has a real bearing on what happens across York. That is why a visitor levy would be a way for people who come to our city to give back, not only through the tourism offer, but to the residents of York to show their gratitude for the enjoyment they have gained. When I first advocated for a tourism tax, as we called it back in the day, we favoured a flat rate because of its clarity and simplicity. I said it should be pinned to the price of a cup of coffee, which nobody these days bats an eyelid at. I acknowledge that the Government have put in a more progressive model of a percentage levied on the cost of accommodation, and I support that approach, but we need to recognise that it will have a bearing on those providers. I have heard from hospitality providers in my city that are struggling at the moment, and we have to recognise that what they pin that on is not necessarily the visitor levy, but the national insurance contributions, which took their toll. Providers say that VAT is a problem and they want to see the Government take action on that. If we are introducing a visitor levy, there must be some trade-offs for the industry. Perhaps looking at VAT again for the hospitality sector would be an encouraging step forward. In other European countries where VAT is lower and there is a levy, tourism has boomed as a result. I ask the Government to publish an impact assessment of the proposals as we travel into Committee stage, so that we can see the impacts while acknowledging that mayors will have to put together their own impact assessments. The way the hospitality sector operates is important, and the detail of the legislation needs tightening up in some areas. In York, we believe the revenue should be hypothecated to York, not wider North Yorkshire, because of the hospitality work our city does as a unit. We believe that if money is raised in our city, it should be spent in our city for the benefit of our residents, as well as for the tourists.

Research from the Labour Rural Research Group emphasises exactly that point. Its latest report on “The Future of the Rural Economy” found that if the levy were introduced, stakeholders would want to see it ringfenced for the area raising that money. That is just as important to rural areas as it is to more urban areas such as my hon. Friend’s, because they want to see the direct benefit that comes from people visiting their area. Does she agree that it would be great for the Minister to look at how that could be mandated?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for that intervention because, as I have heard from other Members across the House today, it would be an important amendment in Committee to enable hypothecation and resource well spent in the locality. Also, it would mean that there is a direct relationship between the tourism sector and residents. I have heard too many times residents in York say to me, “It all goes to the visitors and tourists.” This is about accountability within the locality, and surely that is the piece that is often missing in our politics. Spending determination should not be the domain of the mayor alone. That offer should be developed with the hospitality sector—again, that co-production which is so important. Our hospitality sector would welcome that engagement to ensure that its voice on where the money is spent is threaded through. Hospitality businesses have said that if the levy is used for the promotion of tourism, the locality and services, they would absolutely understand the need for it and the benefit of charging that levy. I believe a proportion should be dedicated to local projects, so that residents can get the benefit of that for community spaces, and a proportion should be spent on services such as street cleaning, and the additional demands on health, policing and other services; there is data to show that that demand comes from outside of our area when tourism comes to our city. It is also right to think about which accommodation is included and which is excluded. As hon. Members know, I have long called for short-term holiday lets to be properly licensed—it is appropriate to ensure that there is a levy on them. However, I would exclude hostel accommodation, like youth hostels and local provision. We have heard about tents; those low-budget options should automatically be removed from the levy. I recognise that new types of accommodation are on the scene. I do not know where these pods fit in, or yurts—maybe the glamping world would not be exempt. It would make for a good debate in Committee, so that we get this right. Paragraph 2(1)(b) of schedule 1 states that a strategic authority should “consult such persons as the authority considers appropriate on the initial prospectus and visitor levy proposal”. I am afraid that is far too vague. The strategic authority must be obliged to consult local authority leaders, MPs, the hospitality sector, and the wider tourism and retail sectors. It should also consult residents and local service providers. Mayors are already far too unaccountable for the decisions they make. I know that is something the Government want to address, but we need to be able to bring in that accountability when introducing a new form of taxation. It is therefore crucial that those stakeholders are listed on the face of the Bill as statutory consultees. The consequential report that the mayor must produce should also reflect the findings of the consultation, not just have “regard” to those responses as set out in paragraph 2(3) of schedule 1. I ask for the Minister to further consider those points. As I have said, family budgets are tight and we need to consider an exemption for children. That option is not in the Bill, but I ask that such a measure is considered. It would be a popular move, and it would enable families to ensure affordability. We have also heard about carers and people on hospital stays, including for treatment—there should be proper exclusions in those cases too. With inflation currently running at 4%, to introduce a 5% charge could mean a 9% increase in the cost of holidays. I therefore ask the Government to consider introducing a levy with a 1% per year increase, so that there is a phasing-in stage and a more gradual approach. Finally, will there be consideration for neighbouring authorities? If there are cliff edges, there could be challenges, and that needs to be debated and considered by the Government.
