It is a fundamentally different plan from the new settlement I have set out today. Their answer is to take away support and walk away. Ours is a guarantee of training, education or a job for every young person, and in return, the expectation that they take it up: opportunity matched by responsibility. The hon. Lady asks about Alan Milburn’s continuing role, and, yes, we hope he will take up a continuing role now the report has been published. I end by saying that the Conservatives wrote off this generation; we offer them a new settlement. That is the difference between us, and one I am proud to stand by.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his statement. I absolutely agree with him that this is an opportunity of a generation and that we must change the status quo. Our young people deserve better, and they deserve the opportunities and support outlined in the statement. I particularly welcome the very rigorous analysis of the causal evidence of what has led to the increase in the number of young people not in education, employment or training. That points very much to the increase in child poverty under the previous Administration. Over 52% of our young NEETs experienced persistent child poverty, and that has been identified as a causal driver of their becoming NEET. I have questions for my right hon. Friend, particularly about the sequencing of some of the interventions and the evidence base, but could he in particular explain what support and opportunities will be available to young people who have special educational needs and disabilities? We know that 80% of NEETs currently fall into that group, and they deserve as much as anyone.

I thank my hon. Friend for her questions. She may have noticed that the child poverty figures published today show a sharp fall in child poverty as a result of actions taken by this Government. She is absolutely right to say that sequencing is important. That is why this is a new system with a new settlement, and it is important that we put support in place before other changes take place. On children with SEND, I work closely with my right hon. Friend the Education Secretary on this question, but we are clear on benefits statements in the Milburn report, and there will be a benefit to help people with extra cost needs.

I thank the Secretary of State for sharing his statement in advance. As Liberal Democrats, we believe that the big lever that needs pulling is the economy. We need to be working much harder with our European neighbours to grow the economy, and we need to scrap the damaging jobs tax. We also need to reflect on how business rates could be altered to provide support and be seriously reformed. Milburn has highlighted that we have lost 1.6 million jobs in our economy. Our young people have had the cost of living crisis and an international pandemic, and the third element in this lethal cocktail is the pressure cooker of social media. We say that it is right to have a greater focus on the state supporting young people into work, not just seeing the way forward through benefits. I have some questions for the Secretary of State about which we are particularly interested to hear from him. Regional inequality is a significant challenge. How can he ensure that we do not see a two-speed approach, where there are good opportunities in some regions and there are well developed elected mayoral systems? We are really happy that the Timms review was co-designed with disabled groups. Is the Secretary of State planning a similar approach with young people to make sure that they are appropriately safeguarded? Finally, will he reflect again on the damaging jobs tax, and cut it for under-25s?

I thank the hon. Member for his questions. He said that economic growth was important. I entirely agree, and I hope he will welcome the latest figures showing that growth is up by 0.7%, once again defying the forecasts that it would not go up by as much. I thought he might also welcome today’s labour market figures showing that unemployment has fallen and that employment is up. He is quite right to say that devolution is crucial in this, and that the voices of young people are important. He will be aware that no employer national insurance is payable for workers under the age of 21 unless they earn more than £50,000 a year, so there is already a tax break in place in the system. Of course, we know that employment costs matter, and we will consider all these things as we move forward.

My right hon. Friend knows that artificial intelligence is already changing jobs and the skills that employers need, with more rapid and profound change likely in future. Four out of five young NEETs have no AI skills or experience whatsoever. What does the Milburn report propose, and what steps will the Government take, to deal with this serious issue and ensure that young people do not face even greater barriers to work in future?

My right hon. Friend is absolutely right to point out the importance of this foundational technological change, which will affect the labour market in ways that cannot currently be predicted and pose a challenge to every Government in the world. There are two important things within that. The first is education and training to ensure that this generation is properly trained to take advantage of this new technology; the second is through our employment policies, looking at people who are having to change careers more quickly and ensuring that the support and help to do that is in place.

Alan Milburn’s analysis is correct. It is good that we are going to treat young people as human beings, not numbers, but does the Secretary of State agree with Alan Milburn that “a deal without consequences is not a deal”? Of course we should be caring, but I ask the Secretary of State whether he is prepared to be tough as well, particularly on the level of benefit, so that work always pays. Will he also accept the analysis that there is no point in destroying real jobs with heavy taxes and then trying to create other jobs through the taxpayer?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his question. He talks about consequences and responsibilities, which I covered in my statement. A new settlement should offer opportunity and hope to young people, and that does come with responsibility. However, I do not see that as a threat. Alan Milburn was clear in his interim report that 84% of young people in this position want to work if they get a chance. I do not believe in the narrative that young people do not want to work—what they lack is a chance to do so. That is where this new settlement can really make a difference.

I thank the Secretary of State for his statement, which I am sure will be welcomed by young people across the United Kingdom. The Scottish Government already have substantial powers to help young people into work, and Scottish Ministers must also take responsibility here. What commitments will my right hon. Friend seek from the Scottish Government to deliver the health and skills support that the reforms depend on and to ensure that councils like South Lanarkshire have the resources to deliver locally? Young people in Scotland should not be left behind.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right that this is a problem throughout the United Kingdom—no part of the United Kingdom can look at itself and say, “We do not have a problem here.” The Prime Minister, the Chancellor and I attended a meeting with the Scottish and Welsh First Ministers in Glasgow a couple of weeks ago where this was a top item on the agenda. It is important that Governments in all parts of the country take this matter seriously. Localised delivery will obviously mean that things can be tailored for local circumstances—that is the intention. This is a problem in Scotland, Wales and England, and we hope that the Scottish and Welsh Governments will take it seriously and ensure that the kind of personalised local support that I am speaking of is available to young people throughout the UK.

The Secretary of State’s statement did not say how he will fund this package. If it is a matter for the spending review, is he therefore unable to say today whether he will fund this package in part by cutting schemes for the over-25s?

The Prime Minister’s first call on all Departments will be reprioritisation to fund support for the next generation, and there is a good reason to do that, because they have their whole lives in front of them. That is the first thing we should do. I have no doubt that it will also be an issue in the spending review, but the first thing we should do is to reprioritise spending to get more support to young people, and I am happy to do that from my Department.

It is a huge breakthrough to have a Government who recognise the plight of young people in our country and will provide them with that extra support. However, receipt of the personal independence payment and universal credit health elements keeps 120,000 young people out of poverty. The question remains: if benefit cuts go ahead, why is it that young people are forced to pay for the new system? Why are we not taxing wealth?

I thank my right hon. Friend for his question, and I appreciate his concern. The truth is that we are putting forward this new settlement because we believe that it is a better deal for young people. Let me give him a figure from another review—this one conducted by Charlie Mayfield, on keeping people in work. He pointed out that a young person who falls out of work and on to long-term benefits can lose up to £1 million in lifetime earnings, with it costing the state a similar sum to support that person. Let us get this support to young people so that they have the experience of earning and making their way. That is what this settlement offers.

The Milburn report gives strategic authorities the job of running the youth opportunity service. We have no strategic authority in Buckinghamshire, and right now there is no plan to join one. What would the Secretary of State say to young people in places like Buckinghamshire about who will be responsible for delivering their service?

The personalised local support that we are speaking of will have to be available throughout the UK, whether or not people have a strategic mayor. That is the way that many of our neighbouring countries and partners do it, and it is the way that we should proceed. There is a good reason to do so, because local travel to work areas and labour markets differ around the country. This is about local authorities as well as mayors getting support to young people in the right place to help them in their local area.

Does my right hon. Friend agree that the concept of responsibility is absolutely vital? Government have a responsibility, as his statement clearly demonstrates, but responsibility also resides with the whole of the state, with businesses, and, yes, with young people too, when the support and opportunity is there. When I met Lincoln Smith, managing director of Custom Heat and Cool in my constituency, he mentioned that his 70-person organisation recommends that it could take on apprentices because it can deal with the HR, the regulation and so on, and then one and two-people businesses or tradespeople could benefit from taking on and using those apprentices. Would my right hon. Friend look at this? Being an active state and enabling young people and businesses will really show that together we can overcome this problem for the long term.

My hon. Friend is right to say that there are responsibilities here. There are responsibilities on us—the Government—to ensure that young people have a chance, and there are responsibilities on young people to take up suitable offers of support. We do need to do more to make things simpler than they are at the moment. I recently met the chief executive of Screwfix, a company that deals with lots of self-employed traders around the country, and he made the plea, quite rightly, to help self-employed plumbers and electricians to take on an apprentice, with us perhaps taking care of the paperwork for them. I think that is a good idea, because many small businesses want to teach people, but they might want someone else to help them with the paperwork.
What did the Secretary of State expect to happen to youth unemployment when the Government he was a part of increased employer national insurance contributions and raised the minimum wage?

The first part the right hon. Lady missed out was that the number of NEETs went up by a quarter of a million between 2021 and 2024, when her Government were in power, and almost nothing was done about it. The second part that she missed out welcoming today’s fall in unemployment and today’s rise in employment.

I welcome the second recommendation in Alan Milburn’s report, which is about treating people as people, not as numbers. Will the Secretary of State say more about how mental health support can be provided to young people at an early stage, so that they can make the most of the opportunities available to them?

One of the differences between the situation today and the situation when I was last in government—I have been around for a year or two, Mr Speaker—is that the proportion of young people in the cohort that we are talking about who are suffering from mental health problems is a great deal higher today than it was when I and my right hon. Friend the Health Secretary were Ministers some years ago. It is a very serious point. The Department of Health and Social Care commissioned a review by Professor Peter Fonagy into this. He was clear that work can be part of the answer and the recovery and is not something that should wait until after recovery is complete.

Today’s report calls for the doubling of apprenticeship completions. However, James Welsh who runs JLMS, an independent apprenticeship and training provider in Eastleigh, tells me that this growth will be difficult to achieve if funding does not reflect the cost of delivery. New foundation standards, such as business administrator level 2, receive just £4,500 for a full year’s training—barely enough to cover exams and delivery costs. Will the Secretary of State review these rates so that foundation apprenticeships remain viable?

We are tilting more of the apprenticeship funding towards young people to try to combat the 40% fall that happened under the Conservatives’ watch. We are fully funding apprenticeships for under-25s now, because we believe it is critical that this funding goes to people who have their whole careers in front of them. We want to work with businesses to make that happen.

No young person should be held back, and that is why I welcome the proposition before us today, but what is really important is that employers do not discriminate against young people, stopping them from securing a job—not least young people who experience severe anxiety or mental health challenges. Can the Secretary of State tell us what steps the Government will take to ensure that employers are accommodating of the needs of young people?

My hon. Friend is right to say that employers are critical. I want to praise the employers who in recent months have signed up to critical agreements with us—the retail sector, the hospitality sector and, at the weekend, the tourism sector. Those three sectors, which hire a lot of people, agreed to take on 250,000 young people in this position over the next few years. We really want to work with employers, because this should be more than a policy; it should be a cause. We can only really crack it if Government and employers work together.

The crisis in youth unemployment is at its heart a crisis in demand. I have lost count of the number of small businesses in my constituency who are asking what the point is of employing a less experienced young person when they will end up paying about the same amount to employ them, thanks to increases in the national minimum wage and the Government hiking national insurance contributions for those over 21. Businesses fear that if it does not work out, thanks to the Employment Rights Act 2025, they will not be able to move them on. That is acknowledged throughout the report, for example in paragraphs 267, 284 and 304. Will the Secretary of State unconditionally accept those recommendations and update the House on what he is going to do?

Arguing for pay cuts for young people is not the way. I saw Alan Milburn being interviewed about this on the television at the weekend, and he explicitly rejected what the right hon. Gentleman has just suggested. I also remind him that the Low Pay Commission looked at this question and did not find a damaging effect on the labour market from recent rises in the minimum wage. It is part of the remit of the Low Pay Commission to consider the effects on employment of the minimum wage rate when it makes its recommendations, and that is a responsibility that it rightly takes very seriously.

In Newport we are already seeing action to support young people, with Connect to Work, a forthcoming youth hub, Beacons Cymru and local businesses creating opportunities, but we need to do more. As this kind of locally driven innovation is exactly what the Milburn report recommends, will the Secretary of State join me in urging the Welsh Government to work as closely as possible with us and local authorities to make this as local, personalised and proactive as possible for young people?

My hon. Friend is right to ask me to work with the Welsh Government. We need to devolve beneath the national level, including in Wales. If we are going to get localised support to young people—we believe that that is right—this has to apply throughout the United Kingdom.

We welcome many of the recommendations in this review, especially as so many of the calls are already embedded in Scotland. However, it does let the Labour party off the hook for its own economic record. We want to see the welfare bill come down, but the idea that the reason for the numbers of young people out of work is that they are lazy or unmotivated is just fantasy. Instead, they have been failed by a Labour Government who have increased job taxes and have overseen a catastrophic decline in vacancies. Is it not true that the Labour Government can only solve this crisis if they accept that the number of young people out of work is a direct consequence of their own stagnating economy?

Perhaps I should not be surprised to hear the SNP reflecting Tory propaganda. If the hon. Lady wants to argue that things are perfect in Scotland, she should speak to the area manager of the Bellshill jobcentre, who last Christmas told me that more than 40% of the youth cohort were on the health journey. Action is needed throughout the United Kingdom, not just in one part of the country. As for young people, she cannot have been listening to my statement, because I said very clearly that they are not snowflakes or shirkers, and that we believe in them and want a better future for them.

I very much welcome this statement and the opportunity it might give to our young people, who have been so badly let down in the past. One particular group that has been let down is young people who are disabled, particularly those with a learning disability. I recently visited TCHC in my constituency, which provides post-16 education for people with a learning disability or autism and ADHD. I asked the young people there, “How many of you would like a job?” Every single one of them put their hand up. However, they told me that they are constantly discriminated against and undermined, and that people belittle their capabilities. Can the Secretary of State assure me that the jobs guarantee will apply to every young person, particularly to those with a learning disability, to finally recognise what these people are capable of and ensure that they are supported to achieve their full potential?

Well, hallelujah to that question! I could not agree with my hon. Friend more. She is right that young people with learning disabilities want to work. I am enormously grateful to Mencap, which recently facilitated a roundtable for me with its national voices council, which is made up of about 10 brilliant young people. When I asked at the end, “How many of you want to work?”, every single hand in the room went up. Young people with learning disabilities have ambitions that, I am afraid, sometimes the state has not recognised and has let fall behind. That should end with this new settlement.
Are there any measures in the Employment Rights Act that have made it more risky to take on more young people that the Secretary of State is now prepared to review?

We believe that young people should have rights, we believe that they should have pay and we believe that they should have opportunities. If the Conservatives’ idea is to take away those things and think that is the answer to the problem, I am afraid that I disagree.

There is some really welcome stuff in the Milburn report and in the Secretary of State’s statement in relation to extra opportunity and extra support, but I want to press the Secretary of State on one thing. I am deeply concerned that a large number of disabled and sick young people are going to be forced into poverty by the removal of PIP and the universal credit health element. Can the Secretary of State commit to ensuring that this does not happen while we pursue the many welcome recommendations in the report?

The report makes it clear that help will be there for those with severe long-lasting disabilities that make work not a realistic possibility and those who will have extra costs. It also makes it clear that we can do better for a number of young people. I remind my hon. Friend of the statistic I quoted in my opening statement: a young person signing on for long-term sickness benefits now, at 20, is more likely to still be on them at 30 than to have had a steady job in the intervening years. Our ambition should revolve not just around someone’s monthly income but around whether or not they have a good future. That is why I say that the exam question that the system has to ask has to change—and it has to change in that direction.

Will the Secretary of State confirm that where someone lives will not determine how much support they can get from the system set out in the review and that rural areas will be funded fairly? Will he also commit to including neurodiversity and special educational needs and disabilities in the Government’s understanding of NEETs? We need a clear, joined-up plan across Government to improve early identification as well as learning, health, work and training support for SEND so that people who learn, think and work differently finally get a fair chance.

The hon. Member is absolutely right that people with neurodiverse conditions should get a fair chance. There is, of course, a great debate about diagnosis, which I do not take part in because I am not medically qualified to do so, but the equation I do want to break is the one between a diagnosis and a life on benefits; we owe those young people more than that. That is why I have advanced the new settlement that I have talked about today.

It is paramount to me that Government Members do not write off yet another generation of young people. To that end, this is precisely the welfare reform for which the country has been crying out for years. Its moral clarity and plan of action is worthy of the best Labour Governments of the past. Will the Secretary of State please commit to fast-tracking the coming White Paper so that the taxpayer gets excellent value for money and every young person has a genuine route into employment?

My hon. Friend is right that action should start now. Action has already started with the youth guarantee, but I believe that we can and should do more. That is why I am already working with my right hon. Friends the Secretaries of State for Health, for Education and for Culture, as well as others, to get this up and running as soon as possible.

The Secretary of State will be aware of the pioneering work of the New Model Institute for Technology and Engineering, our new university in Hereford, and its effect in turbocharging the economy and providing new opportunities for young people, as recognised both by Charlie Mayfield and in the Milburn report. A new think-tank has identified 57 cities and towns around the country that could benefit. Will the Secretary of State offer his support to extra measures to allow these new models to be rolled out in those cities for the public and young people’s benefit?

I am grateful to the right hon. Gentleman for keeping me regularly up to date with the progress that NMITE is making. He is right—it is a really interesting model, doing good things—and if something is doing good things, I am very open to seeing that replicated elsewhere.

I welcome the Government’s significant shift in approach and the Milburn report’s emphasis that there will not be crude cuts to benefits. Instead, reforms to fundamentally change our welfare system will focus on increasing the participation of young disabled people in society to ensure that they can fulfil their potential. I am particularly pleased that Alan Milburn recommends the Government set a target to close the employment gap for young disabled people—that is in paragraph 693 —for which I have argued for nearly two years in this Chamber. It is vital that Milburn’s proposed reforms work in lockstep with the bold action that the Government have set out in other public service areas. Will the Secretary of State tell me to what extent these reforms will close the disability employment gap for young disabled people? Does he have a target for how much he wants to close that gap by? With the creation of the youth opportunity unit, what work will he be doing to ensure a strong connection between reforming mental health, social care, criminal justice and SEND pathways for young disabled people?

I thank my hon. Friend not only for her question but for the many conversations we have had over the past year. She has been strong and consistent in saying that we should do more to close the disability employment gap, and I fully agree with her. We have done some things so far—she will be aware that I lifted travel restrictions on disability bus passes in conjunction with my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Transport, and we have an innovation fund set up for new ideas to close the gap within the Department—and with this report, we put young disabled people front and centre. As I said to my hon. Friend the Member for Thurrock (Jen Craft) a moment or two ago, we will give them the help and support that matches their ambition, which Governments have not always done.

Mr Speaker, “migration…should not become a substitute for building domestic entry routes for young people.” Those are not my words; they are Alan Milburn’s words, on page 71 of his report. As the Secretary of State has not mentioned that elephant in the room, I will ask him: does he share my concern that, according to data from the Centre for Social Justice, for every new, extra young Brit working, there are 27 young foreigners working? Does he agree that we need to reverse the Government’s employer national insurance rise for British workers so that young Brits are at the front of the queue for new jobs?

There is a problem with the right hon. and learned Member’s argument, and the problem is this. Many other countries in Europe without the migration restrictions that she is championing have got far lower rates of inactive young people than we have. I think we should have a properly controlled migration system, but I do not think that is in conflict with championing opportunity, training, education and employment for our own people.

Last week, I brought students from Barr’s Hill school to Parliament to speak directly to the Secretary of State. They made their case for better work experience. The Milburn review highlights that young people who have not done work experience at secondary school are more likely not to be in work, education or employment. Will my right hon. Friend explain how he will work with the Education Secretary to bring schools and employers together to provide better work experience for young people in Coventry and across the country?

My hon. Friend is right to raise work experience. I spoke about mental health problems being perhaps a newer factor in this cohort compared with the situation when I was a Minister in a previous Government. Let me give her another statistic. About 60% of the 1 million young people not in education, employment or training have never had a job. This is not just youth unemployment. It is complete detachment from the labour market—from the sense of pride and purpose people get from getting up and going to work in the morning. We are providing 300,000 more work experience placements through the youth guarantee, which has a critical role to play in positively enhancing young people’s experience and giving them a better chance of getting a job.

Can the Secretary of State go into a little more granular detail about the welcome recommendation that there should be a personalised system for recruiting young people delivered locally? As was mentioned, artificial intelligence is taking an increasing role in so many aspects of life, not least in recruitment processes, and many people complain that they cannot get past the AI barrier, even for an initial interview. How, in practice, is this admirable aim going to be achieved?

The right hon. Member makes a good point. Without going too far into my own anecdotage, when I was a teenager and I wanted a job stacking shelves in supermarkets, I could go into a supermarket and say, “Have you got any jobs?” That is harder for today’s young people, as recruitment is very often online and centralised. On the upside, the right hon. Member talked about personalised help. If he has not done so, I encourage him to go and visit a youth hub in order to see employment advice, health advice, housing advice and debt advice brought together in one place in a trusted venue in the community—often a community centre or a local sports club. That gives an insight into the kind of personalised and local support that we envisage doing much more of.

As chair of the all-party parliamentary group on youth affairs and an MP in one of London’s youngest boroughs, I have heard just how ambitious our young people are and how failed they were by the previous Government. I am proud that this Labour Government are making our young people the political priority they deserve to be. Given the report’s focus on localised support, how will the Government ensure that local councils and organisations are supported to deliver the report’s recommendations?

I believe that local authorities and mayors are up for this; I have discussed it with many of them. They want to do more to help and they have good knowledge of local labour markets. Of course, we will have to work together and we want to do it in a responsible way, but I think we can start now and get this support built up. Critically, in relation to some of the questions that have been asked, it is important that we build up this support before we make other changes to the system. That is a big difference between our approach and that of the Conservative party.
Order. I need questions to be shorter and for the Secretary of State’s answers to be as short as possible.

I welcome today’s report, and particularly the support for young people with mental health issues that often keep them out of the labour market through no fault of their own. For those of us in Scotland, there is a fear that the good intentions and good policies will not filter through the Scottish Government’s inability to implement good policy and overcome the mental health waiting list. Will the Secretary of State give us more detail on how he will work with the Scottish Government?

I am an optimist. I spoke, together with others, in a meeting with the Scottish First Minister a few weeks ago. I think there was acknowledgment that this is a common problem and challenge throughout the UK, so I think we will work together. Crucially, I do not believe that this can all be done at the level of the Scottish Government. We are going to have to get beneath that to get more localised support in local labour markets. That is a challenge for us all and if we believe that personalised support is the right way to go, it should happen all over the country.

I thank the Secretary of State for his statement and welcome the focus on support for young people who across our country are ambitious, creative and full of potential. I welcome the whole-system approach set out by Alan Milburn, from the early years to post-16 opportunities. Those of us on the Education Committee look forward to playing our part in scrutinising the role of the education system in reducing the number of young people who are outside education, employment and training. Apprenticeships are an important part of Alan Milburn’s recommendations, yet just 5% to 6% of young people are able to participate in an apprenticeship. How does the Secretary of State intend to ensure that colleges, training providers and employers work together to increase the number of apprenticeship opportunities available to young people?

My hon. Friend is right about the critical role of education. That is why there has to be a whole-Government response. On apprenticeships, we are already changing the funding to try to get 50,000 more youth apprenticeship starts over the next few years. I will do everything I can to get more apprenticeship opportunities for young people. They are a great start in life for many and the job retention rate for those who complete their apprenticeship course is well north of 90%. They are a great opportunity and I will do everything I can to create more of them.

One million young people need a leg up—one that does not come with the chair being kicked out from under them. The impact of poverty and disability is so clear from the evidence. Will the Secretary of State clearly reject unfair benefit conditions and sanctions and reject cuts for young disabled people, and instead make sure that youth guarantees are statutory so that every Department invests in jobs, youth work, training and further education to make this work?

I have a higher ambition for young people than a life on benefits; I want them to have a job and a future. That is at the heart of the new settlement. I believe that our job and our responsibility is to provide the opportunity, but young people also have a responsibility to engage with that and take it up. That is our approach.

I welcome the report’s hugely ambitious target for 90% of children to have a good level of development before getting to primary school. To achieve that, we will need a further transformation of our childcare system and family support. Will my right hon. Friend commit to working with colleagues across Government to deliver a truly universal, high-quality childcare and family support system in this country?

The problems can often start in the early years, and that is why we have an ambitious target to ensure that children are school-ready. Alan Milburn, in his report, has asked us to go further still and make that more ambitious. It is stretching, but I have worked very closely with the Education Secretary on this and I know that she shares the ambition that, where possible, every child should be ready for school when they start. If they are not, that can have a lasting impact on the child’s fortunes for the rest of their life.

Figures today sadly show that unemployment in my constituency has gone up, including among 18 to 24-year-olds. There is clearly a problem. Bearing in mind that one of my local colleges has warned that funding falls by 17.5% for students who need a third year to complete their studies, does the Secretary of State accept that helping young people finish their qualifications and secure a job is better than allowing them to fall into benefits? Will he work with the Chancellor and fix that funding cliff edge?

I have to remind the right hon. Lady that today’s labour market figures show that unemployment has fallen and employment has increased. I would have hoped that that would be welcomed on both sides of the House. Of course I agree with her that an apprenticeship or a course is better than a life on benefits, and that is at the heart of the new system that we are advancing today.

A life on benefits instead of in work, when a person is capable of working, is no life at all. We do not want that for our young people and our young people do not want it for themselves. One of the central recommendations of the report, which I warmly welcome, is a reduction in national insurance for employers who hire younger workers. It is right and necessary to back the businesses that will help us solve the crisis. Can the Secretary of State confirm when he will do that?

I can confirm that tax is a matter for the Chancellor. There is already a break in the system for employers with regard to employees who are under 21. I am sure the Chancellor listens to all representations about tax, but he has the difficult job of netting off all those representations whenever there is a fiscal event.

The Witham constituency is home to many incredible small and medium-sized enterprises and family-run businesses. They need support to employ and recruit young people, which they are desperate to do, and they do not need higher taxes and more business burdens. The Secretary of State has spoken about personalised, local support. How will family-run businesses and SMEs benefit from that so that they can do the right thing and employ more local young people?

I agree with the right hon. Lady that businesses want to play their part. That is why I welcome so warmly the agreement with the retail, hospitality and tourism sectors, many of whose members will be the kind of small businesses that she is talking about, to take on 250,000 unemployed young people over the next few years. It is an important commitment that affects businesses large and small, and we will continue to work with those sectors and with others, as I said, to take this from being a set of policy proposals from a Government to a cause shared by Government and employers alike.

I signed the reasoned amendment to the last welfare reforms because I thought they were cuts dressed up as reforms, but this is not that; this is a serious attempt to get people back into work. When William Beveridge talked about the five giants that needed to be slain, he spoke about the cross-Government response that was needed. How will we use the youth opportunities unit to make sure that we work across Government to slay the NEET giant in future? We must work with the health service in particular, because the backlogs create such a problem when it comes to getting people into work.

My hon. Friend is right; this is a different approach. He is also right that cross-Government working is needed. Let me be candid with the House: if it is just the Department for Work and Pensions that is involved, it will not happen. It will happen only if the Government work together across the piece. Historically, that has not always been the easiest thing for Departments to do, and that is one reason why we are keen to have more localised delivery, rather than just national Government programmes. That is what the new youth opportunities unit will be charged with overseeing. If we get agreement on the legislation, there is a critical delivery job to be done. That is why the unit has been set up and why it has an important role to play over the next few years.

The hon. Members in this room are, with respect, not the youngest people and not the people who will benefit from today’s announcements, but the young people of this country are watching us today. One of them has written to me and would like to know the answer to this question. He says, “Well done. I am happy to see this, but shouldn’t the money used to fund it be coming from the older, richer generations as well as from young people’s welfare?”

I say the same thing to the hon. Lady as I have said to other Members who have asked a similar question: we have a higher ambition for people than a life on benefits. Let me remind her of the striking figure in Charlie Mayfield’s report: that a young person signing on for long-term benefits could end up losing £1 million of earnings across their lifetime. This is an offer for a better future. That is what young people have been waiting for and what they need, and I want to get on and implement it.

The Secretary of State is right: the system is broken and it absolutely does need to change. There are many excellent things in the Milburn review that are to be welcomed, but the idea that taking away from one group of people is going to get another group of people into work is not one of them. The Milburn review will consign some people to destitution. The author himself has said that it will not be pain free. How can we think that withdrawing benefits from disabled people and putting them into poverty is acceptable?

It is a life on benefits that leaves people in poverty. They are the same people, and what we want is to give them more opportunity so that they can have what everybody wants, which is the ability to earn, to have a job and to have the sense of pride, purpose and dignity that goes along with that. That is our ambition. We are the party of labour. We are doing this not in spite of being Labour but because we are Labour.

Given that the Milburn report states explicitly that the Government’s national insurance increases have “hit particularly hard”, does the Secretary of State agree that we should be allowing the private sector to solve the NEET problem by ending the constant hammering of businesses through increased taxes and new regulations, instead of spending those same taxes on state-subsidised employment that will save only 0.1% of the working-age benefits bill in 10 years’ time?

I agree with the hon. Member that the private sector has a critical role to play. I have said that throughout the statement this afternoon. The Government have their responsibilities, and I intend to fulfil them, along with my fellow Secretaries of State around the Cabinet table, and I really welcome the commitments that we have seen from major employers in recent months. I know that businesses have costs, and that they sometimes make representations to the Government about those costs. I am sure that that will always continue, but we can get beyond that and make this a national cause. The agreements to create 250,000 jobs for young NEETs over the next few years are evidence that that can take place.

The north-east has the highest rate of NEETs in the country, and I really welcome this totally fresh approach from the ministerial team, because only 18 months ago we had a sledgehammer approach, which failed miserably. We need to look at the hidden NEETs. There are 300,000 people among the 900,000 to 1 million NEETs that we cannot find because they are not claiming benefits. Can the Secretary of State say what steps the Government will take to reach out to those hidden people, who probably need more support than most?

My hon. Friend is right to say that the north-east has the highest rate in the country. That shows that what we are tackling is not just an opportunity problem, but an equality problem. On hidden NEETs, the truth is that we know less about them because they are not on the benefit books or the sickness benefit books. Some of them may be able to look after themselves—they are not signing on and can perhaps get work—but Alan Milburn is clear in his report that at least some of the support offer should be available to people outside the benefits system.

I wholeheartedly welcome Milburn’s proposal to reduce employer national insurance for under-25s, because we need to bring businesses on this journey with us. We have fabulous young people across Wales who want to work and will do a wonderful job, so can the Secretary of State confirm that the UK Government expect Wales to play a greater role in delivering these outcomes—we are delighted to do so—and that they will provide the Welsh Government with funding and resources according to our needs, rather than expecting Wales to deliver more with less?

I can certainly confirm that we want to work with the Welsh Government on this, but I hope that the hon. Member will work with me to ask the Welsh Government to do devolution within Wales, so that people in Wales can benefit from a more localised offer, because that is what we want to see throughout the UK.

I also associate myself with the words of thanks from the Secretary of State to Alan Milburn and his team, and I welcome my right hon. Friend’s statement. He referred earlier to the new figures published today showing that 1.6 million children have benefited from the removal of the two-child limit, with 300,000 children lifted out of poverty. Does he agree that this is a significant achievement that we should be proud of, demonstrating the real difference this Government are making to children’s lives, including those in Bradford West, by tackling child poverty and giving young people the best possible foundations to thrive as they grow up and progress into adulthood?

My hon. Friend is right to highlight the figures: child poverty down; unemployment down; employment up. This is a Government who are delivering for the British people, and we will continue to do so through the offer that I have set out today.

I commend Mr Milburn for his report and the Secretary of State for his statement. I have 240 NEETs in my constituency, and one of them is my youngest child. As his mother, I know that work will offer more than a wage. It will provide purpose, dignity and self-worth. He faces the same problem as many of my constituents: they simply cannot get the transport to employment, so may I beg the Secretary of State to include the Secretary of State for Transport in the work that he does, so that young people in my constituency can get themselves to the jobs that he hopes to create for them?

I thank the hon. Member for raising her own experience and I warmly agree with her that work will offer more than a wage. It will offer pride, purpose and dignity, and when we discuss these issues, we should think about what our ambition is for young people. I really thank her for the approach that she has taken today and the way that she has set out her question, and I assure her that I will work with the Secretary of State for Transport on the issue that she has raised. I can tell the House that, in the many conversations I have had with MPs about these issues over the past year, transport has come up a lot. We have to make sure that young people can get to a job.

I thank my right hon. Friend for this statement that gives hope to young people right across the country. Despite what we have heard, 20 years of the Scottish National party has not fixed youth unemployment in Scotland. A mum came to my surgery recently at the end of her tether because her 23-year-old son with autism had lost his local authority internship and had no hope of meaningful work after some years. Does my right hon. Friend agree that Scotland’s local authorities need to play their part to ensure that young people, regardless of where they live, get a good job?

My hon. Friend raises an important question. The last thing we should do is make an equation between a diagnosis of a condition such as that and a life outside work because, with the right support and help, many people with those conditions can work. Not everyone can, but many can. That is what we should be ambitious enough to do, and I hope that throughout the public sector, every local authority in the land and every Government Department will want to play its part.

The Secretary of State has spoken about fully funding apprenticeships for under-25-year-olds, but it is worth pointing out that this fully funded apprenticeship does not include the salary that the employers will have to pay to those young people. Businesses right across my constituency, particularly in the construction sector, are just not able to afford those salaries, given the increases in employment costs under the current Government. I would be interested to hear what he would say to those businessmen and women who want to do the right thing and employ an apprentice but, under Labour’s high job tax and costs of employment, simply cannot afford to do so.

We have had a few exchanges about pay. There are specific pay rates for apprenticeships, and we believe that people should be paid for the work that they do. When it comes to the minimum wage, the Low Pay Commission takes these factors into account when it sets the rate.

I thank the Government for the statement and the many opportunities it will create for young people from all backgrounds to get into training and employment. My right hon. Friend rightly talks about the inequalities that many young people face in getting into training and employment. May I turn his mind to care leavers, four in 10 of whom between the ages of 19 and 21 are not in training and employment? What targeted support will be available to them through the work that has come out of the Milburn review?

My hon. Friend raises the important point that care leavers often find themselves in a difficult position. Alan Milburn’s report specifically addresses this and calls for extra help for care leavers, who, by definition, are not living in the family home. They need extra help, and that is part of the proposals he has published today.

I welcome Alan Milburn’s call to double the number of young people completing apprenticeships. In Walton, Rianna Farbey of Omni Academy has trained hair and beauty apprentices since 2010, but she tells me that apprenticeship starts have fallen because young people cannot find a salon to take them on—for instance, Rock N Rolla hairdresser in Walton says that it has zero margin to do so. The cost of hiring a young person has risen by about £4,000 under this Government. What conversations are being had across Government about easing the strain faced by small businesses and supporting them in creating the entry-level jobs and apprenticeships that our young people are crying out for?

Hairdressing salons are facing particular difficulties. I have had representations from businesses in my constituency that are facing competition from people with rented chairs, businesses operating from back gardens and so on, so I understand the difficulty facing the sector. We are trying to tilt apprenticeship funding more towards young people, including through a hiring incentive of £2,000 for a small business that takes on a young apprentice; if the young person has been unemployed for six months or more, the hiring incentive goes up to £5,000.

I thank the Secretary of State for making a statement on a report that has really listened to young people and directly referenced their experiences over the past decade. He has rightly made the moral case to support young people into work, because of all the benefits that being in work can bring. However, one thing young people raise with me is that gaps in their CVs or a lack of work experience, sometimes because of covid or being unable to find employment, mean that they struggle when applying for jobs. What more can the Government do to work with employers to ensure that young people are not overlooked?

My hon. Friend raises the important role of work experience. We are providing an extra 300,000 work experience placements through the youth guarantee. I am a passionate believer that those can be a critical bridge between unemployment and employment. Once somebody has a few weeks of the routine, the experience and all the rest, they are much more employable candidates. Of course, the work experience has to be of the right quality, but it can play a really important role.

With almost 1 million young people not in education or employment, getting them into work is, of course, a very laudable ambition, but the Government have another ambition, and I want the Minister to explain the cross-over. The Government want an EU mobility scheme, which would bring tens of thousands of EU young people into the United Kingdom—the EU has said that it would like 150,000 visas in that regard. Will those people not be competing for the very entry jobs that we are hoping to provide to our own 1 million unemployed?

The problem with that theory is that countries around Europe that are already members of the EU, with everything that that entails, have far lower rates of youth inactivity than we have. Our rate is the second highest in Europe after Romania, so it cannot just be down to a youth mobility scheme, which involves a far lower level of mobility than EU members have. For example, the Netherlands has a NEET rate that is one third of ours.

I thank my right hon. Friend for the report. Young people in Paisley and Renfrewshire South want to work, but many are stuck on NHS waiting lists or are unable to get the apprenticeships or technical skills that they need to get a job. I wish I shared my right hon. Friend’s optimism that the Scottish Government would invest in these things because it is the morally right thing to do, but in case they need any further persuasion, will he outline how many people he expects to be lifted out of relative poverty as a result of these proposals being implemented in full?

Alan Milburn says that if we get enough people into employment, relative poverty can fall under these proposals. With regard to the Scottish Government, I remind my hon. Friend, and them, that they have received the biggest financial settlement since the inception of devolution, so I would hope to see youth opportunity make some call on it.

As an ex-secondary school teacher, I always take a strong interest in young people, their future and their wellbeing. Too many young people in Bath do not go to school because it does not work for them, and neurodiverse children struggle especially. What steps is the Secretary of State taking to work with the Department for Education so that the national curriculum reflects the focus on good jobs and a good future for all young people?

There is a big chapter on education in the Milburn report, which I encourage the hon. Lady to read. Persistent school absence can have a damaging effect on a young person’s prospects; it is very difficult for them to learn if they are not there. The Government are therefore treating this issue with urgency. Ministers see a million graphs, but one of the most striking to me showed the huge jump in long-term absence from school post covid. We are now dealing in part with the consequences of that.

I thank my right hon. Friend, Alan Milburn and his team for restoring hope for young people across North Warwickshire and Bedworth. Last week, I visited Flannery Plant Hire in my constituency. It delivers skills boot camps across the country, giving young people access to real jobs in heavy goods vehicle driving, plant operations and construction. How will the Government ensure that skills funding reaches such businesses, so that all young people can access support, regardless of their postcode? Young people in this country want a chance to work.

I heartily agree with my hon. Friend that young people want a chance to work, and training in a skill such as HGV driving can be a really good option for young people. We will work with employers in all sectors to try to create opportunities for young people. As I say, we have recently had good results with agreements with some major hiring sectors. The transport sector could be another.

In my constituency, one in six young people find themselves not in education, employment or training. I have been working with Birmingham City University and Birmingham Metropolitan college, which have identified future jobs and are looking at the skills gap so as to train young people who are out of work. Will the Minister support higher education institutions with the resources they need, and will he join me for a visit to see the great work they are achieving?

As a Wolverhampton MP, I regularly find myself in Birmingham. I am sure that the higher education institutions are doing the best job they can. The hon. Gentleman’s question illustrates another point: a number of constituencies have had persistently high unemployment for many years. I hope that he welcomes today’s figures showing that unemployment has fallen and employment has risen. We need to do more to go in the right direction.
I make another plea to Back Benchers: please keep your questions short.

Many young people live in households without access to a private car, let alone their own car, and many live in areas without a decent, or even any, bus service, thanks to the coalition Government’s cuts to local government, which decimated local bus services. Our Transport Committee inquiry “Buses connecting communities” recommended specific action to support under-25s, and our next inquiry, “Getting to work”, will build on that theme by covering all transport. What work is the Secretary of State doing with not only the Transport Secretary but the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government and the Chancellor, all of whom are vital in this area?
I will take your cue, Madam Deputy Speaker. Transport is really important, and the Government have announced a cap on bus fares to try to make it easier for people to get to work.

Every year, the Treasury collects hundreds of millions of pounds more from the apprenticeship levy than gets spent on training. That money is collected for training, and one of Milburn’s recommendations is for all that money to be spent on training—something that the Lib Dems have long been calling for. Will the Minister commit to doing that with the apprenticeship levy?
I have certainly noted that recommendation in the Milburn review. The hon. Gentleman can be assured that I will always fight for as much funding for apprenticeships as possible.

I know personally the despair that comes from being young, unemployed and desperate to work. The north-east has the highest rate in England not only of NEETs but of disability. Unemployment figures released today show that in South Shields the youth claimant count continues to rise because demand outstrips vacancies. Does my right hon. Friend understand how anxious young disabled people are right now, because although the tone has changed, and that is welcome, we do not have all the details? Can he please confirm that the Government’s plans will not leave these young people financially worse off?

I will say two things. First, I point again to the question: where will the jobs come from? We have to co-operate with employers on this, and that is why I have been pleased to announce agreements with retail, hospitality and tourism to hire 250,000 young people over the coming years. Secondly, we are offering a new settlement here, and it will not always be about money. Ambition can be about support and help and helping young people to change their future. That is part of the new settlement that I am arguing for today.

Alan Milburn is clear about the growing chasm in investment for younger and older generations, yet we know from the Budget that school funding is due to fall in the coming years, and yesterday the Education Secretary refused to commit to protecting schools from those cuts. If the right hon. Member accepts Milburn’s recommendation to hold schools accountable for work readiness, added to delivering far more enrichment activities, far-reaching SEND reforms and underfunded teacher pay rises and no extra cash, what is going to give?

I thank the hon. Lady for her question, and for calling for more funding at the same time that she has called for tax cuts. I am afraid that this is a pattern of her party: it supports every spending demand around, but never any of the revenue raisers that mean we can meet at least some of the spending demands. We have to net everything off and do the best job we can, and that is what we will do for young people.

Bristol is a city where there are areas of entrenched deprivation but also massive opportunities, such as in the Bristol Temple Quarter in my constituency and in the Brabazon new town in the constituency of my hon. Friend the Member for Filton and Bradley Stoke (Claire Hazelgrove). What is the balance to be struck between those companies that can be incentivised to take part in this programme and those companies that need to be required to take part if they do not show willingness to step up and provide opportunities for young people?

I do want to work with businesses. I am grateful to the businesses that have taken this seriously and made offers so far, and we will keep discussing it with other sectors. But there is also more that the public sector could do—major Departments, local authorities and so on, as has been mentioned—if this is to be a cause that employers in both the public and the private sectors can help move the dial on.

Will the Secretary of State join me in debunking this myth? In this place, we have demonised and politicised young people. We need to debunk the myth, as was done in the Fonagy review, that there is a widespread overdiagnosis of ADHD, autism, anxiety and depression. That record needs to be corrected. I welcome the announcement to get young people into work and education. Will he confirm that the investment the Government will be making with employers will not be funding vacancies that they already would have employed people for and will not go to their profit bottom lines?

I do not know whether the hon. Member was in the Chamber for my opening statement, but I very explicitly rejected the demonisation of young people and the negative narrative out there about them—that is a narrative I completely reject. Fonagy, in his review, does talk about the diagnosis debate but, as I have said a couple of times, he also said that work can play a critical role in someone’s recovery—not just after they have recovered, but in the recovery, so he is in line with the recommendations of the Milburn report. The equation that I want to break is between a diagnosis and a conclusion that that person then has to spend their life on benefits. Frankly, I have a much higher ambition for young people than that.

Last week I met AJ Taylor, a local business in Brighton with a long record of providing apprenticeships and opportunities to young people. It told me that one of the biggest barriers it faces to doing more to help young people is the absence of any dedicated skills and vocational training centre, and not just in Brighton but across Sussex. The Milburn report recommends an Open University for skills with regional hubs across the country. Does the Secretary of State agree that it would be a big step forward, and does he think a good place to start would be in Brighton Kemptown and Peacehaven?

The report is full of very interesting recommendations. It is over 200 pages long, so we will consider it more fully in the coming weeks. I set out in my statement the main things that I wanted to respond to today, but I have heard the representation my hon. Friend makes for Brighton.

Building on the question of my hon. Friend the Member for Bath (Wera Hobhouse) on school attendance, I have been campaigning to end the current ineffective, punitive approach to tackling school absences. Will the Government commit to replacing it with a supportive approach with alternatives to traditional classroom attendance, to maintain engagement in education when presence in school is not possible?

I am sure the Secretary of State will consider what the hon. Lady has said, but let us be clear that attendance is critical for children. We should all be concerned about the post-covid spike in non-attendance at school. It will have damaging consequences for children, and we should take it seriously.

The Prime Minister rightly recognises that the youth unemployment crisis is not young people’s fault, but the result of decisions made here. I welcome many of Milburn’s recommendations, but if they are funded by cutting disability benefits, the Government will push young people into poverty, undermine their own aims and repeat the very mistakes that they identify as having caused the crisis in the first place. Surely it is not the Government’s view that disabled and sick people between the ages of 16 and 24 are less in need of PIP and the universal credit health element than anyone else.

Let me make clear something that is in the Milburn report. He says that those with severe and lasting disabilities, for whom work is not a realistic possibility, should actually receive more support than they do right now. That is line one of the contract that the welfare state should make with people, and it is something that this Labour Government will always stand by.

Yesterday I met Citizens Advice Thame, which warned me of rising homelessness in Thame, including among young people. What consideration has the Secretary of State given to the removal of UC and PIP in high-cost areas where rents are high and the housing allowance does not cover the full cost of housing?

There are of course issues with rents, but these are disability benefits, and there is something wrong with our system if that is the solution to problems with rent. I tell the hon. Member what would make homelessness a lot worse: the plans of the Opposition party to take £4 billion out of support, because all that would do is end up increasing homelessness, give us less social housing to build and funnel money to people providing the most expensive temporary accommodation.

I welcome the Secretary of State’s statement and report, not least the recognition that this is not about a lack of ambition among young people; it is about the failure of the system to allow them to fulfil it. That is something I heard consistently last week, in Basingstoke Business Week, from both young people and businesses, as it was focused on skills for the future. Will the Secretary of State say more about the support for the nearly 60,000 16 and 17-year-olds who legally already should be in education and training?

That is a good point. I know it is one that the Secretary of State is taking seriously, and the hon. Member is right to say that there should be provision for them in the system we have already. There is more we can do on that before all these extra support mechanisms come into force.

I share the Secretary of State’s ambition that our young people should have better than a life on benefits, but for those reasons I have to reflect my concerns about national insurance. It is one thing to have it for a particular age group, but those NEETs will not stay within that age bracket forever. My constituents who work in hospitality and retail are calling out for a change in the policy on the national insurance increase. Will he confirm to me that he will raise this matter with the Chancellor?

I thank the hon. Lady for her question. It shows that these are problems throughout the UK. On national insurance, I remind her that there is already a tax break in the system for employees under 21 where employers do not pay any national insurance in future. We saw what Alan Milburn has said in his report. The Chancellor hears many representations and, ultimately, tax is a matter for him.

There are over 1,000 people not in education, employment or training in my constituency. From speaking to young people across Erewash, I know that many are frustrated and want help, and it is our job to offer them the hope of good work. Does the Secretary of State agree that the Milburn review represents a major opportunity to transform the support available to young people who are not in education, employment or training?

I think it does represent a major opportunity. As I said, this is a fundamental report. It poses the question: what is the contract between Government and society? That is why it can have a lasting impact, but it will have that impact only if the whole of Government work together to put forward the new settlement that I have advocated today.

We lost my sister Dawn just recently to pancreatic cancer. Her daughter, the amazing Ella, is 22 years old and was born with half a heart, but she and her mum were absolutely desperate that she would live more than half a life. Although Ella is very sad at the loss of her mum, this week she has done herself proud by extending to four days a week her work placement at Matthew’s Enterprise Trust to develop her living and employment skills. Will the Secretary of State congratulate her and say how organisations such as this and the Darwin Nurseries in my constituency can get sustainable long-term funding, to bridge the gap and enable people like Ella to make a valuable contribution to society?

First, let me extend my condolences to the hon. Lady and her family on the loss of Dawn, and let me warmly congratulate Ella. Let me also say that one of the reasons we want more local delivery is so that it can be done flexibly through the great organisations that the hon. Lady has mentioned. Maybe that cannot always be done through big national contracts from my Department, which is why we want to see more local delivery and more flexibility around this.

The social contract with too many young people has broken down, and I welcome the Government’s determination to put that right. In Bedford and Kempston, 8.2% of 18 to 24-year-olds claim unemployment benefit. The young people I meet want opportunities towards a life of purpose and fulfilment—they do not want a life on benefits. Will the Secretary of State ensure that the new youth hub opening in my constituency delivers meaningful pathways into work and timely mental health support, while protecting the welfare safety net for those who are unable to work?

I warmly agree that young people do not want a life on benefits. Alan Milburn found that in his interim report, and he has found that in his final report. Perhaps our ambition has lagged behind theirs. Youth hubs can play a really important role, because they can get the jobcentre out of the jobcentre and get some of the help and services that young people need together in one building, which should be a pretty simple thing, but it has not been happening enough until now.

Work experience should be in the toolbox of every young person to help them move straight from learning to earning, as well as those who are unemployed. However, schools, young people and parents across Mid Dorset and North Poole tell me that they are finding it tougher to find placements, partly due to business and trading reasons but also due to the paperwork. Will the Minister look at an idea suggested by Tammy, who manages the Wimborne business improvement district, to provide liability insurance for employers to remove this barrier for work experience placements?

I have said a few times that I am a great fan of work experience, which I think plays a really important role. I will look at the idea that the hon. Lady mentioned, but sometimes there is a misunderstanding about what is required, some of which applies to children when they do work experience but not to older adults, for whom the paperwork requirements are a bit lighter. Of course, we should make it easy for businesses to do this, because it is such a valuable opportunity for young people.

For far too long our young people have been thrown on the scrapheap. Giving them the skills, confidence and opportunities to succeed and get off welfare is the credible reform that Labour stands for. My constituents in Cannock Chase want to know that this support will be a requirement and that those who refuse to engage for no good reason will face consequences. Could the Secretary of State set out how this will be built into the new system that the report calls for?

Opportunity and responsibility go together. There are responsibilities on the Government to try to help young people and provide opportunities, and equally, there are responsibilities on young people to engage with that and take up reasonable offers.

Alan Milburn talks about the importance of attendance at school and of belonging to school. University of Cumbria research, funded by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, shows that outdoor residentials can improve the self-confidence, teamwork, independence, communication, life skills, leadership, confidence, resilience and aspiration of young people, all of which are vital skills if they are to go on to be successful in finding a job. Will the Secretary of State support my Outdoor Education Bill and persuade his Government that sending young people on outdoor residentials and connecting them with nature can do wonders for their mental health and improve their job prospects?
I have not read the Bill, so I cannot commit to that, but I agree with the hon. Lady: outdoors is good.

I very much welcome Alan Milburn’s report and the Government’s response, as far as it goes. It seems to be a very complex interconnecting set of recommendations. The Secretary of State has not been able to answer on all of them today, but can he confirm that the Government accept all the recommendations? If not, will he undertake to provide a written response, so that we can understand where the Government differ? I accept that we will have to set up a cross-departmental scheme, but there are rumours that some Departments are not fully on board.

The report received a warm welcome in the Cabinet meeting this morning. My hon. Friend is right that it is wide-ranging and contains many, many recommendations. For that reason, we will have to consider it fully and produce a fuller response to it and to the Timms review in the new year. I was able to set out in my statement that we accept the key recommendations of an opportunity and support guarantee, of it being delivered locally, and of a unit being set up in Government to follow through on the delivery.

Around 24,000 young people in Northern Ireland are outside of education, employment or training. If the Secretary of State is to introduce the Milburn proposals, will he confirm that the new tax relief for employers will apply across the whole of the United Kingdom? What funding will Northern Ireland receive for apprenticeships and the additional mental health support that the report recommends? I want young people in Upper Bann to have exactly the same opportunities as those in England.

For the avoidance of doubt, I have not announced any tax changes today. I agree with the hon. Lady that young people in Upper Bann deserve the same opportunities as everyone else. As I said, we recently met the First Ministers in Scotland and Wales. I am very keen to work with the First and Deputy First Minister in Northern Ireland to deliver more opportunities for young people.

My right hon. Friend’s statement today is both visionary for the country and potentially life-changing for so many young people. I want to raise two things. First, I welcome the call for more devolution. Will he ensure that there is accountability as well as responsibility when powers are devolved to mayors and councils? Secondly, small firms often have real difficulties taking on apprentices. Could he look at the Advanced Manufacturing Research Centre in Rotherham and Sheffield, where there are 600 places that are also open to small businesses in the area, so that they can place an apprentice without having all the burdens that often come with an individual scheme?

My hon. Friend mentioned accountability. I think I said in my statement that there have to be agreed standards, accountability and outcome frameworks if we are going to get this right. With regard to the second part of his question, I would be very happy to look at that; I am a huge fan of that institution.

I very much welcome the Milburn report. In my constituency, we are facing a 70% rise in young people with work-limiting health conditions. Although health and skills are devolved, the changes made in Great Britain to universal credit, PIP and national insurance will directly affect our families and small businesses. What discussions has the Secretary of State had with the Northern Ireland Executive to secure fair Barnett consequentials for apprenticeships and mental health support, to ensure that vulnerable young people are not penalised by welfare changes before local jobs are created?

The hon. Gentleman is right to say that support needs to be in place before other changes come in—that is true. He is also right to point out that social security is devolved in Northern Ireland, although the arrangements usually mirror what happens elsewhere in the UK. I am very happy to work with the Northern Ireland Executive and the First and Deputy First Minister to advance an agenda of opportunity for young people in Northern Ireland.
If we look around the Chamber, I can see that a long question will just deny another colleague the opportunity to speak.

The Secretary of State made clear in his response to my hon. Friend the Member for East Kilbride and Strathaven (Joani Reid) that he has been in discussions with the Scottish Government about the implementation of the report. He will share my disappointment that the comments within minutes of the report’s publication were a critique of it. Will he reassure the House, and my young constituents in Motherwell, Wishaw and Carluke, that he will work hand in hand with Scottish MPs, local authorities and colleagues in Holyrood, to ensure that young people in Scotland get every opportunity that young people in England get?

That is the least that young people in Motherwell, Wishaw, Carluke and other parts of Scotland deserve. This is a problem throughout the UK. Our Prime Minister is a great believer in devolution, and he has made an open offer to work with the Scottish Government, the Welsh Government and the Northern Ireland Executive to advance this agenda. I hope that is taken seriously and at face value, and that it results in delivery beneath the level of national Governments. Local, personalised delivery can be valuable in building the right support around a person.

As the Secretary of State will know from his engagement with me since he has been in this role—I thank him for that—my concern has always been about changes that make more young people vulnerable and poorer before mental health and job support is accessed. Young people want to work, as my right hon. Friend saw for himself in February when thousands came through the door at my jobs fair. How will we ensure that the recommendations and policies that the Government are bringing forward will reflect local needs, reach people before any financial support is withdrawn, and be delivered alongside trusted local organisations, including charities, to help young people in education to get mental health support, training and work?

My hon. Friend is a tremendous champion for his area, and specifically the young people in it, and I had an enormously rewarding visit to the fantastic jobs fair that he organised at the beginning of the year. Local delivery can do a lot for the things he mentioned. We must also remember that people with severe enduring conditions that make work an unrealistic possibility will receive continued support—indeed, Alan Milburn recommends that that support increases.
