Given that Capita has missed at least two deadlines, is it not time for the Government to decide to take alternative arrangements for the administration of the pensions?

I share the hon. Member’s anger around his constituents’ experiences; I have constituents in a similar position as well. We have a new rectification plan, which was implemented after the remedial adviser Grant Thorton went in, and we now have five workstreams. Some progress is being made, but we will continue to hold Capita to account. This is Capita’s problem, which it created, and we must make sure that Capita fixes it. As the hon. Member will know, we are looking at arrangements for the future administration of the pension scheme.

I have 36 constituents who have been let down by Capita and many of them landed in trouble with His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs as a result. The Minister says that action is being taken. On my count, the company is responsible for eight scandalous failures, ranging from the Criminal Records Bureau to NHS primary care support, from Army recruitment to the 2023 cyber-attack and now the disgraceful failure that we see here. It is a company whose primary skill only seems to be employing senior ex-civil servants. When will we stop employing Capita, full stop, on the Government account?

As the right hon. Member will know, the contract was signed under the last Government. The Procurement Act 2023 allows the Government to take poor performance into account when looking at giving out future contracts to any suppliers. As I have said previously, the new rectification plan has five new workstreams, including one for complex cases. I think that some of the ones that he referenced are such cases, and I have seen the correspondence that he has sent to me. If he has any further issues, I ask that he write to me and I will look at them again and make sure that those cases are escalated where necessary.

The steps being taken to clear the backlog are clearly not good enough. Otherwise, retired civil servants in Woking would not be contacting me saying that they cannot pay their bills because they are not receiving the civil service pension to which they are entitled. Earlier this year, the Government terminated Capita’s contract for administering the Royal Mail pension scheme. When will they finally do the same for Capita and the civil service pension scheme?

It is important that whatever we do with this pension scheme is in the interest of the members, and that they do not face any further disruption. The hon. Gentleman will be aware of our manifesto commitment to the greatest wave of insourcing in a generation, but my priority at the minute is ensuring that Capita fixes the mess that it has created. Cabinet Office officials are working incredibly closely with Capita. We now have access to its data, and we are monitoring every day to ensure that the most urgent cases are being dealt with. The backlog is big, and I appreciate that many cases, including those of my own constituents, still need to be worked through. If he writes to me with any particularly urgent ones, I will ensure that they are escalated.

The Cabinet Office has set up dedicated MP surgeries through Capita. My caseworkers have described them as a waste of time when it comes to helping civil service pensioners—giving no indication of what has been done, what the next steps are or when they might receive their hard-earned pensions. At an August surgery, we were told that a case had been escalated, but three months later, my 71-year-old constituent, who retired six months ago, has heard nothing. Will this finally be taken out of Capita’s hands and sorted?

I thank the hon. Member for raising that case, and I am sorry to hear about her constituent’s experience. We have held more than 1,000 caseworker surgeries, but it is important to note that caseworkers can only provide updates on the current situation and ensure that the hon. Member’s office has all the up-to-date information. If she writes to me with those particular cases, I would be happy to look into them. However, as I said in my previous answer, it is important that we put members first and do not cause any further disruption to the member experience. Capita has been paid to deliver this contract. It will deliver this service to a good standard, and I will be holding it to account every single day until it reaches the standards that were expected in the beginning.

Last, but hopefully not least, Mr Speaker. Capita’s treatment of many former members of the civil service and their bereaved families has been wholly unacceptable, as we have heard loud and clear in the Chamber today. What I found most frustrating was that one of my constituents, Samantha Vallance, waited five months just to get the initial retirement quote—that is the start of the process—only to find it riddled with errors, sending her back to square one in trying to sort this mess out. How can the Minister reassure my constituent that we will go back to the drawing board with Capita, so that it gets the process right from the beginning, rather than making mistakes from the get-go?

I am sorry to hear of the uncertainty and hardship faced by Samantha and, in fact, so many affected members of the Capita pension scheme. Its performance has been totally unacceptable. We are using all levers at our disposal to ensure that Capita is delivering a good performance at the earliest possible time. As many will know, that includes withholding payments, and we also have a new recovery and rectification plan. The Grant Thornton report was funded by Capita, and we will continue to push Capita to ensure that it is delivered on in full. Capita is very aware of how urgently the Government regard the situation. As I say, every single day, I am holding Capita to account on its progress.

You will be aware, Mr Speaker, that Harlow’s vicinity to the capital means that more than our fair share of civil servants work in the constituency, and many have raised concerns about the issues with Capita. The Minister is right to say that it was the previous Government that signed the contract with Capita, but will she do everything she possibly can to ensure that civil servants in my constituency are getting the pensions they deserve? May I also reiterate the comments made by the hon. Member for Woking (Mr Forster)? There are the same issues with the teacher pension scheme.

I thank my hon. Friend for raising the concerns of his Harlow constituents. I am absolutely working every single day to ensure that the pension scheme is brought up to the good standard that civil servants expect and deserve. In terms of the future of the pension scheme, we are true, as I have said, to our manifesto commitment to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, but I am determined that no member will face further disruption as a result of Capita’s performance. We are working every single day to make sure that that is the case.

When the Minister met me and the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for Hazel Grove (Lisa Smart), the Minister said that she expected the recovery plan to produce visible improvements within the coming weeks. What visible improvements is she able to report to the House today? When can deferred members expect their pensions to be processed?

There have been some small improvements since the hon. Member and I last met—the complex cases are down a small percentage—but I still want to see further progress in November. As I said in my statement to the House and to him and the Liberal Democrat spokesperson as well, I want to monitor progress over the next few weeks and into December, and then I am happy to meet again with the Opposition spokespeople on this matter and to provide them an update.
3. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to prepare for risks to national resilience from El Niño.
18. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to prepare for the potential impact of El Niño on national resilience.

Government investment is protecting communities from severe weather —£2.65 billion on flood defences since 2024, a further £1.4 billion announced in March, £24 billion invested in road maintenance and £2.6 billion to climate-proof rail infrastructure. Alongside investment, our Be Ready campaign is helping households to prepare for potential disruption.

I welcome the appointment of Dame Madeleine Alessandri as the UK’s first special representative for climate security, particularly following her role in the Joint Intelligence Committee’s assessment of ecosystem collapse and biodiversity loss. The assessment warned of catastrophic threats to our food and water supplies, to economic stability and to national security. Can the Minister tell me how this role will ensure that these risks are addressed across Government, and will he commit to finally publishing a response to the report, particularly ahead of this year’s super El Niño?

As I think the hon. Gentleman will know and recognise, the Government did publish the nature security assessment—the first globally of its kind—that sets out the importance of ecosystems to the UK’s resilience, national security and prosperity. Like him, I welcome the appointment of Dame Madeleine Alessandri. She will be working closely across Government to support the work we are doing on climate adaptation, including £1.4 billion for more than 600 flood schemes this year, £65 million to support farmers through prolonged dry weather, £710 million to climate-proof schools and £104 billion to improve water security. This Government are acting not only to prepare people for the threats that climate change poses but, with our commitment to net zero, to address the threat of climate change as well.

With this year’s super El Niño pushing up temperatures at a time when we have already breached 1.5°C in global warming, we can expect extreme weather that could threaten supply chains and cause disruption for millions of people across Britain. What are the Government doing to ensure the nation is resilient against that, both through Government spending and, possibly more importantly, by warning the people of the United Kingdom about the possible effects this winter?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for making those points. Let me say to him that we are taking action to make the UK the most resilient country that it can be, including in the face of our changing climate. That includes investing in nine new reservoirs across the country, more than 600 flood defence projects across England and £2.6 billion to climate-proof rail infrastructure and keep the UK moving. All of this makes us more resilient and contributes to our vital role as a dependable ally.
4. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to improve resilience to cyber-attacks.
6. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to help prevent cyber-attacks affecting food supply chains.

The Government are taking vital steps to strengthen the UK’s cyber-security. At the Budget, £154 million was provided for cyber-defences, including our new national cyber-shield. We have introduced the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill to raise resilience and protect essential services, and shortly we will publish the national cyber action plan with clear actions for Government and businesses upgrading the UK’s responses to cyber-threats.

This country is already under regular cyber-attack by Russia, costing businesses billions and billions of pounds, with a knock-on effect to the British economy and British taxpayers. The response has to be to co-ordinate an effort across the country and across Government with businesses and civil society. In July, the Government said that the civil resilience forum would be meeting this autumn. Has that forum met? If not, when it will take place?

My hon. Friend is right to raise the nature of the threat in that way. We are updating local resilience leaders regularly, and I will convene them shortly. National resilience cannot be built in isolation; it requires shared leadership and action across every sector. That is why our Be Ready campaign has been built with more than 500 partners from charities, businesses, emergency services, local resilience forums and local councils, and it is why we will continue to work closely with all of them to deliver the campaign. I am determined to make us the most resilient country we can be.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his answer. A “deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine consumers’ confidence in it” is how the EU Food and Agriculture Commissioner described the recent fridge and freezer cyber-attacks in Europe. This attack caused millions of euros-worth of food to need to be thrown away. I sit on the Public Accounts Committee, and last month we looked at the resilience of the food supply chain to disruption here in the UK. Does my right hon. Friend agree with me and the National Audit Office that, while UK food supply chains are generally resilient, the risks affecting them are both complex and more likely?

I do agree with my hon. Friend. I recently visited Paris, where we discussed our strong and enduring co-operation on matters relating to cyber-security threats. He is right: food security is crucial to our national security. We work very closely with retailers to protect our supply chain, and we will shortly publish the national cyber action plan, with clear actions that businesses can take to make supply chains even more secure.

Earlier this month, Major General Mike Fayers, the commander of the Defence Cyber and Electromagnetic Force, expressed public concerns that malware hidden in the military network could go bang in the event of a future conflict. We know that the Ministry of Defence has the largest IT infrastructure of any Department and obviously has that capability too. Given that the commander thinks there might be malware in the system, what confidence do Ministers have that the military network and, indeed, wider Government infrastructure are free of any malware from our adversaries?

As the hon. and gallant Gentleman will know, we work very closely across Government, including with partners in the Ministry of Defence and other Departments, to ensure that we are as resilient as we can be, given the nature of the threats, including those he describes. This is a matter that I personally take very seriously. That is why we are progressing work on the legislative front through the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, and we will publish the national cyber action plan very soon.

If the Security Minister is speaking to his colleagues in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, could he perhaps suggest to them that cyber-security be part of the long overdue food strategy, which we are still waiting to get from that Department?
I always listen very carefully to what the right hon. Gentleman says, and I have done so on this occasion. Let me take that away, reflect on it further and discuss it with colleagues in DEFRA.
7. What assessment she has made with Cabinet colleagues of the adequacy of the resilience of the UK’s digital infrastructure.

The Government are taking decisive steps to assess and improve the resilience of the UK’s digital infrastructure. That includes commitments on cyber in the Budget and commitments on AI security, as well as a direction on telecoms with the 2026 statement of strategic priorities for Ofcom. We will continue to work closely across Government and with regulators and industry to identify risks, reduce them, secure networks and maintain digital services.

The public switched telephone network will finally be turned off in January, which means everybody will be dependent on their broadband to make a phone call. Twice in the last five years, many of my constituents have been without power for several days following big storms. If the mobile masts go down without power as well, we cannot even make a mobile phone call, and yet the mobile masts are not considered to be a priority when the power is being switched back on. Will the Minister look at that? Many of my constituents and people in other rural areas cannot make a phone call in the event of a power outage, and it is a really serious problem.

I thank the hon. Member for raising those concerns, which I take very seriously. The fixed telecoms modernisation charter is intended to protect vulnerable individuals during transitions of fixed telecoms infrastructure. I will take her point away and ensure she gets a full response.

The Government’s AI opportunities action plan is driving increased AI and cloud usage across public services for the right reasons. But following the Ministry of Defence’s Afghanistan data breach, my Select Committee highlighted low levels of data hygiene across Government, and our “Rewiring the State” report identified legacy systems as a barrier to successful digital transformation. Has the Minister made an assessment of the resilience of public sector computing infrastructure? Will he confirm whether his Department, the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport or no Department is responsible for setting standards for digital resilience in each Government Department?

I always take my hon. Friend’s concerns on this subject very seriously. She will know that the Government have been focused on strengthening their digital resilience through both a new Government cyber unit and a series of commitments on frontier AI hardening, as well as £210 million for the Government cyber action plan, announced at the Budget. The Security Minister, who is sitting next to me, is the lead Minister for cyber across Government, but I know that DCMS, as the lead cyber Department for Government and public services, will also take the concerns seriously.

To ensure resilience, we must be able to trust the services that we rely on. In light of the US decision to ban the use of DeepSeek in Government systems due to security concerns, what is the Government’s assessment of the risks of using open-weight Chinese AI in the UK?

Open-weight models are used in different areas, both in this country and in the United States. This is a new area of research, and we need to understand the possibility of de-biasing those models and the risks of prompt injections. We continue to lead the world in pursuing that research and securing our public services.
8. What recent progress the cost of living taskforce has made.

Earning back public trust begins with understanding the pressures facing families at the kitchen table. In the last two months, the cost of living taskforce has delivered interventions ranging from the £100 household energy payment for up to 20 million households to the extension of 0% VAT on electricity bills and energy debt relief—and that is just the start.

I welcome the work of the taskforce to date. For many families in constituencies like Uxbridge and South Ruislip, a car is not a luxury but a necessity to get to work, school and vital appointments. In a cost of living crisis, insurers are taking advantage of that by charging exorbitant annual percentage rates on monthly insurance policies—some as high as 53%, more than a credit card interest rate—costing consumers hundreds of pounds extra a year compared with annual insurance premiums. Will the First Secretary of State bring together colleagues across Government to address this poverty premium and protect consumers from unfair monthly charges?

I congratulate my hon. Friend on the work he is doing to highlight this important issue, particularly the issue of the poverty premium, which is so clear in motor insurance. Car insurance is an essential, not a luxury; it is vital to accessing economic opportunities. That is why, as Transport Secretary, I established the motor insurance taskforce with the Treasury. I welcome continued action to bring down monthly APRs, but there is more to be done, so I have asked the cost of living taskforce to work across Government to explore possible interventions to tackle disproportionately high costs.

Families across Wokingham are struggling with rising household costs, while many also face significant care responsibilities. What progress has the taskforce made in easing pressures on unpaid carers and delivering the social care reform needed to reduce financial hardship?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for raising this important issue. Clearly, it is a serious priority for the Prime Minister. He set out in his speech to the Labour party conference in September plans to deliver the national care service; at the heart of that will be the care workforce and the unpaid carers who, day in, day out, deliver an incredible service to their loved ones and our wider society.

Again, this week, I received an email from a constituent—this time in Offerton—who told me they are struggling to make ends meet at the sharp end of the cost of living crisis. We all know that the best way to tackle that is to grow the economy. We also know that the biggest lever the Government could pull is to go beyond Labour’s self-imposed red lines and really strengthen our relationship with the EU. The Conservatives’ Brexit deal, cheered on by their Reform chums, left a £90 billion hole in the public finances—money that could be used to cut taxes or invest in our communities. Families pay for that at the till. Has the cost of living taskforce assessed what a new growth and defence partnership, including joining the single market and negotiating a new UK-EU customs union, would do to prices in the UK—and if not, will the First Secretary ask it to do so?

That is exactly why my right hon. Friend the Minister responsible for resetting our relationship with the EU, the Prime Minister and most of the Cabinet will be in Brussels this evening and tomorrow to address the issues that the hon. Lady has raised. The terrible Brexit deal that the Conservative Government left us with has increased the cost of living, red tape and friction, and that is exactly why the Prime Minister has prioritised improving it.
9. What steps she is taking with Cabinet colleagues to prepare for the commencement of procurement policy note 024.

This Government are committed to delivering good jobs and the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation. The First Secretary of State recently established an insourcing and market-shaping unit. The unit will identify insourcing opportunities, scrutinise departmental insourcing strategies and be a centre of expertise. We recently announced that 2,700 universal credit case workers will be brought into the Department for Work and Pensions. This Government will turn the tide and drive up insourcing.

My constituents want taxpayer money spent on the state delivering where possible, not spent needlessly hiving off capacity to private contractors, so I welcome the public interest test and insourcing strategy coming into force from 1 April next year. However, 120 jobs in Scotland at the Student Loans Company are threatened following the workforce being notified last month that their roles are being outsourced to Capgemini by 1 March next year. Where outsourcing decisions appear to have been accelerated prior to PPN 024 coming into force, will my hon. Friend require in-scope bodies, like the Student Loans Company, to evidence that their decisions are compliant with the public interest test?

I thank my hon. Friend for his engagement on this subject. The insourcing unit is already working across the public sector to support contracting authorities and prepare for the introduction of our public interest test. I declare an interest: I was proud as a trade unionist to have fought for the public interest test, and I am proud as a Minister in this Government to deliver the public interest test. In addition, Departments will set out and publish their five-year insourcing strategies, but that is the start, not the end of our ambition. Delivering that insourcing will benefit those in his Falkirk constituency, my Gateshead Central and Whickham constituency and the constituencies of hon. Members throughout the House. On his specific question, all procurements are subject to a robust set of approvals and we have no evidence that Departments are accelerating any of their decision-making processes.

When considering insourcing, Northern Ireland must be very much part of the process. I hope the Minister will confirm that shortly, but will he ensure that Northern Ireland departments, wherever they may be, can be a part of the policy as we move forward, so that we, as part of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, can benefit from the policy?

On devolved matters, we would encourage the Northern Ireland Assembly to take the same insourcing moves we seek to take as a Government. Where matters are not devolved, of course Northern Ireland will be fully involved in the process.
13. What steps she is taking to improve national resilience.
16. What steps her Department is taking to improve preparedness for civil emergencies.

The Government are taking decisive steps to strengthen our national resilience. We have launched the home defence programme and overhauled pandemic preparedness plans with a billion pounds in funding. Recently, we launched our Be Ready campaign to help households prepare for everyday emergencies such as flooding, and we are actively co-ordinating resilience planning across Government. I am determined to make our country the most resilient it can be.

Food security is national security, so food production is a pillar of that national resilience, and it relies on the very best farmland. As Government pursue energy security through nationally significant infrastructure projects, including huge-scale solar farms, what steps is the Minister taking to ensure that those are limited to and directed towards lower-grade land, so that we strengthen one area of our national security without weakening another?

I recognise the hon. Lady’s long-standing interest in these matters. She is right to stress the importance of the food supply chain. We work across Government to ensure that the food supply chain is resilient, supported by a diverse and highly interconnected network of businesses. We work with the National Cyber Security Centre, the Food Standards Agency and industry to support preparedness and strengthen resilience across the sector. I understand why she raised her other point in this forum, but she will understand that it sits within the responsibilities of other Ministers. I will reflect on what she said and come back to her with a more detailed response.

I welcome the Government’s recent announcement of their Be Ready campaign, which encourages households to keep enough supplies for three days in the event of emergency, but not everyone has the means to stock up. Can the Minister advise what the Cabinet Office is doing to support the most vulnerable in our communities to work with food banks, charities and other local organisations that would be on the frontline of helping constituents, including those in West Dunbartonshire, during a civil emergency?

My hon. Friend raises an important point. I can assure him that cost of living pressures were absolutely at the forefront of our minds as we designed the campaign, and we have worked very closely with charities such as the Trussell Trust across the country to develop the campaign. We recognise that not everyone can take every step, but if households that can take action do so, it frees up emergency services to help those most in need in a crisis. Many of the steps are free, such as signing up for the priority services register, and we will continue to work with charities such as those in my hon. Friend’s constituency as we deliver the campaign.
14. What assessment she has made of the potential merits of insourcing administration of the civil service pension scheme.

The scheme would be a prime candidate for insourcing in the future, and officials are actively evaluating long-term options. I plan to return to the House with a further update once this work is concluded and when it is appropriate, but I am clear that in the here and now, Capita will deliver.

My constituent Inayat Ullah Pathan has served the Ministry of Defence loyally for years. He gave his six months’ notice, but sadly he had to retire last month without his pension. We have heard repeatedly that Capita has missed deadline after deadline. The Cabinet Office has already said that it is considering bringing administration in-house, and the Public and Commercial Services Union has put forward a practical plan to start now. Will the Minister confirm whether she will consider the plan and whether she agrees that Capita’s time is up?

Terminating the contract immediately could trigger an operational vacuum and jeopardise monthly pension payments for hundreds of thousands of our public servants, and I am not willing to do that. We must put the members first at every single stage. We are evaluating the long-term options, but an alternative delivery structure cannot just be readied overnight, which I am sure the hon. Gentleman will appreciate. Our immediate priority remains forcing operational recovery and holding Capita strictly to account. Simultaneously, my officials are looking at the long-term options for the pension scheme.
15. What steps her Department is taking to improve national security.

National security is our first duty. We are spending £298 billion on defence over the next four years, and we are providing record funding for our intelligence agencies. We have strengthened state threats legislation and launched the home defence programme, and we are establishing the national centre for information defence.

My constituency of Stevenage has a long and proud history of manufacturing many key tools for our national security, including military communication satellites, which defend and support our excellent armed forces. In light of the risks to secure satellite communications being experienced by Ukraine in its fight for survival, can my right hon. Friend confirm that the Government place a high value on maintaining UK sovereignty in our own satellite communications?

My hon. Friend is right about Stevenage. Space is a domain of growing competition that is critical for our national security. The defence investment plan recognises that fact with new investments to support sovereignty, resilience and control, including £2.3 billion invested in satellite communications by 2029-30. We are determined to deliver the space capabilities needed to meet the challenges that we face.
19. What steps her Department is taking to support devolution.

The Government’s ambition is to deliver growth in every postcode by moving power, funding and decision making closer to people and places. The Cabinet statement on rewiring the state sets out our plans to develop a new approach to devolution that will empower local leaders, strengthen strategic authorities, improve public services and enable stronger local economies across the UK. We are working closely with mayors and local leaders to deliver that.

Communities such as mine in Ayr, Carrick and Cumnock understand local needs and priorities better than anyone. Through decisions made by this Labour Government at the Budget, the Scottish Government received an additional £600 million for Scottish public services. Does the Minister agree that the Scottish Government should show more faith in public service delivery by devolving powers and more resources from Holyrood to local authorities?

The Prime Minister was clear in his Motherwell speech and at the National Economic Council that devolution to communities and regions is at the centre of his vision for the whole of the UK. That does not mean swapping power from one Parliament to another; as my hon. Friend says, it means going deeper and putting power down into those regions. The Government will always seek to work collaboratively with the Scottish Government, respecting their devolved competence throughout, to progress this work in Scotland and put people at the centre of the places where they live. We are taking forward the work that has come out of the NEC through our offer of joint work to drive regional empowerment through policy sprints, which is being convened by No. 10 North.

The last time we met, the Government were in a bit of a state of confusion about what regional mayors would and would not be able to do with the local income tax and business rates that the Chancellor has allowed them to retain. In September, the Government said that mayors would not be able to offer rebates to taxpayers in their areas, but since then, Lord Houchen of Tees Valley has said that the Treasury has told him he will be able to return those taxes to taxpayers. Is that now the case?

The statement the Prime Minister made, and what was set out at the beginning, was that mayors would not be able to offer a rebate. That remains the position. However, we are working with local mayors and strategic authorities across the country to look at how we can devolve further power—the position of this Government is devolution by default. We will set out the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan very shortly. In that plan, people will be able to see the full suite of powers across Government that will be devolved to regions and local leaders, which is where we believe those powers and resources will be best delivered.

That is a bit concerning, because the Treasury appears to be working on something that the Cabinet Office says is impossible. I hope that the hon. Lady will look at this issue, because as I say, Lord Houchen is working with the Treasury on a scheme that would enable him to return such taxes to the taxpayers in his area. Can the Government confirm that mayors will be able to offer those grants or rebates—whatever the Government want to call them—to individual taxpayers in their areas?

Mayors already have the powers to give grants if they want to. As I said, we continue to work with strategic authorities and mayors on the fiscal devolution road map and the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan, which will be set out in the coming months. I suggest that Mayor Ben Houchen works on delivering for his constituents, which he is not doing very well at the minute.
T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.

At tomorrow’s UK-EU summit, the Prime Minister and I, alongside Cabinet colleagues, will meet our EU counterparts to secure a better deal for Britain. The Brexit deal we inherited has resulted in higher costs for British businesses and higher prices in our shops. We are working to deliver a deal that will add billions of pounds to our economy, boost British businesses, cut needless red tape and create opportunities for young people of all backgrounds. I pay particular tribute to my right hon. Friend the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations for his tireless efforts in our national interest.

Can I get a firm personal commitment from the First Secretary of State that she stands behind the strategic defence review’s commitment to increase the nuclear stockpile to 260 warheads, and that she will not let the strategic spending review dilute either that commitment or the commitment to the Astraea programme? Given that before her time in government, she had supported cuts to the Trident programme, a statement today in this House would be a significant statement of intent from this Government.

It was an incredible privilege to bring HMS Vengeance home on Sunday. I attended the submarine with the Defence Secretary, and it was an extraordinary honour to welcome the crew home after their unfortunate record-breaking tour at sea—they have made an incredible sacrifice for the defence of our nation, and indeed the whole of NATO. As the Defence Secretary and the Chancellor have repeatedly set out, we are committed to reaching 3% of GDP on defence spending by 2030 and to all of our NATO commitments.

T2. Last month, I was proud to join my constituent Ness Abbess as she delivered to No. 10 a letter from bereaved families on the issue of preventable drownings. I welcome the Prime Minister’s response to that letter and his support for the Daily Mirror ’s drowning prevention campaign, but the issue is that water safety sits between four different Government Departments. Will the First Secretary of State use her powers to bring those Departments together? Will she consider appointing a single Minister to drive this work forward, and will she meet me and bereaved families so that we can discuss the vital next steps to save lives?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising that important point in the way that he has. Like the Prime Minister, I warmly welcome the Save Lives at Sea campaign. I assure him that the Government take water safety very seriously, as was demonstrated by the recent roundtable chaired by the Minister with responsibility for water and flooding, my hon. Friend the Member for Kingston upon Hull West and Haltemprice (Emma Hardy). I have listened carefully to his point about deconflicting across Government Departments. I will reflect on it and come back to him with more detail.

The Government’s sanitary and phytosanitary deal with the European Union will require UK farmers to take on thousands upon thousands of EU regulations, even if they do not trade with the EU. Have the Government estimated the dead cost of dynamic alignment for those farmers?

I look forward to discussing the fine detail once we have an agreement over the line in the way that I hope we will tomorrow. On SPS, it is important to recognise that the previous Conservative Government, and indeed our Government, have not diverged a great deal from European food safety standards. Where we have, we have obviously made careful assessments of the impact on farmers.

The right hon. Gentleman will be aware that since we left the EU, it has gone through one of its most profound periods of regulation. There are now tens of thousands of regulations that the UK has never signed up to—that will be an additional burden. If he has done that work on the dead cost, will he publish it so that the House can consider it?

The hon. Gentleman is right to say both that we have assessed where we have chosen to diverge, and of course that there are areas where the EU has changed regulation without our being part of that process of change. I think his question was about farmers. We are, of course, in regular dialogue with farmers about the impact. It is quite difficult to quantify the impact on either precision breeding or the approach to bovine tuberculosis, for example, without the detail. Once the detail is agreed at the summit, we are very happy to come back to this place and talk about the full impacts.

T3. As work is undertaken across Government to improve national resilience and the public’s preparedness for emergencies, what consideration have Ministers given to broadcasting an expert-led national emergency briefing on the climate and nature crisis?

The Government are taking urgent action to tackle the climate crisis and to raise awareness among the public. The Be Ready public awareness campaign provides simple and effective advice on practical steps that individuals, households and communities can take to improve their resilience to a range of risks, including those presented by climate change. Not only are the Government acting to prepare people for the threats that climate change poses, but, through our commitment to net zero, we are acting to address climate change.

Back in September, the Government promised a cross-Government task and finish group on mega-donors that would work at pace. However, 11 weeks and several written questions later, we have seen no terms of reference and no start date. No one should be able to buy the keys to No. 10, so will the First Secretary of State tell us how they are getting on with the task and when they expect to finish?

The Representation of the People Bill is still making its way through the other place. We will be considering work through that piece of legislation. I have asked the group to meet the hon. Lady to brief her on their work, as I did for the shadow Minister. I will ensure that that takes place.

T4. The Government recently delivered almost £16 billion in efficiency savings across Whitehall. However, up to £45 billion more can be found in productivity gains and efficiency savings, so will the Minister ensure that ambitious artificial intelligence and technology adoption plans are at the very heart of next year’s spending review?

Both the 10-year plan and the spending review offer us the chance to put into practice my hon. Friend’s belief that technology should not be the preserve of a few but, through our public services, the driver of opportunity and dignity for the many.

The Minister was asked earlier about digital resilience. Rural areas across North Yorkshire are stressed and concerned, because communities coming off analogue that do not have a mobile signal are stuffed. The commitments from BT and others, to which the Minister referred, are not worth the paper they are written on. The move to digital is happening in January. I urge the Minister to take a look at it.

As the House can see, given the nature of those concerns, which have been raised twice now, there is enthusiasm on the Front Bench to take them deeply seriously. We will do exactly that by responding swifty.

T5. Following the devastating wildfires in High Peak and across the UK this summer and the National Resilience Committee’s warning this week that Britain is “seriously underprepared” for major emergencies, will the Minister accept the recommendation to put local resilience forums on a statutory footing, with clear responsibilities and accountability, so that partnerships such as the Derbyshire LRF have the authority they need to protect our communities?

Let me place on record my profound thanks for the important work that local resilience forums do, not least the vital work they did over the summer and the supporting role they are playing in our Be Ready campaign, including in my hon. Friend’s constituency. The Government are currently leading a post-implementation review of the Civil Contingencies Act 2004, which is considering the merits of putting local resilience forums on a statutory footing. A decision will be taken through the review, and we will present that to Parliament early next year.

People do not have to be white to be English, but the census currently disagrees when it asks for their ethnicity, as do the 10,000 different accounts that have sent me racist messages and death threats since I raised this matter in the Chamber last week. [Hon. Members: “Shame!”] Ahead of my meeting with the Prime Minister to discuss it, will the Cabinet Office reaffirm that Englishness cannot be boiled down to ethnicity and that the census must reflect this?

It was a pleasure to sit on the Front Bench for the introduction of the hon. Member’s recent ten-minute rule Bill. I must say that he gave an absolutely tremendous speech and set out his case incredibly well. To be frank, it was one of the better speeches I have heard in this Chamber. I know he looks forward to meeting the Prime Minister, and I will not prejudge that, but I think and hope that we all, from all parts of the House, agree that Englishness is not a matter of race or ethnicity. Englishness is about the shared culture we share together in this country.

T6. Further to the Government’s commitment to devolution by default, a month ago Cornish MPs met officials at No. 10 North to discuss the powers we need devolved to Cornwall, including economic development funding, housing, transport, post-14 skills and culture. Since then, Cornwall has been formally designated a single foundation strategic authority. Will the Minister meet Cornish MPs to discuss the progress made since that meeting towards devolution in each of those five specific areas?

I was delighted to see Cornish MPs and leaders attend No. 10 North recently to discuss the deal that they want in Cornwall. We are considering all the points they made in that meeting as part of the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan more widely. That work is still ongoing, but we will keep Cornish Members and, indeed, leaders updated.

Following my exchange with the Prime Minister in this place, No. 10 North wrote to offer a meeting to discuss regulating the Isle of Wight ferries. The offer was for a meeting within weeks, but that was two months ago, and we still have no date in the diary. Will the Minister ensure that I get that meeting with No. 10 North without any further delay?
I will ensure that is looked at and the meeting is arranged, and we look forward to welcoming the hon. Member to No. 10 North.

T7. I was delighted that, at the Budget, the Government set out their intention to move ahead with a devolution deal for the Thames valley. I am very determined to get this over the line, so that residents in Bracknell Forest and the wider region can enjoy the benefits that devolution will bring. Will my hon. Friend commit to continuing to work with local MPs and leaders to unlock devolution in the Thames valley?

I agree with my hon. Friend that the opportunities for the Thames valley will be fantastic. Devolution will mean greater powers and funding to maximise economic opportunities across the whole area, including, but not limited to, the measures announced in the fiscal devolution road map as well as those in the forthcoming delivery plan. We are considering all the responses and thoughts given to us so far. The delivery plan will be coming soon, and I look forward to sharing it with Members in this House, people across the country and, most importantly for my hon. Friend, those in the Thames valley.
The removal of peerages Bill was in the King’s Speech. When will it be introduced?
We will provide a further update to the House on our plans in due course.

T8. The Government’s fiscal devolution road map recognises that London has a unique governance arrangement. It is the oldest mayoral model and is out of step with newer combined authority models. If new powers are to work for all of London, which is such a large city, we need decision making to tie directly to local borough delivery. As part of the rewiring the state plans, will the Minister consider reviewing London’s historic devolution powers and ensuring that strategic decision making is fully linked to local delivery?

The delivery plan will not include changes to the London governance structure. I am happy to meet my hon. Friend and other London MPs to discuss their concerns and what change they would perhaps like to see in London, but it will not be included in the delivery plan itself.

Leicester is one of the most vulnerable cities in Britain and is projected to rise fast up the ranking. This summer saw record-breaking heat, and thousands of people up and down the country died. London has its own heat resilience strategy, but Leicester does not. Will the Minister publish a national heat resilience strategy and put adequate funding behind it?
I visited Leicestershire over the summer to engage with local communities and the local resilience forum. Let me look more closely at what the hon. Gentleman has said and I will write to him.

T9. The Minister will be aware that by 2028, London will be the only mayoral authority in the country that is not a combined authority. That means that, unlike Greater Manchester for example, there is no requirement for the Mayor of London to work with the councils that actually deliver services. Will the Minister tell us how she will ensure London is not left behind in the Government’s very welcome drive to devolve power from Whitehall?

As my hon. Friend will know, London has one of the longest standing devolution settlements. The mayor is accountable to voters in every borough. He is scrutinised by the London Assembly and works in partnership with boroughs where responsibilities might overlap. As I said in a previous answer, I am happy to meet London MPs to discuss their thoughts about this issue further. Through “Rewiring the State”, we will work with London partners so that the settlement keeps pace with the changes we are making and, of course, London’s role as a global city, building on the package agreed at the Budget.

The Government have asked the public to prepare for a black sky event. Many people with very severe ME— myalgic encephalomyelitis—are bedbound and rely on electric pumps for nutrition. If we experience a prolonged national or even regional power outage, they would be at very grave risk. What specific provision is in place for them? Will the Minister ensure that national resilience planning fully accounts for people who are dependent on powered medical equipment?

I think the hon. Lady is referring to the recent Be Ready campaign that we launched. This is about raising awareness of simple steps that households can take in their everyday lives to prepare for everyday emergencies. It is part of a process by which we ensure that our country is as resilient as possible, because we cannot have national resilience and national security without resilience at the most localised levels. These are issues that the Government take incredibly seriously. That is why we invested £1 billion in pandemic preparedness and launched the home defence programme. We are doing work in Government now that we have not been doing for almost 25 years. We are determined to ensure that our country is as resilient as it can be, given the nature of the world we are living in.

I support the calls for a reversal of the Tory and coalition-era outsourcing of the civil service pension scheme. The Minister committed to me last month that she would look at publishing a smaller version of the remedial adviser’s report, which I believe would help Members to scrutinise progress of the new rectification plan on behalf of our many constituents affected by Capita’s significant failures. What progress has my hon. Friend made in determining whether that can be published?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question and for the tireless championing and campaigning he does for his constituents on the issue of the Capita civil service pension scheme. On the remedial adviser’s report, my officials are working with the Clerks of the Public Accounts Committee and the Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee on sharing a copy with them. There are a number of market-sensitive issues that need to be considered, but that work is ongoing and hopefully will be resolved soon.

Northern Ireland has an international reputation as a region of expertise and knowledge in tech development. World-leading tech companies such as Fujitsu, WhiteHat Security and Microsoft have chosen to establish their operations in Northern Ireland in recognition of the talent and innovation we hold. What steps will the Minister take to use Northern Ireland-based firms to support the strengthening of the UK’s digital infrastructure?

I have personally witnessed the strength of Northern Ireland’s digital and technology sectors on multiple visits to Belfast. I will take the hon. Member’s points to heart and ensure that we make the most of that strength in the opportunities for digital resilience.
Will the Leader of the House give us the forthcoming business?

The business for next week is as follows: Monday 23 November—Second Reading of the Finance Bill. Tuesday 24 November—Consideration of Lords amendments to the Armed Forces Bill, followed by consideration of Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill. Wednesday 25 November—Opposition day (seventh allotted day). Debate on a motion in the name of the official Opposition, subject to be announced. Thursday 26 November—General debate on inequalities in cancer care, followed by a general debate on lifelong sex education. The subjects for these debates were determined by the Backbench Business Committee. Friday 27 November—Private Members’ Bills. The provisional business for the following week will include: Monday 30 November—Committee of the whole House on the Finance Bill (day one). Tuesday 1 December—Committee of the whole House on the Finance Bill (day two). Wednesday 2 December—Opposition day (eighth allotted day). Debate on a motion in the name of the Liberal Democrats, subject to be announced, followed by, if necessary, consideration of a Lords message.

I thank the Leader of the House for updating the House. I know that the House will want to join me in paying tribute to two great stalwarts of this place who have died this week: David Evennett and John Pardoe. David, in particular, will be remembered with huge affection by many colleagues, he having stepped down only in 2024. We send all good wishes to his family and loved ones. In other news, I am pleased to report that the Scottish Government have now responded to public concern about the annual cost of their hundreds of jobless employee ghost workers. Their position, formally set out this week by Ivan McKee, the SNP Minister for Public Sector Reform, is that they have no idea how much they cost, no plans to find out, and no intention of changing the policy. There is hardly a more hallowed convention of this House than the code of omertà—the vow of silence—that binds the Whips Offices. Don Corleone himself would pale to think of the methods deployed over the years to enforce it. When Gyles Brandreth published a book, aptly named “Breaking the Code”, about his time as a Whip, he received a letter with a black spot the following day. So I was rather surprised to hear about an interview given to none other than Vogue magazine this month, by the new Labour Chief Whip. In it we learned that she loves to collect clothes from the Paris fashion houses Courrèges and Pierre Cardin—brilliant, one might think, and in no way a parody of socialism. The Chief Whip ran off to the left bank when she was 17, in order to become, as she put it, André Breton of the surrealists. Breton’s mantra was, of course: “The simplest Surrealist act consists of dashing down the street, revolver in hand, and firing blindly…into the crowd” —which explains rather a lot. But after a year of living on cheese and wine in France, the Chief Whip said she felt ill—perhaps not surprisingly—which she attributes to “never looking at a vegetable.” Some might say—I couldn’t possibly comment—that she addressed that problem when she joined the Labour party shortly thereafter. It can hardly by coincidental, but it was not quite the cure that she needed. Faithful to André Breton’s mantra, she had barely become an MP, just two years ago, before she decapitated the last Prime Minister. Why? Because, in her words, “After a couple of years, people came away thinking, ‘Well, what is happening for us? We’re just more skint.’” As she says, “the Labour party needed to be saved”. I could hardly have put it better myself, except I would say that the country needs to be saved from the Labour party. The Chief Whip ends her interview in Vogue by saying: “I said all of that stuff before about team-building…But…I’m not going to take any”— expletive deleted— “and I don’t”— expletive deleted— “about.” A bit panicky, one might think, but at least a bit more on message for the Whips Office. The modern art of spinning was invented by a vastly lesser A. Campbell—Alastair Campbell, under Tony Blair —but given the Leader of the House’s 15 years as Deputy Chief Whip and then Chief Whip, I am bound to ask for his views on this topic. Does this interview mark a new direction of spin from the Labour party? Instead of the dark arts, can we now expect some salacious titbits from the Deputy Chief Whip in Cosmo or Grazia , or perhaps a pearl-clutching confessional from the Leader of the House himself in the pages of Hello! magazine? Instead of my asking for a debate, Mr Speaker, perhaps we could all ask the Labour Chief Whip for what she might call an—expletive deleted—period of silence.

Before I respond to the comments of the shadow Leader of the House, I want to welcome home the crew of HMS Vengeance following their record-breaking 217-day submerged deployment. To put that into context, if the crew were to undertake the same deployment today, they would not return until 24 June 2027. Spending seven months beneath the surface as a submariner takes extraordinary professionalism, quiet resilience and personal sacrifice, as well as the silent sacrifice of their families. I just want to place on the record my thanks—and, I am sure, the thanks of every Member of the House—to the members of the 140-strong crew and their families for enduring to keep the UK safe. I join the shadow Leader of the House in paying tribute to Sir David Evennett, who passed away on Tuesday after a short retirement from this House. He served as a Conservative Whip in opposition and in government, in addition to being vice-chairman of the party. I found him a worthy adversary as a Whip, and he was always good company. He was, in my view and that of many others, a genuine and caring man. My thoughts are with his loved ones during this difficult time. In that vein, I know that the whole House will also wish to join me in paying tribute to the former Cornwall North MP John Pardoe and to Lord Davies of Oldham, who both passed away recently. My thoughts are with their loved ones, to whom I send my sincere condolences. An issue frequently raised with me during business questions is access to banking services. Following the review conducted by Richard Lloyd, we have this week announced that we are bringing forward new legal protections through the Financial Services and Markets Bill to protect access to the essential face-to-face banking services that many of our constituents rely on. Another matter often raised with me is the feudal leasehold system. Last week we acted to protect leaseholders by introducing regulations that will improve the fairness and transparency of service charges. Today we are introducing the commonhold and leasehold reform Bill, which will deliver a revitalised commonhold model, much-needed leasehold reform and fairer rules for estate rentcharges. I will turn now to the comments of the shadow Leader of the House. He talked at length about the Chief Whip’s interview in Vogue , which I thought was rather good, actually, and set out not simply what a thoroughly decent person she is, but what a fantastic politician she is. I understand what he says about the role of Chief Whips and what might have happened in the past, but the world does move on. It is not for me to stand here and answer every point the right hon. Gentleman made, because the Chief Whip is more than capable of fighting her own corner. If he is suggesting that these interviews should extend from the Chief Whip to the Leader of the House, then I await offers with keenness, Mr Speaker—although in my case, I think it will probably be less Vogue and more Exchange and Mart .

This is national Road Safety Week. It is 11 months since the Government launched their excellent road safety strategy and I launched my last road safety campaign in Rossendale and Darwen. We have made progress in Darwin with a forward-thinking council, but I am sorry to say that Lancashire county council has completely failed to act in Rossendale. Despite near misses, extensive evidence and harrowing accounts from residents, the council continues to refuse road safety measures where we need them most. For Burnley Road, Rochdale Road, Burnley Road East and Newchurch Road, there is nothing. The repeated excuse is that not enough people have yet been killed or injured to justify action. This is unacceptable, outdated and out of line with the road safety strategy, and it rightly infuriates my residents. Will the Leader of the House join me in calling on the Reform leadership of Lancashire county council to think again?

This Government introduced the road safety strategy and we take these matters seriously. Road safety should be a top priority for all local authorities, so I am concerned to hear about the lack of action from the Reform administration at Lancashire county council. It should be proactively improving safety, not waiting for tragedy to strike. Reform councillors in that part of the world, but also across local government, need to stop making excuses. They need to start listening to calls from my hon. Friend and his constituents and get on with it.

Thank you, Mr Speaker. May I associate the Liberal Democrats with the Leader of the House’s comments on our brave submariners and on the passing of Sir David and John Pardoe? I also disassociate myself with the approach just taken by the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman). I am sure that if the Chief Whip was not a woman, he might not have raised the issue of how she dresses. I have two issues to raise this morning, and I start with the much-awaited EU summit tomorrow. The Bill following tomorrow’s summit will be of major significance, and it is vital that Members are given time to scrutinise and debate the legislation in detail. Can the Leader of the House please confirm when the Bill will receive its First Reading and be published, and how will he ensure that parliamentarians can scrutinise it in this House and the other place? We Liberal Democrats are clear that joining the single market is the biggest lever that the Government can pull to grow our economy, cut taxes and invest in our nation’s defence. Can the Leader of the House please indicate whether the Government will ensure that Members can debate and vote on options to further improve our relationship with Europe and bring growth to our economy? The Leader of the House will also be aware that Cornwall Insight yesterday published its final forecast for the January 2027 default tariff cap. It predicts that energy bills will rise by 26%, taking a typical household bill over £2,000 for the first time. That is an increase of £443 on the current cap. The Government’s current measures will not stop this increase, as the forecast already includes the removal of VAT on electricity bills. The rise will be catastrophic, hitting households in the coldest months of the year. Will the Leader of the House ask the Chancellor to address the House directly on this issue as soon as possible, so that Members have the opportunity to question the Government’s response?

On the hon. Gentleman’s first point, we await the outcome of the summit keenly. The Government’s intention if things go well, as we anticipate they will, is to bring forward a Bill, which we will introduce in the normal way. I assure him that there will be plenty of time for the House to debate these important matters. He asks how he and his party may be able to amend the Bill, or give options to the House. We will be looking at amendments, which will come forward in the usual way. The hon. Gentleman raised the important matter of energy bills. He will know that we have taken action with the warm home discount allowance, with £150 more off bills until 2031. There is also a household energy payment for houses in council tax bands A to D, which will come into bank accounts in January. He acknowledges that we have cut VAT on electricity bills and extended that until 30 June. However, the Government are not complacent on these matters. As we approach what is already looking like a cold winter, his constituents and mine will still be concerned, but the Government are doing everything we can at present. If the Chancellor needs to announce anything further, I am sure he will come to the House in the usual way.

The UK Youth Parliament was established over 25 years ago to give young people a stronger voice in decisions affecting their lives. Elected members campaign on issues such as knife crime, mental health, education and the cost of living. However, its future is uncertain, as its funding is to be stopped. Given that the Government want to introduce votes at 16, does the Leader of the House agree that we should be encouraging our young people to engage with democracy? Will he please arrange for me to meet urgently the Under-Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, my hon. Friend the Member for Lewisham North (Vicky Foxcroft), to discuss the future of the UK Youth Parliament?

My hon. Friend is right to champion inclusion in our democratic process; I pay tribute to him for that. The current funding settlement runs until March 2027, and the Government will take a decision in due course on what happens past that point. It is important that we encourage young people to engage with democracy. His question is timely, given that Parliament Week is next week. I will ensure that he gets a meeting with the relevant Minister to get the answers he seeks.
I call Martin Vickers, who is representing the Backbench Business Committee.

The Chairman of the Committee sends his apologies. I have come off the subs’ bench to stand in for him. In addition to the business announced by the Leader for next Thursday, there will be Select Committee statements from the Transport and Justice Committees. In Westminster Hall, next Tuesday morning, the debate will be on the role of an MP; the afternoon debates will be on access to stroke services in remote areas and on Islamophobia Awareness Month. I hope that the Leader of the House can indicate whether we have been allocated time in the week beginning 3 December, because we have provisionally allocated some debates for days in that week. There is still a long wait for hon. Members who want debates in the Chamber, but we are making good progress with the Westminster Hall debates, and would welcome further applications. As the Leader of the House will know, Samaritans provides a vital service. I appreciate that it is a charity, and that the Government are not directly responsible for it—although of course they do provide some taxpayers’ funding—but 200 branches across the country are due for closure. I have met volunteers from my constituency who work in the Scunthorpe and Grimsby branches, and we have been seeking a meeting with the chief executive of Samaritans, without success so far. I hope that raising this here—and perhaps a nudge from the Leader of the House—might prove helpful.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for that. He is a more than admirable substitute; in fact, he is such a good substitute that I am sure that he would be worthy of being on the bench for Bridlington Town, in anticipation of the hon. Member for Bridlington and The Wolds (Charlie Dewhirst), if it required his services in playing against South Shields.

Indeed. On the future business, I try to give as much notice as I can to the Backbench Business Committee. I cannot confirm the business for the week beginning 3 December yet, but we will do all we can to ensure that the Committee gets all the time it needs and has as early notice as possible of it. The hon. Gentleman raised the important question of what is happening with Samaritans. He was right to praise it for the fantastic work that it does in not just his constituency but all our constituencies; I am sure that the House joins him in his praise. The Government cannot intervene in an independent organisation’s restructuring, but we recognise the valuable contribution made by volunteers. I encourage Samaritans to continue engaging with the volunteers in every part of the country affected during the process. I hope that the chief executive heard him this morning, and will do him the courtesy of giving him a meeting.

Following on from the comments of the hon. Member for Brigg and Immingham (Martin Vickers), Samaritans is an essential national charity that is there for us at our times of greatest need. Unfortunately, the Worthing branch is one of those at risk of closure. It has 100 dedicated volunteers available, day and night, to listen to anyone calling in. Those people have dedicated many years of their life to the service, and we risk losing not only their listening skills but the invaluable community networking and outreach that they undertake. I recognise that, as the Leader of the House said in response to the hon. Member, the Government cannot intervene directly, but I ask him to join me in praising the Worthing volunteers, and to encourage the national charity to engage with local MPs on this issue.

I certainly do that. I will not repeat what I said to the hon. Member for Brigg and Immingham (Martin Vickers), but the Samaritans provide a vital service. My hon. Friend is absolutely right to raise what is happening in Worthing. The Government cannot intervene, as I have said, but I think the Samaritans owe it to MPs to respond in a positive way, and at least explain what they are doing. I think a number of MPs have the same view. If the chief exec is not keen for MPs to go to them, I am sure that Parliament will give a great welcome to the chief exec, if the Samaritans wish to come here and explain what they are doing to MPs.

Road safety, which we heard about earlier, is a major issue in Skipton and Ripon and north Yorkshire. We have 5,000 miles of road, and there have been many deaths and many injured constituents. What more can the Government do to help the council with communications and strategies to reduce injuries and deaths during this Road Safety Week?

I agree with the right hon. Gentleman that this is a dark side to the absolutely beautiful constituency of Skipton and Ripon. The Government have brought forward a road safety strategy, but he makes a good point on communications, and I will take that to Transport Ministers. If he seeks a meeting with them to see what assistance local authorities can get, I am sure that those Ministers will be keen to meet him.

I have been proud to lead the campaign to protect the title of “nurse”. I have worked with the NHS, doctors and the #ProtectNurse campaign to ensure that if someone says they are a nurse, they are actually qualified as one. The Government’s consultation ended last month. Will the Leader of the House give a lovely Christmas present to the NHS and ensure that the Government implement this important legislation soon?

I join my hon. Friend in praising nurses and healthcare professionals in general for their work in what is often a busy period for them. The consultation has closed, and I am sure that Ministers will be poring over the contributions. I cannot guarantee when the response will come forward, but I expect that there will be a response, and that it will be made to this House.

Mr Speaker, may I first join your remarks yesterday, and the remarks made by the Front Benchers this morning, about our late colleague David Evennett? As one of the three, I think, surviving members of the ’83 intake still in the House, I know David to have been a good man, a wonderful constituency MP, a great father and a dear friend, with a very laconic sense of humour. Our thoughts are with Marilyn, his two boys and their family at a very sad time for them. Mr Speaker, may I try your patience just a little, with what might seem to be a parochial issue, though I believe it to be of national importance? For three weeks, a road in my constituency has been closed to school transport, public transport, emergency vehicles and domestic vehicles at the behest of the South African company Trooli, which is licensed by Ofcom to install yet another fibre optic cable. Six businesses—three pubs, one village shop, one butcher, and one tea shop—are all losing money as a result of the activities of this commercial enterprise, which has to be authorised by Kent county council because Ofcom has licensed it. It has to be wrong that a wholly commercial company can disadvantage other businesses without giving them any compensation. Will the Leader of the House talk to the appropriate Ministers to see whether either primary or secondary legislation is needed to address this issue?

The right hon. Gentleman is expressing a frustration that many of us feel in our constituency when we see roadworks that do not appear to be necessary, and that seem to take longer than was envisioned, as is often the case. They seem to happen in an unplanned way. I hope that the company that he refers to, but also Ofcom and anybody else who has a hand in this, has heard what he has said. It is hard to overestimate the effect on businesses, families and children going to school, so I hope that those involved have heard his words. I will certainly take this away and talk to Ministers to see what more can be done—to the point that if this requires legislation, there is a legislative response.

Today is World Toilet Day. It sounds quite amusing, but this is not an amusing issue for the train drivers and other transport workers who are required to work for 11 hours with only one 20-minute break, with a total lack of clean, accessible toilets. Unbelievably, train drivers have had to resort to extreme measures: changing sanitary products in the cab; leaving the train to urinate alongside the railway; or using bottles and lunchboxes. Despite ASLEF’s campaign and the Office of Rail and Road charter, the industry is still not meeting the required standards. Will my right hon. Friend use his offices to secure a meeting with the relevant Ministers to discuss what can be done to provide the dignity that those workers so rightly deserve?

My hon. Friend is a powerful advocate for workers’ rights and he raises an important matter. Welfare provision across the rail network is a vital principle, not least as railways come back under public control. I will be happy, on his behalf, to raise the matter with Transport Ministers and the Office of Rail and Road, and if he seeks a meeting, I will help him to arrange one.

Like many in this House, I welcomed the Prime Minister announcing in his Labour party conference speech the formulation of a national commission on electoral reform. This is the most disproportionate Parliament in history; the Labour party got about a third of the votes, two thirds of the seats and 100% of the power. Despite submitting several written questions, we have not seen the commission’s remit, the membership, the chair or the timescale. My constituents, particularly the 14-year-olds at schools such as Marple Hall and Harrytown who might be able to vote at the next election, are keen to know if the outdated first-past-the-post system will be used at the next general election or beyond. Will the Leader of the House ask the relevant Minister to make a statement to this House on a national commission? We need to fix our politics, so that we can get on with fixing our country. I urge the Government to crack on.

This is a priority for the Prime Minister, and work is in progress on the matter. I am not sure, with due respect, that it is the top priority for all our constituents in the way it seems to be for the hon. Lady’s party, but it is important; I accept that. When progress has been made—we want to make sure, as we change politics, that it is done in a way that changes our country for the better—I am sure that Ministers will want to come to this place and update the House on that.

Meur ras, Mr Speaker. Earlier this week, I met Surfers Against Sewage, who are based in St Agnes in my constituency of Camborne, Redruth and Hayle. Since the clean water White Paper was announced in the King’s Speech, they and many constituents have been eagerly awaiting its publication. Will the Leader of the House update Members and our constituents on when the Government plan to publish that and introduce the Bill to Parliament?

My hon. Friend is right to raise that. In our water system, shareholders appear never to lose and customers never to win. As a coastal constituency Member of Parliament, I know the importance of this issue, not just to those who surf, but to everyone who cares about the state of our waters. We have announced a series of measures to go further in implementing public control. In September, the Prime Minister announced that we would bring forward a strengthened water Bill when parliamentary time allows. I do not think my hon. Friend will have long to wait before that can be confirmed.

I am currently assisting 28 constituents—the number goes up and down—with civil service pension problems. There is a particular irony in the fact that the people affected are civil servants, who have given their career to the bureaucracy that is now so badly letting them down. Capita recently demonstrated that there is not even uniformity in the level and manner of its incompetence: it seems to be finding new ways to let civil servants down all the time. Can we have a debate in Government time to allow right hon. and hon. Members to bear witness to this utter disaster on behalf of their constituents, and allow the Cabinet Office to explain away why there is such institutional lack of grip on the issue?

I do not agree with the final point, because Ministers are working very hard to ensure that the situation improves, but I do understand, because I have similar cases, that it is extraordinarily frustrating for people—in fact, more than frustrating—who are waiting for their pensions. The Government have been clear that Capita’s performance has been unacceptable. It is a complex issue, but it has taken too long to resolve. There have been a number of debates on these matters, and there was an opportunity to raise them at Cabinet Office questions, which we have just had. Ministers have updated the House, and I am sure that they will continue to do so.

The Milburn review rightly identifies that young people lack neither resilience nor ambition, but opportunity on their doorstep. That is particularly stark in Portsmouth, which is joint worst in England for the availability of post-16 provision. I welcome the proposals for early intervention and a new system of support that will help young people to fulfil their potential and will reduce the benefit bill. Will the Leader of the House, who is also a coastal MP, make time for a debate on the unique challenges faced in coastal communities by young people not in education, employment or training?

My hon. Friend is a powerful advocate for her area. As she said, I am a fellow coastal MP, and I am aware of the particular challenges that communities like ours face. I agree that this Government will give hope to young people across all our constituencies, including in coastal areas, and help them to reach their potential. I am sure that the Milburn review will continue to be hotly debated; I encourage her to apply for a Westminster Hall debate so that she can put her questions directly to Ministers and hear answers about how we intend to take it forward.

Stockton’s Labour borough council has turned parts of our town into a free-for-all for houses in multiple occupation, bedsits and bail accommodation, and has volunteered for us to take a disproportionate share of the country’s asylum seekers. Residents see groups of lone men hanging around the town centre, and shoplifting is up 168%. Residents now face plans for a 229-bed HMO near the town centre, which is opposed in the strongest possible terms by Cleveland police, but under Labour’s new rules, councillors might not even get a vote. Can we have a debate on stopping councils cramming ever more HMOs into communities that have already had enough?
