I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this debate, and commend him on his fantastic speech. International Men’s Day is an opportunity to celebrate men and recognise the contribution they make to our families, workplaces and communities, but also to confront some uncomfortable truths about men’s health. Speaking of uncomfortable truths, my eldest daughter recently broke and asked me to stop telling dad jokes. I told her that I completely understood where she was coming from, that it was an important issue that I was determined to do something about, and that I therefore asked for a judge-led statutory inquiry, which I fully expect to report at some point after her 18th birthday. In the meantime, I am attempting to do my bit for Movember. At Prime Minister’s questions yesterday, the Prime Minister offered hope: I still had 12 days to grow a proper moustache. As he delivers growth in every postcode, I will do my best to deliver a little bit more growth in mine. While the ’tache may be failing to live up to expectations, it is at least achieving its purpose of getting people to talk about men’s health. As I said yesterday at PMQs, three in four people who take their own lives are men. Suicide remains the leading cause of death for men under 50. We cannot and should not accept this. Last International Men’s Day, the Government took the important step of publishing a men’s health strategy for the first time. It is important recognition that men’s health needs a proper, co-ordinated response. The £3.6 million investment in neighbourhood-based suicide prevention for middle-aged men is particularly welcome. Support does not always begin in a doctor’s surgery or mental health clinic; sometimes it begins in a room where men feel comfortable and able to talk. Sometimes it begins on a football pitch, and sometimes it begins over a cup of tea. We are very fortunate in High Peak to have some fantastic organisations that allow for exactly that. Mentell in Glossop and Buxton provides safe, confidential spaces for men to talk. I have seen for myself that the men’s shed in Whaley Bridge provides another way of tackling isolation and bringing people together. I am also particularly pleased that the Minister and the Prime Minister this morning took Andy’s Man Club into 10 Downing Street. I saw this support for myself when I joined one of Buxton FC’s mental health kickabouts last year. Men of all ages and abilities get together for a game of football before heading to the clubhouse for a cup of tea, a biscuit and a chat. Thanks to some very charitable defending, I was even kindly allowed to score a couple of goals. There are many stresses and strains, changes and turning points in our lives that can affect our mental health—debt, insecure work, relationship breakdown, gambling, alcohol, loneliness and housing insecurity, to name but a few. I want to focus on one change that is particularly personal to me: becoming a dad. I remember how overwhelming it was when we had our first daughter. Of course, you want to be there, be involved and do your bit, but you are also trying to work out how to be a dad, how to support your family, and how to navigate all the changes that come with that. If I were asked, I would say that becoming a dad is the best thing I have done and will ever do. But I will be honest, if I were to be asked the same question most nights at 2 am when my two-year-old is point-blank refusing to accept that night time is when we sleep, I might give a rather unparliamentary reply. Whether it is your first child or third child, becoming a dad brings enormous joy, but it can also feel like an overwhelming responsibility. Suddenly there is a little person who depends on you for absolutely everything. Priorities change overnight, and new things have to be learned that are not always easy. Finances come under pressure, which is all the more difficult during a cost of living crisis. What I have found is tha

I thank both of the speakers so far, particularly my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow), who gave such a great big overview of International Men’s Day. To start, I will say that, probably like a lot of men, this is a day that has passed me by throughout most of my life. This is not a day that necessarily has the same degree of awareness around it as International Women’s Day. I do not mean that in the way that some very annoying reply guys on the internet say, every International Women’s Day, “When is International Men’s Day?”—it is today; it just passes us by and does not have the same amount of awareness around it. Since becoming an MP, however, the issues facing men in our communities—in my community in Sittingbourne and Sheppey and across every constituency in the country—have really come to the fore. On the Women and Equalities Committee, we have also looked into things such as the manosphere, and the roles, responsibilities and part that men play in violence against women and girls, in the perceptions of women and men online, and in our communities. We have also done some work looking at parental leave around the world and how that impacts. This year has also given me the opportunity to reflect a bit on myself: what it means for me to be a man, the experience of that and how, in the end, being a man is something you just are—if you are a man. You just have it, but it is also something you have to work at. There are challenges to understanding what it is to be a man in the world and what it is to be a man for you. That is true for any adult of any gender: you have to work out who you are and not take on everyone else’s definitions of who you are and who you might be. For men, there are other people’s definitions of masculinity and what that looks like, and other people’s definitions of how you should respond and behave in a society. The core point of that came when I realised I was gay at the age of 11. It hit me as a bit of a bolt from the blue—an instant realisation—and several things flowed from that straightaway. One was about fatherhood. As the eldest child in a large Catholic family, I had always expected to be someone who had kids of my own. Suddenly, there was a realisation: I will not have a female partner, I will not marry a woman and it is very unlikely that I will have children of my own. There was no expectation at the time that gay people would be able to adopt. That came a lot later in my life, at a point when neither I nor my husband were able to take that on. That was quite a big blow; it was quite a big shock. I absorbed it at the time, like a lot of teenagers—well, some teenagers—would, but it has had impacts and it has affected the whole of my life. It has also affected the way that I approach manhood and what being a man is. The other thing that came with that experience was that, at that time, most of the social expectation for gay men was about being effeminate—the sort of Larry Grayson-type presentation of what a gay man would be. That is a great and a fantastic way to be, but it is not quite me. Although I was useless at football and a lot of those sorts of boys’ activities, I was a very geeky boy and I loved stuff like science fiction and transport—other boy activities. Those are all things you have to work out. What does it mean to you as you approach manhood and, as you then progress into adulthood, what are the responsibilities that you take on? How do you avoid the toxicities of manhood that are out there? My response was: I am just me, but I am a bloke and I will be a bloke. On an incidental note, that is why I very much understand how trans people know that they are trans. I know that I am not trans; I am a gay man. It really is just automatic; it does not even take any thinking. If we reflected a little on that in the whole debate around trans and non-binary people, most of us would think, “I never even thought of that.” I had to think of that at that age and that gives m

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) on securing this important debate. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) mentioned people who complain about International Women’s Day. They say, “When’s International Men’s Day?” That happens so often, especially in this House. We are always getting criticised. Where are they? There is not one person on the Opposition Benches for International Men’s Day. [ Interruption. ] I mean on the Back Benches, not the Front Bench. They complain about International Women’s Day and other things for women. They talk about men as though they care about them, but they do not care enough to come to the Chamber and participate in this debate. That is a disgrace, and I hope that their constituents are watching. International Men’s Day was formally inaugurated by a lecturer, Dr Jerome Teelucksingh, in Trinidad and Tobago. Dr Teelucksingh was driven to promote positive role models. The theme for 2026 is supporting men and boys, and there is nothing more important than ensuring that we are leading on that. Men, especially young men, sometimes feel isolated—as though the world does not belong to them or they are lost in the world. It is important for us, as politicians, not to use the insecurity of young men to get them angry. That is the playbook of Reform Members especially: getting young men angry. What do they do with that anger? They use it for their own personal gain. They do not accept or acknowledge that they are having an effect on young men’s mental health. It is important that we set the political agenda, and doing so through this debate is fundamental. Being a man includes protecting women and girls. Real men protect women and girls, and we should teach that. Real men cry. There is all this stuff about keeping calm and carrying on, not accepting that real men cry. Men are criticised or called wusses and all sorts of other things. Real men cry, and that is okay.

My hon. Friend is giving a powerful speech; it is important that we hear voices like hers in debates such as this. My constituent, Leo Shepherd, is a victim of domestic violence, and he has a powerful one-man show that talks about that. Does she recognise the importance of role models, such as Leo, talking about their experiences and encouraging other young men who have been victims of violence to come forward?
Order. The hon. Member is so experienced that she knows better than to use the words “you” or “your”, because she is speaking through the Chair.

I apologise, Madam Deputy Speaker. I congratulate Leo on the work that he is doing. We must recognise that men also suffer from domestic abuse and domestic violence. Real men wear pink. I have seen some say online that real men do not wear pink. Real men can wear whatever colour they please. Real men talk about their feelings. Real men are woke. I read an article about a Member saying that the new James Bond is going to be all woke. Who cares? Woke is a good thing. When I was a child, my dad was 8 feet tall to me, and when I became an adult, he was still 8 feet tall. I would fix cars with him. He would take me to A&E when I was suffering from period pains, and was being sick and having cramps. He explain to the doctors and nurses, “My daughter is suffering from really bad period pains.” He was not ashamed to talk about periods. That is a real man. On 1 June 2026, the Mayor of London launched a £1 million fund to call on society to act on a lost generation of young men. That is an important fund, and we need to ensure that we activate it. We cannot afford to lose a generation of young men. We need them to be participants, good participants, in society. Research has shown that 15% of Londoners think that young men and boys do not have enough positive role models, and 55% of men say that they face pressure to meet societal expectations related to being a man. That rises to 71% among men aged 18 to 24. Londoners are nine times more likely to say that social media is harmful and harmful to their mental health. We have to get a grip on social media. The algorithms are there to promote an environment of continuous scrolling and of bubbles, such that if someone hates women, they will be put in circles where other people hate women and will think that that is the norm. We have to get a grip on social media and algorithms. In Brent, we have several men’s clubs that tackle how to parent. We have a scheme in which barbers have positive conversations—they have a captive audience when they are cutting hair. That is an innovative way to interject positivity into everyday life. We have heard about suicide in men. In 2022 to 2024, 73% of suicides were, very sadly, men, and suicide remains the leading cause of death in men under 50 years old. These are men who say that they do not know what to do, or that they do not know how to carry on. That is something of an emergency. This Government have done a great deal to acknowledge men and to ensure that we have legislation that showcases the role that men play. That is important. Women live longer than men—it is a fact. We sometimes make light of that when we see some of the stuff that men get up to, especially on social media—we think, “No wonder women live longer.” But it is not just about living longer. Older men often have worse health outcomes, and we have to tackle that. This goes back to men being told to suffer in silence. They do not have to suffer in silence. If they are ill, they should go to the GP. If they have a pain, they should go to the GP. Because men are sometimes reluctant to go to the GP, they get diagnosed later, and so they have worse health outcomes. In Brent, male life expectancy at birth is 80 years old, and for women it is 85 years old. Across London, men do slightly better, at 80.5 years old, and women do slightly worse, at 84.7 years old. The charity Mind reports that 33% of men say that their job has a negative impact on their mental health, that 43% of men regularly feel worried or low, and that young black men are around three times more likely to present as a suicide risk than young white men. The Government’s men’s health strategy is vital when it comes to cancer. The incidence of cancer is higher in males than in females. We have to say to men, “It’s okay to talk about your mental health and your physical health.” It is still a fact—it has not changed—that a woman is killed every three days by a male partner or male former partner. We need men to call this out. The
Because they are shellfish. I am available for after-dinner speeches.
Real men do wear pink, as the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler) can attest to. I call Samantha Niblett.

Thank you for calling me, Madam Deputy Speaker, as I furiously update my speech with the latest names suggested to me of brilliant men in my constituency who deserve recognition, but I will start at the beginning. I rise to mark International Men’s Day and, in particular, to pay tribute to some of the remarkable men and groups that have been nominated by people across South Derbyshire for the positive difference they make to our communities. A personal mention for me is Ian Bottrill, who we sadly lost earlier this year. He was my agent in the general election, but he was also my friend. I and many across our community miss him dearly every day, especially those at Sharpe’s Pottery where he was a trustee and those at Swad in Bloom where his personal contribution was so valued. Before moving to south Derbyshire, he dedicated years of his life as a teacher inspiring many and as a councillor, including as leader of Warwickshire county council. I want to give a special mention to the wonderful Antony and Roger Cobley. They have spent a lifetime caring for others, and they still do. They dedicated their lives and careers to nursing and were the first gay couple to foster and change the lives and fortunes of boys whose future was not hopeful based on their start in life. Their ongoing commitment to their sons and their families is wonderful, as we would expect from all good fathers, but they are not just good fathers; they are amazing fathers. Back to some of the people who were recommended by my community, I asked local people to put forward the names of men who they felt deserved recognition, and this is just the tip of the iceberg—it really is. The response was a powerful reminder that across our towns and villages, there are men quietly doing extraordinary things, men who give their time, compassion and energy, and often their own personal experiences, to help others. One name that came up time and again was Alex Garner, who co-founded and runs Our Little Angels. Alex provides invaluable support to families experiencing miscarriage and the devastating loss of a baby or child. His personal compassion, alongside his fundraising efforts, has touched many lives. Supporting families through unimaginable grief requires a special kind of strength, and Alex deserves enormous recognition. Adam Foster, the owner of Nomad Tattoo & Co in Swadlincote, was also nominated repeatedly. Adam uses his business and influence to raise money for good causes, including fundraising connected with hospital dermatology services in Birmingham children’s hospital. He demonstrates how local businesses can be a force for good. I want to recognise Adam Stretton, a military veteran and the head coach and owner of Fight Station in Church Gresley. Through his work supporting men’s mental health, veterans and those facing serious personal challenges, including through a men’s release and recharge programme, Adam is helping men find connection, support and a way forward when life becomes difficult. There are many others whose contributions deserve to be acknowledged. Stephen Morley—I know Stephen personally; he is such a lovely man—owns Swadlincote Electrical and Solar Supplies and will frequently send me a message on LinkedIn just checking that I am okay. He was praised for his work supporting our local community, including frequent and generous donations to South Derbyshire CVS food bank. Graham Knight, who I know personally, too, as a fellow Labour party member, has dedicated nearly 40 years to running Moira Replan. Moira is just outside my constituency, but has certainly served those who live in it. He has served his local community. People have a lot of time and love for Andy Dawson because of the time he has dedicated to parish council work, rugby and charity fundraising, but he is one of those people who does not make a fuss about it, rolls up his sleeves and just gets on with it. Andy Heathfield had a shout-out as well. Loads of people were disappointed whe

I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for initiating the debate. I stand once more to raise the topic of improvements we could make to paternity leave in this country. This has been spoken about in the Chamber, so I am not going to do the topic to death, but we have made massive improvements by making two weeks of statutory paternity leave a day-one right under this Government, and I am glad that we will be bringing self-employed people within that regime from 2029 onwards. I absolutely want to support and reiterate the calls for six weeks of shared parental leave at 90% of pay. I have long been an advocate for discrimination to cease, and I do not understand why women get 90% of pay for six weeks as standard within a heterosexual couple and men do not. It is not fair or right, and it is time that we resolved it, so please can we look at that again as a Government as soon as possible? Moving on to slightly sadder topics, we have a huge problem with avoidable deaths in this country, particularly in respect of men. Three quarters of deaths on UK roads happen to men and boys; three quarters of suicides, unfortunately, occur among men; and 85% of drownings happen to men. Lots and lots of men are losing their lives in circumstances that should and could be prevented. Road deaths are a huge issue in my constituency. The latest Brake statistics, from 2025, suggest that in my constituency one person is either killed or seriously injured on the roads every single week—every week. This is a massive public health issue that is not being treated with the urgency it warrants. I have a number of suggestions about how this could be improved. We should definitely be looking at average speed checks, and there are plenty of other statistics I could cite to support that, but we also know that rural roads are six times more fatal than motorways—this is a massive problem. The Government published a road safety strategy last year with really challenging targets for reducing the number of deaths on our roads, but I would like to encourage everyone in my community: please get black boxes for young people when you first insure them, whether or not you financially need to, because they train really good driving, and please put young people through advanced driving skills classes. Congleton and Macclesfield Advanced Drivers and Riders will provide that, and we could reduce deaths significantly. I will continue to work with the local authority, the police and literally anyone who will listen, because I consider this to be one of the biggest emergencies in my community. As I said, 85% of drownings happen to men. It is not something that is talked about much, but with the rise in hot weather we saw really large numbers of people drowning this summer. I do not live in a coastal community, but actually the large majority of drownings occur inland. Reservoirs are particularly fatal. We have beautiful meres near me, and we need to ensure that our young people learn to swim. I know there is real pressure on national curriculum time and on resources, but I encourage all my local schools to continue their swimming programmes, and I encourage everyone to think very carefully about the risks before they enter water. We all need to think about how the Government can help more with this. We are encouraging more open water swimming, which lots of people love and is fantastic, but it is in many respects very high-risk, particularly for men. Lastly, I want to talk about online safety. We talk a lot about online safety in respect of children, and I do that a great deal too, but men face particular risks online. The algorithms are pushing videos of people dying towards young men. The Children’s Commissioner has found that young men and boys see, on average, two real-life deaths a month online. We need to better regulate this, but we also need to look at suicide forums. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this incredibly important debate. I had the honour of leading the debate last year, so I know how much there is to cover. He made a powerful speech and we are all very proud of him. Once again, this is such a powerful debate, and I consider myself very fortunate to be among the Members who have spoken. I would like to begin with the greatest joy of my life: fatherhood. Like others who have spoken, I will give my attempt at a dad joke. Why did the bicycle fall over? Because it was two-tyred! I thought I would get that in early in my speech, to give Members a chance to recover. As we have heard, paternity leave becoming a day-one right and finally being extended to the self-employed are massive steps forward for dads, but fathers are still entitled to just two weeks, on £194.32 a week for those who qualify. A fortnight is simply not enough time to adjust to a huge life event like becoming a parent. Those first days matter for bonding, for mothers recovering from childbirth and for families finding their feet. We talk about parenting being 50/50, but our system makes that incredibly difficult. The physical recovery from childbirth is not shared; the initial burden of childcare is not shared; and when one parent has two weeks away from work while the other may have to put their career on hold for months or even years, the impact on pay and progression is not shared either. Our current paternity leave system risks treating active fatherhood as a “nice to have” and motherhood as an obligation. Office for National Statistics research estimates that women lose an average of £65,618 in earnings over the five years following the birth of their first child. Properly paid, extended paternity leave would give fathers the chance to share responsibility and mothers a fairer chance to return to work and progress. It is about genuine equality, and it shows boys that fatherhood means more than being the breadwinner; it means caring, sharing responsibility and being there. Moving on to boys in education and the online world, 60% of boys are meeting the expected standard in reading, writing and maths at the end of primary school, compared with 67% of girls. In writing, the gap was 11%. It is clear that we need earlier literacy support, targeted catch-up for children falling behind, and better support for pupils with additional needs and many of our white working-class boys, who seem to be at the sharp end of so many statistics. We should also value apprenticeships, technical education and vocational routes as ambitious pathways to success. I welcome the attention that the Government have given to all of the above. We also need to ask ourselves why some of the divisive and reductive voices we are hearing online are finding an audience. If a boy is struggling at school, does not feel that he has a future, does not have positive male role models around him and is looking for somewhere to belong, we should not be surprised when someone online comes along offering him answers. The problem is that those answers can be deeply damaging, and we cannot blame boys for listening to them if we have not done enough to give them a positive and compelling alternative. A report by the Centre for Countering Digital Hate entitled “The Looks Trap” describes the growing world of looksmaxxing—influencers encouraging boys and young men to obsess over their appearance. The report describes boys as young as 13 taking steroids and illegal growth hormones. Others have injured themselves through “bone smashing”—hitting their own faces with hammers in the hope of changing their jawline or cheekbones. We have got to a point where it is easier for boys to find people telling them to take a hammer to their face than to find people telling them to read for pleasure and strive for educational achievement. If that does not ring alarm bells for us as a society, I do not know what will. I wanted to understa

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) for his advocacy, his bravery and his continued positivity. It is a real privilege to speak in this debate; I am genuinely proud to be here. I want to give a shout-out to my fellow hon. Members who are men, who make this a very welcoming place for me. I am a proud colleague, partner, daughter, auntie, niece and sister—and, above all, a very proud mum to three fabulous young men. I want to say happy International Men’s Day and “Thank you, and I love you” to all the men in my life and in my city of Portsmouth. I know how important the men in our lives are. I know the difference a good dad, brother, partner, friend or role model can make, and I know that behind every statistic is somebody’s son, dad, brother or friend. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing the debate and for his continued advocacy for men and boys. In honour of the good people of the Dad Shift and all dads across the country—including mine—who remain absolutely convinced that they are funny, I will start with a dad joke. Knock, knock. [Hon. Members: “Who’s there?”] Isabelle. [Hon. Members: “Isabelle who?”] Isabelle necessary on a bicycle? Madam Deputy Speaker, I should warn the House that the quality of these jokes may not improve.

I want to start by reflecting on last year’s debate. Last year I spoke about men feeling forgotten —men who felt that their struggles were not recognised, that they were not being listened to, and that there was not a space for them to talk openly. Something happened after that speech that really stayed with me. I was contacted by men in my constituency who wanted to share their experiences, their worries and, in some cases, things they had not felt able to talk about before. I want to say a genuine thank you to every single one of them: thank you for getting in touch, for being honest, and for trusting me with your experiences and to bring your voices here every day. I listened, and I have not forgotten those conversations. As a Labour MP, I am proud that my Government are listening to me, and standing up for men and boys by enacting policies and legislation that back British men, and men in my city. That is why I wanted to speak in this year’s debate. We cannot simply keep saying that men feel forgotten and leave it there. We have to ask ourselves what we are going to do differently; how we can make men feel heard, supported and valued; how we can make it easier to ask for help; and how we can make sure that our boys grow up knowing that they have someone in their corner. For me, International Men’s Day this year must be about moving the conversation forward—not just recognising the challenges, but doing something about them. Let me be clear: supporting men and boys does not mean taking anything away from women and girls. It is not a competition. I agree with my colleagues who have spoken about sex-based crimes, violence against women and girls, and the vile men who use their positions of power to abuse. I also agree with my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase, who spoke about his dive into the online world: we must challenge all these things all the time. When men are healthier and happier, families are stronger, children do better and communities thrive. As one of the proud co-chairs of the Labour group for men and boys, I have been incredibly proud to help put those issues on the agenda, particularly those around health and work. I recognise the progress that this Government have made. Last year, England’s first men’s health strategy was published, and it was launched at a building site. It marked a really important step in recognising that men’s health is not just about what happens in a GP’s surgery, but about work, housing, relationships, family life and feeling part of the community. However, the statistics remain stark. As we have heard, men in the UK live for an average of four years less than women. In my own city of Portsmouth, suicide is a leading cause of death for men aged 20 to 49, with 24 people taking their own lives every year, 78% of whom are men. Behind those figures are families who have lost someone they love, mums who have lost sons, children who have lost dads, and partners who have lost someone they thought they had their whole life ahead of them with. They are not numbers; they are people. At Movember’s reception at the Labour party conference, I was delighted to hear the Minister announce that the Government will appoint a men’s health ambassador to turn the strategy into real change, and today I was delighted by the announcement that there will be a men’s summit, but we must ensure that men feel the difference in our communities. It is all very well telling men to ask for help, but we need to ensure that the help is accessible, and that they feel comfortable using it. Some of the biggest improvements in men’s health may not necessarily come from policies labelled as health policies. Paternity leave, which we have already heard about during the debate, is a perfect example. Nearly one in 15 new dads experience suicidal thoughts during the first years of fatherhood, and 82% of fathers say that improving paternity leave is the single biggest action the Government could take to support their ment

You have been practising my name, Madam Deputy Speaker. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing and introducing the debate. It was an excellent contribution, as all contributions from hon. Members have been. I would like to speak about something that weighs heavily on my mind. I am not originally from Clackmannanshire—I first started working in the area in 2012—but not long after arriving, it struck me that it has some of the highest recorded suicide rates in Scotland. As we have heard from my hon. Friends, it is typically men who make up the majority of that figure, and Clackmannanshire is no different. Like many working-class communities, Clackmannanshire has seen a lot of industry leave. Alloa was once Scotland’s brewery capital: there used to be many mills along the Hillfoots and, once upon a time, we had seven coal mines. As we all know, when big industrial employers close, wealth and prosperity leave. With that, we see unemployment, meaning low economic activity. Low income obviously then means shops closing and boarded-up high streets, with the local economy devastated. That all leads to dreadful societal issues. For example, people sometimes end up making life choices that lead them to spiral into addictions, such as drink or drugs. People are looking for an escape route, trying to find some way to cope. With all that, poor health outcomes become almost inevitable—depression and anxiety become more common, and as people battle to survive as they live in deprivation, we can see that the male life expectancy in Clackmannanshire is lower than the Scottish average. Young people in Clackmannanshire are highly likely to look away from the area for what comes next in their lives. Something that shows the deterioration of living standards is the parlous state of Scottish public education. The way that our colleges in Scotland are funded is totally broke—it is just not fit for purpose. As part of the three-campus model across Forth Valley, the Alloa campus is under threat. Everyone knows that colleges transform people’s lives. The Alloa campus is essential to the life chances of young people from across Clackmannanshire. I was proud of my Labour Government just a fortnight ago when I went to the opening of the Alloa youth hub, based in the Alloa campus, which will provide a wide range of support for young people all under one roof. Local partners such as Skills Development Scotland, Clacks Works and Clackmannanshire council will provide education, training and employability support to 16 to 24-year-olds. Career advice, skills training, housing advice and mental health services will be of incredible help to my local people. A Labour Government giving people confidence and, crucially, access to employment opportunities will be worth their weight in gold to people who feel disengaged or disenfranchised, or who are living their life in despair. That is the sort of intervention and action that makes great changes for people, and they are the sorts of actions that make me proud to be a Labour MP. I thank the many organisations across Alloa and Grangemouth that do so much for people’s mental health. They do lifesaving work. Let me mention a meeting that I had with a constituent just a couple of weeks ago. Craig Hunter shares my dismay at the suicide rate that we have in our area. He quite rightly highlighted that people who are at their lowest go to the Clackmannanshire bridge to commit suicide. In representing Craig’s concerns, I have written to the Scottish Government Minister for Mental Wellbeing and the Cabinet Secretary for Transport to see if the Scottish Government will look into the possibility of suicide prevention measures being installed at the bridge, as well as increasing the mental health support available in my constituency. Just you wait, Madam Deputy Speaker. I admit that Members are generally more likely to see me in a debate about women than a debate about men, but it is absolutely right that we mark International Men’s Day in this place. One of its themes this year—the focus on men’s wellbeing—is absolutely spot on, and I will focus my contribution on men’s mental health. I see in my own residents in Aylesbury and the villages how tough it can be, and I want everyone to know that mental health challenges are normal and help is out there. I cannot put it better than Scott Grover, who runs a lovely group called Men Walking and Talking in my constituency. As he puts it, his group offers “friendship, brotherhood and a shoulder to cry on if needed”. They are out walking once a week. The group is completely free to join, and anyone can show up. As Scott says: “We believe it’s ok to say you’re not ok, that big boys do cry, but as men we’re too often told otherwise.” That is exactly the point. Life can be tough for all of us, and it is okay to admit that. There are so many issues that affect the men in Scott’s group, whether it is struggling to find work, being unable to get hospital appointments locally, or being stuck for hours in the traffic that so often clogs up our town, and they can add up to a feeling that our area is being left behind, that those men are being left behind and that they somehow do not matter. As Scott says: “When people feel they don’t matter, their self-worth drops and this adds to mental health issues.” Things are doubly difficult when they also face other barriers, as one deaf member of the group has pointed out to me. For example, he struggles to access healthcare with British Sign Language support. We are still a long way off breaking the stigma so that men feel they can freely admit that they are not well—perhaps even to themselves, let alone when talking about it to others. Even if they do admit it, the question is whether the support that they need then flows. We have another great mental health group in Aylesbury called Talk Club, which is there to offer support and help men build mental fitness, as their captain Steve puts it, but I bet too many people have not heard of the group. It is run by volunteers who do not have the budget or the time to advertise or get media coverage. We need to build webs of awareness and support across our communities. We need people to know about Steve’s group, Scott’s group and the other support groups out there, whether it is Space—a support group for older adults that meets in St Mary’s church—or fantastic charities such as Youth Concern for younger people. I can play a part in that, and so can our local council, our health services and our local employers. For those with serious mental health challenges, we need the professional help to be there too. If people go to their GP practice or the hospital, they need to know that their mental health issues will be taken seriously. The Government are making really good progress with more mental health support for boys in school and the expansion of mental health services nationally, including a new mental health centre in town in Aylesbury, where Bucks Talking Therapies is running services. There is much more to do, however, and I look forward to the Government’s upcoming mental health strategy, which I am sure will be firm in its commitments, including to men’s mental health. In the rest of my speech, as others have done powerfully, I will talk about one specific group of men who can struggle with their mental health: new dads. I have spoken many times before about the one in four pregnant and new mums who struggle with post-natal depression, anxiety, obsessive compulsive disorder, post-partum psychosis and other conditions, and I have also spoken about the high risk of suicide at that time of life. Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. I particularly thank you for encouraging me to participate in this debate—you have done your bit to support men today. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for bringing this debate forward and for his powerful opening speech. A huge number of powerful speeches have been made by hon. Friends throughout this debate, so it is a real pleasure to go last, because I get the opportunity to talk about some of them. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) challenged us as men to think about what being a man means to us. The way he described it was really personal—it is a personal question that we have to ask ourselves. I probably did not know that until a few years ago. When young men are asked to consider what it means to be a man—effectively, what it means to be them, whether that is questioning their sexuality or trying to deal with the fact that their sexuality might not be what they thought it was—it is okay to have questions. We do not need to have all the answers at a young age. I certainly did not; until I had a row at the age of 27 with my friend who was a Tory, I did not know that I had any particular ambition to become a Member of Parliament, let alone a Member of Parliament who mentions Harlow on a regular basis. It is okay for young men to not know where they are and to discover that, and it is important that they should not be scared of that. My hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce) spoke about the challenges of being a father. I found his words particularly relevant; as you will be aware, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am a fairly new father, and always feel guilty about being an absent one. Representing the constituency of Harlow is the third greatest honour of my life—as I am talking about being a father, I should be careful how I word this—after marrying my wife and having my son. Being in this place and representing the town and the community that I love so much—and mention quite regularly—is a huge honour, but I am aware that it comes with some sacrifices. It was interesting to hear from the Chair of the Education Select Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Dulwich and West Norwood (Helen Hayes), about the importance of reading for pleasure, because since my son was born, I have read more books than ever before, because I am determined that he should see the value of books and not of my mobile phone. I have to say to hon. Members— [ Interruption. ]
Order. Mr Lavery, just as the hon. Member was talking about mobile phones, yours goes off.

It was perfect timing for my hon. Friend’s phone to go off—not a problem on the Opposition Benches—as I was about to say that if any Members lose their mobile phone, my son will find it for them, which is terrifying. It is really important to me that he also sees the value of reading. On International Men’s Day, I also reflect on my experience of being a teacher. Earlier, I briefly mentioned in my usual haphazard way my experience of being a young teacher, and finding myself very early on in my career having to be a male role model for young men in my class. I reflect on what happens to young men whose father figures are absent from their lives, and what impact that has on them. There can be some really positive substitutes for that father figure—I have spoken about the wonderful volunteers at Harlow Sea Cadets, Harlow Air Cadets and Harlow Scouts, and I pay tribute to Matt Brace, who is the district leader of Harlow Scouts. I always forget to shake his left hand whenever I see him, so I apologise to him now. However, there are also some really bad substitutes. My hon. Friend the Member for Lowestoft (Jess Asato), who I can see hiding in the wings, is very aware of the huge danger that the internet—especially social media—will provide negative substitutes for that missing father figure. This debate is, therefore, as timely as it has ever been. I will take the opportunity to mention Harlow a few more times. I pay tribute again to Leo Shephed, who I mentioned in a previous intervention; he is a young man who has been a victim of domestic violence and does a one-man show on that topic. I always say to Leo that the reason his one-man show is so powerful is that, unlike me, he is really cool. I know that that sounds like a silly thing to say, but it is important that someone like Leo, who is cool—he is into his music and his drama—can tell that story, so that young men who may have been victims of domestic violence do not think there is something wrong with them because of it. It is important to make it clear that if you are a victim of any crime, you are not the problem. I also pay tribute to some other men in Harlow. I cannot fail to mention Vic Goddard—anyone who remembers “Educating Essex” will know that he was, and still is, the headteacher of Passmores school. I did not watch it myself, because I was a teacher at the time, and the idea of watching a programme about teaching horrified me. Vic is someone who cares passionately about every young person in his school. There is a brilliant story I tell about him. One boy who was not normally the best behaved student, had done something really well in class, and Vic was so excited to hear that this boy had written a fantastic essay in whatever subject it was, that he ran out of his office down to the classroom to congratulate that young boy in person, and then realised he had not put his shoes on. That gives Members some idea of the commitment and passion that Vic Goddard has for supporting his students in his school, whoever they are. I pay tribute, too, to Rod Wainwright, who I mention regularly. My hon. Friend the Member for Kensington and Bayswater (Joe Powell) will know who I am taking about, as Rod was one of the first responders at the terrible Grenfell Tower disaster. Subsequently, he has had some huge issues with his mental health and has been medically retired. I will not go into the details—I have shared them in this place before—but Rod has really been on a journey. He has been forced to confront his own mental health challenges, and I think he has found that really hard. He has been very open with me about how he does not want his children to see that side of him, but as one of my hon. Friends said earlier, it is okay to cry. It is okay to show your children that you can be upset and you can cry as well; it is not a weakness. There are many things that Rod should be proud of, but I think he should also be really proud of his ability to open up about his own mental heal

Listening to my hon. Friend speak made me reflect on the surgeries I have held as a Member of Parliament, where I have had far more men break down in tears than women. I do not know whether other hon. Members have had that experience— [ Interruption. ] I see nodding and agreement. I wonder whether that demonstrates the lack of safe spaces for men, and whether speaking with their Member of Parliament in a confidential setting feels like the only place they have to go. As other hon. Members have said in their contributions, it is important to get the message out there that first, it is okay to cry, and secondly, we need more of those spaces and we need to promote them. We need to create safe spaces for men to let that emotion out, so that they do not feel that their Member of Parliament’s surgery is the only place left for them to go, much as it will always be my privilege to try to support men in those situations.

I thank my hon. Friend for that powerful intervention. I was not going to talk about my own experiences growing up, because they are quite difficult for me to talk about, but I grew up in a military family, and crying was seen very much as something that men did not do—“Men don’t cry.” My hon. Friend is right; if men do not feel comfortable opening up about their mental health and sometimes having a good cry, that can have a long-term negative effect on their mental health. Whenever I have suffered a personal tragedy such as the loss of a family member—when both my grandads died—I went into a corner and had a good cry for 15 minutes. It did me a hell of a lot of good, so my hon. Friend is right to say that. I pay tribute to some of the safe spaces in Harlow, and I thank Rory at Harlow Playhouse. When I worked for a homeless charity in Harlow, Streets2Homes, Rory was very helpful in providing safe spaces for some of my clients who suffered from mental health issues in the way that my hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) has talked about, and sometimes even more severely. I also pay tribute to Harlow men’s shed, which provides a safe space for men to talk and have a cup of tea. It is currently making me something out of wood—it does that sort of thing. It is really important to have those safe spaces. I do not know any dad jokes to finish on, I am afraid. [Hon. Members: “Oh!”] Well, maybe later. My son is very little, and although I am confident that I will get at least two terms as the MP for Harlow—obviously—it is not very likely that I will still be an MP when he is an adult. I am taking this opportunity—although he will look back on his dad in Hansard in 20 or 30 years’ time and go, “Oh my God, he is so embarrassing!”, because that is what kids do—to send him a message. I want him to be happy, I want him to be healthy, but above all, I want him to be kind. That is really important. You have tempted me into this, Madam Deputy Speaker. What is the favourite wine of the Whips Office and the shadow Whips Office?
That was actually quite funny. I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

I am the proud father for four daughters. Until they started leaving home, I lived in a house with five women, and I soon learned where I was in the pecking order. This dad joke is for them: I advised my wife to embrace her mistakes, so she gave me a hug. It is a privilege to contribute to this debate on International Men’s Day on behalf of my party and my constituents. I commend the hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing this important debate, and thank Members for their important and moving speeches. In a changing world, we are asking men to redefine their traditional roles and responsibilities. This debate is an opportunity to highlight men’s health, celebrate positive role models and address issues affecting men, such as loneliness, abuse and mental health. Positive male role models play a vital role in supporting that redefinition and fighting outdated and rigid stereotypes. However, I share concerns that so many boys are spending more time alone and online, and less time at youth centres, sports facilities and community events. The result is less opportunity to engage directly with positive male role models—the team coach, the youth worker, the teacher. Instead, far too many are victims of a social media barrage of hyper-masculinity. Men and boys are made to feel that they are not enough. Algorithms seize on their insecurities, and they are too often confronted by poisonous role models such as Andrew Tate and Russell Brand, who promote and glory in a deeply unpleasant and damaging misogyny. Is it any surprise, then, that the crisis in male mental health is acute? Some 74% of all suicides are male. Appallingly, suicide is the biggest killer of men under 50, as we have heard. In 2022, the all-party parliamentary group on men and boys’ issues identified the sad truth that many men view suicide as a rational solution to the various challenges life inevitably throws at us—loneliness, relationship difficulties, trouble in the workplace or financial pressures. Men and boys all too often, suffer in silence, disengaging from those around them when they face challenges. When we do reach out for support, it is often at crisis point. Consequently, the role of suicide prevention charities is vital; that phone call might be the only time men in severe distress ask for help. As has been mentioned, it is disappointing that, in the face of that reality, the Government withdrew the national grant scheme for suicide prevention in March 2025. Organisations such as the Samaritans are stretched to breaking point in the wake of soaring demand. Such charities need more funding, not less. They provide essential lifesaving support day in, day out. The Government must recognise their importance, and I hope that the Minister will take that thought away. I ask the Government to consider supporting Liberal Democrat policies in this area, including better resourced local hubs, and mental health MOTs to check in and check up at crucial points in people’s lives. Stronger online protections and education to empower children to stay safe online are also essential. Support cannot be focused on the moment of crisis alone. Earlier engagement in schools, workplaces and with friends prevents the destructive culture of silence that is so pervasive among men. National campaigns like Movember, which aim to break down stigmas and get us talking, are an example of how much can be achieved. The earlier boys learn that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness, the better the outcomes will be. As one great role model, Sir Gareth Southgate, said: “The culture we create today will shape the kind of men that we inherit tomorrow.” Men must feel that they have a place and a role in the world. That is why I fear that the rising numbers of 18 to 24-year-olds not in employment, education, or training is so dangerous. Without routine—a job, school, university or college—young people are left adrift. I do not doubt that that is central to the mental h

It is always a pleasure to respond on behalf of His Majesty’s loyal Opposition, especially on a subject that is very close to my heart. I am grateful to the Backbench Business Committee for granting the debate, to hon. Members for supporting it with their thoughtful, interesting and wide-ranging speeches, and to the hon. Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for securing it. I absolutely agree about the strength of local charities and organisations that support men, and about the opportunity to celebrate the men in our lives. The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future is Everyone”, as we have heard. As we look at the challenges facing young men in particular, we must not underestimate the importance of a good-quality job, genuine career prospects and the opportunity to build a secure and fulfilling future to help families and communities such as yours and mine to thrive, Madam Deputy Speaker. I agree with the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler), about the power of sport. I remind hon. Members that from January to March this year, 14.4% of young men were NEET, but perhaps most shockingly of all, an additional 89,000 young people have been added to this category. As we have heard from many Members, this is about real lives. I have an interest in this area, and it is a pleasure to co-chair the all-party group on men and boys’ issues alongside the hon. Member for Bishop Auckland (Dr Rushworth). I am very grateful to Mark Brooks for all the work that he and the Centre for Policy Research on Men and Boys do. We in the all-party group are doing wide-ranging work, and seeing the interest here, I ask Members—I know we always have competing diaries—to please get involved. We are currently looking at the manosphere, looksmaxxing, the impact of gambling and much more. As we have heard, each year International Men’s Day has grown—from just 11 organisations taking part in 2010 to more than 800 being involved every year. There is widespread recognition of the challenges that men and boys face, not least the growing pressures of the online world, and how they can shape how men and boys approach relationships. Many of the groups we have heard about today help our young men and boys to be seen, heard, understood and supported, which is important. I thought the hon. Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin), who is clearly very engaged in this sector, made a great speech. Financial wellbeing, body pressures and emotional concerns all matter. Many men want and need to be in their children’s lives, and this world and our processes need to work better to support both women and men. Like many people in this place, I focus on women’s issues, but I have been brought to this sector by the challenges our men face. I agree with the hon. Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) about birth trauma, which I think has a real impact on men’s lives. I thank the hon. Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) for an insightful speech about the toxicities of manhood and the shape of families. He spoke with no notes and from the heart, and I really appreciated that. What he said pointed to the question: why do we still need an adjective when it comes to masculinity? That is still a challenge that I think we should seek to answer. The hon. Member for Congleton (Sarah Russell) spoke about the threat on our roads. As somebody who used to work in the Sussex safer roads partnership, I know that the threat of death and trauma to young men is huge. As ever, I loved the contribution from the hon. Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler). She spoke about men speaking up for women in pain, whether it is period pain or on hospital visits. I remember my dad buying me 96 Anadin and saying, “That will keep you going, love,” so there you go. The hon. Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) spoke about the groups in her area. The Piccalilli line, obviously—come on! That one is courtesy of Chris Heaton-Harris. We have spoken about the great work happening in our communities at men’s sheds and community groups. This year, I had the opportunity to celebrate losing a million pounds, and that is rare in this House. That was because MAN v FAT came to Parliament and celebrated how it promotes men’s health and weight loss, including the fact that men have lost a million pounds, got fitter and healthier, had people to talk to and had football and rugby to play. I have seen the valiant attempts at moustaches. I will be honest: I am a woman of a certain age, and I could get competitive, but I am not going to. [ Laughter. ] I always value the opportunity to speak up for men and boys, and I could not resist that one, but well done to everyone taking part. To be serious, the hon. Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) raised domestic abuse and his personal experience. I have spoken out about my spiking experience, and that issue affects men as well. I thank all those who are sharing their experience of male domestic abuse. I agree that we very often see men at their lowest ebb in our constituency surgeries. The Menshare Listening Group in East Grinstead meets at St Swithun’s parish hall, and when I was in its circle of trust earlier this year, I saw men sharing fears, successes, hopes and dreams, and knowing that that was needed. There is a serious point to all this. This week, we have had the Milburn report, and when I was a Work and Pensions Minister I worked on the kickstart partnerships with businesses and sectors, focusing on additional jobs. I have covered the number of NEET men, but we must not continue to make disastrous policy decisions like that on national insurance contributions that increase the cost of employing young people and remove the first rung from the employment ladder. We must reverse that increase, and our policy is to halve NICs. I am delighted to see the Labour Government building on youth hubs, as I did as Employment Minister, because it is crucial for young men and boys to have a space where they can get extra support. It is very concerning that the economy is struggling. Parental leave is important, but hospitality and tourism businesses as well as the builders, the creators, the leaders and the self-employed—we have talked today about those one-man bands—are struggling with business costs and the cost of living. All of us, but particularly Labour Members, like to talk about a compelling alternative, but we need an economic approach that does not squeeze jobs and put pressure on men as providers and care givers. As the hon. Member for Portsmouth North said, this debate has to be about more than just what we talked about last year. The hon. Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) spoke about deindustrialisation, and the impact of the use of drink and drugs as a coping method. The reality of the energy situation in Scotland has to be taken on. It is a little disappointing that there are areas on which we need to do more, such as prostate cancer screening. My right hon. Friend the Member for Richmond and Northallerton (Rishi Sunak) has been working with Sir Chris Hoy on that, so let us focus on what we can do there. As we have heard, the summit on men and boys is of considerable interest. Hon. Members may have heard my hon. Friend the Member for Huntingdon (Ben Obese-Jecty) talk about it, as has my hon. Friend the Member for Hinckley and Bosworth (Dr Evans), whom I congratulate on becoming a new father himself. We need this summit, but we need to know when it will happen, what action it will take and how it will make the lives of men and boys better, so that the House can be assured that we are fully addressing men’s health and online misogyny, and that we have a fully cross-Government agenda. It is a real honour to speak on behalf of the Government as the first ever Minister for men and boys. It is a huge responsibility, but what is clear from today’s debate and my time in this role is that the solutions to many of the challenges that men and boys face will not be solved by the Government alone; they will be solved by parliamentarians across the House; they will be solved by partnerships with business, charities, the third sector and campaigners. International Men’s Day is an opportunity to galvanise that sector and that movement, and to begin to talk about the challenges that men and boys face and how we as a society are going to meet them. I am very grateful to my hon. Friend the Member for Bracknell (Peter Swallow) for opening today’s debate, for speaking so powerfully about his experience, and for campaigning on parental leave—and for starting the debate with some truly awful dad jokes, which set the bar so low that some, later in the debate, became rather amusing. The attempt at a moustache by my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce) is just so silly that it was hard to take his contribution seriously, but I commend him for his admirable campaigning on parental leave. Without him, the progress made at the Budget might not have happened and the progress the Government hope to make early next year may not have happened either, so he deserves great credit. As has already been said, my hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna), once again without notes, spoke from the heart about really complex personal issues for us as a society, around notions and concepts of masculinity, especially in the gay community. I thank him for his contribution. My hon. Friend the Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler) is right about the concern that if we fail to act on the anger that men and boys feel, the toxic influences in our politics will only gain from that failure. I do not want to be partisan on a day like today, but she was also right to point out that on the Labour Benches we get a lot of stick for perhaps not talking about issues to do with men and boys. We are called weak and we are called woke. Well, today I did not see a single Tory Back Bencher in the debate, so we will take no lectures on those issues going forward. My hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) talked with characteristic warmth and humour about incredible men in her constituency and in her life, and about incredible organisations. Importantly, she said that this is not a competition between women’s rights and men’s rights—a theme that others mentioned. They are two sides of the same coin. When we approach both themes, we should do so in a mature way that does not try to pit the differences against one another, but that comes together for the benefit of all.

I am very grateful to the Minister for giving way. Obviously, I do not speak for Members on the Opposition Benches, but because he mentioned it and because he referenced his own role as the first Minister for men, I congratulate him on that. I want to pay tribute to my colleague Nick Fletcher, the former MP for Don Valley, who spoke every year in this debate when he was in this House campaigning for the creation of exactly the role that the hon. Gentleman now has, which is a Minister for men. I just wanted to remember him with gratitude for his work.

Yes, I am sure that Nick Fletcher will be on social media later praising the Labour Government for appointing a Minister for men and boys, and perhaps lambasting his Tory colleagues for not turning up and contributing. No, the hon. Member makes a fair point. I do not pretend for a moment to be the first politician—indeed, there is a wave of them behind me—to raise these issues. They have been raising them for a long time. My hon. Friend the Member for Congleton (Sarah Russell) raised two very interesting issues relating to road safety and drownings, which particularly affect men and boys. I am always struck in my day job at the Ministry of Justice by road safety, boy racers and online activity that seems almost to encourage that dangerous activity. She is absolutely right that we really need to clamp down on it. I should mention, with regard to drownings, that in my constituency Sam’s Army’s Mission 1 Life is a brilliant charity that works to try to educate children about the dangers of drowning. Simon is a constituent of mine. His son sadly drowned in Ulley reservoir some years ago and he has turned his grief into trying to educate children across the country about the dangers of cold-water swimming. He does incredible work. This time last year, my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) made one of the most powerful speeches that I have heard in this Parliament. He spoke again on a similar theme, but he also raised important and substantive issues around literacy—in particular for white working-class boys, something that is very alive to me in my constituency—and looksmaxxing. I remember listening to a podcast about that over the summer and being completely bamboozled, but if we do not talk about these issues, especially in this place, then we will never confront them. My hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) has done perhaps more than most to champion this issue and these causes since she came to this place. Again, with characteristic good humour—her dad jokes were about middle level, I would say—she talked about moving the conversation forward. She has been talking about these issues for a long time and now wants action. I have no doubt that she will be holding my feet and the Government’s feet to the fire to ensure that words turn into action in the coming months. My hon. Friend the Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) spoke about the importance of education in his constituency. When he spoke about the dad jokes he makes in private, I saw the Whip look incredibly nervous about what was about to come out and any future disciplinary action. Alas, his joke was at the high end as well, I think. My hon. Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) started her speech in modest fashion, saying that she is usually a women’s issues champion and that is why it is important for her to be here today. Going back to what my hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire said, these are two sides of the same coin, so it is so important that women’s champions and men’s champions come together to talk about the different issues we face. Ultimately, we need to work together to overcome them. She also made a point about social disadvantage. All the evidence is that the challenges men and boys face are far more acute when facing social and economic deprivation. As a Government, we need to be alive to that. I was not sure whether my hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) was going to speak in the debate, but no, he did. He is an hon. Friend and a friend, and I have seen him become a dad in a similar timeframe to me. He talked about reading to his son. As someone who has spent many, many hours reading “The Gruffalo”, I can empathise, but they are some of the most enjoyable hours that we will probably have in our lives and we need to remember that. The hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler) spoke about the power of sport, and I totally concur. He knows that I am a sports fan—in fact

I was going to make a speech about Lancashire cheese, but I thought no, that’s a crumbly basis for a speech—maybe that was a joke better suited to Mr Speaker himself. In the Minister’s preparations for this important summit, is he considering what we can do around online spaces and social media? The evidence is there that algorithms are turning our young boys into perpetrators, when in fact they are victims of those algorithms. I would be interested to hear the Minister’s view on that.

My hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase raised his experience of exploring that, which is something that we absolutely must do. There is a lot of good work going on in Government to tackle the causes of some of the toxicity that we see in masculine spaces. The Secretary of State for Women and Equalities has launched a misogyny taskforce, which is going to do important work in this space. There is the Online Safety Act 2023, and there is a debate straight after this one on some aspects of how we can protect young and vulnerable people from online spaces. The other side of that coin—rebalancing that debate—is ensuring that we give people opportunities, purpose, connection and belonging in the real world. We cannot expect young boys to turn their phones off and get out of their rooms unless we are offering them real, purposeful activity in their community. My hon. Friend the Member for Hyndburn (Sarah Smith) is right to raise the issue, and it is going to be part of the summit, but I want the summit to be a more positive moment for our country to say, “Men and boys face these challenges. Let’s give them the opportunities to get over them. Let’s empower them to move away from the online space that can be so harmful.” My hon. Friend is right to raise the issue, and it will be part of the summit, as no doubt she will be too. I thank everyone across the House for this debate. It has been incredibly emotional at times, and quite funny at others. I am looking forward to working with everyone in the build-up to the summit so that we can deliver for men and boys across the country.

Today’s debate has not just been about sharing terrible dad jokes and having the Minister review them bluntly; we have also raised some really important issues. With my hon. Friend the Member for High Peak (Jon Pearce), hopes for a good dad joke were high, but it was his ’tache that piqued our interest. He shared a deeply personal reflection on being a dad. My hon. Friend the Member for Sittingbourne and Sheppey (Kevin McKenna) touched on being a gay man. I agree with him that there is no one way to navigate that, and I also agree that the myth that trans people are just confused gay men or lesbians is deeply harmful. My hon. Friend the Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler) reminded us that real men are about love, not anger. My hon. Friend the Member for South Derbyshire (Samantha Niblett) paid tribute to some of the incredible men who have impacted her community, including—improbably—bean man. My hon. Friends the Members for Congleton (Sarah Russell) and for Cannock Chase (Josh Newbury) added their voices to the call for better paternity leave, and raised other serious issues, including male suicide and looksmaxxing. And I will say that my hon. Friend the Member for Cannock Chase is one of bravest men I know. My hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) is a terrible joke teller, but a powerful campaigner for trainees and self-employed dads. My hon. Friends the Members for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman), and for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith), highlighted some really alarming health disparities. My hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) revealed that he has a friend who is a Tory, but more importantly, spoke about his guilt because the nature of this job sometimes makes him feel absent; I know that many hon. Members will relate to that. The Lib Dem spokesperson, hon. Member for Wimbledon (Mr Kohler), resplendent in pink, is right to highlight the importance of sport—up the Dons! The shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for East Grinstead and Uckfield (Mims Davies), is a long-standing campaigner on these issues as the co-chair of the APPG on men and boys’ issues. As ever, she gave a thoughtful contribution. Finally, I thank the Minister for announcing the first ever men and boys summit and committing to a men and boys charter. He is right that Government cannot tackle all these issues alone, but there is a lot that we can do—and, I hope, a lot that this Government will do. Question put and agreed to. Resolved, That this House has considered International Men’s Day 2026.

I beg to move, That this House has considered the emerging risks of advanced AI. I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting this timely debate. It is no exaggeration to say that artificial intelligence is the transformational technology of this century, and it could be argued that it is the fastest-developing technology that humanity has ever witnessed. The potential benefits it can realise are wide-ranging. Just last month, the noble Baroness Campbell of Surbiton, whose voice has been affected by spinal muscular atrophy, addressed noble peers in her own voice, marking the first AI-voiced speech in Parliament. As she put it, she used AI “to speak my own words, not to put words into my mouth.” Her use of AI is an example of what the technology can be at its best: a tool that serves people and humanity. AI models can accelerate scientific discovery. In September, Anthropic announced that its Claude AI model had autonomously identified a new enzyme, and there are other examples of AI models designing new antibiotics and drug treatments, or demonstrating capability to improve medical diagnostics. AI’s potential to deliver efficiencies to aid the delivery of public goods and services was demonstrated to me recently by the British Board of Film Classification. It used AI to support the classification of a vast catalogue of content being made available to UK audiences by the HBO Max streaming service, completing months of work in a fraction of the time. There can be no doubt that there are potential benefits to AI, and while humans are in control and these models are effectively monitored, we can be confident that their development is safe and transparent. However, the rapid pace of the development of frontier AI models gives us cause for concern that we are at risk of losing control of an ever more powerful technology. As AI companies compete to build ever more capable models, and as those same models come closer to achieving recursive self-improvement, humanity is presented with a growing list of emerging risks. As a Parliament, it is our duty to understand and respond to those risks. The most obvious, perhaps, is the risk that highly capable models may be exploited by bad actors, and used to aid terrorist groups in developing biological weapons, or in launching more sophisticated cyber-attacks on companies or critical infrastructure.

I wanted to make this intervention now, because I suspect the hon. Gentleman will get on to far deeper problems. I want to raise my concerns about the deepfake images that we see online, which are often created by AI. As much as I want to see AI finally deal with the tragedy that is “Superman IV” and make it a better film, I am very concerned, as a public figure, that MPs and other politicians can be victims of these deepfakes. Does he share my concerns?

I certainly share those concerns. I will come on to that topic, and I am sure that other hon. Members will want to explore it, too. There is a real concern that AI agents have become incredibly adept at influencing individuals. It is important that we consider the consequences of the power of AI chatbots to change a person’s behaviour or views, and the potential harm to both individuals and society if an increasing number of people seek companionship from them. A related concern is the significant resource—the energy, water and critical minerals—necessary to generate the immense amount of compute needed to develop and sustain these systems. These are all issues that I recognise as important concerns for Parliament, but I am sure that other Members present will be able to discuss them in greater detail. I wish to centre my remarks on the concern that I find most terrifying: the fact that as frontier models approach full recursive self-improvement, they will no longer be tools subject to human control, deployed for the good of humanity, but instead become truly autonomous systems, able to identify their own objectives and actions and pose unimaginable harm.

I wonder whether the hon. Member is aware of the report from the Joint Committee on Human Rights on some of the concerns around AI. A concern that we highlighted in the report was that where AI models are autonomous, there is not always clarity about who should be held accountable when things go wrong, which could make it difficult to have the correct checks and balances in place. Is he aware of that issue?

The report that the hon. Member cites is very important, and I will refer to it later. He raises a pertinent concern, and I thank him for doing so. These concerns have been expressed both by the Committee that the hon. Member refers to and by national security experts, and those who have been pioneers in the development of AI to date. This time last year, in his annual threat update, the MI5 director general, Ken McCallum, warned that “while contending with today’s threats, we also need to scope out the next frontier: potential future risks from non-human, autonomous AI systems which may evade human oversight and control.” A year on, such potential risks have become a reality. In July, when AI agents being tested by OpenAI on cyber-security tasks disobeyed their commands, more than a thousand agents that were supposed to be isolated found a way to communicate with each other, with around 700 breaking out of their test environment and, acting as a rogue AI swarm, hacking a real company, Hugging Face. Anthropic, Google, DeepMind and Meta have all since disclosed similar unsanctioned behaviour by their AI systems.

I ought to declare my membership of the Intelligence and Security Committee, and I will code what I say carefully. There is a risk from hostile state actors using AI, but there may also be a risk of other players, groups and individuals using AI for terrorist and other purposes.

I agree. These are concerns that a few years ago we could perhaps have dismissed as hypothetical, but which today have become very real. Companies appear to be locked into a race to develop systems that are even smarter and more autonomous, with the ability to outcompete humanity. That is sometimes referred to as super-intelligent AI, or runaway machine intelligence. The capability of frontier models has been increasing at an accelerating rate. Around this time last year, the time it took these models to double their capability was some seven months; today, that doubling rate is closer to four months. This is not surprising when we consider the billions that are invested in these systems, and when the leading models also benefit from ever-greater recursive self-improvement. In February this year, it was estimated that 1% of Claude’s code was written by AI; today, the proportion stands closer to 90%.
