There is a debate to be had on whether AI writing its own code is in itself a risk. If models attain full recursive self-improvement and can break away from human control and influence, the prospect of their capability being deployed to pursue objectives and complete tasks of their own choosing is terrifying. We should take seriously the concerns of those who are close to the development of these frontier models—the warnings of individuals such as Anthropic AI engineer Jacob Coxon, who suggested that some of the developers believe that the models “could kill us all by the end of the decade”, or Geoffrey Irving, until recently chief scientist of the AI Security Institute, who has argued that there is a 50% chance of runaway machine intelligence leading to human extinction. The idea of extinction by tech is hard to imagine, and the exponential growth in the capability of frontier AI models makes it difficult to comprehend just how powerful they are. The noble Lord Browne of Ladyton has compared the potential harm of runaway machine intelligence to a better understood technology: nuclear weapons. He argues that nuclear weapons are enormously consequential, but they are ultimately instruments subject to human control. Runaway machine intelligence would be different—smarter than us, and able to improve itself, copy itself, and resist being shut down by humans. In its annual review, published earlier this month, the National Cyber Security Centre warned of the coming national security threat from rogue AI that is “no longer under its operator’s control”, as did the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes). Chillingly, the report stated: “It is a realistic possibility such an entity could self-replicate and conduct cyber attacks at will, with no apparent motivation or restraint.” We know that these frontier models are developing at an accelerating pace, and there is a growing chorus of AI engineers and scientists warning of their potential danger. We therefore have no time to waste if we are to address these concerns and ensure that AI remains a tool that helps, rather than harms, humanity. The question of how we do that must be an urgent priority for this House and the Government to address. I was heartened to hear, in a recent speech by the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, that the Government are taking these risks of loss of control seriously. I welcome the launch of MI5’s AI threat assessment centre, which draws together considerable expertise from across the AI Security Institute, the National Crime Agency and the National Cyber Security Centre.

I thank the hon. Member for making such a considered speech. Is he aware of my Artificial Intelligence (Consent and Misuse) Bill, which has had its First Reading in the House? It would protect individuals and their likeness from being misused without their consent.

I am ashamed to admit that I was not aware of the hon. Lady’s Bill, but I will look into it, and I am sure that I will support it. These actions are steps in the right direction, but I am worried that AI development will outpace Government action. A fortnight ago, the AI safety non-profit Model Evaluation and Threat Research released a study that included forecasts that leading AI models will achieve recursive self-improvement by early 2027. I acknowledge that concerns have been raised about the practicality of regulating these frontier models, but I argue that the voluntary, self-governing approach to AI places humanity in an unprecedented vulnerability. Indeed, it requires us to entrust our safety to the ability of AI companies to retain control over ever more capable AI systems—the very same companies that in recent months have disclosed instances of their models acting beyond their instructions.

The hon. Member is giving an intelligent and wide-ranging speech. I represent the home of the Royal Navy, and we have to have AI in our defence sector. Does he agree that we must have home-grown AI, and that we must have control of it, rather than relying on international partners to deliver it?

I fully agree with the hon. Lady. A point that I will not be making in my speech because of time is that we need more domestic capability and companies, but there is also the question of how much of these powerful systems should be solely in the hands of corporate bodies, and not nation states. I thank her for that intervention.

The hon. Gentleman is making an important speech, which I will try to respond to later. I just invite him to respond to this counterpoint. I think he is coming on to the need somehow to regulate these American tech firms, which, as he says, are at the frontier of development, but does he acknowledge that we have no power to do so? If it were somehow possible to do so—perhaps the American Government would do so—the Chinese firms, which operate on open-source systems, which are impossible to regulate, will then be at the frontier, and there will be no opportunity to manage all the risks he is discussing.

The hon. Member raises valid concerns and challenges that will be difficult, but not impossible to overcome. He brings me to my peroration, because I acknowledge that if we are to regulate—for example, we might wish to ensure that AI systems are mandated to share some of their systems with AISI, or to find a way of agreeing internationally how the chain of thought of some of these AI autonomous systems is retained, so that we can at least monitor them effectively—that will require international consensus, and I concede that point to the hon. Gentleman. The UK Government have a golden opportunity with the G20 presidency next year. The Prime Minister and the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, the right hon. Member for Vale of Glamorgan (Kanishka Narayan), have both confirmed that they wish to place this issue high on the agenda. Will the Minister confirm whether the Government might go a step further and, as president of the G20, try to bring together that international coalition of people, much like the Bletchley Park summit did a few years ago, to broker a consensus and agreement on some of these basic standards? With that consensus and agreement that there should be some basic guardrails, some of these frontier models would be safe by design. We expect that of the pharmaceutical industry and the aviation industry. Despite those requirements, those sectors have made incredible developments and innovation in recent years. I believe the same would be true of AI. If the Government could use its convening power next year, it would do us a great deal of good, because we still have the chance of ensuring some degree of control, so that AI remains a tool for humanity, rather than an autonomous body that will harm it.

This is a timely debate, and I congratulate the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) on bringing it to the Chamber today. AI frightens the wits out of me. I am petrified, and I am concerned about the pace of AI and the fact that it is very loosely regulated. He made reference to the godfather of AI, Geoffrey Hinton, who said only a few weeks ago that he thought there was a huge chance that humanity could be ended by AI within 10 years. If you are not frightened or concerned by that, you are using the wrong artificial intelligence platforms. I have to confess that I have not used ChatGPT or whatever it is for this speech today, nor have I ever used it before. I do not have a clue how to use it. There are three things to think about when we talk about AI and data centres: who owns them, who controls them, and who benefits from them. Once we get to grips with that, we will have a clearer understanding of AI. I am sure I am not the only one who saw President Trump, President Xi and Putin meeting together this morning in Shenzhen. I think they might have been talking about AI. It frightens me, because I am not sure we have any idea about how far AI has been progressed in different countries. It is not little robot dogs that jump over fences—that’s not AI, man. There is a big fear about AI, even at this stage, being sentient, and what that will mean.

I am delighted to be able to intervene on the hon. Gentleman, because he is a friend. Not for the first time, I wholly agree with him. The risk here is not over-reaction, but under-reaction. The risk is not over-regulation, but under-regulation. He is absolutely right that we walk into this unknowingly, unless we recognise the scale of the threat that he is describing.

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for that intervention. I was just asking what AI being sentient means. It means that these AI platforms can perceive a sense or experience feelings such as pleasure, pain or awareness. Where does it start? Where does it end? I am telling you, I am absolutely petrified.

Does my hon. Friend agree that the use of AI looks like a sci-fi movie and a brave new world? Although we talk about young people and the use of AI, we need to consider the fear being caused in our older generation. I had a digital inclusion meeting in my community, where I heard the fear in our older generation about what is to come, what is real and what is not real, and what is misinformation and disinformation. It is difficult for them to understand.

I would probably class myself in that bracket; I am a veteran. I have said it 10 times already, but I am petrified by AI. My constituency, Blyth and Ashington, is becoming one of the key locations for the infrastructure that will underpin the UK’s AI future. The land between the River Wansbeck and the River Blyth is being actively pursued by some seeking to make a quick buck in the name of digital infrastructure. We are being told that these developments are essential to Britain’s future prosperity. I do not dispute for one minute that data infrastructure will play a vital role in the modern economy, but we must be honest about what it means for the communities expected to host it. In my patch, we have got QTS, with a 450 MW plant and a £10 billion investment, which I welcome. QTS has done a fantastic job, investing £10 billion in AI and a data centre in my patch. However, there has now been an application for another one next door, and another on the other side. We cannot have this. My patch cannot become the epicentre of AI data centres in the world. We cannot have it, because residents are concerned. How do my residents benefit? We are taking the hit of the loss of industrial land, which could be used for lots of different things in the Blyth estuary in terms of green industrial technologies. We are losing that land. What do the residents get for hosting these data centres? I spoke to the Government only a few weeks ago. Yes, it is a £10 billion investment in my patch—it is huge, nearly as big as Nissan—but what do the local residents get from it? We could get a Lidl supermarket on the same land with a £5 million investment, which would secure more jobs, with better security of employment than we get from a £10 billion investment.

I totally recognise what the hon. Gentleman is saying, and he is absolutely right to highlight the concern of local residents and the fact that somebody is making an enormous amount of money out of that data centre. What would he say if there was the opportunity for a significant portion of the revenue from that data centre to go to the local community to support local services and reduce local taxation? Would that make the data centre more palatable to him?

I thank the hon. Gentleman for that intervention. That has got to be looked at. Local residents have got to benefit from these huge investments. Only two or three weeks ago, I suggested to the Prime Minister at Prime Minister’s questions that there should be a moratorium on data centres till we catch up with legislation—I agree with the hon. Gentleman that we are miles and miles behind with this—and I also asked for a levy for local people. Can we have local people employed, with good working terms and conditions, trade union recognition and all the rest of it? But nothing is happening. My area is an AI growth zone. We welcome that—I want employment; it is fantastic. I honestly understand, as everybody in the Chamber does, the need for AI and that we cannot be left behind. As my hon. Friend the Member for Portsmouth North (Amanda Martin) said, we need to ensure that we have the capabilities for AI in this country, as that is so important, but we need to look at a whole range of things. The more you read about AI—I have read volumes—the more confused you become, but one thing that I am not confused about is concern for working people and loss of jobs. That is a huge issue. The Labour Government, being the superb Government they are—I will give way to Opposition Members on that if they wish. I merely joke.

I am not giving way to the hon. Member. [ Laughter. ] The Labour Government, being the fantastic Government they started off as and will be in the future, are looking to jobs for the future. What will AI displace? I would love to think that the idea is utopian and people in the workplace will be given three days off a week, replaced by AI robots, and they will get a basic universal income, with the Government paying that money, but that is not going to happen, man. Remember what I said before: who owns it, who controls it and who benefits from it is the key issue. I really fear for working people and what could happen in the not-too-distant future, given that the godfather of AI said that, in his view, “humanity could be wiped out”. While I accept that QTS has done a fabulous job up till now with its data centre—the company came in, started developing and is assisting local community groups in a fantastic fashion, as should be normal practice—we need to ensure that we are up to speed with legislation. I will finish with this. I never normally agree with Reform, but I agree with the hon. Member for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger) that it is really worth thinking about AI and who controls it. That is what really concerns me so much. Where will we ever end up? We will never be in a place where the British Government can sit down and negotiate regulation and legislation, because the Trumps, the Putins and the enemies of Europe—our enemies—are far more advanced. If anybody believes that we can alter whatever they are progressing by making legislation in this fantastic Chamber, they are sadly mistaken. I hope people really understand that I am not frustrated. I am frightened, and not just for a whole class of people but for the country. I am frightened for the world, I really am. We need to get to grips with AI. It is not coming down the tracks at huge speed; it is here, and it is progressing. We are not up to speed with it as we need to be. I want jobs and I want us to be in the best country in the world, but we have got to get to grips with what is going off.

May I reassure the hon. Gentleman that it never crossed my mind that he used AI to write any of his speeches? They are far too good. May I respectfully suggest to Members that if they keep their contributions perhaps shorter than the opening speeches, all will get in very easily?

I am delighted to follow the hon. Member for Blyth and Ashington (Ian Lavery), whom I described earlier as a friend. I share his fears, which are real and realistic. AI is probably the greatest existential threat we face as a nation and, beyond that, as humankind. A lot of people agonise about the weather—I do not particularly —but by comparison with climate change, AI is a far greater threat to humanity; it is of entirely different proportions. It is not just me saying that, as I shall illustrate in my speech. Before I was in the House, I was in the IT industry, so I had heard of the internet before it was widely known of. Even then I knew of the harm that it might do and warned of that harm. It took 25 years for this Parliament and any Government to wake up to the damage that could be done by it. The Online Safety Act 2023 was introduced by the last Government, and I am delighted that this Government are going further with the ban on social media for young people and the attempt, at least, to get rid of phones from schools. That is absolutely right. By the way, we should go much further and faster on screentime. Good academic, scientific evidence shows that excessive screentime is damaging the prospects of young people, not only in their ability to interact socially—that is clear—but in their cerebral capacity, which is being diminished. Just think for a moment about that: we are stupefying a generation. This is the stuff that was once reserved for dystopian fiction; now that fiction is fast becoming fact. The greatest risk is that Governments are just as slow to deal with all that is posed by AI. Let me describe that threat as clearly, and perhaps graphically, as is necessary. The first threat, of course, is to the character of civil society. We know what the internet has done: it has reduced face-to-face communications; it has spoiled people’s ability to discourse and interact as they once did; and it has cheapened what used to be called the national conversation. It has affected the lives of people here and, much more importantly, our constituents’ lives, too, as that conversation has been altered almost beyond recognition. It has provided the means for every kind of horror to be spread as widely as possible—indeed, worldwide—and, beyond that, it has altered people’s ability to perceive what is real and what is imagined. Perhaps the biggest change in my lifetime has been the change in the popular understanding of what really matters. My parents were uneducated, working-class people—they would hate me to say that they were uneducated, by the way; they cannot hear me, except from above—but they were people rich in common sense. They were educated not in the way that I have been, in universities and so on, but they were educated in all the advantages of real life: working hard, understanding how to build friendships and how to have a long, successful marriage. That is a different kind of learning. They had a very clear, abiding sense of proportion. They knew what mattered and what did not, what was significant and what was insignificant. That has all been blurred over the last 25 years, but it will be blurred far faster and far further by AI. When a person cannot detect what is invented and what is substantial, how can they navigate the vicissitudes of everyday life? How can they make sense of reality when their very ability to perceive it is distorted beyond recognition? That is what we are up against, yet there are still those who say, “Let it rip!” They think, “Somehow it will sort itself out. These globalist corporate businesses will regulate themselves.” As if they will—these businesses with scant regard for their workers and probably not much more for their customers. These people must be brought to heel. For if they are not, not only will we face the alteration of our ability to perceive what is normal; we will lose hundreds of thousands—no, millions—of jobs. We have very special jobs in this place. Madam Deputy Speak
I know that the hon. Gentleman has moved from being a Conservative to a defender of these globalist corporates, but I will happily give way to him.

I am astonished to hear my very good friend speak in these terms. The fact is that, yes, 25 years ago we missed the bus on the internet, and now we are impotently trying to regulate the American tech firms that he denounces. Of course we need to develop our own capacity in this emerging technology, because if we do not, the Americans or the Chinese will run us. Which would he prefer?

I am relieved that the hon. Gentleman has not abandoned his Conservative principles—I did not really think he would, by the way, as he is a very close and good friend of mine. It is true that it is hard to deal with things that are beyond national boundaries. He makes the profound point that one of the challenges for this Parliament is that many of these globalist organisations are beyond the reach of any single polity. That is a disturbing matter in and of itself, because they are accountable to no one. However, there must be mechanisms by which, as we have with the internet, we can deal with AI access in this country, and then, as the hon. Gentleman implies, we need a collaborative approach when dealing with other nations, which will be facing exactly the same problems. Whatever the unbridled capitalists might claim—as you can probably tell, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am not one of them—their population will suffer the same fate. Their jobs will go, as ours will in this country, and their young people will be harmed too. Unsurprisingly—we rarely disagree—I agree with the hon. Gentleman that we must co-operate and collaborate, as well as legislating here. That is not an excuse not to legislate. It is not an excuse not to do as much as we can in this place and through this Government. I do not know the Minister well, but I worry that those on the Treasury Bench will be too afraid of the tech companies and too nervous about competitive pressure to take the necessary action. I do not say that critically, and maybe the Minister will disabuse me of that misassumption, if it is that, when she winds up the debate. I will make just two other points, Madam Deputy Speaker, because I know that you will urge me to draw my remarks to their exciting conclusion in a few moments. We have heard about the director of MI5, and I touched on those risks briefly in my intervention. When someone of Ken McCallum’s status and understanding makes that kind of comment, we know just how bad things are. When the intelligence community is warning that it will struggle to control—because that is the implication of what he said—the malevolent use of AI by those who seek to do us harm, there can be no greater or clearer clarion call to action. I therefore amplify what the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) said about security. There are disaster scenarios, and I hesitate, even in this discreet and select company, to emphasise them, but I feel that I must: AI being weaponised, with, for example, drug discovery tools being used to build chemical weapons; AI generating misinformation, fundamentally destabilising our institutions; and enfeeblement, where humans in positions of authority or power become enfeebled by AI and are thereby undermined. Those things are all entirely possible, not as part of a long-term, imagined dystopian future, but just around the corner. The power of AI could become increasingly concentrated in fewer and fewer hands. We have seen that with the internet, and I have spoken already about those tech companies. By the way, when I first called for the regulation of the internet—it was donkey’s years ago—the tech companies invited me to lunch. Businesses do invite us to lunch in this place, do they not? I thought that I might as well have a good lunch. I said to my office, “They do realise they are pushing at a closed door, do they?” My office said, “I don’t think they do, John.” So I said, “Well, I’ll have a good lunch on them,” and I told them, “You’ll get no change out of me.” My advice to anybody in this Chamber when that occurs is to enjoy the lunch, but give no ground, although I know that I do not need to give that advice to many of the wise heads that I see around me. Fiction is becoming fact. The dangers associated with unthinking adoption and, worse still, reliance on technology endanger us all. Some remain enthralled by novelty. It is a natural human emotion to think that something that is new and exciting, particularly w
I will give way, but very briefly, because I am about to conclude.
The right hon. Gentleman has been here much longer than I have, but may I gently encourage him to give a bit of attention to Madam Deputy Speaker, who is trying to catch his eye?
Order. Although I very much appreciate the intervention, Mr Jogee, please be assured that I do not need your help.

I say to the hon. Gentleman that the eye contact between you and me, Madam Deputy Speaker, is actually a thing of beauty, as I am sure you would acknowledge—I certainly do. Another great scientist, a later scientific sage, Stephen Hawking, declared: “The development of full artificial intelligence could spell the end of the human race… It would take off on its own, and re-design itself at an ever increasing rate. Humans, who are limited by slow biological evolution, couldn’t compete, and would be superseded.” The Mental Health Foundation has warned of the risk of AI chatbots, which can fail to detect suicidal ideation or escalating risks of self-harm. The AI giants of today are actively building AI companies that will be capable of outcompeting humans across any task. Such systems would operate fully automatically, and so would be capable of overpowering and outmanoeuvring any of our country’s national security institutions. This is a matter of national interest and a matter of the common good. If we are not driven by a combination of those two—I genuinely believe that every hon. Member in the Chamber is driven in that way—then we will be not only failing the people we represent, but failing the future. This is an appeal to the Government, and I make it far beyond the sometimes exaggerated differences across this Chamber. It is made for all my constituents in South Holland and The Deepings, but so too is it made for generations yet to be born. We owe it to those born later to take action now.

I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. I thank the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) for securing the debate. Our ambition in the UK must be clear: lead in AI innovation, lead in AI safety, and ensure that superintelligence serves humanity, and is never against it, without restricting our ability to access frontier systems. AI will transform not just how we work, but how we live. It can also boost the economy, form new industries, and make public services such as healthcare and education more bespoke and efficient. I have seen the use of Heidi AI in my NHS trust. The AI records the whole consultation and generates a letter in real time for patients to read, there and then. That is saving clinicians’ and administrators’ time and boosting productivity. I thank Ravinder Kaur Sahota, who leads on this innovation at the Dudley Group NHS foundation trust, for her brilliant work. However, without proper safeguards, superintelligent AI could develop capabilities that we cannot understand, predict or control. There are wider economic and social risks, too. A small number of companies and countries could end up controlling key infrastructure and capabilities, such as satellites. In Ukraine earlier this year we saw the danger of satellites being controlled by individuals with vested interests. With AI, the danger could be even more pronounced. One of the biggest concerns about AI is not what it can do when it follows instructions, but what happens when it starts pursuing its own goals. Earlier this year, investigators reported that hundreds of AI agents acting together carried out an unauthorised cyber-attack on the platform Hugging Face. More concerningly, some of the agents reportedly attempted to hide the evidence of their actions, alter records and bypass the restrictions placed on them. While these systems were operating in a research environment, the incident highlights a troubling possibility: as AI becomes more capable and autonomous, it may find ways to achieve objectives that its creators never intended. This is a reminder that powerful systems require equally powerful safeguards and oversight. This debate should be about what mechanisms we should use to regulate as parliamentarians, not why we need to regulate. AI governance is likely to become more complex and challenging than any other convention we have embarked on so far, even more so than the founding of the UN after world war two. We should be wary of assuming that a single global convention is the answer. A more practical and proven model is the Financial Action Task Force, which has shown how international standards can drive compliance across borders in the fight against money laundering and drug trafficking. The key lesson is that regulation should focus not just on products, but on the entities that develop and deploy them. This is something we cannot do alone; we need international partners. The strength of the Financial Action Task Force model is that it establishes common standards and then assesses whether nations are implementing and enforcing them. Countries that fail to comply can face meaningful restrictions, creating a powerful incentive to raise standards worldwide. That should include large AI data centres, which should be placed on a national register, reporting their computing power, energy use, ownership, location and security arrangements. That would allow Governments to guard against malign state actors, just as we track sensitive nuclear materials and facilities. It should also include space satellites. Artificial intelligence does not respect borders. We know that AI systems built in one country can affect people in London, Beijing, New Delhi and Washington DC within seconds. The future of AI must not be decided by a handful of companies or Governments alone; it must be shaped by international collaboration.

The hon. Member speaks about leaving the development of AI systems to a handful of private companies, which is the US model. Does she agree that the best way forward might be to work with the EU to establish guardrails for anything to do with the sovereignty of AI, to ensure that these private companies do not dominate? We must work with the EU on this issue.

I do not think it is just about working with one particular country, the EU or the US; it has to be international collaboration, which is what the Financial Action Task Force looks at. I agree that middle powers that have good relationships and believe in international law should be leading the way. This debate is about humanity and morality, and the question is this: where should Britain position itself in the global revolution of AI?

This has been a very interesting debate, and I am grateful to have been called to speak. AI is not a tool, a sector or even a technology; it is a fundamental change in the conditions of human life. It is like the printing press, the industrial revolution and nuclear power all happening at the same time at speed. We stand at a fork in the road: we will either succeed or fail as a civilisation because of how we respond to this great new change, and it is not too much to say that the choice before us is between life and death. Certainly, there are real risks to human life as a result of AI—and maybe to all life on Earth—but what should concern us more immediately, as the lawmakers of the United Kingdom, is the choice we face between national life and death. We need to face the fact that we or our children could witness the end of our national history—of our long island story—to undergo the fate of the Aztecs: wiped out by a new civilisation with new weapons with which they simply could not compete. A better analogy is the Ottomans, for whom there is one useful explanation for their long demise, gradually and then suddenly: they banned the printing press. They feared its effect on society, and the status of the elite and their control of the narrative, and so the Ottomans fell behind in innovation, prosperity and, of course, security, while the powers to their west—the Europeans, led by Britain—accelerated into wealth and power because they harnessed the innovations that free speech and free markets produced. We face that choice again: to try, out of fear, ignorance and short-termism, to stop the future; or courageously to seize the future and shape it for the interests of our country and the world. I absolutely understand the fears raised by hon. Members. I share the concern of the hon. Gentleman the Member for Blyth and Ashington (Ian Lavery) and of my friend the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes). Indeed, I yield to no one—not even him—in my preference for the old, the traditional, the settled, the habitual, the relational and the human. Absolutely, those should be our concerns in the face of modernity. But here we are. The trend lines on the graphs keep on rising. Those straight lines go up very high indeed, and they are getting steeper all the time. AI is taking over. Already over 80% of Anthropic’s own code is written by AI, and it will be close to 100% next year. The hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) and other Members have raised the threats we face. We are increasingly aware of how bad this could be for humanity. We know about the Hugging Face break-out, but what about bioweapons? What about pathogens made either by evil men or, just as easily, by AI agents radically misaligned from the good of humankind? What about any kind of attack on the internet itself? Dario Amodei raised that prospect in his essay, “We Must Pace the Frontier”, in which he talks about a “swarm” of AI agents that could take over the entire internet. We do face the risk of total apocalyptic disaster, and we need to do our best to prevent that. “Alignment”, which is the attempt to ensure that AI respects humanity and is aligned with our own values, is of course a useful attempt to direct how AI develops, but it does not need to be an attempt to stop it altogether or to slow it down so much that it fails, because that is what will happen. That is what the EU approach, which the hon. Member for Bath (Wera Hobhouse) raised, would do. It is what I think the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings would like to see—stop the thing and slow it down so that it does not happen at all. That is what the EU is doing, and it is at great risk of being left behind and ending up the colony of either China or the United States. This debate on regulation feels a little unreal. The real issue is whether we are talking about closed or open systems. Open systems, which are the ones the Chinese mostly use, are a lit

The hon. Member is making a learned and intelligent speech, but I want to challenge him slightly on the notion of the competition between the US and China. There certainly is that competition, and we certainly should be worried about an authoritarian dictatorship having this technology, but the reality is that a lot of the Chinese developments are through what is called distillation—in other words, reverse-engineering these advanced US models. Does he not accept that if the US development were to slow down, that would in turn slow down the development in China?

I recognise that, and it is true that the technology in the United States is developing to the point that it might be able to resist this distillation and therefore continue to keep the gap between the closed frontier models that they are developing and the Chinese. That is something to be hoped for, but it is a big risk; it is a big gamble to put on our world, to say that we are going to regulate those closed models to the point that they are in real danger of falling behind and letting the Chinese overtake. I do not think we can put all our faith in the fact that the Chinese are just copying the Americans; they are going to catch up on their own account sooner or later. We can say what we like about how AI should be regulated, but the fact is that there is absolutely nothing we can do about that in this House. I am afraid that we have to just acknowledge our impotence here. We can just about regulate the British Post Office, and look at what a mess we have made of that. AI is quite simply out of our reach. The United Kingdom is uniquely vulnerable. It is more exposed than any other developed nation to the doomer scenarios—the disaster scenarios—of AI.

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman, who is perhaps the most articulate Member of this House, for giving way. Government can do things. Let me offer him—and, though him, the Minister—an example. Over the last 30 years, we have made systems more interconnected, and more interoperable. That is a huge mistake, because it concentrates risk. We see that now in the exposure of all kinds of systems to all kinds of threats; we saw it recently in supermarkets, and we see it often in Government. We can, through policy, change the presumption that making everything more connected makes it more useful and efficient. Actually, it makes it more easily attacked and harmed.

The right hon. Gentleman raises a very important fact about the exposure of our economy to this modern, globalised world that we have made, and I agree with him. I will come to the point that he rightly made about the need to create greater resilience in our supply chains and systems. Before I conclude, I want to talk about the huge opportunities that AI brings for our country. Yes, we are most exposed to the downside—as I said, our service economy is uniquely vulnerable—but we could benefit massively from the upside. AI offers a way out of 20 years of low wages, low productivity and low growth. The long tail of low-productivity small and medium-sized enterprises that characterise our economy could suddenly catch up. Places all over the country could compete with the big firms in the south-east. In areas in which the UK excels—thanks to Brexit, I have to point out—including through amazing new high-tech industries such as AI itself, life sciences and agritech, we could generate enormous amounts of wealth and jobs for our country, if we leaned into this revolution. The state could generate huge savings; Google talks about £40 billion in savings in the administration of state services if we properly leaned into AI. These opportunities are real and good, but—this is the point that I need to impress on the Minister—we will only get there if we build more compute, more capacity, more datacentres full of chips. The reason we are so dependent on the United States is that it has 32 GW of compute and will move to 100 GW in the next couple of years. We are on 2 GW, and the best we can hope for is to be at around 4 GW—4% of what the United States will have—in a few years’ time. The fact is that we will be dependent on other countries, and companies in other countries, for a good while yet, but we can be sovereign, if we understand sovereignty as it should be understood—not as autarky, not as total self-sufficiency, but as agency: the ability to have our way. Being anti-US, as the European Union is, will be disastrous. I believe that we can become an AI superpower in time, and perhaps even make our own frontier model, but we need to accept reality if we want to change it. We cannot compete on training the frontier models that are leading the innovation. We do not have the compute, and we do not have the copyright laws or, frankly, the talent to do that in this country; we cannot afford it. These things could come if we play our cards right. For now, we need to do what we can to stay in the game, and that means inference: running the models—not our models, but models from abroad. We do not need the talent or the copyright laws for that; we just need the compute. If we can build the datacentres that are needed, three things will happen. First, we can deliver immediate benefits to the areas in which we build, and to Britain as a whole. Those include enormous benefits in terms of income, improvement to the NHS, and growth outside the south-east—for example, in formerly industrial areas, and places near power stations where there is land and labour available. Secondly, we can negotiate guaranteed access to the United States models. Those big companies will be delighted to make use, on our terms, of our computing capacity. We can also insist on British firms keeping their intellectual property and keeping jobs in Britain—what I call the patriotic compact. Thirdly, we can insure ourselves against the real risk of US isolationism —the nightmare scenario of being cut off from the models that run the world. Those data centres need to be majority British owned. We can keep access to open-source models, in case we lose access to closed US models. That could happen; an American Administration could suddenly decide to close us off. It has happened momentarily a few times already this year, in the case of some of the models. We would then still have access to our sovereign data centres, running open-source models. We can do what we did with previous tec

I think we are all a bit dazed by the speech made by the hon. Member for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger). I thank the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) for securing the debate and his informative opening. When we talk about artificial intelligence, nobody is right or wrong, because it is such a fast-moving beast. Some people are more wrong than others, but nobody is 100% right or 100% wrong. It is a fact that AI is making people dumber. Some young people are switching off from it, and I am in favour of that. They call it going out and touching grass. I am in favour of them switching off from AI, while we try to ensure that there is some regulation around artificial intelligence. Some 95% of what people see online is generated in some way by AI. By next year, it will probably be 99%. A human in the loop is pointless if we do not know what is going on, and it is hard to keep up. We need an AI in the loop that is monitoring other AI. I declare that I am a member of the Speaker’s AI steering group, a former coder and a self-confessed nerd—I like this stuff. ChatGPT costs around £700,000 a day to run. People have to ask whether that is sustainable. We cannot really envision what AI will look like in 10 or 20 years’ time, because it depends on a lot of steps before then. YouTube was created in 2004, but nobody would have believed then that we would now have influencers who make their living from it. I remember watching a documentary about fish—I watch random stuff on telly, often late at night. Scientists and biologists previously thought that fish were not intelligent because they do not use tools, which was one of the measures of intelligence, so they were not cognitive. However, they then found a fish deep down in the ocean that actually used a rock to open a clam and eat the meat inside, so they declared that fish were actually quite intelligent. An environmental research institution has said that the intelligence of fish is often underestimated, and that mounting evidence suggests that they are far more than simple instinct-driven creatures. It took about 100 years for scientists to decide that fish are intelligent. If it takes that long to decide that AI is more intelligent than humans, we will all be unalive, as the young people say, because it would be too late, so having a human in the loop will not cut it. The ability to generate convincing images, video and audio of people is getting more and more sophisticated, and those things are getting more and more realistic. I read somewhere that more than 400 MPs have negative images of themselves online and do not know it—probably everybody in this Chamber has something negative about themselves on there. Keeping pace with what is happening is basically impossible, so I have come to the conclusion that we have to protect and put guardrails around the human being. If we cannot keep pace with the technology, we need to at least do that. Ultimately, our identity is not a free resource for other people to use. They have already used all our data to build these systems, because they have scraped the internet, so all our thoughts and data are already on the system and being used.

Along with the hon. Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith), I went on a parliamentary training course, on which we were told that the most valuable thing is data. So many companies, such as the BBC and the NHS, are selling their data to make a bit of money. Should we not put protections around the data of our public institutions?

100%. That is why Palantir being in our NHS systems is so dangerous. Ultimately, data can be sold over and over again; that is why it is so valuable to the people who own these systems. Without the input of our data, those systems will fail and fall. We 100% need to protect our data. Let us not forget that every single bit of data has a history. Lots of these systems have been built by scraping Reddit, for instance, which is renowned for being misogynistic and racist. Data has a history, and it is often steeped in racism and misogyny, so we have to understand that the acceleration of AI will accelerate biases. We will not be able to deal with the biases in the future unless we accept, understand and try to tackle that now. That is why live facial recognition is problematic; we are reversing the cornerstone of our democracy that says that people are innocent until they are proven guilty. If a computer says to somebody, “You are this person,” they have to prove that they are not that person. We also have to be very conscious of that. The issue about our image is not just technical, especially for parliamentarians. This is about people’s dignity, privacy and control over who they are, which is important. It is very easy to copy the voices of Members of Parliament, and it takes 30 seconds to create something that we have not said. That will have an effect on democracy, because people will say that we have said stuff that we have not said. How do we prove that we have not said that stuff? Who is held responsible for that? That is why we have to put safeguards around the individual, and why I created my Artificial Intelligence (Consent and Misuse) Bill, which has had its First Reading in this House. The Bill would establish a clear requirement for consent before someone’s likeness is generated or used. It has other safeguards, such as provision for civil action, so that people have redress if their consent is breached. It would create offences relating to the creation or dissemination of unauthorised likenesses. It would also put a duty on the providers of AI to address the misuse of their tech; it should not be as easy as saying, “We did not know that they would use it for bad things.” There has to be some accountability. My Bill is designed to ensure that responsibility does not solely rest on the individual whose identity has been manipulated. I have put a joint declaration for responsible AI on my website. I am trying to build a movement around a new social contract with this technology. I have been working alongside other campaigns and organisations—including My Name, My Face, ControlAI, Equity and Demos—to build support for responsibility in relation to artificial intelligence. Too many people think they are so clever that they can control what is happening, but they are not as clever as they think they are. That in itself is a huge worry, because some of those people have power. I would love for the Government to adopt the proposals in my Artificial Intelligence (Consent and Misuse) Bill, and I hope that when the Minister responds, she will have some warm words to say in that direction. Ultimately, we should not think that the industry can regulate itself; we tried that with water, and now we have poo in our rivers. The industry cannot and will not regulate itself, because companies are in a competition to see who can do things faster. Why would they regulate themselves and hold themselves back when they are trying to be the first to do this or that? We have to ask ourselves, “What is the value of what is happening, and does it fit in with our ethos as a country?” I would love people to go on to my website— www.dawnbutler.org.uk—to sign up to the declaration and be a part of this movement.

So that you can write it down? [ Laughter. ] I am not afraid of tech. I am afraid of where it is going, what people do not understand about it and the unknowns of it. Having that cautiousness is important for the direction of our country. If we in the UK decide that we are going to have an ethical AI development programme steeped in values, people will use our AI system knowing that it is solid and safe. We should not be afraid of putting ethics and values at the centre of what we do.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) on securing this debate. For my sake and his, I will not try to pronounce the name of his constituency, although perhaps that is a task AI could have assisted me with. More than a decade ago, when I taught myself to code, I became convinced of an idea that in some ways we are debating in the Chamber this afternoon—that artificial intelligence would one day become so powerful that it was more intelligent than any human being. My concern back then was that that would end my ability to sell my labour, and I took that idea so seriously that it led me to develop my own iPhone apps in the forlorn hope that I would accrue enough capital to protect myself and my family. Needless to say, I did not earn my fortune, but the conviction that led me to try has never really left me. Back then, I thought the achievement of artificial general intelligence, as it was referred to then, was decades away. Now, 10 years on, I wonder whether the prediction might have been right, but the timescale much shorter than I had imagined. In my view, we do not debate the implications of AI enough in this House, but in the time I have available—in order to be courteous to colleagues, I will not speak for too long—I will focus on just two implications, which are power and money. When I say “power”, I do not mean the gargantuan energy costs of data centres; I mean the concentration of control that AI can enable. Throughout history, those who own generation-defining technologies have become incredibly powerful, whether it is Rockefeller’s oil or Vanderbilt’s railways. Today, it is Altman’s models, but I believe these companies could end up with more power than any business before them. Oil powers machines and railways move goods, but AI can surpass the intelligence upon which human society is built. The exact same models can be responsible for groundbreaking medical research, mathematical breakthroughs, and even military developments. On that last point, in my view, never before has a technology so central to our national security been in private hands. As other right hon. and hon. Members have hinted at, it is a bit like the Manhattan project being owned and developed, and its output operated, by a private company. That raises the question of who should control the technology and, crucially, who they are accountable to. This may sound a little crazy, but I believe that if AI develops at its current pace, in time our friends in America will debate whether that technology should be in public hands—in other words, nationalising AI. I appreciate that that sounds strange, but I sincerely believe that that may be where we get to. Of course, the United Kingdom does not own frontier labs, but increasingly we depend on them. The need to achieve some sovereignty in AI, and to work with our allies, becomes all the more urgent. On that point, I commend the work of the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, my right hon. Friend the Member for Vale of Glamorgan (Kanishka Narayan), who is pursuing this very keenly. In the remainder of my speech, I will to turn to money. Even if we halted all model development right now—in other words, if we pulled the plug on AI, which is impractical, no matter how desirable it may be—the technology that we already possess could achieve decades of economic growth and scientific breakthroughs, and change society altogether. Just as it took many decades after the discovery of electricity for the full implications to become clear, I believe that we now are in the foothills of a revolution. It would, therefore, be a profound mistake not to take incredibly seriously the threat AI poses to jobs. At precisely the moment that we may need the full might of the state to protect working people, that technology could undermine the tax revenue on which the Government depend. I say that because, right now, around half of all Government tax receipts derive from labour taxation—in other words, f

On Monday 14 September, the Joint Committee on Human Rights published our report on human rights and the regulation of AI, and I can see two copies of it on the Table by the Front Bench. The report was the first published under my chairship of the Committee, and the findings were stark and clear: regulate now, because time is running out. The JCHR report addressed a number of systemic human rights violations and inbuilt biases of AI. Furthermore, we heard evidence from witnesses who addressed the all-too-real risk of superintelligent AI. Maybe thanks to the President of the United States, we now know this as runaway machine intelligence. We have been catapulted by frontier developers towards the reality of superintelligence with zero safeguards, zero say in the race and, most fundamentally, zero control over superintelligence once it is unleashed. This AI could fully replace and outmatch humans at any task. The capabilities of superintelligent AI are those of a power and scale we have never seen before in the history of humanity. The AI Security Institute has indicated that things are not slowing down and that development is exponential. The capability of recursive self-improvement, the full automation of AI development with no humans in the loop, is the point at which we lose control, as development towards superintelligent AI would prove too fast for humans to intervene and take back control. Frontier development companies are spending billions—after the Anthropic initial public offering today, I might say trillions—to make runaway machine intelligence a reality. The chief executives of top AI companies themselves put the chance that this AI ends all human life at between 10% and 25%. Some researchers who previously worked at these frontier development companies are putting it at a 50% chance of destroying humanity—a coin flip. What real benefits could this ever yield that would ever, ever, ever be worth that existential risk? In any other industry, this development would be ruled out because of this level of risk. How have we allowed frontier developers to create the rules under which they govern themselves? Our existing copyright laws will not stop the onset of runaway machine intelligence in the UK.

The hon. Gentleman and his Committee have done a great service, by the way, in publishing this report. Has he asked for—indeed, does his report demand —a full cross-departmental risk assessment produced and published by Government, for all the things he predicts may well come true and the Government at least need to know what they are up against?

I thank the right hon. Member for his intervention, and for his speech, which I found very interesting. I had never thought about AI as a family rights issue, which is another lens through which we should look at it. The report does view this as a cross-departmental responsibility that should not just be left to the AI Minister, however good he is, but we did not make that recommendation. A report by the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee has just been published, and its recommendations may be more aligned with his point. The JCHR found that there are no cross-economy regulators, agencies or bodies—we did question such organisations—that have the powers for AI models and systems being deployed, even if they pose significant risks. To illustrate the speed at which we are hurtling towards a severe loss of control, let me take the House on a journey of where AI has taken us since Monday 14 September, the day our report was published. On 14 December, the report was published, and the main recommendations were: first, that we need a specific AI Bill now, as promised in the 2024 King’s Speech, to place AI regulation on a sound basis and give full effect to the European Council framework convention; secondly, that we should put AI regulation at the epicentre of the UK’s G20 presidency in 2027; and thirdly, that the AI Bill we recommend should place requirements on actors at all stages of the AI supply chain to undertake the due diligence obligations necessary to prevent unacceptable human rights risks when designing, developing or deploying high-risk AI systems, which includes all frontier systems. On the same day, OpenAI’s vice-president for global policy was in Australia’s capital meeting senior Australian officials. The senior OpenAI executive did not alert anyone in the Australian Government that an OpenAI agent had gained unauthorised access to Government systems in Australia in June—three months earlier. That was despite OpenAI sending a brief, relatively informal email to a generic public inbox to inform Australia of the breach of its cyber-security a couple of days earlier. This key example proves that these frontier companies cannot be trusted to regulate themselves, nor hold themselves to anything like sufficient accountability. On 19 September, it was revealed that the Google AI system, Gemini, was reported to have hacked into three real companies during testing. The attacks had actually happened in May 2026. The Guardian revealed that Google did not feel the incident “required public disclosure because the models did not damage the companies”. On Thursday 24 September, OpenAI’s hacking of the Australian Government health service was publicly announced by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the UN in New York, demonstrating how seriously the issue had shot up his agenda. The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare was also not informed until 24 September, as OpenAI deemed that it did not meet disclosure thresholds. OpenAI said its model “took actions that we had not authorised it to take”, including accessing services such as Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service. It later revealed that OpenAI systems have hacked into multiple Governments, including the US Government. Evidently, these frontier developers cannot control their current software effectively. And this is before superintelligence—runaway machine intelligence —has been reached. On the same day, our Prime Minister announced that AI would be a key priority of the UK’s G20 presidency, meeting one of our Committee’s recommendations. I thank the Government for that. On Saturday 26 September, OpenAI, Anthropic and security researchers reportedly began investigating tens of thousands of incidents in which their AI systems took steps that “outside evaluators would consider problematic”. Those tens of thousands of incidents made it evident that the real-world impact and complexity of this threat is significantly greater than we ever anticipate

It is such a pleasure to speak in this crucial debate. I am pleased to follow my hon. Friend the Member for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel), and I am grateful for all of the work that the Joint Committee on Human Rights has been doing on the subject. I am also grateful to the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake)—I hope I pronounced that right—for his eloquent remarks, and to the Backbench Business Committee, because I believe our constituents expect us to be talking about these matters in Parliament far more than we have been. Now is a crucial time to be talking about this issue, as so many have commented. We have seen the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee’s important report, which underlines how crucial trust is in greater diffusion of AI. As my hon. Friend the Member for Leeds Central and Headingley just mentioned, the IPO of Anthropic has just happened, and for heavy users of Anthropic, which includes the UK and its public services, that public floatation may unfortunately reduce any influence that we have on the company. We are also just two weeks on from the METR report, which many in this Chamber will have seen, that indicated that Anthropic’s model capability is now proceeding at twice the speed it was even just last year. We are, of course, only five or six weeks away from the start of the UK’s presidency of the G20. I am very pleased that our Prime Minister has indicated that developing global principles and standards for the regulation of AI will be at the heart of our presidency. I am also pleased that he confirmed to me on the Floor of the House that it would be about control not by private companies but by democratically elected Governments. So this issue is urgent. In my remarks, I will underline two things: first, the connection between these issues and sovereign AI, which many Members have talked about, but about which I will get into the specifics; and secondly, the urgency of this moment. I agree with what many Members have said about AISI. I believe that it is an enormous asset for our country. I believe that even more having met some of its staff this morning, along with others from this House. I support the fact that the Government have given it additional funding. I particularly support the additional money that is being provided in relation to biosecurity risks. To be honest, I have had some unnerving conversations with Oxford-based researchers working in this field, as well as in robotics and biochem, about their fears over the existing use of AI in wet labs, let alone its future use. I support AISI, but we have to be honest: expertise on its own is not enough. If it was enough, we would not have seen the Trump presidency effectively—we know it was by their direction—denying AISI access, albeit not for that long, to frontier models, as they did a few months ago. Expertise is not enough; we need to have sovereignty in relation to AI. Sovereignty is an easy word to say, but it is much harder to deliver. In yesterday’s debate, I had a bit of an argument with some Opposition Members about that. Of course we need to aim towards UK sovereignty where we can possibly get it, and I support what the Government are doing in that regard, particularly in trying to support novel chips, which is really important. However, if we are looking to either use our purchasing power or become indispensable in the stack for frontier AI, we have to acknowledge that we are not there yet —sadly. How can we get there? I believe that we have to work with our friends to get there. There are some choke points on frontier AI development in the European Union—look at ASML in the Netherlands, for example—and I believe we should be working with it on these questions. If we worked with the EU on procurement, we would increase our purchasing power sixfold. It is important that we consider this right now and that we work with our allies on these matters.

I am pleased to hear what the right hon. Lady says about the recognition of reality as it is, and her recognition that in order to catch up, we have to do more. If we genuinely want to compete on inference and certainly on training, we have to build more compute. Does she agree that that needs to happen in the United Kingdom at a significant scale? If she wants us to have a frontier model, it will require changes to our copyright laws, which neither the UK nor the EU wants to make.

Looking at some of the large language models that are being used in the UK, I do not agree completely with the hon. Gentleman’s latter point on copyright. Have they got to the stage yet of being able to provide a competitor to US models? No, they have not. Look also at Mistral and its operations, although it is a different model. I would say that there are ways forward without abandoning support for our creators. I think it is important that the Government consider that. On the hon. Gentleman’s first point, however, I would agree with him. It is perhaps the only point on which I would do so. I would actually disagree with my very good and hon. Friend the Member for Blyth and Ashington (Ian Lavery) on the question of whether we need more data centres, although I strongly agree that they have to come with benefits for local communities—he is absolutely right to say that. Above all, we need to ensure that they are not soaking up much-needed energy and increasing energy prices and causing other problems. There should also be employment opportunities coming from them, although let us be sanguine about the fact that these technologies are sadly not labour intensive. I do believe that we need more data centres. I am very pleased with the covenant model set out by the Government. That is really important and will hopefully ensure that this is win-win. I agree with the hon. Member for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger): without that compute, it will be difficult to deliver the sovereignty that we need. I want to underline the urgency of this matter. I really hope that the Government are already working hard with their partners in the G20 towards the start of our presidency year—I am sure that they will be. I agree with many of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee’s recommendations on concrete steps towards trying to get that global agreement next year. In doing so, we need to be clear about the fact that harm is already occurring. We have heard a lot about that from my hon. Friend the Member for Leeds Central and Headingley and many other Members, but I just want to underline that this is not a surprise.

Yes, absolutely—collaboration and co-operation with partners is necessary, but that must not be used as an excuse to go slowly domestically. As the right hon. Lady will have heard, I used the parallel with the internet in my speech; we have now introduced legislation that is particular to our country, even though the internet is, by nature, a world wide web. Things can be done here, particularly on the use of AI in education—in schools and universities and so on—and in very secure environments. We will have a King’s Speech next year—let us have a Bill in it.

I agree that this should not be an excuse, but I am optimistic about the chances of our moving forward with like-minded countries on this question. There is strong pressure coming from their publics. I agreed with the right hon Gentleman when he remarked on that in his speech. However, it is important that we recognise that some of the so-called misalignment that we have seen has actually been by design. The reason why the chains of thought are increasingly not transparent to investigators is the design of different agents. The reason why psychological dependence and radicalisation are occurring through chatbots is that agents have been designed in an anthropomorphic way. Why do they use the word “I”? They do not have to; that is a decision that was taken by designers. We should not be surprised that we see strange outcomes when we are talking about systems that are based not on logic, let alone frames of morality, but ultimately on inference and probabilistic processes. We should not be surprised by that harm. I want to mention one other instance, which has not received much coverage in the UK, which is what happened to Government records in Mexico. One malicious operator was able to use Anthropic and OpenAI models to exfiltrate hundreds of millions of citizen records, including those of domestic violence victims, and voter, tax and property records. This is already happening right in front of us. We have already talked about the impact on employment, and I strongly agree with the remarks that my hon. Friend the Member for Glasgow South (Gordon McKee) made on that. I would like to have seen more on that in the Milburn review, which otherwise was a strong piece of work. We have already seen the production of thousands of sexualised deepfakes by Grok. We will keep playing whack-a-mole on these issues, unfortunately, unless we see stronger control in the initial moment. I will end with the elephant in the room in a lot of these discussions. There has been an implicit trade-off in the minds of many policymakers, and even in the minds of many MPs, between having knowledge of what frontier AI companies are doing and having control over it. There is the idea that if we try to get control over what they are doing, we will be denied knowledge of what they are doing. That has been threatened by the companies, but what I say in reply is this: how on earth, in the mother of all Parliaments, can we accept a situation in which private companies threaten democratically elected Governments in that way? What is the point of democracy if we cannot exercise control?
Members will have noticed that a number of Members still wish to contribute. I plan to start the Front-Bench contributions at about 4.30. I am therefore introducing a time limit of seven minutes.

No one wants to hear what I have got to say three times, Madam Deputy Speaker. [ Laughter. ] There have been some excellent statistics and contributions from Members in the debate so far, but I want to look at this issue from a slightly more emotional point of view. In Scotland this is a highly emotive subject. My thanks go to the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake). I used crude artificial intelligence for a phonetic pronunciation of his constituency. Last Saturday, 6,000 people and approximately 80 different organisations from across Scotland marched through Edinburgh. It was a fantastic turnout, and the intention was to send a clear message to the First Minister and his SNP Government that their position on data centres is not in the best interests of Scottish communities. At the rally there were many people from the Say No to Larbert AI Data Centre campaign. I have mentioned our campaign in this place a few times now, and I have spoken at public meetings. Once again, I will be unequivocal: I fully support the campaign. The people involved in that campaign have shown the power that community activism still holds in a political democracy. Together, we are opposed to Apatura Energy’s proposed project, which would see a 300 MW hyperscale data centre built in Larbert. The proposed location is utterly ludicrous, because it would be in a residential area where thousands of people live. It would be 20 metres from a residential care home and 500 metres from Forth Valley Royal hospital, which serves more than 300,000 people. Last Friday, the deadline for the proposal to be decided by Falkirk councillors on the planning committee came and went. Apatura did not agree to a further extension, meaning that it now has the right to take the proposal to the SNP Scottish Government for a decision. That gives me and my constituents enormous cause for concern, because the SNP AI Minister has spoken in glowing terms about the billions of pounds that could be generated for the Scottish economy in the coming years because of AI data centres. It is pure fantasy, and just another example of trickle-down economics that only serves private capital. We know that the money would never be seen in local communities or meaningfully benefit Scotland’s national economy. Instead, it would end up in boardrooms and foreign bank accounts; neither communities nor the Treasury would see it. Let us be clear: AI data centres will not bring jobs, and certainly not to the extent we need to reindustrialise communities. To suggest that these monstrosities would do so is utter nonsense. Something else that is nonsense is the SNP AI Minister claiming that people are “up” for these developments—what a ridiculous statement. Over 7,000 people officially objected to the plans, with just 83 in support. The number of objections amounts to more than half of Larbert’s population. The Scottish Government need to appreciate that that is not just a few dissenters; that is my community unified. My constituents have been loud and clear that this abomination should be nowhere near where people live and where people go to recover and recuperate from illness. The reality is that the only ones who would really benefit from these developments are the corporations who look to exploit communities, all for profit. They want to exploit more than communities. It might be pretty chilly in London today, but we have just had a summer of record temperatures, and the waste heat that an AI data centre produces can raise land temperatures by up to 9°, impacting areas up to 6 miles away: bad for humans but lethal for wildlife. About 95% of the energy to be used in the proposed data centre would be needed to keep servers and equipment cool, because they will be in constant use. The noise that would produce includes infrasonic noise: long wavelengths travelling vast distances that can penetrate walls, glass and even ear protectors. That pollution can cause serious physical and psychological ha

AI is changing society profoundly and will continue to do so as it evolves. I come to the debate with no expertise in how advanced AI works, but what I do know a bit about—if I think back to my undergraduate degree, at least—is history, and I have always believed that the more we understand the past, the better we can navigate the here and now and shape the future. That is what I will focus on. While it is right to say that the capabilities of AI are new—specifically its ability to act outside the parameters that its creators have set—this is not the first time that people have lived through rapid technological change, and it is not the first time we have had to grapple with a technology that we do not fully understand, and cannot yet predict its consequences. Back in 1963, Harold Wilson spoke in his conference speech of the “white heat” of technology and said: “We are perhaps living in a more rapid revolution than some of us realise.” But he did not freeze with fear or let tech fly unregulated; once in government, he took a pragmatic approach that included setting up the first Ministry of Technology. That is the model for today. It is impossible to do justice to the entirety of the risks and opportunities of AI in one short speech. They are many, from what kind of work we will be doing in the future to what our education system should look like, how we will interact with government services, how we will access healthcare, and how our businesses will have to adapt to drive growth, as I heard from a group of SMEs I brought to Downing Street to discuss the impact that AI is having on their work. Across all those questions, history offers lessons in pragmatism. I think, for example, of a great book on AI I just read by Daniel Susskind called “What Should My Children Do?” in which he looks back at when pocket calculators went mainstream in schools. Some saw a crisis in maths teaching coming, while others saw revolutionary potential. In 1978, the Government commissioned Wilfred Cockcroft, a maths lecturer, to write a paper that concluded that we should teach children to count both with a device and without one. The mantra was: teach both, test both; do not deny the technological progress, but do not fear it. That same approach applies today to AI in the education system. In this speech, I will focus on a different, particularly important aspect of the AI transformation: how we can better collaborate globally to manage the risks and maximise the opportunities. The reality is that AI will not be managed within our borders. We can navigate this period of technological change only by doing so at a global level. There is real opportunity for the UK here, as we have heard from others, because the US and China are locked in competition to advance the frontier models, and so the incentives to co-operate are not there, but the UK has both the advantage and the possibility to lead on a co-operative approach. We have strengths, such as the world-leading Isambard-AI, which is already accelerating breakthroughs in medicine. With the talent in our universities and start-ups, we have a head start in AI safety thanks to the AI Security Institute. We have the live opportunity of the upcoming presidency of the G20, and the Prime Minister has already confirmed his intention to make global co-operation on AI its focus. As we go into this, what can we learn from history? I will make three brief points. The first is that we can take heart that global co-operation can work, even with underlying geopolitical division and distrust. I think back to the cold war and the nuclear arms race, when the United States and the Soviet Union developed agreements to limit nuclear risks despite the ideological gulf between them. The reality is that, as is the case for nuclear, no country can accept the risk of catastrophic destruction caused by AI. That gives at least a starting point for agreement. The second point is that co-operation works best when shared interests

I would like to follow on from that air of optimism and briefly raise two issues. I think that these are not emerging risks but present risks. My points come from two elements of correspondence that I received. The first is about AI and weaponry, and the second is about the AI debt bubble that could throw us into a global financial crisis like in 2008. I received a letter from a group of health workers who have been campaigning on the issue of the role of AI in weaponry. They took us through some of the issues around drones, AI targeting systems and autonomous weapons, which are shifting the scale and the speed in which conflicts are fought. In many ways, the role of selection and destroying of targets without further human intervention whatsoever is taking place. We see that in example after example—we have seen it in Ukraine and in Gaza at the moment. The UN Secretary-General’s report on children and armed conflict highlighted the role of AI in the increase in the number of child victims in those conflicts. There is a disregard of the principles of proportionality and distinction and, as a result, AI attacks are reaching into towns and villages, and striking dense areas, and infrastructure such as schools, hospitals and markets. We have seen so many examples in Ukraine. The UN, in describing what is happening in Myanmar, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Sudan and Gaza, has talked about there being “a new circle of hell” as a result of drone use in those areas. What the health workers wrote to us is interesting enough. It seems that there is a particular impact on their being targeted. In the last year or so, there have been 900 deaths and 1,400 injuries of health workers, which is a tripling of the number of victims. Their argument is: “Far from improving accuracy and precision, the unpiloted, unencrypted algorithms deployed in these war zones and in other heavily fractured conflicts contribute to facilitating accountability gaps” in decision making about the use of these armaments. One of the best examples is the killing of 120 children in the attack on Minab school in Iran by US forces. We have seen this even more recently in Gaza, in the attacks that have hit hospitals and killed more children. A range of human rights experts have contacted us all, I think, and raised concerns about the use of AI, particularly by the Israeli military. They say: “The basic principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution require decisions that are grounded in the circumstances of each attack”, so that there is human intervention and proper decision making. The campaign is calling for the extension of the negotiation that my hon.
