Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) mentioned, so that we can get “a legally binding treaty, which prohibits autonomous weapons and systems designed or used to apply force against people and civilian infrastructure, and establish strict restrictions on other forms of military AI.” As my hon. Friend said, those agreements have worked in the past. We may not have got 100% of what we wanted, but we are at the first stage. I think our Government can take a lead next year, because they will chair a range of bodies. The second issue is the risk from AI to economic security in our country and globally. Let me get this plug in: I have invited Professor Damon Silvers, who was one of the advisers to Congress during the last financial crash in the US, to do a briefing for us on Wednesday morning. I received correspondence from the American Federation of Teachers union in the US, which represents teachers and public sector workers. Its president, Randi Weingarten, sent a letter to the Trump Administration in September, urging an immediate investigation into the financial risks from the artificial intelligence sector’s rapid, debt-laden expansion. The union was concerned about the scale of the investment that its members’ pension funds had made in the market, and into AI. It called for the American

I want to start by addressing remarks made by the hon. Member for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger), who is not in his seat, about the importance of relationships and family. It has recently been brought to my attention that AI chatbot toys that are being sold to children—right here, right now—do not have the regulation required. In one example, a toy could tell the child that the child could allow touching by an adult, as long as they consented. This toy was being marketed to children as young as three. What does that do to a child? What does it do to a family if a child gets attached to an AI chatbot toy? Surely they should be attached to their mother, their father, their caregiver. We also now have evidence that adults are getting emotionally attached to AI chatbots. A survey showed that around a third of Americans are romantically involved with AI chatbots. What will that do to our future families and relationships? There is also the issue, which a number of colleagues have mentioned, of deepfakes. Ninety-nine per cent of the tools that create deepfake pornography use women to do so. That can have huge consequences for the way in which men and women form relationships and families.

The hon. Lady is making a powerful and important speech about the character of human relations—the way we interact, the way we form friendship and the way we fall in love. These things are, by definition, peculiarly human, and they are all at risk. We should send a signal from this place—this is well supported by the evidence—that excessive screentime through the internet, and worse still through AI, harms children. Children should be growing up with meaningful relationships of the kind she has described.

I agree with the right hon. Gentleman. I was merely trying to respond to some of the points made by the hon. Member for East Wiltshire. He gave the example of the Ottomans opposing the printing press to perhaps label those of us who seek greater regulation of the development of this technology as—I do not know—Luddites, but the large language models that are driving these machines towards superintelligent AI are surely taking us into Tower of Babel territory. The ultimate human hubris is to assume that we can create machines that will replace and be more intelligent than humans. Sam Altman said: “I think AI will probably, most likely, sort of lead to the end of the world, but in the meantime, there’ll be great companies created with serious machine learning.” That is our future. I will focus on some of the severe warnings about this technology, including those from the former chief scientist at the UK AI Security Institute, who recently estimated that the chance of runaway machine intelligence causing human extinction is “a coin flip”. Paul Christiano, leading AI scientist and OpenAI board member, recently said that he thinks “there is a high risk of AI takeover within the next three years”, leading to a situation where AIs “call the shots, where they have overpowered governments, where we are unable to stop them.” So much for sovereignty, then. When experts give such stark warnings, this House should listen. Last month, I was honoured to be asked to testify to New York city council during its recent hearing on AI safety, to discuss my experience of being deepfaked through Grok, which is SpaceXSI’s AI tool. It keeps changing its name—very confusing. I did that alongside whistleblowers who have been sounding the alarm about what AI companies are doing. One of those whistleblowers, Jacob Coxon, left Anthropic because of his fear about what his employer is building. He told the council, and I heard it there, that the AI companies work on a mindset of “move fast, break things, fix them later.” Today we are talking about the risk of extinction as a result of losing control of autonomous runaway machine intelligence that would be vastly more capable than humans. Surely we in this House believe that this is an entirely unacceptable way to manage potentially catastrophic outcomes. We cannot simply say that because this matter rests with the US or China, there is nothing the UK can do. As we heard from my hon. Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith), humanity has faced risks on this scale before. During the Trinity test for the Manhattan project, scientists warned of a risk that a nuclear detonation could ignite the atmosphere and end up killing the planet. They did the necessary calculations, and only after concluding that the risk was incredibly small did they proceed. They were willing to not go ahead if the calculations had said otherwise. However, as the former Secretary of State for Defence Lord Browne of Ladyton has correctly identified, when it comes to runaway machine intelligence development, we see the opposite dynamic. Leading AI scientists warn us that the calculated risks are staggeringly high, but AI companies are racing ahead regardless. This dangerous, unsafe culture is why these companies cannot be allowed to self-regulate. This goes against all the principles of responsible engineering. Self-regulation is not how we govern any other high-risk sector. We do not allow the aviation industry to mark its own homework after a crash, or the pharmaceutical industry to release new medical products without ensuring that they are safe for people. AI chief executive officers have proposed slowing down AI development, so that we can pace the frontier, but this would only ensure that we arrived at a catastrophic incident more slowly, rather than avoiding it. If you are driving towards a cliff, you do not simply slow down; you stop the car before it hurtles over the precipice. Recent attempts at AI self-regulation have

I congratulate the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) on securing this debate. I am very pleased that we are finally having this essential debate, but I am also extremely concerned. There have been excellent interventions from Members across the House, but it is no wonder we have covered so much, because the last time we had a dedicated debate on AI was in 2023. With that in mind, I hope the Minister for AI will see what has been discussed and can join us for the next debate. Since 2023, we have seen AI win two Nobel prizes and a gold medal at the International Mathematical Olympiad. We have seen AI run a cyber-espionage campaign almost entirely by itself. We have seen Grok release models to create child sexual abuse material. We have seen AI agents break out of their test environment and hack into another company, with nobody telling them to do so, and now we have AI models coding themselves, with Claude writing over 80% of its code. This debate is long overdue, and I hope it will be the start of many more, not one every three years. Because people should be at the heart of what we do with technology, I want to start with Yvonne. Yvonne was diagnosed with breast cancer thanks to an experimental AI system. Jasper, a disabled student, moved into AI-enabled accommodation, making his day-to-day life so much easier. In terms of life-changing breakthroughs, AlphaFold has mapped over 200 million proteins. More than 3 million researchers in 190 countries have used that work, from tackling malaria to looking at plastic-eating enzymes, and it has won a Nobel prize. But we will only realise AI’s potential if we take the risks as seriously as the opportunities. A scam victim paid out £250,000 to an AI-enabled fraud. Creatives across the country—across the world, indeed—are watching their work being stolen. We have heard about the impact of AI deepfakes, whether it is on our democracy or on individuals, and some of the people who built this technology are warning that it could threaten humanity itself within a decade. People across this country are asking what the Government, this place and we as MPs are doing about it. Liberal Democrats have long backed innovation, with the safeguards and trust that make it possible. In April, we published our Liberal vision for AI, shaped by more than 100 industry and civil society voices. Since then, we have sought to bring this debate to the House again and again, because action is needed. My constituent Lin from Ashridge puts it plainly: “the reckless behaviour of tech giants must be stopped before it is too late”, and she is not alone. YouGov found last month that 79% of Britons have little or no confidence in AI companies to develop the technology responsibly. Worse—and we should all listen to this—80% have little or no faith in the Government to regulate it. That is our role, and the lack of public trust is worrying. Recent events show that we cannot capture AI’s benefits unless we confront its risks. A rogue AI agent hacked a Government website in Australia. Our own AI Security Institute testing found AI agents creating fake identities to pressure a real person into accepting malicious code. Criminals, terrorists and hostile states are reaching for the same tools. AI slop is flooding our feeds and our politics, some of it much more dangerous than benign. The AI Security Institute found that AI beat every human persuader tested, including world champion debaters, in drastically moving opinion—I think we should all take them on in this House. Are we better than the AI systems? It seems not. Meanwhile, a handful of the richest men on Earth are deciding the future of this technology at an unprecedented pace, consolidating power in a new AI-driven empire. This Labour Government have been long on promises and short on delivery. While we welcome the £120 million for the AI Security Institute, money is not power. Earlier this week, the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee found: “

I thank the Backbench Business Committee and the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) for bringing forward this important debate, as well as all Members who took part in it. I hope the Minister will not take this as a slight—I think she is a very effective Minister—but it is very disappointing that the Minister for Artificial Intelligence was unable to attend the debate. The debate is focused on the risks of AI, and there are undoubtedly risks and issues that need to be addressed, as there are during any transition or period of rapid innovation and change. In today’s debate, we heard from the hon. Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman) about data centres, as well as from the hon. Member for Blyth and Ashington (Ian Lavery), who also spoke about risks for employment, as mentioned by many other hon. Members. My right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) and the hon. Member for Brent East (Dawn Butler) talked about the risks of misinformation. Many hon. Members, including the hon. Member for Lowestoft (Jess Asato), talked about relational harms and deepfakes. Cyber-crime and the invasion of privacy was mentioned by the hon. Member for Dudley (Sonia Kumar), and implications for our security, in both narrow and broad terms, were talked about by the right hon. Members for Oxford East (Anneliese Dodds) and for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell), and the hon. Members for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger), for Glasgow South (Gordon McKee), for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel) and for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith). We need to address what I consider to be the risks relating to AI: the risk of not embracing this opportunity, and the risk that a lack of clear leadership and direction might now weaken the UK, leaving us subject to the whim of others rather than a leader in a new AI age. Those risks are real and with us today. Many across Government and this House are calling for undefined AI regulation to try to control or limit the future potential use and development of AI tools. However, let us be clear that whether or not the UK adopts those tools, and whether or not we regulate use or creation within our borders, AI innovation will continue and we cannot control what other countries will do. We know that hostile state actors are using AI tools to attack the UK every single day. That will not stop just because we want it to. The best defence is not reports, legislation or even treaties—it is ensuring that we have access to the best AI-backed tools to defend ourselves. This is a matter of security and resilience. We cannot prevent a foreign attack by agreeing it should not be allowed or passing a law to criminalise it—we must ensure we can defend ourselves. Failure to embrace the benefits of AI will risk our security, damage our economy and reduce our influence on the global stage. We need clear leadership, not reports and taskforces that talk about a lot but fail to deliver, and a Government who will embrace this opportunity. Britain is already the third-largest AI market in the world, as seen by growth in the last quarter occurring predominantly in sectors adopting AI the fastest. The opportunities for UK innovation and economic growth, delivering both prosperity and international leadership, are limitless. However, this is about much more than economics. Perhaps AI’s most exciting potential is not what it can do for businesses, but what it can do for people. Take the fight against cancer. Researchers at Imperial College London, working with Google, NHS trusts and other universities, recently reported the largest NHS study to date of AI in breast cancer screening, involving research across 175,000 women. The results are extraordinary. Artificial intelligence in breast cancer screening showed more cases detected and fewer false positives, and that is just one application. AlphaFold, built here in the UK, models proteins, the building blocks of life. AI has the potential

As my hon. Friend knows, I admire him in many ways. We agree on much, but we do not agree on much on this issue. By the way, I find his naive faith in technological change charming. I ask him to consider the closest parallel that we have, which is the internet. When the internet emerged, we were never warned about the ills that now prevail; we were told that it was a wondrous new thing. Someone said to me at the time that everyone will be a publisher—that is the problem! This is not a fear of technology; this is wisdom based on bitter experience.

My right hon. Friend will know that the Online Safety Act 2023 was built around regulating harms, not technologies. I do not believe that there is a single misuse case—beyond a very few narrow exceptions —that is not already covered by UK domestic law. Let me return to my previous point. The Government do not build AI; business does. During covid, we learned the hard lesson that when we focus on immediate risks, we forget to fully consider the long-term impact of the decisions we make. As this House considers the risks of artificial intelligence, I urge the Government not to make the same mistake, and I urge everyone to take pause and reflect. The biggest risk of AI is that we fail to embrace the opportunities that AI innovation presents, the world keeps on spinning and the UK gets left behind.

I congratulate the hon. Member for Ceredigion Preseli (Ben Lake) on securing this debate, and I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Stockport (Navendu Mishra) for making the case for it to the Backbench Business Committee. I also thank all Members who have contributed to the debate. They will have noticed that I am not the Minister for Artificial Intelligence, but I will ensure that all the comments, points and issues raised today are fed back to him. I work closely with him in the Cabinet Office, and I will speak to him as soon as possible. I know he is disappointed that he could not make it here, but he will be at future debates on this topic. AI is developing faster than almost anyone predicted. In recent months, some of the world’s leading researchers, including people building the most advanced systems, have issued stark warnings about where the technology could be heading. We must take those warnings seriously. As AI becomes more capable, Britain must become more capable at protecting its people. AI offers huge opportunities that the UK wants to tap into, from transforming our public services and improving living standards to creating jobs. My hon. Friend the Member for Dudley (Sonia Kumar) referred to her experience of what AI has done for healthcare in her constituency, and I have had a similar experience in my own constituency of Doncaster Central, where AI is being used in some areas to great effect. The shadow Minister, the hon. Member for Runnymede and Weybridge (Dr Spencer), highlighted some of the potential benefits of AI and how it can transform how this country runs. AI is already helping us to discover new cures for diseases and to make our energy networks cleaner, but AI capabilities advance, and we need to ensure that we have the safeguards to keep pace with them. People across the country are becoming increasingly concerned about what the advent of AI could mean for them, their jobs, their children and their safety, and the British public are right to expect that this Government will take that seriously. Our first responsibility, above all others, is to keep the country safe. Our approach is clear: we will independently test models, harden our defences and build infrastructure here in Britain, all to keep the British public safe. Sovereignty has been mentioned a number of times throughout this debate, by my hon. Friend the Member for Glasgow South (Gordon McKee), my right hon. Friend the Member for Oxford East (Anneliese Dodds) and the hon. Member for East Wiltshire (Danny Kruger). Those points have been heard, and they are being taken seriously by the Government. On 12 October, the Minister for Artificial Intelligence set out further action, including extending our frontier AI hardening programme across Government, developing plans to respond to serious incidents involving AI agents, and considering how the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill can better protect our essential services. In the Budget, the Chancellor announced investments totalling over £700 million of new money across Government. That represents significant funding to strengthen the UK’s AI security, resilience and capabilities, as well as the Government’s desire to harness the opportunities to raise living standards and back British industry, ensuring that our country is better off.

Speaking as the person who introduced the cyber-security strategy and the National Cyber Security Centre when I was Security Minister, will the Bill that the Minister has mentioned include what I called for earlier, which is a cross-Government analysis of risk—a risk assessment that stretches across all aspects of government and its agencies? Is that going to be at the heart of that Bill?

I will come to the Bill a little later in my speech. If that does not answer the right hon. Member’s question, I will ensure that the AI Minister writes to him to clarify that point. My hon. Friends the Members for Brent East (Dawn Butler) and for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel) spoke about their respective Bills. I will ensure that the AI Minister is aware of them, as well as the important points that were raised by my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell), and gets back to those Members, if they have not already had a meeting with him. The Government take the full array of risks from frontier AI extremely seriously, as I know does everyone in the House today. AI is advancing at an extraordinary pace, creating risks that do not stop at national borders, and as this debate has shown, it is uncertain how capable those systems will become—or, indeed, how quickly. We do not underestimate any risk, or the possibility that increasingly capable systems may behave in ways that their developers cannot fully control. That is why the AI Security Institute exists: to build a scientific understanding of the risks posed by the most advanced AI systems and develop technical mitigations for them so that policy decisions are grounded in evidence. It will look at complex technical findings for policymakers across Whitehall and our international partners, ensuring that our democratic institutions are ready and responsive to AI’s capabilities and its shifts. AISI, which Microsoft’s president recently branded as world-leading, is working closely with developers to carry out rigorous evaluations of advanced AI models and capabilities. There is much serious and worrying commentary about the most extreme worst-case scenarios arising, which is why AISI’s role will be to focus on empirical evidence that helps us to understand those risks. That is critical—by being empirical and specific about new capabilities and risks, we can take informed and evidence-based action to mitigate them. We are also considering how the regime can be strengthened so that AI, cyber and loss of control risks are better understood and protected against. My hon. Friend the Member for Blyth and Ashington (Ian Lavery) spoke about the data centre in his constituency and the surrounding investment. The data centre covenant was released on 28 October, with five main points: lowering electricity bills, investing in improving local communities, adhering to the highest environmental standards, creating jobs and apprenticeships and driving reindustrialisation, and strengthening Britain’s security. The north-east growth zone will create around 5,000 jobs; there is a local hire commitment for 90% of those jobs, and on social value, QTS has a 10-year framework, including 12,000 local construction jobs. We are determined that local people should benefit in the areas where these growth zones are placed. I have noted the concerns raised by my hon. Friend the Member for Alloa and Grangemouth (Brian Leishman), who underlined his constituents’ views. I will ensure that they are raised with the Department. My hon. Friend the Member for Aylesbury (Laura Kyrke-Smith) mentioned AI in the education system. We are funding innovative work, and we will produce new insights and evidence on AI in education. The AI tutoring tools pioneer programme, run jointly by the Department for Education and i.AI, works with teachers, pupils and industry to develop AI tutoring tools that are safe and designed around genuine educational needs. Together, we are developing new sovereign education benchmarks to assess the safety of AI tools. The world that young people are preparing for is changing rapidly compared with the world that those of us in this Chamber—who are comparatively still quite young—grew up in. Academic knowledge remains essential, but alongside strong foundations in knowledge, young people increasingly need the ability to apply what they know with confidence a

I thank the Backbench Business Committee for granting the debate, all hon. Members who supported the application, and all right hon. and hon. Members who have contributed today. We have heard a range of opinions about the risks of AI, but acknowledging those risks does not mean that we dismiss the potential rewards. We have heard about the vast array of potential rewards and benefits to society—and indeed to humanity—that frontier AI models can bring. The one thing on which I think there is consensus is that AI is a transformational technology and this House would perhaps do well to debate its consequences more regularly. We might not be able to keep up with the pace of that technology’s development, but it is important that we, as the public’s representatives, discuss it. Question put and agreed to. Resolved, That this House has considered the emerging risks of advanced AI.

I am really grateful to have secured this debate to raise the financial position of the Lancashire fire and rescue service, and I thank the Minister for being here to respond. I want to begin by paying tribute to all the staff, the firemen and women, and the people who keep Lancashire safe, be it in house fires, wildfires and accidents on the road, or educating and helping our communities. Every one of them makes a contribution, and when the worst happens, they are the ones who turn up and walk into danger to protect us. I know that Lancashire is very grateful, and I certainly am. Obviously, Burnley and Padiham’s fire stations and fire crews are the best. I pay particular tribute to Chief Officer Jon Charters, who is in the Gallery today; the Lancashire fire and rescue authority; and Councillor Azhar Ali, of Brierfield in my constituency, and Councillors Mark Clifford, Ged Mirfin and Luke Parker, who are also in the Gallery. The purpose of this debate is to seek a sustainable funding solution that protects Lancashire’s fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers, renews essential facilities and sustains the service’s contribution to national resilience, which we know was tested over the summer in tackling wildfires and more. I will set out the local financial position, the action already taken, and four issues on which I would like a response from the Minister. I have known him for many years, and he is a great friend of our emergency service workers, including firefighters, so I know that he will do all he can to aid our endeavours. The Lancashire fire and rescue authority has set a balanced budget for 2026-27, which is to its credit, but its latest medium-term financial strategy shows that a further £4 million of recurring annual savings will be required by 2030-31. I do welcome this Government’s three-year settlement and the strengthened funding floor for 2026-27. A multi-year settlement is certainly what fire services and public authorities more generally have asked for over many years, and this Government have delivered it. However, that on its own has not removed the £4 million black hole. That figure is not a sign that nothing has been done locally—quite the opposite. In 2026-27 alone, the service has made £1.8 million of recurring savings through changes to crewing, including reduced whole-time crewing levels and dynamic resourcing, on top of more than £1.6 million of efficiencies beyond firefighter staffing. Those savings are already in the budget, and the £4 million is what is left after them, in 2030-31. Support services were cut hard through the long years of austerity, and the authority has concluded that, although further efficiencies may remain possible, certain functions need investment, too. I am here today because, alarmingly, the authority’s own blunt financial assessment is that savings to fill the hole on the scale required would have to come mainly from fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers. It is worth being more exact about what that does and does not mean. No specific firefighter posts have been identified by the authority for reduction, but the authority’s judgment is that savings of this size would mean fewer fire engines, and potentially the closure of some on-call fire stations, significantly reducing resilience.

I recently met local firefighters in Blackburn, and I was alarmed and surprised to find that there was just one pump, despite three pumps being available, including the command centre. That means these cuts are putting Blackburn and the surrounding areas at risk. One pump in Blackburn falls short of what the risk assessment for the town has identified. Does the hon. Member agree that we seriously need to look at this?

I think all Lancashire MPs—some are here, and some obviously cannot be here—are as concerned as am I about the funding situation. That is why I have secured this debate, and the hon. Member is right to raise his voice, as he does, for Blackburn. The Lancashire fire and rescue service runs 39 fire stations and 58 fire engines, with an establishment of 600 whole-time firefighters and 423 on-call firefighters, covering busy urban areas alongside a large rural geography, one of the largest in England. It serves some of the most deprived communities in Europe. Five Lancashire districts, including my own town of Burnley, are among those in the most deprived 10th in the country. I say that not to talk down our towns, because I am proud of each one of them, but because deprivation and fire risk unfortunately go hand in hand. The service’s own analysis finds that accidental fires in people’s homes and casualties are concentrated in deprived neighbourhoods. At Prime Minister’s questions in April, I raised the many derelict ex-industrial sites across Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield, many of which are a fire risk or, frankly, have been alight in recent years. I am very happy that the Government awarded £1 million in the derelict building fund at the Budget and I will continue to push for more. At the same time, the service must maintain cover across dispersed rural communities, including through the on-call system. A future funding assessment based on population may miss both sides of that picture, as I am sure the Minister has heard from rural areas as well as from me. But despite pressures, risks and a complicated county to protect, this is also a fire service at the very top of its game. The fire service inspectorate’s 2025 report awarded Lancashire six outstanding and five good grades, with no area graded below good. We are proud of that. Lancashire also holds the national wildfire lead, hosts the specialist national resilience wildfire team in Bacup and this summer supported services in Manchester—it could have been Oldham, Hampshire or Wales—while keeping its own emergency services running at home. It leads nationally on on-call firefighting, firefighter fitness, and on drones and robotics, where a Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government-funded heavy-lift drone programme is now at the testing stage. Its wider capabilities include urban search and rescue, high-volume pumping and international search and rescue deployment capability. Specialist search dog work and the adoption of Lancashire’s assurance monitoring system by other services provide further examples of its contribution beyond the county. Lancashire is about national preparedness, as well as a good local service. That brings me to the four issues I want to raise for the Minister’s attention.
On the subject of Lancashire fire and rescue service, I call John Slinger.

My hon. Friend is making a very good speech. On exactly that point about his local fire and rescue service, he is speaking about how fire and rescue services help one another at times of great need, and this summer was one such example. Warwickshire fire and rescue service saw an enormous rise in the number of incidents—the highest on record, up by 39% from July 2025. Does he agree that this shows that the concern he is raising today is critically important for all our communities, in Lancashire, Warwickshire and across the country? I know that the Minister cares deeply about this issue and will ensure that our fire officers, who are brave and resilient, will get the resources they need.

I agree with my hon. Friend’s intervention, and he has done well to get his foot in the door—you were particularly understanding, Madam Deputy Speaker. I quite agree and I pay tribute to the fire services in Warwickshire, Yorkshire, Scotland, Hampshire and elsewhere. The first issue is council tax. Lancashire’s band D fire precept for 2026-27 is £94.73, against a national average for combined fire authorities of £100.21. That leaves Lancashire £5.48—for those mathematicians in the Chamber—a year below the average, or roughly 10p a week. The fire authority has asked for flexibility to close that gap in a single year from 2027-28, on top of the £5 increase already assumed in its budget, with the final amount depending on the national average at that point. It estimates that this could raise around £2.5 million a year, which is substantial. I know household budgets in Burnley, Padiham and Brierfield are tight—everybody’s are—and I do not take raising bills lightly, so let me be clear about what is being asked. This is not a rise; it is the freedom for the fire authority to decide locally whether around 10p a week extra is worth paying to protect the fire engines, stations and the services that residents need. So first, I ask the Minister whether that flexibility can be provided and whether a decision can be made in sufficient time to inform the authority’s budget in 2027-28. The second issue is firefighters’ pensions. I know a review is ongoing and the Minister will be limited in what he can say today, but if the pension revaluation—there are some hypotheticals here, I understand—brings down the employer contribution rate, the authority wants to keep that benefit rather than see its Government funding cut by the same amount, because otherwise any subsequent saving from the review will give the service no extra spending power and feels like a lose-lose for all involved. No cash figure is attached, so this is about the principle: if there is a saving at a later date, can Lancashire keep it to support its services? Together, council tax flexibility and retained pension savings are sought to close the £4 million recurring gap and protect fire engines, fire stations and firefighter numbers. Neither benefit is included in the current forecast, and the retention of pension savings is dependent on the review outcome and, I understand, is speculative at this stage. My third issue is probably my biggest concern: capital. This issue is completely separate from the £4 million revenue black hole that I mentioned. A 2025 condition survey found that 38% of stations and corporate buildings run by Lancashire fire and rescue service were in a poor condition, with some buildings dating back to the 1800s. I do not speak for Mr Speaker—I would not dare—but he is aware that I intended to make this reference. I will use the authority’s own assessment of the Chorley estate to back up my points about my concerns. The Chorley training facilities were best in class 40 years ago, and they are now at the end of their useful life, as the authority has said. The facilities include buildings that have reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete. On the estate, priorities include replacement stations at Preston and Fulwood, new training facilities at Chorley, and an estate upgrade across the piece. After capital receipts, plans for backlog maintenance and essential works leave a borrowing requirement of around £50 million to get the Lancashire fire and rescue estate up to scratch, with repayments of around £4 million a year. The authority is asking the Government to reinstate capital grants, last received in 2014, for backlog maintenance and essential works across the wider estate. Closing the revenue gap would not pay for these works, and a predictable programme would reduce the need to borrow, or to fund the works using service budgets. My fourth and final issue is the funding formula. The comprehensive review that we are undertaking is intended to inform funding f

Before I respond, can I just say that our thoughts are with Ibrar Ali, the councillor from Bradford, following the horrific attack that took place today? Our thoughts are with him, his family, councillors in Bradford, and local Members of Parliament at this time. I am grateful to my hon. Friend the Member for Burnley (Oliver Ryan) for securing this important debate and giving the House an opportunity to consider the funding of the Lancashire fire and rescue service. I congratulate him on his success in securing funding for the Manchester Road train station access improvements —evidence, if it was needed, that he is an effective and committed champion of the people of Burnley. As my hon. Friend knows, our fire and rescue services do so much more than respond to fires. They work tirelessly to keep our communities safe, including by responding to evolving risks, such as wildfire, and undertaking critical prevention and protection work. I echo the thanks to Jon Charters, the chief fire officer, members of the Lancashire combined fire authority, some of whom are in the Gallery, and all Lancashire’s firefighters and control staff, and the wider workforce, for the work that they do every day to protect communities across Lancashire, Blackburn with Darwen and Blackpool. That commitment is reflected in the service’s strong performance. In its most recent inspection, published in August 2025, His Majesty’s inspectorate of constabulary and fire and rescue services rated Lancashire outstanding in six areas and good in the remaining five. That is a significant achievement, and it reflects the commitment of the service’s leadership and workforce. The Government recognise the importance of providing fire and rescue services with the resources and certainty that they need to protect their communities. The ’26-27 local government finance settlement marked an important step in that direction; it was the first multi-year settlement for local government in 10 years. Nationally, almost £1.95 billion in core funding power will be available to stand-alone fire and rescue authorities in England. At the final settlement, the Government announced a further £15 million for fire and rescue services, ensuring that every stand-alone fire authority receives an increase of at least 3.8% in 2026-27. For Lancashire fire and rescue authority, core spending power increases from £78.1 million to over £81 million in ’26-27—an increase of almost £3 million. I recognise the financial and operational pressures that Lancashire continues to face. The multi-year settlement provides an increase in resources, alongside greater certainty to support effective workforce, financial and investment planning. However, we all know that funding is only part of the picture. The risks facing fire and rescue services are changing, with services increasingly needing to respond to a broader and more complex range of incidents, while continuing their fundamental work of preventing fires and protecting the public. That is why this Government are looking beyond individual funding settlements towards longer-term reform and resilience in the sector. I want to reflect on the work of Baroness Blake in the other place, who gives important leadership on this matter. We are investing approximately £97 million through the new dimensions 2 programme, the largest-scale upgrade to fire national resilience in nearly 20 years. This investment will help to ensure that fire and rescue services have the specialist capability and equipment that they need to respond effectively to major and critical incidents. We also continue to work with the sector on the changing role of fire and rescue services, ensuring that they are equipped to respond to current and future threats. Wildfires are an important example. The Government continue to work with the National Fire Chiefs Council, fire and rescue services and other partners to strengthen national wildfire prevention, preparedness and response. title: Supporting Young People into Work:  Cabinet Discussions

items.txt: 1. What steps he is taking with Cabinet colleagues to support young people into work.

We are working across Government to ensure that every young person has the support and opportunity they need to succeed. The hon. Lady asks about Cabinet discussions. The Cabinet discussed the Milburn report last week, and I announced that the jobs guarantee for young people will be available after 12 months on universal credit. She is right that other Cabinet members are involved, and I welcome the announcement from my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Education, for example, that colleges would be guaranteed funding for 16 to 18-year-olds in the next academic year.

I welcome what the Secretary of State says, but a café owner in my constituency tells me that, with the jobs tax and business rates really squeezing his margins, he cannot afford to take on a 16 or 17-year-old when he could instead hire someone with experience. Youth unemployment is at 15.6%. The jobs guarantee is really welcome, but will the Secretary of State accept that it will not work while it costs businesses so much to employ young people?

I remind the hon. Lady that last week’s labour force figures showed that youth unemployment has fallen, which is welcome. With regard to her café owner, employment costs are of course always a consideration, but if her solution is to reduce pay for young people, I am afraid it is not one I can share.

Over the summer, Cumbria Future Generation and the Cumbria Youth Alliance surveyed young people across the county. Their report found that 44% had turned down a job, apprenticeship or training opportunity because of transport barriers. What is the Department doing to ensure that young people in rural areas such as Cumbria can get to work and training opportunities?

My hon. Friend is right to say that transport costs are often raised in this regard. We have announced a cap on bus fares, and the Secretary of State for Transport and I have also announced a lifting of the hours restrictions for bus passes for disabled people. These are small measures that will hopefully make it a bit easier for people to get to work if they want to.

I wonder whether the right hon. Gentleman has spoken more recently to the Chancellor about the Milburn report—there is much to believe is good in it—and the fact that one of the big things that Milburn hints at is the difficulty of getting young people into work because of the national insurance level being set at £5,000 and 15% for young people. I have just come from a meeting with two charities that both said they are definitely finding it difficult to get people employed. Will the Secretary of State speak to the Chancellor and ask him to cut that tax?

There is an existing national insurance exemption for employers for workers under the age of 21. I also remind the right hon. Gentleman that Alan Milburn said that “the increase in youth inactivity long precedes any recent changes to NICs.” Of course I hear what the right hon. Gentleman says, and I am sure the Chancellor listens to all representations about tax. Tax is, of course, a matter for the Chancellor.

I recently visited the Ealing youth hub at Ealing Green college in my constituency, where young people are already getting tailored one-to-one advice and guidance to help them get a job under this Government. Now, in the next step, Ealing council will be taking the lead on the jobs guarantee scheme as part of the West London Alliance, and this will see 2,500 young people on universal credit being helped into a job across west London, with 562 in Ealing. Will the Secretary of State congratulate Ealing council on taking the lead on this initiative, and will he also wish the best of luck to those young people who will be helped to get a job?

I congratulate my hon. Friend, the local youth hub and Ealing council on the work that they are doing. This illustrates the wider point that the public sector has a big role to play in this. Her local authority, like most across the country, will be a major local employer, and it has a part to play in ensuring the maximum opportunity for young people.
2. What recent progress he has made on implementing the youth guarantee.

We are delivering the youth guarantee to support young people across Great Britain. We have introduced more intensive, earlier support in jobcentres, expanded the network of youth hubs—more than 175 are now open—and introduced a youth jobs grant and the jobs guarantee nationally. I announced last week that, from next April, we will bring forward eligibility for the jobs guarantee so that it is available for young people who have been on universal credit for 12 months rather than 18 months.

I thank the Secretary of State for all that we are doing to champion opportunities for young people. When I last met with my jobcentre in Hatfield, representatives said that employers on the youth guarantee scheme had a mixed record. Some firms were embracing the scheme, and were great partners to work with, but others were more reluctant. Will the Secretary of State tell me a bit more about what work is being done to encourage and incentivise as many businesses as possible to embrace the youth guarantee?

I commend my hon. Friend for working with his jobcentre and local employers. The truth is that we need to ensure that offers such as this are as simple as possible for employers to use. It is a challenge to ensure that the information is as user friendly and as simple to access as possible, especially for small and medium-sized businesses that do not have big human resources departments and so on. However, employers are signing up: earlier this month the waste management company Biffa announced that it would be offering up to 2,000 jobs to young people through the youth guarantee. I welcomed that announcement on a recent visit to one of its sites.

Has the Secretary of State’s Department undertaken a labour market assessment of the Government’s new proposals for the EU mobility scheme, and what those will mean for the implementation of the youth guarantee scheme and the aim of getting more British young people back into work?

I do not share what I think is the implication behind the right hon. Lady’s question—that there is direct competition in this way. I think a closer relationship with the European Union is in our economic interests. It is in the interests of economic growth and business dynamism, and economic growth and business dynamism are what create jobs in the first place.
3. What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
8. What steps his Department is taking to help young people into work.
14. What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
17. What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.
20. What steps he is taking to support young people into employment.

The Government are already investing an additional £2.5 billion through the youth guarantee and the growth and skills levy to support almost 1 million young people to earn or learn. We have recently reached agreements with the retail, hospitality and tourism sectors, which will take on 250,000 young people who are not in education, employment or training over the next few years. In addition, we are supporting employers through the youth jobs grant and the youth guarantee.

The Milburn review calls for colleges to become the “principal technical and transition institution, connecting school to skilled work.” In Wallsend, the Energy Academy is creating a pipeline of skilled workers, preparing young people for careers in the renewables and offshore sector, and it wants to see more apprenticeship places created. What steps is the Secretary of State taking with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero to create more apprenticeships? Will he visit the Energy Academy to see how the green transition can be used to tackle youth unemployment?

I often have quite a full diary after these monthly question sessions, so I hope that a Minister will visit the facility that my hon. Friend spoke about, but I thank her for her question. She is right that the transition to clean energy can potentially create great jobs for young people, and the Energy Academy is an excellent example of the role that colleges can play. I assure her that I am working with the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero to ensure that as many of those opportunities are available as possible.

According to a recent report by Impetus, young people in Hartlepool are at the fourth highest risk in the country of becoming NEET. Does the Secretary of State therefore agree that we must implement the Milburn recommendations in full, including reduced employer national insurance contributions for young people aged 21 to 24, and will he urge the Chancellor and other Cabinet colleagues to act as quickly as possible to ensure that we do so?

I made an initial response to the Milburn report in the Commons last week, and I said at that point that we would issue a fuller response to both the Milburn and the Timms reports in the new year. With regard to national insurance, I repeat what I said to the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) a few moments ago: there is an existing tax break in the system for employees under the age of 21, and Alan Milburn was clear that the problem of youth inactivity long predates any recent changes to national insurance.

Getting more young people into work is crucial for their success and that of our country, so I welcome the Milburn report. What work is my right hon. Friend’s Department doing with hospitality employers to create more entry-level job opportunities for young people, particularly through the youth guarantee and the jobs guarantee?

My hon. Friend may be aware that we recently reached three different agreements across retail, hospitality and tourism to create a total of 250,000 opportunities for young people not in education, employment or training over the next few years. That is evidence that concern with this issue goes beyond the Cabinet table and Government policy circles and is shared by businesses that want to do the right thing and create opportunities for young people.

An initiative led by Middlesbrough council, Mayor Chris Cooke and Middlesbrough college has reduced the 16 to 17-year-old NEET rate to 4.3%, compared with 6.8% regionally and 5.6% nationally. Sadly, however, getting meaningful jobs thereafter dropped significantly, and there is little evidence that disability benefits drive youth unemployment, the real problem being a shortage of suitable jobs. Can the Secretary of State set out what further steps will be taken to ensure that the new apprenticeship incentives are simple, easy to access and high enough to cover support needs, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question —there was a lot in it. He is right to draw attention to the work that he and his local college have been doing, and I am grateful to him for briefing me on that. The issue of 16 and 17-year-olds is important because they should be participating in education—we should not have 16 and 17-year-olds in that position. On future jobs, I made reference to the agreements we have recently reached with several other sectors. On apprenticeships, we are trying to tilt the funding more towards young people, for the obvious reason that they have their whole lives in front of them, and I think the public expect that apprenticeship funding should go more towards young people trying to get their first opportunity in life.
What steps are the Government taking to work specifically with further education providers, such as East Kent Colleges Group in my constituency, to help more young people into sustainable employment?

Let me express my gratitude to East Kent Colleges Group, which covers my hon. Friend’s constituency. Further education colleges have an absolutely vital role to play. They are part of the picture, along with many other recommendations in the Milburn review. But it is true that young people deserve a variety of further and higher education opportunities, and FE colleges like his and like City of Wolverhampton college, which covers my constituency, have an absolutely vital role to play in expanding opportunity.

The Government have spent the past two years making it more expensive for employers to employ young people through their jobs tax, through the burdens of the unemployment rights Act, and through above-inflation rises in the minimum wage. Does the Secretary of State accept that the best way to get more young people into work is to cut the cost of employing them in the first place?

The hon. Member refers to the minimum wage. The precise rate, of course, is set by the Low Pay Commission—an internationally admired model. The Low Pay Commission considered the case he was making and found that there was no evidence to suggest that this had a damaging effect on youth employment. It is of course an important part of its remit to consider the employment effects of any rate that it sets, and we expect it to do that when it sets the rates.

The Secretary of State and the Secretary of State for Education have been boasting about these 250,000 opportunities for young people. However, one supermarket chain was last week boasting to me that it was offering 90,000 work experience placements. Can the Secretary of State outline which of the 250,000 are substantial jobs, which are subsidised jobs, which are work placements and which are, effectively, work experience?

They are jobs, but I also say to the hon. Member that I welcome supermarkets offering work experience as well, because that can be a critical route to a job. When I ask employers, “How much more likely are you to hire somebody if they have gone through work experience?”, they often say “Significantly higher”, so I do not think we should posit these things as against one another; one can be a route to another.

Many employers have explained to me how the removal of the growth and skills levy for level 3 team leader and level 5 operational manager courses is keeping employees stuck in lower job levels, whereas previously those qualifications allowed them to move through the chain and new graduates to enter the market. What work is the Secretary of State doing with the Department for Education to ensure that these important skills can be accessed via the skills and growth levy, so that we can get more young people into those entry roles?

I am lobbied regularly about how the growth and skills levy should be used, including often during Work and Pensions questions, and we take the simple and clear view that the priority for this levy is to create opportunities for young people. They have their whole lives in front of them. I acknowledge that this is a policy choice that the Government have made, and it is one that I stand behind.

The number of young people starting apprenticeships in the hairdressing and barber sector has fallen from over 13,000 to just over 5,000 in the last decade, which has a particular impact on young people with special educational needs as there is double the rate of special educational needs than among NEETs in other sectors. One of the main causes appears to be the level of self-employment in that sector. What is the Department doing with Cabinet colleagues to ensure that these apprenticeships remain open, because the sector believes that there is a risk they will disappear altogether within the next couple of years, and they drive the rest of the businesses on our high streets?

The hon. Lady makes a really important point. This sector faces particular types of competition. She mentioned self-employment, and off-premises work is also a particular challenge in the sector. I thank the hairdressers and others in the beauty sector, who do such important work to create opportunities for young people. Businesses in my constituency have spoken to me about the challenges that she has referred to, and I want them to be able to thrive and continue to offer the kinds of opportunities she spoke about.
In the Government’s response to the Milburn review, how many jobs will be created for young people in Scotland?

We do not have a command economy where we direct people in particular areas to create jobs, but this is a common challenge across Scotland and England and I very much want to work with the Scottish Government on tackling it, because young people in Scotland need to know that their Governments, whether in Edinburgh or here, are on their side.

For months, and yet again today, we have watched the Secretary of State extol the virtues of his youth guarantee. Well, the results from his trailblazers are in, and they are damning. In London, less than half of young people got into work, education or training. In the west of England, they could not even get young people to turn up. With the evidence staring him in the face, will the Secretary of State accept that his pet project has failed and, rather than pouring billions of pounds more of taxpayer money down the drain on subsidised work schemes, will he lighten the load on businesses, the real job creators of this country, so that they can give Labour’s lost generation a chance?

I think that is a very revealing question. I watched Prime Minister’s questions last week, when the Leader of the Opposition attacked the youth guarantee, and now the shadow Secretary of State has nailed her colours to the mast by asking us to abandon it. Let me give her a very direct answer: we will not abandon it, because we believe in young people and want to support them. If the dividing line between us is that we support our youth guarantee to expand opportunity for young people and they would abandon it, then let us have the debate on those terms.
4. What recent progress the Timms review of personal independence payment has made on its programme of work.

The final recommendations of the review of PIP will be published tomorrow. The Secretary of State will then consider the recommendations alongside those of the Milburn review before deciding what changes are needed.

I thank the Minister and the members of the review group for ensuring that the work has been co-produced with disabled people. How will he work with disabilities charities to take forward a new approach focused on what people can do and achieve? Disabilities charities have a track record of success in creating fairer access to employment for disabled people, so will the Government work with them, including those in Scotland, to increase their role in delivering employability schemes?

My hon. Friend raises some important points. When the review is published, the review will call for a fundamental overhaul to rehumanise PIP. He is right about the co-produced nature of the report, and that approach will be vindicated when the House sees it. We will be taking forward recommendations arising from the review to look at how the assessment should be carried out. We will need to engage very closely with disabled people’s organisations and disabled people in the course of that work. He is absolutely right to highlight the important contribution that disabled people’s charities can make to supporting people into work. We have had a stubbornly large disability employment gap for far too long. We want to get that gap down and the contribution of disabled people’s charities will be important to bring that change about.

Several constituents have contacted me about shocking waits of up to a year to get their PIP applications reviewed. While my constituents and I eagerly await the Timms review, does the Minister acknowledge that such delays have a serious impact on people’s lives?

Yes, the hon. Lady is right. There are a number of difficulties with the current system. PIP is a highly valued benefit but the current assessment is not fit for purpose, and tomorrow we will set out proposals to change it.

The Milburn report rightly recognises the harmful disincentives in our health and disability benefits system that keep too many young people who can work out of work. Will the Minister do the right thing in his Timms report, out tomorrow, and recognise the same for the rest of the working-age population, or is he content to create a two-tier system—one system for the under-25s and one system for everyone else?

The hon. Gentleman is right to highlight the serious problems in the system inherited from his party in government. We will be taking forward proposals to change that system, and the proposals in my review will be set out very shortly.

On Sunday, the Minister for Social Security and Disability suggested that, as part of the Timms review, some PIP claimants may be signposted either to support or to services, rather than to receiving PIP. In a world where local authorities are reducing resources and fewer people are volunteering, will he set out his views on how that will work?

I am grateful to the hon. Member for his interest in the review. I know he will be looking at it with great interest after its publication. Tomorrow, we will set out the view that in addition to a cash benefit from PIP, which we are recommending should remain a cash-first benefit, there may well be services that would be helpful to people as part of their PIP award. The Motability scheme already enables many disabled people to enjoy the mobility that they would not otherwise be able to enjoy, and they choose to forgo part of their cash benefit in return for access to the scheme. We think that principle could be applied more widely with the PIP scheme.
5. What assessment he has made of trends in the number of foreign nationals claiming universal credit.

Universal credit is primarily reserved for people settled in the UK. Overall, the proportion of universal credit claimants who are foreign nationals has fallen since August 2025, from 16% to 15.4% in August 2026. That drop comes at a time when the Government are tightening the routes to settlement and rewarding those who make the strongest economic or public service contributions.

Once indefinite leave to remain is granted to a foreign national, they can claim universal credit on the same terms as a British citizen. Last year, foreign national households received almost £12 billion in universal credit, which is a 25% increase in a single year. The Home Secretary tried to toughen the rules, but she was too weak to win her battle with the Labour Back Benchers. Her failure opens the door to hundreds of thousands of new applications for indefinite leave to remain and, thereafter, universal credit. The cheques are written by Labour, but they are paid for by taxpayers. How much will the Home Secretary’s U-turn cost our taxpayers?

Let me remind the hon. Member that the previous Government let migration spiral out of control, and it is now down by 82% under this Government. The Boriswave would have allowed 1.9 million more people to become settled in the UK, which would have significantly increased welfare spending. This Government have taken action to reduce that number through the earned settlement changes, as he will know, and that will save billions of pounds.

Under the system as it stands, Britain is a cash machine for the world, and last week the Home Secretary handed the PIN number to hundreds of thousands of foreign nationals. The Conservatives have a clear alternative: the British welfare system should be for British citizens. Under our plan, non-EU foreign nationals would not be able to claim benefits, saving around £9.5 billion a year. Will the Minister back our plan, or will she continue to spout selective stats while the bill for aid to foreign nationals continues to soar under Labour?

The hon. Gentleman knows that the system he is complaining about is the system that was put in place by the previous Government, and they had 14 years to change it. I will tell him what we are going to do. The Home Secretary has set out significant reforms, introducing earned settlement. As a result, more than 500,000 people will need to wait longer until settlement, which will substantially impact who can access benefits and save billions from the benefits bill.

title: Indefinite Leave to Remain: Welfare Spending

items.txt: 6. What assessment he has made of the potential impact of proposed reforms to indefinite leave to remain on levels of welfare spending.

Our initial estimate is that this change will save billions from the welfare bill. We will work with the Home Office to quantify the welfare impacts alongside the wider fiscal impacts as part of the impact assessment, which will be prepared alongside the immigration rules that will be laid to enact these changes.

People who have arrived in the UK since 2021 will soon qualify for settlement and, with it, full access to benefits. I thank the Minister for that response, but it was quite vague, referring just to “billions”. Has the Department modelled the cost of this policy to the British taxpayer? Does she share my concern that the decision to allow tens of thousands more people to claim at the five-year mark has made reducing the welfare bill—should the Government wish to actually do that—far harder?

As I have already said, these reforms are fair. They will bring down the welfare bill by ensuring that those who contribute and gain access to the considerable rights and benefits that come with settlement have to earn them. In the normal way, when we bring forward the rule changes, we will bring forward the full details in the accompanying assessment.

We often see disinformation about welfare spending, especially online and especially about people who come to the UK to work. Many of my constituents have come to work in high-growth areas and in the NHS, and they pay tens of thousands of pounds in visa fees and extra NHS charges. Does the Minister agree that we should recognise their contribution to our economy and our communities and not demonise them?

My hon. Friend is exactly right, and the earned settlement proposals do just that. It would be wrong to remove benefits from foreign nationals who have followed the rules, settled here, made the UK their home and contributed to the UK economy.
7. What steps he is taking to improve co-ordination with regional mayors on supporting people into employment.

We have committed to give mayors the powers, flexibility and accountability to bring together education, employment, health and local support into a clear route for young people, and we will devolve employment support to mayors, including tailored and specialised support for the long-term unemployed. The “Rewiring the State” delivery plan will provide more detail on planned reforms, including employment support devolution.

Sandon House community centre in Heywood does amazing things, including supporting people into work by hosting a work and skills youth hub, which I visited recently. Following the Milburn review and the Government’s plans to rewire the state, there is an opportunity to fully devolve employment support to our mayors, rather than delegate it. What further steps is the Department exploring to ensure that mayors are being empowered when it comes to devolving careers functions, including long-term unemployment support and the jobs guarantee?

I thank my hon. Friend for her question. I was with her in Heywood just last weekend, and as ever, she is championing not just her town but her entire constituency. It is encouraging to hear about the Sandon House work and skills youth hub, and I thank its people for their efforts—it is a good example of properly joined up work to support young people. The work we are doing on careers support forms part of that wider approach, working with local leaders and services to design support that responds to the needs of local people and places. Our immediate priority is continuity of careers support, following in-housing of that service into the DWP last month, but we will set out more detail about long-term unemployment and the jobs guarantee in the “Rewiring the State” delivery plan.

Wessex will not elect its first mayor until May 2028, and when it does, one mayor will cover four council areas and communities scattered over a huge rural area. Employment support that works in a city region will not reach a young person in a village without a bus, so will the Minister make sure that mayoral employment funding reflects the real cost of reaching people in the countryside?

The hon. Lady makes an important point. It is essential that the Department for Transport plays a key role in how we deliver these services moving forward, and I will make that point in all my discussions.
9. What steps he is taking to help reduce levels of welfare spending.

We are increasing face-to-face health assessments, significantly reducing fraud, and have reduced the value of the universal credit health support payment. Of course, though, there will be more to do following our response to the Milburn and Timms reviews.

Review after review, delay after delay—Milburn is just the latest. While Ministers kick the can down the road, our welfare bill continues to spiral out of control, so when will the Minister finally act and reduce it?

I just listed some of the interventions we have already made, but it is essential to recognise that under the Conservative party in the last Parliament welfare spending, excluding spend on pensioners, increased by 0.6%. In contrast, if we look at the five-year scorecard from now until 2031-32, it is flat across the scorecard period. It was the Conservatives who lost control of welfare spending, not Labour.

I regularly visit Harlow college, which has a wonderful programme to get the long-term unemployed back into education, employment or training. Will the Minister pay tribute to Harlow college for its work to get people back into education, work and training? Can he talk a little more about how the findings of the Milburn review can help support colleges further to get people back into work and off benefits?

It comes as no surprise, Mr Speaker, to hear my hon. Friend say the word Harlow. I do commend the work of Harlow college—as we have already heard today, the role of colleges is central to the transformation that Milburn seeks to bring about. We will respond to his recommendations in due course, but I assure my hon. Friend that I am well aware of the vital role that colleges need to play.

It is disappointing that the Minister could not give my hon. Friend the Member for Berwickshire, Roxburgh and Selkirk (John Lamont) a straight answer to a legitimate question. Alan Milburn’s own figures show new spending of £5.8 billion a year, and after a decade, taxpayers might —might—save £200 million a year, with the Institute for Fiscal Studies calling this “highly uncertain”. Conservatives believe that welfare reform should save taxpayers money, not cost them more. The Government’s plans will mean higher taxes, more borrowing, or most likely both. Given that these reforms will not pay for themselves for at least a decade, who does the Minister expect to pick up the bill in the meantime?

The shadow Minister may be aware that the Prime Minister has already asked Departments to look to reprioritise spending, but I would tread carefully in relation to what the IFS has said about proposals. It was not the Government’s proposals that were described as having “significant uncertainties” but those of the Conservatives. Just for clarity, that is think-tank speak for “the Conservatives stuck their finger in the air long after losing the fag packet.”
10. What steps he is taking to reduce the number of overpayments caused by official error in disability benefit decisions.

We regularly check disability benefit decisions to make sure they are correct. Where we find mistakes, we look at what happened and use those lessons to improve future decision making. We share that learning across teams and focus support where it is most needed. That helps us to make more consistent decisions, ensures that people receive the right entitlement and reduces the risk of incorrect payments.

My constituent’s 12-year-old daughter is blind in one eye and sight-impaired in the other, and she was awarded the higher-rate disabled child element of universal credit in 2018. In awarding that benefit, the Department for Work and Pensions failed to request a certificate of visual impairment. Upon reviewing the case, seven years later, it decided that she did not qualify. My constituent must now repay nearly £27,000 for a mistake she did not make, even though the DWP has admitted in writing that it shares responsibility for this overpayment. The DWP has given her just £400 in compensation for its mistake. Will the Minister review whether it is right for the DWP to recover sums in full when her Department accepts fault?

I thank the hon. Member for raising this particularly difficult-sounding case. We always want to get our decisions right, and we do not want people to end up building up large amounts of overpayment, which they then have to refund to the Department. If it would be helpful, I would be happy to meet her to hear more about this particular case.

I welcome the Government’s commitment to implement the Liz Sayce review and the work they are doing to reassess carers who have been subject to large overpayments due to official error, but too many working carers are still falling foul of complex guidance. What more are the Government doing to stop carers who are working being penalised for these errors?

My hon. Friend is right to raise the situation of carers and the problems in relation to carer’s allowance. She will know that the Government have already acted to deal with problems that have occurred, and we have announced that we will be introducing a taper for carer’s allowance to ensure that unpaid carers who do such an important job can keep more of their earnings going forward.
11. What steps he is taking to help tackle youth unemployment in the Mid and South Pembrokeshire constituency.

Young people in Mid and South Pembrokeshire will benefit from the full breadth of youth guarantee support. Earlier and more intensive support is now available in our jobcentres, the £3,000 youth jobs grant has launched and the jobs guarantee is being rolled out across the country.

In Mid and South Pembrokeshire, the number of 18 to 24-year-olds claiming unemployment-related benefits increased by 29% between August 2025 and August 2026. These young people now account for a quarter of all unemployment-related benefits claimants in my constituency, and 88% of new claimants. I am sure that the Minister shares my concern about those figures, but will he set out what the Government are doing to ensure that young people in Pembrokeshire have access to the support and opportunities they need to build their careers?

I recognise my hon. Friend’s concern for young people in his constituency, and I assure him that we expect the youth hub in his area to open by the end of 2026. It will provide the wraparound employment and other help and support that young people need to get them into work, education or training.

Last week, I asked the Secretary of State whether the UK Government would provide the Welsh Government with the funding needed to deliver the ambitions of the Milburn review. Unfortunately, rather than answering the question, the Secretary of State chose to make a political point, so I want to ask the question again. Can the Secretary of State confirm that the UK Government will provide funding based on our needs, so that the Welsh Government can deliver the changes recommended in the Milburn review and best serve our young people in Wales?

The hon. Lady will have noted the Prime Minister’s correspondence last week calling for a closer working relationship with the Welsh Government. As for the specific question of funding, the Welsh Government have received a record settlement, and I am confident that they will do their utmost to help young people into education, employment or training.
12. What steps he is taking to tackle fraud in the welfare system.

The Government remain determined to combat benefit fraud. We have already delivered the Public Authorities (Fraud, Error and Recovery) Act 2025, which introduced the most significant new anti-fraud powers for a generation, and since the 2024 autumn Budget we have committed ourselves to delivering £21.6 billion in fraud, error and debt savings by 2031-32. In last month’s Budget we announced five new measures to strengthen welfare delivery, increase payment accuracy, and protect public money.

On Saturday, I was doing what I do on most Saturdays—knocking on doors in Newcastle-under-Lyme. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear!”] Members on both sides of the House are welcome to join me, particularly those wearing red rosettes. The message from my constituents was clear: people want fairness and support for those who need it, but they have little tolerance for those who take the proverbial. Does my hon. Friend agree with my constituents and me that the more we can do to tackle fraud the better, and may I urge her to go further and faster in doing exactly that?

My hon. Friend does a fantastic job for the people of Newcastle-under-Lyme. I absolutely agree that the welfare system must be fair, both to taxpayers and to those who genuinely need support. We are determined to tackle benefit fraud, using data and enhanced checks to identify incorrect claims and taking firm action when fraud is found. Through the Jobs and Careers Service, we are ensuring that those who can work receive the help and support that they need to get a job.

The Minister for Communities in Northern Ireland has claimed that £200 million has been retrieved from benefits cheats in the last three years. What assistance can the Government give to enable a proportion of that saving to be retained by the Northern Ireland Executive?
My hon. Friend the Pensions Minister, who is also a Minister in the Treasury, informs me that that is precisely what we are doing.
T1. If he will make a statement on his departmental responsibilities.

Since our last question session, the Government have set out their initial response to the Milburn report. The final report of the Timms review will be published tomorrow, and I have announced that the jobs guarantee will be available to young people who have been out of work and receiving universal credit for 12 months.

After years of young people being hit by cuts imposed by the Tories and by the Tory-Liberal Democrat coalition—for instance, the scrapping of the future jobs fund and of the education maintenance allowance—the Milburn review is a breath of fresh air, and constitutes an ambitious programme for the future. Can the Secretary of State tell us how many of the 250,000 jobs that the Government recently secured for young people from businesses around the country will be supporting young Londoners here in our capital city?

London is very strong in the retail, tourism and hospitality sectors, so I think that a significant proportion will be doing so.
