The commitment is for employers to recruit through their usual hiring processes, and decisions on where opportunities are offered are for individual employers and are not directed by the Government, but I am sure that this will expand opportunity for young people in London.

Last week Alan Milburn told the nation that this Government finally had something to say about sickness benefits. As we have been saying for months, they should stop handing out cash to people with mild health conditions, offer support instead and bring down the sickness benefits bill. However, we hear that the Timms review, which will land tomorrow, will not stop benefits for anyone or save a single penny. Two landmark reviews, one week apart, are pulling in opposite directions. Which does the Secretary of State back, Milburn or Timms?

I always have to remind the hon. Lady that the system she attacks is the one that the Conservatives created, legislated for and brought in. She asks about the two reviews. We want to see maximum participation in work, training and education—as I always say, for people to live the fullest life, particularly young people with their whole lives in front of them. I set out my initial response to the Milburn report last week, and we will respond fully to both reports in the new year.

That clearly was not an answer to my question. This next one is very straightforward, so I look forward to a very clear answer. We have been told that the Government have accepted Milburn’s recommendations. Last week, Alan Milburn told us that his proposals mean that some people will lose money, but the Prime Minister said that no young person will lose out from a cash point of view. They cannot both be right, so I ask for a simple yes or no from the Secretary of State. Will any young person lose out under Labour’s plans?

The answer is quite simple and has been given in the lifelong earnings of someone we can help into work. If we can help them into work, they will gain; in fact, they will gain a million pounds over their lifetime. I hope the hon. Lady welcomes that.

T2. I have a constituent who has a lifelong disability and uses the personal independence payment to pay for his transport to work. Under the Milburn review, his PIP might be replaced by a discretionary payment from a flexible health and disability fund or by an additional cost allowance, but it is not clear which. He is not a NEET, but he worries that he will lose some support. Can the Secretary of State or a Minister help by guaranteeing that young disabled people in work will not be made worse off?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising his constituent’s concern. He will know that the Milburn review contained a number of recommendations on how we deliver a new settlement for young people, including proposals for a higher payment to those with the most severe conditions and for those with additional costs to continue to have those costs met. Although I appreciate that his constituent wants certainty about his support, the Government require a little time to consider the recommendations in full. We will respond to all the proposals in the review early in the new year.

When the disability living allowance transitioned into PIP, 600 deaths, most of which were suicides, were linked to the DWP. What lessons have been learned from that, and what action will the Secretary of State take following the Timms review?

I have to point out that that happened under the coalition Government, of which the hon. Gentleman’s party was a part. Of course, benefit transitions periodically take place as Governments legislate for new benefits, and we must take care to look after people during such a transition. The system cannot be frozen in time. It needs to adapt to the future, and we will do this with care, which is the right way to do it.

T3. In recent weeks we have been pushing hard to ensure that the apprenticeships on offer to young people in Dorset actually meet the needs of local employers. That has especially been the case for growing the number of apprenticeships with defence companies at Dorset Innovation Park. With that in mind, what steps is the Minister taking to strengthen the partnership between employers and education providers so that more young people can study, train and work in the communities where they grew up?

My hon. Friend is a great champion for Dorset, and he is right to say that our education and training offer must support local growth and local opportunities. I know that education institutions, including Yeovil College and Bournemouth University, are doing great work. Local skills improvement plans, and our extra investment in apprenticeships, are designed to ensure that young people have opportunities to obtain the skills that local employers in Dorset need.

T4. Some 25% of young people in London are looking for work. The primary reason that the rate is so high is that businesses cannot afford to employ young people. The Milburn review recommends changes to national insurance contributions for 21 to 24-year-olds, but that falls far short of reversing this Government’s jobs tax. The Government acknowledge that serious action is needed to tackle the NEETs crisis, so why will they not remove their self-imposed barriers to employment?

Alan Milburn said that “the increase in youth inactivity long predates any recent changes to NICs.” He was very clear about that. I believe there is hope with the recent agreements with the retail, hospitality and tourism sectors, which, as I said in response to my hon. Friend the Member for Bermondsey and Old Southwark (Neil Coyle), can be of particular benefit to parts of the country where those sectors are strong. However, I do not rest there. We will continue to do what we can to open up opportunities for young people in the hon. Lady’s constituency and throughout the country.

T5. Folkestone and Hythe will soon be benefiting from one of the Government’s new youth hubs, and alongside our Labour councillors’ Future Ready initiative, this will help to drive down youth unemployment, but what additional measures are the Government taking to tackle this seasonal and structural problem in coastal communities such as mine?

I am grateful to my hon. and learned Friend for championing young people in Folkestone and Hythe. Alongside the new youth hub, we are providing earlier and more intensive support in our jobcentres, delivering the £3,000 youth jobs grant and, from the end of November, providing guaranteed jobs for young people on universal credit through the jobs guarantee scheme.

The Government have announced a new MoneyHelper pensions dashboard, which will help to trace pension pots that were previously considered lost. Does the Minister anticipate that fewer older people will be eligible for pension credit as a result of this new MoneyHelper tool?

I thank the hon. Member for bringing up the pensions dashboard, which has had a mixed history, but in recent years has been making real progress. I am very glad to have announced last week that we will see its launch in 2027. That will enable us to boost pensioners’ income by making sure that more pensioners get hold of the money they are entitled to and can plan in advance for it. We do not see a material effect on pension credit numbers.

T6. I was delighted to see the launch of Alan Milburn’s final report last week and particularly his emphasis on action to tackle the NEETs crisis locally in order for that to be effective. In my constituency, I have been leading the Aspire project, a mentorship programme that connects young NEETs with Kirklees college, C+K Careers and local businesses. With that in mind, will the Minister outline how the Department will support projects such as Aspire in my constituency in providing individualised support to NEETs?

I thank my hon. Friend for and congratulate him on the work he has been doing to support the Aspire project in his constituency. It sounds very similar to the approach that Alan Milburn is advancing in his final report. We will respond to his recommendations in full in the new year, but we have already committed to adopting a personalised and tailored approach, locally delivered, to provide wraparound support for young people to help them into education, employment or training.

Woking’s world-class car manufacturer McLaren recently announced it would expand, creating 1,000 extra jobs. Will the Secretary of State agree to meet me so we can seize this expansion as an opportunity to reduce the number of local NEETs and get them into training or work?

Let me congratulate McLaren. I visited McLaren some time ago—I think about a year ago—and saw the absolutely fantastic work taking place there. The opportunities there for young people are simply wonderful. I would be very happy to discuss this further, and I will make sure that the hon. Member gets a meeting with a Minister in the Department.

T7. My constituent Amy is concerned that the Child Maintenance Service is pushing paying parents to breaking point. How will the Government improve enforcement against ex-partners who will not pay their way, and as direct pay is scrapped, how will they minimise cost to parents?

My hon. Friend is a powerful advocate for his constituent Amy. This Government are clear that parents have a responsibility to support their children, and we are determined that those who can pay do pay. That is why we are reforming the Child Maintenance Service to act earlier on missed payments, speed up liability orders and take enforcement action more quickly, helping to prevent arrears from building up.

Nickel Support in my patch is a fantastic social enterprise helping adults with learning disabilities into the world of work. It previously presented their work to a Minister and a constituency visit was under consideration. Will the Minister commit to that visit today?

The hon. Gentleman will be pleased to know that I have received a full briefing on the meeting with my predecessor about the work of Nickel Support in his constituency. I know that officials are very happy to continue that conversation with the organisation in his constituency that does such important work.

T8. According to a recent Institute for Public Policy Research report, young people in Newcastle-under-Lyme face some of the biggest regional disparities when it comes to starting their working life. What more can be done to support young people in Newcastle-under-Lyme and across north Staffordshire into good, well-paid work?

We are very keen to support people in Newcastle-under-Lyme. I believe the youth inactivity agenda that we have been focusing on is not just an opportunity agenda, but an inequality agenda too. My hon. Friend is absolutely right to point out the disparities in the levels of opportunity around the country. That is why I am pleased that last week unemployment was down and, in the figures released a week ago tomorrow, youth unemployment was down too.

My constituent Mary’s adult son Peter is profoundly autistic and has very severe learning difficulties. He cannot talk or play games, and Mary explains that his main pleasure in life is going out for visits in his Motability car. However, the mileage limit on Motability, introduced earlier this year, means that his ability to do that has effectively been halved, and he risks becoming extremely anxious, potentially harming himself or his carers. Will the Secretary of State work with Motability to introduce an exception for journeys necessary for mental health or behavioural regulation, to help people such as Peter?

As the hon. Member says, a new limit has been introduced by Motability—Motability itself is in charge of the arrangements for the scheme—but it has introduced a concession on the 10,000-mile limit for particular purposes. Whether that applies in her constituent’s case I do not know, but I will be very happy to look at it with her.

T9. I welcome the Milburn review and the Government’s commitment to delivering a new youth opportunity service. Will the Government ensure that young people with education, health and care plans who receive support up to the age of 25 can access the new service when their EHCP ends, so they do not fall through the cracks?

I thank my hon. Friend for her welcoming words on the Milburn review. Her point about transition points and potential cliff edges in the system is well made. We will carefully consider the whole report in due course and come back with a full Government response, but I am absolutely cognisant of the importance of avoiding cliff edges at either special educational needs and disabilities stage, or in later life for people with additional needs.

My constituents Ahmed and Hussain have invested everything they have into their coffee trailer, Espresso Street Coffee, only to be hit by licence fees and a “computer says no” bureaucracy. Will the Minister please back a licence fee waiver for young first-time traders?
I ask the hon. Member to write to me on behalf of his constituents, and we will look at what he says.

T10. My constituent Dawn and her child have not received child maintenance for over a decade. Arrears exceed £50,000, but her child’s father has moved around and, due to errors, has evaded enforcement and any payment. Will the Minister tell us what action will be taken so that Dawn and others like her can get the support they need, and can I have a specific meeting about Dawn’s case?

I share my hon. Friend’s concern on behalf of her constituent. The Child Maintenance Service has a range of robust enforcement powers to pursue unpaid maintenance and ensure that children get the financial support they deserve. Where payments are not made on time or in full, the service can deduct directly from earnings or bank accounts and, where necessary, take stronger enforcement action, including taking control of goods, forcing the sale of property, and seeking disqualification from driving or from holding a passport.

Two thirds of people in Northern Ireland, some with poor mental health, were denied disability benefit but went on to win in a tribunal. What steps is the Minister taking to ensure that a culture of compassion is embedded at every stage of the assessment process, so that disabled people feel listened to?

As the hon. Member may have heard earlier, the final recommendations of the Timms review on PIP are being published tomorrow. I know that he will be looking at the recommendations with great interest.

With permission, I wish to update the House on Thursday’s coalition of the willing meeting in Berlin and Friday’s UK-EU summit in Brussels. Before I do so, let me say that it is deeply disappointing that consensus was not reached at COP31. This moment—after the summer the world saw—called for ambition. Instead, we were presented with a deal taking backwards steps on the climate, and we could not support it. I attended and addressed COP31 because I wanted to leave no doubt about the UK’s commitment to our 2050 target. Shifting to clean, home-grown power is a solution to the climate and cost of living crises, as well as bolstering energy independence and national security. It is vital to the UK and the world’s long-term interests, and we will now consider how, as we take on the presidency of the G20 next year, the UK can rebuild global leadership on climate. The meeting in Shenzhen of the Presidents of the United States, China and Russia provided the backdrop to the Berlin and Brussels meetings, and emphasised the urgent need for Europe to get its voice heard in discussions about its security. Huge progress was made at both meetings. By common consent, this coalition meeting was the most impactful to date and certainly the best attended. Crucially, we were joined by representatives of the US President, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, suggesting a welcome move towards one conversation and one negotiation. The meeting was unanimous on two points. First, there must be no discussion about Ukraine’s security without Ukraine in the room, and no discussion about Europe’s without Europe. Secondly, a successful conclusion of the former, and a ceasefire, must be in place before any decisions about the latter. The meeting heard directly from President Trump on his journey home from China. He pointed to loss of life on a devastating scale, particularly on the Russian side, and the need to build on progress made by the Abu Dhabi talks. In summary, the message out of Berlin was undeniable: Europe’s resolve to defend Ukraine and defend itself is strengthening, and the coalition of countries will stand with them for as long as it takes. The joint statement agreed at Friday’s summit in Brussels further strengthens UK-EU alignment on these critical security issues, with a clear commitment towards building a “stronger Europe in a stronger NATO”, through the EU-UK security and defence partnership. It says we will jointly face Russia’s persistent and evolving hybrid attacks, as well as developing a dialogue on democratic resilience, countering foreign information manipulation in our democratic processes. The agreement will also improve economic security here at home. Friday was a landmark moment. There is a clear consensus among the British public: almost three quarters of people want closer ties with Europe. In the last decade, the existing Brexit deal has had a negative impact on UK growth and added to cost of living and cost of business pressures. It has become harder for our businesses to export to the EU. People were promised more control over immigration, but it has not materialised, as the rise of the small boats crisis in the years after Brexit demonstrates. We lost co-operation. Too many bridges with old friends and neighbours were burned in the process of leaving, and that has damaged Britain’s national interest. The agreement reached in Brussels on Friday holds out the very real prospect that the next decade can be a better one for Britain than the one we have just lived through. The ability to draw a line on a decade of drift and division is in our hands, and I believe we should take it. I thank the Presidents of the European Council and Commission, António Costa and Ursula von der Leyen, for the warmth of their welcome on Friday. From here, we should build a new, more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbours and largest market. [ Interruption. ] The Opposition seem to forget that the EU is Britain’s largest market. Ahead o

There are a lot of things one can say about the deal that the Prime Minister has brought back, but “Congratulations” is definitely not one of them. When the Conservatives agreed Britain’s trade and co-operation agreement with the European Union—the deepest trade agreement any country has with the EU—we agreed a review for 2026. There is nothing unusual about two trading partners sitting down and seeing where improvements can be made. However, when you want to renegotiate, it is spectacularly foolish to tell everyone how desperate you are for a deal and that you are willing to pay any price to get it, as the Prime Minister did last week—so of course he did not get a good deal. When Labour negotiates, Britain loses. The truth is, this was not really about reducing the cost of living. The Prime Minister has treated this negotiation as a political performance, committing Britain to becoming a rule taker from Brussels—something he had no mandate to do—because he thinks, wrongly, that it will help his political fortunes. The Prime Minister has made many claims about Brexit that have turned out to be false. At PMQs last week he said that British exports are down since Brexit, when the figures show that, actually, they are up. Why should we believe a word he says? He said that this package could be worth up to £17 billion—“could be” is doing a lot of heavy lifting. What he failed to say was that the “could be” was by 2040. Last week, I complained that he was waiting 10 years for everything—now he is waiting 14 years. The Prime Minister’s entire economic case for the deal rests on more people coming to Britain; he has clearly not learned any lessons. The Conservatives want a high-growth, low-immigration economy; one where growth means that the people who live here are actually better off. That is what good growth actually looks like, and that is not what the Treasury says we will get from his scheme. All sorts of things were promised a year ago but have not come to pass. What has happened to e-gates? There is nothing here. Even touring musicians were made promises that are absent here. The Prime Minister has oversold this deal at every level. Let us look at the mess of pottage that the Prime Minister has brought back. He selectively and half-quotes many organisations. The worst thing ever to have happened to British farmers was this Labour Government. The British Retail Consortium says that his deal on food and agriculture “is unlikely to have any impact on prices”, and the deal does not even come into force until March 2028. The Fresh Produce Consortium is even more withering: it has said that his deal will actually put prices up. Inflation is rising now—the weekly shop is getting more expensive now because of this Labour Government—and he is making things worse. We need lower energy costs to get our economy growing. British businesses are already struggling. Manufacturing is being driven out of our country by the highest energy costs in the developed world. This deal makes those energy bills more expensive and makes it harder to bring them down in the long term. The right hon. Gentleman congratulates himself on the youth experience scheme. That deal was started by Keir Starmer, who said that he wanted no more than 30,000 young people coming to Britain. This Prime Minister has agreed to up to 300,000 over three years. As one EU diplomat told the Financial Times about Labour, “We sit on our hands and they cave in the end, same as always”. Under Labour, there are almost a million British young people not in education, training or employment; now, thanks to his deal, they will be competing with 300,000 Europeans for the few jobs that Labour has not managed to kill yet. As it stands, the deal is not concluded. Perhaps we should be thankful. We did our deal in 2019 on Christmas eve, and on Boxing day we published the text. This deal was signed on Friday; it is now Monday afternoon and still we have seen nothing. Where is it? We know that t

The right hon. Lady ended by saying she would bring a deal that lowers food costs, lowers energy costs and increases growth. That is exactly what this agreement does. It is not just those on this side of the House saying it: there is a line-up of British businesses and representative organisations all saying the same thing. It sounds dangerously like she cannot bear to bring herself to recognise that, and to stand for the things that the Conservatives used to stand for. They used to call themselves the party of business. Today, they are quite happy to saddle British businesses with mountains of red tape. That is the reality of where they are right now. The right hon. Lady says that the Conservatives delivered the will of the people. Well, I have it here that she also said that it was a “mistake” for the Conservative Government to take us out of the EU without “a plan for growth”. So which is it? Did she say that or did she not say that? She did say that, they did take us out without a plan for growth, and we are having to deal with the reality of that situation. We know now that the UK is the joint fastest growing in the G7, and that there is a deal on the table that will add further to British growth in the years ahead. That is why we have every right to be proud, as the pro-growth party in this House. I am worried about where the Conservatives are finding themselves. It is confusing, to say the least. They have spent the whole weekend bringing out a line-up of former Prime Ministers, one after another, to say that we should not even begin to talk about Brexit, but the reality of their position is that they are committed to reopening Brexit because they have committed to leaving the European convention on human rights. That very policy means they would have to renegotiate Brexit, so they need to get clear about what their party policy actually is. To turn to some of the specifics, the right hon. Lady said that I sold away the negotiating position. At that time when I stood at the Dispatch Box, it was not clear at all whether “Made in Europe” would be part of this deal. I went in to bat on that very issue, and I got an agreement that gives security to the British car industry, the British steel industry and the aluminium industry. That is all about negotiating a good deal for Britain, and she should see and learn how it is done. She says that exports are not down, but in fact they are down in real terms since 2018. She minimises the growth that this agreement will bring, but it is growth that British economy desperately needs and I do not understand why she turns her back on it. She says that more people are coming—this from the party of the Boriswave! Why should we listen to any of them? This plan will help us to build growth in the years ahead. On tuition fees, we are in a negotiation that will carry on after this agreement. Let me finish on the Makerfield test; I am proud to do so. What did my constituents tell me they wanted, when I stood on their doorsteps in the by-election? They said that they wanted lower food costs, lower cost of living, lower energy costs, more control of immigration, and more collaboration on immigration and the small boats. This deal delivers every single one of those things, and that is why Members on this side of the House will resolutely support it. People across the country will today look at a Conservative party that cannot face up to the mistakes it made years ago—mistakes that damaged Britain and left us where we are today. The Labour party will have none of it. We are drawing a line under the mess that the Conservatives left, and we are putting Britain back on a stronger path for the future.

The Prime Minister is right to look to reset our relationship with the EU, yet in one area, tackling modern slavery, we will be going backwards if we are not careful. We have good transparency laws, but the EU will implement laws that will really bite businesses that do not tackle modern slavery in their supply chains. I tabled an amendment to the Immigration and Asylum Bill, which we debated last week. I hope that the Prime Minister will work with everyone across the House who believes that we need to tackle modern slavery more effectively.

I say to my hon. Friend that that is absolutely our intention; this is an area where we have to work together if we are to get the progress that we want. In the document, she will see references to working to tackle organised crime in relation to illegal immigration and modern slavery. That is a very powerful reason why the House should support the agreement.

I thank the Prime Minister for advance sight of his statement. A youth mobility scheme, a food exports agreement and linking our emissions markets are all things that could and should have been part of the original Brexit deal, and would have been, if the Conservative party had not botched it so badly. They are all steps that our party has been calling for since then, so we welcome them. However, I would like to ask the Prime Minister about one particular line in the deal that he signed on Friday. The deal reaffirms the Government’s commitment to the trade and co-operation agreement—the Brexit deal signed by Boris Johnson, backed by the leader of Reform, the hon. Member for Clacton (Nigel Farage), and voted for by the Labour party. It says that the deal “functions effectively”. Does the Prime Minister stand by those words? Whether people voted leave or remain, I think the whole country can see that Boris Johnson’s deal is not functioning anything close to effectively. It puts up barriers to trade with our closest trading partners, ties British firms up in reels of red tape, and has created the small boats crisis by cutting us off from a returns agreement with Europe. This failing deal is costing our country tens of billions of pounds every year—money that Conservative and Labour Governments have taken out of people’s pockets by freezing the income tax thresholds. It has pushed up the cost of living and closed off opportunities for British people to live, work and study across Europe. It has made our country poorer, weaker and less safe. Does the Prime Minister really believe that Boris Johnson’s trade and co-operation agreement is functioning effectively? If not, will he make it his priority to replace Johnson’s failed agreement and get a totally new deal for Britain now? Millions of British people hit by Brexit’s higher taxes and higher bills cannot wait until after the next election.

I can tell the House that I will take a pragmatic approach at all times, be guided by the evidence, and make changes where we need to make changes. We did need to make changes in relation to food, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme, and the right hon. Gentleman is right to point to all those things. Why were they not in the original deal? The Conservatives, particularly the right hon. Member for North West Essex (Mrs Badenoch), stand there saying that they are the expert deal makers, but 10 years of lived experience tells the whole country that they are not expert deal makers. No one needs to hear me say that, because people have lived it themselves. In terms of the trade and co-operation agreement, this deal takes steps to improve it. The right hon. Gentleman has just heard me say that we will continue to look at further options for the long-term relationship. I think he probably agrees that Europe in 2026 is not Europe in 2016, and Britain in 2026 is not Britain in 2016. Looking to next year, the politics of Europe could change considerably. We need to go into the further consideration of options with all those factors in mind. I stick by what I said: we are not rerunning the referendum and the arguments of 2016, but looking pragmatically at the world as it is now, and that is what I will do as Prime Minister. I will lead in the best way I can to get growth going, get opportunities for young people, bring down the cost of living and get greater control of immigration. Let me say unequivocally that I believe in the deal we have negotiated. I think it is good for Britain; it is in our national interest. The House should support it.

Does the Prime Minister agree that it is quite extraordinary to hear the Leader of the Opposition lecturing us about trade deals? I mean, seriously—Liz Truss’s Trade Secretary is trying to tell us that Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal, signed on Christmas eve, cannot be improved. All the trade deals that she and Liz Truss secured for Brexit Britain do not amount to a hill of beans. For example, she said that the comprehensive and progressive agreement for trans-Pacific partnership deal would bring “significant” benefits to the UK. If 0.06% of GDP is significant, then how would the Prime Minister describe his deal—massive, gigantic, colossal, or maybe gigante, écrasant or even gewaltig?

I would describe it as good progress. I would also say to the Chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee that this is a future-facing deal. The Leader of the Opposition was at the CBI just now, saying that Europe is “not the market of the future”. She repeated something similar at the Dispatch Box. Again, I say to the Opposition that this is our largest market—40% of our exports, 50% of our imports. On what basis do we turn away from it, and say that it is not a priority? She is finding any reason she can to dismiss it, but the Opposition would start to get the ear of the country again if they were to work with us, and get this Bill through the House.

Clearly, this reset is a prelude to the Prime Minister’s sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum, but has he considered this point? If he overturns the result of a referendum that should be a once-in-a-generation event, the SNP will launch a relentless campaign to have another referendum in Scotland, so in return for marginal gains from rejoining a bloc with an ever-declining part of world trade, he could be creating new bitterness and division, and be putting the Union at risk.

This deal is not a prelude to anything. It is a pragmatic approach, and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach. If it is in Britain’s national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I will not. There is no fixed opinion here; there is no fixed destination. As I said to the House a moment ago, Europe could change again in the next year or 18 months, and obviously we will have to watch how life changes, but where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress. Can anyone in the Opposition parties, or indeed the right hon. Gentleman, say that the last decade has been good enough for Britain? Well, I cannot. It has not been good enough—for our young people, or for anybody. Where we can make that better, we should.

I warmly welcome the Prime Minister’s willingness to reckon with the disastrous impacts that Brexit has had on our country’s economy and communities, and the work that he is doing to bring us closer once again to our friends and neighbours in the EU. The subject of university tuition fees is central to the deal that he is delivering. The Education Committee published a report earlier this year that documents the extreme financial precarity of many of our universities, which have the potential to be powerhouses of economic growth and opportunity. As the Prime Minister continues to progress negotiations with the EU, will he guarantee to do so in dialogue with our universities, in a way that bolsters their financial sustainability, rather than adding further pressures to it?

I can give my hon. Friend the Chair of the Education Committee that assurance. That is a separate negotiation from the three main deals. We will keep the House regularly updated on progress, but my hon. Friend is absolutely right to point to the critical importance of the UK higher education sector as a powerhouse for growth across all our regions in the years to come, and we will do everything we can to protect that.

When the Prime Minister came to office, he rightly and sensibly cancelled his predecessor’s digital identity card process and policy. How does he justify involving Britain in Europe’s digital ID system, as part of his EU reset process, and risking us having to put that into effect, without this Parliament having any say whatsoever?

The UK is not joining the EU digital identity wallet. This agreement does not commit us to doing so, or to adopting the EU’s digital identity system. It does propose a digital partnership, but that is to deepen co-operation across our digital and technology sectors. That is the reason why it was warmly welcomed by the European chief executive of Vodafone on Friday.

The bottom line is that the deal the Prime Minister has brought home is in our national interest. The Conservative party’s collective amnesia is something to behold. I am old enough to remember when Boris Johnson turned the air blue with his four-letter description of what his botched Brexit deal could do for business. This deal is good for business; it is welcomed by business, and to oppose it is to oppose what is in business’s interest. I want to ask the Prime Minister about “Made in Europe”. It risked destroying any possibility of our reindustrialising our country in the way the Prime Minister wants. Can he confirm that we no longer face that peril, and that we will instead join forces with Europe in standing up to unfair competition from China?

The evidence that this is in business’s interest was right before me in Sittingbourne this morning, at a Morrisons distribution depot. There was a stack of paper on the table for one shipment to its store in Gibraltar. No joke, it was that big. This agreement would sweep it all away, but the party of red tape over there on the Opposition Benches is quite happy to leave businesses battling away with it. It is unbelievable, given where that party once was in this House. “Made in Europe” is an evolving concept, and we have negotiated language that gives us considerable comfort about the impact on British industry. We want to work with Europe as a trusted partner, because we face the same issue, particularly from China. This is about facing it together, rather than disrupting supply chains between the UK and the EU, which are still very integrated. We are dealing with the same issue, and the language that the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations secured is really positive in that respect.

The sanitary and phytosanitary agreement will require us, in future, to close our market to any product to which the EU closes its market. The EU has already closed its market to beef imported from Brazil because of its concerns about antimicrobial resistance. If the principle of alignment is good, should we not be doing the same?

That is why we negotiated hard to ensure that British experts are in the room and are consulted when these decisions are taken. It is a very important part of these arrangements that we have a voice in those decisions.

May I congratulate the Prime Minister on the deal that he secured for Britain last week? I am proud to have been the first Chancellor in more than a decade who sought to strengthen, rather than to sever, our relations with the European Union. Does the Prime Minister agree that the best way to build on the very strong growth and productivity numbers that we have achieved over the past two years is to continue to strengthen both our security and economic relations with our nearest neighbours and trading partners?

I agree strongly with my right hon. Friend. May I pay tribute to her in her role as Chancellor for laying the ground for this agreement that has reached, and to the former Prime Minister too? They were both acting in Britain’s best interests and they enabled us to reach the agreement that we reached on Friday. It is pragmatic, but I agree with her completely: all the evidence points to the fact that this will boost Britain’s security, boost our economy and increase our exports, all of which are good things. If the Conservatives have different ideas about how we achieve all those things in the next decade, it is time we heard them. I am really grateful to her and to the former Prime Minister for all their efforts to make Friday’s deal possible.

Despite their enthusiasm for the EU, Ministers in Keir Starmer’s Government repeatedly ruled out trading away our control of gene editing, given the opportunities to boost farm profitability and improve nature, yet the Prime Minister did not even mention that in his speech. Is that because he does not think those sorts of details matter, or does he accept that he is giving away control over growth opportunities that could be such a boost to our farming community?

Actually, I do understand the importance of the issue to our farming community. We have secured agreements on precision breeding that will ensure that we can protect British interests as part of this deal.

May I congratulate the Prime Minister on the conclusion of an excellent summit? If we want to deal with the cost of living crisis that we see across the country, get growth in every postcode and increase the money we are able to spend on public services, does he agree with me that the best lever available to our country is closer co-operation with the European Union? When he thinks about the options going forward, which one does he think will deliver the best growth?

In this Parliament we will honour the red lines in the manifesto and we will get the maximum for Britain within that context, and I believe that the deal we got achieves that. As we look to the Parliament beyond this, the work that I have set in train will help inform decisions in the Parliament beyond this one. It is important for me to say again that the world has changed and will continue to change. We need to test any options against that reality, but in my view we should always be pragmatic and choose whatever option secures the best deal for Britain.

Further to that answer from the Prime Minister, given the hard-line, doctrinaire approach on display from both the Commission and EU member states last week, does he really believe that this one-size-fits-all approach that would see Britain rejoining the European Union, with a commitment to join the single currency, no borders and no rebate, would remotely be in the national interest or command the support of the British people, including those people who voted remain last time?

I have made no such commitment about the currency and will not be making any such commitment about the currency. The right hon. Gentleman talks in terms that I think show the problem with the Conservatives: hard line and doctrinaire, for years they have gone to Brussels and insulted people; they have gone there and damaged goodwill, and that has been against the British national interest. It is in our interest to work with people when they are our nearest neighbours. It became very plain to me, as part of this negotiation, the depth of the damage they did to relations with people with whom we have shared so much in the past. That is the damage that this Labour Government are correcting.
I call the Chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee.

Everyone in this Chamber should be concerned by the failure to agree at COP31, especially given that the figure of 1.5°C in global warming has been breached. If anybody thinks that is a good thing, they should see Russia’s fingerprints all over that failure. I welcome the Prime Minister’s commitment to use the presidency of the G20 next year to recommit to climate action around the world. At a conference this morning, Rain Newton-Smith, the director-general of the CBI, said that the Prime Minister made progress on Friday. Will he build on the ambition that she has called for today by giving our exporters support through linking the ETS and giving all of us and our constituents support through linking the electricity schemes as well?

We will make sure that we can extract all the value we possibly can from this agreement. The electricity linking opportunity could take a significant number of pounds off bills in the UK, particularly in Northern Ireland, as I have said. [ Interruption. ] I am surprised by the noises from the Conservatives—it is like the cost of living does not matter. Well, it does not matter to them and many of the people they know, but it matters in Makerfield and many other constituencies across the country. We will take pounds off bills wherever we can, and we will keep the House updated on that point. It comes over, does it not? The CBI—the Confederation of British Industry—says that this is progress, but the Conservatives say that it is not. What a position they have got themselves into.

This agreement has been widely welcomed in Edinburgh, which, as the Prime Minister will know, was one of the strongest areas for remain in the country. We have heard that the agreement will deliver for food and goods, but can he go further and tell us what he can push for in the sectors on which Edinburgh is so dependent, such as the finance, creative and research sectors?

I point again to the opportunity for touring artists. That is not just about musicians; it is about performers of all kinds. I do not think they have had enough of a hearing in the 10 years since. They lost opportunity, and no one has talked about that enough, in my view. The creative industries are one of Britain’s finest exports, and bringing back visa-free touring would mean a great deal for the many people who perform at the world-leading Edinburgh festival every year.

The Leader of the Opposition says that the Prime Minister should not reopen the EU debate, but will he reflect that you cannot reopen something that never closed in the first place? As somebody who is open-minded about the future of our relationship with the EU, including perhaps rejoining one day, but not at any cost, I implore the Prime Minister to carry on communicating, discussing and negotiating with the EU. That is the only way that we can ground the future debate in fact, not the fantasy we hear about from Members on the Opposition Benches.

I assure my right hon. Friend that that is exactly what I intend to do. I will not be listening to the voices of the former Prime Ministers the Opposition wheeled out, one after another, at the weekend, because they are asking us to stay stuck in the past and to accept a substandard deal, and we will not be doing that. As I have said, the confusion among Members on the Opposition Benches is unbelievable. They are committed to reopening Brexit because of their position on the ECHR, so which one is it? They are so split on Europe and so terrified of discussing it these days, but we are going to discuss it to get benefits for Britain.
Will the Prime Minister at least give a clear and unequivocal statement that it would be unthinkable for any Prime Minister to try to take the UK back into the EU without a referendum?

I welcome the Prime Minister’s statement on the UK-EU summit. Given that Slough is the youth capital of Britain, I particularly welcome the youth experience scheme and ongoing talks about the youth mobility scheme, which will give our young people back the opportunities that their parents took for granted, such as the ability to work, live and study in mainland Europe. However, given the considerably raised threat level, we must also ensure that British businesses and supply chains are supported by further defence agreements with our European allies. Can my right hon. Friend shed further light on ongoing talks regarding Security Action for Europe—the SAFE project—and the Made in Europe scheme? What are the Government’s ambitions for those schemes?

Obviously, the SAFE talks concluded last year, and we will only ever sign agreements if they are in our national interest, as I have said today. British firms have access to SAFE on standard third-country terms, and that will remain the case—this agreement does not affect that. More broadly, though, we are seeking deeper co-operation on defence, particularly defence procurement. Through the multilateral defence mechanism, the Chancellor is working hard to build partnerships with EU countries and others to procure jointly and get those costs down.

BMW’s decision to pause a planned £600 million investment in the Mini plant was a real blow to my Oxford constituents. The 10% tariffs on electric vehicles exported to the EU would have made that investment even harder, and one constituent who works at the factory told me that while he voted for Brexit, he would now be open to rejoining, because he feels that his job has become so precarious over the years. Will the Prime Minister confirm with clarity whether those tariffs are definitely not going ahead? Furthermore, is it true that if that happens, the quid pro quo would be us aligning our tariffs for Chinese EVs? Jobs are on the line, so can he be clear with the industry?

I can assure the hon. Lady that we care very much about the issues she is raising and the manufacturing of the Mini in her constituency, at Cowley. We are doing all we can. The Business Secretary and I have met the company; it is paused at this moment in time, and I point the hon. Lady towards language in the agreement that should give her some reassurance, but we have not reached a final conclusion yet. We are happy to work closely with her, because we know—exactly as she says—that these issues will be on the minds of many of her constituents.

I know only too well the painstaking work that goes into the final weeks before a UK-EU summit, so I congratulate the Prime Minister on a deal last Friday that is good for growth and good for jobs, that will bear down on the bills people face, and that secures more tools to secure our borders. Does he agree that the priority now has to be swift implementation, so that people can feel those benefits in their lives?

I want to praise my right hon. Friend for the groundwork that he, too, laid for this deal—he possibly did more on the detail than anybody, and we really appreciate what he has done. He is right that we need to act swiftly to show our intent, which is why I have asked the Chief Whip to put the European partnership Bill before this House before the end of this week, and we will be looking to have Second Reading this side of the Christmas break. We want to get on with this—we want to get it in place to make sure we meet the deadlines of the deal.

With regard to the Prime Minister’s UK-EU deal on freedom of movement for young people, the UK wanted the number to be capped at under 50,000 a year. The EU wanted that number to be 100,000 a year. It seems that agreement has been reached at the EU’s higher number of 100,000. What does that say about the negotiating skills of our people-pleasing Prime Minister? Talking of freedom of movement—if that is how what happened in No. 10 today can be described—perhaps the Prime Minister’s time would be better spent polishing up his negotiating skills, rather than concentrating on the choreography of a dance routine of a TikTok influencer.

My goodness, that must have looked good when the right hon. Lady did it in front of the mirror in her office, but I am not sure about this Chamber. I find it hard to take lessons from the party of the Boris wave—she was right in the middle of all of that. The Conservatives let net migration get out of control, and the point they miss completely is that when young people come from Europe to study here, they develop an attachment to this country; they have a lifelong affiliation to it that continues in Britain’s interests, the same as when young Brits go abroad. I thank the right hon. Lady for that performance, but I think she should spend a bit more time in front of the mirror next time.

In joining others in welcoming this agreement and the economic benefits it will bring, may I encourage my right hon. Friend to continue to put to one side the voices of those who want to go back to the past and instead to seek to negotiate a closer economic and security relationship with the European Union? For the reasons that he set out at the beginning of his statement, we live in a more uncertain and a more dangerous world, and working more closely together with our European friends and neighbours is absolutely in our country’s national interests.

When I look at what has happened in the last decade—not just Brexit, but covid, the invasion of Ukraine and all the other challenges—we have to ask: have we been put in a stronger position? Were some of our enemies not both developing plans to invade other countries and seeking to weaken the democratic resilience of other European countries? That is exactly what we have been living through in the last decade. As we go into the next, we should have our eyes wide open to all those threats. Those of like mind—the democracy that we are and the club of democracies that we were once part of—should work together, because it is in our common interest to do so, whether economically or for defence and security. My right hon. Friend is absolutely right, as is customary, to put it in the way that he does.

The Lake district is Britain’s second-biggest visitor destination after London, yet 53% of hospitality and tourism businesses within the lakes say that they are operating below capacity because they cannot find enough staff. That is why Cumbria Tourism, myself and others have fought so hard, for so long, for a youth mobility visa scheme, and I welcome its inclusion in this agreement. What conversations has the Prime Minister had with Britain’s world-class tourism and hospitality industry to make sure that it gets the youth mobility visa scheme in practice that is of most use to it and to our economy?

We will work closely on that. It is similar to the arrangements we have with Australia and New Zealand. That is what we have in mind when we are looking to negotiate this scheme, and we want to make it beneficial for our hospitality sector and the hotels in his constituency. The hon. Member is absolutely right to put it in the way that he does, and we will design the scheme with his comments in mind.

When the Prime Minister was Mayor of Greater Manchester, he was resolute in his opposition to extremism of both left and right. When he said in Makerfield that it would be wrong to reopen the debate on Europe, because it would be divisive, and then he does exactly that in Brussels, does he recognise that that leads to cynicism and a loss of trust in parliamentary democracy? Where there is a loss of trust in parliamentary democracy, we get extremists.

My hon. Friend will have to go back to what I actually said. It was around the 10-year anniversary of the referendum, and I was talking about rerunning the referendum. I am not proposing, at this moment, to rerun the referendum— [ Interruption. ] Well, I am not proposing it, and I have said it clearly this afternoon. I hope he would agree that I am somebody who does take care about what I say and sticks to what I say. I have inherited a situation—I referenced my right hon. Friend the Member for Torfaen (Nick Thomas-Symonds) a moment ago who did the groundwork on a deal—where it was entirely in keeping with the Labour manifesto that my hon. Friend the Member for Blackley and Middleton South and I were elected on to develop that deal. We promised the public of Makerfield and the country that we would deliver closer ties with Europe. That is what this deal does, and I do not think it helps anybody for him to stand up and say that somehow I have broken that trust, because I have not.

The Scottish National party welcomes both the agreement and today’s statement. Brexit has been disastrous for Scotland, so we welcome any action that brings us closer to the EU and, hopefully, back on the path to rejoining it, and we look forward to working constructively on the European partnership Bill as it progresses through the House. The Prime Minister recently promised that he would not go over the heads of the devolved Administrations. Can he guarantee today that the Bill will contain nothing that removes, strips, waters down or overrides the existing powers of devolved Parliaments?

I will ask the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations, my right hon. Friend the Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer), to ensure that all those conversations are had with the devolved Governments. It is very important that this agreement is implemented respecting all the arrangements that we have with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

I welcome the sanitary and phytosanitary agreement to achieve a better deal for our farmers and consumers and give everyone in the UK a welcome reprieve from the cost of living pressures. The last Labour Government, of which my right hon. Friend was a proud part, banned fur farming here in the UK back in 2004, but despite that, we continue to allow the import of products from this cruel trade. Given that fur is not an agrifood and is therefore not part of the SPS agreement, can the Prime Minister assure me, and the House, that the new agreement will not prevent this country from strengthening our own animal welfare standards by banning the import and sale of all animal fur?
It was a specific point of negotiation that all our domestic controls over animal welfare were retained, so I can give my hon. Friend that assurance.

This terrible EU deal— [Interruption.] They do not like the truth, Madam Deputy Speaker. This terrible EU deal will increase immigration, with 300,000 people under 31, making it harder for young British NEETs to get back into work. The Prime Minister told his constituents that he would not reopen the EU debate, and he has done exactly the opposite. He is treating them like fools. What does he say to his fellow Labour MP who told the BBC’s “Newsnight” last week that the Prime Minister was treating leave voters like “thick northern racists”?

I find myself as confused by the Reform party position as I am by the Conservative party position. The leader of the hon. Gentleman’s party famously said—he said it on the radio just two weeks ago—“Brexit has failed.” That is what he said. If anyone searches for it, that is what will come up. Am I right? [Hon. Members: “Yes!”] The hon. Gentleman does not know. Well, he should look it up. That is what the leader of his party said. He has criticised the Brexit deal that the Conservatives negotiated. If that is his position, why would he not admit that it is his position, and why would his party not then argue for something better? It sounds as if he is arguing for the status quo, when the leader of his party has said that it has failed.

I, for one, welcome the Prime Minister’s statement. Let me begin by drawing the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests concerning my membership of the Musicians’ Union. When my niece was touring Germany with the musical “Kinky Boots”, along with Johannes from “Strictly Come Dancing”—I know that the Prime Minister is a real fan of “Strictly”—they had to interrupt the tour to come back to play Stoke-on-Trent, and, I think, Sunderland as well, because of the 90-day rule. The alternative would have been trying to apply for visas, and all sorts of bureaucracy. Is it not ludicrous that they cannot do a tour of Germany, and indeed of Europe, without having to interrupt the tour in this way? What more can the Prime Minister tell us about what he will do to establish touring rights so that musicians and other artists can stay out in Europe and there is freedom of movement?

I know how much my hon. Friend cares about these issues, and I do too. I would routinely hear prominent voices in the Manchester music industry saying how difficult it had become, to the point at which they had given up on doing it. How sad is that? British bands who were listened to all over Europe are having to withdraw from touring. I was therefore really keen for that wording to be secured in the agreement, and I am going to try hard to turn it into something positive—I hope, visa-free touring for British performers. I think that that would be a really good way of projecting the best possible image of our country around Europe, and this is one area in which I hope that perhaps not everybody, but as much of the House as possible, will get behind it, because it is what our musicians and other performers deserve.

May I give the Prime Minister a gentle admonishment for his response to the hon. Member for Blackley and Middleton South (Graham Stringer)? He has been nothing but honourable throughout this debate, and it does not do the Prime Minister any good to attack his hon. Friend, who made a simple statement. He must know that, since he got elected to be Prime Minister, he has hardly done anything else but talk about the EU and what the Government were going to do with the EU. [ Interruption. ] It is true. The Prime Minister has provided figures such as £9 billion in savings, and apparently huge elements of growth going as far ahead as 2040, yet when we ask for the detail of how they are produced, nothing comes. The other day, I asked a Foreign Office Minister at the Dispatch Box whether they could lay out the details of the £9 billion savings that they claimed, and the answer was: “No, we don’t do that, because we’re the Foreign Office.” I find that rather peculiar. Will the Prime Minister now accept and admit— [ Interruption. ] I would not take too much advice from the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer), if he does not mind my saying so. The reality is that the issue here is something that the Prime Minister has not mentioned. Is it not true that before he was allowed to engage in any discussions or deals, he had to cut the fishing target for all British fishing, which will now cost more than £6 billion over the same period? That is not in his costs.

That was a long question. From my point of view, I have had no discussions about fishing as part of this deal. On the exchange I had with my hon. Friend the Member for Blackley and Middleton South (Graham Stringer), all I can say is that I stick to the facts. I was talking about rerunning 2016, and I have not done that. I have inherited a situation in which there was a deal on the table, and it is entirely in keeping with Labour’s manifesto. I have to act and lead in the national interests of this country. I believe that this deal is in the national interest and in keeping with the manifesto. That is why I have taken it forward.

Either we can keep our head in the sand, or we can act when things are not working. UK goods exports to the EU last year were 14% below the 2019 level in real terms, and one story that illustrates that is from a business in my constituency. The owner told me that it took four days for his goods to be on the shelves in Germany before the Brexit deal, but up to 40 days after the Brexit deal. Does the Prime Minister agree that the direction of travel that we are now taking to see closer relationships with the European Union is vital for supporting businesses and families in all our constituencies to take up more of the opportunities that that will bring, and gives a message of hope that things can be better than they are?

I agree very strongly with my hon. Friend. It is our job in this House to remove barriers and red tape from businesses where we can, particularly when they do not serve the wider public interest. Seeing what businesses are having to deal with to export was something of a shock, to be quite honest. I come back to the main point: in the times that we are living in—we have all felt it—sticking with something that is patently not working is the worst kind of politics.

I very much welcome this deal, but it is a timid and piecemeal approach, and does not deliver the full economic benefits that joining the single market would. As a result of this approach, the Prime Minister is left haggling over university tuition fees for EU students for the next six months. Is this deal contingent on reaching a deal on tuition fees? If he cuts tuition fees for EU students, how is he going to compensate our world-leading universities, whose finances are already very fragile?

I refer the hon. Lady to the President of the European Commission’s words on Friday. In relation to tuition fees, she spoke about the deal being on a separate piece of paper—in other words, it is a separate deal. I think that answers the hon. Lady’s question. We will seek a constructive deal with the European Commission that is in both its interests and ours.

I congratulate the Prime Minister on his deal with the European Union, which will mean cheaper food in shops in Ealing Southall, less red tape for businesses and more opportunities for young people. My constituent Mary from Northfields is concerned about a very specific impact of Brexit, which is the £150 she has to pay each time she goes on holidays to Europe and takes the family dog, Toby. Does the Prime Minister agree that, for people such as Mary and for Toby the Shih Tzu, another benefit of this deal will be multi-use pet passports that will save pet owners in Ealing Southall both time and money?

I have good news for Mary and Toby the dog: breaks in Europe are going to be much less stressful for both of them in the future, and for the many British families who have had to apply for pet passports, involving a lot of cost and paperwork, so that is a really positive thing. My hon. Friend mentions the cost of food in her constituency. Again, the Opposition try to dispute it, but every single big British supermarket and retailer has come out and said this deal will lift pressure off the weekly shop. Why are the Opposition unable to welcome something that is so obviously in the interests of their constituents and ours?

The Prime Minister has made optimistic claims about the impact on GDP of this deal by 2040, and he has also spoken about farmers and sanitary and phytosanitary arrangements, but does he accept that this deal will leave some farmers and food producers worse off? Will he reflect, as the hon. Member for Newport West and Islwyn (Ruth Jones) did, on how the deal raises concerns about animal welfare standards? We have the highest animal welfare standards in this country. Finally, why has he sacrificed this Parliament when it comes to being able to make laws that affect the future of our country?

The estimate is the Treasury’s estimate—it is not my estimate—and it has done the detailed work to back up that claim, and as I said a moment ago, we have specifically negotiated the ability to keep Britain’s animal welfare standards as part of this deal.

Brexit has damaged our economy, made us poorer, increased costs to businesses and families, taken away opportunities for young people and made the cost of living harder to bear, so I welcome the Prime Minister’s determination to take practical steps to relieve those harms. At a time when major world powers are shaping the future of our continent without our say, does he agree that closer co-operation with our European allies, particularly on defence and security, is vital to our national interest?

I very much believe that. Let me come back to something I said earlier. I think 10 or 15 years ago our enemies had a clear plan to invade neighbouring countries—that is, Ukraine—and at the same time weaken the cohesion of Europe and the ability of Europe to fight what they were doing. Sadly, they succeeded on the first, but I do not believe they have succeeded on the second. As I said at the start of this statement, the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday was magnificent in the solidarity among all the different countries and in the strength of the resolve expressed by all the leaders. Russia tried to break the resolve of the European Union and it tried to break its cohesion; it has failed.

I genuinely welcome the shift in tone from Labour—the recognition that Brexit was disastrous, a dog’s breakfast and deeply damaging to the UK—and the steps taken last week with this agreement. However, given the scale of the challenges that we face globally on security, the climate and the cost of living, does the Prime Minister not recognise that we need bold and brave politics, not baby steps, so when will he set out a pathway to the truly brightest future for Britain—in other words, to rejoin the EU?

I will set out a bold plan for Britain next month, so the hon. Lady does not have to wait too long—a plan to reindustrialise Britain, to give young people a new education system, and to create new opportunity and growth in every postcode. It is on the way. As part of that, we will consider what is the right long-term relationship for Britain with its largest market and nearest neighbour.

First, I thank the Prime Minister for his statement and for his commitment to strengthening our relationship with Europe. The deal he has secured is the right approach towards deeper co-operation, boosting growth, removing barriers and, more importantly, creating opportunities for young people. I welcome his commitment to making progress on touring artists and musicians, but we need to see concrete action that will rebuild ties, reduce barriers and cut costs. When the Government are looking at options, will he commit to ensuring that they include practical solutions, from work permits to easier movement between countries, that will be mutually beneficial to our musicians and artists here, as well as in Europe?
I certainly will give my hon. Friend that assurance and I look forward to working with her on precisely that.

I wonder, did the Prime Minister hear the chief executive of the Fresh Produce Consortium on the radio at lunch time, who said that his deal will add more than £300 million in costs to those importing food into the UK and that that would need to be passed on, with the result that food prices would be higher, not lower?

That is, I am afraid, not a majority view. I read out the long list of business endorsers for this deal. I will not do it again. I will look up that interview, but the vast majority of people—I come back to it: people from Morrisons this morning showed me the pile of paperwork that they will no longer have to complete. [ Interruption. ] The right hon. Gentleman rolls his eyes, but that is just a fact. They welcome it warmly. I will look at what the Fresh Produce Consortium said, but, as I say, it seems to be an outlier.

I very much welcome the deal. Frankly, being lectured by those on the Opposition Benches—they oversaw a deal in which up to 20,000 British businesses gave up trading with Europe altogether and our food exports were cut by a fifth, and food prices are rising—is a bit like being lectured by Henry VIII on marriage or by Hannibal Lector on veganism. Now, they want to make things even worse, not just by rejecting any progress at all and defending the status quo, but by ripping up our membership of the ECHR, which underpins international trade treaties such as this and gives other nations confidence in debating and negotiating with us. Will the Prime Minister promise my constituents and all businesses who have been affected that, as he sorts out the mess that Brexit has made in our economy and our society, he will not make the same mistakes as them?
Before the Prime Minister rises to answer that question, can I ask Members please to keep questions short?

Oh, I can certainly give my hon. Friend that assurance: we certainly will not be repeating the mistakes of the Conservative party. As she says, they are committed to reopening Brexit—it is their party policy. It is just an ideological position that they have, rather than a practical position which is about helping businesses and consumers where we can.

This betrayal of Brexit will result in higher energy prices, food prices and greater contributions to the EU. The Prime Minister said that this is about breaking down barriers, yet in Northern Ireland we still have goods that cannot be sold, taxes that have to be paid and paperwork that has to be filled in. Can he specifically tell me what will be the role of the £140 million 10-acre border post in the port of Larne in my constituency? Will it now be redundant, or will it remain a symbol of our detachment in Northern Ireland from the GB economy?

I would have thought the right hon. Gentleman might have welcomed the fact that this agreement will remove 90% of the SPS checks in the Irish sea that were introduced by the Conservative party. That surely is good news, is it not?

Penicillin was Britain’s gift to the world. It transformed modern medicine and it remains vital today, yet Europe’s last major penicillin manufacturing plant is reportedly at risk of closure. I welcome the Prime Minister’s progress on health corporations with the EU, including plans for earlier warnings of medicine shortages, but warnings alone will not solve the problem if we lose the factories that make our medicines. As I listen to Opposition Members reject the Prime Minister’s closer engagement with Europe, can he explain how facing alone a risk such as that would make our medicine supply safer? Will he commit to making pharmaceutical manufacturing a priority in the next stages of the UK-EU reset?
I assure my hon. Friend that we will continue to work with European Commission partners on exactly the issues that she raises, including on the critical issue of the supply of medicines.

I welcome the Prime Minister’s statement as an attempt to reverse some of the damage done by the Conservative’s botched Brexit, but thousands of young people will be excluded from the youth mobility scheme—the very cohort who started their working lives during covid, when placements, graduate jobs and chances to work abroad dried up. Will the Prime Minister consider extending the age limit to 35, in line with our schemes with Australia, Canada, New Zealand and South Korea?

I understand why the hon. Lady raises that point and speaks up for a generation who were badly affected by the way things changed. The agreement is for a youth experience scheme up to the age of 31, so I am afraid I cannot give her that assurance. But still, the fact that people up to that age will have the freedom to work, travel and study in Europe is clearly a major step forward.

Automotive manufacturers will be keen to see further actions protecting against the rise in Chinese dumping of electric buses and cars. Will the Prime Minister expand on the progress being made to avoid the rules-of-origin cliff edge that still threatens to push up export costs for our domestic manufacturers in a matter of weeks?

The rules of origin are extremely important for the automotive industry. I am aware of Alexander Dennis—ADL—and other manufacturers in my hon. Friend’s constituency. We will talk to the European Commission about this matter tomorrow, and the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations will keep my hon. Friend updated.

I thank the Prime Minister for the steps that he has taken to strengthen our relationship with the European Union. As we look to the future, will the Prime Minister’s 10-year plan include a dispassionate consideration and assessment of the widest possible range of options for the UK’s future long-term relationship with the EU?

The plan will not set them all out, because we have to go into an informal process of discussion. As I said before, the world has changed, it keeps on changing, and we need to be pragmatic in that regard. But yes, at the next UK-EU summit, I would hope that those options will be laid out and that all parties in this House will be able to consider them as part of their next election manifestos, so that we inform the discussions in the next Parliament as much as we possibly can.

I welcome Friday’s deal, particularly the commitment by the UK and the EU to avoid any measures that would harm each other’s automotive industries. I was pleased by what the Prime Minister just said about rules of origin; in his discussions tomorrow and those ongoing up to Christmas and the new year, can he please ensure that that issue is treated with the urgency it deserves, given that we have a cliff edge on 1 January?

I think I should correct the record: I believe that Cowley is in my right hon. Friend’s constituency, and not the constituency of the hon. Member for Oxford West and Abingdon (Layla Moran). I am very aware of how serious the concerns are. We are doing everything that we can to support the manufacturing of the Great British Mini in my right hon. Friend’s constituency. I believe we have taken a step forward and I hope that her constituents will be reassured by this deal. To repeat, “Made in Europe” was not on the table as part of this negotiation; I put it on the table, and we got it in the agreement. That is good negotiation, and I hope it will turn into something meaningful for my right hon. Friend’s constituents.
Will the Treasury compensate universities for any loss of fee income?

The right hon. Member is getting ahead of the talks. He has heard me say in this House that the British higher education sector is one of our major strengths, and we will ensure that nothing is done to damage it.

I welcome the inclusion of climate ambition in the G20 presidency. Last week’s EU summit marked a step change compared with the hard Brexit negotiated by the red tape Tories. In my constituency, we have businesses that will be able to return once again to trading with Europe and young people—as well as performing artists, consumers and shoppers—with better opportunities. Can the Prime Minister confirm that this deal will pass the Putney test as much as it passes the Makerfield test?

I think it passes the Putney test with flying colours. My hon. Friend has coined a new phrase in this House: the Opposition used to call themselves the red wall Tories, but they are now the red tape Tories —because that, it seems, is what they stand for.

The Prime Minister has just said that the British people will be the boss and decide what comes next, but dynamic alignment, which is at the heart of the SPS agreement, means that we have to take on EU laws without a seat at the table—no ifs, no buts. Legally, how is dynamic alignment possibly allowing the British people to be the boss?

Many food producers are already aligned. As I said before, we negotiated to ensure that British experts are in the room when decisions are being implemented, and they will be consulted. It is an important step forward that we have secured. What the hon. Lady has to justify to businesses in her constituency is why she is turning her back on a deal that will further their interests.

This deal will bring a wealth of trading benefits to so many in the UK. As the Prime Minister says, it is in the long-term interests of our young people. Will the Prime Minister say how young people will benefit from the youth experience scheme and the criteria for a visa?

The details are to be worked up, but my hon. Friend is absolutely right that the deal restores to young people freedoms that were lost at the time of Brexit. As I said, they have in many ways been the biggest losers. Many people in this House took those freedoms for granted when they were young, but have gladly removed them from the next generation. I think young people can have some hope with this deal that things that might give them the chance to broaden their horizons will once again be possible.

Food export volumes to the EU fell by a third between 2019 and 2024. I welcome cutting red tape for farmers, growers, and cider and cheese producers, right across my constituency, but the UK must influence, if not vote on, the rules it aligns with. Will the Prime Minister now go further and drop his red lines, go further still to a customs union and access to the single market, and ensure that the UK has a seat at the table at all critical moments as we move forward?

I am aware of the wonders of Glastonbury cider, and I want it to have the widest audience possible. I would say to the hon. Lady that it is one step at a time. We have to be careful at every stage to ensure that we are in tune with public opinion, which, in my view, is telling us that the public want a deal of this kind. In a recent poll, 73% said that they want closer ties with Europe. That is what the people are saying. They have not been heard by the Opposition, but we will not ignore them. We will continue to take that pragmatic approach going forward.
Order. I really do want to get in as many Members as possible, so please be brief.

Companies, particularly those in the food and drink sector in my constituency, have learned the hard way how costly post-Brexit trading arrangements are, no matter the size of the company. Will the Prime Minister outline how being able to both import and export more easily with European markets can benefit the G65, G66, G67, G68 and G33 postcodes?

I do think the deal will bring growth in every one of those postcodes—good growth.
