Scotland stands to gain greatly from this deal, as it can face the longest export journeys; when we consider perishable products that could be spoiled by delays at the port, this deal is clearly in my hon. Friend’s constituents’ interests. I remember that she stood up in this House and spoke of constituency examples of businesses with containers stuck at the port, which cannot be in their interests. I believe that this deal will remove those delays.

As someone who campaigned to leave the EU and took part in two referendums, it saddens me that the Prime Minister is embarking on a policy that will result in yet another divisive referendum. As he will know, my constituency is heavily dependent on the energy sector, due to energy-intensive industries and farming. Can I urge him to draw some red lines that say that in future negotiations he will agree to nothing that imposes further regulation on the energy sector, that damages the support that the Government are giving to Scunthorpe steel or that prevents the farming community from developing new processes that will improve their yields?

I am not proposing that we have a referendum or do any such thing. I am advocating a very cautious, pragmatic approach if we are to go any further down this road. On the industries that the hon. Gentleman has just mentioned, is he aware that the emissions trading scheme linkage would be massively beneficial for big British industry and would significantly reduce its costs? Much of that benefit is to be found in his constituency. I know that he is an advocate of the steel industry, and this will seriously help that industry.

This afternoon we have seen Project Fear raise its ugly head again with the way that the Opposition speak about the youth experience scheme. Does the Prime Minister agree that this is a wonderful opportunity for young people from across all our constituencies, from London to Makerfield to Clacton, who will be able to go to 27 countries to learn more and bring back their learning to support this country to be a thriving economy?

I agree completely; it is time for a bit more hope and positivity in this country. We want to open up people’s horizons rather than close them down. Rather than a language of distrust about our European partners, let us start working with them again to bring benefits for both sides.

Does the Prime Minister recognise the bitter irony that, in the week that Alan Milburn makes sensible recommendations about getting NEETs back into work, he is allowing 100,000 people from abroad to come and compete with them for jobs? Will he confirm that it was when he was retreating, having been defeated in battle, that the proposal for foreign students to come here and not pay their dues—to pay domestic fees—was brought in? In other words, was it not introduced at a very late stage in the negotiations? Was the Prime Minister both defeated and ambushed?

Neither. We had a good, positive discussion throughout. Hence, we have a constructive deal that has responded on many of the things that we wanted to see. At the scheme’s steady state, the Home Office estimates that around 14,000 young people will come in from Europe every year. The point that the right hon. Gentleman and his Opposition colleagues are missing is that this is within the context of a bigger economy where there are more opportunities to get the kind of jobs that people will seek, such as those in retail and hospitality. He needs to broaden his perspective and think of a bigger British economy that has more positivity and is more open to Europe. I think that will be a good thing for young people in this country.

The UK’s food system is remarkable, but it is also complicated. While overall it will gain, of course it is possible to find particular sectors that will struggles. The same goes for universities. The Prime Minister will know from his own experience at the University of Cambridge that European students in UK universities can be life-changing. I would like to see more European students in our universities, but he will also know that our universities are very different—they are not all the same—so can he give me an assurance that the sector will be properly consulted and the impact on different universities will be taken into account?

I can certainly speak from personal experience about the life-changing effect of young students from the European Union coming to Cambridge University —sometimes life-enhancing as well! I take seriously the resilience of the UK higher education sector, and I understand that these proposals could impact differently on different universities. It is really important that throughout whatever happens, we safeguard one of Britain’s critical strengths: our higher education sector.

I must say, that is the most expensive dating agency I have ever heard of! The Prime Minister has evidently got a cunning plan to hand back control to the European Union, but does he accept that the EU is still committed to political unification and a United States of Europe?

Well, that is probably rerunning the language of the past. Let’s move on a little, shall we? I think the Conservatives need to get themselves out of the rut they put themselves into in 2016 and have never got out of. Let us open up again and start talking in a more modern, constructive way about where we may go from here.

The Prime Minister talks about bringing back hope, and he will know the value of the creative industries in doing that, so I was pleased to hear him speak today about making it easier for musicians to tour in Europe, which cost an extra £208 million between 2020 and 2024, with millions of pounds extra for carnets, red tape and additional costs for our musicians. Could he furnish us with some examples of how it will be easier for our musicians, orchestras and bands to tour in Europe, and for Europe’s cultural offering to come here as well?

Obviously, we have not concluded the discussion—I am happy to involve my hon. Friend within it—but I remember bands from Manchester saying to me that they could not take merchandise with them as it was too complicated, and therefore they could not stack up a tour financially. That was a very common experience. We need to try to solve those issues and remove those barriers as part of these discussions.

I had the best possible start to UK Parliament Week by spending the morning with children from Hazel Grove primary school. They had two asks for me as their MP. The first was to get better play equipment for Torkington park—I will not ask the Prime Minister about that—and the second was to help their families with the cost of their energy bills. We know that the UK and the EU working together on energy bills could help to bring them down, but the talks will not conclude till next year at the earliest. Will the Prime Minister commit to seeking membership of the EU’s internal electricity market? Will he also publish an estimate of what that would save on bills to give the children of Hazel Grove primary school some light at the end of the tunnel?

We owe it to the children of Hazel Grove, their families and the hon. Lady to put before the House the assessment of what we could do through the linking of electricity trading in Europe, and we will do that. To further my answer, the chief executive of National Grid, who was with us in Brussels, pointed very much to the opportunity to bring down bills if we were to pursue that route. There are wider considerations, but, as a Government, we will look at anything that brings down the cost of electricity bills.

It is not just big supermarket chains: small businesses are also welcoming the deal. Will the Prime Minister build on his considerable achievements on youth—also, it seems, on touring musicians—with mutual recognition between EU and UK qualifications in his next round of negotiations?
We have made progress on mutual recognition for architects, and we are looking to take that to other professional sectors as well.
Vibes and empty promises of hope will not pay the bills of hard-working British families. How much, in British pounds, will the Prime Minister’s deal save British families doing their weekly shop?

Is it not good enough to have M&S Food, Morrisons, Tesco, Aldi and Lidl all coming out and saying that this deal will lift the pressure off the weekly shop? I could show the hon. Member a photo of what Morrisons showed me follows every shipment; from that, it is obvious that this deal will reduce cost pressures, and that will be passed on to the public. Conservative Members should be asking not how much these measures will remove from bills, but by how much their resistance in the House to backing what we are doing will put food bills up.

In a dangerous world, relations with our largest trading partner must be governed by our national interests, not nostalgia or narrow ideology. Unfortunately, the deal we inherited from the last Government failed on every single one of those terms. The Conservatives were too afraid of the siren voices from Reform to do right by the British people then; regrettably—and I do mean that—it sounds like they remain afraid of those voices. I am particularly excited by the opportunities on the table for young people, but the Prime Minister will know that in the past not every young person—that includes our care leavers—was able to fully take advantage of them. Can we kick-start a conversation about how we ensure that every young person in Britain can benefit from the opportunities he has announced today?
I am absolutely on the same page as my hon. Friend, and we will do precisely what he asks.

In Scotland, taxpayers are concerned that they will pick up the tab for EU students receiving free university fees in Scotland again. Can the Prime Minister assure Scottish taxpayers that they will not be picking up the bill for anything he agrees on student fees?
We have not concluded a deal. When we do, we will bring it before this House.

I warmly welcome the Prime Minister’s statement. Reducing friction and costs at the border with our biggest agricultural partner is good news for farmers, consumers and our economy. Can he reassure my farmers in High Peak that the Government will support them through the implementation of this deal, and that the UK will be able to advocate on their behalf?
Yes, I can give them that assurance. It is really important that we enable British farmers to become exporters once again and help them to take advantage of these new opportunities.

The Prime Minister says his EU reset deal has passed the Makerfield test. Well, in order to pass the Isle of Wight test, he will need to tell us a single item at the supermarkets that will reduce in price as a consequence. Can he?

As the hon. Gentleman may have heard, I was in Morrisons in Sittingbourne this morning, and it has a store on the Isle of Wight that it services from that depot. Morrisons says that this deal will lift the pressure off the weekly shop. What does that mean? It means that it will not be as expensive as it would have been had we not had this deal, so why is the hon. Gentleman against it? What is his answer to the people going into the Morrisons store in his constituency when they say, “Why did you oppose a deal that could have taken the pressure off the weekly shop?” I would love to hear that conversation.

Over the weekend, I spoke to the managing director of Coquet Island Shellfish, a significant business in my constituency that exports millions of pounds-worth of shellfish and seafood every year to the continent. To be clear, the business is delighted about the SPS deal, but it has short-term problems with its exports to French ports, where there has been some obstructive behaviour by the French customs and hundreds of thousands of pounds-worth of its produce has sadly been lost. What more can the Prime Minister do in the short term, between now and March 2028, to aid the overcoming of those barriers to businesses such as Coquet Island Shellfish?

The Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations, my right hon. Friend the Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer), is very much having discussions with European colleagues about those types of issues, and we are working to minimise that type of disruption.

Last week, the Foreign Affairs Committee visited British troops who are serving in Estonia. Most of them will be away from their families for many months, and they receive longer separation allowance to recognise this, but they are taxed on it. Will the Government consider removing tax from longer separation allowance?
I am struggling to work out how that is relevant to the statement—
It might be a good idea, to be fair to the right hon. Member for Tonbridge (Tom Tugendhat). Yes, it might be, so I will have a look at that proposal.

In my constituency, families are still feeling the squeeze of high food prices while local wholesale businesses, of which I have many in my constituency, have spent years dealing with the post-Brexit red tape. Does my right hon. Friend agree that this new EU agreement will both back local businesses in my constituency of Barking and help keep food market prices down for families, fixing the mess that the Conservative party left behind in this country?
I am very pleased that the leader of the red tape Tories was in the House to hear my hon. Friend’s excellent question.

I thank the Prime Minister for his statement, in which he said of the small boats: “By losing access to intelligence and the ability to return people, it has become harder to stop these crossings.” He went on to say that he had done something on intelligence. Did he ask for the power to return illegal immigrants to EU countries as part of these negotiations? If not, why not?

I am trying to work out whether the hon. Gentleman is in favour of that, because he—or his party—gave it away. We are trying to take steps to get back the collaboration that we once had—the collaboration that they waved away. We have a significant step forward, which is to be a partner in the channel action plan. If he looks at the agreement, he will see it says explicitly that it will involve intelligence and data sharing. That is invaluable to UK Border Force.

I congratulate the Prime Minister on securing this historic agreement, especially on the youth experience scheme, for which I have long been an advocate. Does he agree that a clear dividing line is now appearing in our politics—on this side of the House, the pro-Europeans looking for every opportunity to maximise support for young people, and on that side of the House, the Brexit fanatics who, by rejecting this deal, will continue to hold young people back?

Every week the Leader of the Opposition comes here demanding major cuts to support for young people. Now, with her deputy, the hon. Member for Brentwood and Ongar (Alex Burghart), saying that he would rip up this deal even though it gives a major opportunity to young people in their constituencies, they are closing down opportunities. They are really revealing themselves this afternoon.

Why should the British public trust the Prime Minister that costs will come down when, so far this afternoon, he has not been able to tell us what they would be with a reset or without a reset? To my mind, there has been far too much “could do”; does he need to be honest and say that they might not?

I am quoting practically every big British retailer, and the hon. Lady is choosing not to hear what those retailers are saying because it is inconvenient for her to hear what they are saying. They are saying that the removal of major red tape will enable them to lift pressure off the weekly shop. We are talking of prices some 14 months hence, and so we cannot give precise prices, because who knows what will happen between now and then? The red-tape Tories really need to get themselves in position; they cannot come here calling for lower food prices while defending mountains of red tape on our businesses.

Small businesses, often family run, are the backbone of our economy in Aylesbury and the villages. Many have raised with me their challenges in exporting to the EU, which involves so much red tape. One of my local hauliers told me that his European contracts are at risk because his drivers cannot be on the continent for more than 90 days. I therefore commend the Prime Minister for his ambition to get our relationship with the EU working again. Does he agree that that is a good thing for my local businesses?
It is a great thing for my hon. Friend’s local businesses and businesses represented by colleagues across the House. They will take careful note of those not supporting it.

How on earth can the Prime Minister attempt to justify the reported reduction in tuition fees for EU students coming to the UK while the Government that he leads continue to impose VAT on independent education—the irony being that that would be illegal under EU law?

Small businesses that want to export to the European Union have for several years now been rule takers; they have had to follow European rules without any say in shaping them. Now, at last, we are going to be decision shapers, and we have a chance of a seat at the table. Will the Prime Minister assure us that the diplomatic mission in Brussels has the staffing and technical expertise we need to make this opportunity work for Britain?
My hon. Friend is so right—British experts, back in the room, getting a good arrangement for our country. That is exactly what it is to have a win-win deal.

British scientists are leading the way in developing a vaccine against bovine tuberculosis—a disease that has devastated so many of our farming communities, including dairy and beef farmers in my constituency—yet EU rules prohibit cattle vaccination against TB. The NFU has warned that this agreement could prevent British farmers from benefiting from that breakthrough. Can the Prime Minister guarantee that British farmers will be able to use this vaccine if our scientists succeed, rather than being held back by EU regulations?

We have negotiated carve-outs in certain areas. If the hon. Member sends me the specifics of the case— [ Interruption. ] Well, at least let me have a look at the detail and I will come back to her with an answer to pass on to her constituents.

I welcome the Prime Minister’s deal negotiated on Friday. A youth experience scheme and closer trade partnerships make direct rail services to the continent more important than ever. Will he restate his commitment, alongside the Department for Transport, to get direct rail services open once more in Kent and put forward a financial package to ensure that Ebbsfleet and Ashford station can be—
I do favour the restoration of direct European services from the stations that my hon. Friend mentions—it has infrastructure implications. I will take a close look at it.

I am sorry to say that parts of this EU deal are a bit of a dog’s breakfast, which is a bit harsh on what my black Labrador had for breakfast this morning. In the run-up to the deal, the Cabinet Office released a video in which the Minister for Intergovernmental Relations and European Relations, the right hon. Member for Lincoln (Mr Falconer), who is sitting next to the Prime Minister, complained about the inconvenience of deworming tablets when moving pets between the UK and Europe—an “inconvenience” that helps prevent people from getting a serious zoonotic disease. Is the Prime Minister 100% certain that this deal will protect the UK’s biosecurity, animal health and public health?

Yes, I am 100% certain. Conservative Members can find whatever reason they want to oppose it, but the vast majority of people in— [ Interruption. ] Excuse me? Oh, “the Conservatives”—I thought it was aimed at me for a second. The vast majority of people in the British veterinary community support this deal.

I welcome the statement and the Prime Minister’s observation that three quarters of people in the UK would now like closer ties with Europe. In Colchester, we value our existing ties with Europe through twinning partnerships, historical military links and our export strengths. On that last point, does the Prime Minister agree that exports from Essex to Europe will improve as a result of this deal?

Yes, I am pretty certain that they will. I come back to the fact that the NFU states there has been a 30% reduction in agricultural exports. That will have been felt in counties right across England. This deal will change that, and I am sure that Essex will benefit.

The Prime Minister’s approach to negotiations puts him in the sorry position of a home buyer who after the first viewing tells the estate agent it is his dream home and that he will not go anywhere else, and then is shocked when he gets asked for the asking price—except it is all of us paying the asking price. How much will it cost to join the electricity market?

Like so many on the Opposition side, the hon. Member is getting it completely wrong. The comparison is between what I put on the table today and what he left behind with his Government, so what is better: what he left behind or what we are putting on the table today? Does the Opposition really want to defend the status quo which has hurt growth and lifted food prices? Does he really want to do that? It sounds like he does, and I do not think he will win that argument.
UK agrifood exports to the EU have fallen 32% since 2019. Does the Prime Minister believe that this deal can reverse that, and what would a good result for farmers look like in five years’ time?

I do believe that this deal could reverse that, and we want to get agricultural exports back up to where they once were. When they are at that point, that will be at the level that we would want to see.

Listening to Conservative Members, I find it possible that they have not learned anything from the last 10 years and do not understand their own position on the ECHR and Brexit. With that in mind, I ask the Prime Minister why last week the Labour party voted with the Conservatives and Reform against joining the EU migration and asylum pact.

As I say, we have to take one step at a time, and we do not want to go ahead of British public opinion, and I am not doing that. I believe that what I am doing today is squarely in tune with what people are saying they want: closer ties with Europe.

The deal’s measures that strengthen defence industrial co-operation between the UK and EU will be particularly welcome in my constituency, which has a long and proud history of contributing to our country’s defence industry with thousands of high-quality jobs in the sector. Can my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister outline the benefits he expects to see from that closer co-operation to Stevenage and the rest of the country?

We are already seeing that closer defence collaboration. It is evident in our response to Ukraine. What I confirmed on Thursday in Berlin was that we would supply two fast attack boats built in Britain but done in partnership with Norway. That type of collaboration is increasing as we move into a new world. I mentioned before that my right hon. Friend the Chancellor is looking to build countries behind the multilateral defence mechanism. My hon. Friend will see an ever-increasing focus on defence, but more innovative ways of funding it, too.

I agree with the Prime Minister that young people coming to study in this country builds friendships and relationships that can last a lifetime. However, does the Prime Minister agree that there is a concern that we are going to charge European Union students who come and study here the same as British students while at the same time charge overseas fees to our friends in the Commonwealth, who are also our friends and clearly are a benefit to this country?

We have not concluded the arrangement and we will debate it when we do, but I agree in principle with the hon. Gentleman that when young people come and study here, they develop an attachment. As part of resetting our relationships with the EU, I am also resetting relationships with the Commonwealth and was glad to be able to start to do that properly at the recent Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua.

I thank the Prime Minister for his statement. My constituency is home to East Midlands airport, the largest carrier of small air freight in the UK, so I know how important it is to smaller exporters. Will the Prime Minister update the House on how he will ensure that small businesses are supported to maximise their opportunities to export goods to Europe in this deal?
We will work with the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade to make sure that type of practical support is put in place to maximise the benefits of this deal.

There is no voice, no vote and no veto on key issues like animal disease outbreaks or crop protection products. This deal requires Britain to pay towards the European Food Safety Authority and other EU agencies, plus a management fee, yet there are no specific costings in the detail. In the interest of transparency, will the Prime Minister set out what those additional costs will be for taxpayers and British food businesses?

As I said, the European partnership Bill will come before the House later this week. We will publish all the technical and legal papers to support consideration of the Bill, and I give the hon. Gentleman an assurance that the material he seeks will be published as part of that.

I thank the Prime Minister for visiting my constituency this morning and spending so much time with the fantastic team at the Morrisons distribution centre, discussing with, and hearing from, them about what the impacts of this deal will be on their work. On the way to Sittingbourne, he will have gone through the garden of England and that heartland of ultra-productive orchards. Will the Prime Minister outline to my farmers—my apple and pear growers—the impacts of this new deal on their potential to export across Europe?

I thank my hon. Friend for being part of the visit this morning, which, as he says, was great. It was great to meet his constituents. His constituents will benefit greatly from this deal, and fruit growers in particular because their produce is time-sensitive and needs to get over to those markets quickly. I can guarantee his constituents that their exports to Europe will get there much more quickly than has been the case for the last six years or so.

We were told that Brexit would save us £350 million a week, but the Conservative Brexit deal has been costing us £250 million a day in lost revenue to the Treasury, so we welcome the Prime Minister’s attempts to rebuild our trading relationship with Europe. We need to improve trade with Europe for farmers and agricultural businesses—we need an SPS agreement—but can we have an assurance that we will double-down on port biosecurity, because illegal meat and the illegal movement of animals from Europe are putting the livestock industry at risk of a notifiable disease outbreak, like foot and mouth?

Of course we would not want to take any risks on that front— [Interruption.] Opposition Members laugh, but this is why it is important that British veterinary experts are back in the room overseeing the arrangements.

Operation Brock, the entry-exit system, relocating border checks to the Sevington inland border facility, and the loss of international train connectivity—that is what a hard Brexit brought to my constituency. While the Conservatives and Reform continue to defend the damage caused by the status quo, what does the Prime Minister say to my constituents and people in Kent about how this new deal will improve their lives and help restore opportunities for their communities?

I say to my hon. Friend’s constituents that the agreement will take practical steps that will make life better. He mentions the hard Brexit. It was harder than the one that people thought that they were voting for in 2016, and that was the manner in which the Conservatives did that deal, burning our bridges. That is what we are trying to repair, and the deal that we reached on Friday, with good spirits in Brussels, puts us back on that path.

It is clear that the EU is demanding cheaper tuition for EU students, and it is also obvious that this Prime Minister has a habit of capitulating. He has said that he will bring a deal to the House regarding any offer on EU students, but before that, can he guarantee to the House that any deal to offer EU students cheaper tuition will not result in UK students paying more for university, or in fewer university places being available in this country?

We will have our clear red lines in that negotiation. The hon. Gentleman talked about capitulating. I say again that “Made in Europe” was a real threat to British industry when I came into this job. I put that issue directly on the table, and we have negotiated a good deal. What would the Conservatives have done with “Made in Europe” with their isolationist approach? It would have been heading straight for the British car industry as we speak, and they would have nothing to say about it.

Does the Prime Minister agree that when Conservative Members oppose making it easier for British businesses and farmers to export to the EU, reducing red tape, helping our brilliant bands to tour, and giving our young people freedoms again to study and live in the EU, they are putting petty ideology ahead of the national interest?
As my hon. Friend says, what is not to like about this deal?

Our businesses, farmers and consumers were told that the Irish sea border was gone, but that was never the lived, economic or political reality. While we await the final text and see the direction of travel of this agreement, will the Government start removing the bureaucracy, the red tape and the barriers that are holding back our businesses, or at least put a pause on the implementation of any further bureaucracy?

I distinctly remember Boris Johnson saying there would be no checks in the Irish sea, but the hon. Gentleman knows and Northern Ireland knows that that has not been the reality. This deal removes 90% of those checks on agrifood coming into Northern Ireland. How do the Conservatives defend the status quo that would have trapped Northern Ireland in that position? We are trying to help to remove 90% of those checks and potentially get significant reductions in energy costs in Northern Ireland. We will keep working at that because we believe that his constituents deserve those benefits.

I know that my constituents would want me to thank the Prime Minister for keeping his focus on the cost of food in the middle of the cost of living crisis, and that they will welcome the removal of pet passports from 2028—Cheshire has a great many pet lovers. He will be familiar with Chester zoo, and one of the lesser-known effects of Brexit was that it made international conservation efforts and breeding programmes difficult, because moving animals across borders became so bureaucratic and problematic. Will he give Chester zoo and other zoos around the country some reassurance that the implementation will focus on the need for those conservation programmes to go ahead?
I think this deal helps with that type of conservation work, but I would not want to say that here without knowing for sure, so I will write to my hon. Friend.

Sovereignty is not divisible, so will the Prime Minister have the courage to be clear from the Dispatch Box that his deal means in that in certain areas the United Kingdom Parliament is no longer sovereign but subject to qualified-majority-vote decisions, which are equally under the jurisdiction of the European Court of Justice? Will he reinstate the European Scrutiny Committee, so that this House, and this House alone, can scrutinise the flow of European law coming into this country?

I would want this House to scrutinise the effect of this deal very much, but in relation to food and farming, the truth of the matter is that people have retained alignment with the European Union, but they have just had a load of cost and paperwork at the same time, and we are removing that. The hon. Gentleman should start thinking about the practical benefits, rather than always taking a highly ideological approach to these issues.

Despite the assurances of the previous Government that Brexit would not increase barriers to trade, I have lost count of the number of businesses in my constituency that have faced increased export costs or have had to stop exporting to Europe entirely as a result of their rubbish Brexit deal. Does my right hon. Friend the Prime Minister agree that this Government must tear down the barriers to trade that the Conservatives threw up?

I agree very strongly with my hon. Friend. Those barriers are hurting businesses in East Worthing and around the country. It is absolutely time to tear them down and stop defending a status quo that clearly has not worked.

In just 39 days’ time, UK automotive manufacturers face a 10% tariff on electric vehicles being exported across the channel into Europe, not as a result of anything new in Europe, but as a result of the ratcheting up of the TCA negotiated by the Conservative party. Brexit’s adherents talked about the necessity of running down the British car industry prior to 2016, so what assurance can the Prime Minister give that our car sector has a bright future? Will he also acknowledge that the best way to secure that future is through a single market and rejoining the customs union so that these future tariffs can be parked forever?

We are working hard to protect the car industry. The rules of origin that the hon. Gentleman talks about will be the subject of a discussion that the Minister for European Relations will have tomorrow, and he has assured me that he will update the House on progress shortly after.

Madam Deputy Speaker, did you know that Britain’s biggest beansprout producer hails from Dunstable? Too often, its products get stuck at the border, wrapped up in red tape and literally rotting. I know that the Prime Minister is a hopeful man, but, after the negotiations, would he also describe himself as full of beans?

I am upbeat today. It was a really good thing to be in Brussels and working practically to improve things and stop those delays. I do not know how frustrating that must be for one of the businesses in my hon. Friend’s constituency. Seeing a whole container or lorryload of produce going off because of bureaucracy —who supports a status quo like that?

It has felt very much like the Prime Minister is rolling the pitch this afternoon. Whether he goes early in May 2027 or goes long into 2029, if he is not rolling the pitch to set the UK on a path to rejoining the EU, will he commit now not to make rejoining the EU a manifesto pledge for the Labour party at the next general election?

I am not rolling any pitch this afternoon; I am being proud and confident of the deal that we have secured. I am standing here saying that I believe in it, and I believe it is in the best interests of Britain. I will carry on taking practical steps that are in the country’s national interests. I will happily stand against the hon. Gentleman and members of his party at the next election and show how this party has put this country back on a more positive and constructive path for the future.

I welcome this deal and the help that it will bring to businesses in Southend West and Leigh. Our historic cockling industry tells me about the impact that the Tories’ disastrous Brexit deal has had on its trading relationship with countries such as Spain. Does the Prime Minister agree that this deal will support the Leigh cockling industry to trade more frictionlessly and will save it money?

I am well aware of the unique nature of the Leigh cockling industry, and those particular kinds of products are hard to export if we have paperwork delays. The industry stands to benefit greatly, and I will ensure that it does.

Brexit is the biggest con that our country has been sold in a generation. Millions of good people who voted to leave the European Union wanted a better Britain, but they ended up with a Brexit bonfire. The deal that the Prime Minister has talked about will take us closer to where we need to be, but does he agree that to correct the Tories’ mess, we need to rejoin the single market to get Britain growing again?
We will honour our manifesto, and the deal that we propose does precisely that while making several important steps forward for the country, as the hon. Gentleman says.

This deal is a good deal for Britain, and it draws to a conclusion a decade of division, paralysis and decline on the issue of our relationship with the continent. What steps will the Prime Minister take to ensure that we spend far more of the next decade focusing on the issues that unite our communities than we did in the last decade?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right —we need to draw a line, and we need the next decade to be better than the last. There has been too much division and too much turbulence. This is all about setting the country on a strong, clear and uplifting path. That is what the 10-year plan for Britain will do next month.

Instead of healing old wounds, uniting the country and shifting the national conversation towards growth, prosperity and a positive future, we appear to be going backwards, reopening the most divisive debate in recent British history. What is the logic of reigniting these divisions at a time when the country needs calm, reconciliation and a new political direction—a politics that unites and heals? Can the Prime Minister explain his strategy?

We do not heal divisions if we stick with a status quo that clearly is not working and has caused damage to growth in every constituency in this country. How does that help move people forward? Moving people forward means recognising that that has not been good enough and putting something better on the table. That is exactly what I have done this afternoon; it is just a shame that the hon. Gentleman has not been listening for the last hour and a half.

Fifty-two per cent of Shrewsbury’s constituents mirrored the UK Brexit vote, but 10 years later, they have realised that a hard Brexit has caused more harm than good. Irrespective of politics, there is now consensus that we need a better economic relationship with the EU to support 40% of our exports. Friday’s summit deal delivers exactly that, cutting red tape, supporting farmers and progressing our membership of the electricity market—economics, not politics. Can the Prime Minister clarify for the House that whatever path this country chooses in 2029 when it comes to a political relationship, the Bill we are discussing today is about an economic deal, which offers a better trading relationship for businesses, and which stands on its own two feet?

I can absolutely confirm that we are taking a significant step forward today. It has already given businesses a sense of greater optimism about the future, as they have said to me since the weekend. In particular, young people will see more opportunity than they had before. It is a good day for Britain.

Brexit customs declarations have cost British businesses £7.7 billion since 2022, and it does not appear that anything agreed on Friday will change that. Even the SPS deal will not apply until 2028, so what are the Government doing for the Welsh manufacturers and importers left out by this package?

We can only go as fast as we can go. I am introducing the Bill this week, and I said that it would have its Second Reading before Christmas; that is pretty fast. I do not know how I could go any further, but if the hon. Gentleman can tell me how, I would be open to going further.

Many of my constituents are proud to work at Nissan, just across the constituency boundary. That factory is central to the economy of the north-east. Does the Prime Minister agree that this deal is good news for the automotive industry, for my constituents’ jobs and livelihoods, and for the prospects of reindustrialising the north-east of England?

I am well aware of the critical importance of Nissan to the north-east. I think people are underestimating the importance of what we have managed to negotiate on “Made in Europe”, and particularly the way that what we have in the document offers support for the British car industry. It was a big effort; I spoke to practically every European leader about it. We threw a lot at it. We have got a good arrangement. It is interesting that it was almost minimised by the Conservative party, but it will give comfort to a lot of people working for Nissan.

On 22 July 2024, I asked the last Prime Minister if he would deliver a youth mobility scheme to benefit young people across our country, like my constituent Rose. I welcome the fact that more than two years later, we now have a deal, but it comes too late for Rose and a whole generation who have missed out on opportunities because of the hard Brexit delivered by the Conservatives. For those thinking of the opportunities ahead, can I ask the Prime Minister what he and his Ministers will do to bring forward the implementation date from the backstop of January 2030? Also, I listened to what he said about the President of the European Commission. Are negotiations on tuition fees in any way linked to the other three pillars of this deal?

As I have said, the President of the European Commission said no; it is a separate piece of paper. Those were her words at the press conference on Friday. I agree with the hon. Gentleman: I want to see the benefits for young people as quickly as we can possibly bring them in. That will depend on how quickly this House can progress the legislation. Before they have even seen the Bill, the Conservatives have pledged to repeal it. That is such a short-sighted approach to take. At least look at the measures and see whether they have any merit. As I say, they are stuck in an ideological position and in the past, and sadly that has been on show this afternoon.

The chemicals industry is a key sector in my Mid Cheshire constituency. Once implemented, the emissions trading scheme linkage will give businesses access to a larger market, and will provide exemptions from the carbon border adjustment mechanism, reducing barriers to trade. That is an important step forward that I warmly welcome. Does the Prime Minister agree that we should go further in reducing barriers for the chemical industry by implementing the chemicals annexe of the trade and co-operation agreement, and that we should start with mutual recognition of UK and EU REACH?

I am glad that my hon. Friend recognises that there will be significant benefits for the biggest emitters; I know this will significantly reduce their costs. I am prepared to look at what he says, but at the moment, I am focused on implementing this particular deal.

My constituents in Strangford are paying the penalty for breaking the bonds with Europe and exiting the EU. It seems that these deals will come with a re-entrance fee. We paid to leave, and now it seems we will pay to have a closer relationship with the EU. Is it not a fact that Michel Barnier and others in the EU just cannot wait to punish the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland once again?

No, I do not think that is the case at all. If we can do things to address the issues that the hon. Gentleman and other Members from Northern Ireland have raised in this House, why would we not do them? I have heard complaints about the border in the Irish sea. Northern Ireland was promised that there would be no checks, but the reality has been different. We have to work in a pragmatic way to get progress where we can, and we have made progress for Northern Ireland with this deal.

The Prime Minister will know that the UK is the world’s third-largest market for artificial intelligence, and is a leader in quantum and other emerging technologies, too. It is clearly in our national interest to deepen our partnership with the EU in this area. Can he provide any update on how the UK intends to use the EU-UK digital partnership to consolidate our position as a leading destination for technology investment and AI adoption?

The digital partnership presents a really big opportunity for Britain, and for my hon. Friend’s constituency, given its strength in that area. I will work with him to make sure that we take that opportunity in full.

I welcome the deal, and heard what the Prime Minister said about data exchange, but we have not gained access to either Eurodac or the second-generation Schengen information system, SISII, both of which are critical to tackling small boats. Will the Prime Minister commit to securing access to both databases to make our borders more secure?

I would love to secure access to both those databases, and that will be precisely what I put on the table as part of discussions on the channel action plan. SISII is possibly more realistic and achievable in the shorter term. When we lost visibility of all that data, we definitely lost the ability to control illegal immigration. The Conservatives promised to take back control, and we were given the opposite. It is time to say that plainly to the public.

Yellow leaf in the vast sugar beet fields of East Anglia threatens yields and farm income in my constituency. Gene editing, which is different from gene modification, is led by our brilliant UK scientists. It allows natural breeding processes to accelerate, so that we can protect against this disease. Does the PM agree that such science, which has the potential to solve much of the problem of worldwide hunger, must be supported as we create agreements with our EU friends, and boost trade and prosperity?

The Esher and Walton test is important, as we are the single biggest contributor to the Exchequer outside London. In my constituency, businesses are struggling. As the engines of growth, they need a boost. The deal is a start, so it is shocking that the Conservatives decry it. They are showing that they have nothing to say on economic stewardship, growth, business or the young. They should never be trusted with the economy again. The Prime Minister said that incremental steps will only take us so far, so will he dump incrementalism and move towards the biggest boost to GDP, which will come from entering the single market?

I have been very clear that the red lines of our manifesto mean something. We will honour them, but we will do so while getting the best possible arrangement we can in this Parliament. We can take steps now to deliver a deal for British businesses that will be much better than what they had before. That will lower costs for British consumers. This is a good deal, and I look forward to the hon. Lady helping to get it through the House as quickly as possible.

Many European leaders have said that they developed an affection for Britain because of Blur, Beckham and Bournemouth, where many of them spent their time at English language schools. Will the Prime Minister set out how his deal will help the English language sector, which has taken such a battering under the Conservatives’ hard Brexit? How will his deal help Bournemouth?

It was interesting being in Brussels and the Netherlands over the weekend, where people were saying, “This is better. We can work with Britain again. We feel more positive about Britain again.” The Conservatives created a lot of negativity about Britain. People thought we had changed and had become a different, unwelcoming country. Let us be honest: the Conservatives did a lot of damage to the national interest through how they conducted those Brexit negotiations. The new approach that we are taking—the constructive approach pioneered by my right hon. Friend the Europe Minister—will be good for Bournemouth and for Britain.

The Prime Minister has repeatedly called this a good deal for Britain. What about the United Kingdom? This is a deal that continues the partitioning of the United Kingdom by an international customs border down the Irish sea. The result is that the same customs paperwork will be required to sell from Britain to Belfast as from Britain to Berlin. He is the Prime Minister of the whole United Kingdom, so why did he not even try to recover sovereignty over customs in Northern Ireland?

Has the hon. and learned Gentleman even been listening? I have spoken this afternoon about the removal of 90% of checks in the Irish sea in relation to agri-produce. I am working with the bad Brexit deal that Boris Johnson left us, and I can only do so much in one go. I have mentioned Northern Ireland repeatedly in this House this afternoon, because I care about Northern Ireland and his constituency. I am proud to have taken these steps forward for the great people of Northern Ireland.
Can the Prime Minister guarantee that a row over tuition fees will not delay an SPS deal? My farmers in Tiverton and Minehead want to produce food, not battle with over-zealous paperwork.

I can definitely give that assurance to the hon. Lady and, through her, to the farming community in her constituency, which is significant. The paperwork is devastating, as I have said this afternoon. We want British farmers exporting again, and that means making it much easier to do that. That is what this deal will do. It is good for British farming. I think it will increase exports. That is why the whole House should be behind it.

Last week, the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland refused to pull the Stormont brake, despite all Unionist Members of the Legislative Assembly backing its use. Northern Ireland businesses, farmers and consumers remain under the jackboot of EU law, and the Irish sea border posts are still standing. When the Prime Minister struck his deal with Brussels, did he secure a date for dismantling those border posts, or did he simply agree to put the rest of the United Kingdom under the same EU rules that Northern Ireland has been left under? When are the border posts coming down?

We will look carefully at the implementation of this deal and how it affects Northern Ireland. I am working with the Northern Ireland Secretary to address ongoing issues relating to the budget. We all have to take care to work with each other, at this moment, to deal with the issues that matter to the hon. Lady’s constituents and to people across Northern Ireland—and we will, as I have said in the House this afternoon. May I conclude by saying that we have had a good exchange this afternoon, but I think it is important that we move forward in a slightly better way? I ask this of everyone, on all sides. This is definitely one for problem solving, not point scoring. Let us take a practical mindset to this deal. Let us get the best deal we can for Britain, and then we will all be able to enjoy the benefits in our constituencies.

With permission, I will make a statement on Myanmar. On 19 November, the International Court of Justice found that the Myanmar regime had committed genocide against the Rohingya people. The judgment represents the first finding of state responsibility for genocide since the 1948 convention on the prevention and punishment of the crime of genocide, and it lays bare what the actions of the Myanmar regime meant for the Rohingya: indiscriminate and targeted killing of civilians including those fleeing their villages, summary executions, widespread sexual violence, and the burning of people and homes. The court concluded that “the only reasonable inference that can explain Myanmar’s actions is an intention to destroy a substantial part of the protected group, namely the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State.” The UK’s long-standing approach is that any determination of genocide follows the reasoned judgment of a competent national or international court, after a credible judicial process. With the ICJ’s judgment that test has now been met, and today I can confirm that the United Kingdom formally acknowledges the genocide committed against the Rohingya. For this Government, and, I would argue, for the whole international community, our response to a crime as profoundly shocking as genocide must reflect our values, and must be matched by clear action. We should also act cognisant of the fact that the appalling targeting of civilians by the Myanmar regime continues to this day, as do the discrimination against and persecution of Rohingya and other communities. Airstrikes are happening regularly across the country, hitting schools, hospitals, markets and places of worship, and there is also ongoing violence on the part of the Arakan army, which it is right to call out. This morning I met courageous Rohingya campaigners, who emphasised to me the importance that they attach to the recognition of what has happened, and the fact that they had felt too long ignored by the international community. Today I am setting out a package of measures, against the Myanmar military, in pursuit of accountability, in support of the Rohingya and the people of Myanmar, and to build international pressure on the regime to end the suffering. Let me deal first with action against the Myanmar military. On Thursday we ordered the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attaché, because we will not tolerate a serving representative of Myanmar’s military remaining in post on UK soil. I can announce today that we have also imposed sanctions against four Majors General and a Brigadier General—senior military figures who oversaw troops who carried out egregious civilian killings and repression of the population across Myanmar. We know that the Myanmar military has systematically used lethal air power against its own people. I do not believe that the British people want any UK companies to have any links to such practices, so we will introduce new legislation in the coming months to stop the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar which is used in such horrendous attacks. These are our initial steps, but we will also scrutinise all major companies in Myanmar, particularly those linked to the military regime, and we will take further sanctions action where it is justified to deter or disrupt violations of international law and to stand against impunity. Secondly, the United Kingdom, as United Nations Security Council penholder on Myanmar, will use our diplomatic influence to increase international pressure for accountability and to end the humanitarian crisis. To that end we will raise this as an urgent issue at the Security Council this week, and we have called a dedicated Security Council meeting in two weeks’ time to strengthen momentum for action. We know that the Security Council has too often been divided on Myanmar, but division should not become an excuse for UN inaction. Let me start by thanking the Foreign Secretary for advance sight of his statement. I am responding to it in place of the shadow Foreign Secretary, my right hon. Friend the Member for Tonbridge (Tom Tugendhat), because of his registered interest as a member of the Leadership Council of Fortify Rights. I want to be clear at the outset: we absolutely condemn the atrocities committed against the Rohingya. Murder, rape, forced displacement and other serious abuses demand accountability. However, it is also important to note that condemning atrocities and establishing the specific legal crime of genocide are two very different things. Genocide requires a specific intent to destroy a protected group as a whole or in substantial part. As was emphasised recently in a report from Policy Exchange, broadening the definition of genocide risks undermining the clarity or seriousness of this international crime, and as Ukraine’s former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba argues in his foreword, the charge must meet the legal test if it is to retain its authority. As the Foreign Secretary has said, this is the first time the ICJ has found a state directly responsible for committing genocide, but the Court divided 9-6 on that central finding. It concerns me greatly that the dissenting judges raised substantial questions about proof of intent, the standard of proof, and the treatment of evidence. Those questions deserve careful consideration, and a clear response from Ministers. We do not believe that the Government should have intervened in this case, given the risk of encouraging a broader interpretation of genocide. Our role should be to defend the clarity and rigour of the established legal test, and we cannot allow legal standards to become subordinate to political objectives. Britain must defend the integrity of international law and resist its weaponisation. Does the Foreign Secretary agree that where genocidal intent is inferred from a pattern of conduct, it must be the only reasonable inference, as established in Croatia v. Serbia, and will he defend that standard? What consideration has the Foreign Secretary given to the dissenting judges’ concern that the majority’s approach risks shifting the burden of proof on to the respondent state? What assessment have Ministers made of the reliability of the UN investigative material relied upon by the Court, particularly where underlying witness records were unavailable for examination? What assessment has he made of the implications for British service personnel, defence partnerships and military operations if the threshold for establishing genocidal intent is relaxed? I turn to diplomacy. We absolutely support the expulsion of Myanmar’s defence attaché and the summoning of its chargé d’affaires, announced by the Foreign Secretary last week. What response has he received, and what further diplomatic pressure will follow? Given that the UK is the penholder on Myanmar at the Security Council, what concrete outcome is he seeking from the urgent session he requested, and how is he working with regional partners to secure that? On sanctions, we supported targeted action in government. We will support further targeted measures against those responsible for atrocities and those sustaining the military, but what assessment has the Foreign Secretary made of the effectiveness of existing measures? What further co-ordinated action will he take to restrict the Myanmar military’s access to finance and supplies, and to tackle sanctions evasion? Alongside that pressure, we must not lose sight of the humanitarian situation. The Foreign Secretary has spoken of this today, but what support will the Government provide for vulnerable communities inside Myanmar and for Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh, and how will he ensure that it reaches those who need it? We on this side of the House unequivocally condemn these atrocities. We demand accountability, and we stand with the Rohingya, but the questions we have put to the

I had hoped that today would be a day for bipartisan consensus across the House. Before I respond to the substance of the right hon. Lady’s remarks, let me say that I do not doubt her condemnation, and the condemnation of those on the Opposition Front Bench, of everything that was done by the Myanmar regime, but I deeply regret her questioning of the role of the ICJ in this case. Let me explain why. It has been a long-standing view on both sides of the House that the determination of genocide is not a matter for us to call out as politicians before a competent court has reached a judgment. That is a very important linchpin of the approach, which I think has united both sides. The most competent court—the apex court: the International Court of Justice—has now reached its view. It is true that it is a majority view, but a majority view is the view of the Court, just like it would be in our courts, so I deeply regret the right hon. Lady’s seeking to unpick this judgment. I have read through the summary judgment in a lot of detail, as I am sure she has. I am not a lawyer, but I do not think that my job is to second-guess the judgment of the competent court. At a time when international law and international courts are under threat across the world, it is so important that we respect the Court, and let me explain why. If the British Government come along and say, “The ICJ may have ruled that, but we just disagree in this case,” it gives carte blanche to every other Government in the world to start saying, “The ICJ may have reached this conclusion, but we ignore the judgment of the ICJ.” This is the first response. I urge those on the Conservative Front Bench, the shadow Foreign Secretary and his colleagues to think hard about what it means to uphold international law. I would have thought a basic requirement of that—given that the judges have spent a number of years examining all the evidence, looking at the legal arguments and coming to a conclusion—is to respect the judgment.

On days like this, it is tempting to see the very worst of humanity, but my reaction to this judgment was to be moved by The Gambia. It is a country whose people are unlikely to have frequently visited Myanmar or even to have met anyone from there, but who stood up in the highest court in the world, argued in defence of a persecuted people and demanded that there should be justice. It was an act of international solidarity that, frankly, we need to see more of. Does the Foreign Secretary agree that the ICJ’s vital work in coming to this determination serves as a reminder that, despite the continued attack on international law—including today, very disappointingly, by His Majesty’s Opposition, which is a new low—justice and truth will find a way? Frankly, the brave men and women who worked to achieve the determination deserve our full support.

Characteristically, my right hon. Friend speaks incredibly well on this issue, and those who took forward this case are to be praised. Today I had the privilege of meeting Tun Khin, who is the president of the Burmese Rohingya Organisation UK. It was an incredibly moving occasion, because he obviously wants action to be taken, as we all do, but he also wanted recognition. He felt that, for the first time, there is actually recognition of what happened to the Rohingya people.

The Liberal Democrats stand with the people of Myanmar, including the Rohingya. The ruling by the International Court of Justice is hugely consequential. Those responsible for genocide against the Rohingya must now be held to account, democracy must be restored and the Myanmar military must cease its human rights abuses. I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s swift decision to expel Myanmar’s defence attaché, and to call for an urgent UN Security Council session and for targeted sanctions against the military. Given the UK’s position as the penholder on Myanmar at the Security Council, I urge him to pursue the steps that will now follow this landmark judgment, to ensure accountability and push for long-term political solutions. Will the Government ensure that there is a time-bound plan to support the implementation of this ruling that includes a safe voluntary return for the Rohingya? I declare an interest as a vice-chair of the APPG on nutrition for development. In October we visited Cox’s Bazar, where 1.2 million refugees from the Rakhine region have sought refuge in the world’s largest refugee camp. Severe funding shortfalls mean that food has been rationed, with further rationing to come, yet the Rohingya’s 10-year stay there means that they have dropped off the news agenda. There is expected to be a funding shortfall of $229 million for the Rohingya operation next year, meaning that it is only half funded. Will the Foreign Secretary commit to stay the course, provide additional humanitarian support to the Rohingya and Myanmar, and resource the UK mission to Myanmar and to Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh so that it can provide that support? Finally, I am saddened by the comments of the shadow Minister, the right hon. Member for Aldridge-Brownhills (Wendy Morton). His Majesty’s Opposition should do better than that, and should not argue for the moral abdication of a structure that we, the British, largely constructed. Can the Foreign Secretary confirm that the legal positions that the UK set out in its intervention during the ICJ judgment remain the Government’s position on the genocide convention, and will the Government apply them consistently going forward?

There were lots of questions there, and I agree very much with the thrust of what the hon. Lady said. On her initial point about the time-bound nature of taking action, she is completely right. Our objective from the moment of this judgment has been to really apply international pressure on the regime. I think we should be frank in this House that there was a sense that a normalisation of the regime was happening across the world, and we do not want normalisation given what has happened. I think that is very important, and I have been in communication with lots of partners over the last few days—as has Baroness Winterton, the Minister in the other place, who is doing an excellent job on this issue—about how, in this moment, we can create pressure for action on the regime. I undertake to the hon. Lady to seek to do so through the UN and other mechanisms, and we will continue to report back to this House. We are doing some justice to the Rohingya by actually calling this out, but we will be doing real justice if we get change, so that is my objective. I will look at the points that the hon. Lady made on humanitarian aid and so on. The final point I would make to her—I did not say it to the shadow Minister—is that it is important to say that our intervention in this case was on facts of law. It was not to intervene on one side or the other, but to assist the Court, and I think it was very important we did that.

I really welcome the ICJ ruling, because I genuinely believe in international law. I also welcome and support the actions outlined by the Foreign Secretary, especially calling a special meeting of the Security Council. However, if the Myanmar Government failed to implement the ICJ’s judgment, what would the UK Government, as the penholder and as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, do to ensure that it was then implemented? I am particularly thinking about how two of the permanent members have been supporting the Myanmar Government for a very long time.

My hon. Friend characteristically gets to the absolute nub of the issues we face. As I said in response to the Liberal Democrats, we want to use all the means at our disposal to seek to create pressure on the regime. I think it is worth saying that a resolution 2669 was passed by the Security Council in December 2022, and that was an important resolution on Myanmar. We will be saying to all countries across the world, including our partners and others, that with this finding of genocide—the first ever finding against a state of the crime of genocide—the UN has got to act. As I said in my statement, at a time when international law and multilateralism are under threat and under duress, this is a test. This is a test of the international community, and in my view the international community must not fail.

I welcome what the Foreign Secretary has said. I visited Myanmar in 2018, and I met villagers in Rakhine state who were forced by soldiers to stand in front of me and tell me there had been no atrocities and no genocide, and the fear in their eyes told me everything I needed to know. Is not the uncomfortable truth that the commander-in-chief of the Myanmar armed forces at the time of the genocide in 2017 is today the President of Myanmar, and is that not why it is absolutely essential that firm action is taken? Today, we are seeing atrocities being committed—rapes, torture, villages being burned, hospitals and schools being bombed by air force military—so does the Foreign Secretary agree with me that the stronger the international response, the greater the likelihood that the atrocities will stop, and the stronger the international response, the stronger the likelihood that genocide will not be repeated? Does he also agree that the UK has a particular role, as penholder in this situation—where there has been a genocide—to make sure that in this century there are no more Rwandas, no more Bosnias, no more Darfurs and no more Myanmars?

The right hon. Gentleman spoke very powerfully, and I do want to repeat my praise for him and his work on this issue. He has done incredibly important work with my hon. Friend the Member for Bethnal Green and Stepney and many others across this House. I think he is right to say that General Min Aung Hlaing is directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened. The International Criminal Court prosecutor has applied for an arrest warrant for the general for crimes against humanity. The United Kingdom has sanctioned the general. I think the right hon. Gentleman’s wider point is right, which is that this is about the international pressure we can apply. As I have said, one of my purposes in the last few days, as it will be in the coming weeks—I was talking to Julie Bishop about it this morning—is how we rally the international community, particularly the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, to really make sure that this is a moment of change, not just a moment of outrage but then the status quo. I look forward to working with all Members of this House on that.

I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s strong response following the historic ruling of the ICJ that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya people. The signs were there long before 2017. In 2013, when I visited Rakhine state with the support of Burma Campaign and Refugees International, the Burmese military had already committed horrific crimes and displaced 140,000 people. However, it took the rape, torture and murder of thousands, and the expulsion of 700,000 to Bangladesh in 2017, before the world really took notice. It took our Government many years before they backed The Gambia’s case against Myanmar—under the last Government, and I am grateful to them for doing so. I welcome the sanctions on jet fuel that the Foreign Secretary announced, but will he commit to a regular round of sanctions, including on Myanmar’s oil and gas extraction sector, the state banks that are financing arms, and the mobile phone company that is tracking and enabling attacks on human rights activists?

I thank my hon. Friend for the great work she has done on this issue. The first part of her question is so right. When we read the pages of the judgment, it is a frankly horrifying account—a compelling and horrifying account—of what happened, and she is right that the world has taken far too long to wake up to this. It is true to say that in the UK, we have had 19 rounds of sanctions since the coup of 2021. We will definitely look at the specific points she raises about telecoms, and oil and gas; we undertake to do so. I was very clear in my statement that this is simply the first part of what we intend to do. We will keep looking at how we can put pressure on the regime through both our domestic action and working with partners.

As a Conservative who sees our own country’s safety, and indeed the projection of our values, in our support for strong international institutions, I also welcome the Secretary of State’s statement, but here is my confusion—or, I guess, frustration. As he knows, the genocide convention contains not just a duty on us to enact the judgment of the Court, but a preventive duty. My first question to him is: does he regret that British Governments have not acted earlier, and if they had done, does he think thousands of lives might have been saved? In particular, the Secretary of State will know that the judgment marks out violence against children as a particularly sharp aspect of this genocide, and says that no claimed counter-insurgency can justify the violence perpetrated against children. In that regard, what are the implications for British Government conduct in Sudan and, in particular, in Gaza, where, as he knows, this continues, even with a ceasefire? One child has been killed every day since that ceasefire was instituted.

Those are typically intelligent questions from the right hon. Gentleman. On the first point, I think we can all regret that more was not done earlier. We cannot look at this account of what happened, and think anything other than that the international community did not do enough, and we all bear a responsibility. On the right hon. Gentleman’s point about the violence against children and all the things that are there, he is absolutely right. On Gaza and Sudan, part of my purpose as Foreign Secretary is to intervene and make a difference in terms of our values. On 8 September, we made the statement on the two-state solution and Gaza. We are seeking to rally the international community on Gaza and the outrageous blockage of aid. My invitation to all Members of this House is to work with us on these issues. I will not pretend there are not trade-offs for Government between values and interests, but as the Prime Minister said in his speech last Monday, pursuing our values is not only right in itself, but, as he said at the beginning of his statement, the right way to serve our interests.

Nothing prepared me for working on multiple occasions with the Rohingya as they fled over the border: dead bodies; babies burned on fires, with parents having to choose whether to jump in the fire to pull them out or run with the children still left alive; and mutilations on a scale I could never have imagined experiencing. I applaud the judges who bravely, in the face of a lot of pressure, did the right thing last week and called out what we all knew to be true: a genocide has been committed. Given that the perpetrators will stop at nothing until they finish what they have set out to do, may I ask the Foreign Secretary what our Government are doing to act at great haste to save as many lives as possible now that there will, I believe, be renewed and redoubled efforts to kill as many people as possible?

My hon. Friend speaks very movingly about her experiences and I thank her for her work. My answer is that, in this moment, following the finding of genocide, we have to rally the international community and create the maximum possible pressure, on all countries, to say to the regime in Myanmar, “Enough is enough.” That is true of all countries, including all P5 members. That is my responsibility as the Foreign Secretary, and it is the responsibility of the UK Government and other Governments. I have been pleased at the extent to which Governments across the world are starting to rally on this issue—it is why we made a very early statement last Thursday—but I totally agree with her that there is much more to do. Frankly, in this case, the best thing we have at our disposal is shining the spotlight of the judgment harshly on what is happening to try to get change.

Although the ICJ’s landmark ruling is extremely welcome, the US Holocaust Memorial Museum’s Early Warning Project identified the Rohingya as one of the world’s vulnerable populations most at risk of genocide back in 2015. In 2018, when I was a member of the International Development Committee, I heard UN officials state that the conflict had the hallmarks of genocide and I heard first-hand accounts in Cox’s Bazar that year. The world failed to act on those early warning signs and retrospective court judgments have come too late for those who are not here to witness that result. We must not be afraid to call a genocide a genocide and act decisively when appalling crimes like these have been committed. Real justice must now be delivered for the Rohingya. How will the UK prevent the ruling failing, when Myanmar’s military regime is unlikely to comply and when major powers in the UN Security Council, such as China, Russia and possibly the US, may oppose any meaningful action?

By standing up and saying what we believe needs to be done, and rallying as many countries as possible to our cause. That is what we have to do. On the basis of the conversation so far in this House, I think I can do so with the support of this House. It is so important that we do that. The hon. Gentleman is right to point out the challenges. That is the world as it is, but we live in the world as it is. Our job—I know he agrees with this—is not to succumb to inaction in the world as it is, but to try to shape it. That is what I am pledged to do.

As chair of the all-party parliamentary group on Rohingya, and having returned from the camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh only last week and seen first-hand the suffering of families who have waited for justice for far too long, I welcome this genocide judgment. However, it will not alone deliver that justice. As the Foreign Secretary has acknowledged, the international community cannot recognise that genocide while allowing Myanmar’s military to continue to carry out these horrific crimes with impunity. Now is the time for the international community to act, so I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s statement, particularly the broad sanctions and the welcome aid that is massively needed by the 1.2 million people who have been forgotten by the world. As the penholder on Myanmar at the UN Security Council, what further action will the Foreign Secretary take to ensure that other members of the Security Council understand that this substantial judgment leads to serious consequences for Myanmar’s military, including cutting the weapons and money sustaining the war crimes and holding those responsible for genocide to account?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question. He is absolutely right to draw attention to the 1.2 million refugees in Bangladesh. One of the most moving things on the day of the judgment was seeing those in the refugee camps watching the judgment being played out; it was incredibly moving. On my hon. Friend’s point about the international community, I undertake to him and this House that we will do absolutely everything we can to rally the international community, including the UN and the P5 on this issue. I do not pretend it will be easy—I have already been in touch with our UN ambassador about this—but this is a moment that tests the international community and we have to respond.

The refugees from Myanmar fled to Bangladesh in their hundreds of thousands and that community has grown substantially over the past nine years. The Bangladesh Government have struggled with what to do with that huge influx of refugees. There have been a lot of problems in the camps, as we know. What discussions has the Foreign Secretary had with the Government of Bangladesh? Clearly, the Rohingya refugees will not return any time soon, until there is a clear change of Administration and Government in Myanmar. What discussions has he had about what support the UK Government can give to alleviate the suffering of the refugees in the camps?

The hon. Gentleman raises a very important question. Governments of both parties have contributed, I think over the last 10 years, hundreds of millions of pounds to Bangladesh, but he is right to say that this is a very difficult situation. I do not have an easy answer for him. We are in touch with the Government of Bangladesh—I met the Foreign Minister recently. He is also right to caution that, given what is happening in Rakhine state at the moment, the refugees will not be able to return quickly. Therefore, making sure that they lead their lives with as much dignity as possible is part of our collective task.

I really welcome this moment of recognition and the Foreign Statement’s fulsome statement.
