Will he undertake to look carefully at the World Food Programme, as so many children are facing starvation in Cox’s Bazar? Secondly, will he work across the House to try to convince those on the Opposition Front Bench that this was always a bipartisan issue, going right back to the first sanctions on aviation fuel introduced by the former Member for Berwick-upon-Tweed—I supported her 100% when I was on the Opposition Benches. We must speak with one voice from this House on the question of international law.

My hon. Friend speaks very well. Indeed, she was a Minister who covered these issues. I will look at the point she makes on the World Food Programme. I also agree with her that bipartisan consensus would be much better on this issue.

There are obligations on states to prevent genocide as soon as we become aware of a serious risk of it. The recognition of the genocide against the Rohingya by the British Government has taken nine years; the recognition of the genocide committed against the Yazidis by Daesh also took nine years for the British Government and was made on the basis of a ruling by a German court. Will the Foreign Secretary give further consideration to the Genocide Determination Bill, introduced in the other place by Lord Alton, to extend what is deemed to be a competent court?
I think Lord Alton has written to me about that Bill, and I will undertake to look at it.

On Friday, I had the enormous privilege of running an extraordinarily successful Islamophobia awareness event in my constituency with my team. The news of this judgment was extremely fresh and painful. Does the Foreign Secretary agree with the conclusion of our meeting, which was that this country should stand up to systemic Islamophobia, antisemitism and racism, both at home and abroad?

I agree with my hon. Friend—we should stand up to racism at home and abroad. The facts of this case will resonate with people, not just in the Rohingya and Muslim communities, but way beyond. That is why it is important that we rise to the moment.

I thank the Foreign Secretary for the way he delivered his statement and for British support for the case that was taken to the Court. That is absolutely important. The fundamental question, of course, is what happens if the Government of Myanmar carry on with their murderous regime against the Rohingya people? I absolutely welcome the Foreign Secretary’s commitment to the following of international law. While this is a definitive judgment from the ICJ concerning Myanmar, there is also the question of advisory judgments and the duty of member nations that support the ICJ to prevent genocide from taking place in any circumstance around the world. That includes Sudan, Congo, and of course, the Palestinian people in Gaza. We need to have a rethink, because I welcome the Government’s support for the principle of total adherence to international law.

I agree with the right hon. Member, particularly on his first point about how we should have no illusions about the regime that we are dealing with in Myanmar. The ordering by the Court is important, and we must put maximum pressure on the regime to implement the rulings, but we know the record of the regime. That is the conversation we need to have with other international partners. On the right hon. Member’s wider point about our responsibilities on genocide, to relieve suffering across the world and to follow international law, those are really important points.

I draw the House’s attention to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests, and a visit I undertook to Bangladesh and Cox’s Bazar with the APPG for nutrition for development. I thank the Foreign Secretary for the decisive action he has taken to call out the hideous acts of the Myanmar regime. It is very good news that the judgment gives Rohingya refugees a right to return, but it is clear when one visits the camps that they are pretty permanent establishments. What conversations has the Foreign Secretary had with the Bangladesh Government about giving the Rohingya the opportunity to work and have a livelihood while they are still there?

My hon. Friend is the second person to raise the issue, and he is right to do so. I have had conversations with the Government of Bangladesh, but I undertake to him and to the hon. Member for Harrow East (Bob Blackman), who also asked about the issue, to further intensify those conversations. In all respects, the judgment has got to be a moment when we focus on the plight of the Rohingya people, both those who were murdered and those who are refugees in Bangladesh. We must do everything we can to relieve their suffering.

I welcome this very important ruling from the ICJ and the steps that the Foreign Secretary has outlined on sanctions on the Myanmar regime in relation to the genocide of the Rohingya. However, the judgment also has wider implications, because, as we have discussed, as a signatory to the genocide convention, under article 1, the UK has an obligation to act to prevent genocide, as well as to punish it after it has been definitively agreed by an international court to have occurred. To quote from the judgment: “the obligation to prevent genocide does not allow a State that is in a position to act in the face of a serious risk of genocide to remain idle… responsibility for breach of the duty to prevent genocide is not conditioned on a finding that genocide has occurred.” In relation to Gaza, given that the UN independent international commission of inquiry has concluded that genocide has occurred, when did the Foreign Secretary last undertake an assessment of the serious risk of genocide in Gaza, and why will he not take the further actions that are obvious, such as stopping all arms exports and instituting sanctions on all those responsible?

I will deal with the two parts to the hon. Member’s question. The first part repeats an important theme that has been raised by another hon. Members: conflict prevention. That needs to become much more part of what we do, as a Government and across the world—identifying risks of genocide, war crimes and other things, and taking actions to prevent them. On her second point, I would say to her that we are taking action on Gaza, including sanctions against Tsav 9. We will continue to look at further measures, including for getting humanitarian aid in.

I too welcome the ICJ ruling, and thank the Foreign Secretary for the swift action, at home and on the international stage; it must be the start of the military regime being held to account for their horrors in Myanmar. It is important that this should be the renewal of a strong and determined international coalition that stays the course on the path to a sustained peace. Can the Foreign Secretary confirm that he will—as I think he has intimated he will—continue to work closely with the Bangladesh Government, who have taken so much of the burden of the needs of the Rohingya refugees? Will he also work to keep on the international stage the situation facing children—those who are malnourished, and the millions who are out of education, due to displacement and armed conflict, including the quarter of a million Rohingya children with no access to education?

My hon. Friend speaks with great authority on these issues, having been a Minister dealing with questions on Myanmar. I absolutely undertake to work with the Government of Bangladesh, as I have said before, on these questions, including on the education of children. She is right to raise that, and there are some charities doing incredible work on this issue in Myanmar, and trying to improve the conditions. She is right that we have to do both those things.

As many Members have said, nothing quite prepares one for the kaleidoscope of emotions one feels when visiting Cox’s Bazar and meeting the Rohingya. I had the opportunity to do so with the all-party parliamentary group on Bangladesh, and one of the things that stood out for me was the young people asking for an education to better themselves, their community and their homeland when they eventually go back. We showed the best of who we were in 2022, when we opened our doors to Ukrainian students. Now that a genocide has been committed against the Rohingya, will we facilitate safe routes to education for young Rohingya survivors of genocide, or a way to invest in their camps, so that they can get an education there?

I will take away the hon. Gentleman’s points, but I think he speaks very wisely about his experience of visiting Cox’s Bazar, which has been mentioned by other hon. Members. The issues of education and the conditions in Cox’s Bazar are important, and we will definitely focus on them in the weeks and months ahead.

I too welcome the statement on the ICJ ruling of genocide by the Myanmar military regime, but the international community has to reflect on why these rulings take so long, and do not stop atrocities as they are happening. I welcome the Secretary of State saying that further action will be taken, and I have a few questions. First, why is only one diplomat from Myanmar being expelled, when all of the diplomats represent the military regime? Secondly, as other hon. Members have said, the aim of a genocide is to wipe out a people; that is why the education of young people in Cox’s Bazar is so important. It will train them, and enable them to return to Myanmar and have the best opportunities. It will also enable the Rohingya to stand up, as a people whom Myanmar’s military regime was trying to wipe out.

This gives me the chance to say that since 2017, the UK has provided more than £457 million to support Rohingya refugees and host communities in Bangladesh. My hon. Friend is absolutely right about the importance of education, which was mentioned by others. On her first point, the reason we singled out the defence attaché is because of the military links, but we do not rule out taking further action, including against representatives of the Government of Myanmar. This is about how we can take effective action and put effective pressure on the regime.

I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s statement and the finding by the ICJ, although I am seriously perplexed by the absurdity of the response from His Majesty’s Opposition. I certainly hope that they are not trying to undermine the rule of law and the Court’s findings. Only a few weeks ago, the Foreign Secretary said that there was ethnic cleansing and war crimes committed on the west bank, and potentially war crimes committed in Gaza. Given that the UK supported the application launched by The Gambia relating to the genocide of the Rohingya, will the UK now become a signatory to the application against the state of Israel?

What we have done in this case is support the work of the Court with our factual submission. I said very clearly in my statement on 8 September that we support the work of the ICJ in the so-called South Africa case, too. I concur with the first part of the hon. Gentleman’s question: it is very important that we support the work of the Court and uphold international law.

I, too, have worked as a surgeon in Bangladesh, although long before this conflict. I visited Cox’s Bazar, which is indeed a beautiful place; now, we hear it is the home to the largest refugee camp in the world. What exactly are we in the United Kingdom to do to support the humanitarian effort for the Rohingya? I note that the statement announced an additional £5 million for 350,000 people, which is about £14.20 per person.

We want to take action across a whole range of fronts. I have mentioned that we are one of the largest humanitarian aid donors, and mentioned the work that we have done in relation to the Government of Bangladesh, which we do within the aid budget that we have. We will do absolutely everything we can—everything it is possible for us to do—to support those in both Myanmar and Bangladesh to relieve the suffering. The best way we can help to relieve the suffering is through pressure on the regime to change its practices and to change course.

I, too, welcome the Foreign Secretary’s acknowledgment of the ICJ ruling and hope that Britain will now help to secure justice for the Rohingya. Given the seriousness of the situation in Gaza and the risk of genocide, will the Foreign Secretary expressly confirm whether this Government recognise that there is a serious risk of genocide? As a signatory to the genocide convention, Britain has a legal obligation to take all reasonable measures within its power to prevent genocide once that risk is known. Does the Foreign Secretary genuinely believe that sanctions against individuals and entities involved in violence and settlement activity on the west bank, alongside statements calling for humanitarian aid to enter Gaza, are sufficient to discharge that obligation? If not, what further action will the Government commit to?

As the hon. Member will know, we announced a comprehensive set of measures on 8 September, including a new sanctions regime relating to the illegal settlements. We announced further action on Gaza after the extension of the global human rights regime, and have rallied the international community to shine a spotlight on what is happening in Gaza, and to seek to drive aid in. I undertake to him that we will do absolutely everything we can to relieve the suffering in Gaza. As I said in my statement, genocide is a finding that comes from a competent court, and there is a case that is being considered by the ICJ.

I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s statement and welcome the ICJ’s ruling that the military junta controlling Myanmar has been committing genocide against the Rohingya. Sadly, although that is the most revolting of its crimes, it is just the tip of the iceberg of the ways that it is repressing other ethnic and religious minorities, and committing human rights abuses against its political opponents in Myanmar’s diverse society. It is disappointing that until today, the UK had not introduced new sanctions on the military regime for two years. I welcome the announcement of the sanctions on jet fuel for use by the Burmese military, but will the Foreign Secretary look at further sanctions against the Burmese state banks, the oil and gas extraction industry that funds its war machine, and the communications network that the Government use?

The answer to the last part of my hon. Friend’s question is yes. On the first part, I could not agree more; what the military regime is doing is systematic oppression, not just a genocide, against the Rohingya. There is a pattern of repression against a whole range of minority groups in Myanmar. My hon. Friend is right on both points.

I welcome the Foreign Secretary’s statement and the decision from the International Court of Justice, which is a significant step forward for the Rohingya people. The ICJ judgment is a reminder of the importance of international law; frankly, I was shocked to hear the position of His Majesty’s Opposition. How will the Foreign Secretary ensure that the UK continues to play its role, and that we do all we can to support international justice?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right about this. I do hope that the Opposition, perhaps helped by some of the wise people on their Back Benches, will think hard about their position on these issues. Now more than at any time since the second world war, these institutions and the idea of international law are under threat. People will be looking at Britain and asking whether we are upholding these norms, whether we stand for them, and whether we abide by them—and I think we should.

I thank the Secretary of State for his statement today and for his commitment. Given the recent International Court of Justice judgment on the Rohingya and the continuing persecution of religious minorities in Myanmar, including Christians and Muslims, as chair of the APPG for international freedom of religion or belief, I ask the Foreign Secretary to outline the concrete steps the British Government are taking with international partners to ensure accountability for those responsible for the most terrible crimes—murder, rape, mutilation, destruction of homes, schools and hospitals, and displacement—as well as to protect freedom of religion and belief and human rights, and to secure humanitarian assistance for communities facing persecution.

The hon. Gentleman speaks a great deal of sense on this matter. This is a genocide, and an attack on freedom of religion. He is correct on that. As he will know, my hon. Friend the Member for North Northumberland (David Smith) is our envoy for freedom of religion or belief. It is so important that around the world, including in Myanmar, we fight for that freedom.

I thank the Foreign Secretary for his sobering statement on this landmark judgment. I visited Myanmar in 2013; even at that early point, I saw violence rising against the Rohingya people, which has escalated so terribly since. Since becoming an MP, as part of the British Group of the Inter-Parliamentary Union, along with others in the Chamber, I have had the privilege of meeting some of Myanmar’s exiled politicians, who continue to work for justice at great personal risk. Would the Foreign Secretary enable a dialogue with those brave exiled politicians as part of his work on the ICJ judgment?

I thank my hon. Friend for that question; yes, I would very much like to do that. When I met the representative of the Rohingya this morning in my office, he asked me whether I would meet some of the community in this country, and I said that I absolutely would. My hon. Friend is right to draw attention to her experience in 2013; reading the report, it is clear that, unfortunately, this genocide was a long time coming. Well before 2017, there was a systematic pattern of oppression of the Rohingya people, which led up to the terrible events of that year.

I had the privilege of visiting Myanmar during perhaps one of the last moments of hope before the precipice. Does my right hon. Friend agree that a rising economy, foreign direct investment and development finance are no substitute for early-stage prevention work of the kind that his Department can be so successful in delivering?

I thank my hon. Friend for his question; he is so right about early warning systems across the international community on atrocity prevention and the actions we need to take. The judgment that the Court has found should drive us all to think about how we can do better at atrocity prevention, working with international partners, rather than having to deal with the appalling consequences of a genocide nine or 10 years after the event.

I strongly welcome the Foreign Secretary’s statement and the leadership he is showing on the international rule of law. The need for accountability of the perpetrators of these atrocities is fundamental for victims. That includes Myanmar’s military leader, for whom I believe the ICC has a pending arrest warrant. However, that Court is under threat. I recently met the vice-president of the International Criminal Court, who explained to me the personal impact on judges and officials, which holds them back from doing their duties. What steps can the Foreign Secretary take, working with our European allies, to protect the international rule of law, and particularly to protect the International Criminal Court from attack so it can get on with doing its job?

I am really glad that my hon. and learned Friend raised that point. The threat to the ICC is real. I am working with my Dutch counterpart and others to seek to protect the Court. We have expressed our strong disagreement with our US allies on this question. The Under-Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, my hon. Friend the Member for Bridgend (Chris Elmore) will be at the Court next week, and I undertake to do everything I can to protect the work of the Court, because it is so important. Lastly, I say to all Members in this House who take an interest in these issues that I undertake with the team of Ministers to keep working on them. This cannot just be a one-off moment when we react to the judgment. I recognise our responsibilities to the people of Myanmar and the Rohingya.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. This point of order relates to the timeliness of ministerial correspondence. On 16 August, I sent an important and time-sensitive case to the Ministry of Justice, which transferred it to the Department of Health and Social Care on 2 September. My team has consistently chased up the Department for a response, because my constituent is now quite rightly frustrated and questioning the efficiency of my team, rather than the Department at hand. I am sorry to bother you and the House with a point of order regarding this, and I know that you are not responsible for ministerial correspondence, but could you advise me how I can chase the Department through other means in order to get a much-needed response to my constituent?

I thank the hon. Member for giving notice of his point of order. As he will know, and as he has mentioned, the timeliness of ministerial correspondence is not a matter for the Chair. However, I know that his comments will have been heard by those on the Treasury Front Bench, and I trust that they will take steps to ensure that the reply is forthcoming.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Earlier, during the Prime Minister’s statement on the UK-EU summit, the Leader of the Opposition claimed that the UK already has “the deepest trade agreement any country has with the EU”. As you will know, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein are all members of the European economic area, which gives complete and untrammelled access to the EU single market. Switzerland’s European Free Trade Association arrangements follow close behind, and Turkey has a customs union with the European Union. Madam Deputy Speaker, I am sure that you and the House would agree that that long list of exceptions is perhaps rather too long for the Leader of the Opposition’s point to stand. As a former Trade Secretary, and someone who has congratulated herself on never making gaffes, I am sure she would welcome the opportunity to clear up this wholly uncharacteristic error. Could you recommend how that can be achieved?

I thank the hon. Member for advance notice of his point of order. As he knows, Members, not the Chair, are responsible for the content of their statements—otherwise we would have another full-time job on top of the one we have.
The reasoned amendment in the name of the shadow Chancellor has been selected. I call the Minister to move Second Reading.

I beg to move, That the Bill be now read a Second time. The Budget last month was a Budget to provide breathing space now and fresh hope for the future. It backed British business to unleash growth in every postcode and kick-started the changes needed to put our country on a better course. It was a Budget to steer Britain through global economic storms and a Budget built on fiscal discipline, which now, more than ever, underwrites every promise that we make to the British people. The economic context for this Budget was shaped by the impact of the war in the middle east. Labour has always sought de-escalation and taken the right judgments when it comes to our economic national interest. That is in stark contrast to the Leader of the Opposition, who was rather gung-ho about this conflict at the start. In March this year she said: “I have made it very clear that the Conservative party also stands behind America taking this necessary action”. —[ Official Report , 2 March 2026; Vol. 781, c. 586.] Yet this is a conflict that the Office for Budget Responsibility forecasts has added £14 billion a year to debt interest costs. It is against that backdrop that the Chancellor faced a choice at the Budget. He could have followed the route that the Conservatives always tend to go down, which is to sacrifice economic stability, borrow irresponsibly and make unfunded spending promises—exactly the same kind of irresponsibility that led to the disastrous Liz Truss mini-Budget. Still, to this day, the shadow Chancellor maintains that there were a lot of good things in the mini-Budget, and still, to this day, the British people are paying the price.
On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. It is my understanding that when the Minister is moving the Second Reading of a Bill, he should actually speak to the Bill that is before the House.

I hope that the Minister is getting very close to saying everything he needs to say—maybe he was giving some background information. We have a lot of people down to speak, so perhaps we should get straight to the point.

Of course, Madam Deputy Speaker. I look forward to the Opposition parties’ spokespeople forensically going through the measures of the Bill only and not making any political points in their remarks. Instead of taking the irresponsible path chosen by the Conservatives, the Chancellor chose the responsible route: to keep the public finances under control, to protect working people, to back businesses and to invest in Britain’s future.

For the second time we have seen a rise in taxes on rented properties. Could the Minister tell me what that will do to the already reducing supply of private homes available to rent and what it will do for rents for those who are the most in need of somewhere to live?

I am grateful to the right hon. Gentleman for raising the issue of housing supply and the cost of renting in this country. The Government have made very significant progress in reforming our planning system to enable more homes to be built, which is the ultimate way we can bring down the price of renting in this country and make housing more affordable. I am sad to say that at every single opportunity the right hon. Gentleman and his party have voted against the planning reforms that the Government have put forward to improve the operation of our housing market. Things would be much worse with regard to housing if they were still in charge. For families, the Budget will mean a £100 household energy payment to support up to 20 million households in January, along with the extension of the VAT cut on electricity bills and a further freeze on fuel duty. To help fund this support, the bank corporation tax surcharge will be increased by three percentage points. The increase is time-limited and will end on 31 March 2028, as is set out in the Bill. The Tories opposed this measure at the Budget. Their choice is always more borrowing, and again today they are making the wrong choice for families across the country by opposing higher taxes on banks to fund £100 off council tax for 80% of households in England.

I very much welcome the commitment to reduce fuel duty for a certain period of time, but in Northern Ireland we are already facing higher costs for fuel because of logistics—we have to bring everything in and take everything out, and there is a cost to that. Have the Government considered a concession for businesses in Northern Ireland that are paying a higher premium for fuel because of the distances and costs involved?

I thank the hon. Member for his question. I am aware that the rural economy is really important in Northern Ireland, as well as in other parts of the country. As well as continuing to freeze fuel duty, we have cut the fuel duty on red diesel. The Budget extended that cut, because we know that cost of living impacts are affecting not just families but businesses in the rural communities that make use of red diesel. I turn to businesses more broadly. The Budget also confirmed a reduction in bills by up to 25% for more than 10,000 eligible businesses from next April through the British industrial competitiveness scheme. In the first week of this new Government, we increased business rates relief for pubs, clubs and music venues from 15% to 35% from April next year. At the Budget, we went further, taking around 70,000 more high street properties out of paying business rates altogether. For other businesses in those sectors, the Budget froze business rates in real terms for two years. To pay for that new support, we are taking action through the Bill to increase the rate of machine games duty for higher stakes machines and to level the playing field by clamping down on VAT evasion through online marketplaces.

The Highbridge social club in my constituency is run by volunteers and has provided services to the community since 1914. Its treasurer has written to me to say that the increase in machine games duty will cost the club £1,500, on top of the national insurance rises. This Government’s tax increases are putting the club in danger. What advice would the Minister give the treasurer of the Highbridge social club? The Minister’s tax rises are putting a valuable community asset at risk.

I thank the hon. Member for raising that issue about the club in his constituency. The 5 percentage points increase in machine games duty is a limited increase, targeted at higher stakes machines. Pretty much all the machines found in pubs and clubs across the country should not be affected by that increase, but I will be happy to pick that up with him and have a conversation to discuss the impact on the club in his constituency. The support for businesses will deliver some breathing space now, but, as the Chancellor said at the Budget, “The only way we keep Britain’s families and Britain’s finances secure for the long term is with an economy that is growing strongly” —[ Official Report , 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 307.] —and one that continues to grow strongly, as it has been recently. To achieve that, we must do more to help firms start, scale and stay in Britain. Britain does not lack ideas, and nor do we lack entrepreneurs, but too often we invent the technologies here in the UK and see the jobs and profits go somewhere else. The Bill contains a significant package of tax reforms to help founders, investors and talented employees across the UK. I am pleased to say that they have been welcomed across industry. For example, the Startup Coalition said at the Budget that it was a “good day” to be building a start-up in Britain, while the ScaleUp Institute praised the important work we are doing to address scale-up challenges. That includes action to help businesses attract and retain the talent they need to grow while giving employees a greater stake in the success they help create. Our research and development reforms will help make the claims process simpler for around 40,000 businesses and enable more companies to access the £65 million of relief. Our changes to our venture capital schemes will make them easy to use and help more investment reach early-stage and growing companies. The Bill also increases the trading allowance from £1,000 to £3,000, providing additional tax relief for people starting small businesses or earning income from side hustles. To ensure that the UK remains the best place for ambitious founders and early investors to build their companies, the Bill will legislate for a new capital gains tax founders’ relief: a 10% rate on lifetime gains of up to £10 million for the founders or early investors in high-growth and innovative firms.

I would like to make progress. Many Members wish to speak, we are constrained to 10 pm and I have already taken a few interventions. [ Interruption. ] As well as measures to fund breathing space now and to help kick-start good growth in every postcode, the Bill contains a number of measures to modernise the tax system and ensure that everyone pays their fair share.
Order. I want to ensure that the Minister has not made plans for the evening as the business can go well beyond 10 pm.

The Minister, as ever, is being extremely generous. He is talking about making sure that businesses stay here and do not go elsewhere when they grow up, and he has talked about small businesses. What about large businesses such as Compass Group? Why is it looking to go to New York? Has he spoken to its representative? What will he do to ensure that such companies do not leave our shores because of excessive taxation by this Government?

I thank the right hon. Member for his question. I have not personally engaged with that particular business on this matter, though I am sure that the Department for Business, Innovation and Trade will be in conversation with the people there and will want to understand the reasons behind that decision. We are looking at what more we can do to deepen capital markets and support the stock exchange, and we recently made changes to stamp taxes on shares, but of course we need to continue to look at this important issue; I hope that there are areas of cross-party consensus that we can work on, because it is such an important topic for the future of our country.

The Treasury Committee heard conflicting evidence from Helen Miller of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, and Alex Depledge, who until recently was adviser to the Government on such start-ups—in fact, she started her first businesses in Shoreditch; she eventually sold one of those on. The key support that these fledgling businesses need is in getting that finance early doors. Will the Minister lay out the detail of how the Government will support them at that point? A tax break later on is all very well for those businesses that do succeed, but it is in the early stage that they need support. Perhaps he could give us some more information on that.

I thank my hon. Friend for all the work she does on the Treasury Committee, and I thank the Committee for its important work scrutinising and challenging us on the Budget. We increased capitalisation for the British Business Bank at the Budget, and we continue to work with it to reform and improve its effectiveness and performance so that it can get funding out more quickly to start-ups, supporting them to access the finance they need. We are also looking at reforms. We have made reforms to our pension system to support more funding staying in the UK—those reforms were challenged by the Opposition. We need to continue to look at what more we can do to help the smallest businesses. One area of particular interest to me and to the Government is procurement: how we can help growing and fledgling businesses to get their first contract with the Government—that stamp of approval from the NHS or the Ministry of Defence to show that their product is viable, and to help get the cash flow. We have changed the procurement framework so that it focuses not on a whole smorgasbord of issues, but on British businesses and British jobs. Those are some of the things that the Government are doing.

I would like to make a little progress, if I may. First, the Bill will help taxpayers get their tax right first time while strengthening the ability of His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs to identify and tackle non-compliance. It paves the way for the introduction of e-invoicing, saving businesses time and effort, and modernises the rules for error correction to help ensure that the right tax is paid. Those measures form part of a wider package announced at the Budget to close the tax gap, raising an additional £2.3 billion in 2029-30 and taking the total raised across this Parliament from closing the tax gap to over £12 billion. Secondly, the Bill will ensure that the tax system keeps pace with changes in our economy. That includes the introduction of an electric vehicle excise duty from April 2028, because as more drivers make the switch to EVs, we need a sustainable long-term replacement for fuel duty that supports the public finances while backing the transition to cleaner transport. Thirdly, the Bill will address unfairness in the tax system. The Bill resolves the question of VAT for the largest taxi companies, ensuring that they play by the same rules no matter where they are located, while still protecting smaller, local firms. It also introduces a high-value council tax surcharge. Under the current council tax system, a £10 million property in Mayfair can pay less than a family home in Darlington or in Blackpool; the Bill will ensure that is no longer the case. Providing breathing space for families and businesses now, and ensuring that we meet our fiscal rules with a buffer, even after the impact of the shock from the middle east on our shores, also required further tax changes at this Budget. First, as I have set out, the Bill provides for an increase to machine games duty and, separately, a time-limited increase to the bank surcharge. Secondly, we are maintaining the key features of the corporation tax regime that support investment, including the 25% rate and the top-ranked regime in the OECD for capital allowances. The Bill introduces greater up-front relief for new investment, increasing the first-year allowance available for main rate plant and machinery from 40% to 50% while reducing the main writing down allowance from 14% to 12%. Thirdly, the lifetime limit for business asset disposal relief in capital gains tax will decrease from £1 million to £500,000, which will mean no change for three in four claimants. Fourthly, the rates of tax on income from property and savings will increase by a further 2 percentage points from April 2027—an additional contribution from those with income from assets, while keeping the rates of tax paid on earnings unchanged. Around 84% of income tax payers will see no increase in their income tax bill in 2027-28 as a result of this change, and half the revenue is expected to come from the top 10% of households. The Government have also confirmed that we will no longer go ahead with the cut to the tax-free amount that people can put in a cash ISA. If the Conservatives oppose these measures today, they must set out how they intend to fund the breathing space we are providing, including on household energy bills. Every policy in our Budget is fully funded, because fiscal responsibility underwrites every promise that this Government make. We will not repeat the mistakes of the Conservatives, who left us with billions of pounds of unfunded spending commitments and borrowed like there was no tomorrow. We are taking a different approach. We will invest in public services, we will keep borrowing falling year after year and we will meet our fiscal rules, delivering breathing space now alongside fresh hope for the future.

I beg to move an amendment, to leave out from “That” to the end of the Question and add: “this House declines to give a Second Reading to the Finance Bill because, at a time when taxes are at a record high, borrowing and debt are increasing, and the OBR has confirmed that household net incomes are set to fall and that growth next year will be lower than this year, the Bill does not take the necessary action to bring down the deficit, or increase growth, and because the Bill is the result of a Budget that will lead to higher spending and borrowing; believes that it is wrong to penalise savers, landlords and homeowners with increased taxes to pay for more welfare spending; further believes that it is wrong to add to the tax burden on businesses; and instead calls on the Government to support economic growth by cutting taxes, reducing the rate of employers’ National Insurance contributions for young people, and abolishing Stamp Duty and Inheritance Tax on the family home.” “Is that it?” Those were the words of the Leader of the Opposition when she first heard this Budget. This is a missed opportunity, and the Chancellor has simply kicked the can down the road. We may have a new Labour Chancellor, but we have failed to change the fact that we have an old Labour Budget: high tax, high spending and high welfare. I am afraid Labour does not get it; when you tax something, you get less of it, and this has been the biggest tax-raising Parliament in our nation’s history. Since coming into office, the Labour Government have increased the jobs tax, imposed the family farm tax, introduced a family business tax and taxed independent schools. They have hiked capital gains tax. They have extended inheritance tax to pensions. They have increased taxes on entrepreneurs and investors, and by extending the freeze on income tax and national insurance thresholds, they have hit people’s take-home pay. I could go on, but as the Work and Pensions Secretary put it, Labour MPs spend their time asking, “Who can we tax next in order to pay benefits to others?” Today, we have a Bill that I can barely lift. It has 455 pages, and includes nearly 100 new ways to squeeze the pips out of our economy and to punish the wealth creators, those who create jobs and those who work hard, those who save hard and those who grow the food we eat. The party in government does not seem to realise that economic growth comes from enterprise, from investment and from hard work, not from continually finding new ways to tax those who work, create jobs and generate wealth. This country needs lower, simpler, fairer taxes. We should be making it easier to buy a home, easier to start a business and easier to save, and easier for families to get ahead. At a time when the world is becoming more dangerous, we need to strengthen our economy so that we can properly fund our national defence. A strong economy is the absolute foundation of a stronger country. The decision in this Finance Bill to increase tax rates on those who save sends entirely the wrong signal. People who have done the responsible thing—who have put money aside and built up a nest egg—should not be treated as an easy source of revenue. Higher property income taxes for landlords will inevitably mean that many tenants will end up paying the price through higher rents. Members do not have to take it from me; that is what the Office for Budget Responsibility says in its report. For many people, rent is their biggest outlay, and this Budget will drive up their cost of living. When Labour taxes landlords, the tenants get the bill.

I thank the shadow Minister for the wisdom of her words. When it comes to the 2 percentage point hike on savings and property income, this legislation applies to Scotland and Wales. There has been no indication whatsoever that there will be any help for those in Northern Ireland. That is an anomaly to be fixed by the Government and by the Minister. Does the shadow Minister believe that it is time the Government looked at fairness across all of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, to ensure that we in Northern Ireland can have the same opportunities and flexibility as Scotland and Wales? At this moment, we do not.

I congratulate the hon. Gentleman on standing up for his constituents very effectively in this place. I agree with what he says. Reducing the value of business asset disposal relief in this Finance Bill sends a worrying message to entrepreneurs: take the risks, create the jobs and build the companies, but do not expect the tax system in this country to recognise your contribution. The high value council tax surcharge, which Labour misleadingly brands a mansion tax, is simply a family homes tax. It is yet another example of a Government who treat home ownership as a problem to be taxed, rather than an aspiration to be encouraged. The increase in the bank surcharge may be levied on the banks, but it will not be borne by the banks alone. The costs will seep through to the economy in higher mortgages, lower business lending and the wider cost of borrowing. In the end, what Labour calls a tax on banks risks becoming a tax on aspiration, on home ownership and on growth. The test for any Finance Bill is simple: will it make Britain more competitive, more attractive to investment and more likely to grow? We all recognise the need for sound public finances, but sound public finances are built on a strong economy. This Finance Bill takes more from taxpayers while doing too little to create the growth that would make higher taxes unnecessary. Britain under Labour is living beyond its means. We are locked in a doom loop of high spend, high debt and higher taxes. At the end of the last Parliament, when the Office for Budget Responsibility forecast what growth would be under the Conservatives’ plans for the economy, it said that the economy would grow by 8.5% between 2024 and 2028. Now it is saying that, over that same period, growth is going to be 2% weaker at 6.4%. That alone is worth £60 billion to our economy. This Government inherited inflation that was bang on the 2% target, but new figures show that it has risen by 3.6%. In fact, inflation has exceeded the Bank of England’s target in every month since Labour’s first Budget in October 2024.

Does my hon. Friend agree that the Government are responsible for those higher inflation figures through their excessive borrowing and public expenditure, and through giving in to the rail unions, the junior doctors and any other unionised workforce that simply asks them for more money?

My hon. Friend is spot on. In fact, the Governor of the Bank of England pointed out that the October 2024 Budget would feed through into the economy in higher prices. Unemployment is 248,000 higher and the number of payroll jobs has fallen by more than 200,000 since Labour took office in 2024. The number of young people not in jobs, training or education has increased by nearly 60,000—a town the size of Loughborough— on Labour’s watch. In fact, youth unemployment in Britain is higher than in Bulgaria, Slovenia and Hungary.

The hon. Lady will know that that problem did not arise under this Labour Government. Numbers went up massively in the final years of her Government. In a spirit of generosity and hope for those young people, does she not support this Government’s measures to try to get those young people into work and boost our economy? We need those young people working.

I just point out to the Chair of the Treasury Committee that 60,000 suggests a very fast rate of increase, and that youth unemployment in this country is now higher than in Bulgaria, Slovenia and Hungary. There is no question but that increasing the cost of employing a young person has increased the number of young people out of work. That is a simple mathematical fact. Pay growth in this country has fallen to its slowest rate in five years.

It is unimaginable that Gordon Brown would come out well from a comparison on support for enterprise, but 18 years ago entrepreneurs’ relief was at 10% up to £1 million; it is now at 18% for half that figure—nothing for inflation. Enterprise in this country has been dissuaded by a Government who have no understanding of private business, and no understanding that it is the pursuit of profit and growth that provides the dynamism to allow ordinary people to have better lives.

My right hon. Friend is spot on. In fact, by continuing that approach to entrepreneurs under the 14 years of Conservative-led Governments, we created more than 1.1 million new businesses in this country. That is something to be truly proud of—unlike the fact that the national debt has now surpassed £3 trillion. It has gone up £275 billion since Labour entered office, and the tax burden is set to reach a historic high of 38.5%. In fact, over this Parliament, Labour is borrowing £308 billion more than it would have under the plans they inherited. To pay for that, the Government must hike taxes by £75 billion every year. In case the Minister and Government Members did not hear that correctly, I repeat that that has all happened since July 2024. We have a better plan. We have set out more than £70 billion in savings, including in the welfare budget. We will use those savings to do two things: first, pay down the deficit; and secondly, cut taxes to jump-start growth. We will abolish stamp duty for all primary residences, abolish inheritance tax on the family home and repeal Labour’s family homes tax. We will scrap business rates for thousands of high street businesses, and halve the jobs tax on young people’s jobs. Labour is creating a lost generation, isolated and powerless. Labour has an ever-rising working-age welfare bill, which is now costing each taxpayer £4,000 a year. It is simply not fair to ask for more and more in tax from those in work to pay for those who are not. We cannot go on like this. We need lower, simpler and fairer taxes.
Would the shadow Minister, as the Liberal Democrats would, consider reducing the VAT rate on electric vehicle charging points?

I will stick to the tax cuts that I have already outlined, which are attractive and significant. I hope that the hon. Gentleman will join me in the Lobby to vote to end this socialist doom loop by voting down this tax-and-spend Finance Bill.

One thing on which I agree with the Opposition spokesperson, the hon. Member for West Worcestershire (Dame Harriett Baldwin), is that this is a very large Bill—I counted 469 pages, so we may need to recount. We already have a very complicated tax system, and Budgets from different Governments over the years have made little changes here and there, making it difficult for many businesses and individuals to navigate. The Office of Tax Simplification was retired under one of the previous Conservative Chancellors from the last Government; that is something we perhaps need to reconsider. Does the Minister disagree with Helen Miller, who gave evidence to the Treasury Committee after the Budget? She said: “We have a tax system that is a mess”— she does not mince her words— “It is far more complex than it should be. And that is because, Budget after Budget, chancellors make seemingly small tweaks that lack principle and don’t systematically move us to a better place. This approach gives us more complexity and more instability. Both have real economic costs.” Does the Minister acknowledge this complexity? I know that he thinks deeply about taxes and is clear about his plans for taxes when he comes to the Committee. Of course, he chairs the HMRC board, so he has a direct hand in how our tax system works. Does the Treasury acknowledge the economic complexity the system may create? Is there any analysis of the long-term impact when these proposals are put into a Budget? I appreciate that any Government must deal with the here and now. We are in a cost of living crisis. There is the war in Iran, and the ongoing war in Ukraine—huge challenges not just for our country but for the world. We still have instability in the White House, which is causing challenges. However, we need to think long term about tax complexity. It is difficult for people doing their tax returns and difficult for businesses to navigate. The Bill includes the temporary increase in the banking surcharge. I must put on the record the Treasury Committee’s disappointment that that leaked out before the Budget statement. At 10.45, there was a story on Bloomberg stating that the tax would be 6% for 15 months —very specific details that had not on the whole been speculated on, as far as I could see, in any media in advance. By 10.46, there was trading on the markets. This was market-sensitive information. When the permanent secretary came with the Chancellor to the Committee a couple of weeks after the Budget, we were pleased that he was robust about his desire to undertake a leak inquiry and to ensure that this does not happen again, but we have heard this before, and I am a little weary of it. Governments of all colours say, “Oh, there’s a leak; we’ll have an inquiry.” The Chancellor did upbraid me for saying that we never find anybody—perhaps I was a bit pessimistic, because occasionally someone is found—but this is a serious matter. I applaud the Chancellor for making it clear that he wanted to lock down and avoid the leaks we have seen in previous years. On the whole, that worked, but this was an egregious leak. I hope that the Minister will back any findings from the leak inquiry by the permanent secretary. The bank surcharge is supposed to be temporary. We heard some speculation that it might not stay that way, so it would help if the Minister was clear about that. The Bill legislates for it to end on 31 March 2028, and I like to take things in good faith. It is important to note that Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of J.P. Morgan—speaking on Thursday, as reported in The Financial Times and then picked up in other media—was trenchant in his anger about the tax, and said that he will seek to offset it. He can be as angry as he wants—it is the Treasury that is making the decision to tax the banks. Will His Majesty’s Treasury and the Minister ensure that they are watching the impact of this tax and measuring what happens when they introduce a surcharge of this sort? Having

I am extremely grateful to the Chairman of the Treasury Committee for giving way. I think it may have been to her Committee that Helen Miller of the Institute for Fiscal Studies pointed out that not one of the 98 measures in this Budget had a positive growth score, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility. Could she comment on that feature of this enormous yet non-growth-producing Budget?

I could get into a long and detailed explanation of how the OBR scores growth. It sets a de minimis level that must be reached before a measure is given a growth score, but growth is not impossible. This Bill outlines measures that have a smaller effect than the OBR would score, but in aggregate, they can still deliver growth, albeit in small amounts. That is partly due to the situation that we are in. This was not a Budget of big, sweeping changes. I am pleased to say, as a Labour and Co-operative MP, that this is not a Government who have found the magic money tree; they are being prudent with the public finances, and are not over-promising and under-delivering through the Budget. That caution is right; we saw what happened back in 2022 when caution was thrown to the winds. Hopefully, the right hon. Gentleman is still sore about the damage that did to the British economy, mortgagees and the British public, who gave their verdict firmly in the 2024 election. It is right that we have steadiness.

The Chair of the Select Committee describes the Government’s approach as cautious and prudent, but their figures assume £500 million a year from permission being given to the Rosebank oilfield. Does she regard that as a prudent and cautious stance? Does she assume that the permission will be granted?

That is being scored by the OBR as a potential, but it involves a quasi-judicial process, and it is a matter for the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero to determine. Given her experience, I am sure that she will weigh up all the issues. Until that decision is made, we cannot be sure what the outcome will be. I turn to the cash individual savings account. The Treasury Committee was firm in its view—cross-party, of course—that slashing the £20,000 ISA cash limit to £12,000 was not the right way to get British consumers to invest. Keeping the amount at £20,000 is a good thing. People rather valued the ability, in theory, to claim this. Of course, most people get nowhere near the £20,000 limit in a year, but that does not mean that we should not always encourage people to invest. It is interesting that the Government have added tax on savings. I wonder if they are hoping that the extra tax, at both tax levels, on earnings from savings will drive savers to invest instead. Of course, as it is, the tax will eat away at the capital, so anyone with cash savings will find that their capital is not keeping up with inflation, even with the higher interest rates emerging because of inflation. I commend the Government—in fact, the former Chancellor, my right hon. Friend the Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves)—on biting the bullet and finally implementing a tax on low-emission vehicles, a so-called EV tax. The possibility was raised a number of times with the Public Accounts Committee, when I chaired it, and with the Treasury Committee. As we phase out petrol vehicles and fuel duty, there was always the elephant in the room of how that hole in the Exchequer would be filled. It is right that we consider driving to be a pollutant, and not just because of fossil fuels; there are other pollutants from driving. We should not discourage driving where it is necessary, but we should ensure that this issue is considered in the round. That brave decision was long overdue. I welcome the move to increase the amount of money that people can earn from side hustles from £1,000 to £3,000, tax free. Madam Deputy Speaker, if you want to see a side hustle, come to Hackney South and Shoreditch, where everybody is doing something on the side, partly because of the cost of living challenge and the cost of housing in my area. A lot of innovative entrepreneurs are starting little businesses on the side, which one day might grow into something more. It is great that they can now earn £3,000 without having to think about tax. That will encourage them to grow that bit more, and perhaps some of the next interesting businesses in our country will come from my constituency, as well as other places up and down the country. This small but important measure from the Government has a big benefit for many people in my constituency. This is a large Bill, and I hope that the Minister will answer the philosophical question about tax simplification. I appreciate that this Government have inherited a complex tax code, and a tax system that was not just down to them, but they have added to it, and that seems to be the general direction of travel in this country. It will be a Herculean task to reverse that and make tax more simple; that is not easy to do. I would be interested to learn the Minister’s thoughts on this—if not now, then when he no doubt appears before our Committee to explain tax and his approach to delivering for the Exchequer.

We needed a growth Budget but did not get one. We all know that only by growing the economy can we cut people’s taxes and bills and create good jobs. Earlier this afternoon, the Prime Minister stood at the Dispatch Box and celebrated the growth that he hopes to get from his timid EU-UK reset deal, but we Liberal Democrats know that only through a real growth and defence partnership will we get the real growth that we need to change people’s lives. We are again calling on the Government to join the single market, the customs union and a new European rearmament bank, so that we can have joint financing and joint procurement. Such a partnership would enable us, in time, to raise the income tax threshold to £15,000. In short, if we can grow the economy, we can put more money in people’s pockets. The need to grow the economy is urgent. Buried in the detail of the Budget was a damning conclusion from the Office for Budget Responsibility: living standards are not set to improve. This was repeated, though it got very little coverage, by many other organisations. The Resolution Foundation has said this will be a “lost decade for living standards.” Paul Johnson, formerly of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, has described this as “an unbelievably awful decade.” The Joseph Rowntree Foundation has said that this will be the “worst ever Parliament for living standards”, and even an OBR member, who should be impartial, said that British households were facing a “grim picture.” This is a bleak outlook for British families. Against that backdrop, the Government’s cost of living package was too timid and not well targeted. I was, and remain, sorely disappointed to see that the Government’s energy support is linked to the outdated council tax system when it did not need to be. It is estimated that using the outdated council tax system will result in up to 1.4 million people on very low incomes not benefiting from the £100 payment; but wealthier people, who may have retired early, travelled the world and downsized, will receive that £100. That could have been avoided.

During the covid pandemic, I looked in detail at how these schemes giving money back worked. Often there was a data issue, but the approach being taken here is simple, and it means that nine out of 10 of the poorest households will receive the money. It obviously does not cover everybody, but it is one of the simplest and cleanest ways of approaching this. What would the hon. Lady’s alternative be?

I am glad that the hon. Lady asked the question, because we have set that alternative out repeatedly over the last six to eight months. We have called for an essential energy guarantee. It would use existing Department for Work and Pensions data, which would be shared with energy companies, as well as the child benefit data used by His Majesty’s Revenue and Customs. By combining that data, the Government could reduce the cost of essential energy, using an analysis provided by Ofgem every three months of what counts as average energy use. We would provide a discounted rate on the first half of that energy. That would result in an increase in support for households in which there were disabled people or children. This idea has been set out by the New Economics Foundation, and others have looked at it as well. We have set it out in detail; and I would be happy to share the details with the hon. Lady, in case her Committee is keen to support it.

The hon. Lady is making an interesting speech. Has she done any work on how these two data sets would be merged, the complexity of managing that data while maintaining its integrity, and what the costs might be?

It is my understanding that work has been under way on that in Government for several months, and that the collation of the data was supposed to be complete by this autumn. I have not seen a Government update on that, but those data sets already exist. The Government could have used that data to provide a more targeted scheme that provided an average of £100, while high energy users could have received up to £180. That is another way that this could have been done. It would have been a social tariff—something that I believe a number of Labour Members have supported. This is a mechanism the Government could have used. It is unfortunate that some people will lose out, and that the measure is, as a number of think-tanks have said, unnecessarily untargeted. It could have been better targeted if the Government had used the data they already have.

I would ask Governments, including the previous Conservative Government, to avoid trying to find fixes to help people on low incomes directly with their energy costs. If they want to do that, they should go through the DWP; then they would not get caught up in all this. If they want to hand the money over, they should hand it over, in recognition of high energy costs, but they should not find some bespoke system, which is inevitably over-complex and expensive, and all too often misses the people they want to hit.

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his intervention. I am not quite sure whether he thinks that he is agreeing or disagreeing with me, but I was suggesting that we use DWP data, which I think is the point he was trying to make. Using DWP data and some HMRC data would have allowed a more tailored approach.

I am grateful to the hon. Lady for allowing me to explain. I would recommend going through the DWP. Do not just use its data; go through the DWP. Do not try to come up with another complex system that might look good for a headline for the weekend—Governments tend to like those. The Government should just go through the DWP, and put more money in the pockets of people on lower incomes, if that is what they think they need to do. Do not create a parallel system.

I am grateful for the clarification. Just to explain, this essential energy guarantee could use the system already in use for the warm home discount, in which the Government share limited DWP data with the energy companies, and the energy companies then provide a refund to the customers. The system exists already; we could use it with this data as well, but discount essential energy in the first instance.

I really care about data use. I was privileged, in a previous life, to work with large data sets. One problem for those working with two data sets is the lack of a primary key. It means that they cannot get the two pieces of information to talk to each other. The hon. Lady is right that a lot of information exists in Government, but connecting it is really challenging. She made a point about using DWP data and giving it to the energy companies, but in her original conversation about this, she was talking about two separate Government databases. Is she proposing that both sets of data go across? If so, there is a significant risk of overlap. Or is she aware of something connecting those databases?

An essential energy guarantee would initially use the data that the Government already use, and share with energy companies, for the warm home discount. That data already exists; the mechanism exists; and people already benefit. The difference under this system is that there would not be a one-off payment. There would be a discount on energy use up front; it would reduce the cost of the first chunk of energy that people use. There is the additional potential benefit of our using HMRC data on child benefit to provide an even bigger additional discount to families with children. The scheme could be carried out using the first data set or the second. I would like to see Government using both data sets, but if they can only use the first, that will still provide more support than the scheme that the Government have designed. I shall now move on from the technicalities of this proposal— [Interruption.] As we can see, I am across the detail.

Riveting stuff; there we go. Many people will be aware that last week, Cornwall Insight predicted that energy bills would increase, and could rise by 26% next year. That is a £443 increase next year. I am surprised that we have not had a Government statement on this issue. This warning came out last Wednesday or Thursday, I think, so we have had a couple of days since in the Chamber, and we have not had a Government statement about how they intend to respond. Age UK has said that this rise would be “frightening to many older people who…simply have no room left in their budgets to absorb another energy price increase.” National Energy Action has said that “actual energy bills will be higher than at the peak of the 2023 energy crisis, after the government stepped in to put a cap on prices and provide bill rebates.” The £100 that has been announced in the Budget will be swallowed up almost instantaneously on the first day of next year, so I urge the Government to come forward with a statement to say how they will respond to that challenge.

I commend the hon. Lady for setting out the case. Rural communities account for 40% to 50% of my constituency. In Northern Ireland, 68% of people depend on heating oil, but in Strangford 80% of people depend on heating oil to heat their homes. The impact will be greater for them, so the Government need to give assistance to rural communities such as those in Strangford, Northern Ireland and across the whole of the United Kingdom.

I agree with the hon. Gentleman. My party has been at the forefront of calling for a cap on heating oil costs as there is in other areas. I represent St Albans, but from my speeches he will know that I am a Suffolk girl, born and bred, so I know that in rural communities the cost of heating oil has gone through the roof and I am familiar with the challenges that people are facing. Moving on to businesses, we welcome support for small businesses. Raising the small business threshold will support a number of businesses, but it is still tinkering around the edges rather than delivering the fundamental reform of business rates that this Government promised in their manifesto. If we are serious about breathing life into our high streets, we have to reform the outdated broken business rate system. Does the Minister have any update for the House on the review that he commissioned on fair and maintainable trade and how it affects our pubs? Many pubs are still struggling because of the number of tax increases that we have seen. In a debate in Westminster Hall earlier today, there were calls for an independent commission to look at reforming council tax and stamp duty. I would add business rates to that list of broken property taxes. Will the Government consider the call for an independent commission to look at these outdated, broken property systems?

On the subject of small businesses that are not on the high street, I met a sole trader on Friday morning at my surgery who is concerned about making tax digital. I declare an interest as a landlord who will be affected by making tax digital. That will not bother me, but there will be a huge cash-flow impact on small traders, because they will have to pay their tax quarterly. Does she agree that we need to look at how to mitigate that cash-flow impact, because it is lack of cash that makes people go out of business, not planning to make a profit?

I thank my hon. Friend for her incredibly well made point. People often say that the phrase “making tax digital” is making tax incredibly complicated and making it almost impossible to run a business. Thinking more broadly about the way our Government work, we often talk about digital exclusion in this place, but in my surgeries I am starting to see digital exhaustion. People of all ages, including older people, are struggling to access public services. The digital systems are just too complicated and require too many bits of ID, so people end up going around in circles with three different websites or apps not talking to each other. It is a huge problem for small business owners who are just trying to run their business. We Liberal Democrats have objected to the Government’s increases in alcohol duties, because we see that businesses on our high streets, particularly hospitality businesses, are suffering death by a thousand cuts, whether from the increase in business rates, the jobs taxes or anything else. Alcohol duty is just adding more pain, and ultimately it will put up the price of a pint, which many see as an indicator of how much money they have in their pocket. The UK should be the best place in the world for a start-up to scale and stay, but the new capital gains tax founders relief has been described variously by people as “bonkers”, “dreadful” and “a pointless lottery”. It is estimated that around 600 people at best will benefit, but it could undermine productivity and growth. That is not exactly the ringing endorsement that I believe the Government were after. Have the Government reviewed their plans since those concerns were pointed out? On business asset disposal, the Government’s measures do not close the loophole and could hit genuine entrepreneurs. There are many reasons why we support the Government on taxing the banks. We have long called for increased taxes on our banks, and to those who say that it will harm competitiveness, all I would say is that under the botched Brexit deal, our financial services have suffered. Those who want to increase the competitiveness of our financial services should be backing our call to join the single market.
Under the Liberal Democrats’ plans to join the single market, how much have they budgeted for the United Kingdom's contribution towards the European Union budget?

We believe there is a growth dividend of £29 billion by year 5, of which £2 billion will be paying for the membership, so there will be a £27 billion net growth dividend to the UK from joining the single market and the customs union, reducing red tape and making it cheaper for businesses to do business here in the UK. Finally, we can all agree that stronger economic growth remains the only durable route to improving living standards. A new partnership with the EU could secure the growth dividend that I have just described, but unfortunately the Budget before us is not a growth Budget. That is why in our amendment we have set out all the reasons we cannot support the Finance Bill this evening.

I will focus on a couple of key revenue-raising clauses in the Bill that demonstrate how the Chancellor made the right choices in his recent Budget. I will also highlight some welcome support for small producers in a rapidly growing industry. I start by discussing the temporary increase in the bank corporation tax surcharge. As others have noted, the measure temporarily increases the surcharge rate, setting it at 6% from 1 January 2027 for a period of 15 months, returning to 3% from 1 April 2028. Undoubtedly, the banks will not have been overjoyed at the measure, but the change was required to help fund the household support measures announced in the Budget. The £100 household energy payment that will be given to 20 million households in council tax bands A to D in England in January is much needed, and has certainly been welcomed by my constituents in Rochester and Strood. The Chancellor and his ministerial team have been doing a good job listening and responding to the concerns raised by the banks and other financial companies about what they consider to be disproportionate bureaucracy. The Government are targeting a 25% reduction in the administration cost of regulation by the end of this Parliament, and the Budget identifies up to £640 million a year of new gross administration savings. The Government are also establishing a better regulation executive to drive a more streamlined and proportionate regulatory system that will better support growth, innovation and investment. In my view, the banks are not doing too badly from this Government, and once again I would point out that the increase to the surcharge is temporary and for a clear purpose. The Government have struck the right balance in raising revenue to meet current fiscal challenges, while minimising impacts on the UK’s competitiveness and growth in the real economy. The other revenue-raising measure I would like to highlight is the increase in machine games duty from 20% to 25% for higher stakes machines. I understand that the measure has a carve-out for machines in pubs and seaside arcades, which will be protected as they are lower-stake machines. The revenue raised will help to fund the many support measures announced in the Budget for businesses that are key ingredients for our vibrant high streets—the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors. Many of my local high street businesses will benefit from the Chancellor’s decision to increase small business rate relief from £12,000 to £18,000, therefore taking many of them out of paying business rates all together.

This weekend I popped down to my local high street in Eccleshall and talked to some of the local businesses that will be lifted entirely out of paying business rates. Olive’s Italian restaurant is over the moon, as is Johny Todd based in Stafford. Does my hon. Friend agree that initiatives like this will make a fundamental difference to our high streets in supporting the smaller businesses that are at the heart of our towns?

Absolutely. A lot of hon. Members have had conversations with local business owners in recent years about business rates, and I agree with my hon. Friend that the Chancellor’s measures are extremely welcome. I look forward to speaking to lots of my local businesses about it.

The hon. Lady is speaking to her local businesses, as I am, particularly on the high street. They are screaming out about the impact that the jobs tax is having and their inability to recruit young people and retain staff. Does the hon. Lady acknowledge that that is a major factor affecting our high streets just now?

There have certainly been challenges in recent years in employing young people. We have just had the Milburn report, which has recommended some changes and which will be something for the Chancellor to consider as we move forward. Let me also talk about the decision to freeze business rates for other businesses in the retail, hospitality and leisure sectors in real terms for the next two years, which will provide really welcome breathing space. I understand that around 900 high street businesses in Medway, where my constituency is located, will benefit from that change. Once again, this is about making a clear choice about the kinds of businesses that we want to support on our high streets and in our town centres.

The hon. Lady is being most generous in giving way. She said earlier that seaside arcades enjoyed a carve-out. I am aware of no such carve-out for seaside arcades in Withernsea in my constituency or up the coast in Hornsea where they are so important to those towns. If their machines are not covered by this tax increase, that is a carve-out, but if they have machines that fit this measure, they will be taxed the same as any other location. That is true, is it not?

Maybe I was imprecise in my language. Lower-stakes gaming mechanisms are more likely to be in those kinds of locations and therefore far less likely to be impacted by the increase. Let me talk about alcohol duty relief. I really welcome the improvements to the small producer relief in the Bill, which will help a lot of small independent breweries to invest in their businesses, expand and compete against the global brewers that tend to dominate the sector. I welcome that as both a member of the Campaign for Real Ale for about 17 years and as an MP with a fantastic independent brewery, Moot Brew, in Halling in my constituency. Combined with the new right to a guest beer, I hope that the extra relief will supercharge its business as well as other small breweries.

It is great to hear the hon. Lady speaking up for breweries and beer, but does she agree it is somewhat anomalous that small vineyards, such as Hendred Vineyard in my constituency, will not benefit from small producer relief? The relief currently applies only to alcohol of a relatively low grade, even though many people drink wine just as sensibly as they drink beer. Does she feel that her Government should tackle that omission?

As somebody from Kent, I am a big supporter of the English wine industry. The Minister will have heard the hon. Gentleman’s contribution, and I hope that he will give it some consideration. I thank the Chancellor for fixing the quirk of the alcohol duty system that previously prevented a lot of smaller breweries from entering the market with lower-strength beers. We know that the appetite for lower-strength beers is growing, particularly among younger generations, so that is a really important step forward in supporting the growth and business model sustainability of small independent breweries. I note that that has rightly been welcomed by the Society of Independent Brewers and Associates. The Chancellor made the right choices at the Budget, many of which are in this Bill. He has managed to maintain fiscal discipline while providing much-needed support to households and high street businesses.

This Finance Bill illustrates that this Government have learned nothing over the last two years. Specifically, they have learned nothing about two fundamental and obvious principles of economics. One principle was referred to by the shadow Minister, my hon. Friend the Member for West Worcestershire (Dame Harriett Baldwin), in her opening remarks: if we tax something, we get less of it. The second principle is that if we misalign incentives, we should not be surprised if we end up with undesirable outcomes. This Government have learned neither of those lessons. Let me take the first principle.
