One would think that over the last two years, in which Labour has levied more than £60 billion of additional taxes on our economy, the Government would have learned that lesson. Some £25 billion of those additional taxes came by way of the jobs tax, the increase in national insurance and the reduction in the threshold at which the tax kicks in. That had a devastating effect on jobs. If we tax something, we get less of it. There are 100,000 fewer jobs in hospitality and leisure, and some 120,000 fewer jobs in retail alone, according to the British Retail Consortium. It is because the Government not only increased the headline rate but reduced the threshold at which the tax kicks in that it has had a disproportionate effect on lower earners, women, part-time workers and, critically, younger people, who are desperate to go out and get their first job. Is it any surprise that today we have approaching 1 million people not in education, employment or training in our country? In his recent review, Alan Milburn has pointed out that that figure stands at over 15% of young people. To his credit, in a review that, I have to say, I find rather mixed in its merits—none the less, there are some merits in it—he also accepts that those taxes on jobs are too high, and he calls on his own party to reduce them. Had the right decisions been taken on spending, there was an opportunity in this Budget to do just that, but that opportunity was comprehensively missed.

I am sure the right hon. Gentleman knows that there are now more young people not in education, employment or training than there are job vacancies in the whole UK. Even if every single job went to one of those young people, around 300,000 of them would still be without a job. Does he agree that if we want to grow the number of jobs in the UK, we need not to only cut the jobs tax, but to join the single market and the customs union to bring back the jobs that left the UK under the botched Brexit deal of his party?

It is perfectly conceivable to have a thriving economy, if an economy is properly managed—I will set out in a moment how that works. [ Interruption. ] Well, we are setting out as a party exactly how that works. We could have a thriving economy in which unemployment was not up at about a five-year high, as it is at the moment, and in which we did not have eye-watering levels of youth unemployment. I remind Government Members that under the last Labour Government, youth unemployment went up by about 44%, while under the last Conservative Government, it went down by about the same proportion. That is because we had a focus on job creation through getting the incentives right and getting taxes down, particularly on employment. It does not stop at jobs. This lesson about tax is present in many of the actions that this Government have taken. It is there in the farmers who will be clobbered by the farm tax. It is also there in schools; we have been reading just this weekend that the application of VAT on private education has meant that, according to the Independent Schools Council, about two thirds of private schools are reporting lower rolls than they had before. The Government forecast that 37,000 children would have their education disrupted and would move from the private sector to the state sector by 2030. That figure has already been met. That is an example of the aspirations of people up and down this country being sacrificed on the altar of socialist envy.

When we talk about the removal of the loophole that allowed private schools to escape paying VAT, we often hear people say that the number of kids in private schools has gone down this year, but is that not due to a falling birth rate as much as anything else?

The fact of the matter is that if you put up the cost of something by 20%, you should not be surprised by what happens. The hon. Gentleman cannot get away from that. Incidentally, there were other measures that discriminated against private schools, such as the removal of the reliefs that they previously had with respect to business rates and other costs. This Government estimated that 37,000 fewer pupils would be going to those schools—not because of demographic change, but because of the application of VAT. That grim milestone has been reached now, not in 2030, when the Government said that it would be reached. What do we find in the lessons that I have laid out for the Minister? What have the Government done? They have gone and put up taxes yet again. They have put up taxes on savers. We want to encourage people in our country to save for their retirement, yet they have put an extra 2 percentage points on savings. There have put an extra 2 percentage points on income earned through property. As my right hon. Friend the Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) pointed out, that leads to one simple conclusion: there will be fewer people acting as landlords, providing tenanted accommodation for people to take up. The implication of that is that there will be fewer and fewer opportunities for people to move around to where the work is, and they will have to face higher rents. We have heard about the banks, and the increase in the bank surcharge from 3% to 6%. PwC carried out an extensive piece of work for UK Finance looking into the relative levels of tax faced by banks around the world, and the reality is that we are becoming less competitive—certainly compared with the United States of America. As has been pointed out, in many cases the costs of that additional tax will ultimately be borne by the people and businesses borrowing from those banks. The OBR itself says that profits will flee our country as a consequence of the additional taxation. I think somebody mentioned Jamie Dimon of JP Morgan, who is reported as having said—in a private conversation, I believe—that he expects an “example” will be made as a consequence of increasing taxation. The clear implication is that in many instances, tax will not actually be raised as a result of this measure. JP Morgan is the kind of bank we should be encouraging. It is one of the world’s leading banks, and it has recently announced that it is going to invest £1 billion in building new office space in Spitalfields, yet we are putting up taxes on that bank and on others. The Conservative principles on taxation have to be these. First, taxes should be as low as possible, and as a consequence, they need to be as broadly based as possible. They need to be as simple as possible. They need to be fair, and certainly progressive—I absolutely accept that. If we meet those conditions, people do not try to avoid tax, because they accept that it is fair. We narrow the tax gap, and as a consequence, we raise more money. Turning to the alignment of incentives, the worst area of all is welfare incentives. The Centre for Social Justice has illustrated that a family with three children in which no one works, if they are receiving housing benefit, health benefits and personal independence payment, will receive about £46,000 in untaxed income. If a family who have children are working, with one full-time worker and one part-time worker on the national living wage, they are not taking home £46,000—they are taking home £28,000. A person would have to earn £71,000 before tax to equal the £46,000 that the family on benefits are receiving. That is simply not right, yet there is nothing in this Budget to get to the bottom of those disincentives, nor does the Milburn review say anything of any major substance about that. This Government have abolished the two-child cap at great expense, which once again is sending the wrong signals when it comes to incentives.

The right hon. Gentleman is making a customarily detailed speech. He references two people working on the national living wage—something that his party has said has gone up by too much—and he talks about the abolition of the two-child benefit cap, which in my constituency has raised hundreds of children out of poverty. If he is opposed to higher wages and opposed to Government support for poorer families to lift children out of poverty, how does he recommend it happens?

The best route out of poverty is employment. It is to get the incentives right so that we create more jobs. Rather than destroy jobs—as this Government have done, as has been set out in previous contributions—we create jobs, and then we create better jobs. That is the way to raise people out of poverty.

What would the right hon. Gentleman say to the woman I visited in my constituency who had left an abusive relationship, been in temporary accommodation, and finally got a one-bedroom flat that she and her three daughters lived in? She was working in a good job, but one of the children was regularly ill. She had to take so much time off work that she could no longer sustain her job, so temporarily—she hopes, because she really wants to go back to work—that extra money going into the household to support the third child has been a lifeline to ensure that her family do not drop through the floor. Is that not what lifting the two-child benefit cap was really about?

Of course, I cannot comment on the specifics of the case that the hon. Lady raises, but let me make an important general point. There are many, many people up and down this country who work extraordinarily hard and make huge sacrifices in order to afford to have a larger family. It seems entirely wrong to say to them, “If you go out and work and do the right thing, you will get no benefits—you will just have to struggle”, whereas for others it is a case of “It doesn’t matter what size family you choose to have, the state will pay for it.” I think that is fundamentally wrong, and I think most people in this country feel exactly that way. When it comes to businesses and the wealth creators, along with the increases in national insurance contributions, the national minimum wage and so on, we have ended up in a position where people are trying to get out of our country to go to places that have better opportunities —places that have lower taxes, do not confiscate profits and do not think that “wealth creation”, “job creation” and “making money” are dirty words. Those places welcome these people with open arms. Very high net worth and very successful people are going to jurisdictions such as Italy and, more recently, Greece rather than to our jurisdiction, because we have got our incentives fundamentally wrong. What is there in this Finance Bill in that regard? It reduces business asset disposal relief and requires self-employed people to start divvying up their tax earlier than they previously did, which presumably means that during some transition period, they will be finding on average twice the amount of money to send to the taxman than they did before. When the Chancellor delivered his Budget, and in his commentary around it, he made a great virtue of the fact that this was a steady as she goes, not rocking the boat, cautious Budget. He had to do that because businesses were petrified that they were going to face the kinds of decisions they had already faced under the previous Chancellor, the right hon. Member for Leeds West and Pudsey (Rachel Reeves), and her two ruinous Budgets.

On Friday night, I spent a wonderful evening celebrating an institution in my constituency called House of Bread, which supports people who are homeless and going through really troubling times. Most of the people who were there that night, including local Conservatives, spent the evening thanking me for having a Government and a Chancellor who were prepared to invest £432 million for homeless people in the Budget. Does the right hon. Member agree that through priorities like these, this Government are making sure that those who need support get it?

The hon. Lady rases an important point—homelessness is a critical and deep scar on our society, and I accept that. However, my point is on something deeper than that. If we are to address those wrongs, if we are to defend our country appropriately, if we are to deal with an ageing population who need ever more support, including healthcare, social care and so on, and if we are going to deal with intergenerational unfairness, with younger people not getting a fair crack of the whip and so on, then we need a growing economy. My point is this: if we misalign the incentives and set taxes too high, we will not achieve that, and that is of no value to the people the hon. Lady was helping the other evening. In not doing very much, the Chancellor took a conscious decision. He chose to kick the can down the road, as the shadow Minister, my hon. Friend the Member for West Worcestershire, said. He chose to duck the big issues. He chose to exemplify a Government who have no backbone to take the tough decisions we need as we lean into the requirement for greater defence. Of course, we have forecasts that are underpinned by unrealistic assumptions about what is going to happen to the public spending envelope nearer to the end of the forecast period. We all know that is pie in the sky—the Minister knows it is a fantasy. That will have to be faced up to at some point. The wrong decisions were taken in this Budget in that regard. The final thing I want to talk about is headroom. The Chancellor would have us believe that it was prudent to have cut headroom from £23 billion to £15 billion, because that is what you do when times are tight. Well, no, you do not actually—when times are difficult, you increase the headroom. If he had come forward with the average headroom as a proportion of GDP since the OBR came into existence, it would have been up at more than £40 billion.

Not just yet. We live in a world of external shocks. We saw it with the financial crisis in 2008, with covid and with the Ukraine-Russia war. We are seeing it now in the middle east. It will not be long before there is another crisis. The situation that we have at the moment, where we have slim headroom—slim because the tough decisions around spending, particularly on welfare, were not taken—will leave us brittle going forward. This Budget is a missed opportunity. It is also an abrogation of responsibility.

Budgets are rarely glamorous, but they are the nitty gritty—the important nuts and bolts that define this Government’s agenda and allow them to make the improvements we are making. We have the jobs guarantee, £2,000 for businesses to take on young apprentices and £100 million on local apprenticeship services. We have money off energy bills, capped bus fares and much more. That is why I am glad to stand here and support the Bill. The Bill is a substantial piece of legislation, but Members will be relieved to hear that I will refer to only some aspects of it. First, I welcome the changes to air passenger duty for private jets, ensuring that their use results in a greater contribution to the public finances. Many of my constituents will regard it as simple common sense that those choosing some of the most carbon-intensive forms of travel should make a greater contribution than ordinary families travelling on commercial flights. When households are continuing to feel pressure on their finances, that is a reasonable and proportionate approach. The Bill also recognises that the tax system must evolve as we move towards cleaner forms of transport. As more drivers switch to electric vehicles, revenues from petrol and diesel will inevitably decline, as Members have mentioned. The challenge for the Government is to maintain funding for our transport infrastructure while continuing to encourage the transition to cleaner vehicles. It was therefore good to see cuts in the Budget to the price at lower-powered public chargers. That should save the average user about £150 a year, and it is £100 million of welcome funding over two years. However, the transition must be fair. In Warwickshire, constituents in Rugby, Bulkington and the surrounding villages have raised concerns with me about the cost of charging for those without off-street parking. I have written to the relevant Minister about ensuring that residents who rely on public charging infrastructure mechanisms are not unfairly disadvantaged. There is real potential for innovative solutions, including, as one of my constituents mentioned, municipally-owned community charging networks that would reduce costs while expanding access, because we need to ensure that EVs are available to all our constituents. I also welcome the time-limited provisions relating to the banking surcharge. Banks play a vital role in our economy and in supporting businesses and households, but it is entirely reasonable to expect institutions that benefit from the stability of our financial system to make the appropriate contribution to the public finances in return, to help ease pressures on working people and families. The choice before us is clear: we can ask those with the greatest capacity to contribute a little more, or we can place a greater burden on working families and small businesses. Most people in my constituency of Rugby, Bulkington and the surrounding villages would consider that choice to be straightforward. I welcome measures that modernise our tax system and tackle avoidance, particularly in the digital economy. The Budget will ensure that VAT collection is shifted to online marketplaces, and we have provisions on crypto assets and electronic invoicing. Those all recognise a simple reality: our economy is changing and our tax system must keep pace. This Government have increased enforcement and compliance powers, and they are funding HMRC appropriately to make sure that that can happen. Businesses on Rugby’s high streets should not be undercut by competitors gaining an unfair advantage through weak tax compliance. Honest businesses that play by the rules deserve a level playing field, and I struggle to understand why any Member would oppose measures designed to reduce fraud, tackle tax avoidance and create a level playing field for honest businesses. What message does it send when the Opposition vote against this legislation, as they will this evening? On the Government Benches, we believe that th
We now come to a maiden speech. I call Adnan Hussain, the hon. Member for Blackburn.

It is a privilege to rise in this House to represent Blackburn, the town that I am truly proud to serve. To speak for its people in this Chamber is an honour that I do not take lightly. Every constituency has its own character, history and aspirations, and I believe that a Member’s first responsibility is to understand the people who have placed their trust in them. Contrary to the demands of tradition, I have allowed myself the time to really absorb the mood, needs and wants of my constituents. I wanted to listen, to understand the challenges facing our communities, and to consider carefully the contribution that I could make on their behalf. However, with the threat of a snap election ever looming over our heads—although we are constantly reassured there is not one on the horizon—I thought that it was high time I delivered this speech. Let me begin by acknowledging those who have represented Blackburn before me. The constituency has a distinguished parliamentary history, having been represented by figures who have left their mark not only on this town but on the wider political life of our country. That is a legacy to respect, but also a responsibility to carry forward. The responsibility of representing Blackburn does not begin or end with any one individual; it is part of a continuing relationship between this House and the people whom we serve, and I approach that responsibility with humility, determination, and a clear sense of the work that remains to be done. Blackburn was built on industry, it is sustained by enterprise, and its strength has always been its people. Our mills in Blackburn helped to power Britain’s industrial revolution. Generations worked hard, raised families, and built the communities that we know today. That spirit is still with us. We see it in our factories and family businesses, in our shops and community groups, and in the people who give their time to help others. We have much to be proud of. Our task is to turn that pride into opportunity. When we speak about growth, we should ask what it means for the people we serve. Can a young person find a good job without having to leave the town they call home? Can a small business take on another worker? Can a family pay their bills and still have something left at the end of the month? Those are the tests that matter. For Blackburn, growth must reach the streets and communities that have waited far too long to feel its benefits. Our industrial past gives us a place to start. Each year, the Festival of Making brings Blackburn together. It brings old skills and new ideas together. It celebrates what we have made, and shows us what we could make next. We should bring that same ambition to our economy. In addition to our world-class services economy, Britain needs to acknowledge that we must make more. We need more industry in order to keep up with the rapidly changing face of world economies. Modern manufacturing, engineering and new technologies can bring skilled jobs, better wages and greater strength to our economy. Blackburn should be part of that future. We should bring our empty mills and industrial sites back into use. We should help our colleges work with local employers so that young people gain the skills they need, and we should help our manufacturers find the space, funding and connections to grow. Our young people should have the chance to build the industries of tomorrow in Blackburn. Our small businesses matter just as much. Behind every shop, every family firm and every new business is someone who took a chance—someone who worked long hours, who put their life savings on the line and who believed they could build something of their own. When they succeed, they create opportunities for others. We should make it easier for them to start, to grow and to take on other people, and we should do more to keep the pound local. When we shop locally, when businesses buy from local suppliers and when public bodies use local firms, more of that money

I welcome the hon. Member for Blackburn (Mr Hussain) to the House. As he mentioned, he has illustrious predecessors: Barbara Castle, Jack Straw and, more recently, Kate Hollern. I noted that he advocated very strongly for his community, and for more growth in his town, and I appreciate that. It is a privilege to speak tonight on the Finance Bill. I want to focus on four areas: the effects of the Bill on residents; its effects on high streets; entrepreneurs; and issues related to planning, and setting the right framework to encourage growth. The Budget offered breathing space and hope for the future in what we cannot doubt is a challenging international climate. First, residents in Reading are hard pressed by the cost of living crisis. Many of my residents live in older homes on terraced streets across the town, or in 1930s semis, and the cost of heating those homes is considerable, so I wholeheartedly welcome the Government’s measures on energy—particularly the £100 of support—and the measures to tackle standing charges. I also welcome the measures to deal with the cost of travel, which are so important in getting people to work. The recent freeze in fuel duty, the freeze in rail fares and the reduction in bus fares will all provide residents with very real help in getting to work, and will help employers with the recruitment and retention of staff. I should also mention the very positive support for EV charging, which is important at this time. I would like to respond briefly to points made by the Lib Dem spokesperson, the hon. Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper). I think she was somewhat over-optimistic about the idea of putting together two complex Government datasets to deliver help in a more targeted way. It is essential to have a simple system for delivering help. It is very easy to imagine a perfect solution to a difficult problem, but in my experience as a civil servant in a number of Departments some years ago, it is extremely difficult to manage Government data. Many of the databases are on legacy systems, and some of them, sadly, are not able to talk to each other. That has been a problem for successive Governments.

In a moment. I also noted the comments made by the right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) on this matter. I gently refer the hon. Member for St Albans back to the essential need to deliver real help immediately. The second point we really should be clear about is the help for high streets in the Finance Bill. Reading and many towns of a similar size—the hon. Member for Blackburn hinted that this was the case in his Lancashire constituency—have vibrant town centres, but small independent businesses are often under real pressure. Reading town centre has an above-average number of independent businesses, but they face many pressures. One of the biggest is the cost of business rates, so I welcome the fact that 70,000 high-street businesses will no longer have to pay business rates. There are a whole host of other measures, but that central point is hugely important. It will help many family-run and other small businesses in Reading, the major shopping town for central southern England, and in many other parts of the country, so I welcome that.

I will in a moment, but I would just like to finish the point about high streets. It is essential to celebrate them, and to recognise that the Government have, once again, given sensible, targeted support to businesses.

I am very grateful to the hon. Gentleman for giving way. He spoke about the reference by my hon. Friend the Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper) to the Liberal Democrats’ proposals for a more targeted scheme to help households with the cost of energy. The hon. Gentleman spoke about being a civil servant, as I was. Does he think it is regrettable that the various agencies of the state have not used the last four to five years since Liz Truss’s effort to provide energy support to think about how they might integrate those databases more effectively, in order to provide more targeted support? Would he suggest, perhaps, that they work a bit harder in future?

The hon. Gentleman makes some interesting, but I think slightly unsubstantiated, points. The challenge is to deliver help now, quickly, through an existing IT system. The problem that we have, as do many large organisations—we saw this recently in issues around the world relating to Microsoft and others—is the difficulty of trying to rely on making quick changes to complex IT systems. That is an unwise approach. That would be a kind way of describing what his party is proposing; it is unwise and untested. It is much better to go with a system that we know works, and is deliverable in the near future. I am very pleased with the Government’s work to support entrepreneurs, and in particular with the founders’ relief support, which in my constituency will offer many growing small businesses and founders a powerful incentive to grow further and take more risks to generate more jobs. In Berkshire—the hon. Gentleman represents a seat in Oxfordshire—there are 300,000 jobs in tech and telecoms in a county with a population of 800,000 people. Those firms are growing rapidly and offer real growth to the UK economy. It is important to reward those setting up those firms and offer them an incentive and drive growth, so I wholeheartedly welcome that measure. It is one of a raft of measures to support small businesses, and that should be noted and supported across the House. The final area that it is important to highlight is planning reform. We heard earlier about some of the benefits and the huge importance of planning reform in driving economic growth, and I would hope that there is a growing consensus on this matter. I would like to describe some of the problems in my town centre. As I said, our part of southern England is lucky to be an area of relatively high growth and enormous potential, but there are significant obstacles thrown up by the planning system, none of which I think any Member would particularly want to support. Let me describe the situation that faces me every day, when I walk or drive to Reading station. There is £1 billion of investment in the Station Hill area on one side of the station, but there are a series of empty sites on the other. That is down to the complexity in the planning system. The Chancellor and other Ministers should be commended for their work to simplify the system.

It is interesting that my hon. Friend raises a situation in which one side of a town—in my case, Stafford—has masses of investment. In Stafford, that is the side with the town centre; but on the other side of the tracks, planning restrictions mean that we do not get investment and growth. Does he agree that it is imperative that the Chancellor looks at the situation in places like Reading, and perhaps even Stafford, to see whether there could be further investment on both sides of the train tracks, to help growth in our towns?

My hon. Friend makes a good point. The potential solution to this issue is using some of the devolution measures that the Government have highlighted. Through mayoral development corporations, there will be more scope to simplify planning, and to bring sites together, which will make them more attractive to developers. I hope that more parts of the country will benefit from that. There were other measures in the Budget, and it is interesting to note the strategic work around planning, as well as other simplification measures. Those four areas of the Bill particularly interest me, and they are hugely important for my constituents and local businesses. I also welcome the wider thrust of what the Chancellor and Ministers from the Treasury have been saying about the importance of fiscal discipline, and the measures offering breathing space now, and hope for the future. We have seen that the fundamentals of the UK economy remain strong; we have recently had some interesting data about the UK having the second-highest rate of growth in the G7. The Government’s measures to deal with national debt have been commended by the International Monetary Fund, so I think we are heading in the right direction. This is a sensible Budget and a sensible way forward. The Budget offers four key measures for my town, and many other parts of the country, that I would commend.

In his Budget speech, the Chancellor said that the Government had two guiding approaches. First, on immediate action, the Government sought to provide breathing space for families and businesses. Secondly, when it came to the big structural changes, the Chancellor wanted to unlock good growth in every postcode. He said that the Government would deliver more devolution and local leadership, and “back British businesses”. Those phrases were repeated by the Exchequer Secretary to the Treasury when introducing this debate. What would help families and businesses in every postcode would be this Government delivering real and sustained growth. I want to test the Government’s claims and the measures in the Bill against the experiences of businesses and residents in Bicester and Woodstock, who want to see good growth. Businesses need the confidence to employ and invest; infrastructure must be ready to support new development; and councils need the resources to deliver the services on which growth depends. Those practical tests must guide a Government who promise good growth in every postcode. First, I will address infrastructure and cumulative development. In his Budget speech, the Chancellor offered “cheaper, faster grid connections”, yet that is not what new businesses and home seekers have experienced in my constituency, where the default connection date is 2037. In Bicester and Woodstock, new housing, businesses and major projects are competing for capacity on the same electricity network and roads, and from the same public services. In North West Bicester, grid constraints have delayed thousands of homes well into the 2030s, leading to a deficit in the housing land supply. Homes, investment and the economic activity that they would have supported are postponed. The Government tend to assess major proposals in isolation, each of them competing for Treasury funding and tax breaks. That approach fails to adequately account for the fact that several developments will depend on the same infrastructure at the same time. Ministers should fund infrastructure ahead of demand and ensure that decisions account for the combined impact of development. In the context of cumulative development, the Government’s plans for data centres are key. In his Budget speech, the Chancellor promised that there would be “strict tests that data centres must meet”. —[ Official Report , 28 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 308.] However, we need details about those tests. There are two huge centres proposed in my constituency—one for 100 MW in Kidlington, and one for 435 MW in Bicester. That is sufficient to power 1.4 million homes. Data centre investment needs a coherent national plan that considers what facilities are for, where they should go, and whether sufficient electricity is available. Residents and businesses need to know whether prioritising a data centre’s connection will delay their own connections or affect their electricity bills. One development in my area was consented as a warehouse; then it quietly changed to a data centre under the same planning code, without adequate opportunity for residents and the local council to scrutinise that change, although there were clear impacts on already strained grid capacity. Ministers should commission an independent assessment of projected AI electricity demand against available grid capacity. They have not committed to publishing the impact assessments that I requested for my constituency. Those assessments should be published before priority area is granted. Communities also need to know what benefits they will receive, how commitments under the covenant that the Chancellor spoke about will be enforced, and what happens if they are not met. We need only look across the pond to see what happens to Governments when they do not listen to residents’ concerns about data centres.

The hon. Gentleman makes an important point about data centres ending up in warehouses. Can he tell the House whether that was done through the loophole of permitted development, which avoids any local scrutiny of planning applications?

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his question. I do not wish to delay the House too much on detailed matters, but I believe it was classified as use class B8, which relates to warehouses; because there is some confusion as to how a data centre should be classified, it is treated as a warehouse for data, and there is therefore no need to apply for a change of use. Residents in my constituency did not become aware of the fact that this large warehouse, which had been consented in 2023, would be converted to house a data centre, with the consequent impact on electricity demand, until a small landscaping condition was applied for. Through that measure, local residents became aware that the purpose and use of the land was to be radically changed. The Budget includes an allocation of £150 million towards the cost of large asylum centres. One is proposed in my constituency at MOD Bicester, as hon. Members may have heard me speak about. The cost is likely to exceed £270 million, however, simply to set up a centre on that one site that has never had accommodation and has no potable or sewage water or electricity connections. The Government’s approach to MOD Bicester raises basic questions about the stewardship of public money. Ministers justify large asylum accommodation sites by claiming savings against hotels, but Parliament needs to and should see the full development, operating and local service costs to assess that claim. Any comparison must include the costs of remediation, utilities, transport, security and displaced defence activity alongside clear assumptions about occupancy and the operating period. Ministers should publish a transparent comparison with alternatives before making further financial commitments. The Chancellor made devolution deals a centrepiece of his Budget, yet they were built on the wreckage of the botched approach to local government reform. Oxfordshire, Cherwell and West Oxfordshire councils are expected to accommodate growth while maintaining services for existing and new residents after the latest round of local government reorganisation hokey cokey. Reorganisation and an extended transition bring additional costs and uncertainty to councils in my constituency; Oxfordshire county council, for instance, will have its budget slashed by £24 million next year by this Government, while Cherwell and West Oxfordshire also face cuts. Yet councils still have to plan, retain staff and deliver services through the now extended period of transition. Funding must be predictable and reflect growth, existing service pressures and transition costs. The Government’s preferred option of three unitary councils in Oxfordshire will also condemn the proposed North Oxfordshire council to financial insecurity. It fails to meet the financial sustainability criterion set out by the initial local government reform proposal. Establishing this unitary proposal for Oxfordshire will also swallow areas in my patch, such as Kidlington, into greater Oxford, with their residents facing the double cost of the higher existing council tax under Labour-run Oxford city council and their current parish council precepts. Ministers should therefore explain how their settlement will give councils the capacity to deliver the growth the Government expect of them. The Government have invested in East West Rail. My constituents want to see real benefits from the new train line, yet completed infrastructure delivers its full economic benefit only when people can use it. It is a farce that two years and two months after successful trial runs of trains between Bicester and Bletchley, passenger services still have not begun. Railway infrastructure has sat dormant for two years while commuters and employers wait for passenger services. Each delay postpones benefits for Bicester and the wider growth corridor, including access to jobs and opportunities for businesses. Ministers should work urgently with the RMT to accept sensible, safe operating arrange

Many times over the last two and a half years I have spoken about the old Stanton ironworks that existed for over a century and a half in my constituency. It built ordnance during the second world war, and, Madam Deputy Speaker, if you look down on almost any road that is older than I am, you will see an iron grate that was made at Stanton—you can tell because they all say “Stanton” on them. Have a look next time you are outside. I have raised Stanton repeatedly for several reasons. The ironworks was vital to Ilkeston, the largest of the two towns in my constituency. It was the heart of the town’s economy. It was integral to the development of the strong community, which has significantly outlasted the ironworks itself. Quite simply, the town would not be what it is today without the ironworks. As New Stanton Park—the brand-new business venture on the old ironworks site—grows, the former ironworks remains as vital in its contribution to Ilkeston’s economic future as it was to its economic past. I think, too, that the Stanton Ironworks represents the narrative that the Labour party was birthed to tell. Over a century ago, the Labour party was founded by workers—at the factory, in the shipyard, down the mines —to defend, fight for and give voice to their communities. Our party was formed as a means to represent manual labour, but with time we have evolved, as has the nature of work. I fear we too often remain romantically focused on some guy swinging a hammer in Stanton ironworks instead of focusing on what work looks like in 2026 for many British workers. With that in mind, I would like to speak about what this Bill, and the Budget more broadly, will do for Britain’s modern workers—the workers on whom our society depends and who I do not think we talk about nearly often enough. I want to talk particularly about the impact that the Budget and this Bill have on service workers, who represent between a quarter and a third of all workers in Britain today, depending on who you ask. Service jobs are often transient, precarious and very poorly paid. It is the least that we can do for these workers, whose substantial role in our economy is so under-discussed, to make sure that their pay keeps up with the rate of inflation. We have done that in this Budget by yet again raising the minimum wage. Meanwhile, the Conservatives and Reform, whose Members are once again not here, I note, call for our lowest-paid workers to be made poorer. I think that is a disgrace. Turning to carers, whether it is paid or unpaid, care is very hard work. It is demanding, emotionally exhausting and, often, invisible. We should be very grateful to all those who provide care, whether they do it professionally or because they must. Carers are performing an invaluable service, filling the gaps left by a social care system that has been neglected for far too long. That is why it is so important that this Budget has abolished the carer’s allowance cliff edge. The old rules punished those who sought to balance paid employment with caring responsibilities, threatening to take away their carer’s allowance altogether if they earned a penny over the limit. Ending that cliff edge is an enormous step towards giving carers the recognition, respect and support that they deserve. Another group I want to highlight is the self-employed, who make up a comparable portion of the working population to public sector workers. They are the builders, the electricians and the plumbers—ultimately, the tradespeople we rely on in modern life to service our homes. They are doing long, often unsociable hours, often across six or seven-day weeks, with poor workplace protections compared with their conventionally employed counterparts. The historical lack of protection is why finally giving self-employed fathers and their partners paid parental leave is such a significant breakthrough. That leave allows—

I am sorry to interrupt my hon. Friend, who is making a wonderful speech, in full flow, but the group of workers he just referenced are exactly those whom the Conservative party in government excluded from any covid support whatsoever. That excluded group of people still had to go out to work because they were not entitled to help and support. Does he share my frustration that the Conservatives talk the talk, but when it came to an opportunity to help they were nowhere?

I thank my hon. Friend for making an excellent point. I agree with him completely. It was shameful at that time, long before I was elected to the House. It was difficult to talk to some of my closest friends, who are in the trades, about how much they were suffering through covid and how difficult they found it. The leave that we have brought in allows dads to take time away from work without hurting their livelihoods, so they can spend precious time with their new families. It is only right that we close the gap in the social contract between conventional and self-employed workers in our society. The measures that I have outlined do right by my hard-working constituents and their families in Erewash. Ultimately, it is about giving them the respect they deserve. That is respect for those who care for their loved ones without complaint or acknowledgment; respect for those who leave home before dawn to get the job done and come home late at night exhausted; and respect for those who just want to spend time building their own home as well as ours. People who contribute so much to our economy, our society and our country deserve recognition for their hard work, and they deserve a proper reward. The Budget, and the Bill, have those workers at their heart. For that reason, I am proud to support the Bill to allow us to deliver on our promises.

The debate has been really interesting so far. One of the stand-out aspects of this Finance Bill is that it has clearly missed some fundamental opportunities to look at economic growth, future investment changes and real propositions for our country and our economy as well as for Britain’s standing in the world. It is pretty clear that the British economy was going in the wrong direction, but having changed Prime Minister and Chancellor of the Exchequer, the new Prime Minister and the new Chancellor’s Budget, rather than changing course, continues to do one thing only, which is to put Britain on the regressive pathway of higher taxes, more borrowing, more debt, increasing the burden of restrictions and regulations on businesses, and ultimately restricting the economic freedoms of British households and British businesses. Instead of doing the right thing, the Labour Government continue on this regressive, backward-facing treadmill. It is not helping our country one bit.

The right hon. Lady spoke about the economic freedoms of British households. Does she think that having a properly functioning NHS that treats citizens when they need treatment free of charge helps them to get back to work and to contribute to the economy, thereby enhancing their economic freedoms?

The NHS has been there serving the country for decades, doing the right thing by those who need it; frankly, all of us use the NHS. The point I want to make is that the hon. Gentleman’s Government, by increasing taxes by £75 billion over the last two years, are sucking the economic oxygen out of our economy and our country. There was an opportunity for the Labour party in government to put Britain on an alternative path by reducing taxes to help working households—that term that Labour Members so often love to use and abuse—keep more of the money they earn and have more money in their pockets, and freeing businesses to recruit and employ more people, give people better pay and, importantly, unleash a new wave of investment, economic growth and job creation. As I have said repeatedly in this House, I personally think that it is the duty and responsibility of every single Government not only to back business but to back the British people to earn more and to keep more of the money that they earn. Language is everything in this place, and what I find so astonishing is that what Labour has served our country is not more breathing space—to use that overused term—but more taxes. Instead of using the Budget to make choices to support investment in defence, the Government have constantly taken away money from the fundamental areas where the state needs to invest more to grow our security, and to grow investment in R&D and other aspects of defence that would serve our country well and make Britain strong when it comes to our standing in the world. Another example is innovation and infrastructure. We have just heard the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller) speak about an important rail infrastructure project, and the farcical situation—with no explanation from the Government—of a train station not being used and commuters having to go elsewhere. That is absolutely unacceptable for a project that has rightly had years of investment. It is no different in Essex, and in the Witham constituency. Funding for the A12 widening scheme was put in place—and guess what happened? The Labour Government chose to withdraw that funding and put the money elsewhere. I have also just had confirmation from the Department for Transport that the A120 dualling scheme—which would support economic development, more housing to meet Labour’s targets, new job creation in Essex, and everything to give the construction sector the ultimate boost that it needs—is now being parked firmly in a lay-by somewhere and will not see the light of day. It is businesses that feel the consequences of these decisions, not just through the tax burden that keeps on rising and the squeeze on consumer spending, but through people not being given the jobs they need through the opportunities created from these major infrastructure development schemes. This Finance Bill could have been used to reverse the extension of the freeze on income tax bands. No Labour Member who wants to speak about working households should forget the implications of fiscal drag and its real impact on working households.
The right hon. Lady is absolutely right to mention fiscal drag. Can she explain why she voted for it to be an incredibly long part of every Conservative Budget that she supported in this House?

The hon. Gentleman can correct me if I am wrong on this, but I do not think he was in the last Parliament, when I consistently spoke about this issue. I have spoken up for the changes that are needed to ensure that fiscal drag does not happen and that we see changes to income tax band thresholds. The hon. Gentleman and all Members must recognise that inflation going up puts pressure on wage growth, and it is possible that even more people will be dragged into paying higher levels of income tax. This has an impact on—guess what?—consumer demand and the pound in people’s pockets. About one in four earners will be paying the higher 40% tax rate by 2031. This Bill could have been used to reverse Labour’s jobs tax, but instead all it does is cement and gold-plate it. We know that these measures, especially the lowering of thresholds for employer contributions to £5,000, added over £600 to employment costs per employee, damaging the ability to sustain and create jobs. This Bill does nothing to ease the pressures that businesses face, and with the roll-out of the Employment Rights Act 2025, they face new burdens in the months and years ahead. We have already heard my right hon. Friend the Member for Central Devon (Sir Mel Stride) speak about this in relation to the Milburn review, which came out last week, and we have already debated this subject in the House. The impact of this regressive step on businesses and their ability to employ people is really disturbing. Is it any wonder that the OBR has said that, as a result of the measures Labour has introduced since coming to power, there are greater pressures on interest rates, inflation, unemployment and household disposable incomes than previously forecast? Well, there you go—it is not rocket science. Labour is not giving households breathing space; it has taxed the oxygen out of the economy. Many measures in the Bill should be questioned—I am being polite in using that term—and there are a few areas on which I would like the Minister’s response. First, the Government have said that the bank corporation tax surcharge, in clause 7, will support their efforts to provide temporary breathing space. Taxing banks has always been seen as a popular measure—it is, if I may say so, a lazy measure—but I have to tell Ministers that taxing banks, like taxing oil and gas companies, can have unintended consequences. Again, that is not rocket science. At a time when interest rates are creeping up, mortgages are difficult for first-time buyers to secure, and borrowing, as we have heard, is getting costlier, what Labour thinks is a harmless measure to business will have significant consequences for the economy. Will the Minister confirm what impact the increase in the surcharge on banks’ profits will have? Will the increase be temporary, running to the end of March 2028, or will Ministers be coming back next year to extend it—to do that good old Labour thing of asking for more? Labour’s obsession with using headline-grabbing tax increases to demonstrate that it is punishing those it perceives to be rich and wealthy has led to the imposition of the high-value council tax surcharge—Labour’s so-called mansion tax—through clauses 97 to 115, which is part 3 of the Bill. This new tax will not get the housing market moving and may not raise the levels of income intended. Ministers have already downgraded the original forecast, with proposals for deferral, discounts and exemptions—I am sure that the list of exemptions will grow and grow. The tax will create complex administrative issues for the councils forced to administer it. It will be left to local councils to issue the bills and pursue debts, despite the fact that the revenues raised will not go to the councils to invest in local services, but into the consolidated fund for the Government to spend. Councils, which will be issuing the bills and having to deal with the consequences, will not see a penny back, other than some funds for administrative costs.

It is a pleasure to follow so many excellent contributions, including by my colleagues on the Treasury Committee and others. I am pleased to welcome the Bill because it brings into effect crucial measures that give families and businesses the bit of breathing space they need at an extremely difficult moment for the global economy. It also provides fresh investment in our economy to ensure that it can continue to grow. Whatever narratives the Opposition have sought to set out about socialist doom loops or oxygen being sucked out of the economy, the fact is that our economy continues to grow well compared with others in the G7, and the IMF has recently taken the opportunity to compliment the UK on its fiscal consolidation—that is, on our management of the public finances. There is more to do in both those areas, but I believe that this demonstrates we are on the right track. I join my hon. Friend the Member for Stafford (Leigh Ingham) in welcoming the Budget’s confirmation of the support going to local authorities to meet the Prime Minister’s crucial agenda to offer all those sleeping rough on our streets a route into accommodation. This funding of £200,000 for the current year, with further sums to follow in subsequent financial years, will allow Dartford to work with community groups such as Porchlight and finally see homelessness numbers begin to head down after significant growth in recent years. There is a shocking statistic that between 2010 and 2025 the number of those rough sleeping in this country rose by 171%. That is, and should be, completely unacceptable to all of us in the House. Another underappreciated and important measure in this Budget is the significant reform and strengthening of the soft drinks industry levy. That has been one of the most successful public health interventions in recent years and I commend the Conservative party on introducing it. I have the privilege of being the co-chair, along with the hon. Member for Chelmsford (Marie Goldman), of the all-party group on dietary health. We strongly support the Government in their implementation of the policies set out in the NHS 10-year plan to tackle obesity. Strengthening the levy was one of the key measures in the 10-year plan so I welcome its inclusion in the legislation. The changes will see reduced sugar content for drinks in the scope of the levy from 5 grams to 4.5 grams, as well as the removal of the exemption covering products like bottled milkshakes and prepackaged chilled coffees which are bought in shops. They are both drinks that have tended to be extremely high in sugar, which the public often know very little about; change has been needed for some time. This is likely to lead to the reformulation of the drinks rather than substantially increased revenue for the Treasury, but in this case we would, I think, all welcome the steps. I applaud the Government’s measures through the Budget to support our high streets and help retail, hospitality and leisure businesses. All Members across the House will welcome 70,000 more high-street businesses being entirely exempted from paying business rates. Since the Budget, I have had the opportunity to go out speaking to businesses in my constituency and this news has been warmly welcomed by, among others, Thaiger Thai Shack, Ali’s Cafe and Albion’s Bakery in the centre of Dartford, some of my and Dartford residents’ favourite spots to eat; long may they continue to thrive as a result of the help the Government are giving them. As has been said, this is in part funded by the measures in the Bill to increase the rate of machine games duty for higher risk machines, a step many of us who are concerned about gambling harms have advocated taking for some time. I am pleased to see that in the Bill, while protecting pubs and seaside resort areas which use and profit from lower- stakes gambling arrangements, which should continue. I share the concern expressed by many Members this evening about the potential impa

The essential energy guarantee that we have called for has been called for by various different think-tanks. The data exists already—the Government have the data. If they wanted to, they could use a first tranche from the DWP data, which is already shared with energy companies, to apply a lower cost for essential energy. That is exactly the same mechanism that is used already. If the Government chose to do so, they could use a second tranche from HMRC data, but that second tranche should not deter the Government from using the first tranche of data that they already use—it is just as simple and it is more progressive.

I thank the hon. Member for her explanation, but I still do not think she has completely convinced us that this is something that we could do quickly. She said earlier that she understood that the necessary databases had been merged. Understanding that that may be the case is not quite the same as a mechanism for getting money into people’s bank accounts quickly. We should be honest and open with people that energy bills are obviously going to rise substantially, and that the Government cannot totally compensate all households for the increases that are coming. As has been pointed out by other hon. Members, Cornwall Insight’s forecast suggests that the cap will rise by 26% in January. I hope Ministers will keep looking at how we protect the most vulnerable, particularly those in lower-income, high-energy use households who will struggle to cut their energy consumption this winter. Finally, I have two quick comments. I want to record my disappointment that the Government have been unable to help those who are repaying student loans with any extra support in this Budget. One thing they could have done, which I advocated for strongly alongside my Select Committee colleagues, was to unfreeze the repayment threshold for students. That would have been the best way to get help to as many students as possible, across all income bands, as quickly as possible. I hope that will be something that the Government return to in future Budgets, as it is important that we help people who are starting in their careers who are struggling with those repayments. I recognise the impact of a change made at last year’s Budget. Last week, we had the hugely welcome news that 300,000 children across Britain, including hundreds of children in Dartford, are benefiting from no longer living in poverty following the scrapping of the two-child cap. I commend the Government for proposing to make that change and sticking to their guns so that we lift young people—who should not be growing up in households with no money—out of poverty. All in all, I commend the Bill to the House and I will be fully supporting it.

It has been an interesting debate so far. Like the Finance Bill, the debate has been massively varied because there are so many different measures on so many different topics, as the Budget touched on so many different things. I congratulate the hon. Member for Blackburn (Mr Hussain) on his excellent maiden speech. It showed how much he cares about the people of his constituency and how much he wants them to have opportunity in the future. For me, whether or not people have opportunity is one of the measures of privilege, but that should not be the case—everybody should have opportunity and we should all be working towards that. On that note, I will try my best not to be a socialist doom loop. On my grumpiest days, perhaps we end up in that place, but I will try not to do that today. On the Budget, the OBR talked about the fact that we are going to have the “worst decade” for living standards, so we have a situation where members of today’s generation are going to be the first to be poorer than their parents. Their real household disposable income will not go up in any reasonable way over the short or long term. The Government can talk about this being a Budget that involves breathing space, but that is not the reality for people, given what we are facing this winter and how cold it is already. My constituency, a city constituency next to the sea, has already been white in the past few days, so imagine how much colder it is further inland. With the massive increase in energy costs and the costs that Cornwall Insight has suggested will be coming next year, we do not have breathing space. People are looking at the fact that Labour promised in its manifesto that energy bills would be £300 cheaper, and as of next year they will be about £1,000 more expensive than Labour promised. That is not breathing space—that is a tightening of the financial situation and an increase in the cost of living crisis that people are facing. The Government keep talking about the help with energy bills being provided over the winter, but they are providing a council tax rebate—not an energy bill assistance scheme—for people in council tax bands A to D. The benefit to the Government of announcing that is that it does not apply in most of the UK, geographically. If a council tax rebate is announced, it applies in England, then the devolved authorities can make the decisions that they like. If the Government had a discount like the warm home discount, as the Lib Dems suggested, it would apply across England, Scotland and Wales, but unfortunately not Northern Ireland. However, it would at least apply over far more of the UK than what has been announced, which is simply a council tax rebate. The Scottish Government have promised that we will put the rebate in place in Scotland, but there are far better and more progressive ways. Across the income spectrum, people were promised far cheaper energy bills by the Labour manifesto than the Government have delivered. There is a significant disparity in the figures. Whether people are earning lots of money or very little money, what was promised has not been delivered.

I am sure that the hon. Lady spends a lot of time reading the Labour manifesto. We said that we would deliver a £300 cut by the end of our term. When that manifesto was written, none of us could have predicted what Trump has done in Iran or the war. She must accept that that war has had a real impact on our ability to deliver that pledge, but the target date for that pledge is the end of this term.

I am really glad to hear the hon. Member recommit to delivering a £300 reduction by the end of the term. I would love to hear Ministers on the Front Bench explain how people will get a £1,300 cut in the next few years or months until the next general election, or however long the term lasts. If an election is called in May, I will write to the hon. Member for Edinburgh South West (Dr Arthur) and ask him where each of my constituents’ £1,300 is, so that it can be delivered by the next election as part of the pledges made in the Labour manifesto. Let me return to the Budget and the confidence rates of the OBR. I wonder about the Cornwall Insight prediction about the price of electricity, gas and energy, which is higher than was predicted even at the time of the Budget—perhaps even higher than the OBR imagined that the price cap would go as a result of the changes made. Energy prices are more expensive than was expected, even at the Budget, and we will see an increase in those prices. The Budget’s confidence levels in being able to deliver the fiscal headroom that the Chancellor laid out were about 54% to 56%. That is not a good confidence level, to be honest. If I was going to cross the street, I would prefer more than a 54% chance that I would make it across alive. I do not think that around 54% or 56% is great. That is not brilliant; I would not take those odds. We have seen a change in that because of the ongoing crises in Iran and globally. It is perhaps the case that the OBR’s projections are not as accurate as they could have been—who can work that out at this point? Given the changes in the international market already, can Ministers tell us whether the OBR’s projections are mince now? Are they rubbish? Is it the case that the Government will not make their fiscal targets because of energy prices being higher for longer than predicted? Is it therefore the case that real household disposable income will be even lower than predicted, given that we saw incredibly low growth in it? Even though we have seen tiny growth in household disposable income, the Government are calling it breathing space. If we see a reversal in that because of changes in the international markets, will people see absolutely no growth or a regression in their household disposable income, instead of the minuscule growth that the Government have promised? It will be interesting to see how things go as time goes on. On that point, what will the Government do to prove to us how much money they have raised from each of the many tax measures in this Budget? To gently argue with some Conservative Members, there are a number of tax measures in the Budget, but not all of them are new taxes; many of them are slight changes to taxes, and some of them are reductions in taxes. There are new taxes, but there are also many tweaks to taxes. As the Chair of the Treasury Select Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier), said, one of the problems we have in the tax system is that constantly adding extra things and making changes makes it far more complicated than it needs to be. Will we get information from the Government in two years’ time about whether all the measures in this Budget have delivered the tax that the Government told us they would? The Treasury is monumentally bad at providing that feedback—at doing post-implementation checks on whether or not tax rates have delivered—which makes it really difficult for us to provide scrutiny. If the Government tell us that a tax will raise £1 billion over three years and then do not tell us how much it actually raised, it is very difficult for us to pass good legislation next time. It would be great to have a commitment that we will get an out-turn on all the taxes and changes that have numbers beside them in the Red Book or the Blue Book. That would be incredibly useful. Returning to energy prices, I am really concerned about the disproportionate impact that the removal of gas standi
Order. May I gently encourage Members to reflect on the time? Perhaps we could have slightly shorter speeches, if at all possible.

Three weeks ago, I stood up in the Chamber and told Members about the Turkey Inn in Goose Eye, a much-loved pub run by hard grafters who had to cut their opening hours from seven days a week to just four because of this Government’s lack of support. Today is a Monday, so tonight, as we debate the Finance Bill, that pub’s doors are closed, when it would want them to be open. That is the reality of what the Chancellor’s “breathing space” Budget looks like to my constituents, and to businesses across Keighley and Ilkley. The Finance Bill was the Government’s chance to think again—to listen to the pubs, shops and family businesses up and down the country who told them loud and clear that this Budget gave them absolutely nothing. Let me start with what is not in the Bill. There is no relief on Labour’s jobs tax. Employer’s national insurance stays exactly where it is. There is nothing at all to help employers meet the 3.9% rise in the national living wage—on top of the “Unemployment Rights Act”—and there is no real cut in business rates. The so-called real-terms freeze in those rates hits many of my businesses, and the British Retail Consortium rightly called it out as just “smoke and mirrors”. The Chancellor told the House that the gaming machines and vape shops would fund a breathing space that would help our pubs, shops and cafés, but the Bill raises machine games duty on higher-stake machines to 25%. EY estimates that that puts 9,000 jobs at risk, and could cause nearly 1,000 betting shops and casinos to close. That is not supporting businesses on the high street; it is shutting down another part of the high street. As for pubs, far from providing breathing space for them, the Bill raises alcohol duty again. Pub closures are now outnumbering openings by nine to one, and in some parts of the country by 24 to one. The Prime Minister calls pubs “cherished venues”, but the support that he has offered barely scratches the surface. My constituency—from Goose Eye to Haworth to Silsden to Ilkley—is blessed with so many pubs, and with brilliant brewers as well; there is Timothy Taylor’s, Goose Eye Brewery and Wishbone Brewery, to name but a few. Does the Minister know by how much the costs of the average pub have risen under this Government? The landlords in my constituency whom I meet regularly tell me every single month that their costs are going up under this Labour Government. It is high time the Government stopped talking about how important our pubs are and our hospitality sector is, and actually did something about it. I call on the Government to act, because the Bill does nothing for them. Businesses in my constituency and across the country are tired of this Prime Minister’s empty rhetoric. They want a Government who actually do something and who support the jobs that many of our constituents want to do. Then there is how this Bill treats people who build businesses—the backbone of our local economies. The Bill halves the lifetime limit on business asset disposal relief from £1 million to £500,000. About 10,000 business owners will be worse off every year, yet at the same time the Government have introduced the new founder’s relief, which will help only about 600 people a year. What fantastic logic: cut relief for 10,000 people, and create a new one for 600. Can the Minister explain the thinking behind these two measures, which clearly contradict one another? The reduction could adversely affect retiring farmers, partners, and rural and urban businesses that sell or transfer their businesses, a partnership interest or shares in a qualifying trading company. For an individual who realises a qualifying gain of at least £1 million, and who has not previously used any of their lifetime allowance, the reduction could increase the capital gains liability by up to £300,000. Individuals, including constituents of mine, who are contemplating retirement, succession or a business disposal will now be looking hard at what their prospects a

First, I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. The Government are saying this is a Budget to help with the cost of living. According to them, my constituents are getting a breathing space. Unfortunately, this winter, energy bills will be £450 higher than they were last year, yet the Government are trying to convince us that a £100 energy payment and a couple of pence off food items will change the fortunes of families choosing between heating and eating this Christmas. The same goes for fuel. Since the Iran war began, petrol prices have risen by 33%. That means the average family is paying an extra £24 every time they fill their tank. The Chancellor has extended an existing fuel duty cut, but it does nothing to bring down prices at the pump today. Drivers are being protected from a future tax increase, but they are being denied relief when they need it most, and that is now. With all these savings being wiped out by the cost of living, residents in Birmingham Perry Barr are looking at this Budget and simply asking one question: what has changed? With this Budget, the Labour Government promised fresh hope, but in reality they are giving us nothing but broken promises, with no ambition, no substance and no commitment to addressing the issues that keep families in poverty and people out of work. In my constituency, a quarter of young people are waking up with nowhere to go and nothing to do. Just this year alone, the number of graduate jobs has halved, and businesses cannot afford to bring on apprentices and trainees as they did before. When the job market is broken, entry level jobs are always the first to go, and that is exactly what we have seen. In the past year alone, the number of graduate jobs has fallen by almost half. One in four young people cannot find work, and many of those who can are paying hundreds of pounds each month in interest on student loans that they will never pay off. Thanks to the Government’s changes, some graduates will struggle to put food on the table and pay their rent, all so that the Treasury can make £700 million in profit each year. Rather than squeezing the few students who do find work, we should be raising repayment thresholds, lowering interest rates and creating more of the jobs that allow graduates to pay off loans without entering poverty. Young people in my constituency deserve better than unemployment and a graduate tax, yet the Budget fails to offer an alternative. Once again, we have had a Budget full of promises about giving power back to communities, but for residents in Birmingham, the most important question remains unanswered: where is the funding that our city desperately needs? Since Labour’s Birmingham administration bankrupted Birmingham city council, residents have seen community assets sold, local services slashed and council tax bills rise by more than 24% in just three years. Thanks to this Government leaving it short-changed by £43 million every year, West Midlands police has 550 fewer officers and 500 fewer police community support officers than in 2010. Our communities continue to face serious crime and antisocial behaviour, but unfortunately this Government are not doing much to help. The Government have also withdrawn Birmingham’s highway private finance initiative funding, which would have gone towards building roads and fixing potholes. Our city was promised funding since 2010, but this Government have now pulled the funding that would have assisted us with £450 million of costs. It is a similar story with Birmingham’s supported exempt accommodation pilot, which the Government scrapped in May. Birmingham is expected to house vulnerable people from across the country, while the Government stall on delivering the powers needed to regulate this sector. Worse still, while we wait for these powers, Ministers have withdrawn funding from the very enforcement pilot that is keeping rogue providers in check. We cannot be expected to do mo

The Chancellor promised the country breathing space, but we are all holding our breath. What he has delivered is a Budget of little substance with no real plan to grow the economy. For too many of my constituents, its help passes them by while its costs land squarely on their doorsteps. I will start with what the Government got right, because it is something the Liberal Democrats have long campaigned for. Our high streets are the heart of our communities in Esher and Walton, and the smaller independent businesses that keep them alive deserve a fairer deal. From April, up to 250 retail, hospitality and leisure properties in Esher and Walton could move on to small business rates relief. However, that relief counts premises, not businesses. A local business running a café and a small shop may only be able to claim small business rates relief on one property. I urge the Minister to look again at how the rules treat small independents with more than one modest premises and to make sure this support reaches them in full. Rates relief means little when it is given with one hand while the Government are piling on costs with the other. Riverside Pantry, the café at East Molesey cricket club, one of the oldest cricket clubs in the world, employs 30 local people and its owner, Sam, is passionate about giving young people their first job. That matters, because hospitality provides almost a third of first jobs for 16 to 24-year-olds. These entry-level jobs are where young people learn the skills that get them ready for every job that follows. Given the NEETs crisis, they have never been needed more. Every café that cuts a shift or shuts its door closes off another first step into work. Sam tells me it is getting harder by the month. The higher rate of employer national insurance and rising minimum wage costs, coupled with food inflation and energy bills that keep on climbing, only see prices getting higher and higher. The very businesses that give young people their start in work are being squeezed from every side. Sam is not alone; I could cite many restaurants. The Good Earth in Esher has seven sites across London and the south-east. It cannot expand, it cannot take on any more staff and it is looking at the premises it has already. Our only Michelin star restaurant in Esher cannot face the cost of food prices any more. The George pub in Walton is owned by Manil, whose dream was to open a pub. It opened only this year and he is putting his own money into the pub that is losing money every month. These are not failing businesses; they are community pubs, cafés and restaurants at the heart of Walton, Esher and Molesey being crushed by costs they cannot control. All these businesses have called for a cut in VAT on hospitality. The Liberal Democrats have called for that and we have laid out how we would pay for it to give businesses like these a real incentive to take on young people. I want to turn to energy bills, which as we have heard are projected to rise by 26% in January. The £100 energy payments go to only 40% of households in my constituency. We have had a long conversation about the targeting. The Government have chosen to target this help using bands based on what a home was worth in 1991. Those bands say nothing about what the people living in it earn today. Think of the pensioner who has lived in the same family home for 40 years, now getting by on a modest fixed income and dreading this winter’s bill. This is not targeting; it is a blunt instrument that will leave six in 10 households in my constituency without any help at all. Most of my constituents are shut out of the help in the Budget, but many of them will be first in line for its cost. The higher value council tax is again bolted on to a property tax system that is decades out of date. For households that are asset-rich but income-poor, everything depends on the deferral scheme and the Government are yet to publish it. Will deferral be available as of right to pensioners

I try this with every Liberal Democrat who speaks in these debates, so I will try with the hon. Lady. On 1 April 2019, six Liberal Democrats, led by the now leader of her party, the right hon. Member for Kingston and Surbiton (Ed Davey), voted in this place against joining a customs union. That vote fell by three votes. Why did the Liberal Democrats do that?
