I clearly was not here in 2019, so I cannot answer for the MPs that were, but I certainly will not apologise for the Liberal Democrats fighting Brexit tooth and nail, which we continue to do. The resulting growth dividend of our proposals could do many things, not least ease the cost of living, and it will help the young. I share the regrets expressed by other Members about the failure to tackle plan 2 student loans. There is a lack of ambition in this Budget, but the one bit of ambition that I did spot was on devolution. I cautiously welcome the announcement of a strategic mayor for Surrey, but it comes after Surrey being the only unitary authority going out in this round. As the local authority at the vanguard of the devolution wave, it is critical that residents see it as a success. The finances of the new East Surrey authority are imperilled by significant debts from Conservative-run Surrey, which notably ramped up over the last 24 months before the Liberal Democrats take over; the Government’s fairer funding review, which reduced annual funding by £180 million in year 3; and the cost of implementing local government reorganisation, which was grossly underestimated. It is regrettable that there were not more transitional support funds in the Budget, and that there was not a review of the fairer funding formula. People believe in democracy if what is outside their door is working. My constituents are paying out more, yet feel that they are receiving much, much less. My constituents work hard, save hard and care deeply about their communities. My constituency is the single biggest contributor to the Exchequer in the country outside of London, but local businesses are being squeezed from every side. The Government seem to see the south-east as a source of revenue, not a source for growth: save, and you pay more tax; build a business, and the relief when you sell it is halved; earn a pay rise, and frozen thresholds take a bigger slice. Where is the help for those who want to start a business, take on staff and get on in life? Where is the plan for growth? At a moment that demanded ambition, the Chancellor chose to tinker around the edges. Until this Government find the courage to fix our relationship with Europe, every Budget will do the same. Esher and Walton deserves better; it needs more than the wasted opportunities in this Budget.

The Chancellor closed his Budget by promising two things: breathing space now, and fresh hope for the future. The Government tell us that their ambition is good growth in every single postcode, and now the Finance Bill is before us this evening. The reasoned amendment tabled in my name highlights areas where I feel that the Government missed the mark. I will go into brief detail on four simple questions. I ask these questions as a constituency MP, first and foremost. Does the Bill deliver for the constituency of Leicester South? Will our young people benefit? Will our small businesses benefit? Does it actually close the gap between those who have, and those who struggle? I will start with the last question. The first thing that households feel is that the Bill extends the freeze on income tax thresholds, leaving the personal allowance at £12,570. Had it kept pace with inflation, it would be around £16,000. The OBR tells us that the freeze is equivalent to adding 4p to the basic rate, and that it will take £29.3 billion a year from workers and pensioners by 2027-28. This is not breathing space; it is a tax rise in everything but name, and it falls hardest on the nurses, bus drivers and shopkeepers in our constituencies, whose wages rise just enough to pull them into paying even more. Disposable incomes are set to fall by £1,050 over three years. The help that has been offered in this Bill is absolutely minor, and I will not pretend otherwise: £100 off energy for homes in bands A to D; gas standing charges removed; and VAT taken off household electricity. That is welcome, but fundamentally it is a plaster over a wound that the Government themselves are opening. I welcome the Government’s decision last year to listen to my campaign to scrap the two-child benefit cap. One of my first acts in this House was to table an amendment to do exactly that. The Trussell Trust says that scrapping the cap has protected 415,000 children from severe hardship. That is what happens when this House listens, and I ask it to listen again.

The hon. Gentleman is right to underline the issue of the two-child cap. In Northern Ireland, our advantage was 65,000 children lifted out of poverty, too. The hon. Gentleman was right to push it, but he was not the only one—we pushed it as well to ensure that we could do it together.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his intervention. I feel it more acutely because in Leicester, close to four in 10 children grow up in poverty; in my constituency, the rate is nearly double the national figure. Yet this Bill keeps the local housing allowance frozen. More than half of private renters who rely on it have faced food insecurity this year. Modelling by the Trussell Trust shows that linking the allowance back to real rents would lift 105,000 people out of severe hardship. Lifting the two-child cap was the last fight; this appears to be the next one. Who actually carries the burden? The bank surcharge came in at 3%, not at the expected 8%. There is no 2% wealth tax on assets over £10 million, which would raise around £24 billion. The Government have not delivered the digital services tax they promised and do nothing serious to stop multinationals offshoring their profits. Set that beside the families in my constituency choosing between the rent and the food shop—when the Government choose who carries the load, it should not be them. There are some good measures in the Bill for young people. Apprenticeship training for under-25s will be fully funded, and small firms can receive up to £8,000 for taking on young apprentices, which I welcome. However, the £100 million to expand mayoral apprenticeship brokerage goes, as we would expect, to mayoral areas. After months of graduates watching student loan repayments swallow their pay, the Bill is silent. There is nothing on the repayment threshold and nothing on the years before the debt is written off. A generation is being asked to pay a graduate tax for decades, and then told to save for a home. It is simply not possible. The Your First Home scheme lets a first-time buyer purchase with a 2.5% deposit and a 20% Government loan. The instinct is definitely right, but the scheme applies only to new build homes built by developers who decide to sign up. Someone walking the Victorian terraced streets of my constituency would not find many new show homes. The loan is not a gift, either: interest starts in year six, and what the homeowner owes grows with their home’s value. For a young person renting, repaying a student loan and earning a lower youth wage, even 2.5% is a mountain. A first home scheme that works only on new estates will do little for the young people of LE2. On small businesses and young entrepreneurs, I will give credit where it is due. Raising full rates relief to £18,000 of rateable value will take many small shops off the rates bill altogether, and tripling the trading allowance will help a side hustle to become a business. The Budget even admits that too often, young founders succeed not because they have the best ideas, but because they have family money behind them. Let me briefly tell the House about two young men in my constituency. Ahmed and Hussain saved, invested their money, time and effort, and started a coffee trailer, Espresso Street Coffee. It is exactly the kind of enterprise that this Government say they want. Yet at every single turn, they have faced obstacles from the local council, from the administrative burden to the costs that deter them from their designation—a viable local business. No one in particular is to blame, but, because the system is built to say no, in the end, it came down to the adage, “computer says no”. I want to very briefly speak about Leicester and the devolution gap. This was billed as a devolution Government, and I welcome the direction that has been set. From next year, mayors will keep a fifth of business rates; from 2028, they will keep a share of the income tax their residents pay. But the Government’s own fiscal devolution road map is blunt: the highest level of fiscal devolution will be available only to areas with mayors. Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland have a directly elected mayor, but this Budget rewards strategic mayors, who lead combined or strategic authorities. Leicester is not part of that. We are st

It is a pleasure to respond on behalf of His Majesty’s official Opposition. As ever, I refer the House to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. I congratulate everybody from across the House who contributed to today’s debate. In the interests of all colleagues, I will keep my remarks relatively short compared to the voluminous speeches we have heard tonight. Let me first pay tribute to the hon. Member for Blackburn (Mr Hussain), who made his maiden speech. It was two years and four months in the drafting, but I can tell him that it was worth the wait. I notice that he is not actually here—you know what these newbies are like! It is what it is. More experienced colleagues made extremely positive and comprehensive contributions, not least the Chair of the Treasury Committee, the hon. Member for Hackney South and Shoreditch (Dame Meg Hillier), who highlighted, quite rightly, the complexity in our tax system and asked the Minister to confirm that the bank surcharge will remain temporary, as is put into legislation through this Bill. My right hon. Friend the Member for Witham (Priti Patel) also asked about that, and I look forward to the Minister’s response. I am not usually in the business of praising Liberal Democrats, and I do not want to end up on a leaflet, but the hon. Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper) did quite rightly warn the House that energy bills are about to go up by 26% next year. That should concern all of us. My right hon. Friend the Member for Central Devon (Sir Mel Stride) gave a characteristically detailed speech, highlighting in particular the 1 million NEETs that we now have in our country, and that he believes that the growing tax burden is making that situation worse. My right hon. Friend the Member for Witham, in addition to talking about the bank surcharge, lamented the loss of key infrastructure projects in her constituency, in particular the A120 dualling scheme, which I am sure is of great concern to many. Finally, my hon. Friend the Member for Keighley and Ilkley (Robbie Moore) spoke about the impact of this Finance Bill on pubs and hospitality, not least the Turkey Inn in Goose Eye, which I am still to receive an invitation to. I thank him for his contribution as well. I am reminded that this is the third Labour Finance Bill that I have scrutinised from this Dispatch Box. First we had the 2024 “Halloween” Budget, with a Finance Bill that scared the living daylights out of business and culled jobs. Then we had the 2025 “Nightmare Before Christmas” Budget, which targeted working people and punished family businesses and farmers. This year, the Government have made a sequel. In my opinion, every trilogy has a disappointing third episode, and this is no different. This actually is “The Hangover Part III”—the country has woken up with a headache, the wallet is empty and there is a man in Downing Street that nobody remembers voting for. It is a new cast but exactly the same plot—taxes higher, businesses raided, and aspirational hard-working families punished just for doing the right thing. This was meant to be third time lucky for the Labour Government. But if at first you don’t succeed, it’s tax, tax, and tax again. Every warning light on the dashboard is flashing red, but the Chancellor is stood there staring at it, thinking how wonderfully festive it all looks. They have changed the Chancellor and they have changed the Prime Minister, but they still have not changed their high-tax, anti-growth policies that got us into this mess in the first place. Even Labour MPs are unsurprised: just look at what Labour’s own Ministers are saying about the Government’s performance. Even the Chief Whip did so recently in a highly unusual interview in a fashion magazine— Vogue . It has often been said that Chief Whips should be seen and not heard, but she has been seen, heard and photographed, and what she said was remarkable. She said that after two years of a Labour Government, people out there cam

It is a pleasure to close Second Reading of the Finance Bill. Like the hon. Member for Grantham and Bourne (Gareth Davies), I will keep my remarks short, but let me thank all right hon. and hon. Members for their contributions. Before I turn to the points they have raised, let me reflect briefly on the purpose of this Bill. The Budget delivered by my right hon. Friend the Chancellor last month was about providing breathing space now and fresh hope for the future. In the face of global economic storms, we chose to act by providing breathing space now on the cost of living and the cost of business, by creating the conditions for good growth in every postcode and by focusing on the changes that our country needs to be on a better course. All this while maintaining the fiscal discipline on which our economy depends. I turn to some of hon. and right hon. Members’ contributions. Let me start by congratulating the hon. Member for Blackburn (Mr Hussain), who is now in his place, on his maiden speech. He spoke with great pride about the people in his constituency and the role that his constituency has played in our country’s industrial heritage. He also spoke about the importance of opportunities for all in the next generation, and I am sure that is a sentiment that we all share across this House. We heard from two shadow Ministers this evening. The hon. Member for West Worcestershire (Dame Harriett Baldwin) selectively erased what had happened before July 2024 in her recounting of history. The hon. Member for Grantham and Bourne (Gareth Davies), for whom I have a great deal of respect, was worried about ending up on a Lib Dem leaflet; I am not quite sure what they have got planned in his constituency. I must take exception to his comments about living standards, because the truth is that real household disposable income per capita has increased in this Parliament by 1.8%, compared with a fall of 1.7% in the last Parliament. The last Parliament is the only Parliament on record during which living standards declined. That is not a record the Conservatives should be proud of. We also heard from the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for St Albans (Daisy Cooper), who very bravely attempted to do a live workshop about data sources here in the Chamber this evening, which certainly provided some interesting food for thought. She spoke about the £100 that we are giving through the council tax system to 20 million households across England in July, to help with the cost of energy bills. I can assure her that, should any struggling households not be caught by that mechanism, there is an additional £100 million pot, available through local councils, so that they get the support they need. The hon. Lady also raised a question about business rates and our review of the methodology for valuing pubs and hotels. I can assure her that, while that call for evidence has now closed, that work is ongoing and we will be updating the House as soon as possible. We heard from the right hon. Member for Central Devon (Sir Mel Stride), who was quite bold, I thought, to imply what he thought we should learn from our last two years in government, while showing no self-awareness whatever about what he could learn from the 14 years that he had in government. I like to think that it was his own brand of “Melsplaining”. He also spoke about welfare, forgetting that welfare increased by £88 billion over a decade during which the Conservatives were in power. We also heard from the hon. Member for Bicester and Woodstock (Calum Miller), who spoke about data centres. I hope he will welcome the data centre covenant that the Chancellor announced at the Budget, which is important for communities across the country. The right hon. Member for Witham (Priti Patel), for whom I have a great deal of respect, spoke as well. I thought at one point that she was making the case for greater public investment in infrastructure, so I wonder whether she might be walking through
Before I put the Question, I yet again remind Members of the importance of attending the wind-ups if they have spoken. Question put, That the amendment be made.

I should probably start with an apology for keeping the House so late on a Monday evening. I am grateful for the House’s time. I would also like to say how grateful I am to have the opportunity to bring this important Adjournment debate to the House. I pay tribute to my neighbouring Members of Parliament for their support since the announcement of the closure of Leweston school, particularly the hon. Member for North Dorset (Simon Hoare), whose hard work, support and knowledge have been invaluable throughout. I also express my gratitude to the Minister for the kind offer of a meeting in two weeks, alongside the hon. Member for North Dorset and the right hon. Member for Gainsborough (Sir Edward Leigh). I am angry—not just at the decisions that resulted in the closure of Leweston school, but at what happened after the school closed. I am angry at a group of people who demonstrated a complete lack of urgency when it came to protecting people and property, who failed to support staff, who attempted to take credit for work done by others, and who attempted to pass responsibility for their mistakes elsewhere. This is a group of people who took over a school that had served the community for 135 years and closed it in less than a year. In December 2025, Leweston came under new ownership. Concept Education operated the school, and established the Catholic Schools Trust to hold the land and buildings. The directors of one are the trustees of the other. We need answers not only about the competence of Concept Education as the operator, but about the decisions, responsibilities and oversight of the charitable trust that owned the property.

It is truly incredible that VAT on private schools can lead to closures and what may happen as a result. Similarly, in Northern Ireland, without warning, St Anne’s primary school was given only 35 minutes’ notice before the Department of Education publicly announced its closure. Does the hon. Member agree that there must be rapid and effective communication with staff, parents and pupils when closures are being considered? That would help to reduce the uncertainty and distress if school closures do occur—and, unfortunately, there will probably be more of them.

I thank the hon. Member for his intervention. I shall be listing some recommendations that I would like the Government to look at in order to prevent such circumstances from arising again, not least the introduction of a minimum notice period. I am not a lawyer or an accountant, and I am not alleging that every failure was deliberate or malicious or attempting to prejudge any investigation. Whether these failures arose from negligence, incompetence or something more serious, they cannot be ignored. What is clear is that 550 students were left with no school place at no notice, 54 staff were left unemployed, and parents were left tens of thousands and, in some cases, hundreds of thousands of pounds out of pocket. The necessary regulators and the police must look at the evidence and use their best judgment, but when wrongdoing is established, those responsible must be held to account.

I thank my hon. Friend for giving way, and for the great speech that he is making. Does he agree with Robert from West Coker, who was head of engineering at Leweston, that it is unacceptable that staff have been let go with zero warning and zero consultation, and does he agree with me that the Department for Education must do all that it can to help staff, pupils and parents from Yeovil and beyond with the transition to new schools that are actually in their areas?

My hon. Friend and neighbour is entirely right. While the local authorities have done everything possible to accommodate the students who have been displaced, the fact is that we are asking the state school sector to absorb an enormous number of students at very short notice. There will invariably be problems associated with that, and I hope that the Department for Education will provide assurances about how it plans to support local councils in their plight. The financial difficulties facing the school did not appear overnight. The company’s accounts described declining pupil numbers, substantial discounting of fees, rising operating costs, pressure on cash flow, regular financial updates, and a business dependent on further funding and investment to continue trading. It states that during 2026, before the summer holidays had even started, management information and cash-flow forecasts showed increased pressure on working capital and liquidity. The owners knew that the school needed a huge amount of capital to remain viable, but the parents did not. They continued to pay fees, deposits, money for school trips and, in some cases, substantial lump sums for future terms and academic years They did so on the reasonable understanding that their children would receive the education and activities for which they had paid.

After years of dedicated service as a music director at Leweston, Rachel, from Milborne Port, has suddenly been left jobless after its sudden closure. Her own children were at the school. They have been offered alternative places, but those are guaranteed only if Rachel secures another job. Does my hon. Friend agree that displaced teachers and their families who have lost fees that were paid up front should receive immediate financial support? Does he also agree that there should be an immediate investigation of the school’s financial dealings, especially given the recent change of ownership, and its management?

My hon. Friend and neighbour is absolutely right. There is a litany of failings and of families who have been affected by this and who understandably want answers, both from Concept Education and from the Department for Education. I hope the Minister will take this opportunity to provide answers for them and for us. What I want to know, and what those families deserve to know, is what happened to that money. Was it kept for its intended purposes, or were funds transferred elsewhere within the wider group? Relevant authorities must look into whether the ownership arrangements provided the proper protection for the school and the people who depended on it. The impact on the students has been enormous. Many began the new half-term without a confirmed school place. Ofqual has confirmed that it cannot arrange transfers between examination boards, which leaves some pupils at risk of having to relearn substantial parts of their GCSE or A-level courses. For pupils with special educational needs and disabilities, the disruption is even more serious. They need continued continuity of specialist provision, trusted relationships, support plans and properly managed transitions. Children with education, health and care plans must not lose the support to which they are entitled because their school has been closed. One pupil, who is paralysed, had specialist facilities at Leweston that local schools are unable to match, which means that he no longer has a school place and is losing his confidence following his paralysis. Concept knew the impact that the closure would have on students, yet it did not organise a managed closure or tell parents in advance. It did not inform Dorset council and give it time to arrange alternative places. In fact, it was me, not Concept, who alerted Dorset council to the closure. With only days until the start of the new half-term, Dorset council had to organise state school place allocations, emergency admissions, nursery placements, EHCP-supported pupils and the transferability of funded childcare places. The council and its admissions teams have worked extremely hard, round the clock, in exceptionally difficult circumstances. Local schools have stepped up, with some prepared to exceed their published admission numbers to accommodate Leweston pupils. One local school identified 60 to 70 pupils in its catchment seeking places, and developed plans to accommodate them across several year groups. Taking additional pupils requires teachers, support staff and resources, but because the pupils arrived after the school census, receiving schools will not automatically receive the funding through the usual mechanism. Already stretched state schools should not be expected to absorb those costs without additional support. Teachers and support staff were dismissed at short notice. Some have not received wages for work that they have already completed, and some were hired just two weeks before the closure. People with mortgages, bills and children to feed were left without the money they had earned. One member of staff described being unable to afford the petrol to attend a meeting at the school. Another explained that they were struggling to pay for food for themselves and their daughter. Some former employees have been unable to make benefit claims because they lack proof of redundancy or the insolvency reference number needed to progress their applications. They were told that insolvency practitioners had been appointed weeks ago, only to discover that this has still not happened. That delay has left staff without wages, redundancy support or access to financial assistance. There are also concerns about pension contributions that have been deducted from salaries but not paid into the relevant schemes. Some staff, who live at the site, have lost not just their jobs but their homes. Others who remain on site have been left without heating, because the school has not paid its heating bills. My brilliant casework team have bee

I thank the hon. Member for West Dorset (Edward Morello) for raising this important issue, for securing the debate, for highlighting the issues around the closure of Leweston school and for touching on the Government’s decision to apply VAT to private school fees—although I appreciate the debate is focused primarily on the school in question. As a former teacher, I know the central role that schools play in their communities. When they close, the impact on pupils, their families, school staff and wider communities can be significant. However, private schools are independent institutions and decisions about ownership, financial sustainability and closures are all currently matters for their proprietors. Private schools, like many private organisations may face business pressures from demographic change, financial viability and operating costs, and, as schools, they are subject to changing parental demand and fluctuations in pupil numbers. On the specific case of Leweston school, I recognise the significant impact that this type of closure, especially at such short notice, can have on pupils, parents, staff and the wider community, but it is the responsibility of the private school and its proprietor to make decisions regarding the future operation of the school. It is very clear to me that the owners of the school have not communicated with the notice that families or pupils should reasonably expect a responsible owner to do. To close a school with immediate effect, leaving pupils displaced is not an acceptable way for a responsible owner to act. The hon. Member set out in such detail the full state of the problems with the closure of Leweston school and his rightful anger at the way in which it has been handled. In circumstances such as these, where a private school has closed, local authorities provide invaluable support for families whose children need a state-funded school place. I would like to place on the record my thanks to the hon. Member’s constituency staff for the role they played in supporting pupils and also to the local authority team in Dorset. The Department’s relevant regional team is working with Dorset and Somerset councils to ensure all pupils needing a school place can be accommodated. All the pupils who have special educational needs and disabilities have now secured alternative places and the majority of the remaining pupils have secured places in other private schools. Turning to the matter of VAT, given its inclusion in the title of the debate—I appreciate it is only referenced in passing—it is worth setting out that the impact of the VAT policy has not led to any market change in the rate of private school closures. The statistics show that since the introduction of VAT, closure rates are still lower than the 10-year average. On average, 75 private schools, including independent special schools, have closed per year over the last 10 years. Only 60 private schools closed in the school year the VAT changes were introduced and only 67 private schools closed in the 2025-26 academic year, the first full year the VAT changes applied. The VAT measure is expected to raise more than £1.5 billion this year, increasing to £1.7 billion per year from 2029. The business rate measures are anticipated to raise £70 million this year, increasing to £90 million per year by 2029. At the autumn Budget last year, the re-costing of the VAT measure showed that it will raise around £40 million more than we originally forecast. That funding supports vital investment in education, benefiting the overwhelming majority of children, who attend state schools. We recognise the valuable contribution that many private schools make. Private schools offer educational choice, bursaries and scholarships. I am particularly familiar with the brilliant work of organisations such as the Royal National Children’s Springboard Foundation, which supports children who are looked after into excellent educational opportunities. 1. What recent assessment she has made of the potential implications for her policies of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency’s proposed increase in registration fees for level 2 category dental devices from April 2027.

I recognise the hon. Member’s concern about the potential impact of the proposed increase in MHRA registration fees, particularly on smaller firms. The MHRA has consulted publicly on the proposals, and the Government will carefully consider the responses. We remain committed to a regulatory system that protects patient safety while supporting a thriving and innovative medtech sector.

I thank the Minister for his answer, and I am glad that the Government will review the consultation responses carefully. The Dental Laboratories Association is aware of the MHRA’s plan to increase the fees for medical device registration from £300 to £511 per global medical device nomenclature level 2 category. That is an increase of 70%, which is materially and operationally unjustifiable, and will fall on the shoulders of independent laboratories, which are already struggling with the cost of doing business. Given the MHRA’s operational independence, what will the Minister do to ensure that it is not inadvertently putting dental laboratories out of business?

It is important to remember the context. The landmark Cumberlege review identified a shortfall in the regulation of such devices. It is important that the manufacturers set to benefit from registration are making a contribution that is no longer fully subsidised by the UK taxpayer. Consultation on the cost response will follow shortly.

May I take this opportunity to congratulate my chief of staff, Stefan, and his wife, Emma, on the birth of their second son yesterday? Does the Minister agree that a national urgent care safety net means that, for the first time, people in dental pain in Harlow will no longer be left with nowhere to turn?
I do welcome that development, and am happy to go into more detail about it with my hon. Friend.
2. What steps she is taking to help increase consistency in access to NHS-funded fertility treatment.
3. What steps she is taking to support equal access to NHS-funded IVF provision.

The support that people get to have a baby should not depend on where in the country they live, but variations in access to NHS-funded fertility services have been a problem for many years. Our women’s health strategy commits to ensuring that every woman can access those services. That means we expect such services to be commissioned by integrated care boards solely on the basis of patient needs and the relevant National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidelines. We are currently assessing the level of provision in each ICB to ensure that it lives up to those commitments.

I am grateful for the Minister’s response. In North and West Yorkshire—this affects the Secretary of State’s constituency—residents are offered only one cycle, whereas in the north-east and north Cumbria, they are offered three. Can the Minister give a timeline for when the review will take place, so that people who are getting only one cycle can get three?

I pay tribute to the right hon. Gentleman for all his work in this area; he has been involved in a long-standing campaign. He will be pleased to know that work is already under way and that the results from the ICBs are expected imminently. After an assessment and review of the information from the ICBs, we will move to the next steps.

Similarly, the NHS in Greater Manchester has reduced NHS-funded IVF provision to just one full cycle, despite NICE guidelines recommending up to three cycles for eligible patients. The NHS in Greater Manchester pressed ahead with the change despite 74% of consultation respondents opposing it. The consultation cost the public around £4,000, and it seems to have been entirely ignored. England has a falling birth rate, with fewer than 600,000 babies born last year. We should be making it easier, not harder, for people to start a family. Does the Minister agree that access to fertility treatment should not depend on someone’s postcode or ability to afford it? Will she commit to ending the reduction in NHS-funded IVF provision?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this important issue, and I agree that access should not depend on someone’s postcode. As I have set out, work is under way to identify what is happening in ICBs around the country. Once we understand that, we can determine the next steps towards more equitable access across England.
4. What progress she has made on the reorganisation of the NHS.

Subject to passage of the Health Bill, NHS England will be brought back into the Department of Health and Social Care next April. My statement on 4 November set out the next steps for how those changes will be delivered, but the purpose of the reforms is to help us get back to what the NHS does best—caring for people where they need it most—and ending the duplication and fragmentation of our national health service system.

I thank the Government for their reversal of the abolition of Healthwatch and local Healthwatch organisations, and I pay tribute to Charlotte and Helen at Healthwatch Bromley because it has been very unsettling for them. With the support the Government are now giving, will the Government agree to a minimum funding standard to account for the different size of Healthwatch organisations across the country?

I agree with the hon. Member that Healthwatch plays an important role across the country. That is why I took the decision to ensure that Healthwatch, and so the local patient voice, can continue. We are also strengthening the voice for patients and the focus on patient experience at the national level, with a new director in post. He will know that the funding decisions also reflect the allocations and ICB allocations, but I hear his point.

I am pleased to see the Government making progress on NHS reorganisation. The all-party parliamentary group on eye health and visual impairment recently published its report, which found that only just over 3% of blind and partially sighted people found the NHS app to be fully accessible and inclusive. As the Government continue to make progress on moving from analogue to digital, does the Secretary of State agree that it is vital they ensure the voices of disabled people are part of that reorganisation? Will she also agree to meet me to discuss how we can remove some of those barriers, and has she received a copy of my report?

I welcome my hon. Friend’s point. We clearly need to improve digital access to NHS services across the country. Those reforms are moving at pace and are making the NHS much more accessible, but she is absolutely right that all other ways to access GP services have to exist and that we must ensure that all reforms are as accessible as possible. I would be happy to follow up directly on her specific points.

The Amos review identified 748 recommendations to improve maternity safety, but the body responsible for implementing those recommendations—the National Quality Board—is chaired by NHS England, which is being abolished from next April. Will the Health Secretary confirm that the NQB will continue, will be co-chaired by the Care Quality Commission and will not just catalogue recommendations, but will actually decide on them with a person and a date by when they will be implemented?

The former Health Secretary makes an important point about the challenge of recommendations that are never implemented. We are setting up a new hub within the Department to keep track of recommendations, some of which are duplicates and some of which contradict each other. We will shortly be setting out a first action plan on maternity services based on the work of the maternity and neonatal taskforce. We also expect the National Quality Board to continue.

Following the abolition of NHS England, what arrangements will replace the patient voice function of the specialised blood disorders clinical reference group, and how will organisations representing people with haemophilia and other bleeding disorders be involved in specialist commissioning decisions?

My hon. Friend makes an important point. I can tell him that we are setting out many of the specialist commissioning functions, which will continue to be done at a national level. It is important that that takes place alongside the expansion of strategic commissioning by ICBs. We expect patient voice to be taken into account at every level when it comes to commissioning, and we are strengthening the patient voice directly in the Department as well as part of these reforms.

The Government’s reorganisation has become a re-re-reorganisation, with a quango for a quango, the famous “regional tier” integrated care boards in limbo and costs mounting daily—not on hospital consultants but on management consultants. Could that help explain why we still have no workforce plan, why the waiting list is over 7 million, and why those long delays in A&E just keep getting longer and longer?

The right hon. Gentleman is the man who supported the Andrew Lansley reforms in 2012, which did such incredible damage right across our NHS. We are taking the final steps to reverse the damaging Lansley reforms by bringing NHS England back into the Department of Health and Social Care, reducing swathes of bureaucracy right across the country. We are on track to save £1 billion a year as a result of those reforms, because the duplication and fragmentation that his party introduced has damaged the NHS and undermined the frontline.

The Government said this reorganisation would eventually save £1 billion a year but cost £1 billion to get there. Guess what? The costs are going up, and the savings are coming down. On top of that, there is now the impact of the Employment Rights Act 2025, because it turns out that the No. 1 user of zero-hours contracts in this country might be none other than the national health service—I say “might be” because it also turns out that the Government do not know. That could cost the NHS a further almost £1 billion a year. Will the Government reorganise away from bank staffing, will they exempt the public sector from the Employment Rights Act, or will they cut something else to cover this spectacular oversight?

One of the things we have been doing since the election is reducing the dependency on agency staff. That is how we have improved efficiency across the country, ensuring that our NHS staff are properly supported and protected in the important job that they do, caring for all of us. I think it is a huge disappointment to the whole House that the right hon. Gentleman is not interested in that. We are also undertaking a massive turnaround in the NHS. When his party were in office, in 2011, there were only 123 12-hour waits. When it left office in 2024, there were 430,000. That is the collapse in performance under the Conservative party.
5. What steps she is taking to help improve maternity services at St Helier hospital.

I have met a number of Members to discuss the issue of maternity services at St Helier hospital, where we are committed to ensuring safe, high-quality care. The board at the hospital is considering the safest option to address the water and estates challenges. Of course, maintaining patient safety and staff safety must be the highest priority. I understand that the trust board is making a decision at the beginning of December.

I thank the Minister for meeting me and colleagues at very short notice to discuss ways to keep maternity services accessible for my constituents due to further failures at St Helier hospital. She knows that the water safety issues in the women’s health block mean the trust is facing difficult and expensive decisions and that, at the same time, lift failure has closed the paediatrics block and the re-ablement unit has been closed due to structural failures. I know the Minister understands the urgency of our pleas, but it would be remiss of me not to take every opportunity to ask that she redoubles efforts to work with the Treasury so that we can bring forward our new hospital, which will secure women’s health and maternity services in Sutton and deliver a brand-new, world-leading hospital for our patients.

The hon. Member is quite right: it would be remiss of him not to advocate on behalf of his local trust, as many Members do. Further to the Secretary of State’s comments, the state of the estate that we inherited after the last 14 years is well documented. We have put the new hospital programme on a sustained footing, and we have ensured there is money allocated to it, which was not the case when we came into power. The capital budget is on a longer-term, sustainable footing. I am happy to continue to meet Members across the House to get these hospitals built quickly and on time for the patients they are designed to serve.
6. What steps she is taking to help ensure that high-quality healthcare is available to people closer to where they live.

It is important that people get the highest quality of healthcare closer to where they live. That starts with improving access to GP care. As a result of the work we have done, there are now 24 million additional GP appointments a year compared with before the election, and we have now announced neighbourhood care reforms, including new neighbourhood support teams, to help the frailest of patients stay well and safe at home.

In recent months I have been deeply impressed by the way healthcare providers in Southend East and Rochford, including North Shoebury surgery, have thought outside the box to deliver proactive and patient-focused services. What measures is the Department putting in place to ensure that this sort of high-quality care is available to people closer to their homes?

The hon. Member is absolutely right about this: we know that some people end up in emergency care because they could not get early enough support and care at home. That is why we are giving GPs £40 million this winter to identify the frailest patients and put in place home care plans, and from next April, we will roll out new neighbourhood support teams to help the frailest 1% of the population across the country. This is a fundamental change in the way that we provide NHS care, and will provide those patients with support and care in their own homes.

As an ambassador for Prostate Cancer Research, I support local testing events in communities up and down the country, including a very successful one in my own constituency this weekend, organised by Wensleydale Rotary club. Does the Secretary of State agree that community groups play a vital role in raising awareness of and testing for prostate cancer, and will she join me in thanking those groups, including Rotary, the Lions and the Graham Fulford charitable trust, and the medical volunteers for all their efforts, which are saving men’s lives from community to community?

I thank the right hon. Member for his advocacy and campaigning on prostate cancer, which affects so many men across the country. As he will know, the Government will roll out England’s first targeted prostate cancer screening programme, as recommended by the UK national screening committee. We have asked the committee to keep the programme under continual review. Men who are not covered by the screening programme and who are concerned can also talk to their GP about getting a prostate-specific antigen test based on informed choice. He is right that raising awareness about prostate cancer is critical, and many campaigning organisations do an amazing job on that.
7. What steps she is taking to improve NHS maternity services.
8. What steps she is taking to improve NHS maternity services.

The Health Bill, currently passing through Parliament, will include provisions for a new maternity and neonatal commissioner to help drive up standards, and shortly we will publish the first action plan based on the work of the maternity and neonatal taskforce. Every family deserves the very best start in life.

My constituent, Megan, is expecting her third baby, usually a cause for celebration, but she is scared. She has seen maternity care fail and watched her midwife break down in tears. That is sadly no surprise, with three quarters of midwives having considered leaving in the past year and 80% feeling that their unit is not safely staffed. Will the Minister commit to better supporting midwives, including Lib Dem calls for 52 hours of protected paid training for every midwife every year?

Support for the workforce is a critical part of the work we are doing through the taskforce. We are considering introducing a new modern services framework, a set of national standards for maternity and neonatal care. When I was a Health Minister 25 years ago, we were introducing national standards around maternity care. Those were cancelled and dropped, so it is important to introduce new standards now.

My constituents in west Somerset are served primarily by North Devon district hospital and Musgrove Park hospital, yet North Devon hospital’s maternity unit remains closed and Musgrove continues to face significant pressures. For families in some of the most remote communities on Exmoor, including villages and hamlets such as Porlock and Culbone, the nearest consultant-led maternity care can be more than an hour away by road. Does the Minister accept that it cannot be right in modern Britain that expectant mothers risk giving birth on the side of a B road because maternity services are too distant to reach safely? Will the Government act now to end this unacceptable situation?

I agree that it is deeply unfair on families that North Devon maternity services continue to be closed. NHS England is meeting daily with the trust leadership to provide support and to ensure progress. The trust has been working on different ways to seek to recruit the additional staff it needs to keep services safe, because fundamentally the problem comes down to issues around recruitment. It has been offering additional financial incentives for relocation. We will continue to support the trust and to maintain that pressure and work in order to get those services safely opened, as rapidly as possible.

In April, the Royal College of Midwives commissioned a review into its workplace culture. Unlike a similar review by the Royal College of Nursing, the findings and recommendations have not been made public. If the review has not already been shared, is the Secretary of State able to confirm that she will request sight of the recommendations and seek assurances that they will be acted on?

I can tell my hon. Friend that we work with all the royal colleges on what improvements need to be made, but issues around culture and the need to have really effective multidisciplinary teams and workforce teams as part of maternity services are crucial. That is part of what we are looking at through the maternity taskforce.

Maternity readmissions within six weeks of birth have risen by more than a third in just three years, and data shows that at least one in five baby deaths last year may have been preventable. In June, the Government promised a maternity and neonatal commissioner; nearly six months on, no one has been appointed. How many avoidable tragedies have to occur before this Secretary of State gets a grip on maternity services?

Let me point out gently to the hon. Member that the maternity and neonatal commissioner was introduced by us through an amendment to the Health Bill so that we can bring it in on a statutory basis. His party had 14 years to address this issue, and the work that we are doing is already improving the work around maternity services. One of the issues around those critical weeks immediately after birth, which are so incredibly important, is that mothers and families used to be supported by Sure Start, until his party abolished it.

Delay is clearly a pattern with this Government when it comes to mothers and babies. Nearly three years after the Hughes report on sodium valproate, the Patient Safety Commissioner has described a “stark lack of Government response”. There is no redress scheme and no timetable, and children harmed before they were even born are still waiting. Ministers promised a decision in this Parliament, which is no comfort to the families who have waited decades. Will the Secretary of State finally commit today to a date for a Government response on the Hughes report?

Again, the hon. Member’s indignation does not reflect his own party’s responsibility throughout this period. The Public Health Minister has been holding a series of meetings on exactly this issue, because we and she take it so seriously, and we will report back to the House in due course.

The Conservatives drove maternity centres to breaking point, but the Labour Government have been in power for more than two years, and I am afraid that they are not moving fast enough. The national maternity action plan is delayed until next year, and the recommendations of previous inquiries are outstanding. Today’s statistics show that rates of postpartum haemorrhage continue to rise and, worst of all, the budget for maternity services has effectively been cut by £80 million because of the removal of the ringfence. That funding would have paid for much-needed nurses, midwives and consultants, and dedicated safety funding has been gutted as a result. Will the Secretary of State restore that funding?

We will produce the first action plan on maternity services and reforms before Christmas. We will then continue with further work, including around the modern services framework and new standards for national maternity and neonatal care, because that is important. We are also investing in new capital funding for maternity units. I will gently point out to the hon. Member that her party was in government when the previous national framework of standards on maternity care was cancelled.

Let me focus on the issue of safe staffing, because it remains a critical problem. Just last week, the General Medical Council released a report outlining the pressures on obs and gynae trainees, who are more likely to report heavy workloads, feel short of sleep and have a higher risk of burnout. Our written parliamentary question has revealed that the number of midwives quitting early in their career has climbed, as 1,669 midwives under the age of 35 left the profession last year alone. We are still waiting for the workforce plan, which was originally promised for summer 2025. When will we receive it?

We already have an increased number—in fact, a record number—of midwives working in the NHS this year. That is important, so that we increase care and support for women during pregnancy. We are also providing investment for an additional 1,000 temporary roles to help newly qualified midwives join the NHS, to ensure we improve care for mums and babies at that critical time.

Carers and unpaid family carers will be at the heart of our national care service. We will publish a five-point plan for the social care workforce next month, setting out immediate steps to improve recruitment, retention and retirement and building on the announcements we have already made on fair pay and pensions. Last week, we were delighted to announce the appointment of my hon. Friend the Member for Shipley (Anna Dixon) as the Government’s champion for unpaid family carers. She will work directly with unpaid carers and support the continued delivery of the unpaid carers action plan, as well as shaping the new national care service.

I thank the Minister for that update. Last week I met a constituent who is the sole carer for her 56-year-old brother as well as for her elderly parents. She also organises Dancing with Dementia, a wonderful service in Westminster. I work closely with City Carers Community in the City of London, who are unpaid carers for their loved ones. I hear what the Minister has said about workforce planning, and I would be grateful for her comments on how we will be supporting the assessment process for care needs. That is something that many unpaid carers struggle with, and I know the Government want to see action taken.

I thank my hon. Friend for her question and—through her, if I may—thank the organisations she mentioned, which do great work with carers. On assessments, part of our work is to support social workers and others, to ensure we have the workforce we need as we move towards the national care service. I would be very happy to discuss that further with my hon. Friend.

The Minister will be aware of the tragic case of Matilda Davis, a parent-carer who did not get the support she needed after telling her social worker that she was having suicidal thoughts. After my hon. Friend the Member for Stratford-on-Avon (Manuela Perteghella) raised that case at Prime Minister’s questions, the Prime Minister committed to mandatory suicide prevention training for frontline social workers. It was the lack of that training that let Matilda down, yet a freedom of information request by her brother Joel has revealed that only three local authorities in the country are making it mandatory. With 41% of parent-carers at some point having thoughts of taking their own lives, will the Minister meet me and my hon. Friend so that we can discuss every opportunity to make good on the Prime Minister’s promise?

I thank the Chair of the Select Committee for that very important question. I will of course meet her, and I will also raise that point with Professor Louis Appleby, who leads our advisory group on suicide prevention. As we refresh the national suicide prevention strategy, we need to incorporate this important work.

I am hugely grateful to my hon. Friend the Minister and to the Secretary of State for the opportunity to represent the 6 million unpaid family carers in Government. I look forward to working with my hon. Friend and with hon. Members across the House to champion unpaid carers in this place. My hon. Friend will know that last week, Carers UK published its “State of Caring” survey. That survey identified that about one in three carers are not known to their GPs, so will she work with me to improve identification of carers by GPs and across the NHS?

I thank my hon. Friend for agreeing to take on her role—I know that all the unpaid family carers up and down the country will be at the top of her mind and at the heart of the work she is doing as we build the national care service. We ought to think about identification in the context of the remarks that the Secretary of State just made about protecting frail older people better. We cannot care for people unless we care for those who care for them.

Unpaid carers clearly pay a hugely important role in supporting so many people, but too often, they struggle to balance that with employment. Carers UK has suggested that each day, 1,500 people leave paid employment because they cannot get the balance right between their unpaid care duties and their employment duties. Will the Minister support the call of Carers UK and so many other carers’ organisations to introduce paid carer’s leave, to support unpaid carers to remain in employment while supporting their loved ones?

I thank the hon. Lady for her important question. Part of the purpose of building the national care service is to take some of that burden off family carers, so that they can get on with life and fulfil their hopes in employment and other areas, knowing that their loved one is cared for safely.
10. What steps she is taking to help reduce waiting times for elective and emergency treatment in Medway.

I thank my hon. Friend for meeting me recently with other hon. Friends to discuss the trust. I commend his work in supporting it. Whether it is elective or emergency care, we want all patients seen as quickly as possible. Despite record pressures for emergency care, more patients are being seen within four hours. In Kent and Medway, we have improved performance on the 18-week target from 59.8% to 63.9%, so more people are being seen more quickly. We are determined to improve performance further in Medway and across the country.

I thank the Minister for meeting us last week to listen to our concerns. Under the previous Government, accident and emergency waiting times soared. There has been increasing demand across the country, including queues at my local Medway Maritime hospital just yesterday. What more can be done to share best practice, including for improved corridor care, so that we do not see repeats of those queues going into the future?

I thank my hon. Friend for the work he is doing with the trust. The trust is working alongside NHS England to use oversight and expertise to improve conditions for patients and staff. There are also the many measures we have introduced to improve flow of patients from contacting primary care through the entire system. We will continue to do that to see sustained progress. His area has had some long-standing challenges that go back many years. We are committed, along with him and other hon. Members, to ensuring that that progress is sustained.

11. Whether she has made an estimate of the number of residents in England who are unable to access NHS app functionality for managing hospital appointments because they are registered with a GP in Scotland.

Arrangements for patients registered with a GP in Scotland while residing in England are made by the appropriate English and Scottish authorities. The NHS app is available to all patients registered with a GP practice in England. Patients registered in Scotland should use MyCare.scot.

I very much enjoy the convenience of the NHS app, but it strikes me as slightly ironic that I can use it to order a prescription and pick it up on the Scottish side of the border, just 8 miles from where I live, but my constituents living on the English side of the border cannot use the same app to book their NHS appointments. May I press the Minister for a date when the guidance governing cross-border care will be updated?

Arrangements on the Scottish border are made through service-level agreements between relevant bodies. These arrangements are expected to be reviewed following completion of the Health Bill to support greater consistency and alignment. I am happy to carry on our conversation at our planned meeting on Wednesday afternoon.
12. What steps she is taking to create a national care service.

The Prime Minister set out a vision for a national care service and Baroness Casey’s independent commission will recommend next summer how that should be taken forward. In the meantime, we are already taking important steps to strengthen support for unpaid carers and the social care workforce. Last week, as a down payment on the national care service, I announced how neighbourhood support teams would start coming together to support the most frail and vulnerable people in our communities.

I thank the Secretary of State for her answer, but does she agree that the best model for the national care service is one that is free at the point of delivery, just like the NHS, and funded by society as a whole, rather than through an adjusted triple lock?

The Prime Minister has set out a plan for free personal care, and that should have alongside it an adjustment to the triple lock, where pensioners will still see their pensions go up in line with inflation or by 2.5%. Pensions will also track wages. That is the right thing to do. The adjustment will also allow us to provide a better deal for elderly people, who currently face such huge pressures from social care bills in old age.

Delivering care to 50,000 people in urban Manchester is very different from the challenges of delivering care to 50,000 people in rural Cornwall or the Isle of Wight, which Policy Exchange calls “The Rural Penalty”. Does the Secretary of State accept that the system must be designed, and funded, to meet genuine challenges of geography, travel time and local need, rather than being based on population numbers alone?

The health service does need to respond to different communities and different conditions, in rural Britain and in coastal areas. As the hon. Member will know, that was reflected in the chief medical officer’s recent report, and we take it extremely seriously. We want more devolution so that we can ensure services are most effectively designed for the communities where people live. Neighbourhood support teams will be providing support at home rather than expecting people to travel long distances for care or health support.

We are, of course, still awaiting much of the detail of the Prime Minister’s proposed national care service. However, the Secretary of State must surely accept that if a third of people with dementia remain undiagnosed and many others with complex conditions are not yet accessing services, the £18 billion a year estimate for such a service is highly unlikely to reflect the true level of unmet need, and the eventual cost of the scheme will almost certainly be significantly higher than that advertised.

I look forward to the cross-party talks with the hon. Member, and I hope we can build some consensus on the need to create a national care service. Families across Britain have been let down for far too long, partly because political parties and Governments have turned away from this difficult issue rather than asking themselves, “What practical steps can we take? What can we do, step by step, with, for instance, the social care workforce and the neighbourhood support teams, to build services that better reflect today’s needs?”
13. What steps she is taking with the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions to support employers to prevent ill health.

Being able to work can be every bit as vital to our health as any treatment that we receive, which is why, alongside all the work being done by our colleagues in the Department for Work and Pensions, we are supporting access to talking therapies and to the healthcare that matters most for participation in work. Prevention starts with young people. Professor Fonagy’s review showed that there is more to do, and we will soon publish a new mental health strategy responding to the issues that he identified.

In 2023, when I sat on the Opposition Benches, I wrote a report called “Healthy Britain”, which set out a framework for a cross-Government, cross-sector approach to the health of the nation, with a particular focus on prevention and early intervention and a holistic approach to physical, mental and social wellbeing. I am delighted that the Labour Government have focused more on this agenda, but what are the Government doing to turbocharge that work so that, when possible, we can prevent people from becoming sick in the first place and build a strong, healthy nation with the many benefits—including, of course, economic benefits—that that brings?

I thank my hon. Friend both for the work that she did in opposition and for her continued championing of this issue. We have much more to do to create a healthier Britain, and she will have heard the comments of the Prime Minister and the Chancellor on the subject of prevention. This matters nowhere more than in mental health, and, as I have said, we will soon publish our strategy, which has been supported by colleagues across Government, including the Department for Education in respect of children’s mental health and the Department for Culture, Media and Sport in respect of participation.

Some of the most important work to help employers to prevent ill health in my constituency is carried out by the NHS veterans outreach service. Does the Minister agree that the reorganisation that has taken place in the NHS should not mean that those key personnel lose their jobs, and may I pay tribute to the campaigner Steve Summers, a Wellington veteran who has campaigned indefatigably to prevent those services from being cut?
That work sounds incredibly important, and I am sure that the decision makers in the hon. Gentleman’s area will have heard what he has said.
14. What steps her Department is taking to support women affected by diethylstilbestrol.

May I start by paying tribute to my hon. Friend for all her work on DES and for representing her constituent Jan Hall? My hon. Friend raised this issue at our last oral questions, and I can confirm that the review with the University of Exeter is moving forward, with the publication of protocols setting out how the research will be conducted. Its findings will then be reviewed by a clinical steering group, and will inform decisions on screening and guidance.

I thank the Minister for her answer. It appears that there is still no mammogram screening pathway for DES-exposed women, who are 30 times more likely to get breast cancer. These women require routine screening far before the age of 50. What steps has the Department taken since I last raised the issue of enhanced access and screening for DES-linked cancers?

My hon. Friend is right to raise this issue. To improve clinical awareness, the notice to cancer alliance directors was reissued on 26 October to ensure that affected women are identified and supported, in line with the existing guidance. My officials are engaging with NHS England on concerns about the guidance on DES not being easily accessible, and I would very much welcome a meeting with my hon. Friend and campaigners to hear directly about what more we can do.

I thank the Minister for her answers, and I thank the hon. Member for Bournemouth West (Jessica Toale) for bringing forward the question and outlining the dangers of DES, which was used from the ’40s to the ’70s. It is still being used in exceptional circumstances, but if there is a proven history of disease and people will unfortunately lose their lives, is it not the case that it should never be used?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for making that point. My understanding is that DES is not being used, but I will go away and seek advice from officials about that. Clearly, clinical decisions are made, but I will certainly get an answer for the hon. Gentleman.
T1. If she will make a statement on her departmental responsibilities.

This morning the UK Health Security Agency published new figures showing that 5,258 people died this summer due to extreme heat. That is three quarters higher than the previous record in 2022, and it is well over double the number of winter deaths last year. I offer my deepest condolences to all those who lost a loved one this summer. The numbers are a stark reminder of the human impact of climate change, which is why I have asked the NHS to prepare for summer as seriously as we do for winter, and why we have our new heat taskforce and an initial £32 million to provide better cooling and ventilation in hospitals. The unprecedented summer has increased the challenges for the NHS for the winter, so we are also investing £1.9 billion over several years in urgent and emergency care facilities, with 25 new and expanded urgent care schemes and centres open or due to become operational this winter, alongside the support for GPs to help care for people at home.

Next Monday, after a decade of campaigning by local people, the new Lace Hill health centre in Buckingham will finally open its doors to patients, and I pay tribute to the Swan Health team for all their work in getting this over the line. When I met them recently, one of the issues that they raised was their ability to hire the GPs and nurses that they need. Does my right hon. Friend have an update on how she is working with GP practices to ensure that they have the workforce they need?

I join my hon. Friend in congratulating Swan Health and Dr George Gavriel, who works at the practice. I also congratulate my hon. Friend on the role that he has played in campaigning and arguing for investment in this new, modern facility, which is so important to the community. We have already increased the number of fully qualified GPs by 10% over the past two years and, as a result of the work that we have done, there are 24 million additional GP appointments. My hon. Friend rightly points to the importance of the workforce, and we will continue to support them.

First, may I thank the Minister for Public Health and Patient Safety for correcting the record after our last Health and Social Care questions? Now that the Government are aware that people are waiting so long in A&E, I hope that we can see some improvements. Waiting lists more generally are rising and have been since Easter, and for those waiting for a procedure or an operation, the waiting list is higher than it was last month, last year and since the general election. Is the Secretary of State aware of that, and what is she going to do about it?

I can tell the hon. Member that 615,000 fewer patients are waiting over 18 weeks for non-urgent hospital treatment as a result of the improvements in elective performance since the general election. We have instigated a major turnaround programme after the Conservative party took this country from the lowest ever waiting lists to the highest ever waiting lists.

T3. This month, the all-party parliamentary group on fertility called for a national fertility strategy. We have heard about the realities and problems of accessing treatment, including the additional barriers faced by same-sex couples who have to pay privately for donor insemination before being considered on the NHS. Does the Minister agree with me that this gay tax must finally be ended, and will she meet me to discuss a national fertility strategy?

I pay tribute to my hon. Friend for her work as chair of the APPG on fertility, and I know that she has been raising a number of these issues for some time. As I set out in my earlier answers, work is under way to look at what is going on with ICBs at the moment, but I am of course always very happy to meet Members.

T2. Has the Secretary of State asked her officials for an up-to-date evaluation of whether the Humber and North Yorkshire integrated care board is able to deal with an extra 1,200 illegal immigrants who may be housed at Linton-on-Ouse, because three years ago the ICB said that it could not deal with an increase of that size?

I do not know the details of the issue the right hon. Member raises, but ICBs’ responsibilities extend to all their resident population, and we continue to work with Home Office Ministers on any such implications that may need to be dealt with to ensure that they can do so.

T5. Bradford’s A&E unit was designed to cope with 200 patients a day, but it now receives three times that number. Frankly, it is unacceptable that patients continue to be treated in cramped and outdated facilities, despite being promised a new A&E years ago. Bradford patients and NHS staff deserve way better, so will the Secretary of State meet me to agree a clear route to funding a new purpose-built A&E for Bradford?
As my hon. Friend knows, we are looking at a number of issues in Bradford and the wider area, and I am very happy to meet him to discuss them.

T4. Major estates failures at Stepping Hill hospital occur several times a year, which hospital leaders say is seriously disrupting care. Most of the estate is officially in a poor or bad condition, and too many patients are spending their final hours with the privacy of only a curtain as there are not enough side rooms. Will the Secretary of State visit Stepping Hill to see the challenge for herself, and will she set out a timetable for future funding decisions so that patients and staff know when essential rebuilding will take place?

I commend the hon. Lady, who is a strong campaigner for Stepping Hill. As she knows, there are other issues with the state of that estate. I think she is talking about end-of-life care in particular, and my hon. Friend the Minister for Social Care and Mental Health is looking at that, but I am happy to continue talking to the hon. Lady about how we can continue to improve that estate.

T6. I recently visited Greenwich & Bexley community hospice and heard how its budget for next year is likely to result in severe reductions in end-of-life palliative care. When the Minister for Social Care and Mental Health spoke at the Hospice UK conference recently, she set out some excellent goals for improving end-of-life palliative care. Does she realise, however, that unless hospices get extra funding urgently, as set out in the letter from Hospice UK to the Department of Health and Social Care this week, they will be unable to fulfil those pledges?
I thank my hon. Friend for that important question. I am extremely seized of the issue he mentions. We have a lot to do on end-of-life care, including on the important work that hospices do.

T8. For over 40 years, Princess Alice hospice in Esher has looked after my constituents in their final weeks and months of life, yet due to rising costs and with less than a quarter of its funding coming from the NHS, it is about to have to make £3.5 million-worth of cuts, which will affect services for my constituents. Will the Minister agree to meet me and other south-west London and Surrey MPs, so that we can talk about finding a sustainable way forward for Princess Alice hospice?

I am always happy to meet colleagues, and I have met a number of them already to discuss their hospices. I am happy to meet the hon. Lady, because, as I was just saying, this is an extremely important issue.

T7. My constituent Philip Scott recently passed away due to oesophageal cancer. This cancer is particularly prevalent in the north-west of England, yet access to testing remains a postcode lottery, with ICBs pointing to a lack of national guidance and sustainable commissioning. Will the Minister work to remove these barriers and support a co-ordinated roll-out across the north-west, with a view to making this lifesaving technology available more widely?

I recognise that access to capsule sponge testing remains variable, including across the north-west. The National Institute for Health and Care Excellence has now published draft guidance recommending sponge tests as an option for detecting the cancer. I can confirm that we will work with NHS England on implementation once final guidance is published. I am very happy to work with my hon. Friend to ensure north-west coverage.

T9. After our successful community campaign, the Helme Chase maternity unit in Kendal reopened two years ago, but it was closed for nine months because it could not be safely staffed with enough midwives. What is the Secretary of State’s plan to tackle maternity staffing shortages in rural areas to secure the long-term future of treasured units such as ours in Kendal?

The hon. Member makes an important point. This is an issue I have discussed with NHS England, because it is important that mothers in labour and women across the country do not have to travel huge distances. That means recognising that there are different pressures in rural areas. He is right that there have to be safe staffing levels. We therefore need to look more widely at what the NHS can do nationally to support areas that struggle to recruit, while recognising that the safety of mothers and babies is paramount.

Last week’s Health Committee report concluded that investment and funding arrangements are blocking GP practices from developing and expanding. I can concur with that. In my constituency, local GPs cannot employ extra clinical staff, including GPs, because of a lack of space, yet rooms in their practices are locked by NHS Property Services. Over at least 15 years, the NHS has not taken on the space that has been provided for GPs by residential developers in agreement with the planning authority. Is NHS Property Services fit for purpose?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for raising this issue. I very much expect that ICBs will work with local GPs to maximise the utilisation of NHS estates for the benefit of patients. I would be very happy to discuss this issue with her.

As of February this year, only 5% of the innovative medicines fund had been spent. Friedreich’s ataxia, Parkinson’s, Alzheimer’s and motor neurone disease—the list goes on—are all clinical conditions that desperately require further research and funding. What steps are the Government taking to release more of those funds, so that they can be spent sooner?

The hon. Member is absolutely right that this is a health inequalities argument at the heart of the innovative medicines fund. We are committed to securing rapid patient access to effective new medicines. We are also changing the funding responsibilities for medicines, exiting managed access with a consultation in early 2027. NICE evaluation is and remains vital, but this can help to speed up the process to access vital drugs in accordance with our plan.

The Women and Equalities Committee published two reports in the past year on cosmetic procedures. In addition to telling me when we might expect a response to those two reports, will Ministers tell us whether they intend to implement all the recommendations, including ensuring that only qualified plastic surgeons deliver surgical procedures?

I thank my hon. Friend and her Committee for the report. As she knows, I set out my initial responses in a letter on 27 October.
