We are currently engaged in a consultation on our proposals to introduce regulation in this sector, and the Government will respond shortly on the wider breadth of issues that the Committee has raised.

Thirty thousand women each year experience severe pregnancy sickness—hyperemesis gravidarum. My wife was told by NHS employees that she should not have got pregnant if she did not want to be sick. Women really need to be listened to within the NHS and get the support that they need. Will the Minister meet with me and the charity Pregnancy Sickness Support to discuss this further?

Let me say how sorry I am that the hon. Member’s wife was given that response. Clearly, all mothers should have proper support during pregnancy, and women and parents should be listened to. That is a critical thing that has come out throughout the maternity taskforce, and I will ensure that the hon. Member and campaign groups get a meeting with the Minister responsible for maternity services to pursue this further.

Steve Sharman, a resident in my constituency, is campaigning for better support for dads experiencing paternal post-natal depression, because, sadly, many men find it hard to navigate the system and support varies enormously from place to place. Will the Minister please outline what steps are being taken to improve the support available to dads like Steve?

The Minister with responsibility for men’s health and I are working together to ensure that perinatal services are more father-inclusive, and we will have more to say about it in the mental health strategy.

A constituent of mine was discharged from Leeds after a cancerous tumour removal, referred to the GP for wound care, and then referred by the GP to community support staff, who said they could not help—my constituent had to get a friend to do it. Will Ministers please speak to the ICB and ensure that post-operative wound care is available and stated before people leave hospital?
I would be grateful to talk to the right hon. Gentleman about that case and see what we can do to make clear what the provision should be.

After months of escalating symptoms, my constituent Georgia remains in significant pain with complex endometriosis, but requests for cross-border referral to specialist centres in England have been repeatedly refused. Does the Minister agree that location should never be a barrier to treatment, and access to specialist services in England for Welsh patients should be made available?
I absolutely agree and I am very happy to meet my hon. Friend to discuss the case he raises.

The Lobular Moon Shot Project has made a very modest request for an investment of £20 million over the next five years into lobular breast cancer research. I know that the Prime Minister is sympathetic to this, because he has said so. He also promised to meet people from the project last month. Will Ministers use their good offices to ensure that this meeting takes place, and will they confirm that they are interested in supporting this investment proposal?

Investment of this kind—embracing innovation in health and accessing speedier treatment or discovery—is absolutely part of the work of this Government. We would be happy to have further discussion with the hon. Member and related parties.

South Tyneside has one of the highest death rates from mesothelioma in the UK. I have been working with local NHS teams and Mesothelioma UK to establish a hub in my constituency, building on the excellent work of the existing multidisciplinary teams, yet my requests for a ministerial meeting have been unsuccessful. Will the relevant Minister please meet me?

Does the Minister welcome the Plaid Cymru Welsh Government’s intervention in the Betsi Cadwaladr health board today, with stronger oversight, new governance appointments and clear improvements targets, and does he recognise that addressing health equalities in north Wales will benefit communities on both sides of the border?

The City of Durham has been a growing dental desert in recent years. The latest practice to hand back its dental contract was Burgess and Hyder in Esh Winning, leaving thousands of patients concerned about where to turn for affordable local dental care. Will the Minister reassure my constituents that tackling the crisis in NHS dentistry remains a priority, and set out when exactly he will launch the overdue consultation on the new dental contract?

We are committed to improving access to NHS dentistry. Across the country, nearly 3 million additional NHS dental treatments were delivered in 2025-26 compared with the year before the 2024 election. Some 81% of those who wanted to access an NHS dental appointment received one, more than 50% of whom were children needing urgent treatment. We will build on this progress and will shortly be publishing the intentions for further reform of the dental contract.

My constituent Don, in Kings Langley, has been a taxpaying UK resident all his life. He is now retired and, like all pensioners, deserves to be able to use an NHS dentist. Notwithstanding what the Minister has just said about dental care, Don has been unable to register himself at any of the seven local practices despite three years of tireless effort. Will the Minister confirm that he will work cross-party and across the House to ensure that every constituent has access to first-class dental services?
The hon. Member is absolutely right and speaks to an experience that we will have all seen at constituency level. He has my full attention on this—I am very happy to look at the case in question.

The UK is renowned for medical innovation; indeed, it is a global hub. Does the Minister agree that the Birmingham health innovation campus is one of the best places to pull together academia, NHS and private research to provide novel solutions to complex medical problems?

I agree with my hon. Friend, who is a brilliant champion of his constituency. It was a pleasure to join him at a recent showcase of the life sciences work led by the University of Birmingham. Our life sciences action plan is a Government priority, with fast access to trials both a bid to end existing health inequalities and a growth initiative of this Government.

Yesterday, the Royal Devon university healthcare NHS foundation trust extended North Devon hospital’s maternity unit suspension for another two weeks. The Prime Minister and Health Ministers have stated that the maternity unit will reopen. Will the Secretary of State tell us what the Department of Health is doing to help the trust make that happen so that mothers do not have to travel for more than two hours to give birth?

As I said in response to an earlier question, NHS England is meeting the trust leadership every day in order to continue to support the trust and to ensure that pressure is maintained in order to get recruitment in place so that the unit can be safely staffed. That is critical, because everyone wants to see the unit opened as swiftly as possible.

This year’s GP patient survey, highlighted by the Alzheimer’s Society and reported in the Daily Mail yesterday, found that just 47.8% of respondents with dementia or Alzheimer’s disease felt confident managing issues caused by their condition, compared with 82% of those who have had cancer. What action will the Minister take to improve support for people facing dementia—the UK’s biggest killer—to close that confidence gap?

I thank my hon. Friend for her leadership on this issue. As she knows, we are soon to publish a new modern service framework on dementia, because diagnosis is one thing; getting people the care they need is another. We have to see improvements in all areas.

My constituents find it almost impossible to access NHS dental care. Will the Minister explain why, despite being provided with extra funds, the NHS is providing fewer dental treatments in Somerset than it was before the last general election?

I am acutely aware of some of the specific challenges faced in the south-west, particularly in Somerset. I would be happy to speak with the hon. Gentleman to ensure that he is involved in conversations about the plans that I am putting in place to address those issues specifically.

Health visitors are the universal safety net for babies and pre-school-age children, but the Department’s health visitor workforce figures, published in September, confirmed significant workforce losses, wide variation in provision, and growing pressures on services supporting babies, children and families. Will the Secretary of State outline what she is doing to address this unsustainable situation, and will she meet me and the Institute of Health Visiting to discuss this matter?

I thank my hon. Friend for her campaigning on this matter and will happily meet her to discuss it. The role of health visitors is incredibly important; I see it as the heart of the Sure Start health services that we are so determined to bring back.

It is Bereavement Matters Season, a national initiative led by the charity AtaLoss, which was founded in my constituency. Will the Minister commit to giving Bereavement Matters Season national recognition, which would embed greater awareness of grief and access to bereavement signposting across our health and social care system so that no one is left to grieve alone?
I thank the hon. Lady for, at the very least, giving that campaign national recognition by raising it in the House. I will consider the campaign as we move forward to improve end-of-life care.

The Minister will be aware that, earlier this month, the Public Service Ombudsman produced a report called, “Strengthening NHS wheelchair services: commissioning with confidence” on the need to improve NHS wheelchair services. What assessment has she made of the report? Will she meet me, in my role as chair of the all-party parliamentary group for wheelchair users, to discuss it?
I have met the ombudsman, which raised the report with me. I will happily discuss it further with my hon. Friend.

I realise that health is a devolved issue, but in NHS Grampian we have a serious issue developing. We have recently heard shocking revelations from two whistleblowers alleging that at least 19 avoidable deaths were covered up. Will the UK Government ensure that any investigation is truly independent and that the SNP will not be marking its own homework?

As the hon. Gentleman said, health is a devolved matter, but we obviously take whistleblowers’ allegations very seriously. I hope that the authorities in Scotland will deal with that in the proper way, give those whistleblowers the hearing they deserve and take the appropriate action.

Retired nurse Sarah Whitlow—granddaughter of Sir Alexander Fleming—came to see me last week. She asked me to find out what our Government are doing to counter the growing problem of antibiotic resistance.

I thank my hon. Friend for his excellent question. I will shortly join Health Ministers from around the world in Abuja at the conference on antimicrobial resistance. Resistance of that kind poses significant challenge. The Government are committed to playing their part where market failure has occurred and market incentive is required.

I welcome the Minister’s commitment to hospice care, but cuts are coming right now to the in-patient unit and home visits at Princess Alice hospice in my constituency. Will the Minister give that her most urgent attention?
I will. I am sure that all who work in hospices up and down the country will be most relieved that so many hon. Members have raised the matter of hospices today.

Sickle cell disease is the fastest growing genetic condition in England and Wales, affecting over 19,000 people. At a recent meeting, my local sickle cell patient support group spoke to me about many issues, including the bypass unit, community outreach and medical exemption certificates. Will the Minister please meet me to discuss that further?

Following the decision to extend Palantir’s contract for NHS England’s federated data platform, what assessment has the Minister made of comments made by Palantir’s founder Peter Thiel, publicly expressing hostility towards the NHS? Has he considered the serious concerns raised by Keep Our NHS Public about patient confidentiality and public trust?

I refer the hon. Member to the statement to the House last week in which the Government announced a new procurement of the NHS federated data platform. Services will continue until 2029, before the contract then ends. The FDP is here to stay. This is not a conversation about the politics of the providers’ executives or the territories of its other customers; it is about continuity of care. This is the right decision. The FDP principle is one to defend, not to attack.
To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office to make a statement on the UK civil service pension scheme and the performance of Capita plc.

Before I begin my response, I declare that I have a Capita pension from the Prison Service under the civil service pension scheme. We are aware of the announcement that Capita issued to the market yesterday, including on the appointment of its new chief executive officer, Pablo Andres. The Government routinely monitor the financial health of our strategic suppliers. It would not be appropriate for us to comment on the wider commercial position of Capita as a company, as that is a commercial matter for Capita and its shareholders. Capita’s performance on the pension scheme has had unacceptable impacts on people who have dedicated years of their working lives to serving this country, and they deserve better. We are using the most stringent commercial levers, including requiring deliverable plans and withholding payments under the contract that was signed under the last Government. To hold Capita to account, we mandated that it appoint an independent remedial adviser at its own expense. The report identified many weaknesses in Capita’s rectification planning, from technology implementation to its overall ambition, which fell well short of restoring the quality services that members deserve. To address that, I agreed with Capita executives that Cabinet Office officials would work with it to develop a credible, workable and realistic recovery plan for which Capita alone will be held to account. Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita’s systems and data to provide us with firmer assurance of the accuracy of the management information and to allow even stronger challenge on Capita’s direction and performance. I have put in place dedicated teams to work alongside Capita to agree priorities, improve quality and processes, and ensure that pensions are paid correctly. The new recovery plan is made up of five workstreams. They cover casework across every level of complexity, major statutory exercises, including the McCloud remedy, and the underlying technology and infrastructure needed to fix delivery. Rightly, we have required Capita to prioritise the oldest cases first, tackling the root causes in those legacy cases, and that is already unblocking similar queries across the system. That is why Capita is now issuing more quotes for complex cases that are less than three months old. Simultaneously, members with complex cases are now supported by a dedicated team and a specialist helpline. For non-complex cases, including retirement quotes, we have seen some improvement and, as I announced in my recent statement, there is now a fortnightly dashboard where members can view progress. Although that is some progress, there remains a lot more to do, and there are still too many people waiting on the pensions they are owed. I will continue to hold Capita’s management team to account and apply the strongest possible commercial levers under the contract to rectify the situation for those who still have not received the service that Capita should have already delivered.

Thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting this urgent question on such a critical matter. The Minister speaks well about the supposed progress, but we have been here before. On 22 April, we discussed this matter and the then Minister, the right hon. Member for Torfaen (Nick Thomas-Symonds), said all the same warm words. The sad truth is that for the 1.7 million members of the pension scheme, the situation is getting worse, not better. When Capita took over the contract, there were about 86,000 outstanding cases; there are now almost 160,000. It is worse than at the beginning of October. I have constituents who are suffering. The number of MPs in the Chamber today indicates that many have constituents who are suffering. We will hear from them, I am sure. It is not good enough, and I warned of the problems. I warned in April that the company faced a financial crisis and that the Government needed a plan B. I said then that the market value of the company was £350 million. It had debts of £500 million. Yesterday, the share price collapsed by 70%. The market value is now £75 million. The chief executive has resigned. The company talks about a rights issue of £190 million. It will be lucky. That is the reality. This company is a critical supplier to the Government. It has over 80 contracts—some £7 billion-worth—running over many, many years. They include the Ministry of Defence’s Army recruitment, Royal Navy training, the Department for Work and Pensions and NHS England. This company is too big to fail. We cannot face an equivalent of Carillion plc, but that is where this is going, and I worry. It is all very well saying that we must rely on the commercial company and the shareholders, but there is no guarantee that the shareholders will pony up. This company could well go bust in the next three months. The reality is that the Government need to have a plan B, a plan C and a plan D. That might involve ensuring that Capita can merge with another outsourcing company or underwriting the share issue, or it might have to involve taking it in-house. I look forward to the Minister’s comments.

I thank the hon. Member for bringing this important issue to the House today and for the questions that he has raised. On what has changed compared with six months ago, following the report of the remedial adviser, Grant Thornton, a new rectification plan was set up in conjunction with the Cabinet Office. Previously, Cabinet Office officials did not even have access to the Capita data and could not see for themselves what the picture was. That is now different, and we have full access to the Capita operation so that we are able to see what is happening with the civil service pension scheme. The rectification plan was built on the back of that, so I think that Members can have more confidence that transparency is there in a way that it was not before, and that we are therefore able to tackle some of the root issues. We still have nearly 150 civil servants from the surge team working with Capita. That has not changed, and it will not change until the pension scheme scenario improves. On the wider issue of contingency, the Government routinely monitor the financial health of all their strategic suppliers, particularly ones as big as Capita, and we work across Government to ensure that relevant contingencies are in place. I am not in a position to discuss that in detail in the Chamber, but that is now routine and lessons were learnt on the back of what happened with Carillion to ensure that the Government do not find themselves in that position again. Capita has up to this point been transparent with the Government and let us know what its position is. While that continues, we will work with it, but it would not be appropriate for me to go into the intricate details of the contingency planning in the Chamber now.

I actually feel sorry for the Minister, given her position. She has inherited a terribly difficult situation with Capita, a company that had previously failed to run pension schemes but was handed this scheme last December on a contract let by the previous Government. When the company took over the scheme, it clearly did not have the systems in place to run what is actually a fairly simple job: to administer and pay out pensions. I would just say to the Minister, as I said in the Public Accounts Committee some time ago, that I do not believe a word Capita says any more. If she is in that position as well, does she now recognise that there has to be a fall-back position, and that we have to look seriously at a plan to take this scheme in-house, because I do not think anyone in this Chamber believes that we are going to be in a different position in six months’ time if Capita carries on with it?

The remedial report identified that Capita did not have ready what it said it had ready when it took over the scheme. It said that it was going to have the biggest AI-enabled pension scheme ever known, and that clearly was not the case. Its performance has been abysmal, as I have said a number of times in this Chamber. I am not here to make excuses for its performance or for the position that it is now in. In relation to the future of the scheme and bringing it back in-house, it is our manifesto commitment to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and we have not moved away from that at all. My priority at this point is making sure that the service is restored as quickly as possible and that members get the pension they deserve, so I think we need to do everything we can to deliver for scheme members, and then we will look at the future of the pension scheme. As I have said before, we have officials working up different options for its future, as we are with procurement across Government in order to fulfil our manifesto commitment.

Will the Minister tell the House when she was informed of the resignation and what assurances she has received from Capita’s incoming chief executive that October’s recovery plan will not be derailed? Given Capita’s £85 million profit warning and £25 million in extra remediation costs, is the Minister still satisfied that it has the capacity and the resources that it will need to deliver the rectification plan? Last Thursday, I reminded the Minister that she had said five weeks ago that she expected to see visible improvements over the coming weeks. She replied that there had been “small” but insufficient improvements on some “complex cases”. Can she give the House any further update? Specifically, when will the 1,800 complex cases delayed for over a year, including bereavement payments and McCloud remedy cases, finally be cleared? What further contractual penalties or payment withholdings beyond the £10 million already retained will the Government impose? Why have the Government continued to hand Capita further contracts, such as Synergy, when it was already clear that it was failing in its existing commitments to pensioners? Will the Minister now use the powers introduced by the previous Government to consider whether Capita should be debarred from future contracts as a result of its failures? Finally, will the Minister now bring forward contingency plans for use if Capita is unable to fulfil its contract or if it becomes necessary to remove the contract because of its continued failure to deliver required improvements?

Capita has been open and transparent with the Government, and I was given information beforehand about the problems that it faced. That is in line with the agreements we have with Capita and all strategic suppliers on transparency in all Government contracts. It gave us and the permanent secretary pre-sight of that. As it stands, the rectification plan is still in place and will continue to run. We have been very clear with Capita that we expect the foot not to be taken off the pedal and that if we are to work to support it, it needs to continue to work on the rectification plan with Cabinet Office officials and the 150-strong surge team that we have put in place. I will continue to monitor that, as will officials, and if there is any change in the level of service, I will obviously address that with Capita and return to the House to set out the next steps. Capita still has significant resources from the Government, including the 150-strong surge team, the officials that are working on this every day and anything else that we can give the company to try to bring the service back up to a decent standard. As it stands, we believe that it has the resources it needs. We will continue to monitor the situation on a daily basis, and if there appears to be any change in its ability to deliver, or in the service that it is delivering, we will of course address that immediately. In relation to the 800 cases and the McCloud remedy, as I said in my recent statement, I will make sure that I update the House on McCloud before the end of the month, and that will happen very shortly. There has been a small improvement on the complex cases. I am happy to write to or meet the Opposition spokesperson to discuss the exact numbers, because I do not have them with me, but we are updating the dashboard on a fortnightly basis, and there is an explainer on the dashboard detailing the breakdown of which complex cases have and have not been dealt with. On debarment and procurement law, as I have said before in the Chamber, I am not in a position to say which companies, suppliers or contractors may or may not be considered for debarment, but as the whole House knows, that option is now available for the Government to consider in any circumstances, and general poor performance from suppliers is something that we can consider across Government when looking at issuing new contracts, in a way that we could not previously. On contingency planning, as I said in my initial response, we work with all strategic suppliers across Government and make sure that contingency planning is in place. Part of that is having transparency with suppliers—which, up to now, we have had with Capita—to allow us to put contingency plans in place. As I think I said in oral questions last week, we have been working on contingency in relation to the pension scheme, irrespective of the announcement that was made yesterday. For all the reasons that have been discussed in this Chamber many times, it would not be appropriate for me to go into the details of that, but it is being done in line with Government policy on having contingencies in place for all contracts of this nature.

I have taken up lots of cases of delayed civil service pensions that have led to severe hardship. It can also be very distressing for members of the scheme approaching retirement if they cannot obtain timely quotes on future pension entitlement. That can affect vital decisions for them and their families. I hear the Minister’s mention of improvements, but when does she expect that all pension scheme members will be able to receive timely quotes, so that they can plan ahead?

I concur with my hon. Friend: the service from Capita has been appalling. I will not make any excuses for that today, or on any day. There is an improvement in non-complex, business-as-usual cases being seen in under 30 days, but there is still a big backlog of complex cases, giving us a mixed picture. I said to the House recently that I expect to see significant improvements by the end of this month and before Christmas. We will continue to monitor that, and will return to the House with an update if Capita’s performance does not appear to be moving in the right direction.

Civil servants have given years, often decades, of service to this country. They planned their retirement carefully, and they deserve to know that the pension that they earned will arrive on time. However, almost a year after Capita took over the civil service pension scheme, far too many of them still cannot be sure of that. The problems remain. In just the past couple of weeks, yet another constituent, Karen from Offerton, contacted me because she has been waiting for more than two months for her pension, despite providing six months’ notice before retiring. Karen currently has no income. She has repeatedly been in contact with Capita, as her initial quote was incorrect, but Capita has failed to say when it will fix it. That is yet another example of Capita’s failure. We have discussed these issues many times. Does the Minister feel that she has the tools she needs, through the Procurement Act 2023 or other legislation, to hold Capita properly to account and to get this situation sorted, or is she seeking additional powers?

I thank the hon. Member for her contribution. I will continue to work with her and other Opposition spokespeople on the issue. If she wants to write to me about the case she raised, I would be happy to look at it. On the tools at our disposal, we have used all the contractual levers we can, and we will continue to do so. Capita has now been transparent, and has allowed our officials access to all the information that we need. This is a difficult situation for all our scheme members. Before we look at any other options that may cause future disruption, the priority has to be the option that most benefits them, and gives us the best chance of getting the scheme up and running to a good standard for members. I am working on this issue every day, as is the Cabinet Office. Capita is under no illusions about the fact that we expect it to continue to work, day and night, to improve its performance on the contract.

I declare an interest as the chair of the Public and Commercial Services Union parliamentary group. I thank the Minister for the hard work that she has put in, and for the open access that she has given to the trade unions. May I say, as an aside, that I think the Opposition have some front to come here and be critical, having signed the contract themselves? After this long period of failure by Capita, it is time not only to reject the ludicrous suggestion that we give the contract to another outsourcing company, but to take up the civil service union plan of bringing the administration back in house as fast as possible. We could then look at the technical and computer solutions that are needed; the plan would give us the breathing space to do that. This is now a matter of urgency. We need to go back to the solid administration of a directly provided service.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his engagement with me on this matter. As I have said previously, all Government Departments routinely do contingency planning in relation to strategic suppliers, and this case is no different. I want to ensure that what we do now is in the best interests of scheme members, and we are working with Capita to ensure that the situation for scheme members improves as quickly as possible. He knows my views. He knows that I am committed to the Labour party 2024 manifesto, and so to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation; I have not moved away from that, and neither have the Government. However, in this initial period, we need to ensure that scheme members are the priority, and that services resume for them as quickly as possible.

May I thank the Minister for briefing my Committee properly, and the Government for changing the tax rules on lump-sum payments within a week of my raising it in the debate on the Budget? That will provide some reassurance to pensioners in the scheme. We are about to approach the 12-month anniversary of the scheme going live. Sadly, there have been some tragic and dreadful cases in that time. I heard of one poor lady who was living on benefits because she could not get the bereavement payments she needed after her sister’s death. I have heard of a member of parliamentary staff, not far from this Chamber, who is having to delay his retirement by a year because he cannot even get a statement from the scheme. If the rectification plan does not work, what further steps can the Minister take? For understandable reasons, she does not want to discuss that in the Chamber this afternoon, but if the worst happens and, for some reason or another, Capita cannot carry out the remainder of this contract, she must have a proper contingency plan in place.

I thank the hon. Member for his engagement with me and the Department on this matter. He rightly highlights some of the truly tragic cases that have come to light as a result of Capita’s failure. I have said before in this House that it should be absolutely ashamed of its performance. We have seen evidence that it has stepped up in recent months and begun to rectify the problem, but it is inexcusable that it let the situation get to this point. My position on that has not changed. On contingency planning and what further steps we can take, I have to be careful about what I say in the Chamber, as the hon. Member understands. It is important that we stabilise the situation and that Capita can continue to deliver the pension scheme. However, I assure him that the Government are working across Departments, as we do in relation to all strategic suppliers, to ensure that the relevant contingency plans are in place. People are working around the clock on that.

The Minister was right when she described Capita’s administration of the civil service pension scheme as unacceptable, and I want to offer her a few Mid Derbyshire-centred insights from my burgeoning bag of casework on the issue. Gary was due to retire following a brain injury. He was a civil servant at the Department for Work and Pensions, and had asked for his pension calculation three months before he retired; it has not been forthcoming, and the case has been going on for more than a year. Helen’s partner, who died, was also a civil servant. The pension arrangements were supposed to support Helen with some money, but she is living off her savings. Both cases have been going on for over a year, and my caseworker Emily is tearing her hair out. Will the Minister make the case to Capita that the human reality of its failure to deal with these issues is that it is causing misery all over the country?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising the very real hardship that has been faced as a result of Capita’s failure. I certainly do not want Emily to tear all her hair out, so we will definitely continue to work at pace to resolve the situation. I have met the Capita executive team regularly since I took up this post, and will meet the new chief executive very shortly. I will continue to relay the day-to-day impact of its performance on people’s lives. These are not just numbers; they are people’s realities. My hon. Friend highlighted that very well. I assure him, his caseworker and his constituents that I will not let up on ensuring that Capita faces the realities of its failure.

I am grateful to the Minister for her answers so far. What practical steps can older people affected by this scandal—particularly the bereaved, and those who are not au fait with computer technology—take when they receive, alongside their payments, what one of my constituents describes as a very confusing letter? Is it not understandable that, after this fiasco, people lack confidence in the accuracy of the calculations? Is there a non-technological way that people can check that accuracy?

I thank the right hon. Member for raising that important point. In November, Capita was writing to everyone who has a complex case, to detail where their case was in the system. That was a written letter. There is of course a phone line as well. Phone line waiting times are probably one of the biggest successes that Capita has had in recent weeks, and most phone calls are now being answered in under 30 seconds, so that would be another way that members could contact Capita to find out the status of their case, or if they have any queries. Of course, if he wants to write to me about any particular cases, I am happy to look at them.

Despite improvements that the Cabinet Office have made, my caseworkers and constituents are experiencing a dreadful lack of communication from Capita. Even when some payments are made, there is often no paperwork or explanation. People are being left in the dark; it is a disgrace. What is the Minister doing to ensure that Capita communicates properly with our constituents?

I know my hon. Friend has been diligently campaigning on this issue in recent weeks and months on behalf of many of her constituents who have been affected. On the communication, anyone with a complex case should have had a letter already from Capita this month, or will get one in the next week, as it committed to writing to everyone with a complex case, setting out their situation. When I meet the new chief executive very soon, I will feed back on the need to ensure that paperwork and communications are issued with payments, so that people have the breakdown. We still have the surgeries for Members, which caseworkers and Members can attend to get an update from Capita or the Cabinet Office on the status of a case. I appreciate that people do not always get the answer that they want, but hopefully that will provide reassurance about where the case is in the system.

I would like to ask about the procurement process, because right now, a supplier can be in breach of contract, have money withheld every month, miss most of its targets and still bid on other Government contracts. What conversations are taking place in Government on revisiting those procurement guidelines, and ensuring that the debarment thresholds are not too high, so that a provider that is clearly failing cannot secure other Government contracts?

The Procurement Act 2023 provides Government with the statutory power to launch a formal investigation that can lead to debarment, either for severe breaches of contract or for poor performance. That is different from what happened before; it allow us to take into account poor performance, and not just technical ways that a company has failed. I am not in a position to confirm or deny whether a supplier is under active consideration for, or subject to, a debarment investigation, but I reiterate that it is an option that Government now have when there is poor performance by any strategic supplier.

I thank the Minister for the sterling work she has done. This is undoubtedly a poisoned chalice. Capita’s running of this pension scheme has brought so much misery and despair to many tens of thousands of people—many of them hard-working people on the lowest of low wages. Does the Minister not agree that a red line has been crossed? Would she think about convening an emergency meeting with all those concerned, including the PCS union, to discuss bringing the entire contract back in House?

As I have said, the performance of Capita has been totally unacceptable, and it is nothing that any public servant or anyone in this House should expect; we would not accept it among ourselves. I have had a meeting with PCS and all the other unions that represent members who have been affected by this since I came to office, and I am happy to continue having those meetings, to keep people updated on where we are. We committed in our manifesto to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, and sitting next to me is the Minister for procurement, my hon. Friend the Member for Gateshead Central and Whickham (Mark Ferguson), who is working on this closely across Government. My priority at the minute, as I said, is ensuring that we get pension scheme members their money as quickly as possible, and I do not want to cause any further disruption to that. I am keen to ensure that this rectification plan works, and that Cabinet Office officials and our 150-person surge team remain working with Capita on the scheme to ensure improvement as soon as possible; and then, of course, we will continue to fulfil our manifesto commitments.

The private sector does not always get it right, but neither does the public sector. In this case, the private sector has gone badly wrong and is causing huge financial hardship for my constituents and for people up and down the country. I congratulate the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) on securing this urgent question and thank you, Mr Speaker, for granting it. It is concerning that a company that is clearly failing has 80 Government contracts. That should be of severe and grave concern for the Government. When contracts like this are awarded to the private sector, there clearly needs to be more competition and more choice. We should look at where the contract is given and whether it should be in the public sector. If it should, I will support it. I am not ideological. What my constituents want is delivery and—to quote the Prime Minister—pragmatism. At the moment, constituents are spending hours on the phone—60 hours in one case—quotes are wrong when they come, and payments are severely delayed, causing many people financial hardship. I will reference one constituent, Mr Mark Churm of Apley, who has given consent for me to raise his case. Many people in my constituency are suffering right now, but would the Minister please look at his case at least?

I would be more than happy to look at the case the right hon. Member raises. If he writes to me about it, I will personally look at it and get back to him as soon as possible. On the contract and further steps we could take, we have a new public interest test coming in from April and, obviously, the Procurement Act 2023, as I have mentioned in previous answers, gives Government more scope to monitor poor performance. I agree that we need more competition, and I refer him to the speech made by my right hon. Friend the Member for Sheffield Heeley (Louise Haigh) about ensuring that we have sufficient public control in markets so that we do not find ourselves in situations like this with public essentials.

Nearly a year on, Capita’s failures are still causing uncertainty for people approaching or already in retirement after years of serving in our civil service in good faith, including at MOD Abbey Wood in Filton. Could the Minister please set out what powers remain available to the Government under the contract, including formal step-in powers, and what would it take for the Government to use them?

We have currently withheld nearly £10 million in contractual payments due to failure, and Capita has taken a voluntary 10% reduction in its monthly payments from Government, so we will continue to monitor that. I am not in a position to discuss step-in powers at this time. I go back to my earlier answers: we are working across Government to ensure that the relevant contingencies are in place for all our strategic suppliers, and Capita is no different given the announcement yesterday. We will continue to work to ensure that pension scheme members experience as little disruption as possible.

Significant numbers of my constituents have been badly affected by Capita’s failures. I have raised this in the Chamber before, and my caseworkers have done lots of work on this. It is an outsourcing omnishambles, frankly. The Minister has set out the steps she is trying to take to sort this out, but fundamentally it highlights a bigger issue: outsourcing is not working and it does not work. The Minister said the performance of Capita has been “totally, totally unacceptable”. In this context, why are the Government still signing new contracts with Capita, such as the recent UK Health Security Agency contract? She has talked about the Government’s commitment to a wave of insourcing, but where is the timetable? Surely it needs to happen now so that we have no more of these failures.

On insourcing, a new unit has been set up and is working with different Departments on insourcing strategies for contracts across Government. That work is ongoing, and I know the Minister for procurement will report back on that when he is ready to update the House. On bringing the Capita contract in-house, I sympathise with the hon. Member’s position—as someone who signed up to Labour’s 2024 manifesto commitment on insourcing, it is my ideological position as well—but I do not want to do anything that will lead to further or increased disruption for scheme members. We are seeing some improvements—I will not overstate them as it is not for me to defend Capita—on, for example, complex cases coming down, phone line answering and some of the business-as-usual non-complex cases. The improvements are not enough, and I continue to hold Capita’s feet to the fire to see further performance improvements, but the scheme members have to be our priority in the coming weeks and months, to get service up to a good standard, and then we can work on what comes next.

My constituent David Ferriday gave 30 years of service to the Crown, and despite retiring roughly six years ago, he says he has still not been able to retire properly because of Capita’s abject failure in the administration of his civil service pension. With dozens of case reference numbers, unexplained payments and no meaningful communication, he feels completely failed by this process. Will the Minister intervene directly in cases like David’s? Does she agree that this kind of gangster capitalism is exactly why outsourcing always fails the public, and that we should not let Capita anywhere near any future Government contracts?

I am sorry to hear of the experience of my hon. Friend’s constituent. I am more than happy to look at that case personally if he writes to me, and I will make sure it is actioned. He highlights Capita’s generally abysmal performance and, as I say, I will make no excuses for Capita in this House or any other forum. It has shown that when competition is insufficient and contracts are signed that potentially should not have been or the relevant checks are not done, as was the case under the last Government, we find ourselves in this position. But this Government are committed to making sure that this scheme gets into a far better position for scheme members, and we are, of course, committed to the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation.

The Minister has referred to complex cases on several occasions. I have a number of such case among my constituents, and they are clearly causing very serious problems. The Minister referred to her officials now having full access. Are the Minister and her officials satisfied that sufficient resources are being put into dealing with complex cases?

The Cabinet Office and the Government have given a huge amount of resources and that will continue to support the scheme and get the service to a good level. I am more satisfied now than I was when I started this job that Capita is putting in sufficient resources. It has stepped up its game. There is a question to be asked about why it did not put more resources in sooner, and that is something I am sure will be discussed long into the future. The priority now is making sure that the resources of both Capita and the Cabinet Office are used to their maximum potential. As it stands, there is sufficient resource, but both Capita and the officials need to crack on to make sure we get those numbers down.

I thank the Minister for her statement and for all her work to try to get this contract back on track. Like so many MPs, my office has a number of bits of casework relating to Capita, and one of the really frustrating things is the capacity we are having to use as MPs to push these cases along for our constituents—constituents like Linda, who has been waiting almost a year for her pension—because of the timeline for complex cases. Could the Minister provide an update on when our constituents should expect to get a resolution and when payments will start to be made to those with complex cases?

I totally sympathise with the strain this has put on many constituency offices; I have also had a lot of casework in relation to Capita’s failings on the pension scheme. I am a little reluctant to put dates and deadlines on things, because that has happened before and then they were not met, but the approach has changed: we are now looking at the oldest cases first, which tend to be the most complex and therefore could take many hours or sometimes even days to resolve. That is why it may seem that some cases have taken a lot longer than others. I am hoping that, by having that member-led approach and starting with the oldest and most complex cases, more cases will be resolved more quickly as solutions get identified. I have said previously in the House that I expect to see significant improvement in weeks and certainly in a small number of months.
Order. Everybody has a case to be told. We need to try to speed up, so that everyone can at least get their name on the record. We will have a first test of that—I call David Chadwick.

My constituents are also facing lengthy and arduous fights to secure their own money from Capita, which we all agree has made a huge mess. Will the Minister commit to ensuring automatic compensation for affected constituents?

Compensation can be sought through the usual route, through the Pensions Ombudsman, which I know some members are already pursuing. I am happy to write to the hon. Member separately about how his constituents can pursue that. Interest is applied to all delayed pension payments from Capita, and that is done automatically by Capita when people receive their money.

My constituent who formerly worked at Kew Gardens waited nine months for his pension lump sum. I am very glad to report that he finally received his payment last week, which I hope is a sign that the Minister’s relentless focus on Capita’s performance is finally achieving progress. Will she continue to pull out all the stops to ensure that the other cases I have raised with her Department receive the payments they are due without further delay?

I thank my hon. Friend for her update and a little bit of good news. I can assure her that I will continue to work every single day to make sure that Capita is held to account and push to improve its performance. While some progress has been made, there is a huge amount of progress still to make, and until Capita is working within the agreed performance indicators that were set out in the contract, as far as I am concerned, the job is not over.

I have a constituent who is left with less than £100 a month because of Capita’s mistakes. Capita simply cannot be trusted to handle people’s lives or their money. I will not put words in the Minister’s mouth, but reading between the lines, I expect that she does agree with me and the rest of the House. Can she confirm that Capita will not be granted any further contracts? The public do not trust them, and neither should the Government.

I do agree with the hon. Member that Capita’s performance is abysmal, unacceptable and everything else that everyone in the Chamber has said today. With regard to other contracts, that is not something I can personally commit to in the Chamber—I am not overseeing the decisions that all Departments make—but I refer her back to the Government’s new powers under the Procurement Act 2023 to investigate poor performance and look at debarment. They are a new lever at our disposal.

I thank the Minister for her assiduous attention—she has been quite superb—and I declare my interest as a member of the PCS parliamentary group. In last week’s Westminster Hall debate on the Department for Work and Pensions’ Synergy contract, the Under-Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, the hon. Member for Nottingham South (Lilian Greenwood), cited the costs and risks of reversing existing outsourcing arrangements, but today’s events show the costs and risks of continuing with these outsourced contracts. I know that the priority is getting people paid, but surely the Minister must now task the insourcing unit with examining both the civil service pension scheme and the Synergy contract and developing plans to rebuild the skills, expertise and operational capacity within the civil service necessary to bring these essential functions back in-house.

On the insourcing of the scheme and contracts more widely, we have a new insourcing unit that the procurement Minister is leading on. On the scheme itself, we want to ensure we prioritise scheme members and their needs. As I said in my statement, we have already begun to look at different options for the future of the scheme and I will be receiving advice on that in the not-too-distant future, alongside and in parallel to ensuring Capita continues to pull its socks up a lot higher and delivers for scheme members across the country.

Capita is a reverse Midas: whether on the civil service pension scheme, medicals for armed forces recruitment or a plethora of other contracts across Government, it has repeatedly failed. Will the Minister confirm whether conversations have been had with the senior executives at Capita so that they will not be allowed to fail upwards any longer, and that no further contracts will be even entertained until Capita has sorted out the ones it already has?

As I have set out in previous answers, the Procurement Act 2023 allows Government to take into account previous performance. I have met Capita executives on multiple occasions since I became the Minister for this portfolio, and I made clear in no uncertain terms that their performance is wholly unacceptable. The chief executive officer has now gone and my office is currently arranging for me to meet the new CEO in the coming days. I will be repeating exactly the same to them: improved performance is absolutely imperative, and if there is any sign that they decide to take their foot off the pedal in relation to resolving the civil service pension scheme and improving the service, I will continue to ensure that there are consequences.

I thank the Minister for all her hard work on this matter since she picked up the poisoned chalice. Despite that, things are simply not getting better for many people. A constituent of mine, in her 90s and with dementia, has been waiting 14 months for her late husband’s civil service pension payment to be processed. Paperwork has been lost and there have been repeated assurances, but no action, just more hardship and distress. She is unable to pay her care home fees and her family are getting more and more concerned. Will the Minister intervene to bring this hardship and others to an end, using every possible lever?

I am desperately sorry to hear the circumstances of my hon. Friend’s constituent. If she writes to me with the details, I will take it up directly. It sounds like a case that should have been resolved before 1 September, so I am more than happy to take that up and ensure Capita deals with it as soon as possible.

I believe that the Minister deserves credit for the attention she is giving to this issue. I was grateful whenever she made Cabinet Office officials available to deal with individual cases, but I was appalled when I met those officials: they had had no access to the correspondence that we had shared, and they had no knowledge that my constituent had sought a forecast in January, retired in April and had not received a penny for six months. I was grateful that that case was resolved, but it should not have taken the conflict of that call and my disappointment to see progress. I have another constituent who is in the same position, but has been waiting one year for any payment at all. Does the Minister believe that Capita will still be in a position to resolve this issue and the many tens of thousands of others across the United Kingdom, or should it just go?

I am sorry to hear about the experience that the right hon. Member had. I will speak to him afterwards to find out the date of his meeting, so that we can get to the bottom of why the information had not flowed between the two. We definitely want to ensure that the surgeries we are holding are as smooth and efficient as possible, so I am sorry to hear that was not the case. If he writes to me, I am happy to take up the other case he raises. Capita will be delivering on this contract: it has been paid to do a job, so it does not get to just walk away and leave everyone else to clear up the mess. I will continue to push every single day. I will meet the new executive and make absolutely clear my expectations on what Capita will deliver and the progress it will be making, alongside looking at future options.

It has been heartbreaking to see the frankly impossible position that too many of my local civil service pension holders have been put in by Capita’s complete mismanagement of the scheme. It should clearly never have been given the contract by the last Government. I am grateful for the Minister and her Department’s support in driving forward some improvement, but it is clear that there is more to do. As we rightly prioritise getting more of my constituents their long overdue pensions, how can we ensure lessons are learned, so that we do not see future failed outsourcing that leaves my constituents picking up the pieces again?

In line with our manifesto commitment to have the biggest wave of insourcing in a generation, the procurrent Minister has set up an insourcing unit, working across Government to look at plans for how every Department can insource more services. That is where we are at now: there are too many examples of lack of competition and market failure letting people down time and again.

May I start by thanking the Minister for her clear dedication and the work that she is putting into this issue? I am sure the whole House appreciates it. The Minister will only be aware of the information that she receives, so I bring her attention to the fact that my team tell me that the dedicated casework clinic that they use has very little effect. Will the Minister take a close look at that clinic, see if it is worthwhile and bang some heads together?

I will check in with the casework clinic when I leave the Chamber to ensure it is working as effectively as possible. One issue is that the casework clinic can sometimes just update where a case is in the system, which is not necessarily where someone wants it to be. Staff at the clinic can at least give an honest answer about where a case is stuck in the system, even if they cannot resolve that, which I know can often lead to disappointment that we cannot move things forward straight away. I will take that away and see if we can be any more effective in how those casework surgeries are being delivered.

I thank the Minister for her support on the Exeter cases that I have raised with her. However, we are still seeing waits of over two months for some of those cases. Some of them are simple admin changes, but more importantly some of the cases are people with life-limiting or very severe illnesses. Will the Minister set out how Capita is prioritising the most vulnerable and time-essential cases that we need to solve?

Absolutely. Capita should be prioritising the oldest cases as well as cases of significant urgency, particularly where there is significant ill health. If my hon. Friend wants to write to me with the specific cases that are not being actioned, I will take them up as I have done with other correspondence. Anyone who is facing a life-limiting illness should be in a priority case load and Capita should be dealing with it as soon as possible.

I thank the Minister for her thorough answers and evident dedication. Jill Hughes MBE of Nefyn received a civil service pension until her death last December. Some 11 months later, her widowed husband David has yet to receive the dependant’s pension, even though Capita admits the case is not complex. Mr Hughes is now in a care home and he is at a financial loss directly because of Capita’s inaction. It appears to be civil service pension and UK Government policy not to pay interest on delayed payments to bereaved dependants for a number of months. Does she agree, therefore, that this looks very much like an incentive for a profiteering organisation to delay payments, even in non-complex cases?

I thank the right hon. Member for raising that particular issue. I will take up with Capita the issue of not paying interest: it should be paying that alongside the payment, particularly when lump sums are issued and have been delayed. That has been agreed, so I will take that up with Capita after the statement has finished.

First it was the £90 million contract with the Ministry of Justice, which failed to deliver interpretation services in our courts. Then it was the £1.3 billion contract with the Ministry of Defence, which failed every year to meet recruitment targets in the Army. Now it is the civil service pension scheme fiasco, costing the Cabinet Office some £239 million. Wherever we look, the previous Government signed up to public contracts that effectively fleece the taxpayer, so my question is very simple: what will the Minister do to ensure that this track record of failure, which sits specifically with Capita, is ended once and for all?

I thank my hon. Friend for the points he has raised. For exactly the reasons he highlights, this Government have set up an insourcing unit specifically to look across Government at different contracts in different areas of Government service, so that we can look to insource in the future. Capita’s performance has been totally unacceptable, and we will not be letting it off the hook. It needs to deliver and it needs to deliver fast.

Karen Allum and Janette Woolgar are just two of several of my constituents who face several months of delays in their payments. For the sake of all of them, what deadline has the Minister given Capita to get this right and have a reasonable service standard? On the question of compensation, with such widespread failure affecting so many people, is it reasonable that they will all have to go through additional hurdles? Can the Minister insist on some kind of standardised and easy-to-access compensation for those experiencing such significant delays?

I thank the hon. Member for the points that he has raised. I will take the compensation issue away with me after this urgent question. At the minute, the primary focus is on trying to get money out the door to scheme members and to get the scheme up and running, but I understand the point that he raises. A huge number of people will want compensation as a result of this issue, and that needs to be managed effectively. I will take that point away and discuss it with officials. At an appropriate time, I will be able to update the House on that, but my priority now is ensuring that people such as Karen and Janette can get their pension.

A wife with a husband who retired with early-onset dementia should never have had to face delays. A mam who is a guarantor on her daughter’s house and facing financial insecurity should never have faced delays. I am certain the Minister knows that this is not just about the contractual or administrative failure of Capita; it is about families’ dignity, wellbeing and financial security. Will she assure this House and my constituents that the Government will use all the new powers to ensure that Capita is awarded no further Government contracts?

I really sympathise with the words of my hon. Friend. We hear so many heartbreaking stories; I have seen so many of them in my own constituency and in the correspondence that I receive. I assure her that the Government will use all the levers at their disposal when looking at how we contract out Government services in the future, and that is why we have the insourcing unit.

Like everybody else in this House, I have a long list of cases of people who have been treated appallingly by Capita. I thank the Minister and the civil service team for everything that they are trying to do in coming up against the ineptitude of Capita, which its own staff are also hit by. It strikes me that all those people are sitting at home today, and what is going through their minds is not whether Capita will get any more contracts, the insourcing or whether that will be the new Government practice; it is what will happen to their pensions and whether they are in safe hands. That is the question they will want to be answered today, and they need reassurance about it. Can the Minister give that?

I believe that I should wish the hon. Member a very happy birthday. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear!”] I completely understand the concerns that she raises on behalf of her constituents. I can provide her with the assurance that, as with all strategic suppliers, the Government work across all Departments to ensure that we have good contingency plans in place for any eventuality. That is not just with Capita, but with all strategic suppliers, so Capita is no different. As she will know from my previous statement, we are already looking at contingency because of the state that the pension scheme was in, but the priority is making Capita continue to improve on its service so that we can get money to people as quickly as possible.

Alarm bells were ringing last week when Capita told my constituents waiting on delayed payments that interest on those payments would not be automatic and would be taken on a case-by-case basis. Can the Minister reassure us that interest on delayed payments will not be jeopardised by Capita’s rapid share price fall over the weekend? What material actions is she taking to build up in-house capacity so that the Government can finally reverse this Tory legacy outsourcing?

The Cabinet Office and I have been very clear that we expect that, despite the announcement yesterday, there will be no change in Capita and the service that it is expected to deliver in relation to the pension scheme. As my hon. Friend will know from previous statements, the Cabinet Office is looking at all the different options for the future of the pension scheme, and I will report back about that at the appropriate time. I know that he has campaigned really hard on this matter.

Order. This urgent question is already an hour long, but I am conscious that we all have constituents badly affected by this issue. I will endeavour to get everyone in, but it would be very helpful if we could have short questions and answers. I call Sammy Wilson.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker—I was just about to sit down. May I thank the Minister for the action that she has taken and the access that we have to Cabinet Office officials and to Capita? In fact, only this morning, Helen—a constituent of mine—had her case resolved after nine months. Despite the promises that we have had of significant improvements almost every time this issue has been raised, thousands of people still find themselves in a situation where they cannot get their pension. Although I have no ideological opposition to outsourcing the services of Government, is it not the case that Capita has been so chaotic in this contract, and Government action to change that has been so ineffective, that we really have a case to say, “Bring this in-house”?

I am glad that the right hon. Member has had some good news this morning from one of his constituents. Although I am heartened to see that there has been some small progress in delivering the scheme, I am very aware that there is a lot more to do, and we continue to fight for that every day. With the contract itself, the priority must be no further disruption for members. We are working towards that every day, but, alongside that, as I have said before, we are looking at how the future scheme could be delivered, and the insourcing unit is looking across Government at how we can better procure insourced contracts in different Departments.

Outsourcing has clearly failed. The Minister has said that the Government have worked with Capita on a workable and realistic recovery plan on which it will be held to account, but, beyond Capita sending correspondence to my constituents saying that their cases are complex and signposting them to an internet page, nothing has got better. I realise that she is doing an extremely hard job, but will she emphasise in her meeting with the new CEO of Capita that the current system is just not working for my constituents?

I assure my hon. Friend that I will not hold back when I meet the new Capita chief executive about my expectations, the expectations of the Government and the expectations of the whole House for what we want to see from them in this contract. They will be left under no illusions, just as the last one was not.

I will not hold back either. There has been a lot of praise for the Minister today, but every day the situation is getting worse. It is a year ago this month that this Government decided to hand over the contract to Capita, even though the waiting list had grown to 86,000 with MyCSP and the Cabinet Office, in which the Minister sits, knew that Capita did not have the technology in place to take on the contract. This Government made that decision and are responsible, and John from Withernsea is still waiting, seven months on. After 30 years in the Prison Service, he has not received a penny or even a quote, and this Government should apologise. Does the Minister agree?

I am sorry to say that I do not agree. The right hon. Gentleman should look at his own party and the last Government, which signed off the levers that this Government have available. The decision taken to hand the contract over at the time was— [ Interruption. ] It was the best option on the table at the time, because of yet another poor contract that was signed by the last Government. I accept that this is a terrible situation for all scheme members. I was a prison officer, and many of my own former colleagues get in touch with me about this issue, and it absolutely needs to be resolved. However, trying to throw the blame for this issue at the current Government and not acknowledging the role of the last Government or, frankly, just focusing on getting this situation better totally misses the point. The Cabinet Office and officials are working day in, day out to improve the situation. This Government are taking steps to ensure that this issue never happens again by looking at insourcing options for the future not just for Capita, but across Government.

Things are so bad that I find myself agreeing with the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice). One of my constituents has been waiting since she lost her husband. She contacted me in January, and we still have not heard back. A third of the cases that have come to my office have been solved, but two thirds have not. This contract is not working, so will the Minister look at what options we have to ensure that Capita is not on the table for future procurements like this?

If my hon. Friend writes to me about any specific cases, I am happy to look at them. As with all strategic suppliers in this situation, we are looking at all contingency plans available, and our insourcing unit is working to look at future options across Government for such contracts. I understand his sentiment and can assure him that the Government are working on the issue.

I think it is safe to say that the Capita situation is an absolute catastrophe. Mark has given nearly 30 years to the civil service and cannot get a single annual benefit statement, while Julie received a quote in June that differed significantly from the one she was given when she left. She queried it, chased it and was promised a new quote, but it has never arrived. Six months on, she is paying all her bills from her savings, and interest on late payments does not cover that. Will the Minister commit that everyone affected by this scandal will be fully protected from financial loss?

It is absolutely right that no scheme member should be footing the cost for Capita’s failure, and if the hon. Member wants to write to me about that case, I will be happy to talk to Capita about it. Some funds have been available to support members, including the Government putting up transitional interest-free loans. However, as I said in a previous answer, I will take up the wider issue of compensation once we have the scheme up and running. I am happy to report back on that, because I accept that a lot of people have suffered as a result of Capita’s failure.

As I mentioned last week, this issue affects a number of residents in my constituency of Harlow. Like many Members, I am deeply concerned about Capita’s failures. What has the Minister’s Department learned from this absolute fiasco? What can she do to ensure that in future we prioritise insourcing and, if we do have to outsource, we ensure that we have trusted providers?

As I have mentioned, we now have our insourcing unit in the Cabinet Office—the Minister for insourcing, my hon. Friend the Member for Gateshead Central and Whickham (Mark Ferguson), is taking a lead on that—which is working across Government and across Departments to look at how we can insource more contracts, or at least ensure that there is better competition so that we are not continually rewarding failure. If my hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) would like to write to me about any specific cases, I would be happy to take a look at them.

I am very pleased that since the last time I spoke to the Minister about this issue, Anna has received her 17 years-worth of widow pension back pay, but I still have nine other priority cases that are waiting. Carol retired in July 2025 after several years of cancer treatment. She has still not had her lump sum and has gone back to working part time, and last week I was told by Capita that it needed more details from her old employer. After over a year, how many more details does Capita need to be able to get Carol her pension?

I am not going to stand here and make excuses for Capita’s poor performance, and a level of poor performance has been shown in what the hon. Member has just described. We have had quite a few exchanges of correspondence on the cases in his constituency, but if he has not sent that one to me yet, I will take a look at it if he does so.

Capita misled my caseworker, and other Members have said that they do not believe a word it says, yet the Minister says that there is the necessary transparency for contingency plans. Does she really have full confidence that the civil service has access to all the data so that if Capita does fail, civil service pensioners will not suffer further harm?

Cabinet Office officials now have full access to Capita’s system, so they are able to look at specific cases one by one. That is a relatively new thing that happened only as a consequence of the new rectification plan that was put in place after the remedial adviser went in, and I am confident that we have that level of transparency. However, if the hon. Member wants to raise with me particular instances in which she feels Capita has misled her office, I will take them up with the chief executive when I meet him.

I have to declare that my husband is a civil servant. Many of my constituents have been impacted by this issue. What I hear—and what I have heard before—is that this is about continuity of service and maintaining a lack of disruption, but constituents are already disrupted. We have presumably paid Capita to carry out this contract. How much money is being spent to remediate this botched Capita contract, and at what point will we cut loose from it and actually deliver for our constituents? Will it be next year, or the year after?

I totally understand the points that the hon. Member raises. I do not want the disruption to get any worse, so whatever we do now has to be about delivering as quickly as possible for scheme members, regardless of what we are working on in parallel in relation to the future of the scheme itself. The Government will seek for Capita to pay back any additional costs we have footed in order to assist it. We have withheld almost £10 million in payments, and Capita is voluntarily receiving 10% less each month in contractual payments. We will use all the levers at our disposal and continue to withhold that money for as long as possible until Capita improves its service and meets the performance indicators that are set out in the contract.

I invite the Minister to share in my frustration and anger at the way GCHQ workers have been treated. These are people who have dedicated their careers to keeping us all safe, and who are now being totally failed by the system that the state they kept safe has set up for them in retirement. Will the Minister look at what is happening with those GCHQ people? As and when the charade of Capita comes to an end, will she also look at setting up a specific scheme so that, in future, GCHQ workers are properly looked after and do not have to put up with Capita, or another company like it, letting them down?

I agree with the hon. Member’s sentiments about GCHQ and the incredibly important work it does. If he is referring to specific cases, I would be happy to look into them if he writes to me about them. I am probably not in a position today to commit to a brand-new pension scheme for GCHQ, but we are looking at the pension scheme as a whole—at its future and how to ensure that the service it provides is improved for all its members.

I have to say that I am running out of pejoratives to describe Capita’s performance. Just this morning I learned that Capita has been busily and callously closing unresolved complaints where individuals are still owed money. To my mind, this appears to be nothing more than an attempt to massage its performance figures. Is the Minister aware of that practice, and how can complaints possibly be considered closed when pensioners are still waiting for money that is rightfully theirs?

I agree—it is not acceptable if complaints are being closed when the points have not been actioned. If the hon. Member raises those cases in writing with me, I will take them up with the chief executive when I meet him.

We must never forget that real people, many of them in dire circumstances, are the victims here. I raised one such case when this matter was last before the House—I gave the Minister the details of a constituent who is a stage 4 cancer patient, and who has been waiting since April. I am very disappointed that, despite supplying those details, there has still been no progress in that case. Time is running out for my constituent, but it seems that time never runs out for Capita.
I am sorry to hear that the case has not been resolved. I do remember it, and I will take it up as soon as I leave the Chamber today.

My constituent Sarah retired from the civil service this year after notifying her employer five months in advance. Nine months after retiring, with my support, she should finally receive her pension this week. How can it take someone nearly nine months to get their pension after they retire, and what assurances can the Minister give all my constituents impacted by the Capita pension debacle that Capita will face penalties for the impact it has had on people’s lives?

I am sorry to hear about the experience that the hon. Member’s constituent had. I am glad that they now have their money, but I recognise that lots of people are still waiting to be paid. Nine months is totally unacceptable, and I will not make excuses for that. Turning to the future arrangements for the pension scheme and contracts more widely, the Procurement Act 2023 allows the Government to look at poor performance when issuing new contracts, and we will continue to do that. We also have the insourcing unit, which is working across Government and across Departments on how we can bring more contracts in-house, so plenty of work is going on across Government to ensure that we do not find ourselves in this situation again.
