Does the Minister acknowledge the extreme financial hardship that the Capita pension scandal is causing for our constituents? A constituent of mine was told by Capita to sell their car in order to make ends meet. Does she also accept that, regardless of someone’s immediate financial circumstances, everyone who has worked hard to retire deserves to make use of their pension in the early years of their retirement, when they are healthiest?

I agree. It is frankly disgusting that a representative of Capita advised someone to sell their car in order to support themselves financially—it is a complete outrage. I will raise that case with the chief executive and ensure that Capita staff and people dealing with scheme members are properly trained, particularly those dealing with sensitive cases. We continue to work every single day to improve this service, and I will relay all of the hon. Member’s points to the chief executive when I meet him.

Laura from Wareham told me that one of the compensations of a lower salary in working time was the promise of a good pension, which she now feels is at risk. She explained that the lump sum due to her in April would have reduced her mortgage payments, which are due to go up in January by £600. Laura has a very simple question: will the compensation from Capita cover those mortgage payments that she never expected to make?
I ask the hon. Member to write to me with that specific case so that I can take it up with Capita.

Steven has dedicated more than 40 years to public service and yet has dwindling savings to get by. Tim, after several errors, has waited more than 18 months for his pension payout from Capita. Given these urgent cases, which have come from all parts of the House, when will there be an assessment and more clarity on whether Capita can live up to this contract? Is there a contingency plan if it cannot?

Contingency planning for that situation is already in train, as it is across all our strategic suppliers for any major contracts. Whether it was in my last statement on this issue or during oral questions, I mentioned to the House the contingency planning being done by Cabinet Office officials for the pension scheme. I can provide assurance that that work is being done.

First, I thank the Minister for her endeavours, which are appreciated by many of us in the House. Many widows and retired civil servants in my constituency of Strangford are in real distress, while waiting months for Capita to process their pensions. Warm words will not pay the heating bills this winter. Will the Minister guarantee that every bereavement and hardship case in that specific 32,600-strong backlog will be cleared before Christmas? Will she set a clear deadline or a target to bring this service back in-house, if Capita fails yet again?

I assure the hon. Member that there will be no warm words exchanged between me and the chief executive when I meet him again. There were not with the last chief executive, either. Warm words are not on the table. I am reluctant to give specific dates or deadlines, particularly because we are focusing on the oldest and most complex cases first. Sometimes they can take days just to resolve. There have been issues around Capita not being clear about what information it wants from members. That can elongate a case. Some of the “business as usual” cases are moving a lot faster, as they do not have the same complexity. As I have said, I expect to see significant progress with Capita in the coming weeks and few short months. The dashboard comes out every fortnight, so people can see for themselves what is happening with the caseloads and where the numbers are going up and down. There is an explanation alongside the dashboard, breaking the numbers down between business as usual and the longer and more complex cases.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker, I apologise, but I forgot to declare an interest at the beginning of my question. Can I please put on record that I am the vice-chair of the PCS parliamentary group?

With permission, I would like to make a statement on the final report of the Timms review of the personal independence payment. PIP provides vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long-term health conditions. It contributes to the additional costs they face, and aims to help them to live independently, to participate in their communities and often to work. PIP was introduced 13 years ago. Since then, lots has changed, but PIP has never been fully reviewed, and it has not kept pace, so the Timms review was launched in summer last year. The review was co-produced with disabled people, the organisations that represent them and other experts. It is the first time that the UK Government have co-produced a review of this scale. I express heartfelt thanks to my two co-chairs, Sharon Brennan and Dr Clenton Farquharson, and to the 12 steering group members, whom the three of us recruited from more than 340 applicants. The group has met for a full day on 15 occasions since January, with lots of other discussions in between. The whole group has shown exemplary commitment to the task. Each of the 15 members, including me, had one vote. Almost all 12 of the steering group members had lived experience of disability or long-term ill health, as well as a range of other expertise. The review heard from more than 40,000 people and organisations, including more than 38,000 responses to the call for evidence, 138 community workshops, and evidence from clinicians, charities, deaf and disabled people’s organisations, academics, frontline practitioners and international experts. I thank everyone who shared their expertise and their experiences—often very personal ones—with us. This was an ambitious review, and it asked big, complex questions. Co-production means that every participant does not necessarily agree on every detail, but we created the conditions for people with different perspectives to test the evidence and shape the outcome as equals. The review’s report has been submitted to my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State, and the Government will now consider its findings. I will turn to the review’s central conclusion: the system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset. The review is clear that PIP remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It does not consider people’s needs, aspirations, barriers or extra costs—it is just about what someone cannot do. Many find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and too often it leaves people fearing that work, health treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it. Secondly, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution towards the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey, reviewed by the steering group, showed that PIP does not always target the highest levels of support at those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions better reflecting individual circumstances. Thirdly, the system offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs. The review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not just some adjustment of the form or descriptors. It does not prescribe a final set of eligibility rules, because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected Government, accountable to this House, but it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made. Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cu

I thank the Minister for advance sight of his statement. What a contrast this is with last week when we gathered for the statement on the Milburn review. It was a packed Chamber— [Interruption.] It’s your review! They do not like to hear it, Madam Deputy Speaker, but I remember well that, only a week ago, the Prime Minister and the Chancellor were both here to tell the country that they finally had some kind of plan for welfare, if only for the under-25s. Today we are here to talk about their plan for sickness benefits for everyone, but the Prime Minister does not seem to have made it. After the fanfare of Milburn, all the trumpets have been muted for Timms. It is almost as if the Government were hoping that no one would notice the Minister’s statement. The Timms review had a rather inauspicious start in life. It was set up to appease Labour Back Benchers after they had floored the Government’s last attempt at welfare reform, prohibited from making savings. The Minister himself has said that the spiralling costs of PIP are “not a great concern”. I respect the right hon. Gentleman, but I have to say to him that he may not be concerned about the cost of benefits, but people out there are. They can see the bill heading up and up. PIP alone will go up to £41 billion a year under this Government, and they know that they will be left footing the bill. Worse still, the Minister’s recommendations in the round make PIP easier to get; we will see more claims and an even higher bill, as the Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned. No wonder: we know that all Labour MPs ask is, “Who can we tax to pay more in benefits?” Of course Labour Back Benchers love welfare, but can the Minister not see that to a public struggling to make ends meet and sick of a welfare system that is out of control, a plan that refuses to make savings is simply a kick in the teeth? That said, it is not all bad. We agree that PIP looks too much at what people cannot do, not at what they can, and leads people to fear that working will make them worse off. We support fast-tracking PIP for people near the end of life, and reducing onerous reassessments for people with lifelong progressive conditions. Many who claim PIP do not have extra costs, and we welcome greater scrutiny, and yes, there should be more differentiation between awards for mild and severe conditions, but can the Minister tell me what evidence of their extra costs people will be required to provide? Will this be ongoing, or a one-off check with no accountability? Will the plan to move from cash to support have teeth, or will it be nothing more than optional, and enticing, Motability-style freebies? Why is there no proposal to tackle the extraordinary growth in the number of claims for mild conditions—for mental health and ADHD? Why is there no plan to require face-to-face assessment, or to crack down on those who are gaming the system? The review has taken over a year, but all we have is a report that tinkers around the edges of a failed system, with more spending, fewer checks, and a complete absence of substance. Of course, this is not the only review in town. Last week Alan Milburn also proposed changes to the disability benefit system, based on the plans that we have set out—shifting from cash to support for milder conditions, and reducing the total amount spent on sickness benefit. Two “landmark” reviews commissioned by the Government, landing one week apart, say completely different things. The Minister has tried to make out that they fit together, and that they have much in common. Pull the other one! They may have similar diagnoses, but their proposals are poles apart. What a mess. Which side is the Prime Minister going to pick: Team Milburn or Team Timms? Or will he freeze in the headlights and avoid the argument, refuse to choose, and create a two-tier system with one rule for under-25s and another for everyone else? This is no joke. Two hundred billion pounds—that is what the working-age welfa

I sympathise with the hon. Lady, who is feeling so lonely on the Opposition Benches because so few of her hon. Friends are present. I am grateful to my hon. Friends for being present in such large numbers and showing real interest in this work. Once again, she has set out her familiar attack on the system with which her party left us when it left office. Let me pick up some of the points that she has made. The need to reduce the costs of welfare has been spelt out very clearly by both the Prime Minister and the Chancellor. The Government want the welfare bill to come down, but the way to do that is not through crude cuts that then just show up somewhere else in the system—and the hon. Lady has delivered a list of the crudest kind of cuts. What we recommend in the review is an entirely new assessment focused on people’s needs and the costs arising from them, unlike the current assessment, which does not ask about people’s costs at all. We will set out the implications for the cost of the whole system in the White Paper that will be published in the new year. The hon. Lady asked whether I envisage a system in which it is easier to claim. I do not believe that claiming disability benefits needs to be dehumanising, which it currently is. We want a completely new approach to assessment that, unlike the current one, is not just about what someone cannot do. We can do a better job by asking about needs as well as costs. I do not believe that the assessment needs to be a traumatising experience, which it has been for too many people under the current system. The hon. Lady made a point about face-to-face assessments, and the review says that we want more of them. She will know that, for understandable reasons, face-to-face assessments were shut down during the pandemic, and the previous Government never really restarted them. It has been down to this Government to restart face-to-face assessments. We are now up to 20% of all PIP assessments being carried out face to face—a dramatic improvement on the woeful situation left behind by the last Government—and we will continue that process. The hon. Lady is wrong to say that we are tinkering with the system. This is a fundamentally new approach to the assessment for PIP, and I commend it to the House.

I congratulate my right hon. Friend, his co-chairs and all members of the steering group on coming up with this report. From what I have read so far, I think it is incredibly constructive. I particularly like the approach of framing future developments around the principles that he has set out. It is a personalised and positive approach rather than, as he has described it, the dehumanising system that was too often associated with the PIP process. As my right hon. Friend rightly explained, PIP contributes to, but does not wholly cover, the thousands of pounds in extra costs that disabled people have to pay by virtue of their being disabled. I have to say that I have been concerned about the conflation of PIP with out-of-work support. I am reassured by what my right hon. Friend says, but how can we ensure that, as we move forward—we will have the White Paper in the new year and legislation at the end of next year—the support provided by PIP is not lost? We need to have support for disabled people to cover their extra costs, and it should apply to everyone of all ages.

I am grateful to my hon. Friend, the Chair of the Work and Pensions Committee, for her question. She is absolutely right to say that we need a more personalised approach than the one we had in the past. All of us will know constituents who have significant extra costs as a result of their disability, and this benefit is there to contribute to those costs. She is also absolutely right to highlight—the review is very clear about this—that PIP is for people who are in work, as well as those who are out of work. Indeed, one of the points that was made to us in the debate last summer by a lot of people claiming PIP is that they need it in order to afford the cost of getting to work. It is very important that that support is maintained, and the review is determined that it shall be.

I thank the Minister for sharing his comments and the report in advance of today’s statement. It has been a very busy couple of weeks. There was very much a Mardi Gras feeling around the Milburn report, but it has been strangely quiet around the Timms report—it could even be seen as the “Tiny Timms report”, given the lack of media interest in it. [ Interruption. ] The reality is that we need to manage the benefit system appropriately, but PIP is there to support people to do things that many other people throughout the country take for granted. The fact of the matter is that people who are disabled are so much more likely to have high levels of deprivation, so it is very important to get this right. The Liberal Democrats welcome the fact that the Minister has worked really well with people with disabilities, and we want to make sure that that happens throughout the Department for Work and Pensions. It is very interesting to see how the two reports have taken a different approach to young people, which has led to uncertainty and anguish for them. It would be extremely helpful if the Government could get a grip on that. Some answers from the Minister would be really welcome. First, what conditions are included when he speaks about “severe” and “degenerative” conditions? Finally, will the final report apply to all claimants or just new ones?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for his questions. As one of my hon. Friends said from a sedentary position, it is the first time I have been described as “tiny”, but I welcome the hon. Gentleman’s interest in the report and the evidence that he submitted to it. Let me comment on his questions. There will need to be careful planning around who will be eligible for the fast track that we will introduce. It will be a minority of applicants—those with the most severe and enduring conditions—but we will need to specify that more fully. What conditions count as degenerative will probably be easier to establish. The Department’s policy in the past has been that if people are on a high rate of benefit and their condition is degenerative, they ought not to be frequently reassessed, but actually they have been. The policy that was there on paper has not been applied as rigorously as it should have been in practice. We are going to change that and make sure that the policy is applied in the future.
Order. More than 50 Members are standing. In order to get in as many as possible—it probably will not be everybody—short questions and short answers would be very helpful.

It is interesting that today’s review, which has been co-produced with disabled people, says that PIP remains a “vital” source of support, whereas the Milburn review, which was not co-produced, wants to scrap it. A 24-year-old and a 26-year-old with the same health condition will receive radically different support for independent living under the two reviews. Why is age, rather than need, being used as a determining factor in whether someone receives support with the extra costs of disability?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for his interest in this work, but the Milburn report is clear that young people who have additional costs arising from their disability should be eligible for support. Moreover, the two reviews have a good deal in common. Both want to see greater participation, and I think my hon. Friend would agree with that. Both reviews call for fundamental reform of the system, and both want more personalised and more localised approaches. The review that has been published today does not make age distinctions or talk about different age groups, but Alan Milburn’s report argued pretty compellingly that given the crisis of young people not in education, employment or training that developed after 2021 and the overriding importance of young people, including young disabled people, being able to get into work at the start of what should be their working lives, a different approach is needed for young people. The Government will respond to the two reviews in a single White Paper.

I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman on producing this report. I know only too well from personal experience how difficult it is to get this right. Disability living allowance was failing, so we introduced PIP to try to deal with the problems, but here we are again. I simply offer him my support. There are good elements in the report, and the approach to progressive disease is absolutely right, but does he recognise that the driver of so much of the extra expenditure has been the massive growth in mental health issues? That is illustrated by one of the diagrams in his report. The question is, how will he deal with the requirements on mental health problems, given that on the other side of the fence, unemployment sickness benefit is going to be taken away?

I am grateful to the right hon. Gentleman, who I recall once resigned from the Government over issues related to this area of policy. He is right that there has been a huge increase in the incidence of mental health issues among those applying for PIP, and there is indeed a graph in the review that sets that out. The crucial question for this system is: who has extra costs arising from their impairment, whether it is a mental or physical health impairment? If there are significant additional costs, this benefit should be available to contribute to those costs, but if there are not really any costs, it should not be; I think that is the right way forward.

I am grateful to the Minister for his statement, and for working closely with me after accepting, at the Dispatch Box last year, my amendment to ensure that the review was co-produced with disabled people and disabled people’s organisations. The Timms review is clear that we must fundamentally overhaul the system in order to rehumanise PIP. The Milburn review also states that those who have no realistic possibility of working, and who currently receive PIP, along with the health element of universal credit, should receive more support. Will the Minister set out how the Government will implement the Timms review, alongside recommendations in the Milburn and Mayfield reviews, in a way that ensures that the reforms join up cohesively, and work together? We want to ensure that, for people in receipt of these benefits, there is not inadvertently a negative cumulative impact of changes resulting from the reviews, and we want to ensure that disabled people can fulfil their potential.

That is the crucial point, and my hon. Friend is entitled to a good deal of credit for the approach taken in this review. She is also absolutely right to underline the importance of rehumanising PIP, which I think is a good slogan to take forward from this report. We now need to come forward with a cohesive response to the recent reviews, and indeed to other work going on, including that by Sir Charlie Mayfield. That will be set out in a single White Paper, which my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State will bring forward quite early in the new year.

PIP provides vital support to individuals who have additional costs in their day-to-day life because they have a disability, but they are jumping through hoops and constantly answering the same questions. Can the Minister confirm today that people who need support just to get the same standard of living as everybody else in society will not lose out as a result of his review, or subsequent Government legislation?

The intention of the review is precisely to ensure that those who have additional costs as a result of disability continue to receive this benefit, and this will go forward in a fair and sustainable way. The hon. Member absolutely rightly makes the point about the obligation that is placed on people, far too often, to give the same information time and again in different assessments in different bits of the system. One proposal in the review is that we should introduce a digital profile, which starts to be populated at the start of the process, so that if people want to pass on that information to other bits of the system, they can do so without having to answer the same questions all over again.

I welcome the removal of repeated reappraisals of people with lifelong or degenerative conditions. That will save the system money, give the individual dignity, and make the system more human. I have a simple question. Implementation will always be the key issue, and in the past, some of the best proposals have floundered because those implementing procedures have not always stuck to the aims set out at the beginning. Has the Timms review made any recommendations to the Government about how implementation should work? Will the Minister be involved in discussions to make sure that this actually meets the aims that he has set out?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. She makes the point that reducing the number of reassessments will save the system money. It will free up assessment resource, which we can then use to do a better job, for example, for those with fluctuating conditions. She is absolutely right about the importance of a very well planned implementation programme, and that is what we are determined to draw up.

There seems to be cross-party unanimity that the Minister will add to his already deservedly popular reputation by ensuring that people with profound and permanent disabilities no longer need to go for repeated reassessment. Can he confirm, however, that the widely reported rise from 2.7 million people claiming PIP to 4.1 million is largely because of mental health claims? Is there a projection of how much further this rise can go before there is some way of discerning which people are profoundly mentally disabled and which are not?

There are indeed projections of that. I thank the right hon. Member for his kind remarks. As I have said, I think the key is to have an assessment that correctly establishes whether people have additional costs arising from their impairment, whether it is a mental health problem or a physical health problem. At the moment, the assessment does not ask that question at all. The benefit has always been intended to contribute to additional costs, but the assessment does not ask about them, and we want an assessment that does.

Can the Minister outline how disabled people, who co-produced the review, will continue to be involved as he drafts the White Paper, and will he consult Scottish Ministers and disability groups on any learning implications for citizens’ support in Scotland?

On my hon. Friend’s latter point, yes, I certainly will. Indeed, I am looking forward to speaking to the Scottish Minister this afternoon, and I spoke to the umbrella body for disability organisations in Scotland yesterday. Co-production has been a key feature of this review, and as we take this work forward, it will be very important to continue to engage with disabled people and disabled people’s organisations, who have a very important contribution to make.

The very first Health and Social Care Committee report this Parliament was called “Adult Social Care Reform: the cost of inaction”. In it, we argued that the result of failure to grapple with social care, particularly for working-age adults, will be seen in other parts of the welfare system. It looks as though the Minister’s review has come to a similar conclusion. My question is about the Casey commission. The report says that there needs to be close co-ordination. Has this already started? What is the mechanism by which the Minister’s review will feed into the Casey review, and how do we ensure that joined-up working across Government actually works this time?

Those conversations have begun, and I am delighted that my hon. Friend the Minister for Social Care and Mental Health is in her place on the Front Bench. As I have mentioned, when it comes to the assessment for this benefit, and the future national care service, there is an opportunity to ensure that people do not have to give the same information in two—or quite often more—places. Indeed, we suggest in the report that the digital profile I mentioned could be contributed to the national care service, if a care assessment is needed. Those conversations will carry on.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his statement, and for his engagement with me and the all-party parliamentary group on disability on this issue. I welcome his review, but does he agree that despite the fact that PIP was designed to contribute towards the extra cost of living with a disability, there is still a perception that PIP is linked to being in work? Does he agree that it is vital to have a lot of engagement, but also to educate people about the fact that PIP is there to contribute towards the extra cost of living with a disability, and is available to both those in work and those out of work?

I thank my hon. Friend for the close and supportive interest that she has taken in this work, through her APPG role. She is right to underline that PIP is a benefit available to people whether or not they are working. She is also right that there is often confusion on that point. The report is very clear, and I shall be very clear on that, whenever I have the opportunity, as will she.
What assessment has the Minister made of the likely impact of the proposals in his report on the size of the benefit bill?

We will set that out in full in the White Paper that is to come. As I have said, the key is to have a new assessment, which we will develop, that correctly assesses whether people have additional costs arising from their disability, and, if they do, awards them a benefit. We will set out the full details of that and the cost implications in the White Paper.

I thank my right hon. Friend and the steering committee for their work on this vital and very sensitive issue. I particularly welcome the acknowledgement in the statement that the system does not adequately take account of fluctuating need, which I think is relevant for people who have long covid or multiple sclerosis. Will the Minister expand a little further on what that might mean for the White Paper, when it is published?

There is a very clear recommendation in the review that we need to do a better job of assessments in cases of that kind. As I said, we will free up some assessment resource as a result of a couple of the recommendations that I referred to, and that will mean that we can do a significantly better job of them. We will need to work out carefully how to do it, but we need to. The criticism that the assessment does not do a good job for people with fluctuating conditions is probably the single most commonly heard criticism, and we are determined to do better.

Young disabled people in my constituency have been watching this process, and have been very worried about what it will mean for their dignity and their future, so I really want to thank the Minister for the approach that he has taken, through the report, and the consideration that has been put into coming to the House today to make these announcements. One of the biggest misconceptions is that PIP is an out-of-work benefit, so I appreciate the effort the Minister is making to take a more human approach to this. I am proud that the Scottish equivalent, the adult disability payment, has been described by the Resolution Foundation as “kinder”, but not more costly, and agree that this is the right objective. Can the Minister confirm with confidence that any changes that follow from Timms and Milburn will not remove crucial support for young people in Scotland? Will he continue to work positively with the Scottish Government on the quasi-devolved elements of welfare and employment, to ensure that we can all get this right for young people across Scotland?

Yes, I can give the hon. Lady the assurance that we will work closely with Ministers in Scotland. We took evidence during the review from Edel Harris, who recently undertook a review of the adult disability payment in Scotland. That was very helpful, and we will ensure that those connections remain.

I warmly welcome the ambitions of the Timms review, and particularly the ambition to develop a system that is more of a conversation than a confrontation. Will my right hon. Friend reassure my constituents that the adversarial and often cruel culture of the Department for Work and Pensions will be overhauled? Unless the Department is re-humanised, any PIP reforms will fail.

We talk in the review about the need for a different approach, and a different cultural approach. It is important that we have a system in which people understand the outcome of assessments, and feel that they can trust the system. That is what we are working for.

My constituent Tracey, who has stage 4 cancer, was awarded PIP under the SR1 special rules for end of life. Her cancer is terminal, but she is likely to outlive this time-limited support. She applied to transfer the PIP to the standard pathway, and that is finally being agreed, but at a reduced rate, and she now faces a lengthy mandatory reconsideration of her case. The Minister’s review rightly says that people with severe, well-evidenced conditions should be fast-tracked without unnecessary consultations. Will the SR1 be updated, to prevent people in Tracey’s situation from suffering long waits and excessive reviews, and will he make sure that Tracey’s mandatory reconsideration is dealt with urgently?

I would be happy to look at that case, if the hon. Lady wants to drop me line. We talked in the report about the importance of looking at how mandatory reconsiderations work. I was at the Royal National Institute of Blind People this morning, talking about the report, and I met somebody who had a successful mandatory reconsideration experience. I know that is not always what happens, and we are going to look at this.

Following the Milburn review last week, the House has been presented with this review, which also recommends changes to eligibility for disability benefits. The Minister will understand the deep anxiety that disabled people will have about reviews that recommend changes to eligibility, when no specifics are provided. May I press him to say which disabled people will be impacted by the changes to the eligibility criteria, and what criteria he will recommend to the Government?

The key will be that the assessment needs to correctly establish whether people have additional costs. If they do, they will be eligible for this benefit, which will make a contribution to those extra costs. Nothing is going to change overnight arising from this. Our aim is a better system that addresses the barriers that disabled people face and that many of them have been in touch with us about. We will set out the details in the White Paper.

The Minister is very polite about the Milburn review, but will he make it clear that his review and its principles cannot support arbitrary age discrimination in people’s benefits? May I ask him to push back loudly against the idea that PIP is an out-of-work benefit to be chopped and replaced by work support? It is not. People who work more pay more tax and PIP enables that. Will he make sure to remind Alan Milburn and the Cabinet about that principle as often as necessary, because we keep hearing the opposite?

We probably need to remind journalists of that more than anybody. I am happy to do so—I looking forward to having a conversation later. The point Alan Milburn has made is that it is vital that young people, including young disabled people, have the opportunity to be in a job at the start of what should be their working life. That is what his proposals are aiming to achieve.

I thank the Minister for attempting to give us a report that is co-produced, which is really welcome. We should not lose sight in this place of the data from the Joseph Rowntree Foundation that shows disabled people make up 61% of people in destitution. As the report is considered alongside the findings of the Milburn report and the seemingly disappearing Fonagy review, can the Minister assure the House that no disabled person will be pushed into poverty by these reforms? Will he commit, at the Dispatch Box, to co-produce the White Paper with the disability movement? Will he publish a full destitution impact assessment before any legislation relating to his findings is brought forward?

There will, of course, be the full set of assessments published at the time. We are aiming to develop a new assessment that correctly establishes whether people have additional costs arising from disability, which can indeed push people into destitution in the way that my hon. Friend says. If they do, this benefit is there to help with those additional costs. We are determined that that should continue to be the case.

The Timms review being co-produced with disabled people and organisations was a welcome change from previous reviews, but my constituents fear that the new PIP claim process will now be drafted by civil servants, with no co-production at all ahead of a White Paper in the new year. Naturally, uncertainty as to the direction of travel creates stress for those receiving PIP, so can the Minister guarantee that disabled people will also co-produce the new assessment process?

I can guarantee that there will be extensive discussion and engagement with disabled people throughout the process leading up to the White Paper. We need to hear those voices and we will continue to do so.

I commend my right hon. Friend and the co-chairs for their excellent work co-producing the review with disabled people and their carers. My constituents who rely on PIP and who joined me at a roundtable told me they found the assessment stressful, confusing and adversarial, with too many repeated assessments of conditions that will never improve, so I welcome today’s recommendations to make the whole process simpler. Will he provide assurance to those family carers who currently receive carer’s allowance as an automatic entitlement, that this will continue, and that those at end of life will be fast-tracked and not subject to reassessment?
Yes. We envisage that PIP in this fundamentally reformed version will continue to be a passport to carer’s allowance in the way that it is now.

Diolch yn fawr, Madam Dirprwy Lefarydd. One recommendation in the report is to move towards support based on direct assessments of disability-related costs. While this could be a positive move for some people, I worry about where the definition will be drawn for what is considered a disability-related cost. How will the Government ensure that less visible but essential everyday costs are recognised, and will they work with disabled people and disability organisations in Wales, and the Welsh Government, to ensure that Wales’s specific context is recognised?

Yes, I can certainly give the hon. Lady that assurance. Yesterday, the co-chairs and I met with Rhian Davies from Disability Wales. We will continue those conversations, and it is important that we listen to the voices of disabled people, including those in Wales, as we draw up the definition of how the new assessment will work.

In my constituency, 11,586 individuals receive PIP; they are all on tenterhooks, anxious for the Timms review. Other hon. Members have mentioned one specific group: those suffering from fluctuating conditions, who are really poorly one day, but possibly not as bad the next. Will my right hon. Friend assure that group that their PIP will be protected, and not impacted by any changes to the eligibility or assessment criteria?

As I have set out, the assessment criteria changes will reflect whether people have additional costs arising from their disability. Getting that right for fluctuating conditions is a very important part of the process. In theory, the assessment is supposed to do that at the moment; in practice, it frequently does not. We will be doing a good deal of work on that, and it is likely that we will put in more assessment capacity to look specifically at this issue.

The Joseph Rowntree Foundation’s research shows that 61% of destitute people are also disabled, while young people face a disproportionate risk. In Leicester South, where child poverty is double the national average, the Minister will agree that there are a lot of frightened families. Will the Minister rule out removing PIP for under 25-year-olds, as the Milburn review proposes, and publish a full assessment of the impact on destitution before the White Paper and any changes the Government make?

There will certainly be a full set of assessments with the White Paper. I will correct what the hon. Member said about Alan Milburn’s report, which is very clear that the system will need to continue to contribute to the additional costs faced by disabled young people—that is not at risk.

Our welfare system must be there for those who need it most, including those who rely on it to stay in work and live independently. After years of welfare changes under the previous Government, with people being written off and told what they cannot do, naturally, any change can feel unsettling. What does the Minister say to people in Filton and Bradley Stoke who rely on such support?

I hope that my hon. Friend’s constituents will take encouragement from the review. She is absolutely right that there is a lot at stake here and a lot of people depend on these decisions. People can see that changes are needed for this benefit to be fair and fit for the future, and to be sustainable for the long term. That is what we are determined to deliver.

I welcome the two sensible and humane changes that the Minister has proposed, namely for those who have lifelong, degenerative diseases and the fast-tracking of those who have serious and well-evidenced illnesses. However, there is concern about the full cost of the benefit bill and the PIP bill—as has been said, it is due to go up by £15 billion by 2030—so what are the cost implications of the recommendations? Secondly, given that these issues are devolved to Northern Ireland, what discussions has the Minister had with the Communities Minister in Northern Ireland about implementation?

I have spoken regularly to Gordon Lyons—I am speaking to him again on Thursday. The Prime Minister and the Chancellor have been clear that we need to reduce the benefits bill, and the proposals that we have set out will lead to a White Paper, where we will spell out exactly the implications for future spending.

There are nearly 10,000 people in South Shields who rely on PIP, one of the highest rates in England. Although the Minister’s words will have given some relief to disabled people, he will know how worried they are waiting for the details on the White Paper. I heard his earlier responses, but there remains a difference between this co-produced review and the Milburn review. The Milburn review will see half a million disabled young people losing PIP. Will the Minister please confirm that such crude cuts will not be in the White Paper?

The determination that motivates the Milburn report is that young people should have the chance to be in work, and that there should be a substantial improvement in employment support, not least for disabled young people, who often face barriers to work. Those barriers do not need to be there; the system needs to remove those barriers, which is what we are determined to do. I say to my hon. Friend’s constituents that it is very much in the interests of those who depend on this benefit that it be sustainable in the long term. These changes will help to ensure that it is.

I thank the Minister for the inclusive style of the inquiry that he has undertaken, and I hope that this principle will continue into the next, probably much more difficult, stage. When he announced the review, he said that it would all be paid for within the envelope of the Office for Budget Responsibility predictions on expenditure. Will the Minister confirm that PIP will be determined by the needs of the individual as assessed, not driven by some Treasury forecast or restriction? Many people in receipt of PIP are terrified of the future and appalled at the inhuman way they have been treated. I thank the Minister for recognising the inhuman nature of the application of PIP assessments until now. I hope that changes quickly and does not wait for another review.

We will certainly be cracking on with it. A lot of people who depend on PIP have been worried by the scale of the increase in the number of people claiming it, and whether that meant it would not be there for the long term. We need to ensure that the benefit is sustainable for the future. On co-production, I point the right hon. Member to chapter 6 of the report, which says that co-production will not be appropriate for every stage. Only the elected Government can take decisions about major spending elements, and we take responsibility in making them.

I grew up in a household with disabled parents, and my parents were at their best when they could live independently. PIP is critical for independent living. In my constituency, I want everybody to get the best shot at life, which means going into the workforce. Will the Minister explain how PIP will be reformed to enable independent living, while also ensuring that more disabled people go into the workforce? Work does not just provide purpose and dignity; it provides a means to a better life.

My hon. Friend speaks from the heart and he is absolutely right. When changes were proposed in the summer of last year, a lot of people claiming PIP made the point to us, as I have mentioned, that they used their PIP to get into work. That raises the question of what more we can do in PIP to remove barriers that hold disabled people back at the moment. There is also lots of other work going on, such as the Connect to Work programme, which is now rolled out across England and Wales. We are seeing encouraging results from that, but there is more to be done. I agree with my hon. Friend about the great importance of opening up those opportunities.

The review recommends that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support they receive, but in many parts of the country, especially in rural areas, those services have been reduced or have collapsed altogether. Will the Minister tell the House what services our constituents will be signposted to?

There is a variety of different kinds of services: some may be health services, while others may be services provided locally by a charity, for example, which people can be made aware of. I take the hon. Lady’s point that the picture varies in different parts of the country. At the moment we have the Motability service, where people choose to forgo their cash benefit in order to access, say, a wheelchair-adapted car. That system works well. There might be other kinds of equipment that could be made available on a similar basis, whereby people would choose to take the equipment or the service and forgo their cash in response. As her question hints at, the picture will be different in different places, and the Government are, of course, working to improve services in every part of the country.

It is welcome that the review recognises that PIP is a vital support. However, as the Minister will understand, there is deep fear in our communities, in the light of Milburn’s recommendation that PIP should be scrapped for the under-25s. Can he reassure many of our constituents today that they will not face a cut to their personal independence payments?

Alan Milburn’s report is clear that support for additional costs for young people will continue to be in place. However, the absolute overriding ambition in his report is to ensure that disabled young people around the country have the opportunity for work, many of whom have not had that opportunity up until now as barriers have been in the way. We need to see those barriers removed and improve the Government’s support, and we are determined that that should happen.

I have to declare that close family members are in receipt of PIP. I am relieved to hear from the Minister today that there has been a full acknowledgement of the harrowing process that many people have to go through just to try to qualify for PIP, and I am glad to hear that there is an understanding that there is an issue around mandatory reconsideration itself. I have veterans coming into my office every day of the week who are being put through the most harrowing and humiliating exercises. However, I feel that there is a tension between this review and the Milburn report. Can the Minister assure my young constituents who rely on PIP that they will not be penalised for wanting to have a life?

We want young people, and everybody, to be able to have their fullest life and fulfil their aspirations and ambitions. That is exactly what is driving this work on the part of the Government at the moment. The hon. Lady is right to use the word “harrowing” about the experience that a large number of people have with PIP, which I think is the case because the process simply requires them to run through lots and lots of things that they cannot do, over 42 pages. We have to do better than that.

I thank the Minister for his diligence and his experience. Not everybody in this House knows what they are talking about, but he certainly does on these issues, and I thank him for his work. [ Interruption. ] No, I do not want a job—don’t worry. I am focused on making sure that my constituents stay in theirs. The Minister will know that many in the Parkinson’s world, such as Parkinson’s UK and many back home in Newcastle-under-Lyme, have major concerns about the inadequacy of PIP assessor training, which leads to people with Parkinson’s losing support, with a rate of wrong decisions that is, on average, 10% higher than for any other condition. Can the Minister reassure me that the work on assessor training will be co-produced and that he will work with Parkinson’s UK and other condition-specific organisations and charities to get this right?

I will certainly enjoy continuing to work with Parkinson’s UK. Parkinson’s is actually a good example of a degenerative condition where lots of people with the condition who are on PIP are being reassessed frequently, and it is not clear what the purpose of that is. That is the point that Parkinson’s UK has made regularly to us, and it is right. Yes, we do need to do a better job on assessor training.

I certainly welcome the removal of the reassessments for those with some of the most severe disabilities. A number of my constituents have had to have that reassessment, and it causes immense anxiety. On PIP itself, the questionnaire and the telephone conversations are quite stringent in detail. A lot of people are now heavily reliant on that support, which they desperately need. Can the Minister confirm that this is not just a smokescreen to make those questions a lot harder so that we can stop many people receiving the support they need?

I welcome the Minister’s statement, which is very welcome indeed. It is not surprising that there is not a single Back Bencher on the Tory Benches, because they left behind the scheme that we inherited, which is dehumanising, confrontational and has stigmatised tens of thousands of people. Going further back, it was Mrs Thatcher—the Tories’ heroine—who drove tens of thousands of unemployed mineworkers and others on to sick pay, because they were told that they would be left the rest of their lives without a job. It is true today that in my constituency there are still thousands of men who have not worked for 40 years who were instructed to go on to sick pay. That is a shameful record that we must reverse. I think this is a step in the right direction. I will make one further point. The employment rate under Thatcher meant that only two out of every three people who were available for work could get work. Now that figure is more than 75%, and it is increasing month on month. I urge the Minister to be careful not to fall into a moral panic and begin to cut things that might lead to destitution simply because there are loud voices on the Opposition Benches.
Order. You are a very experienced Member, Mr Trickett, and should have known that that was a very long question—almost as long as the question asked by the Liberal Democrat spokesperson.

My hon. Friend is absolutely right about the high and rising employment rate that we have at the moment, and we are determined to keep it that way. He is also absolutely right that the Opposition have a lot to answer for.

The Minister has often referred to the assessment resource, which is, in fact, a private company that has been conducting both the assessments and the appeals. It is that service that has been described as adversarial and dehumanising. What additional resource, training or contract change will he put in place to cover appeals, the fast-track route, or even how it assesses practical services as part of the overall support, in order to actually make that service humanising and supportive?

The hon. Gentleman is right that these services are contracted to a number of providers, and those contracts will be in place until, I think, the early 2030s. The report talks about training, and we will need to talk to the providers about how that is best done. Something important that came out very strongly in our discussions towards the end of the review was that people want to see a more professionalised assessment service, and that is what we will be looking to achieve.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his statement today and for his continued engagement with me and other colleagues. I welcome the commitment to rehumanise the system—something my constituents and I have been crying out for. Last year I tabled an amendment to end outsourcing of assessments to profit-making companies such as Capita and to bring assessors in-house. Does my right hon. Friend agree that we cannot rebuild trust in the system while private contractors remain at its heart, and will he explore whether we can end those contracts much sooner?

Actually, the review does not call for the contracts to be brought back in-house. To be frank, that is partly because our Department is not terribly highly regarded in some circles, either. I think we can provide a good service with the current arrangement, but it is going to take some work along the lines set out in the review.

I thank the Minister for his statement and all those involved in the review, particularly WECIL—the West of England Centre for Inclusive Living—which is based in Fishponds, in my constituency. Much has been reported about the co-production process with disabled people. Will the Minister give us some examples of how that process has actually strengthened the review, and would he recommend it as an approach to his ministerial colleagues?

I send thanks to WECIL and to the Public Service Consultants, to whom WECIL was a subcontractor. WECIL’s particular role was helping in our shaping recommendations workshops, which took place across the country. I particularly remember one that I attended in Birmingham—I found it a very helpful day, talking to disabled people about their experience, facilitated by a member of staff from WECIL. I think there is a lot to be learned from that approach.

May I bring my right hon. Friend back to the potential conflict between his report and Alan Milburn’s report? People have mentioned the Joseph Roundtree Foundation report that says that nearly 4 million people are living in destitution. Any reduction in people’s income will push more into destitution. The withdrawal of PIP and access to the universal credit health element is a withdrawal of a means of support. In addition, it is the withdrawal of a passport benefit to other benefits. Although he has said that support will be provided under the Milburn report, that is not defined, and the level is not indicated in that report. May I ask him to address with his colleagues the contradiction there could be between his report and last week’s report?

I do not think there is a contradiction. As I have said, the commitment to that support is there. I think my right hon. Friend would agree with the point that Alan Milburn makes: the really crucial thing for disabled young people is to have the opportunity of employment. Many can gain access to that, given extra support, and that is the extra support that we want to provide.

I thank my right hon. Friend for his open and constructive engagement throughout the process. I particularly welcome the recognition of fluctuating conditions, as no two days may be the same for people living with Parkinson’s, MS and endometriosis. I want to come back to the assessment. He spoke of capacity and just touched on training. Will there be a comprehensive review of training for assessors, which is currently where things fall down for people with fluctuating conditions?

PIP is a lifeline for so many people, helping them to meet the extra costs of living with a disability. It supports people in work as well as those who are not in work. I therefore welcome the Timms review’s recognition of PIP as an essential benefit. But that makes me even more alarmed by the proposals in the Milburn review to take that essential support away from so many young disabled people as that risks plunging huge numbers of young disabled people into destitution. Does the Minister not agree that sick and disabled people need that support whatever their age and that extra employment support for young people, which is very welcome, should be funded not by cutting disability support but by taxing the wealthiest?

But if we can support young people much more effectively into work at what should be the start of their working lives, they will be significantly better off throughout their lives. That is the goal we want to achieve.

I thank the Minister for visiting Morecambe. As my constituents there said, PIP is there to help with the extra costs of disability; it is not an unemployment benefit. I therefore welcome his proposals and the focus on the actual costs of disability as well as, of course, the Government’s wider work on prevention, because preventing ill health is how we will bring the bill down. Will he outline to my disabled constituents how the PIP process and outcomes will change for them if his proposals are put in place?

I thank my hon. Friend for hosting that helpful workshop in her constituency. The key change, as I have said, is that we want a new kind of assessment. It does not need to be dehumanising, as the current one is. It needs to focus on people’s needs and the costs arising from those needs. It also needs to establish properly who has additional costs arising from disability. We want to ensure that the benefit continues to be there to contribute to those additional costs for those who have them.

It is right that disabled people have had their voices heard at the heart of this report. I look forward to reading the detail. It is clear that the assessment process will be pivotal to how we move forward. Will my right hon. Friend ensure that disabled people are part of the co-design of how the assessment process advances, as well as the training of assessors? Alongside that, will he extend that principle to young people who also need that support?

The next step will be the work leading up to the White Paper, in which, as I have said, there will be extensive engagement with and involvement of disabled people. We will need to hear the voices of disabled people as we do the detailed work between now and publication of the White Paper.

I welcome that people with the most severe conditions and terminal illnesses will no longer need to go through the process again and again. Will people with severe mental illnesses be included in that group? What additional support will be available to people with fluctuating mental health conditions who are at work, as well as those who want to return to work?

For the group that my hon. Friend rightly highlights, the key is improved employment support. For example, the Connect to Work scheme, which is now up and running throughout England and Wales, includes support for people after they have started work so that, if they do run into a problem early in their job, they can fall back on the support provided to help see them through that.

I wholeheartedly congratulate my right hon. Friend on his statement and the work he has done. The co-production model clearly has much to recommend it. I think I speak for everybody in the House in wanting to see that continued through to the White Paper. May I take my right hon. Friend back to the tension point between the two reviews? We have a different proposition altogether here, for which I am grateful, but there are additional costs from disability, which of course is no respecter of age, and the potential differential between the ages of 24 and 26 under Milburn may lead us to inadvertent age discrimination. I ask him to take those issues on board. Lastly, if there is any ability to take forward his excellent proposals between now and the White Paper, perhaps he might consider doing that.

It will take a bit of time to plan and implement the changes I have announced today, so I do not think we will see much before the publication of the White Paper. I put to my hon. Friend the point that I put to a number of our hon. Friends: what is really important for young people at this critical stage in their lives is to give them the chance of a job so that they can earn a living for themselves. That is the crucial, overriding ambition that we want to see achieved.

Will my right hon. Friend join me in thanking the thousands of disabled people who submitted evidence, making his review so meaningful? I welcome the change of culture and the acknowledgment of the substantial costs faced by some disabled people. Will he assure me that the system will provide appropriate support to those with fluctuating, unpredictable and sometimes acute conditions, such as MS?

That is very much our ambition, and we are determined to achieve that. I join my hon. Friend in thanking all those people—over 38,000—who contributed to our call for evidence, and others who contributed to other engagements undertaken as part of the review.

I welcome the Timms review and its extensive engagement with disabled people and the organisations representing them. PIP should be about enabling people to live independently by meeting the additional costs of their conditions, not creating further barriers. How will the Minister ensure that the proposed reforms deliver more personalised, dignified support that properly recognises fluctuating and lifelong conditions and does not result in people losing support that they genuinely need?

We can develop a more personalised system. For example, stage one, as proposed in the review, is an initial gateway, which is a conversation with people about their aspirations and the barriers they face. That would help to route them through the assessment process and better reflect their personal circumstances, which the current system does not.

Let me say well done to my right hon. Friend. One thing the report shows clearly is that disabled people are not a homogeneous group. At one end, we have people with lifelong conditions, who should not have to face a lifetime of reassessments and reviews. But is it really right that PIP is used, at the other end, for people with drug addictions and alcoholism? In those circumstances, we should be giving them support rather than finance to fund their addictions.
My hon. Friend has raised this matter with me previously. He is absolutely right on both scores, and we are looking at the latter point.

I concur that our welfare system is not fit for purpose, but behind it are vulnerable people, often with fluctuating and lifelong conditions. I seek assurances from the Minister that he has truly listened to disabled people, and their representatives and advocates, who will be there to shape the reforms as they advance. Will he also explain how the reforms will ensure the proper stewardship of taxpayers’ money?
Both those objectives are absolutely right, and we are determined to deliver on both of them.

I thank the Minister for his statement and for his extensive engagement to date. Will he reassure my constituents that fast-tracking those with severe and degenerative conditions will help to improve the quality of life for the most vulnerable in society? Removing those repeated reassessments will undoubtedly provide them with a better experience, but will also save taxpayers’ money into the bargain.
My hon. Friend is right on both of his two points as well. I think we can achieve those things.

I welcome the Minister’s statement, the review and, in particular, the proposals for those with the severest conditions that are unlikely to improve—an issue that is raised consistently by my constituents in Basingstoke. One of the many things that the Timms review and the Milburn review have in common is the proposal on the ability to exchange cash payments for services. Will the Minister say a little bit more about that and whose choice that would be—the claimant’s or the Government’s?

The review is clear: it should be the claimant’s choice. The model here is Motability, where that is the case at the moment. At the shaping recommendations workshop that I mentioned, I met somebody who said that what she really would have liked was to have been able to give up her PIP in exchange for a particular kind of lifting bed that she had great difficulty in finding. She eventually did find one at a chain of bed shops; it cost a great deal of money. It may well be that a lot of people want beds of that kind. Maybe that kind of equipment could be provided on this basis as well.

Personal independence payments were designed to pay for the additional costs faced by disabled people, including those in work, but too often the assessment process created by the previous Government has concentrated on what people cannot do, and, as a result, has penalised those who have a job. Does the Minister agree that focusing PIP assessments on need rather than diagnosis, as the report recommends, will allow more disabled people in Ealing Southall to gain and to retain employment?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. Sometimes, for people on PIP, one of the real fears about going into a job is that if they start one, the DWP might come along and say, “Oh, you don’t need your benefit any more then”, and then take it off them. We have addressed that with our Right to Try regulations. There is more that we need to do, but I agree that changing the nature of the assessment will help significantly as well.

A common issue described to me is the failure of the existing PIP system to recognise the fluctuating nature of many conditions. For many, the solution to that failure has been absurd: people with genuine need forced to lie. I appreciate that the Minister has recognised the fluctuating conditions issue. Will he commit that the reforms will deliver a system where good people in need are not punished for being honest?
That is absolutely our ambition, and I am hopeful that we can do a better job specifically for people with fluctuating conditions, of whom there are many.

Madam Deputy Speaker, I am one of those Back-Bench Labour MPs who love welfare—according to the shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for Faversham and Mid Kent (Helen Whately). And do you know why? It is because it saves lives. I welcome the Minister saying that he wants to replace a dehumanising system. That is long overdue. Nothing frustrates disabled people more than being signposted to services that do not exist, and nothing makes them more worried than speculation about policy changes. Similar to the Milburn review, the aims here are good, but I have concerns about how they will be paid for. Will the Minister categorically promise that there will be no cuts that make people poorer?

Our ambition is to make people significantly better off. That is set out in the terms of reference for the review, and I think the recommendations will help. My hon. Friend will see the details in the White Paper that follows.

I thank the Minister for all the work that he and his co-chairs have done. An injection of compassion and a focus on the cost of disability is the right approach. I have met constituents who have fluctuating conditions that are often invisible, are rarely understood by assessors and that predominantly affect women. They agree that the current system is undignified and broad brush. Will my right hon. Friend explain what the review concluded about how those varying costs might be considered?

We have talked about the fluctuating conditions point; I think we can do a better job there. We do not envisage that the assessment will come up with “fifteen pounds and something pence” for each person. What I suspect may well happen is that there will be a larger number of payment bands than there are at the moment to reflect the varying nature of the conditions to which my hon. Friend rightly draws attention.

Can I declare that my daughter is in receipt of disability living allowance? Those of us who are advocates for people who are non-verbal or who have learning disabilities know the complexity of the system—continually having to produce the same information or the same paperwork. I therefore welcome the single digital profile and the benefits it could bring. Will the Minister say a little bit more about how that may save costs both for families and for the taxpayer?

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for all the interest that he has taken in our work during the course of the review. I was very pleased to have on the steering group a member with a learning disability. The digital profile, which we envisage being populated from the initial gateway on, would be available for the person who has applied for the benefit to use in whatever way they chose: for other bits of the benefits system, for a carer’s assessment if they subsequently went through one, or perhaps for applying for a disabled facilities grant or something of that kind. The point that he makes is a very important one and it is often made to us: people are asked time after time after time to provide the same information to different bits of the system. We think we can do better than that.

I thank the Minister for his statement and for the incredible amount of work that he has done, in collaboration with disabled groups, to get the report to us. He is right to say that those people who have the highest need should get the highest amount of support. As it is the last question, may I ask him to reiterate that and explain how the reforms will benefit those with the most severe conditions in my constituency of Harlow and across the UK?

That is very much the objective. I am delighted to reiterate that point and I thank my hon. Friend for giving me the opportunity to do so. We want an assessment that correctly establishes who has additional costs arising from disability. Evidence that we have looked at in the course of the review shows that quite high awards of PIP sometimes go to people with very low costs—or sometimes to those with no costs—and the other way around is true as well. We want to do a much better job, and I am confident that we can.

With permission, Madam Deputy Speaker, I would like to make a statement following the conclusion of the COP31 climate summit. This year’s climate conference sought to confront a hard truth: that the world is on course to exceed 1.5° of warming by around 2030. We all know what this will mean for communities at home and abroad. At around 1.4° of warming today, we are already seeing the impacts. Here in Britain, this summer brought record heatwaves, droughts and wildfires, and it was people’s homes, their livelihoods and the communities that they love that were impacted. And not just that: lives were lost, too. As my right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care informed the House earlier, the UK Health Security Agency released data today showing that we saw a total of 5,258 heat-related deaths in the UK over 2026. We cannot stand by and let this be the new normal. Overseas, we saw the devastation on the Nepal-China border with heartbreaking scenes of communities destroyed. Around the world, communities on the frontline of the climate crisis are seeing their homes destroyed and their livelihoods threatened. Climate change is here, and as we overshoot 1.5°, the impacts will be felt in country after country, the world over. So I went to COP31 clear about the challenge we face, and about the urgency of taking climate action. The target of 1.5° remains the right target. As the UN Secretary-General has said, overshoot does not mean surrender; it means redoubling our efforts. We arrived in Antalya determined to work with our partners to reach consensus on the need for urgent, ambitious action. COP31 delivered important progress across the wider negotiations, especially through the action agenda, but as the House knows, parties were unable to reach consensus on the cover decision. After concerted negotiations and tireless efforts to up the ambition, the substance that was proposed in the final cover decision did not meet the moment and we were unwilling to support it. It moved us backwards on the science when we needed to move faster. It failed to reaffirm our existing collective commitment to transition away from fossil fuels and our commitment to keep 1.5° within reach. It compromised where we needed bold collective ambition, and I was immensely disappointed by this outcome. We were not alone in standing up for these issues. We stood alongside small island developing states and some of the least developed countries on the very frontline of this crisis, which could not accept this as an adequate outcome. Now we have a responsibility to uphold and protect the Paris agreement. We have a duty to protect communities here in the UK, across the Commonwealth and in the countries most vulnerable to climate shocks. Although we could not find consensus on the cover decision, COP31 saw success beyond this. We worked with partners around the world and made progress that was not reflected in the proposed cover text. The technical negotiations delivered progress on areas including the global goal on adaptation and just transition. Conferences of the parties are increasingly about turning commitments into action through the action agenda, which was a significant focus for the Turkish COP presidency. We saw the strongest ever backing for mobilising action, with 119 countries using the closing event to recognise the wider implementation that is happening. That is concrete progress, and it demonstrates the global momentum for the energy transition. I am proud of the UK’s role in this effort. More than ever, it has strengthened our commitment to multilateralism and our resolve to work with partners in every region of the world to drive action ahead of COP32. I want to thank the UK’s negotiating team, led by Kate Hughes, and everyone across the UK civil service, business and civil society who contributed to this effort. I have seen at first hand their dedication, hard work and determination to make progress. Together we focused our e

I thank the Secretary of State for advance sight of her statement. This Government told the British public that if we led the world on climate policy, the world would follow. Ministers have lectured industry, imposed extra burdens on households and sidelined concerns about competitiveness, all on the basis that Britain would provide the model that others would emulate, but even with 100 private jets touching down at Antalya, a British delegation of 255, and 92,000 people at the largest conference ever, the whole thing collapsed. After months of speeches, declarations and moral grandstanding, the outcome was failure. The truth is uncomfortable: while Britain has been busy making itself poorer in pursuit of climate leadership, the world’s major powers have been moving in a very different direction. The United States did not even send a delegation to the conference. Instead, it is pursuing what it openly calls “energy dominance” to win the race for artificial intelligence and future technologies. Does that not expose the central flaw in the Secretary of State’s approach? The rest of the world is focused on energy security and growth; meanwhile, this Government remain trapped in an ideological cage that assumes all nations share Britain’s priorities. It is obvious that they do not. Perhaps the most revealing moment of COP31 was when the proposed text omitted any reference whatsoever to fossil fuels. That is because everyone can see that the world has become more dangerous and our energy security is at risk. This so perfectly demonstrates why the Government’s approach is misguided. The Secretary of State believes that if Britain loses enough jobs, sacrifices enough investment and abandons enough industrial capacity, others will surely follow. I wonder what the GMB general secretary thinks of that. At COP31 we saw the reality: Russia, India, Saudi Arabia and other major producers of oil and gas are not following Britain. They are pursuing their own interests, and that means it is time for us to stand up for ours. I will ask the Secretary of State some basic questions. First, does she believe that other countries are following this Government’s example when it comes to energy security? Secondly, what assessment has she made of the impact on British competitiveness when countries such as the United States are explicitly pursuing energy expansion while we restrict our own domestic production? Thirdly, she made reference in her statement to maintaining “momentum behind forest finance”. Does that mean she is committing long-term to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility? Finally, what was the total cost to the British taxpayer of sending 255 people to COP31? The gap between Britain’s climate policy and the realities of international politics has never looked wider. The Prime Minister is still trying to govern on vibes alone, and while he may think he looks cool on TikTok, it makes him a laughing stock on the international stage. He flew all the way to COP for a three-minute speech, probably written by ChatGPT, in which his main point was to show the world that Britain would show leadership. But leadership is meaningful only if others follow—ask Keir Starmer. The events of the past week suggest that no one is following Britain. Showing leadership would be to fight for cheap energy at home, maintaining prosperity, competitiveness and energy security. The Energy Secretary could start by approving Rosebank rather than briefing against it. No one will be persuaded by her virtue signalling; they will be persuaded by innovation, growth and prosperity. After the collapse of COP31, it is the Energy Secretary’s duty to refocus on delivering that.

I am going to try to compose myself because I thought that was a shameful and shocking response. The hon. Member should hang his head in shame, because if against the backdrop of the science and overshoot, that is what he thinks is an appropriate response, he needs to think again. Let me answer the hon. Member’s specific questions. First, Britain has provided a model that other countries are following.
