We were the first country to put in place a Climate Change Act, and it has been replicated the world over. There was a time when the Conservatives agreed with us and there was consensus on the need for action. Businesses were at COP31 in force because they can see that this is a global economy—a sector growing to $3 trillion, with $2 trillion in clean energy last year alone. The UK can be at the forefront of that. China, which he mentions, is stealing a march. It is moving fast on this because it sees the opportunities at home and abroad. Even if the hon. Gentleman will not recognise the realities of climate change and the duty we all have to protect our communities, and therefore to act, he should look at the economic opportunity: £110 billion in clean energy alone has been unlocked by this Government in the last two years. There is a huge opportunity to build the industries of the future. That is why businesses are clamouring. The hon. Gentleman says that countries are not following. On the path to electrification, 80 countries signed the 35 by 35 pledge put forward by the Türkiye presidency. Country after country can see that this is not just a response to climate change. Critically, the dependence on global fossil fuel markets, which was compounded by the Conservatives when they were in government, has left us acutely exposed. We are experiencing a cost of living crisis today because we are too dependent on global fossil fuel markets. The response to that is clean energy and electrification. Whether we care about climate change—which we Government Members do—affordability, or investment in our businesses and communities, this is the way forward, which is why country after country is following suit. I end by quoting the shadow Secretary of State, the hon. Member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine (Andrew Bowie), from when he had a grip and some foresight and cared about the country: “We are not rowing back on anything. Net zero remains on the statute book, and we are going to smash the target.” That was in 2023. Something profoundly tragic has happened to the Conservative party. I ask Conservative Members to look at the evidence, the science, and what is happening in the world, and to join the side of the reasonable.
I call the Chair of the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee.

As the shadow Minister mentioned Russia, let us talk about Russia. Russia had a booklet at COP advocating what it called the benefits of global warming. In Russia, of course, climate change includes the disastrous release of billions of tonnes of methane from the melting of the permafrost in Siberia. Russia was also instrumental at COP in blocking the reaffirmation of collective commitments to the transition away from fossil fuels in the final agreement. Does the Secretary of State agree that those in this place who want to delay or reverse the energy transition should think long and hard about the fact that they are not only supporting the damage done by climate change, but putting themselves on the same side as Putin’s murderous regime?

I could not agree more with my hon. Friend. In the end, we are standing alongside countries across the European Union and the global south that are on the side of change. Whether it is action on reducing methane, which we must take, or recognition that we must transition away from fossil fuels, on which we had collective global agreement at COP28, everyone can see the direction of travel that is required for the climate, and to protect our communities and ensure our energy security. We Government Members know which side we are on. I caution the Opposition; they should to reflect on whether they want to be standing on the same side as Putin.

The failure to reach a final agreement at COP31 is a deeply concerning missed opportunity. I have worked for many years in some of the most climate-vulnerable islands and countries, and I know how desperately worrying this news will be for them. It is worrying for the vulnerable people at home in the UK, too, who face the consequences of our overshooting 1.5°C, such as heatwaves like the ones we had this summer, which led to a record-high 5,258 heat-related deaths in England. Heat-related deaths are avoidable deaths. Let that sink in. I respect the advances that were made at COP, and the country negotiators who drew a line in the sand. The UK was right to stand alongside the EU and refuse to accept a deal that made no mention of the need to phase out fossil fuels—the largest driver of climate change—or the commitment to keep 1.5°C within reach. But rejecting a bad deal is only half the battle; climate ambition and leadership means doing at home what we promise internationally. We Liberal Democrats are increasingly worried that this Government risk failing that test with some of their measures, such as cutting £2.5 billion from the warm homes plan; proposing to weaken the zero emission vehicle mandate; and considering approving Rosebank, in the face of our climate commitments to global science-based targets. At COP31, the Prime Minister promised “a new era of British leadership over the next decade.” Rowing back on climate action targets is the sort of thing we have come to expect from Conservative leadership; it is not what we in this House want to see. Will the Secretary of State turn the worry that many are feeling about the results of COP31 into hope, by agreeing to our calls for a national electrification strategy, with targets; by maintaining the zero emission vehicle mandate; by restoring the warm homes plan; and by ruling out Rosebank?

I share the hon. Lady’s concerns about our failure to reach a collective agreement. She must know that we and our negotiators did everything—for 36 hours at a stretch, with no sleep—to try to get a deal that was commensurate with what we believed was needed. We will continue to work and we will continue to fight. Progress was made, the action agenda moved forward, and commitments were made in the technical track. We are committed to playing our part in the coming year, working with our partners across the world, to deliver action, because we understand how important that is. On the hon. Lady’s point about replicating our domestic work internationally, I reassure her that we are absolutely resolute about climate action at home. This matters, because our communities are at the heart of this. We have seen the impact if we get this wrong. The first duty of Government is to protect our communities, as I have said, so we will ensure that we take action. We are governed by carbon budgets, which are legally binding limits for carbon emissions. Every decision we make is within the carbon budget. We will ensure that we take balanced action to drive carbon reduction while we protect our communities. I am proud that the UK has managed to reduce its emissions by 54% since 1990. We have done that at the same time as growing our economy by 85%, so it can be done. We will take that balanced approach. We will absolutely continue to drive the warm homes plan forward. Yes, there were cuts, but we have worked to ensure that we protect the schemes for low-income households. Alongside that, we have launched the warm homes loan. It has had record interest and support; we are now looking to scale it up, so there is a balance there. We are also looking to ramp up and scale up through devolved programmes. We are consulting on the ZEV mandate, but we are clear that the end destination of getting to zero emission vehicles by 2035 absolutely stays. Again, everything we do will be done in the context of maintaining our carbon budget, so that we are delivering on our climate commitments.

The vacuous, weasel words that we heard from the shadow Minister shame a party that once had a proud track record on the fight of this generation’s life. The vast swathes of empty seats on the Conservative Benches show that that party has completely given up. The Minister is absolutely right not to sugar-coat the fact that this was a considerably disappointing COP. The UK Government were attempting to take positive steps. It is true that there are many people on the same side as us, but there are also powerful voices calling on the world not to take action. We heard positive things in Antalya about the UK’s role in providing climate finance, and about using the power of the City to support developing nations in getting the investment to make the transition. Will she tell us more about the steps that the UK Government are taking, working with our private sector partners, to ensure that nations that are unable to fund climate actions can get the support that they so urgently need?

My hon. Friend is completely right to emphasise the important role of climate finance. We are on a journey, but we have a responsibility to support vulnerable countries and the least developed countries in going on this journey with us. We have exceeded the investment made in climate finance in the last period. Going forward, we have committed £6 billion of international climate finance investment. Alongside that, there is £6.7 billion of UK-backed investment that will go through financial institutions. We are working with the private sector to unlock billions of pounds for clean energy electrification, unlocking grids and supporting adaptation. There is a huge amount that we need to do, and we are absolutely clear about the commitment that we must make to supporting others making this transition.

I agree with most of the Minister’s statement, but obviously this is a disastrous outcome, because global warming is probably the single greatest threat. Labour is the party of working people. I am worried about my working constituents in Scunthorpe, where companies are going out of business because we have the highest energy costs in Europe, and my constituents who work in the North sea oil and gas industry. Instead of trading insults across the Chamber, surely we should find some sort of balance. We produce only 1% of global emissions. There is no point in trying to meet an arbitrary target by exporting emissions, as we are doing. Surely the solution is to gradually reduce emissions, without killing off jobs in the working economy.

Let me start with the point about us accounting for only 1% of emissions. The countries that account for 3% or less of emissions together account for 50% of global emissions, so we must all play our role, but the Father of the House is absolutely right to say that there is a balance. This is a transition, and Government’s responsibility is to get that transition right—to take the action that we need to take, in a way that protects our communities. The right hon. Gentleman talks about the acute cost of electricity. Our energy costs are some of the highest in Europe because we have an energy system that is not working and that is far too dependent on global fossil fuels. We must break that dependence. Critically, we have a privatised system that does not put affordability and the consumer—business or domestic—at its heart, and we are absolutely determined to change that. We care about our workers. For me, one of the travesties is that if we look at the North sea, we see that between 2016 and 2024, some 75,000 jobs were lost there. That happened on the Conservatives’ watch. We need to support a just transition, but that will not happen unless it is intentional. We are committed to doing the hard graft to support a balanced transition.
We have to move much faster, with shorter questions and on-point answers.

It was good to see the Secretary of State at COP. In my bilateral meetings, including with Democratic US representatives, I felt a lot of optimism and will for action—a coalition of the doing, as one person put it—but the cover decision did not reflect that, and I am pleased that we rejected it as completely inadequate. How are we delivering on our climate goals, both domestically and internationally, despite the failure of the cover decision?

I will keep it brief, Madam Deputy Speaker. We are clear about our carbon budgets, and we will do everything that we can to deliver them. Clean electrification and clean power are absolutely critical. We have set out a road map, and we think that, through that, we can achieve the double win of reducing carbon emissions while responding to the affordability and cost of living crisis. We are taking action at home, but alongside that, we will continue to work with our partners to ensure that there is a coalition of the willing acting on electrification, methane, and our forests and oceans. Critically, we will also work on providing climate finance to support countries that are struggling, vulnerable and at the heart of this crisis in making the transition.

I entirely agree with the Secretary of State on the importance of protecting the Paris agreement. Looking at the regrettable conclusions from this COP, I think it is probably better, or at least more realistic, to leave it as it is than to have some sort of structural sticking plaster. Does she agree with two points? First, there is now an opportunity to look again, under the UN’s auspices, at the value of these mass conferences and the way in which they are structured. Secondly, let me reinforce the point that it is the poorest people in the world, particularly in Africa, who suffer first and hardest from climate change. Prioritising adaptation not only helps the poorest countries, but helps stop migration and displacement.

I agree with everything that the right hon. Member has said. There is scope to improve the process. One of the tragedies is that there were some good proposals in the cover decision on how we could begin to reform the process, so that it can have the impact that it needs to have. He is absolutely right; the poorest are at the very forefront of this. Adaptation is key, and we are determined to do our part to support adaptation; I chaired the adaptation track, and we came to an agreement on that. There is a question about the finance to support that, and we are committed to supporting that. However, adaptation cannot be a substitute for mitigation. We are about to overshoot 1.5°C, so we have to both adapt and mitigate if we are to have any chance of staying at 1.5°C.

The Prime Minister said at COP that we would see a new era of climate leadership from the UK. Does the Secretary of State agree that we can show that climate leadership by refusing consent for Rosebank?

That was a very good try from my hon. Friend. As he well knows, that is a quasi-judicial process, so I will not go into the specifics. What I will say, though, is that we are very clear that there is a climate and environmental test for any consenting decision, and we need to ensure we meet that test.

Unlike the shadow Minister, I do not believe that growth will come from clinging to the technologies of the past. How will the Government use their presidency of the G20 in 2027 to rebuild the coalition for the energy transition, and how will they support British businesses to lead on that?

I thank the hon. Member for that very good question. We are clear that the G20 is an opportunity for us to hold the space and make advancements from COP. There is a very strong strand on resilience, and we are clear that we want to work with partners across that. There is also a critical piece on electrification and how we improve the energy system—if we are going to electrify, huge amounts of investment need to go in. We have to work across boundaries to deal with common issues.

I was slightly surprised to hear the Opposition spokesperson’s comments in light of the investment that Tata Agratas is making in his constituency, which is creating hundreds of jobs at an electrification plant. Maybe he is just following the Opposition party lines, but I am sure Tata will be very disappointed to hear what he has said. I was deeply disappointed by the outcome of COP. As I understand it, some good technical work was done on electrification, and I thought the Prime Minister’s presence there underlined the importance we gave it—it was really reassuring to hear him say that the UK is determined to lead by example, particularly in light of the Jackdaw decision. Will we have the same leadership on Rosebank? I will try one more time.

I thank my hon. Friend for asking that question again. As he knows, the process is quasi-judicial—my favourite word—but the Prime Minister was really clear about our commitment to, and endorsement of, the electrification pledge. We think there is a huge opportunity to drive clean power, but also to ensure consumers benefit from it by having the kit in their homes, such as solar, batteries, EVs and heat pumps. We are clear that that is how we will drive down bills, and critically, it is an investment in every single community—we are creating jobs for our people. This is the opportunity of the future.

While the failure of COP was deeply disappointing, I welcome the fact that the UK Government refused to sign up to an agreement that—as the Secretary of State said—would have been a move backwards. Does she recognise that approving Rosebank would be exactly the same sort of move backwards against the things she talked about in her statement? It would be a failure to live up to our commitments, and an abdication of our responsibility to uphold the Paris agreement to transition away from fossil fuels and keep 1.5° within reach. It would render the Prime Minister’s pledge of “a new era of British leadership” on climate utterly hollow.

We are committed to transitioning away from fossil fuels. We have introduced the Energy Independence Bill, and the reason there is a ban on new exploration is that we are clear about that pathway. We are in no doubt about where we need to be in 2050, but within that, we will ensure that we manage our existing fields. We will do all of that in a way that is consistent with our carbon budgets—when we consented Jackdaw, I said I was confident that that decision was consistent with our delivering net zero and with our carbon budgets. We can and will operate within our existing climate commitments.

I commend the Secretary of State for her leadership on these issues. With the UK responsible for less than 1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, many of my constituents are sceptical that actions in the UK will make any difference. That is why global partnership and climate diplomacy are so important, but does the Secretary of State share my concern that approval of any new or existing fossil fuel projects risks undermining our efforts to take global leadership on this issue?

Having spent the week with countries abroad, there is no doubt that people see the leadership we are providing and recognise and respect it. To come back to the point I have already made on consenting decisions, whatever decisions we make will be consistent with our carbon budgets and our climate commitments. We are not resiling from the end state of net zero or from the transition that we must go through.

One area where we are most definitely not showing leadership is on deep geothermal. The Secretary of State might remember coming as a Minister to our all-party parliamentary group meeting two years ago, and progress since then has been painfully slow. This week we saw the news that in the latest auction round, zero money has been allocated to deep geothermal electricity projects. Does that not make even stronger the case for a set-aside fund in the new money that the Government have announced from the North sea, so that we can definitely get this industry off the ground?

I know that the hon. Member has been an avid, consistent and passionate advocate for deep geothermal. We are looking at everything in the technology mix and how it can help us do the transition. I believe he has spoken to my ministerial colleague, my hon. Friend the Member for Leeds North West (Katie White). We will continue to engage and we will continue to work with him, because if there is an opportunity, we are keen to ensure we are exploiting it.

Over the past few years, the language of the COP has moved from saying that we will phase out fossil fuels to saying that we will phase down fossil fuels, to saying we will transition away from them. This time, there was no mention of fossil fuels. I congratulate my right hon. Friend on her decision not to support the cover decision. It is clear that the battle lines are now drawn. We heard in her speech about Dame Madeleine Alessandri being appointed as the climate security person. We now need a coalition of the willing to fight this battle. That is a battle not just for the environment, but for security. That was made clear by the Intelligence and Security Committee’s report earlier this year. Will she now ensure that we observe what the UN Secretary-General said and do not despair about overshoot, but redouble our efforts, present a coalition of the willing and secure the future of this planet?

I thank my hon. Friend for his leadership in this area. He has been a strong and consistent voice for climate action. He is completely right in his analysis and, critically, that the way forward is to develop a coalition of the willing. I believe that such a coalition exists. We are committed to playing our part to support that over the course of the coming year in advance of Addis Ababa. He is right to point out that climate change is an energy security issue, but it is fundamentally a national security issue. The Ministry of Defence has done its own analysis and concluded that climate change is a national security issue. The imperative for us to act is absolutely clear on every single front.

I must say I have been hugely disappointed by how far the Conservative party has fallen on this issue. Voters in Oxfordshire know full well that if they want action on flooding or heatwaves, and if they want to secure their own community’s future, we do that by tackling climate change at every possible level. When the Liberal Democrats put that on the front of our manifesto to take over from the Conservatives on Oxfordshire county council, not only did we win, but we got a majority. What are this Government doing to encourage climate leadership at council level? We can show people that we can lead at all levels, everywhere in this country and abroad.

The hon. Lady is completely right. There is a huge role for councils to play. One reason that we are pushing to devolve the warm homes plan is that we know that upgrading our buildings, our communities, our schools and our hospitals will be critical not only for adaptation, but for the job of mitigation and electrifying people’s homes. Regional and local government can play a powerful role, because they know their communities and their communities trust them. If we want to deliver the scale that we need over the course of the next decade, it must be through local government.

I share the Secretary of State’s disappointment that despite the UK’s effort, a consensus was not reached at COP31. The urgent need for action against the climate crisis has not changed, and neither has what the science is telling us. With that in mind, how will her Department, looking forward from COP31, use Britain’s position on the world stage as a climate leader to drive international progress?

My hon. Friend is completely right, and there is a huge opportunity with the G20 presidency for us to continue the work. That work is climate leadership and ensuring that we are filling the space and building that coalition of the willing, but it is also the critical job around clean energy and electrification. There are common challenges in country after country about grid connections, how we build energy access and infrastructure. There is huge amounts that we can share as we go on this journey and support others so that we do it collectively.

If a policy is to be effective, it must command general support, so I welcome what the Secretary of State has been saying about the importance of multilateralism, but given that China, the United States and India between them create 50% of the world’s emissions and we create 1%, what can we do that will be effective unless they are acting as well? Which, if any, of those three countries are reducing their emissions significantly?

The right hon. Member is entirely right. China is streets ahead of anyone on this journey: it is on course to deliver 35% electrification by 2030. In respect of EVs, solar and renewables, it is stealing a march on us, and what India is doing on the ground is staggering. Regardless of geopolitics, countries recognise the direction of travel. They recognise that this is about climate—and their communities are at the very heart of the impacts of climate change—but, critically, they also see the economic opportunity. They know that this is the route to home-grown energy, they know that it is the route to lowering bills, and they know that it is the route to energy security. We must continue to ensure that there is collective action and we must continue to ensure that we are taking everyone on this journey, but I would not doubt the work that is being done on the ground, because everyone can see where all this is headed.

The very disappointing failure to secure an agreement reaffirming transition away from fossil fuels must make the UK determined both to use other channels for international co-operation on climate action and to accelerate our own transition to cheap, clean power. What will be the next steps to roll out floating offshore wind generation in west Wales, and to increase the opportunities for local supply chain input into construction and maintenance, thus creating more and better jobs for my constituents?

We need a mix of renewables and nuclear to secure a clean energy system. We have been looking for bids for allocation round 8, and have made it clear that we want to ensure that where there are opportunities we are taking them, throughout the country. As my hon. Friend has said, this is not only about the infrastructure that we are building but the investment in our communities and the jobs that we are creating. There is an opportunity for every part of the country that we are absolutely committed to unlocking.

There must be agreement that fossil fuel emissions have caused this crisis, and there must be agreement about how we provide adaptations for the countries that need it most, but we are struggling to secure unanimity in the House, let alone every nation involved in COP. The Secretary of State has said that she is seeking to improve the COP process, so might she consider different ways in which that agreement could be reached? Despite the rogue players out there not allowing us to arrive at unanimity, we know that a majority of the countries at COP agreed and that there is a majority view that can drive this agenda forward.

I think that all parties are now reflecting on how we can improve the process. As I said, the presidency had some proposals about how we could do that, and I suspect that all the UN’s agencies and the institution itself will be thinking about how to do it. However, we should remember where we were before Paris. We were on course for 4°, but collective action—that multilateralism, however painful—has moved us to a place where we are now on course for 2.8°, and if all the countries deliver what they have said they want to deliver in terms of national contributions, it will be 2.1°. Multilateralism does work. It is painful and it is painstaking, but it works.

Even when multilateralism stumbles, it gives us an opportunity to demonstrate, through our own domestic decision making, what could be done. As the Government move towards a decision on a third runway at Heathrow, may I ask the Secretary of State to remind her colleagues that expansion at Heathrow would pump out about 4.4 million tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, in addition to the other climate-changing pollutants? Moreover, it would break our carbon budget and undermine our commitments with regard to the Climate Change Act 2008.

We have been really consistent. Any proposal from Heathrow about a third runway will need to be consistent with our climate commitments, and we will hold that position. We are very clear that we must deliver our carbon budget, and we will work with all parties to ensure that any proposal sits within that. Ultimately, there is a test, and it is for Heathrow to meet that test.

The point at which the UK lost its leadership on climate change was under a Conservative Government. Today the UK Health Security Agency reports that more than 5,000 deaths in England this year were linked to the extreme summer heat, after our hottest summer on record. The climate crisis is not some way off; it is now. Does the Secretary of State agree with Al Gore that it is outrageous that a handful of petrostates have a veto power on any mention of fossil fuels in the COP31 agreement? What will the UK Government do to keep the multilateral consensus-based process on track, or does she think there is a different way for states to tackle the climate crisis collectively?

I agree with the hon. Lady and Al Gore that it is outrageous that we did not reach a consensus on the scale of ambition. It is a process, and ultimately countries have gone on this journey, painful as it is. At some point, all countries signed up to the transition away from fossil fuels. There is a process, and we will work with all parties to ensure that we are moving forward collectively, because this is a collective action problem. It is not enough for us to act if we are not acting in concert with others, so we will work with all sides, including those that are a bit more resistant, in order to move forward.

The failure of COP31 is unsurprising, given that the fossil fuels lobby repeated exactly the same arguments used by pro-Rosebank Members of this House. Collectively dragging our feet means food prices soaring, unliveable towns and lower living standards. Is it not time that politicians had the honesty to admit that we cannot ignore the environmental limits on growth and that capitalism, based on consuming more of the Earth’s resources every single year, is not an economic policy but a death cult?

My hon. Friend is a very passionate advocate for climate action. Of course we need to adjust our economy in response to climate change, but as a country we have delivered a 54% reduction in carbon emissions at the same time as growing our economy by 85%. I believe that the two are possible, but it requires the Government to be intentional about it. It requires deliberate policies to think about how we can ensure that we do the transition in a way that is good for our economy and, critically, that we do it in a way that is good for our communities.

I thank the Secretary of State for her statement and for the work that she tried to do at COP. Understandably, her statement mainly focuses on the issue of fossil fuels, but there is a passing reference to biodiversity and the security and future of our oceans. Could she say something about how the Government intend not just to protect biodiversity, but to enhance and improve it? We need to reduce, restrict and stop illegal overfishing of the oceans; the loss of many animals and habitats because of that; and the deep levels of pollution, which lead to people eating polluted fish. That crisis is equally as bad as all the others.

The right hon. Member is right to raise nature. My colleagues in the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs were with us at COP and made advancements on this issue. We are very clear that in the fight for climate, nature is an ally. When we think about carbon reductions, our forests and oceans have an absolutely critical role to play, which is why we went into this COP looking for action. We are putting investment into that and building partnerships to ensure that we can protect and preserve our forests as well as our oceans, because that is a critical part of how we respond.

Although COP ended without agreement, Nvidia has seen its stock increase by 30%, taking the company to a nearly $4 trillion market capitalisation. Meanwhile, my constituents in Larbert continue the campaign to prevent a hyperscale AI data centre from being built in a residential area, which is next to a care home and a hospital that serves over 300,000 people. What is the Secretary of State doing to stop international investors and tech oligarchs with no regard for our climate trying to shape Britain’s industrial future for their own gain, at the expense of communities?

We are very clear that there is an economic opportunity from AI, but we need to ensure that we shape it so that it works for the benefit of our communities. That is a combination of focusing on strategic AI projects that have impacts on our wider supply chain and, critically, of ensuring that, where there are data centres, they have a very clear community benefit, whether in what we extract from the companies to invest in communities that host AI centres or wider impacts for the supply chain, chip manufacturing and other things that may come out of this. My hon. Friend is right to raise caution, and I know that communities are worried about AI, but the Government are committed to ensuring that this is AI for good and AI that fundamentally works for our communities.

The collapse of COP must mean accelerating clean energy, including emerging technologies such as tidal stream. Projects such as Morlais on Ynys Môn need long-term certainty, yet tidal stream received no budget allocation in the latest CfD, which is sending a worrying signal to the sector. What steps is the Secretary of State taking to provide long-term support for tidal and wave energy?

As I have said, we know that there has to be a balance of projects, and we want a balance of projects, particularly those that will benefit different parts of the country. In thinking about the balance in that suite of projects, we are trying to manage their ability to play a role in our clean energy drive, and about their affordability and cost. That is a difficult balance, but when we open our auctions we are asking for projects that can meet the test of both delivering the clean energy we need and, critically, of doing it at the least cost. Candidly, consumers would expect nothing less from us.

The Government were right to hold firm on what the science tells us and, indeed, on what our own bitter experience of wildfires and flooding tells us. What will the Government do now to build on the political partnership in evidence at COP between the UK and some of the world’s most climate-stressed countries?

My right hon. Friend has been a clear and passionate advocate of this agenda, and she is absolutely right that we must work with partners. We will work with partners in the EU, but also with those across the least developed countries as well as island states at the very forefront of this. There is an IPCC piece that is the science foundations of everything we do, and critical work needs to be done to ensure that the science leads climate action. There is also work we must do to ensure that a coalition of the willing is up for acting. Irrespective of COP action, there is a huge amount that we must come together to progress, and we are determined to do so.

The Government said they could not sign the COP31 agreement because it did not come close to meeting the scale of the challenge. If we are going to meet the scale of the challenge, the public need brave leadership. They need to know what that challenge really looks like, and what they can do. Will the Secretary of State support a national emergency briefing fronted by the Prime Minister and delivered by experts to inform the public, and some official Opposition Members, about the true nature of the challenge we really face?

My hon. Friend the Minister for Climate Transition met the organisers of the national emergency briefing, and we had a Westminster Hall debate on this critical question. Engagement and recognition of what climate change means for our communities are absolutely critical. We know that we cannot impose this transition on people, so we need a conversation with the public about what this means. There is also an opportunity if we get this right—because there is a downside, but there is also an upside—and we as a Government are absolutely committed to having that conversation, engaging with our communities, working with our local leaders, who will be critical to such a conversation, and driving consensus for the scale of ambition that we all know we need.

The failure of COP31 is a bitter disappointment. Climate change is the single biggest issue we face, and it is caused by fossil fuels. The Government were right to refuse to sign up to an agreement that does not take account of that incontrovertible scientific fact. Does the Secretary of State agree that, given that Britain was one of the first countries to industrialise, we have a special responsibility to lead the world in tackling climate change and decarbonisation, and will she be working with our European allies who also refused to sign up to the statement to ensure that that happens?

Let me reassure my hon. Friend that we are clear both about our historical responsibility and about the partnership we need to move forward. Countries are following the UK’s example: we pioneered the Climate Change Act 2008 and now 76 countries have taken it on; we were the first G7 country to phase out coal; and we were one of the first major economies to ban new exploration for oil and gas licences. We are leading and others are following. We take that responsibility to heart.

I was at COP31, too. The strapline was “dialogue, consensus, action”. We saw lots of dialogue. We even saw a consensus between two camps—the polluting countries and the polluted countries—but what we did not see was action. In particular, the Minister spoke about the lack of action on adaptation, which is obviously not just a problem abroad. The Minister told this House that 5,258 people in the UK died from the heat this year alone. Will she commit to a properly funded adaptation plan here at home, and also for the frontline countries?

My right hon. Friend the Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs will be coming forward with our responses, but the hon. Member is right to raise adaptation. Climate change is here and all countries now need to ensure that we are scaling up adaptations. We are investing a record amount—£10 billion—in flood defences. We are investing in upgrading our schools and hospitals, and we are investing in upgrading our homes. We understand that there is a huge amount of work to do, but we are committed to making sure that we play our part, because ultimately this comes down to protecting our communities, which is the first duty of Government.

COP31 was a disaster in our battle against climate breakdown. Let us be clear: the world is being held hostage by a fossil fuel mafia hellbent on using its wealth and power to stop necessary action to maintain its profits. It even kept the words “fossil fuels” out of the draft text. As the United Nations Secretary-General said, “fossil fuel interests keep making a killing while killing our planet.” Is it not time that Governments around the world confronted the fossil fuel giants and put humanity’s future before their dirty, obscene profits? Does that not need to include a rejection of Rosebank?

I think most countries recognise that we need to transition away from fossil fuels. What I would say—and this is where there is a need for empathy and balance—is that for some of the states actively working against this, this is the heart of their economy and their livelihoods. So part of what we need to do is ensure that, as we have that conversation about what transition looks like—I am very clear that we have to make that transition in a way that works for all our communities, both at home and abroad—we have got to work with those who at the moment are wholly reliant on oil and gas to power their economy, to help them make that transition. I have been very careful in how we manage that, because this is a hard thing that we are all having to do and are trying to do. The more that we can do that in collaboration and allyship, understanding and seeing things from the perspective of those who come at this issue from a different perspective, the more progress we will make as we go forward.

I may be in the minority in this place today, but I believe this needs saying. At COP31 the utter madness of net zero was laid bare. All the leaders flew there in their jets while increasing the tax burden on flyers around the UK. None of them took non-fossil fuel methods of transport to get there. Given that the major global emitters of fossil fuels refused to sign the transition deal and that the UK accounts for less than 1% of global emissions, how can the Government justify punishing others with domestic policies that raise energy bills and risk de-industrialisation?

First, as a Department we are always clear that, whatever the emissions from taking a delegation to any COP are, we offset that through other measures, and we will do that again. I hear people consistently trying to juxtapose climate action against affordability. I do not believe there is a tension there. Yes, we are having a cost of living crisis, but what is driving that? It is our dependence on global fossil fuel markets. What is the way out of that? Breaking that dependence. How do we do that? We do that through clean energy. If the hon. Member does not believe in climate change, fine; that is up to her. That is not where I am. Ultimately, whether it is a question of climate or a question of affordability, it is the same answer: clean energy electrification. That is our route out of the bind, so I do not believe there is a conflict and I think it is disingenuous when Members suggest that there is.

Going to COP and giving a statement with no reference to fossil fuels is a bit like going to a lung disease conference and not mentioning smoking. It is cause and effect: we know that fossil fuels have been putting fuel on the fire of the climate crisis, so does the Secretary of State agree that we have to be persistent in trying to encourage working together globally on the issue, ahead of the UK getting the G20 presidency?

I completely agree with my hon. Friend. We have to be at the forefront. There needs to be a transition, but the thing that we are all grappling with is how we do that transition in a way that works for communities. At the heart of this issue are people—their lives, jobs and livelihoods. That transition is incredibly hard for every country that is going through it, but we make progress by learning from and supporting one another. We are a step ahead of other countries on this journey, and we have a responsibility—whether through technical assistance, financial support, or collaboration on unblocking private investment—to do our bit to help others go on this transition.

The Minister is absolutely right that we have already felt the impact of global warming. More than 65 families in my constituency felt it when there was freak rainfall and flooding. It is disappointing that COP31 did not reach an agreement, but it is even more disappointing that America failed to turn up, given it makes 10% of pollution. What work will the Government do to build a relationship with our allies and lead on this issue, so that we leave a better planet for future generations?

We are working with all countries. There was a huge presence from American states. When I was at New York Climate Week, it was incredibly clear to me was that there is a massive amount of action happening at state and local level to drive this transition. Ultimately, I come back to the fact that there is an imperative to protect our communities, and critically, there is a huge economic opportunity, recognised by lots and lots of countries and states.

I strongly welcome the Prime Minister’s attendance and leadership at COP31. It was significant, especially at a time when some petrostates are trying to undermine the process, and when the public can clearly see and feel the effects of our heating planet. Does the Secretary of State agree that global co-operation on the climate is too important to fail?

My hon. Friend is completely right. In the end, this is a collective action problem, so we need multilateralism. It is too important to fail. We are very clear about the leadership role that the UK can play. We have an opportunity with the G20 presidency to ensure that we are holding space for multilateralism. We are committed to doing that, because it is the only way that we will solve the problem.

The failure of COP would have been a disaster in any year, but particularly this year, when we have seen such devastation from wildfires and drought. One of the groups of people particularly impacted by a changing climate are farmers. I see that back home in Norfolk all the time. Could the Secretary of State say what the Government are doing to support farmers with the adaptation needed to respond to that changing climate?

Agriculture and the farming community have a huge role to play, and our farmers are at the very heart of advocating for climate and adaptation action, because they can see the impact on their farms, businesses and communities. The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and DEFRA are working closely with the farming community to help unlock the solutions and respond to the situation.

Turkey made zero waste a central theme of COP31. This morning, the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee held a stakeholder roundtable on the circular economy. We heard that there is enormous expertise and pent-up investment in the UK, but the Government’s circular economy growth plan has been chronically delayed. This cuts across multiple Departments, including the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. Will the Secretary of State speak to counterparts in DEFRA so that we can get the plan out the door and start to seize the growth opportunities that other nations are steaming ahead with?

My hon. Friend is completely right to talk about the opportunities of the circular economy. I hope he will be reassured that we are working closely with our colleagues in DEFRA. This is a really important part of the puzzle. There are huge opportunities and investors that are willing to step into the space, and we are committed to working across Government and with them to unlock those opportunities.

I was deeply disappointed that there was no agreement at COP31, and I find the official Opposition’s luddite attitude simply baffling. I mean, change tack, man—there aren’t enough luddites out there for you to win. I was also deeply disappointed to hear about a possible dilution of the ZEV mandate to 50%; with existing flexibilities, that would increase demand for petrol to the equivalent of double the annual output of Rosebank, and would almost certainly lead to the breaking of a manifesto commitment. I ask the Secretary of State to confirm that she is still committed to the banning of pure petrol and diesel vehicles by 2030—not hybrids by 2035, but pure petrol by 2030.

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this important point. We are committed to zero emission vehicles by 2035. As he knows, we are going through a consultation at the moment, and we are looking at options for the trajectory. Irrespective of that trajectory, though, we know that EVs are hugely cost-effective for consumers—it is between £800 and £1,400 cheaper to have an EV, so the market is booming. We are seeing record EV sales because consumers can see the opportunity. We will do our bit to ensure that we continue to support that trajectory, but, candidly, I think the market is going to outstrip us.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. We are in the middle of UK Parliament Week, and I commend the team for their work on that. Our young people are self-evidently the future. Can my right hon. Friend reassure them and the House that there is hope on this vital issue, and that British leadership will be central to overcoming the problems of climate change in the future?

I thank my hon. Friend for ending with that question. I genuinely believe that there is hope. What gave me hope was sitting opposite countries from across the world and seeing that, for all the disagreements and the rancour, there is absolute commitment to the Paris agreement, and resolve that, ultimately, for many communities this is existential and we have to act collectively. We have the technology and the pathway, and we know what needs to be done, so I am hopeful. I am also very clear that the UK has a fundamental leadership role to play, and we are determined to play it.

Before we come to the ten-minute rule motion, I should inform the House that the case relating to Elkin and Bell Funerals has been referred to the Court of Appeal by the Attorney General under the unduly lenient sentence scheme, and it is therefore sub judice. Mr Speaker has granted a waiver to allow the case to be referred to during this debate. The facts of the case and the convictions may be referred to, but Members may not discuss the sentencing review or matters that might influence sentencing decisions, such as the seriousness of the offences or the length of the sentences originally imposed.

I beg to move, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to require the Secretary of State to prepare and maintain a register of funeral directors, private mortuaries, direct cremation services and certain other persons who transport or hold the bodies of deceased persons; and for connected purposes. It has been three years since I first met Ministers to register my horror, because I had just discovered that anybody—no matter their background, expertise or resources—could set up business as a funeral director. Since then, there have been numerous meetings and numerous Ministers; the Government have said a lot and done almost nothing. The disturbing fact remains that in the funeral industry, there is no minimum qualification, no registration, no licensing, no inspection, no formal regulation and, crucially, no dedicated legislation to fall back on when things go wrong. In fact, the funeral sector is almost completely unregulated. Of course, this matter remains as pressing as ever. Last December, Gosport funeral directors Richard Elkin and Hayley Bell were convicted after a court heard they had kept 46 bodies on their business premises in an unrefrigerated room. Bailiffs entering the premises found two bodies stored without refrigeration in a dilapidated room with water leaking through the ceiling. One of those bodies—that of an elderly gentleman who had been left for 36 days—was badly decomposed. Elkin and Bell were brought to justice only by using a jigsaw of non-purpose-built legislation, including the offence of carrying on business with an attempt to defraud, causing a public nuisance, and a Victorian common-law offence of preventing a lawful burial that dates back to the times of the grave robbers. Imagine the hurt of those families who believed that the body of their loved one had been properly cared for, respectfully placed into a coffin and cremated with dignity, only to find that instead it had been left to rot on a rack at the back of the funeral parlour—it is almost unimaginable. We put enormous, unquestioning trust in those who care for the bodies of our loved ones when they die. There have been a number of high-profile cases across the UK, but in the case of Elkin and Bell, 46 grieving families were robbed of a proper grieving process because they had been left to worry about how their relatives’ bodies were mishandled. That is before we talk about those left wondering whether there were others besides those 46. I have therefore been calling for the Government to urgently bring forward proposals to establish a proper framework of regulation around the death pathway. The real horror is that this will not be an isolated case—it could be happening out there in our communities as I speak. Under the law as it stands today, anyone can set themselves up as a funeral director without any meaningful supervision. The Fuller inquiry, whose report was published in July last year, made five recommendations to the Government. Almost a year and a half later, the promised response has not arrived. Those recommendations were quite simple: first, that “The UK government should establish an independent statutory regulatory regime for funeral directors in England”; secondly, that “These regulations and standards should be considered within the overall care and journey of the deceased”; thirdly, that “mandatory information be given to customers by funeral directors to provide transparency about the care of the deceased”; fourthly, that “Direct cremation businesses should also be considered” as part of the reforms; and fifthly, that “the benefit to customers and the need for public confidence outweigh the difficulties that may be experienced by some businesses” in adjusting to a new regime. On 1 September, the Government took the meaningful step of committing formally to introducing legislation. The Secretary of State said that the Government would “bring forward comprehensive proposals to ensure respect and dignity for the deceased in eve

I draw the House’s attention to the fact that financial privilege is engaged by Lords amendments 2, 15 and 18. If any of those Lords amendments are agreed to, I will cause the customary entry for the waiving of Commons financial privilege to be made in the Journal . After Clause 3 Military homes standard
I beg to move, That this House disagrees with Lords amendment 2.

With this it will be convenient to discuss: Lords amendment 18, and Government motion to disagree. Lords amendments 11 and 25, Government motion to disagree, and Government amendments (a) to (r) to the words so restored to the Bill. Lords amendments 1, 3 to 10, 12 to 17 and 19 to 24.

The Government invite the House to agree with Lords amendment 1, 3 to 10, 12 to 17 and 19 to 24, which we tabled in the other place. We invite the House to disagree with Lords amendments 2 and 18, which were proposed by Baroness Smith of Newnham, and with Lords amendments 11 and 25, which were proposed by the Opposition. In disagreeing with Lords amendments 11 and 25, we will propose Government amendments to the restored Reserve Forces and Cadets Association provisions to the Bill. Lords amendments 1 and 3 to 7 respond to recommendations made by the Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee. The Government considered the Committee’s recommendations carefully, and the amendments simply ensure an appropriate level of parliamentary scrutiny for both the armed forces covenant statutory guidance and the code for victims in the service justice system. Lords amendments 8 and 9 ensure that the provisions enabling transfers between the regular and reserve forces operate as intended. Lords amendment 10 modernises the way in which reservists can be contacted by allowing call-out and recall notices to be served by email. Lords amendments 12 to 14, 16 and 17 make provision in relation to assaults against members of the service police and create an offence of impersonating a member of the service police. Lords amendment 15 concerns immigration fees for eligible armed forces personnel and their families. It requires regulations to provide for specified fee exemptions, which I confirm will be implemented before the end of September 2027.

I wholeheartedly support Lords amendment 15 on the issue of immigration fees for Commonwealth personnel. Having brought two amendments to the House, which sadly were voted down, I am reassured that the Government have accepted the Lords amendment so that we can finally get this pushed through and Commonwealth veterans can receive the support that they need for their families.

I, too, am very much looking forward to implementing our manifesto commitment. Lords amendments 19 to 24 are technical and consequential amendments. Amendments 19 and 20 clarify the Crown immunity provisions applying to the Defence Housing Service, while amendments 21 to 24 ensure that the transitional arrangements for the reserve forces operate as intended. The Government recognise the intent behind Lords amendments 2 and 18, and single living accommodation continues to be a priority for Defence. This is why the Government commissioned an independent review into single living accommodation, led by Natalie Elphicke Ross OBE. That review has now been published and, given the scale of change being proposed, it is essential that we take the time to get this right and put in place the foundations needed to deliver meaningful change for our people. However, recognising the need for change does not establish the case for the approach taken in Lords amendment 2. While the amendment allows for military-specific regulations, it would nevertheless make the civilian statutory requirements a mandatory minimum benchmark. The review expressly recognises that single living accommodation has a distinct function within service life and recognises operational requirements, cohesion, military culture and ethos as reasons why those arrangements can differ from civilian settings. As the Minister for Veterans and People set out in his written ministerial statement, we are already taking steps to drive this work forward. Air Marshal Sir Paul Lloyd, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff, will oversee this important work, supported by teams from across Defence. The Ministry of Defence is already looking at the review’s recommendations, and the immediate focus will be on how best to refresh the existing defence minimum standard to ensure that it better meets the needs of our people. I can speak of my own personal commitment to this issue, as someone who has experienced single living accommodation, and I take seriously the need to improve the standard of accommodation for people who work so hard in the defence of this country. Turning to Lords amendments 11 and 25, the Government strongly disagree with the other place’s decision to remove the provisions that establish the Reserve Forces and Cadets Association as a non-departmental public body. The RFCA provisions are in line with the 2019 Sullivan review, which recommended that the Council of Reserve Forces and Cadets Associations and the 13 reserve forces and cadets associations should be consolidated into a single executive NDPB with a national headquarters and strong regional structures.

I welcome the measures in the Bill, but representatives from my local reserves and cadet community in Medway have raised concerns with me about Government amendment (n), which states that the RFCA may appoint “no more than six representative members” to be drawn from the chairs of regional councils. Their concern is that without stipulating a minimum number of representatives in the legislation, the number could drop to one or even zero, when to meet the standard governance expectation of a higher number of non-executive directors than members of the executive, a minimum of three would be required. I wonder if the Minister will reconsider this aspect of the Bill.

I assure my hon. Friend that the Bill provides for regional council chairs to be represented at national level, and it establishes a national council where regional experience will be valued. We highly value the regional input, and that is why we have suggested these changes.

The reserve forces and cadets associations in Northern Ireland look after local sites and support our reserves, cadets and adult volunteers. Will the Government guarantee Northern Ireland a seat on the governing body that will make decisions about those sites and the resources they receive?

To reiterate, it is highly important that we have regional chairs that represent the broad spectrum of voices from across this country. As I said before, the Bill provides for regional chairs to be represented on the national council, and that should provide representation across the country.

I want to add my support for our fantastic reserve forces and cadets associations across the country. The fact that we have had interventions on this issue from across the House demonstrates the respect in which these organisations are held. As we move on to the new structure, may I thank the Minister for listening to concerns and for making sure that we still have a powerful regional voice while also having a strong national body to support our reserves and cadets?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right to highlight the huge amount of work done by people with a huge passion for our reserve forces and cadets. I very much recognise the immense amount of work that they do and the importance of ensuring that their voices are represented. The findings of the National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee reinforce the case for establishing a single NDPB. Those successive independent reviews reached a consistent conclusion: the current structure does not provide the level of accountability, governance or financial assurance expected of a modern public body responsible for significant public expenditure. However, the Government very much recognise that the current RFCAs remain essential to Defence’s relationship with reservists, cadets, employers and local communities. That is why there must be the requirement that the RFCA establishes regional councils to maintain those connections. The Government have tabled amendments to strengthen those connections, and will ensure that the future NDPB retains a strong regional dimension and continues to benefit from the local knowledge, community connections and experience that have been the hallmarks of the associations over the years. The amendments will make several changes. First, they clarify the regional councils’ leadership and composition, providing for chairs and arrangements for appointing presidents and vice-presidents. Presidents will be appropriate lords lieutenant, where available, preserving the RFCA network’s constitutional, ceremonial and community links. Secondly, the amendments allow for a number of regional chairs to become representative members of the RFCA, ensuring that regional perspectives can be brought into discussions at the national level. Thirdly, they will establish a national council comprising regional council chairs, service representatives and others appointed by the RFCA. This formal forum will enable regional experience, advice and expertise to inform the organisation’s work and help to maintain strong links between the centre and regions. It is important to be clear that this reform is not about removing local engagement. Rather, it is about combining strong national governance with strong regional delivery, ensuring that local knowledge, employer engagement and cadet support, and community links remain central to the RFCA’s work. In conclusion, the choice is not between reform and tradition. The Government’s approach delivers both by preserving the regional connections, civic leadership and volunteer contributions that have been central to the RFCAs’ success, while introducing the accountability, transparency and assurance that are necessary for the future. I therefore urge the House to support the Government motion.

It is a pleasure to speak on behalf of His Majesty’s Opposition on this late stage of ping-pong, or Lords amendments, on the Armed Forces Bill, which, I remind the House, had its Second Reading back in January. For the record, yet again when we are discussing important matters that affect our armed forces and their families, not a single Reform MP is in the Chamber to participate in the debate.

In a moment—I’m on a roll here. When are the plastic patriots in Reform finally going to realise that if they are constantly going to cite their admiration for those who serve in uniform, they are expected in return to turn up when we debate the future of those people and their families, including their terms and conditions of service? Reform, yet again, is AWOL when it matters on defence.

Will the right hon. Gentleman be transparent with the House? Was he so confident that Reform would not bother showing up today that he put it into his speech, knowing that he could read it out because Reform Members would not bother turning up?

As a Front-Bench spokesman, one sometimes has to extemporise, but for the record I typed both those paragraphs of my speech this morning. Having got that off my chest, may I commend Ministers for not objecting to Lords amendment 15, the essence of which is to waive visa fees for the families of foreign and Commonwealth personnel? It is an open secret that the new Veterans Minister has been sympathetic to the cause. I am pleased to see that this policy change, which Conservative Members argued for strongly on Report, has now been made. In particular, I congratulate my now Front-Bench colleague, my hon. Friend the Member for Huntingdon (Ben Obese-Jecty), on making much of the running on this issue during the Bill’s passage and, indeed, prior to that, and on helping to secure such a positive outcome, which has been welcomed by the Royal British Legion; it has earnestly campaigned on this matter for some time.

I represent the Labour constituency with the largest amount of SFA in the country. I judge how the Government are doing on this by whether I see refurbishment happening on my SFA estates, and I absolutely do. On the Defence Housing Service, the people have been put in place, and I am getting much fewer complaints about the time it takes to get repairs done and those sorts of issues. I got a lot of complaints about that when I became an MP. Government is about choices. Does the right hon. Gentleman recognise that this Government have to balance a lot of really difficult choices, but are doing the right thing and refurbishing houses that were not fit for purpose when we inherited them?

I know that the hon. Lady speaks up strongly for her military community, so perhaps I could meet her halfway. I will absolutely believe what she tells me about what is going on in her constituency if, in return, she will believe that we are genuinely annoyed, because all the way through the Bill process, dating back to its Second Reading in January, the Opposition have been repeatedly promised that this money would be ringfenced, and would not be raided to meet short-term funding pressures. The permanent under-secretary, in his letter to the Chairman of the PAC—not to the hon. Lady, and not to me—admits that that has happened in this Parliament, to the tune of approximately £2 billion. I ask the hon. Lady to appreciate that this is not faux anger. We spent months asking this question, and we were told time and again that the Government would not do what we now know they have. We have it in writing. I turn briefly to amendment 2 in the name of the Liberal Democrats. We have considerable sympathy with what the drafters are trying to achieve by seeking to set minimum standards for both SFA and SLA. This matter was discussed during the earlier stages of the Bill, so I will listen carefully to the Lib Dem spokesman. I see a raft of Liberal Democrat Members in the Chamber, but I presume that the spokesman will be the hon. Member for North Devon (Ian Roome).

In which case, I should point out that the hon. Gentleman is an RAF veteran. I congratulate him on his appointment to the Front Bench. We look forward to his explaining how the amendment would work in practice and expanding on the details of the proposal, including whether the standards will apply to transit accommodation, of which the MOD has much, and what the implications might be for the rent charged to young, predominantly single soldiers if these standards were to apply. I am sure that he has thought that through. We will listen to that in a moment. For the record, I note that he is wearing a Royal College of Defence Studies tie. In summary, we commend the Government on doing the right thing by waiving visa fees for foreign and Commonwealth personnel who serve this country in uniform, and now for their loved ones, too. However, we continue to disagree with the Government on their attempts to replace the RFCAs with a national quango, and we are deeply unimpressed by Labour’s introduction, with great fanfare, of the Defence Housing Service through the Bill, only for it to breach its own ringfence and denude it of cash, having repeatedly promised for almost a year not to do precisely that. Our armed forces and their families really do deserve better than that.

I rise briefly to address three matters of particular interest to the Defence Committee. First, Lords amendments 2 and 18 concern standards in military accommodation, particularly single living accommodation. This has been a long-standing concern of the Committee. We have seen the consequences of years of under-investment, poor maintenance and unacceptable living conditions for our service personnel. The Committee has not taken a view on whether the statutory military homes standard proposed by the Lords is the right legislative mechanism, but there should be no doubt about the standard we expect. Our service personnel should not be asked to live in accommodation that we would regard as unacceptable for anyone else. The Government have published the Elphicke Ross review, which recommends a new decent SLA standard across all permanent single living accommodation by 2032, overseen by a new office for military accommodation. Those commitments are welcome, but important questions remain. If the Government are asking this House to reject a statutory standard, will the Minister explain what status the new decent SLA standard will have, when it will be published, what interim milestones will apply before 2032, and how Parliament can hold the Government to account for meeting them? I turn next to Lords amendments 3 to 7 on the victims’ code for the service justice system. Through our work on women in the armed forces, the Committee has heard powerful evidence about the experiences of victims. I welcome the Government amendments requiring the code to be laid before Parliament and brought into force through secondary legislation, but the real test will be whether victims see a difference in practice, and whether they are properly supported, kept informed and treated with dignity throughout the justice process. The voices of victims must remain central as the code is developed and maintained. Finally, I welcome Lords amendment 1 on the armed forces covenant. The Defence Committee has supported the extension of the covenant duty, but we have stressed that much will depend on the accompanying statutory guidance. It is right that the Lords amendment preserves an appropriate degree of parliamentary scrutiny over the guidance. These changes matter to the daily lives of our service personnel and their families, and the Defence Committee will continue to scrutinise whether the improvements promised in the Bill are delivered in practice.

Thank you for your kind words earlier, Madam Deputy Speaker. The Armed Forces Bill champions many new measures to strengthen our armed forces, which continue to have Liberal Democrat support. That includes the expansion of the armed forces covenant, action on defence housing and better support for victims of service offences. However, as the Bill returns to this House, we want to speak yet again in support of a better standard of housing for all serving armed forces personnel, both those in service family accommodation and those in single living accommodation. Every member of our armed forces deserves a decent standard of housing, but the Government continue to reject Liberal Democrat amendments to the Bill that would demand improvements to single living accommodation, just like the kind I lived in while serving in the Royal Air Force. Lords amendment 2 would require the Government to agree to a minimum housing standard for single living accommodation at least as good as the decent homes standard on behalf of more than 77,000 service personnel. That standard should cover everything from building safety to heating, plumbing and laundry facilities—a baseline to be agreed within six months of the Armed Forces Bill being given Royal Assent. The Lords amendment, from my noble friend Baroness Smith of Newnham, mirrors what the Liberal Democrats pushed for in this House during earlier readings of this Bill, and my hon. Friend the Member for Tunbridge Wells (Mike Martin) and I pushed for that again when the Bill was in Committee. The Elphicke Ross review into single living accommodation was published barely a fortnight ago, and it is completely clear about the need for a decent housing standard for military accommodation. Second only to emergency repairs, recommendation 2 of the review says that the Ministry of Defence “should introduce a new Decent SLA Standard”. Specifically, it says that military accommodation should be “safe”, “warm”, “clean”, “functional”, “secure” and “private”. It also says: “For too long, poor conditions have been institutionalised by an outdated accommodation grading system that compensates substandard living with discounted rent, rather than driving the necessary improvements”. It also warns of the disaster that happened when the last Government did not back words with actions: “In 2022 an attempt was made to address the poor state of Defence accommodation. The Defence Minimum Standard (DMS) was introduced to provide a baseline for acceptable accommodation. This attempt failed because there was no funding, no implementation plan, no timetable for improvement and no mechanism for enforcement.” This time last year, the former Secretary of State for Defence, when talking about improvements to defence housing, wanted to tell our armed forces: “We are on your side”, so it is disappointing to see that the Government have proposed to reject the Lords amendment entirely, letting single living accommodation fall behind. Can the Minister tell us whether the Government will make a separate commitment on this matter? If not, as my hon. Friend the Member for Lewes (James MacCleary) has already asked the Minister, how many of the 19 recommendations of the Elphicke Ross review will be either delayed or ignored? There are no doubt dozens of Labour Members with forces accommodation in their constituencies that house thousands of personnel. How will they answer that question? I urge them to think about the conversations they will have with young serving personnel in the future. The independent review says that the Ministry of Defence needs to move on from “fix on fail” building repairs to planned lifecycle maintenance and better accountability. Nor is this just about money. The report is clear: “Many of the failings identified by the review work can be addressed at relatively low cost but with better oversight, monitoring and determination.” At the Select Committee, Ministers claimed it was not “appropriate” to judge single l

This Armed Forces Bill makes a number of important changes that will strengthen our national defence and better support our men and women in uniform. Having spoken at a previous stage of the Bill’s passage, I am glad to see it come back to this House as it nears the end of its progress through Parliament. We are here to discuss a number of amendments, which I will come to shortly, but given the Bill’s important provisions, I hope we can reach agreement so that Ministers can crack on with implementing the vital measures it contains. Why is this Bill so important? As we all know, Parliament is required to renew the legislation every five years in order to maintain the armed forces. Ministers could simply have tabled a Bill to do that; instead, what we have in front of us is a genuinely ambitious set of changes to the law that will strengthen our defensive capabilities in a number of key areas. First, as Members across the House have mentioned, it puts the armed forces covenant into law to give much greater weight to the need to support our service personnel and their families in communities across the country. Secondly, it establishes the Defence Housing Service. I disagree with the right hon. Member for Rayleigh and Wickford (Mr Francois)—I think that service will provide clearer leadership, greater coherence and greater investment in military accommodation. In my previous speech on this Bill, I set out for Ministers more detailed thoughts on how that could best work. The Bill also improves our resilience by expanding our reserves pool, grows our whole-of-society approach, and expands life chances for young people by growing our cadet forces. Finally, it modernises the law to give service personnel much-needed new powers to tackle the threat from incursions and hostile surveillance by drones. On my visits to operational bases in this country and abroad as part of the armed forces parliamentary scheme, I have seen for myself just how much of a growing issue that is, and I am glad that the Government are making specific provision for it. Those measures, and the many others contained in the Bill, are very welcome, and I think they will make a real difference. Turning to the Lords amendments, Lords amendments 11 and 25 refer to the Government’s proposed change to the legal form and governance arrangements of the reserve forces’ and cadets’ associations. I followed with real interest the debates in the House of Lords on this issue. While there is clearly disagreement about the best future approach, it is important that we recognise that there is a lot of consensus. There is widespread agreement that our reserve forces and cadets play crucial roles and deserve the very best support. There is strong support for the strategic defence review recommendations that the strength of reserves and cadets be expanded. There is also recognition that activities to organise and promote reserves and cadets in local communities and to employers are central to their success. As we heard from the Minister, under the proposed new arrangements there is a clear, ongoing commitment to ensure regional and local work will be maintained by the establishment of regional councils across the UK. What remains in contention and is whether the new body will remain an unclassified arm’s length body with Crown status or will become, as we have heard, a non-departmental public body. My view is that the argument for the latter is relatively straightforward. In 2019, as the Minister set out, the Sullivan review recommended improvements to governance, financial reporting, audit and other arrangements relating to the reserve forces and cadets associations. We know that those issues still need to be addressed, because the National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee found inadequate arrangements for monitoring the financial performance of those bodies. In September last year, the Public Accounts Committee wrote to the Government chasing progress on what was bei

Bedworth hosts one of the largest Armistice Day parades in Britain—it is known as the town that never forgets. Across North Warwickshire and Bedworth, people are incredibly proud of our armed forces, but that pride must be reflected in the way in which we treat and support armed forces personnel, veterans and their families. It was an honour to serve on the Select Committee on the Armed Forces Bill earlier this year.
