We heard from service personnel, military families, charities and those working in the service justice system. There has been progress, but it was clear that much more still needs to be done. I particularly welcome Lords amendment 1, which maintains parliamentary scrutiny of the regulations bringing the armed forces covenant guidance into effect. The covenant makes a simple promise: serving personnel, veterans and their families should not face disadvantage because of military service. Military families move around the country, spend long periods apart, and often have to rebuild their lives around the demands of service. The least we can do is ensure that they are not left behind when accessing public services. Taking part in the armed forces parliamentary scheme with the Royal Navy has enabled me to hear at first hand from serving personnel. For a family who have fought hard to obtain the support that their child needs in a local school to be nearly there, and then for redeployment to a different county to return them to the bottom of the pile, is unacceptable. That child should not be worse off because one or both parents are serving our country. The same is true of NHS waiting lists. I heard of a particularly difficult example: that of an officer and his wife who had been undergoing fertility treatment for some time. He had to make a choice: to turn down a promotion so that they could stay in the area to continue their treatment. They had a happy outcome, but that officer’s career progression was slower because the covenant was not working in the way that it should have been. Our Committee heard that, although the covenant had made a difference, support had not always been delivered consistently. In some places, the needs of armed forces families have simply not been properly understood. This Labour Government were elected on a promise to extend the covenant across Government, and the Bill takes an important step towards putting that right: for the first time, the legal duty will extend to central Government Departments, and will cover a much wider range of services, including childcare, employment, social care, pensions and benefits. However, implementation matters. Our Committee recommended clearer guidance and proper evaluation so that the covenant is delivered consistently. I have seen what good practice looks like locally: Warwickshire police has achieved gold status in the defence employer recognition scheme, and has developed an armed forces network to support veterans and their families. We should be encouraging more organisations to follow that example. Lords amendments 3 to 7 relate to the victims code of practice in the service justice system, about which I feel strongly. During our Select Committee inquiry, I asked witnesses what the new code should look like and how it should help victims to navigate the service justice system. Zoe Jackson, from Aurora New Dawn, stressed that victims needed to know from the beginning what support they could expect, and Emma Norton, from the Centre for Military Justice, also raised concerns about the protections available to victims whose cases are dealt with in civilian courts. We cannot expect victims to have confidence in a system if they do not understand their rights or the support available to them. That is why our Committee recommended comprehensive training and education alongside the introduction of the victims code, and I am proud that this Labour Government are strengthening the service justice system as part of our wider mission to halve violence against

I served on the Select Committee on the Armed Forces Bill, and I have spoken in previous debates on this Bill. The reason I wanted to do so is that a clause from my ten-minute rule Bill, which gives the Royal Fleet Auxiliary access to the independent Armed Forces Commissioner so that they, too, have someone with whom they can raise issues and grievances, was accepted as part of the Bill. I do not think it is common for a Back Bencher to make law, so I wanted to see it through and to mention it again. I wish to speak initially to Lords amendments 11 and 25, by which the Lords decided to remove the provisions that established the Reserve Forces and Cadets Association as a non-departmental public body. As Members have said, there are currently 13 regional reserve forces and cadets associations across the country, and the original provision in the Bill was to replace them with one unified body. Successive independent reviews have reached a consistent conclusion that the current structure of the reserves does not provide the level of accountability, governance and financial assurance expected of a modern public body that is responsible for significant public expenditure. Our Select Committee reported that unifying the RFCA into a non-departmental public body was a long-overdue reform from the Sullivan review in 2019, and we did support the proposals. We also suggested that the National Audit Office be invited to carry out a review of the new body two years after it is set up, to ensure that the concerns in the review were addressed. Has the Minister considered that part of our report? One of the points raised in evidence to the Select Committee on the Armed Forces Bill was just how difficult it is to gather data on reservists. We heard striking evidence about how hard it is to find veterans and reservists, right down to getting hold of their addresses, and finding out where they live and who they are. The Royal British Legion, in its briefing on the amendments, pointed out that not only would the RFCA, as a new single body, create the potential for clearer oversight and co-ordination, but the change would create the potential for improved data collection. If the separate associations were co-ordinated and merged, there could be better central insight into the demographics, locations and needs of reserve forces, cadets and their families, which obviously has the potential to inform better support for them as a group. However, the local and regional links in the RFCA remain essential to the Ministry of Defence’s relationship with reservists, cadets, employers and local communities. That is why there was a requirement in the Bill that the association establish regional councils to maintain those connections, and the Government did bring forward amendments to schedule 6 to strengthen those connections, but none was moved on Report due to the peers removing the provision. The Government’s approach would, I hope, deliver the best of both worlds by preserving the regional connections, the civic leadership and the volunteer contribution that have been central to the RFCA’s success while introducing the accountability and assurance necessary for the future. With Lords amendment 2, the Lords proposed a decent homes standard for single living accommodation. On 10 November—very recently—the Government published the review of SLA led by Natalie Elphicke Ross OBE, which has been mentioned. That review obviously needs consideration by the Government before it is put into effect. It recognises that SLA has a distinct function in service life, and recognises operational requirements, cohesion and the way single accommodation in the military will differ from family accommodation in civilian life. I want to use this moment to raise an issue raised with me by constituents, which is the impact of alcohol in SLA, and to request that the MOD recognises this issue. I know the MOD is taking steps to reduce alcohol-related harm in the military. Natalie Elph

As the Member of Parliament for Aldershot, the home of the British Army, and the chair of the all-party parliamentary group on the armed forces community, I am incredibly proud to speak in support of the Bill. For the community I represent, the measures in the Bill will make a tangible difference. I want to use my speech to highlight some of those positive changes and also areas where I think the Government could go further.

I thank hon. Members for their contributions to this debate. I will briefly respond to some of the points that have been raised. Lords amendments 11 and 25, which were mentioned by a number of Members, are all about modernising and improving the governance of the RFCAs to better support the vital work they do in their local communities, as well as supporting the work of reserve forces and cadets. I assure my hon. Friend the Member for Truro and Falmouth (Jayne Kirkham) that we will keep those changes under review. A number of Members spoke to Lords amendment 2. I remind the House that our commitment of £9.2 billion over 10 years remains ringfenced. Within that, we expect to modernise nine out of 10 SFA homes. Indeed, we have already done over 2,000 so far—and over 1,000 this year. The right hon. Member for Rayleigh and Wickford (Mr Francois) is absolutely right to note the connection between the standard of accommodation and retention. I am well aware of that, because that is also my story. I assure him that as we have seen outflow go down by 7% this year, reversing the trend of the previous four years, I am reassured by the direction of travel. My hon. Friend the Member for Slough (Mr Dhesi) rightly raised the SLA review, as did others, and I assure them that we are considering the recommendations deeply and it is appropriate that we do so. I assure all those who spoke to that issue that it is close to my heart and that of the Minister for Veterans and People. Let me address some specific points raised by the hon. and gallant Member for North Devon (Ian Roome). Given how military accommodation is organised and delivered, the decent homes standard is not appropriate. He is absolutely right to speak passionately about the importance of having SLA that reaches minimum standards, such as being warm, safe and secure, and having the amenities and the wi-fi that people would rightly expect today. However, although we may agree on the principles, we disagree on the practicalities of his suggestions. The SLA review, which the hon. and gallant Member mentioned, recognised that military SLA needs a unique standard, because of the unique nature of the community that it serves—one size does not fit all. He is absolutely right to speak passionately about the impact of substandard accommodation on many of our serving personnel. Again, that is a story that I know well. I will turn briefly to the Members who spoke passionately about Lords amendments 3 to 7. It cannot be restated enough in this House how important it is to listen to, believe and support victims through what can be a difficult process to find justice. It is important that we never stop asking ourselves what more we can do to support them. I will respond to the point made by my hon. Friend the Member for Truro and Falmouth about alcohol—an issue she is absolutely right to raise and that can be very troubling to read about. We have a number of information campaigns and we do encourage our service personnel to ensure that they look out for each other and that boundaries are respected in leisure time, but we need to do more. My hon. Friend also raised the issue of those with children who live in single living accommodation. Again, while there are some arrangements currently—welfare houses and so on—we do recognise that for those who do not have full-time care of their children, for whatever reason, those arrangements are not as good as they could be. We are actively looking at this point in order to recognise this cohort. I thank all the Members who have spoken passionately about the armed forces in their constituencies and of how proud they are of their constituents who serve either as cadets or within the armed forces themselves, or in the wider armed forces community. It is incumbent on us all to serve those who serve us and to work as hard as we can to do right by them. title: Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill

items.txt: I draw the House’s attention to the fact that financial privilege is engaged by Lords amendments 48 to 52 and 54. If any of these Lords amendments is agreed to, I will cause the customary entry for the waiving of Commons financial privilege to be made in the Journal . After Clause 58 Review of the effectiveness of the NIS regime
I beg to move, That this House disagrees with Lords amendment 107.

With this it will be convenient to discuss: Lords amendment 108, and Government motion to disagree. Lords amendments 1 to 32. Lords amendment 33, and amendments (a) to (i). Lords amendments 34 to 106 and 109 to 112.

It is a pleasure to bring this important Bill, which has cross-party support, back to the House. Lords amendment 107 would require the Secretary of State to undertake a comprehensive annual review of the effectiveness of the network and information systems regime. Many issues are raised by this amendment, and I consider the Government to have listened and responded to them carefully. First, the Bill already requires a post-implementation review of the regime. Following concerns raised in the other place, the Government tabled Lords amendment 42 to reduce the timeframe of the review from every five years to every three years. That will allow us to undertake a meaningful and more timely review. Secondly, we have listened to concerns about the sectors in scope of the regime. In the other place, the Minister for Space, Cyber and Regulatory Reform made a clear commitment at the Dispatch Box to assess whether critical sectors not already in scope should be part of the regime and report back to Parliament within 12 months of Royal Assent. I can commit to going further. I confirm that the Government will table an amendment when the Bill goes back to the other place to this effect, so that it is on the face of the Bill. To allow for a flexible approach, it will require the Secretary of State to lay a statement within 12 months of the passage of the Bill, setting out which further activities should be specified as essential under this regime. I can commit that, to inform this statement, the Secretary of State will consider whether activities and services within the UK’s critical national infrastructure sectors should be brought within scope of the regime. I can also commit that we will go further and consider advanced manufacturing, electoral infrastructure and political parties within 24 months of Royal Assent.

The Minister is showing responsiveness and flexibility, and I think he understands that, although the Bill does enjoy cross-party support, there is a need to get it right. Part of that is recognising that this is a highly dynamic environment and that technology moves very fast. What is probably in the their lordships’ minds is that that requires a very regular reappraisal of the appropriateness of the application of policy. To that end—I raised this point last week when we debated artificial intelligence—I wonder whether the Minister might look at the whole issue of interoperability and interconnectivity. My fear is that we are concentrating risk, and when we review these matters we might want to consider that in a cross-departmental way.

The right hon. Gentleman makes that point well. The reason we have not accepted Lords amendment 107, which would require a 12-month review of very wide aspects, is purely that we need this legislation to bed in. It is because it is such a dynamic environment that we need to ensure that the legislation beds in and then assess how it is working. The Minister in the other place has committed to making a verbal statement on this matter, but we are also going to put it on the face of the Bill and, as I said, advanced manufacturing, electoral infrastructure and political parties, which were raised in the other place, will be considered. I fully appreciate the dynamic and fast-moving nature of technology and cyber-security risks, which are increasing all the time. We are trying to put in place a piece of legislation that is both dynamic and has time to bed in, so that businesses and Government can take the time to assess whether it is working properly, but I take the point, and the Minister in the other place did so too by making that concession. I hope that that satisfies the right hon. Gentleman.

When I was Security Minister, I set up the National Cyber Security Centre and developed the strategy. I was very conscious then that the dilemma for policymakers, Government and the House is that our processes, by their nature and their thoroughness, require time for proper scrutiny, as the Minister is making clear. However, the world that we are trying to legislate for is moving rapidly. There is sometimes a mismatch between those two things. It may well be that the Bill has to be sufficiently flexible to allow for that kind of dynamism. I think he recognises that, and I am grateful to him.

That is the contradiction in all this. At the start of his first intervention, the right hon. Gentleman said that we have to get this right, but we have to get it right at pace, and with flexibility, which are two competing aims in this place. We need a regime that responds to the dynamism and fast-moving nature of the technology, but at the same time, we have to take the time to get this right. The Minister in the other place rejected the proposal for a 12-month review, on the basis that we would be reviewing something that would not have had time to bed in, but we will give a commitment that we will make changes to the Bill in the other place, when the Bill goes back there, to reflects the concerns of the noble Lords.

What about sovereign capability? The public sector, whether it be the UK intelligence community or other Government Departments, cannot do everything, so the partnership with the private sector is important, particularly for capital-intensive networks. I get that the Government cannot do everything and cannot afford everything, and that partnership with the private sector is absolutely critical, but does the Minister accept that there is still a place for sovereign capability? Regulation cannot cover international private sector companies—US companies, for example, that for political or trade union reasons will not take a particular action that the UK Government want them to.

Governments of all colours have recognised that the UK has to have a debate about tech and AI sovereignty. In parts of the tech stack, we should have greater AI sovereignty, because we are good at that stuff in this country, and in other parts, it would be impossible for us to try to compete. I accept the point and the challenge that if we are not in control of the levers, and they are controlled by other jurisdictions, it becomes much more difficult to determine how to regulate. We have to promote AI sovereignty for the technologies in the tech stack that we are good at. We have put in place the AI sovereign wealth fund, and we are ensuring that the national cloud infrastructure project is a partnership with the sector. There are not many suppliers, but we want to make sure that we use big Government procurement to ensure sovereignty in the cloud, and that we are seeding fledgling companies here. This is a process, but through our commitment to procuring quantum, and our £2 billion investment in quantum, the Government are showing industry very clearly that we are challenging for AI sovereignty in the tech stack in areas that we are good at. However, there are parts of the tech stack in which we will not be able to challenge.

The Minister is being very generous with his time. The Government are trusting more and more people, be it in the education, IT or defence sectors. I get that; it needs to happen. However, will the Government at least consider whether any new legislation, parallel to the Official Secrets Act 1989 or the National Security Act 2023, needs to come before the House? Arrangements cannot be made just on trust. Some defence and other companies sign the Official Secrets Act. It seems as though we will have to trust more people, in more sectors. My view is that this is a risk to national security, unless we have legislation that can sanction individuals or companies that do not fulfil their obligations.

That is a key challenge across the entire international community when it comes to defence and the sovereignty of nations. I am sure that the right hon. Gentleman is referring to the defence field in his question about the Official Secrets Act. This Bill is about making sure that we have the best possible platform for cyber-security and resilience across the whole economy, including for defence and defence contractors. There are constant discussions in Government, as there would have been when he was in Government, about how far technology needs be embedded, and what needs to be done to protect it through regulation. That is a key issue, given that the technology is moving so fast. The right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) rightly talked about the dynamism and fast pace of technological advances in this area; we have to be cognisant of that. There is a balance to be struck between access and sovereignty, and between doing things at pace and doing them right. These debates will continue. The Bill has had such support across parties and across Parliament because we need to get it through as quickly as we can. I was talking about Lords amendment 107. Let me run through the other reasons why we have not accepted it, and what we are doing instead. I recognise the desire to situate the Bill in the Government’s wider strategy to improve UK cyber-security and resilience, and I am pleased to commit to the Government publishing the national cyber action plan before the Bill receives Royal Assent; the Minister gave that commitment in the other place. I am concerned that the prescriptive and wide-ranging annual review in the Lords amendment would be a distraction from the successful implementation of the Bill, and disruptive for the regulated entities covered by it. I urge the House to recognise the efforts made by the Government to address concerns raised by their Lordships, and to support the Government in ensuring the timely passage of this critical legislation, as well as the steps being taken to recognise the issues raised by Lords amendment 107. Lords amendment 108 would require the Government to establish and maintain a register of foreign powers. As the Minister explained in the other place, a statutory register to inform the use of powers is both unnecessary and unhelpful. Cyber actors do not always operate along strict national boundaries, and risks are multifaceted; they may come from states or state affiliates, from criminals or from the technology itself. To inform action using these powers, the Government will seek holistic expert advice from across Government, including from the UK intelligence community. A blunt register risks undermining dynamism. I am sure that the hon. Member for Runnymede and Weybridge (Dr Spencer) will make the point that businesses want more information, but in my view a register would work against that. Cyber actors are agile and can work through proxies, affiliates and front companies, so the lines between state, state-affiliated and criminal activity are often blurred. A register would create false certainty in both directions. Specific foreign powers on the list will look like the only threats, and we know that foreign powers would be let off the hook if they were not included on the list. Ultimately, businesses would be fed a simplified reality with regard to the risks.

Just over a year ago, Jaguar Land Rover was hacked. The Government made a decision to bail it out to the tune of £1.5 billion, and there has been no attribution, and no repercussions since. On national preparedness and resilience, does the Minister not think that businesses might need the context, so that they can know where some of those threats are?

I accept the question, but the NCSC’s annual report mentioned several countries in its analysis of cyber-threats. That does not need to be written into the legislation or in a register; that would not give that dynamism. We do not shy away from this issue. In fact, the knowledge that the public, parliamentarians, businesses and the NCSC have in this area is pretty extensive. The NCSC has talked about state-level actors, and the number of countries involved. The Jaguar Land Rover case that the hon. Gentleman mentions, and the disruption it caused to businesses, should be a wake-up call for people in every single boardroom across the country. Cyber-security should be higher up on their risk registers, and responsibility should be taken at board level. Let me go back to Lords amendment 108. The vendor risk framework will be underpinned by guidance, enabling businesses to take a holistic risk assessment of their supply chains. The trust groups established by the NCSC will continue to support organisations in sharing information confidently and securely. Finally, there will always be a delicate balance between national security, economic prosperity and diplomatic relations. Opposition Members will know well, from being in government, that this is a tightrope. This House has grappled with this issue before, most comparably during the passage of the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021, in which it was agreed that suppliers and investors should be assessed on the evidence, case by case. A statutory register of foreign powers would upset that balance and give businesses neither the certainty nor the guidance that they require. A case-by-case risk assessment, backed by guidance, industry collaboration and expert security advice, is the only sensible way to do this, so we ask the House to reject Lords amendment 108. That brings me to the remaining amendments made in the other place, which I urge the House to support. The first of them relates to vendor risk management. The priority of this Government is of course national security, and we will not hesitate to take action against hostile actors who seek to disrupt our way of life. The Bill not only bolsters the regulatory framework to safeguard our most essential services every day, but provides emergency backstops in the face of serious national security threats. In the other place, we strengthened those protections with a new vendor risk management framework. New powers will enable the Government to direct organisations, supported by guidance and a mechanism for self-referral to Government, to take action against risky procurements. That goes back to the question asked by the right hon. Member for The Wrekin (Mark Pritchard). Lords amendments 48 to 51, 95 and 96 insert new clauses that provide for this new power of direction, introduce essential delegated powers to secure the longevity of the framework, and establish key requirements to ensure transparency.

The Minister will know that under the National Security and Investment Act 2021, two Chinese tech companies were called in for review, and then another Chinese tech company was retrospectively called in. Given that the Act contains retrospective powers, is there an ongoing review of tech companies that have contracts with the Government? They may not be Huawei-badged, but they may have links to third countries about which we have concerns. Might a retrospective review under that Act help with some of the issues that the Minister is talking about?

I do not know the answer to the right hon. Member’s question, but I will get some advice from the Box about whether that Act is directly applicable, and will come back to him on that. As a result of the amendments that we added to the Bill in the other place, risky procurements—or procurements that might be a risk—would have to be dealt with through the Bill’s vendor risk management system. However, I will see whether any retrospective action could be taken on the issues that he raises.

On the vendor risk register, does the Minister accept that intelligent electronic devices, which are found in multiple organisations and have multiple vendors, pose a great risk, and that if these amendments are to be effective, we need greater depth?

What we need is to get the Bill on a statutory footing as quickly as possible. The amendments we have made in the other place on the vendor risk management system are about companies having a reportable way of making sure that the Government know about risks. They should be assessing their own risks, and where there are risky procurements, the Government should be able to take direct action. I think that goes to the point that the right hon. Member for The Wrekin made. These issues have been much discussed in the other place, and we made these amendments to strengthen the Bill in this area. This package of amendments complements the Bill’s national security powers of direction, enabling Governments to act before and after vendors become embedded in supply chains. I am thankful to the other place for its engagement on this issue, which has strengthened the Bill and created the comprehensive package of amendments that is in front of the House.

My hon. Friend is making a great speech. Just for clarification, we on the Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy raised concerns about managed service providers and the importance of diversity. The hon. Member for Exmouth and Exeter East (David Reed) made a point about the JLR attack, but having a limited number of suppliers and MSPs can have massive impacts across our economy, as we saw with the attack on the food chain and freezer units a week or so ago. One of our proposals was to put a provision on that in the Bill. I recognise that pace is now urgent, but will the Minister consider that for the future?

My hon. Friend is right about diversification, vendor lock-in, and there not being a wide array of choice in the marketplace for various aspects of technological embeddedness, in supply chains or otherwise. I absolutely get that challenge. There is a balance to be struck between flexibility and certainty in the regulations. I am very happy to look at the examples that my hon. Friend has given, but he is correct that in such a fast-moving technological landscape, we have to make sure that we cover as many bases as possible. The reason for this Bill is to update the 2018 regulations to bring managed service providers into scope, alongside others, and the review that I have announced tonight will look at whether that scope should be widened further, if things transpire in other parts of the economy. This year, AI incidents have shown that we face a new challenge in cyber-security. It is vital that our essential services remain well protected against novel risks. We have brought forward changes that will help us better understand why incidents involving AI occur, and help us share lessons across regulators and regulated entities. Lords amendments 33 to 40 and supporting amendments update the delegated powers in the Bill, clarifying that through future regulations the Government will be able to use in-house expertise such as the AI Security Institute to collect vital information about the causes and impacts of AI loss of control incidents occurring in essential services. I thank Members, particularly the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith), who is not in his place, for campaigning on the topic of information sharing. Lords amendments 21 to 24 restrict overseas information sharing by NIS regulators to our Five Eyes partners, European economic area countries and Switzerland only. Cyber actors do not respect international borders and these amendments ensure that we can co-operate with our international partners without any risk of compromising our values.

I begin by thanking the Minister here and the Minister in the other place for their collaborative approach to these stages of the Bill. The UK faces a rapidly evolving threat landscape, to which we must be able to react and respond to ensure security. Those who seek to undermine our security and our critical national infrastructure are constantly adapting the tools and technologies they use, and our legislation must be capable of adapting with them. We must be clear about the threats we face, and in order to remain relevant, the legislation must address the actual risks, not just the tools that may be used. I put on record my thanks to colleagues in the Lords for their careful work in scrutinising and strengthening the Bill. The amendments before us raise important questions about how we measure the effectiveness of our cyber-security regime, how we counter threats from hostile states and how we ensure that our legislation keeps pace with emerging technology. Keeping our critical national infrastructure secure is essential in the modern world, so I hope that Ministers will consider the substance of these amendments carefully and make improvements where possible, while putting the security and resilience of the UK first. I will specifically address Lords amendments 107 and 108 and our amendments to Lords amendment 33, concerning autonomous systems. Amendment 107 would require the Secretary of State to review within 12 months the effectiveness of the Act and the network and information systems regulations, including on sectors within scope, the regulatory framework under which NIS regulations operate, and the obligations that could be placed on organisations and technology providers to improve their cyber-resilience. At its heart, the amendment raises an entirely legitimate question: how will Parliament know whether this legislation is actually working? Under the Government’s present approach, we would wait several years for a post-implementation review, but cyber-threats will not politely stand still while Whitehall evaluates the legislation. We need to know whether strategically important sectors remain outside this regime, whether regulators have the powers, information and capacity they need, and, ultimately, whether these reforms are making Britain’s critical infrastructure more resilient. To help answer that, we have been calling on the Government to publish their national cyber action plan and to provide greater clarity about the strategy sitting behind this legislation. I am grateful for and very much welcome the commitment that the Minister has made this evening at the Dispatch Box, in particular committing to publishing the NCAP before Royal Assent. Publication cannot be the end of the story; the real test is outcomes, and this House will continue to scrutinise and hold the Government to account, to ensure that the revised regime is actually making our critical systems safer. The brings me to Lords amendment 108, tabled by my noble Friend Viscount Camrose. Ministers have repeatedly resisted our calls for them to address the issues of threats from foreign state actors, and I therefore welcome support from the other place for a provision that would require the Government to establish and maintain a register of foreign powers considered to pose a risk to the UK’s critical network and information systems. A register would provide a clear and reviewable framework for identifying the foreign powers that pose a threat to our critical infrastructure. Nowhere does the need for clarity matter more that when we are talking about China, yet nowhere is the Government’s position more opaque. We have seen that again in recent weeks. Just as the Government finally acknowledge the risk that China poses in terms of cyber-attacks, espionage and foreign interference, the Defence Secretary makes the case for closer ties with China, hosting its Defence Minister here in Britain—the first such visit in 26 years. So which is it? If China poses

Given the importance of the issue to our national security—this is not a political point, but a technical point about which Department should be leading on this—my hon. Friend may or may not agree with me that it might sit better in the Cabinet Office or the Home Office under the Security Minister, although I have the greatest respect for this Minister, as he knows.

The amendment concerns duties performed by the Secretary of State under part 3, which are quite broad in terms of statements and directions, particularly when it comes to business. What we have been asking is this: how can business be clear about responding to the threats and the duties that are imposed on it by the regime if the Government do not make that clear directly? I understand what my right hon. Friend is saying—that this provision needs to be much wider in many ways—and I wish I had the ability to table an amendment that was much wider than the narrow scope of the Bill, but until we see some leadership from the Government on this issue, we are restricted in terms of what we can do, or at least try to do, with the Bill to drive this forward.

I am grateful to my hon. Friend for being so generous in giving way. Members should know that this is probably my last intervention—I am sure that many are watching the TV screens elsewhere in the House and will want to get to dinner. They are probably shouting at me at this moment. My hon. Friend mentioned parliamentary oversight. The Intelligence and Security Committee, of which I am a former member, does a great deal of work already, but the Government’s “whole of Government” approach to security, which I support, should also be subject to oversight by the ISC. The memorandum of understanding between the Government and the ISC is currently out of date. It needs to be updated and it needs to include new responsibilities, such as those that we are discussing today.

I thank my right hon. Friend not only for his intervention, but for his expertise and his contribution to the debate on this particularly important issue. I hope that the Minister has been listening and has noted what has been said. Let me now turn to my amendment (a) to the Government’s Lords amendment 33, which deals with autonomous systems. From the start, I have been unconvinced that the Government’s amendment is necessary. I think that the powers and measures set out in the original clause 31 are sufficient to address the reporting requirements, so I am not convinced of the need for this Lords amendment in the first place. In fact, I think that, if anything, it risks muddying the waters. As a responsible Opposition, however, we take at face value the Government’s concern that the Secretary of State should have the necessary powers. We need to clarify some of the language and the scope of those powers, particularly around loss of control. That being the case, it is essential that the provisions are robust and workable in order to address the risks, not just the latest tools that may be used. Lords amendment 33 focuses specifically on the loss of control of an AI agent. Although that is the relevant technology in use today, the regulation of just this technology presents the risk that the rules become obsolete very quickly in the face of future innovation. The principle is simple: regulate the harm, not the technology. If the Government are correct to say that there is a gap in the reporting requirements on AI agents and loss of control, the harm is the actions and operations of autonomous systems. Today the technology is agentic AI, but who knows what will be here tomorrow, next month or next year? We should not rush to regulate and make bad, unworkable law that rapidly senesces and becomes obsolete. Instead, we should build up from the basic principle of regulating the harm, not the technology. I hope that those on the Government Benches will take the purpose of our amendment (a) in good faith and support it in the Aye Lobby.

It is a great pleasure to speak in this important debate. Holding it late on a Tuesday night, following a late sitting on a Monday evening, may not be ideal, but given the shifting tectonic plates of AI and the economy, and the level of interest in AI and cyber, the timing of this debate is absolutely critical. I welcome the Bill, as I did on Second Reading and have done throughout its passage. I particularly want to speak to Lords amendment 33, which I see as a necessary attempt to address AI, but I want to share my concerns about the effectiveness of this attempt. No doubt I will do so again when the Minister comes before the Science and Technology Committee. In debates, and in justifying the Bill, the Government have emphasised time and again the social, economic and national security costs of cyber-attacks. I absolutely recognise and support that, and it is incredibly important—in fact, one might argue that the Government are late in addressing the challenges. We are discussing the Bill at a time when AI is putting a booster rocket under the cyber-security challenges coming from criminals, non-state actors and state actors. We have had example after example over the past weeks and months, so it is hugely important that we address this issue. I am glad that the Government are taking the opportunity to address the AI challenge, but Lords amendment 33 does not do so. Lords amendment 33 introduces a new clause, entitled “Functions of the Secretary of State: loss of control of artificial intelligence agent”. It gives the Secretary of State functions in cases where “a security or operational compromise in relation to a relevant network and information system is or may be attributable to loss of oversight or control of an AI agent”, and in cases where there is a risk of such a compromise. The meanings of “AI agent” and “loss of oversight or control” are to be set out in regulations made by the Secretary of State at a later date. I suppose my first concern is with the language, which is semi-anthropomorphic. If someone loses control of a plane, for example, either they are a bad pilot, or the plane is badly designed. Someone should not be able to “lose control” of a technology that is in the market and on sale.

The hon. Lady has a great deal of experience, and I defer to her on many of these matters, but has not the Hugging Face hack identified that some of the autonomous systems we are building will operate and we are going to have to play catch-up to understand what they have actually done?

That is exactly the example I was coming to, because I imagine that Lords amendment 33 was designed some time over the summer to address the Hugging Face incident. The hon. Gentleman says “we are building” such systems. Well, for a start, I am not building them; they are being built by companies—hugely valuable businesses, as we saw with Anthropic’s valuation. If they cannot control—or rather, I would say, design—tools and technologies that can be used by those who purchase them to achieve the ends or tasks they are supposed to achieve, then that is bad design. I think the hon. Gentleman’s position is that this technology is so amazing that it is beyond human control or understanding, but that should certainly not be the case yet, and we have the AI Security Institute to test and to confirm that such technology is secure. His intervention goes to the heart of the issue: if this AI technology is beyond control or comprehension, what is it doing being sold in our markets? The Hugging Face incident was described as a loss of control, rather than as badly designed software or applications; that was partly anthropomorphisation of AI, but it also increased interest. The Science and Technology Committee has identified hype as one of the four key barriers to the effective digital transformation of the public sector, and I think that is what this incident was. Lords amendment 33 gives the Secretary of State powers over those who are seen to have lost “oversight or control of an AI agent”, but I would argue that it is actually those who have made, designed or developed the AI agent who have the power or ability to set the guardrails for achieving the tasks it is meant to achieve. I am concerned that this is, in effect, giving the Secretary of State power over those who do not actually have any power in this regard. AI is already in so many applications, and people who buy such applications, which have often not been tested, have no power or ability to change or control them. That point is at the heart of this. For example, the Bill extends the scope of the NIS regulations to data centres, large load controllers, and managed service providers and their suppliers. I have argued that it should be extended further, because it is very hard to argue that cyber-security is of critical importance only in one or two sectors. Who would have thought that fridges could be an example of critical national infrastructure being undermined by cyber-attacks or a lack of cyber-resilience? Agentic AI may already be embedded in managed service providers. The Bill describes a managed service provider as a medium or large enterprise that provides ongoing management of a customer’s IT systems under contract, where the provider connects to or accesses the customer’s networks and information systems. That could describe just about any AI-based or IT-based business right now. Look at how AI is being portrayed and sold—and I do not mean Jensen Huang’s semiconductor activities. AI is being sold as a must-have. [ Interruption. ] I didn’t think I could make an AI speech without reference to Jensen Huang at the moment! AI is being sold to businesses of all sizes, but in particular to medium-sized enterprises that often do not have their own chief technology officer. It is being sold as a must-have, with messages like, “If you are not deploying AI, you are food for the fishes” and “Everything is changing and everyone must change with it, so AI is an essential part of any IT management system.” I do believe it is important that we embrace the benefits that AI can bring, but it is also important that we empower business and industry to do so securely. That brings me to the concern about putting the responsibility to control AI on businesses without empowering them. The Government’s Cyber Essentials scheme is one tool by which the cyber skills of small and medium-sized enterprises are brought up to standard.

I think what the hon. Lady is touching on is liability; what I am hearing relates to safety by design. Does she agree that we need a serious discussion about where liability sits with AI systems—the question of who is responsible for outcomes, especially when SMEs are using this software, too?

The hon. Lady anticipates the end of my contribution, which makes me think that maybe I should get to it faster—but yes, we need a comprehensive AI regulatory package that includes safety by design principles. That has been discussed by members of my Committee. On Cyber Essentials, will the Minister respond to this particular statistic? In 2024-25, 55,000 Cyber Essentials certificates were issued. There are about 6 million SMEs in this country, so at that rate it will take about 100 years before all small businesses are brought up to the cyber standard. Is it not essential that before we put such responsibilities on businesses deploying AI, or as we do so, we ensure that they have the tools and skills to do so in a well-informed and effective way? Right now, there is no testing for AI services. There are no guarantees that AI is safe. I would argue that any frontier model AI products and services sold in this country should, for example, have been through the Artificial Intelligence Security Institute’s testing process. That is not the case at the moment. The Competition and Markets Authority indicated in a statement today that normal consumer protections apply to AI services. I am not sure where that leaves businesses. My key question to the Minister is: why is he putting the responsibility for AI behaviours on the buyers of AI, and not, it would seem, on the sellers? I was contacted by a major cyber-security company making exactly that point. What does “control” mean in this case? What if there was never any control, because AI models are non-deterministic and the concept of control may not be appropriate? What about the concept of safety by good design? Are we not taking a rather whack-a-mole approach? Would it not reassure business and ensure a more comprehensive approach to cyber-security to bring in specific AI regulation that included safety by design and that was based on principles, rather than one specific scenario which may or may not occur? Will the Minister give me an example of a scenario that Lords amendment 33 is designed to capture? Will he set out to me what he sees happening, what the benefits of the provision would be, and where the responsibilities and liabilities would lie? To go back to the Hugging Face incident, it was noticeable that although a criminal act had been committed—it is criminal to hack—nobody was charged. Indeed, Hugging Face was then bought by the company that had undertaken the criminal act. The question of liability is not solved by this amendment. Will the Minister also indicate how long he believes it will take to set out some definitions here, particularly on “AI agent” and “loss of oversight and control”. Will he tell me if there will be an AI Bill that sets out a regulatory framework, rather than taking a whack-a-mole approach? Also, telecoms networks are regulated by the Telecommunications (Security) Act 2021, so they will not come under the jurisdiction of the provisions on AI agents and losing control—unless, I suppose, they are in a supply chain for a regulated organisation. Perhaps the Minister could clarify whether that is correct? I welcome the Bill and its provisions. The attempt to address some of the issues around AI is very well meaning, but I strongly feel that it needs to be part of a comprehensive, well thought-through and principles-based approach, and I am not sure that Lords amendment 33 achieves that.

For our constituents, cyber-security is not an abstract debate. It is about whether their company can pay their salary, whether the food supply chain is stable and food makes it to their table, whether the council can keep its services running, and whether the personal details that they hand over when registering to vote stay safe. Last year’s attack on Jaguar Land Rover was the most economically damaging cyber-event in UK history, costing an estimated £1.9 billion and hitting more than 5,000 organisations. Earlier this month, hackers took remote control of supermarket fridges and freezers in at least six European countries and warmed them until tonnes of food had to be thrown away. Researchers have found that more than 800 refrigeration and building control systems linked to British retailers can be reached over the open internet. This impacts the weekly shop for every family in our constituencies. The Bill was our opportunity to get ahead of those threats, to strengthen the systems that we all rely on and to secure our digital sovereignty. When it comes to building that sovereign capability, the IPPR offers a really solid framework: building where we can get ahead; shaping regulation and procurement; and partnering with other middle countries, such as the EU. The Minister talked about the AI sovereign fund. I will gently push on that, because I have talked to companies that are looking for investment from the fund and it seems that the definition of sovereignty is not actually that clear. We are not necessarily even talking about AI sovereign models, so I want to push for clarity on what the AI sovereign fund is funding. We need to think about this in terms of a whole digital sovereign strategy.

It has been brilliant watching the Bill go through Parliament, seeing that we can create this law domestically. The hon. Member mentioned closer ties with the European Union, and we have recently been discussing the EU-UK reset. Does she see any issues with closer relations with the European Union and our ability to regulate AI?

I do not. I think partnership is about how we get the best out of working together. We need to get the balance right. The UK is in a really excellent position, but actually the Government have not used that opportunity. Some AI models have been released in the EU sooner because of market size. Companies there are getting access to advanced models before the UK. We need to look at this matter in the round in order to get the best for our economy and our security.

I have broken my own embargo, but there we are. On sovereign capability, the hon. Lady will know that the European Union is looking to build its own cloud capability, which I think makes sense, given the ups and downs of the transatlantic relationship over the past few months and the political views of some of those who are in charge of the big tech companies. Does she think that is something the UK should do independently, so that we have our own sovereign cloud capability, or at least something we should work on closely with partners and allies across the world, not just in the United States?

When the Liberal Democrats talk about a digital sovereignty strategy, it is about being realistic about this and looking at where we can build and get ahead. There is also an important element of leadership here—how can the UK develop those capabilities if we do not even start? DeepMind was started in the UK, yet in the past two years, people have told me time and again that we cannot build those models here. If we have given up, then of course we cannot. We also have to back British tech and businesses. When it comes to AI models—I will touch on other elements, too—we do not need frontier models for every single application; some need something smaller and more predictable. Whether it is building, partnering or shaping, we need to take this seriously, and sooner rather than later. In June, I asked the House to back our digital sovereignty strategy so that our critical infrastructure does not depend on a handful of foreign suppliers. Unfortunately, the Government turned that down, but we will keep making the case. In the light of the Microsoft outage, I ask the Minister what assessment has been made of the reliance of the Government and public services on foreign suppliers, because that is vital to our cyber-security and resilience. Turning back to the amendments before us, I thank colleagues in the Lords who have worked hard on improving the Bill. Lords amendment 107, which was passed with the support of Liberal Democrat colleagues in the other place, would require a comprehensive review of the NIS regime within 12 months of Royal Assent, building directly on what Liberal Democrats have argued from day one. On Second Reading, I warned that “the Bill leaves the back door wide open by leaving out key sectors”. —[ Official Report , 6 January 2026; Vol. 778, c. 190.] In Committee and on Report, we tabled amendments to bring in councils, political parties, electoral infrastructure, manufacturing and retail. I would just like to clarify what we are asking the Government to commit to. Our first ask is to carry out that review within 12 months, covering all 13 of our critical national infrastructure sectors. As has been mentioned, the fast-paced change of cyber-security and the threats we face mean that it is critical to review it sooner rather than later. As I said on Second Reading, the Government do not consider their own public services essential enough, although I appreciate that that is being reviewed. Councils hold some of the most sensitive data our constituents have, from social care records to benefit claims, so they cannot be an afterthought. Secondly, we would like a commitment to review the sectors that fall outside critical national infrastructure but are still of high importance to the UK, including political parties, electoral infrastructure and advanced manufacturing. Our democracy is a target. Between 2021 and 2022, a Chinese state-affiliated actor compromised the Electoral Commission’s system, exposing the names and addresses of an estimated 40 million voters. Yet political parties—the organisations through which the British people exercise their democratic voice—sit outside this regime entirely, although I appreciate that that is being reviewed. Thirdly, we want to look at accountability at the very top. As I have said before, security must be board-led to ensure that each lock, door and window of our house is built securely; Baroness Lloyd also said in the House of Lords that the forthcoming security and resilience requirements will mandate board-level governance. I urge the Government to say on the record that those requirements will make the boards of regulated organisations accountable for their cyber-resilience. Turning back to AI, Alexandr Wang, who is head of AI at Meta, said this week that superintelligence is coming, and that, “How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.” It is really important that we tackle this issue. The regime-wide review proposed

The hon. Member is making an excellent speech. She knows that I have tabled my Artificial Superintelligence Bill for discussion on Friday. A regulator is essential in the field of AI. However, I have concerns about Lords amendment 107, because the AI Security Institute, set up at Bletchley, is a research organisation. We are rightly proud of it, as it is the best in the world. It has some of the finest scientists and researchers assessing the most powerful AI. As we know, AI is the fastest moving technology in history. However, we need to ensure the independence of AISI so that it can continue to do its work. We do not want to restrict its research powers in any way. Does the hon. Lady therefore agree that the Government need to bring forward a separate mandatory regulator as part of an AI Bill, rather than rolling those roles together?

The hon. Member, as always when there are synergies across the House, has predicted what I am about to talk about. I do agree. We welcome the amendments to take on the AI threats, but we need to look at future-proofing the legislation. If it is not AISI that will take that on, we need to have a single AI regulator that helps to keep us secure in the face of increasing cyber-security threats from AI. The Liberal Democrats support Lords amendment 107. We have pushed for it at every stage of the Bill, and the other place has agreed. Our asks of the Government are simple: to review every critical national infrastructure sector within a year; to review political parties, electoral infrastructure and advanced manufacturing; to make boards accountable; to ensure that the AI security regulations have the clarity and teeth they need, and a regulator; to take a holistic approach to our digital resilience; and to look at our sovereign capabilities. Our constituents and every business in our supply chains deserve nothing less.

As hon. Members have said this evening, the frontline of hostile state attacks is no longer just in Government networks; it is the fridge in the blood bank, the e-charger on the street and the meter on the wall. I welcome the Bill as the very first step in recognising the real threats that our country faces from cyber-attacks and the need to develop not only defence but resilience. This month, we have seen refrigeration systems hacked in supermarkets across Europe and blood banks in France—I warned about that earlier this year—and we have already seen that EV chargers in the UK are exposed in a similar way. Much of this everyday kit connects to the internet through internet of things small cellular modules, more than 70% of which are manufactured by Chinese firms. Through over-the-air updates, equipment in this country can be changed or switched off from outside it. Hostile states are building leverage over our infrastructure, as we have seen today from Russia and Iran, and we know that China is working towards that in the long term. I therefore welcome Lords amendments 48 to 51, to which the Minister referred, on vendor-related directions, which will give the Secretary of State for the first time the power to stop kit from risky suppliers being installed or used in systems that we all depend on. However, as I have said in the House before, our problem has rarely been a lack of laws; it is often the lack of enforcement. Such powers will be only as good as the will to use them. Energy must be near the front of the queue. We have already seen the EU act on inverters, and the Government rightly turned down the Ming Yang investment in Scotland on security grounds. The equipment on our grid deserves exactly the same scrutiny. Will the Government work with companies in the UK and our allies on a trusted supplier standard so that operators know what is safe to buy before they install it, not afterwards, and to give them the correct information they need to ensure that they are protecting their businesses as well as our national way of life? I also welcome Lord’s amendment 8, under which operators will have to weigh an incident’s impact on the economy and on the day-to-day functioning of society. That means that, for the first time, the Government will hold incident-by-incident evidence of what the attacks cost. I have called that the “Putin tax”, which leads to higher bills, lost business and disrupted services, each of which is paid for by our businesses and our constituents every single day. Will the Minister expand the data being collected, so that it is collected by attacking state? In that way, we can finally put a number on how much foreign actors are costing taxpayers in this country. Powers and reporting duties are only as good as the people who use them. Someone has to spot the attack, someone has to understand the attack and someone has to stop it, yet 57% of UK businesses have a basic cyber skills gap and more than half of cyber teams across Europe are understaffed. In the other place, the Minister for Cyber promised security and resilience requirements, including skilled, accredited people with senior responsibility for resilience. Will the Minister tell us when that consultation will begin and confirm that it will set a clear standard for qualifications and board accountability? On Lords amendments 107 and 108, which have been discussed extensively this evening, I see why the Government have come to their position, and that an annual review and a statutory register might not be the right tools. However, I believe that the aims behind the amendments are correct. I think that Members from all parts of the House would agree that law enforcement needs all the help it can get to confront the attacks and this affront to our democracy, and providing a register would go some way towards plugging existing holes in the legislation and increase our resilience against what has been described by our security services as our most pres

I refer Members to my entry in the Register of Members’ Financial Interests. After a recent career in cyber-security before coming to this place, I was proud to work with the shadow Minister in Committee. Lords amendments 107 and 108 build on that work, while amendments (a) to (i) to Lords amendment 33 seek to broaden its scope and effectiveness. Together, they are fundamental to ensuring the resilience of our critical national infrastructure. Lords amendment 107 seeks to ensure that our regulatory regime remains fit for purpose. I suggest that the effectiveness of the regime will depend on the quality and frequency of regulatory scrutiny. It is not just about enforcement, but about nuance. Compliance does not necessarily mean that an organisation has fully understood its cyber-risk. Does it have a cyber-security plan that makes clear that it understands and will mitigate inherent weaknesses in legacy infrastructure? Are regulators consistently demanding returns from operators of essential services and following up on shortcomings? Will the Minister address how that will be achieved consistently across regulators? On Lords amendment 108, I consistently raised in Committee the risks associated with intelligent electronic devices from individual manufacturers being deployed across multiple sectors of our critical national infrastructure, from water, electricity and rail to oil and gas. The register of foreign powers that pose a cyber-threat is useful, but it would be strengthened by understanding how IEDs and essential services could be deployed against us by those nations. The devices may be manufactured in such countries, or they could be manufactured elsewhere and then compromised by hostile actors, and they are spread right across the sectors that could compromise us most effectively. The Government have introduced vendor-related powers in Lords amendments 48 to 51, but for those powers to be effective, the Government need to have sight of the equipment in use across our critical national infrastructure, and to identify where several sectors rely on the same suppliers, and which of those suppliers might have had their devices compromised. How will the Government identify those shared dependencies, assess the risks that they pose, and alert operators when action is needed?

It is a pleasure to speak in this debate. I promise I will not go on too long. [Hon. Members: “More!”] Cross-party support already! I draw the House’s attention to the fact that my father-in-law, Professor Robin Bloomfield, is a professor of system and software dependability at City and St George’s University—I finally got his title correct. Also, the Kao data centre is in my constituency of Harlow. I thank the Minister for his opening statement, and particularly for his commitment to looking at increasing the scope of the Bill. We had conversations across parties in Committee on the scope of the Bill, and whether it could be extended to other potentially vital infrastructure. We live in uncertain times, and bad state actors, used by foreign powers, will seek to undermine our national infrastructure and our democracy using the internet and AI. We need to be alive to that. I rise to speak against Lords amendment 107. Although I am sure that it is well-meaning, I am concerned that it could have unintended consequences. It would require the Secretary of State to conduct an annual review of the effectiveness of the national infrastructure and security systems regime, and to lay that review in front of Parliament once it was complete. As you will know, Madam Deputy Speaker, I am always a huge supporter of parliamentary scrutiny, not least because it allows me to give a matter scrutiny. However, it is very likely that the foreign powers that we have concerns about are observing said debates and said scrutiny, so if the report highlights any potential weaknesses in the network and information systems, those powers will be aware of those weaknesses, which could put us at risk when they seek to exploit those weaknesses. Finally, Madam Deputy Speaker—I promised I would be short—I reiterate the concerns expressed by Members from across the House about the Hugging Face incident that the hon. Member for Exmouth and Exeter East (David Reed) mentioned. How does the Minister see Lords amendment 33, or other Bills in this place, being able to look at OpenAI’s potential liability for that incident, and what can this Government put in place to protect systems in the wake of that? We need to be aware of the emerging threats around cyber-security and AI. I welcome the fact that this Bill seeks to address those threats. Bad state actors controlling AI is worrying, but AI controlling AI is truly terrifying.

With the leave of the House, I will quickly sum up and answer some of the questions from Opposition Members and my hon. Friends. First, I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Harlow (Chris Vince) for his brevity, which we really do appreciate, as well as for his work on the Bill Committee. He is right that the Committee took a collaborative approach, which got us to a much better place. The amendments tabled in the other place show that the Government have listened to concerns; we brought amendments forward on some areas, and gave strong reasons for not doing so on other areas. I thank my hon. Friend the Member for Dunfermline and Dollar (Graeme Downie). I want to go to the heart of the matter of the foreign register. The NCSC reports annually on resilience issues. Its annual report was very succinct—I think there was a question from the Opposition spokesperson, the hon. Member for Runnymede and Weybridge (Dr Spencer), about the threats, which the annual report set out clearly. It stated: “China continues to be a highly sophisticated and capable threat actor, targeting a wide range of sectors and institutions across the globe, including the UK.” That is from the report, so it is not a secret. That does not have to be written in the Bill, through the register of foreign powers that Lords amendment 108 would provide for.
Briefly, does the Minister agree that it would be helpful to quantify the cost of the threats that the NCSC has highlighted?

Quantifying is quite difficult, as is attribution. The JLR situation showed us the costs, but the sophistication of the threats and the wide range of them mean that quantifying them might be quite difficult. The Opposition spokesperson challenged the Government on a number of issues, including the definition of AI and whether the term “automated system” should be used instead. The reason we refer to AI and AI agents is that that is where the harms are happening; the hon. Gentleman talked about basing the provision on the harms, but if he looks at the Hugging Face incident, he will see that the relevant amendments have been made in order to widen the scope in relation to AI, newer technologies and the increasing number of threats.

The Minister was very specific in what he just said; he said that the Government use the term “AI agent” because that is where the harm is happening at the moment. He should reflect on the fact that not only is harm happening through operational technology with autonomous systems, but it could, as my hon. Friend the Member for Runnymede and Weybridge (Dr Spencer) pointed out, happen with systems that have not yet been invented. Why is the Minister restricting himself to this phraseology?

That phrasing is in the Bill because the Bill is about extending the measures to cover where we are, in terms of the threats. The mention of AI agents relates to what we are trying to achieve with the Bill. The incidents mentioned by the Chair of the Select Committee—my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West (Dame Chi Onwurah)—and the hon. Member for Exmouth and Exeter East (David Reed) show that the scope needs to be extended. Let me turn to the contribution from the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, the hon. Member for Harpenden and Berkhamsted (Victoria Collins). There were a number of questions about small businesses and boards. I think this is the third time in less than seven days that I have said from the Dispatch Box that every single board and every single business in the country needs to reflect on the fact that the risks are real and ensure that it is as cyber-resilient as possible. The NCSC has free tools. On 3 November, we launched a Cyber Essentials funding package for eligible UK small and medium-sized enterprises, which is designed to address the barriers that small organisations face in implementing cyber-security. We understand that this issue has to be on the risk register for all small businesses, and we are trying to put the building blocks in place to ensure that happens. I might have to write to my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne Central and West about a practical scenario in relation to Lords amendment 33. How it will work is a matter for consultation, but we will obviously involve the Select Committee in how that comes together. There was a question about putting AISI on a statutory footing. We do not think that that is desirable. My hon. Friend the Member for Leeds Central and Headingley (Alex Sobel), who is no longer in his place, spoke about the reasons for that. Given where AI is at the moment, we need voluntary relationships with AI labs across the globe. The collaborative approach lets us keep pace with fast-moving technologies. We remain committed to ensuring that the AISI is fully equipped for its vital role, and we will keep the House updated as that work progresses. It is a tremendous, world-leading organisation, of which we should be incredibly proud. The Bill is fundamentally about protecting our most essential services from those who seek to do us harm. It is targeted—it balances business burdens against the threats we face—but also ambitious in its protection against threats to our national security. It is thorough and flexible. In the other place, we strengthened the Bill further with a robust vendor risk management package, tightened incident reporting, strengthened intelligence gathering following an AI loss-of-control incident, and a guarantee that information will not be shared with countries that do not share our values. I thank Baroness Lloyd for her work and urge both Houses to conclude the Bill’s passage, so that we can begin the important task of implementation. Lords amendment 107 disagreed to. Motion made, and Question put, That this House disagrees with Lords amendment 108.— (Ian Murray.)

Saltend Chemicals Park, just outside Hull, is one of the most important industrial sites in East Yorkshire. It is owned and operated by the px Group. Across its 370 acres, companies including INEOS, the Mitsubishi Chemical Group, Triton Power, Air Products and Yara—though currently mothballed—make chemicals and provide the power, gases and services on which other businesses depend. Saltend matters to the region, because it provides skilled technical jobs. It matters to British industry, because its companies supply one another and businesses far beyond the Humber. It matters to the country, because we need the capacity to make foundational chemicals here in Britain. Last year, Vivergo ceased producing bioethanol and animal feed at Saltend. The Government’s trade deal, unfortunately with Donald Trump, gave US ethanol tariff-free access to the UK market for 1.4 billion litres a year, equivalent to the size of the entire UK market. Vivergo was already struggling, but its owner said that after that deal its position was made untenable. The Government did not provide the solution needed to keep it open, and it shut, with £700 million of investment by a great British company, ABF, lost in the process. I said at the time that the Government had offered the British bioethanol industry to the Americans on a plate, and we saw the consequences at Saltend. We cannot, tonight, bring back the production lost at Vivergo, but we can act while there is still time to save the INEOS plants. Three INEOS chemicals plants at Saltend have stopped production. All 245 staff remain employed, and the plants and the skills are still there. The time to save them is now. Those jobs matter enormously, but the country also stands to lose something harder to replace: the capacity to make these foundational chemicals. At Saltend, INEOS makes acetic acid, acetic anhydride and ethyl acetate, which are used in the production of medicines, food preservatives, packaging, ink and adhesives, to name just a few. Most of us, of course, will never see those chemicals themselves, but we see and rely on the products made with them. If we lose the capacity to produce those chemicals here, British industry will become more dependent on supplies from overseas. That is a question of industrial resilience and, ultimately, national security. The Government rightly say that they want to reindustrialise and, in particular, to reindustrialise the north, and I want the Government to succeed, but keeping the industry that we already have is the first test of that ambition. INEOS is an anchor tenant at Saltend Chemicals Park. That phrase can sound abstract, so let me explain what it means. Businesses there share services, power and steam: what one company produces, another one uses. They invest on the basis that the park works as a whole, with people working together. I have spoken to Mitsubishi Chemical about the effect of INEOS’s stopped production on its operation and investment. It is midway through a £500 million investment there, which is now on pause. I have spoken to Triton Power, which supplies electricity and steam to the park. When industrial demand falls, the economics of providing those services change too. Neither company told me that it was about to close, or would be forced to close by the INEOS shutdown. What they showed me was that the loss of an anchor tenant would be felt well beyond that anchor tenant’s business. About 800 highly skilled and highly paid people work across Saltend Chemicals Park, with thousands more in the supply chain. I do not suggest that every one of those jobs is immediately at risk, but the park’s future as a place for skilled technical work depends on keeping its businesses connected and investing. A decision that appears to concern those three INEOS plants could shape what happens on the other plants across the site for years to come. That is why I ask the Minister to look beyond the immediate payroll, important though that is. Once a chem

I congratulate my hon. Friend on securing this debate, which is important not just to his constituency but to the whole Humber region. We have seen the Lindsey oil refinery and some smaller companies go out of business because of the energy costs. Does he agree that the main focus of Government policy has to be getting energy costs down?

I entirely agree with my hon. Friend. He is right to highlight the industrial losses that we have already suffered on the south bank, but also on the north bank. As I say, Vivergo has gone. It was the largest bioethanol plant in the United Kingdom. He and I have for many years tried to move from E5 to E10, to get the bioethanol into UK petrol and give that a future going forward. That, too, was lost. If we lose these businesses, we lose the foundations of the very industry that the Prime Minister rightly wants to champion and grow. The good news is that INEOS is not asking for money. It believes that it has a viable future if it can bridge through this period. It is not just getting through the higher gas prices that we currently have; it is actively looking at shipping in gas from the United States. If it can bring in gas at American prices, the company can be viable. The cost of moving chemicals from China and America to Europe is so high that if we have a competitive gas price that allows us to make them in the UK, INEOS believes that the site will dominate those chemicals for decades to come, so there really is a prize to be gained here. I entirely accept that the Government must test that proposition. They should examine the costs, the timetable, the company’s contribution and the commitments it would make on production, jobs and investment. I am certainly not asking the Minister for a blank cheque, and I know that he will not be in a position to offer that tonight, but a rigorous decision must also be a timely one. Having been a Minister for nearly eight years, I know that the Government can move slowly. If the answer arrives after the workforce have gone, or restarting is no longer possible or is so expensive that it will not go ahead, the Government will have tested a proposition that no longer exists.
