I met the Minister, whom I am delighted to see in his place, earlier this month. He engaged seriously with this problem, and I am grateful to him. Officials have been speaking to INEOS. I believe that the Government understand the importance of the business and do not want to lose it. We now need that engagement to produce a workable route to a decision. INEOS is the largest chemicals company in the UK by sales, and it is important. I have a fairly simple view of industry in the UK. At the base we have energy, and one of our problems is that we have such expensive energy. We need to work on that, and the Government are seeking to address it. Above that we have chemicals, data centres, steel and other industries that are typically suppliers to other businesses downstream. If we do not get those foundational layers right and they are not there, then whatever innovative ideas there may be and whatever political will there is, we will not have the industrial strength that this country needs, let alone in a dangerous world in which we need to be able to make things for ourselves. As recent years have shown, we cannot always depend on even some of our previously closest allies. As I say, I believe the Government understand the importance of the business and do not want to lose it, and we now need that engagement to produce a workable route to a decision. The £350 million critical chemicals resilience fund was announced in May. The published scheme describes support for new capital projects, with grants of up to 50% of eligible project costs. INEOS says that it needs support for operating costs first and capital investment thereafter, and those are different things. We should not assume that a fund intended to strengthen chemical production can meet this particular need merely because it has “chemicals” in its name. INEOS has told me that its exchanges with officials have been constructive and that it is ready to proceed, yet it has not yet received the invitation and the full set of rules it needs to apply to start the dance, as it were. The Government have said that the fund should be open to eligible applications by the end

I am grateful to the right hon. Member for Beverley and Holderness (Graham Stuart) for securing this debate. I thank him for his engagement with the Government generally and myself personally on the issues in his constituency. He is a staunch supporter of the economic interests of his constituency and of the wider Humber, Yorkshire and Lincolnshire regions. I hope he knows that his concern, passion and aspirations for this sector very much reflect those of the Government, and my own too. I hope that the desire to reindustrialise the nation with the chemicals sector, and manufacturing industries more broadly, can be achieved by working together. I will come to the right hon. Gentleman’s core and specific questions, but I will first turn to the context. The chemicals sector’s contribution is particularly pronounced in his part of the world, playing an integral role in the wider web of chemicals clusters in the north-east and north-west of England, plus in Grangemouth in Scotland. The sector employs over 90,000 people directly. I know at first hand its contribution to local economies through well-paid jobs, its customers and its supply chains. Given that context, I will try to address as many of the specific issues raised as possible. First, I acknowledge how vital the chemicals sector is for delivering our industrial strategy at, as he puts it, the base of the pyramid, not only because of the direct footprint the chemicals sector has in our economy, but because it is part of the supply chain for so many of our most important manufacturing sectors, as well as critical national infrastructure sectors, like water, energy and defence. We have seen the impact of successive Governments stepping back and allowing the slow deindustrialisation of this proud sector, including at Saltend. I know the right hon. Gentleman will agree with me that this trend is no longer sustainable for our country or for his community. The UK has been at the cutting edge of chemistry, with innovations across the chemicals spectrum, including the very process that INEOS currently utilises at Saltend. The Government have not been inactive in dealing with the challenges facing industry. Members will have seen the action we have taken to secure important supply chains elsewhere. That includes our interventions to ensure production at INEOS in Grangemouth and the action we continue to take to safeguard carbon dioxide production via Ensus in Teesside. As the right hon. Gentleman says, energy costs and volatile gas prices continue to dog the industry. They remain high because of continuing geopolitical instability, particularly in Ukraine and the middle east. Alongside monitoring and responding to immediate pressures, we are determined to tackle the underlying competitiveness challenge from high energy costs, rather than leaving British businesses exposed to international fossil fuel price shocks. Our longer-term ambition, as we will set out in the 10-year plan, is to get UK energy costs in line with those of our European counterparts, helping to provide the conditions for firms to invest, grow and compete internationally. Our commitment to heavy industry is evident through the significant interventions we have made on steel, including in the emergency legislation we passed to keep British Steel operating. That brings me on to the specific support we are putting in place for chemicals. As the House will be aware, not least because the right hon. Gentleman just spoke about it, that we have announced the critical chemicals resilience fund, which will provide key support to producers, and strengthen the resilience and long-term sustainability of key production assets. The co-investment we will make in the chemicals sector, in partnership with industry via the resilience fund, will deliver significant economic and resilience benefits. It will also help to ensure that our most important chemicals assets are less prone to disruption, as well as delivering wider benefits t

On the issue of capital expenditure and revenue costs, clearly the issue for INEOS at Saltend is revenue. The rules for this fund initially appeared to preclude support for that. Can the Minister make any comment on that?

I will not get into applications from the Dispatch Box per se, but the right hon. Gentleman is right that the critical chemicals fund is focused on that long-term resilience and tilted towards capital expenditure there. We are having the wider conversation with INEOS about how we can help it get back to production as quickly as possible. Members will be aware of the closer relationship we are pursuing with the EU. INEOS is a great example of the close integration of our supply chains and why it is important that we work together with the EU to tackle common challenges. INEOS Acetyls supplies a significant proportion of its product into Europe, and it is important for sectors such as pharmaceuticals and defence. From the conversations that both my officials and I have had with the company, we understand that one of the biggest challenges the business faces is ensuring that there continues to be a sustainable market to sell into in Europe, and there is a fragile balance that needs to be maintained in order to do so. In short, it is a business that cannot operate without having certainty of market access. Trade flows can be impacted by additional barriers and frictions that we are working with the EU to minimise, similar to the measures that were announced last week at the EU summit. However, they can also be impacted by unfair trading practices from regions that often have lower standards and a much higher carbon footprint than we do. That is another area where we are collaboratively working with the EU to protect our critical industrial assets and strategically important manufacturing bases. For this reason, I am sure that the EU will also agree that it is in our collective interests to help the Saltend plant, and many other businesses in a similar position, to overcome their challenges. The alternative is becoming more reliant on imports from other nations such as China, and this brings risks, particularly given the geopolitical environment that we are living in at the moment. Linked to the financial support we are offering, the Secretary of State recently asked the UK’s Trade Remedies Authority to undertake an analysis of import trends across the chemicals sector, as well as insight on a number of chemical products, using the powers conferred to him under the Trade Act 2021. The findings, which will enable my Department to consider the extent to which market distorting practices overseas may be undermining the sector’s future, have been submitted to the Secretary of State. We will be building on the findings via further dialogue with the members of the sector that are the most impacted by unfair trade practices. This Government are expending significant resource to deliver on the reindustrialisation agenda, and I am personally invested in ensuring that the UK’s chemicals sector has the environment to overcome the immediate challenges it is facing, and, in the coming years, to grow. That of course includes Saltend. I thank the right hon. Member for securing the debate, and for all the work he is doing on behalf of his constituents and the wider chemicals industry. I am sure he will keep doing that work going forward. Question put and agreed to.
1. What steps he is taking to support the Northern Ireland Executive to tackle violence against women and girls.
7. What steps he is taking to support the Northern Ireland Executive to tackle violence against women and girls.

Today is the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women. Such violence is a scourge on society that we must do all we can to eradicate, and we must challenge the patriarchal structures that enable perpetrators. Ahead of the 16 days of action, I look forward to welcoming the Minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls, my hon. Friend the Member for Pontypridd (Alex Davies-Jones), to Northern Ireland later this week to work on this very issue. This Government will continue to support brilliant organisations like Foyle Women’s Aid in order to deliver on our commitment to ending violence against women and girls.

Today also marks the start of the national roll-out of domestic abuse protection orders across England and Wales. As the sponsor of a private Member’s Bill that would extend the protections offered by those orders to children under the age of 16, I know the potential such orders have to strengthen safeguarding and tackle violence against women and girls. I want victims in all parts of the UK to benefit from the strongest possible protections, so what discussions is the Minister having with the Northern Ireland Executive on sharing best practice from England and Wales, to support efforts to tackle violence against women and girls?

I thank my hon. Friend for the fantastic work that she has undertaken to progress this serious matter, and to ensure that women and girls are safe, no matter where they are. I welcome the progress made by the Department of Justice on piloting domestic abuse protection notices and protection orders. That will start with the Greater Belfast police district early next year. While tailored specifically to the unique needs of Northern Ireland, the pilot will draw on insights gained from England and Wales, and will strengthen safeguards for vulnerable children.

I am working with local housing associations, along with Standing Together Against Domestic Abuse, to improve housing outcomes for survivors of domestic and sexual abuse. I am glad that Standing Together’s domestic abuse housing alliance programme is being piloted by Govanhill housing association in my Glasgow constituency. Does the Minister agree with me that it is crucial that survivors are given specialist support, and would she consider working with the Northern Ireland Executive to promote programmes like Standing Together’s DAHA in Northern Ireland?

My hon. Friend’s hard work highlights the importance of a whole-society approach to improving outcomes for victims and survivors of abuse. While housing is devolved to Northern Ireland, initiatives like free travel and the sanctuary scheme have been essential to support victims and survivors of abuse and, crucially, to help them and their families stay safe in their home. Today, White Ribbon Day, would be as good a day as any for the Northern Ireland Executive to agree a budget and give service providers who are tackling violence against women and girls the certainty that they need for the future.

Tackling misogyny and abuse means challenging attitudes, and football clubs play a real part in that. Clubs across Northern Ireland are leading the way in promoting respect and giving more women and girls a chance to play. As part of the UK-wide bid for the 2035 women’s world cup, what is the Secretary of State doing to help to secure fixtures at the superb Windsor Park, and to allow those clubs to build on the excellent work that they are already doing to tackle violence against women and girls?

Sport has a brilliant role to play not just in tackling violence against women and girls, but in supporting women and girls into secure futures and opening opportunities for them. I know that many in Northern Ireland will be excited about the news. The hon. Lady is right that we have to tackle violence against women and girls across all sectors of our society, whether in the entertainment industry, policing or politics. I am looking forward to welcoming my hon. Friend the Minister for victims and tackling violence against women and girls to Northern Ireland this week, and I will work with her and Northern Ireland Executive members to do just that.
2. What steps he is taking to support the Northern Ireland Executive to increase economic growth.

Northern Ireland has seen faster economic growth than the rest of the UK over the past decade, and I want to build on that success with the Northern Ireland Executive. That is why we awarded Northern Ireland the largest block grant ever and offered an extra £1.5 billion across three years. However, the Northern Ireland Executive are hurtling towards a cliff edge unless they set a budget now. There is an extra £631 million on the table this year if a budget is agreed. They cannot let that go to waste.
Does the Secretary of State agree with me that bringing growth to every postcode is just as important in Northern Ireland as it is across the rest of the United Kingdom?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. In her constituency and across the whole of Northern Ireland, we want to ensure that everybody has the chance of prosperity. That means building on the economic successes in Northern Ireland—for instance, with Bank of America, Thales, Shorts Missile Systems and the work we are doing in cyber-security. However, to give an example of the problem that we have today, Ulster University had to say that it was going to cancel its cyber-security courses. Institutions need to know what their budget will be this year, next year and the year after, if we are to build on economic success in Northern Ireland.

During this period of instability for the Executive, may I urge the Secretary of State to work directly with businesses? He mentioned Bank of America; there is also FinTrU in Derry. Many fantastic businesses need to meet now to develop their 2027 growth plans for the betterment of Northern Ireland across the board.

I am keen to ensure that the British Business Bank, UK Export Finance, and all the different levers of economic prosperity that the Government have in Westminster are available in Northern Ireland. I am happy to work with the Executive on that, but they have to set a budget. [ Interruption. ] I see the right hon. Gentleman nodding; as a former Secretary of State for Northern Ireland, I am sure that he would agree.

Signs of life and vibrancy in the Northern Ireland economy are underpinned by arts and culture, and the Irish language revival is in full swing. Despite that, there is no mention of the arts in the programme for government. BBC Northern Ireland is cutting in-house Irish language production, and the very modest legislation on providing Irish language teachers was brutally vetoed in the Assembly yesterday. What role do inclusion and respect for difference play in supporting the growth of our economy?

As my hon. Friend knows, I am a passionate supporter of the arts and creative industries. They are an important part of economic success in Northern Ireland, whether we are talking about film and high-end television production, dance, music, or indeed the phenomenally successful fleadh that we had recently, which I suspect might be permanently resident in Belfast in future years. We must build on all that, but again, there has to be a budget.

A few weeks ago, I had Lord Sarwar in my constituency to meet Camlin and Smiley Monroe, two incredible businesses. The one thing business needs to thrive is stability. At what stage will this Government act to reform Stormont, end the veto, end the ransom politics, and allow Northern Ireland to thrive?

I completely agree with the hon. Lady about the wonderful businesses in her constituency and around Hillsborough, and more importantly about the need to rewire Stormont so that it works for the people of Northern Ireland. Most people in all the political parties agree; certainly, if you go into a coffee shop in Northern Ireland, people will say, “It’s time we got this sorted.” We need people of good will in all political parties to sit round the table and come to an agreement.

More than 89% of Northern Ireland’s private sector consists of micro enterprises that employ fewer than 10 people and often operate on razor-thin margins. The Secretary of State talks about supporting the Executive in boosting growth, but does he accept that his Government’s hikes to employer national insurance contributions, and rising employment costs, are acting directly as a handbrake on hiring and investment in Northern Ireland and across the United Kingdom?

No, I do not accept that for an instant, and this is a classic instance of Conservative incompetence. The Conservatives always want us to spend more money, but not to raise more money. That is precisely the problem with the Northern Ireland Executive, who refuse to do revenue raising so that they can live within their budget. It is the kind of crazy Lizonomics that failed this country in the past.
3. What steps he is taking to help attract foreign investment into Northern Ireland.

I thank my hon. Friend for the chance to highlight the work that we are doing on this. I am committed to bringing investment to Northern Ireland, and to promoting its unique dual access to the UK and EU markets. That is why in the Budget we announced £1 million to fund an NI investment summit, which will highlight its world-class sectors, such as cyber-security, advanced manufacturing and the creative industries, some of which I have seen at first hand, including at Catagen, AVEVA and Collins Aerospace. This is a whole-Government approach, and as we heard, we recently welcomed the Minister for Trade to Northern Ireland, during International Trade Week, to meet businesses from across Northern Ireland.

Friday’s UK-EU sanitary and phytosanitary agreement represents an important breakthrough in making trade easier and less costly. Will the Secretary of State outline the practical benefits of the agreement for businesses in Northern Ireland, particularly in reducing bureaucracy, strengthening supply chains, and improving choice for consumers, and say how those benefits underline the case for foreign investors turning their attention to Northern Ireland?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right. The new SPS agreement with the EU will boost growth by cutting red tape, reducing border checks and lowering costs for agrifood and retail businesses trading with Great Britain and Northern Ireland. It will help consumers in Northern Ireland to enjoy a wider range of products; the Secretary of State got to see that at first hand at a florist’s. Nurseries and garden centres in Northern Ireland will be able to stock an expanded range of plants, and it will be cost-effective to receive seeds in the post. That is good news for all gardeners and green-fingered people. As I said, positive changes for consumers will be underpinned by the Government’s investment in driving more foreign direct investment to Northern Ireland. That will be the focus of the investment summit, which received £1 million in funding at the Budget and will pitch Northern Ireland to global investors as the gateway to UK and EU markets.

May I suggest to the Minister that the much-vaunted dual-market access is a fraud and a deceit? It has not produced one instance of foreign direct investment, for the very simple reason that if a foreign company comes to manufacture in Northern Ireland, its inputs are restricted by the Irish sea border, and it has to go through customs declarations and much more besides. That is the reason why foreign direct investment is failing to take off in Northern Ireland. Is not the answer to restore Northern Ireland’s economy to what it was—a fully integrated part of the United Kingdom economy?

I thought that the hon. and learned Member would welcome the new SPS agreement, given the concerns that he has outlined. This agreement will provide certainty for Northern Ireland cross-border traders, and will free UK businesses from financial and administrative burdens when exporting energy-intensive goods to the EU. While routine SPS checks will be removed, the facilities for NI ports will remain in place to cover checks for goods from the rest of the world. Those checks actively protect UK biosecurity. Stakeholders and businesses that I have met tell us that supply-chain simplification will make it easier to offer a wider range of products to consumers in Northern Ireland. I know that there is no blue moon, but he could have at least welcomed that.

title: Northern Ireland Troubles  (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023

items.txt: 4. What steps he is taking to replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023.
11. What steps he is taking to replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023.
13. What steps he is taking to replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023.

We Government Members made a manifesto commitment that we would repeal the legacy Act because it was legally flawed, did not have the support of any political party in Northern Ireland, and gave the same immunity to terrorists as to British service personnel. We have made good progress; the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill passed its final stages in the Commons over a month ago, and it will have its Second Reading in the Lords on 2 December.

Nine former four-star officers, including three former Chiefs of the General Staff, have called this Bill’s lawfare a direct threat to national security. The Government’s Armed Forces Minister resigned over it, and the Special Air Service Regimental Association, the Special Boat Service Association and the Special Reconnaissance Regimental Association warn that it leaves veterans facing endless reinvestigation. Can the Secretary of State tell the House which veterans’ groups support the Bill as it stands?

The hon. Lady, who I do not remember taking part in any of the debates on the troubles Bill, will perhaps not have realised that we have made substantial changes to the original Bill, which is what the people she mentioned were referring to. I have engaged directly with a large number of organisations. We will still have a process in the House of Lords to ensure that we get the balanced Bill that we require, but her comments were rather out of date.

On Third Reading of the Bill, the shadow Secretary of State, my hon. Friend the Member for Brentwood and Ongar (Alex Burghart), quite rightly pointed out that “‘essential’ is no bar at all” —[ Official Report , 20 October 2026; Vol. 791, c. 993.] when it comes to new evidence. What amendments do the Government propose bringing forward in the other place to address that issue?

The hon. Member makes a very good point. The definition of the word “essential” is essential to how we progress the Bill in the second Chamber, and that is precisely where we will do that. Let me make it clear that my understanding, our legal understanding and our advice is very clearly that “essential” is a high bar, not a low bar. It is a higher bar than the one in the legacy Act.

Earlier this week, the Secretary of State said: “you don’t defend the British Army by defending the indefensible”. Does he agree that that is reckless language, particularly in the light of his Government reopening the inquest into Loughgall? Will he apologise?

I was literally quoting David Cameron, the former Conservative Prime Minister, who said that directly in the Chamber of the House of Commons. He recognised, as everybody in the Chamber at that time did, that the Saville report was very clear that we do not defend the British Army by defending the indefensible. That is precisely what I was referring to.

Can I invite the Secretary of State to confirm one more time, for those who are hard of hearing in this place, that the equivalence created in the legacy Act between British serving personnel and paramilitaries has been removed from the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill, because that is the right thing to do?

I want to say two things. First, the Bill is primarily about families getting answers. We need do no more than scratch the surface of Northern Ireland politics to discover problems that still exist from the troubles era. For instance, on 9 May 1997, 100 people were gathered in the Parliament bar in Belfast—a gay bar, as it happens. In came a terrorist with a gun, who shot dead a 24-year-old officer of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, Constable Darren Bradshaw. Nobody has ever been held to account for that murder. We need—the families need—answers on precisely that kind of event in Northern Ireland, and that is what our Bill will deliver.

In July, this Government acknowledged that the lack of information-sharing arrangements with the Irish Government was impacting a number of investigations by the Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery. The Secretary of State has said that the Irish Government “will work in lockstep with us so that our legislation and their legislation will come into force on the same day.” —[ Official Report , 19 October 2026; Vol. 791, c. 798.] However, concerns have already been raised about relying on existing Garda structures, and the pressure that will place on their responsibilities. How confident is he that the Republic’s legislation will not face any delays?

As the shadow Minister probably knows, I spoke directly with my counterpart in Dublin last week. I made it very clear that we have to have full co-operation from the Irish Government, not only with the ICRIR, but with the Omagh inquiry, as well as all the different ongoing inquiries that need to proceed. People in Northern Ireland will get answers only if the Irish Government fully comply. I am very confident that we will not only work in lockstep, but dovetail our legislation to ensure that we get those answers.
Can the Secretary of State lay out to the House what action he can and would take if the Irish Government were not meeting their obligations?

I would prefer to ensure that they do, and I am absolutely confident that they will. They gave very clear guarantees last week that they will do everything in their power to ensure that they fully comply. Their legislation is ready to go, and we will not be implementing our legislation until such time as it is. I am very confident that we will dovetail the two together.

Clause 13 of the troubles Bill states that “reconciliation should be promoted”, but it fails to define the term. As one witness said to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee today, we need a definition, and we need agreement on what components are included in reconciliation. That is a point made by many in Northern Ireland civil society, including the WAVE trauma centre and the Community Relations Council. The failure to create a budget is just one of many manifestations of the failure to reconcile. When will the Secretary of State give reconciliation the legal framework that Northern Ireland needs?

I agree with the hon. Gentleman about reconciliation. As I said to the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee, I have always hated this idea that we want a tolerant society, because that always feels like we are putting up with people we do not particularly like. It is much better to have a society based on respect—respect for difference, and respect for different political opinions and views on the future of Ireland. That is precisely what we should achieve.

The Secretary of State was right last week when he said that it would be inconceivable for the Irish Government not to hold a full public inquiry into the bombing at Omagh. I am glad he said that, because the families deserve answers and they are not getting them from the Irish Government. Does he agree that answers to the following questions fall outside the remit of the Omagh inquiry? What Garda intelligence was available about the conversation that Norman Baxter overheard in Mahon Road police station in Portadown, one day before the Omagh bombing? Why was the Finner Camp warning, given the day before the bombing, never confirmed or communicated to Northern Ireland’s security forces? What intelligence lay behind the RUC network transmission, 20 minutes before the bombing, saying that it was going to occur? The Irish have the answers to those questions. Does the Secretary of State believe that they should give them now?

I am grateful for the dedication that the right hon. Gentleman has shown on this issue. As he knows, I met families at Omagh on Remembrance Sunday, and I know that the pain is very, very raw for very many of them. I am very keen to ensure they get all the answers they need. As I have said, and as the right hon. Gentleman referred to, it is not for me to decide on the basis of the evidence that has already been brought forward to the inquiry; it is for the inquiry to decide how credible it is and how to measure it all. To be absolutely clear, though, I think it is inconceivable that there will not be an inquiry in Ireland, and I know the families think it would be very helpful if the Irish Government now laid out the terms of reference for such an inquiry.

I agree with the Secretary of State—not only would it be inconceivable, it would be an absolute outrage if the Irish thought their only role in this was to tie up loose ends after the UK inquiry concludes. The families have a sincere question: what was the intended target? I believe the Irish Government have secret information confirming that the car was in the right location when it exploded outside in the town, not the wrong location, as is believed. If that is right, that is information that the families deserve. They yearn for the truth; it is incumbent that they get it.

I completely agree that it is very important that the families get the full set of answers that they deserve—not only what happened in the United Kingdom, but what happened across the border in Ireland—and I am determined to play my role in ensuring they get all those answers.

title: Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery

items.txt: 5. What discussions he has had with his counterpart in the Republic of Ireland on the role of the Independent Commission for Reconciliation and Information Recovery.

As you have just heard, Mr Speaker, I had productive discussions about legacy issues with my Irish counterparts in Dublin last week. I am confident they will deliver on Ireland’s commitments to full co-operation under the joint framework as they work to ensure their legislation dovetails with ours.

The Secretary of State said that the families deserve full information. It has now become apparent that the Irish Government are not sharing information with ICRIR regarding inquiries to Garda units. Letters go unanswered, so what steps will the Secretary of State take to ensure that the Irish Government engage with ICRIR, rather than waiting on the creation of a new legacy commission?

As I said earlier, I made that point very clearly to the Irish Government, and I will continue to do so. My counterparts in Dublin were very clear that they intend to do precisely that. Of course, it would help if we were to get our troubles legislation through as swiftly as possible so that it can dovetail with the Irish Government’s legislation. We would then be able to have full co-operation on both sides of the border.
8. What discussions he has had with the Northern Ireland Executive on recent events on the Garvaghy Road at Drumcree.

I had meetings with a wide range of people about the stand-off at Drumcree, including several rounds of talks with residents of the Garvaghy Road and with the Portadown Orange lodge, before I reluctantly used my powers under the Public Processions (Northern Ireland) Act 1998. I hope to publish the findings of Justice O’Hara’s review of the Parades Commission shortly, but I am pleased that events passed off peacefully and that the vast majority of parades in Northern Ireland proceed without controversy.

Will the Secretary of State accept that when a court’s judgment is upheld on appeal, yet is not given effect for days, public confidence in the rule of law is weakened? What steps will he take to ensure court orders are properly complied with in future?

I honestly could not hear the hon. Gentleman, but I think he was asking me what steps I will take to ensure court orders are properly adhered to. First of all, it is for the courts to ensure that court orders are enforced, and any breach is a matter for the prosecuting authorities. It is not for me to judge the individual actions of politicians, but I say clearly that every elected representative, whether in this House or in the Northern Ireland Assembly, should abide fully by the law.
9. What recent discussions he has had with the Northern Ireland Executive on setting a budget.

I have repeatedly met the Executive parties to discuss the budget following their initial request for us to intervene. Most recently, on 5 November, I chaired discussions at Hillsborough and reaffirmed the Government’s significant offer of £1.5 billion over the next three years to help the Executive stabilise their finances.

As a member of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee, it does not matter which stakeholders we engage with; the consistent message that comes through is that the lack of an Executive budget is harming every aspect of life and every organisation within Northern Ireland. What can the Secretary of State do to impress on the Executive that they need to take action?

I think all Members agree that Northern Ireland deserves financial and political stability, but that can only be achieved if the Northern Ireland Executive set a budget. If they continue on the course they are on, they will end up running out of expenditure around the beginning of February. They will not be able to spend a single penny in the next financial year. That will hurt every single nurse, every single doctor, every single teacher and every single part of the public sector in Northern Ireland. That is why I strongly urge them to take the responsible decisions and set a budget now.

It is the eighth month of the financial year, yet no budget has been set by the Sinn Féin Minister in Northern Ireland, creating chaos in Government Departments. Does the Secretary of State agree that those foolish and short-sighted Unionists who are calling for the collapse of the Assembly will only aid and abet Sinn Féin in hiding the embarrassment of its irresponsible behaviour? Will he work with my party to try to get a sustainable budget in Northern Ireland?

I will work with all political parties to try to ensure we have the fiscal responsibility and stability that we need in Northern Ireland. I warmly commend those who, despite the difficulties of working in the Stormont system, stick with it and try to ensure that power sharing really works. It would have been possible at the beginning of the financial year to make pay awards and to factor them in for each Department in Government. That has not happened. Every single time that somebody refuses to cut expenditure or adds to the bill, it makes it more difficult to make those pay awards. It is time that the Northern Ireland Executive settled the budget.
Q1. If he will list his official engagements for Wednesday 25 November.

With your permission, Mr Speaker, I will make a statement after Prime Minister’s questions on our nuclear test veterans. Today is International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls. Recognising the growing concern in the country and the need to strengthen all possible measures to protect victims, we are today confirming that we will bring forward the date to January by which non-disclosure agreements can no longer be used to silence a victim of sexual harassment. This morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In accordance with my duties in this House, I shall have further such meetings later today.

We are coming towards the end of National Care Leavers Month, which is a chance for us to renew our commitment to do the very best for care-experienced young people. Southampton’s care leavers came and told me that they just want to be able to build a good future for themselves, but the cost of going to college or work is often money that they do not necessarily have. I know that the Prime Minister loves a bus, and I very much commend him for providing free bus travel for care leavers when he was Mayor of Manchester. Will he now do everything to ensure that this Government can extend that same support to every care leaver?

My hon. Friend is right to say that Greater Manchester had some good policies under the previous mayor, as it does under the current one, too. One of those was the provision of free transport to care leavers up to the age of 25. I hope other areas around the country would look to do the same. We do need to do more to support our young people who have left care and who do not have a mum and dad to fall back on. That is our collective responsibility, and I can promise him today that I will go further as Prime Minister.

The EU reset deal is not yet done. They have still not finished negotiating tuition fees. If EU students paid the same as British students, that would cost British universities half a billion pounds. As Universities UK has said, this deal will do “huge damage” to its sector. Who will the Prime Minister ask to pick up the bill? Will it be cash-strapped universities, or cash-strapped taxpayers?

I think the right hon. Lady has answered her own question. The deal on tuition fees is not done. As the President of the European Commission said, it is on “a separate piece of paper”. It is a separate deal, and we will take that conversation forward, always rightfully mindful of the challenges faced by higher education. But let us be clear about what this deal does do. It gives new opportunities to everyone in the country under the age of 31. It puts more hope on the horizon of young people—hope that was taken away by the Brexit deal, the flawed Brexit deal, that the Conservatives negotiated.

The Prime Minister says that the President of the European Commission has said that the deal is not yet done. On Monday, he said that the Commission saw tuition fees as “a separate agreement”. But— [Interruption.] . Wait for it. But the Council of the European Union, the highest political authority in the EU, has said something very different. On Friday, it issued a separate statement. It said that the agreements on youth mobility, food and energy “shall not precede the conclusion of negotiations on tuition fees; they are part of the same package.” If the Prime Minister refuses to cut tuition fees for EU students, will Brussels still sign his reset deal? Yes or no?

Tomorrow we will introduce legislation in the House that will set the date for the implementation of the deals on food, on emissions, and indeed on the wider youth experience scheme. We will continue discussions with the European Union on the question of tuition fees, but it is what we have said all along, and the Conservative party needs to decide where it stands. Will it stand against a deal that will remove mountains of paperwork from British businesses and British exporters—a deal that the vast majority of Britain’s major supermarkets support because, they say, it can bring down pressure on the weekly shop. The Conservatives were once the party that opposed the imposition of red tape; they are now the red tape Tories standing against a deal that will be good for British businesses, good for British consumers, and good for young people in Britain.

If the Prime Minister spent less time talking to influencers and more time talking to businesses, he would know that the red tape they complain about is his Employment Rights Act. But, Mr Speaker, look at all that whataboutery! I asked the Prime Minister a simple question, and he cannot give a straight answer. Now he is saying that they are still negotiating. It is very clear that this deal is not done, because he cannot just wish away those comments from the Council of the European Union, and he needs to be very clear about what he is doing on tuition fees. When I asked him whether, if he cut tuition fees, Brussels would still agree to the deal—yes or no—he could not answer. On Monday, when the Prime Minister was asked about reducing EU student tuition fees, he said: “We will have our clear red lines in that negotiation.” —[ Official Report , 23 November 2026; Vol. 794, c. 57.] So let us hear them. Will he now rule out EU students’ paying the same tuition fees as British students?

The right hon. Lady has mentioned my talking to influencers. It is true: I have spoken to influencers, and then I have to come to the House and speak to people who are the opposite of influencers. In relation to the deal, the right hon. Lady is referring to the European negotiating position, which is not the British negotiating position. That has not been put on the table, and it will not be put on the table, but she should address the substance of the deal—the overall package. What will the overall package do for growth in the British economy? She dismisses the fact that it adds up to 0.5% to the British economy, billions of pounds extra. Can we as a country really afford to turn our back on growth of that scale? It is the biggest growth measure that we could take in this Parliament. The party of low growth in the last decade is standing against an opportunity to boost British growth. The Conservatives keep on making the same old mistake over and over again. They want us to stick with a failed Tory Brexit deal—the failed status quo. We will not do that. We can improve it, and it is in the British national interest to do so.

It sounds like the Prime Minister does not have any red lines, because when he had the opportunity, he did not say so. Instead, he went on point scoring. I do not know why he is getting tetchy with me again, because if I do not hold him to account— [ Interruption. ] If I do not hold him to account, we know that he will end up giving the whole country away. I know he is not enjoying this—he prefers soft questions from people dancing around Downing Street. That is not what he is going to get from me. I asked the Prime Minister a very simple question. Instead, he wants me to congratulate him on a deal that is not yet done. This is important. This is about our students. Labour froze the student loan repayment threshold until 2030 at the last Budget. Because of that freeze, the Treasury says that British graduates will pay an extra £355 million a year. Those are not my numbers; they are Treasury numbers. Yet he is willing to spend at least £500 million a year subsidising tuition fees for EU students. Why is the Prime Minister making British graduates pay more, while agreeing to let EU students pay less?

The right hon. Lady mentions people dancing around Downing Street. Wait until she hears about the lockdown parties that once happened there. She will be really outraged when she hears about all of those. On the right hon. Lady’s question, surely this is about looking at the whole package in the round and what it can do for the British economy and British businesses. I come back to my point: they are facing mountains of red tape if they are looking to export food to the European Union, and this deal can remove that. British supermarkets say this deal can reduce and lift pressure off prices in the shops. This deal gives hope and opportunity to young people. We have not done a deal on tuition fees, as I said at the start of my answers today. We will keep her posted on the progress of those negotiations, but it is surely about time that this House got behind measures to boost growth in the British economy and lift the life chances of young people, and that is what this side of the House is doing.

Let us be clear about what we have learned today: the Prime Minister is telling us to look into the horizon now that he realises that his deal is not yet done. I was not asking about all those bits. I was asking about tuition fees and students, and what have we learned today? There is no answer on paying half a billion pounds to the EU, no answer on putting British students before EU students, and no answer on whether the deal is contingent on the tuition fees agreement. He claims that he is offering young people hope, but graduates are facing the worst recruitment crisis on record. Hope does not get them a job. Hope does not pay their student loans. Hope does not pay their energy bills, which have gone up today by £440. The Prime Minister keeps promising young people a brighter future, but is it not the case that when we ask for the details, all we get is vibes?

I remember when I first came to this House and made a statement about my approach to this whole question. The right hon. Lady said that I had revealed a negotiating position and that we would not get a deal. Well, we did get a deal. We actually got a deal that removed the threat from “Made in Europe” to the British car industry, the British steel industry and the aluminium industry. She minimises those things because she looks for the negative in everything. She has not got the ability to see the bigger picture and what this deal will do for the economy, but also in building a more constructive relationship with our nearest neighbours. The Conservatives burned those bridges, and they damaged good will with our nearest market. We are repairing it, and we are right to do so.

The Prime Minister is coming unstuck because he spent more time on vibes than on the detail, so let us see where his vibes get us. He mentioned lockdown parties earlier in his statement, and I think he is going to fall off his high horse very quickly. This week, we saw videos of the Prime Minister hosting social media influencers in Downing Street. The words used by one of them on the steps of No. 10 were so offensive that I will not repeat them in this House: disgusting and pejorative comments about women’s private parts, and obscene language that referred to white women as “cheap meat”. This is grotesque. Labour MPs constantly tell us about their commitments to fighting violence against women and girls. Those MPs were silent yesterday; I won’t be! Will the Prime Minister now apologise for debasing his office and for allowing that vile video to be recorded on the steps of No. 10?

An inappropriate video was taken down and the creator has rightly apologised—the right hon. Lady was right to call that out, because it was not acceptable—but I will not apologise for engaging with people who young people— [ Interruption. ]
Order. Mr Snowden, it was Lancashire Day yesterday. I do not need to hear a Lancashire voice today.

I will not apologise for engaging with people that young people themselves are looking to for their information, and I think this House— [ Interruption. ] Not this individual; I am talking about the wider point. The right hon. Lady sneers at TikTokers, she sneers at influencers, but young people are looking to these people for their information, and I will not apologise for doing that. [ Interruption. ] I have already said it was wrong—what was said—and it was taken down. We have done this about six times now, and I have realised that the right hon. Lady has nothing positive to say to the country. She is constantly talking it down in the answers that she gives, and why? Because she is looking over her right shoulder to Reform and to Restore. She comes to this House to make cheap points. I will continue dealing with the big issues—on Europe to boost our economy; on young people, giving them more support to give them hope; on social care and a national care service for our older people. We are working hard, we are turning this country around, and that is what the Opposition do not like. We are giving people hope, and we will not be distracted by her negativity.

Q2. I recognise that there are already guidelines for judges to give juries directions in relation to rape myths, though the timing and consistency of those are a point for discussion. I also recognise that defence barristers must be able to ask witnesses all questions that are necessary and relevant to the case. However, the current system allows cross-examination to go beyond this. Survivors of rape and sexual abuse are being subjected to disproven and misogynistic stereotypes that harm victims and undermine justice. Will the Prime Minister bring together an expert group of judicial office holders, lawyers, academics, campaigners and experts by experience to make recommendations around how rape myths are dealt with in courts?

I thank my hon. Friend. She speaks with real power and authority on this crucial issue, and I agree with her completely. Yes, I will establish the group that she calls for. Today, we have said that we are inviting survivors, parents and young people to take part in a national conversation on these issues—on false rape myths of third-party consent, the age of consent and wider abuses of power. Her expert group can sit as part of that, and I will make sure she is fully part of that conversation.

I welcome the announcement the Prime Minister has just made. As we mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, and girls, I also welcome his commitment to stop non-disclosure agreements being used to silence survivors. Families and pensioners already struggling to make ends meet simply cannot afford an extra £400 on their energy bills next year. At the same time as Trump’s war in Iran is pushing up the cost of living for everybody, a small band of energy network companies are making massive profits at the expense of millions of people. Will the Prime Minister claw back those windfall profits and use them to cut people’s energy bills now?

I recognise that the energy price cap announced this morning by Ofgem will cause concern to many people up and down the country. I do accept that longer term reform of the energy market is needed, and we will set that out in the plan for Britain, to be published next month. The right hon. Gentleman calls for action. Obviously, we took a different form of action in the Budget, which was to put a levy on banks to pay for £100 support for 20 million households across England, starting in early January. What Ofgem has announced is that, for the first three months of the year, families will see about £110 extra on their bills. The support we have provided, alongside the removal of VAT from electricity bills, will give people some breathing space, but I accept there is more to do.

I am afraid the Prime Minister’s help does not touch the sides for so many families and pensioners. I hope he will look at our proposal. He said he wanted to control companies making big, unjustified profits. Well, this is a test of whether he meant it. Moving on, in February last year the Government announced £2.5 billion for the British steel industry, but a freedom of information request obtained by the leader of the Welsh Liberal Democrats revealed today that the Government have not spent, allocated or committed a single penny of that money in Wales. Why on earth not? Will he meet me and my hon. Friend the Member for Brecon, Radnor and Cwm Tawe (David Chadwick) so he can put right this latest betrayal of Welsh industry and jobs?

If I could first go back to energy bills, Mr Speaker, the right hon. Gentleman is right to push for more and I will do more. Next year, we will remove the standing charge from gas bills, and I will seek to do that as quickly as possible, hopefully with the support of the House. On the steel industry, particularly in Wales, he will know that the Government have invested heavily in the electric arc furnace at Tata Steel in Port Talbot. Again, there is more to be done, and I will always meet if he asks me to do so, but he should recognise that we have, as a Government, invested heavily in steel transition in south Wales.

Q5. Yesterday, Sikhs in Smethwick and across the world celebrated the birth anniversary of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. Guru Nanak promoted equality for all and shared three key teachings: Kirat Karo, to work an honest living; Vand Chhako, to share one’s earnings; and Naam Japo, to remember God at all times. I wish all those celebrating a happy Gurpurab. We should thank the Prime Minister for his leadership in the coalition of the willing last week in support of Ukrainian people in the face of appalling Russian aggression. This weekend, I had the privilege of representing this Parliament at the annual NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, where NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said “our citizens need to know that the lights will stay on, that their homes will stay warm, that hospitals, transport, and communications will keep working”.Will the Prime Minister tell the House what the Government are doing to build preparedness and resilience in communities across the UK, including in my Smethwick constituency?

It is such an important question, resilience. I will address the Liaison Committee on Monday on this very issue. What I can point my hon. Friend towards straightaway is our Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, which is going through the House and will protect critical infrastructure, and the Be Ready campaign that we have launched, alongside our commitments on defence spending. He is right to raise these issues, but there is more to do. I join him in wishing all those celebrating a peaceful and blessed Gurpurab.

The Prime Minister will be aware of the Irish Government’s drive towards planning for a united Ireland. Will he remind the Taoiseach and others, even in this place, that the Belfast agreement is based on consent, not a false assumption that constitutional change is inevitable, and that the future of Northern Ireland belongs to its people, not to a political agenda in Dublin? Its true place is as an integral part of this United Kingdom.

The hon. Gentleman is right that the Good Friday agreement is based on the principle of consent, and that is very clearly laid out within it. The important thing, as we approach its 30th anniversary, is that we all remind ourselves of what precisely is in the Good Friday agreement and work very hard to uphold its values. More broadly, the priority now is for all parties in Northern Ireland to come together and urgently agree a balanced budget to protect public services. I am concerned that this has not happened, and along with the Northern Ireland Secretary, I urge all parties to use the additional funding that this Government have offered to agree a budget as a matter of urgency. We can then sure up the arrangements in Northern Ireland and mark the 30th anniversary of the Good Friday agreement in two years’ time.

Q6. This is more of a plea than a question. In the Public Gallery is my constituent, Raneem, and she does not know if her son Ibrahim is alive. Four years ago, when he was six years old, his father abducted him to Saudi Arabia, and she has not seen him since. I ask the Prime Minister on behalf of Raneem: please, will he help bring Ibrahim home?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising this case with me previously. I dealt with one in my previous time in Parliament and I know the pain, to some degree, that Raneem has endured. I know that she is in contact with the Home Office to see if Ibrahim’s British nationality can be established. Home Office Ministers will have heard what my hon. Friend has said, and we will see if we can make more progress. I say directly to Raneem, who is here today, that we will work with you. We will give you all the support that we can to reunite you with your son.

Q3. Diolch yn fawr, Mr Llefarydd. When he came to office in July, the Prime Minister promised to end Whitehall’s resistance to devolution and to listen to Wales. How disappointing then, that he has overruled the mandate given by the people of Wales for more responsibility. He has dismissed the calls of all 22 Welsh councils, TUC Cymru and two former Welsh Labour First Ministers, Carwyn Jones and Mark Drakeford. Last week, the Prime Minister was not persuaded and said no. When exactly did he decide that Wales is no longer worth listening to?

I am listening to Wales, and I have met the First Minister a number of times. I put an offer on the table of deeper devolution around employment support. Let us first work where we have got a clear case and common ground, so that we can get more young people in Wales into work and good jobs. I will never completely rule things out, but at this moment in time, that is the issue that we should work on, where we can agree that there is a case to go further and get deeper devolution down into all parts of Wales.

Q9. The Prime Minister took office promising to move beyond the years of dogma that said that the answer to every problem was to sell off and deregulate. But recent comments about Natural England have raised concerns about the return of lazy narratives, blaming bats and newts for the shortcomings of corporate profiteering. Will the PM back my call for clear red lines on nature, so that there is no more defunding of environmental bodies, no more weakening of environmental protections, and a fully funded plan for nature’s recovery?

This is precisely why I attended the COP31 summit. I wanted to make it clear that I put a high value on all the things that my hon. Friend has mentioned. As a Government, we will continue to work hard to safeguard nature and the environment.

Q4. Jenny’s son is a primary school pupil with special educational needs and disabilities who has not attended school since June. Despite medical evidence, his school refuses a gradual return under threat of prosecution. His is one of thousands of cases nationally. Using fines to force children with unmet needs into school is cruel and ineffective. As the Milburn review said, enforcement cannot substitute for understanding the cause. Last month, I handed in a petition to Downing Street with charities like Square Peg, which is piloting a more compassionate approach in Manchester. Will the Prime Minister meet us to discuss rolling out the approach nationwide?

Our guidance is clear: schools and local authorities should consider whether further support is more appropriate than a fine, as well as considering a pupil’s particular circumstances. I agree with the hon. Lady that fines really should not be used in these circumstances. Perhaps in the most exceptional cases they should, but even then I would be with her in wanting to send that message to all schools in England.

Q10. On Monday it was announced that the UK will host the 2035 women’s world cup; this summer, Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth games. These events inspire excitement and national pride, but sport should be about participation, not just spectating. Tomorrow, campaigners in my constituency will mark the third anniversary of the closure of Whitehill pool. We all know the huge benefits to our mental and physical health of getting out of the house and down to the local pool. Will the Prime Minister back the campaign to save Whitehill pool and join us in demanding that Glasgow city council finally set out a plan to reopen this vital community asset?

I am one of those who believe that we cannot get enough sport and sporting facilities, so I am quite happy to back my hon. Friend’s campaign. I hope that Glasgow city council will listen to what she is saying. These are essential facilities—critical infrastructure at the heart of our communities. It was wonderful news that the UK was confirmed as the host of the 2035 FIFA women’s world cup, to be held in Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland and England. This gives us a huge opportunity over the next decade to build women’s and girls’ sport in this country on a cross-party basis, and I hope the whole House will take it. I know that the news will have excited young women across the country this week.
Order. We are not going to get through the list unless Members keep their questions short, so I need you all to help me now. Let us have a good start with Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown.

Q7. The Treasury has estimated that the final bill for leaving the EU will be at least £34 billion. Following the excellent question from my right hon. Friend the Leader of the Opposition on the Prime Minister’s reset deal, how much money has the Prime Minister provided in this Parliament to fund that reset deal, and how many tens of billions would that lead into if we were to rejoin the EU?

The question is, how much have we also lost in our economy from leaving the EU? I did not agree the deal that the hon. Gentleman and his colleagues signed up to—indeed, that many of them forced previous Prime Ministers into when there was a better deal on the table. That is the challenge that the country has been facing: low growth and, because of that, low ability to finance our priorities. I am doing what I can to repair that flawed deal, to bring more growth to the economy and therefore more resources to the Exchequer.

Q14. This month, Stevenage celebrated 80 years as Britain’s first post-war new town, created by the Labour Government of Clement Attlee to give people the chance of a new and fulfilling life. Ever since, our town has been at the forefront of cutting-edge industries, especially in the defence sector, producing rockets and satellites that keep Britain and our allies safe. Does the Prime Minister agree that the Milburn review must be an opportunity to help a new generation to work in our locally based industries, just as the young generation of 1946 did?

It is excellent news that 13 major defence companies have committed to helping young people not in education, employment or training to access careers across the industry. I hope that my hon. Friend’s constituency will be a major beneficiary of that move.

Q8. Devizes lies at the heart of Wiltshire, surrounded by tourist sites including Stonehenge and Avebury. It is on the brink of major regeneration, yet despite the main line being just two and a half miles away, there is no railway station. The Prime Minister says that he wants growth in every postcode, so will he back my petition and meet me to discuss how the proposed Devizes Gateway railway station could unlock jobs and provide homes and investment across Wiltshire?

I know from my previous role how important transport infrastructure, particularly rail stations, is in unlocking jobs. I will encourage the hon. Gentleman to work with the Department for Transport, but I will also make sure that our Rail Minister meets him to discuss the matter. I will keep an eye on it, too, because I care about his part of the world and I would like to see that infrastructure delivered.

Following the horrific case of Jo Young, who bravely waived her anonymity to allow shame to change sides and who joins us today in the Public Gallery, there have been calls to look at stronger direction for judges and barristers to address rape myths and ensure that sexual consent is clearly articulated by those involved. Does the Prime Minister agree that it is important for the Government to look at the ways in which we can improve the criminal justice system for victims of rape and sexual assault?

I do agree, and I pay tribute to my hon. Friend for her dedicated campaigning on this issue. We are launching a national conversation covering all the issues that she rightly raises. I join her in paying tribute to the extraordinary courage of Joanne Young. Joanne cannot speak in this House, so I want to repeat from the Dispatch Box some of her words: “Consent has to come from the person themselves. No one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed.” Everybody should hear those words. Joanne is absolutely right, and we praise her courage today in this House. More victims will be able to speak out because of Joanne.

Q11. Twenty thousand children were harmed by the sodium valproate scandal, including in my constituency. Children were born with lifelong conditions, including heart defects, limb abnormalities, spinal deformities and severe learning disabilities. In 2024, the Hughes report recommended interim compensation to start last year. A year beyond that, the Government have failed even to publish a formal response, let alone make payments. All the while, victims suffer and die. From the Post Office to the infected blood scandal, it is the same story: we have a recommendation, and then Whitehall drags its feet. Will the Prime Minister end this delay and commit today to delivering compensation for the victims of this atrocious scandal?

The right hon. Gentleman mentions other scandals, and we are about to discuss another one: nuclear test veterans. The pattern is always the same; he is right to point to that. I have campaigned on this issue in the past, and I am not going to take a different line as Prime Minister. I am happy to work with the right hon. Gentleman on this issue. We need to see full justice for those affected by the sodium valproate scandal, and I will work with him to that end.

Today is the national day for children with a parent in prison. I will be hosting an event at which we will hear from young people about how this experience affected them, and from a panel of people who, as kids, saw their dads go to jail because they killed their mums. All I ask of the Prime Minister today is that he put his wholehearted support behind our manifesto commitment to identify children who are going through this experience, so that we can get them the support that some of the people we will hear from later will not have had.

I think we can all agree that no child should pay the price for their parents’ actions and that having a parent in prison should never define a child’s future. My hon. Friend is right to raise these issues on this important day. Later today, the Minister for Sentencing and the Minister for Children will hear from affected families to ensure that their thoughts are reflected in the work that we carry forward on this issue.

Q12. People often say that they want to hold their MP’s feet to the fire. I took that rather literally on Sunday, when alongside 27 others I did a fire walk. As a group we raised £10,000 for Meningitis Now. I joined Angela Cloke, the organiser, and my constituent Rod Adlington, who will be rowing the Indian ocean in memory of his son Barney, who Rod tragically lost to meningitis at the tender age of three. The Prime Minister will know that earlier this year there was a huge meningitis outbreak that tragically claimed the lives of three young people and put dozens in hospital. These outbreaks can be prevented with a MenB vaccine, but, crucially, there is no vaccination provision beyond this year’s one-off programme. Will the Prime Minister acknowledge the bravery of all who joined me on Sunday? Will he meet me, Rod, Angela and the Meningitis Now campaign to protect young people from this pernicious disease?

I am glad to hear that I am not the only one in this House who has their feet held to the fire, and I am glad to see that the hon. Gentleman is on his feet today. I congratulate him and all those who took part in the event on the weekend. I have some family experience of the importance of the MenB adolescent vaccination programme; I am sympathetic to what he is saying. The Health Secretary has just said to me that she is prepared to meet him to discuss the matter and see if we can make some progress.

While visiting Korea last month as the UK’s trade envoy, I witnessed the deep friendship between our two nations, their immense manufacturing and technological prowess and the vast opportunities for British companies across many sectors. With the free trade agreement already agreed, and with our two Governments moving towards signing it as soon as possible, does the Prime Minister agree that now is a great time to elevate this vital trading relationship, to give jobs and opportunities in every postcode of our great country?
I couldn’t have put it better myself. I agree wholeheartedly with my hon. Friend.

Q13. Tiverton and Minehead is a coastal constituency with a rural backdrop, so I know that it will be of particular interest to the Prime Minister. We face myriad challenges, including poor transport connectivity and health outcomes. At the last general election, Labour pledged to double the number of CT and MRI scanners. Unfortunately, Minehead community hospital saw its scanner taken away after the general election. The Prime Minister’s signature maxim is about delivering for every postcode, so will he arrange a meeting for me with the Health Secretary to discuss reinstating Minehead’s scanner and provision in rural healthcare settings? In case he is wondering which postcode would otherwise be left behind, it is TA24 6DF.

Let me just write that down—say it again? [ Laughter. ] No, I fully understand the importance of what the hon. Member is saying. Diagnostic capacity should be close to the community, and that is indeed the programme that my right hon. Friend the Health Secretary is leading. I cannot promise a meeting with her, but we can promise the hon. Member a meeting with a Minister to discuss the issue, to ensure that her constituency and all others in the area have the diagnostic capacity that they need.

With permission, Mr Speaker, I would like to make a statement on nuclear test veterans. This day has taken far too long in coming. The only reason it has arrived is the sheer courage of thousands of ex-servicemen and their families who refused to give in. Our nuclear test veterans stand with all other veterans in displaying all the typical characteristics that we so rightly commend in the British armed forces: service, bravery, dignity and determination. Yet these veterans have been left to stand apart for decades, in a wilderness and with no choice but to fight their own country for recognition and answers. It is hard to know how we can even begin to put that right today, but it does mark the day when we make a start in earnest. Next year will mark the 75th anniversary of Britain’s first nuclear test. Operation Hurricane took place on 3 October 1952 off an island off the coast of Western Australia. It was one of many detonations that was to take place across the 1950s and 1960s in the south Pacific, involving about 22,000 British servicemen, many called up on national service. Many facts about Britain’s nuclear test programme and what happened to the people who took part in it are not known, but one is undeniable: many young servicemen were forced to participate in the witnessing of tests without their knowledge, their consent or personal protective equipment. Archie Hart was 18 years old when his ship was ordered to sail through the fallout of two atomic clouds for eight hours at a time. Within two years, he began developing hundreds of benign tumours, some the size of tennis balls. He later developed aggressive cancer. John Morris was wearing just a shirt, shorts and sunglasses when a nuclear bomb exploded just 20 miles away. He said: “The flash was white, the heat like a blowtorch on your back, then we were knocked off our feet.” When he returned home, he was diagnosed with a blood disorder. His first-born son, Steven, died at just four months old of bronchopneumonia. His parents were wrongly blamed for his death. Members of this House and people watching this may at this point recognise a pattern they have seen before: the people given infected blood who faced questions about their lifestyle; the sub-postmasters and sub-postmistresses branded petty thieves; the Liverpool supporters accused of unspeakable things against their fellow fans. I met John and Archie five years ago and they had a very simple request, like those who had been caught up in the infected blood, Post Office and Hillsborough scandals: they just wanted the truth. It is a sad fact that the vast majority of the 22,000 people who witnessed the tests have died, some many years ago. But they passed on the torch of their campaign over the years, and it is right and fitting that we are honoured by the presence of members of the test veterans community with us today. We salute you all and we know you represent every single person you were proud to serve alongside and every single person who was caught up in this. We are also joined by families affected: wives who have fought for husbands, and children and grandchildren for fathers and grandfathers. You have been through what no British family should, but today we recognise the depth of your commitment to the loved ones you have lost. Those servicemen and their families were able to take their first steps out of the wilderness five years ago on the 70th anniversary of the first test. Boris Johnson as Prime Minister was right to call for the Nuclear Test Medal in 2022, finally recognising their service and their sacrifice. Their courage deserved such an honour; it contributed to the creation of the UK’s nuclear deterrent that we rely upon today to keep us safe. But a medal on the chest is no substitute for knowing the truth in your heart, nor is it sufficient for decades of questions unanswered and justice denied. There is a very significant reason why this is an urgent issue of now and not just one of the past. I

Order. I thank the Prime Minister for bringing this statement to the House. It has run over, so there is some extra time for the Leader of the Opposition and, obviously, for the leader of the Liberal Democrats.

I thank the Prime Minister for making this statement. We on these Benches will always stand up for our brave veterans; as Conservatives, we value the sacrifices made by those who serve in our armed forces, including Britain’s nuclear test veterans. The stories of the nuclear veterans that the Prime Minister laid out in his statement are absolutely harrowing. These men were exposed to radiation in the service of our nation, and for decades they have been campaigning for answers. I pay tribute to members of the test veterans community for all that they have done, and I thank Members on both sides of this House who have campaigned with them, not least my right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes). Back in 2022, the country finally recognised our nuclear test veterans, when Conservatives introduced the Nuclear Test Medal. We gave these men the honour and recognition they deserved. I hope that they will now get the answers that they deserve, too. I have some questions for the Prime Minister. Can he clarify—I could not quite tell from his statement—if this inquiry investigates whether previous Ministers were misled by officials? Will it make recommendations on compensation? If compensation is awarded, has provision been made by the Government for that money? Will veterans and bereaved families have a straightforward process to claim? There is another important issue. These events took place in the 1950s and 1960s. Record-keeping has changed enormously since then. What guarantees has the Prime Minister been given by the Ministry of Defence that the records the inquiry will be looking for actually exist, and that they are accessible? What powers will a non-statutory inquiry have to demand these documents? If I can make a broader point: how a country treats its veterans tells us a lot about how a nation values service and sacrifice. That is why, in government, the Conservatives introduced the armed forces covenant, veterans ID cards and the veterans railcard. We launched Operation Fortitude to tackle veterans’ homelessness and Operation Courage to support veterans’ mental health. The Prime Minister is absolutely right to talk about justice for the nuclear test veterans today, and I commend him for that, but I would like to take this opportunity to urge him to please take a closer look at veterans who served in Northern Ireland. As he is opening this inquiry today, his Ministers are simultaneously reopening the door to legal proceedings that remove protections for another group of elderly veterans who served our country. This is something that Labour’s own Armed Forces Minister has warned is causing those veterans untold anguish. I hope the Prime Minister will take a closer look at that group as well. Our nuclear test veterans have waited decades for answers. They deserve those answers and they deserve justice, so we support an inquiry that delivers for these veterans and their families.

I thank the right hon. Lady for the support that she has given for the nuclear test veterans independent panel. It is very important that the panel visibly has the support of the leaders of both the Government and the Opposition, and hopefully of other leaders in this House. That gives the panel the backing it needs to do its work and it matters greatly, so I thank her for that. The right hon. Lady asked about the work of the panel and the questions it will consider. On whether previous Ministers were misled, Tobias Ellwood, who was a Defence Minister in the previous Conservative Government, has said on the record that he was misled. I have said on the record in the past that, during my time as Health Secretary, I was misled over the infected blood scandal, and other Ministers have been in that position as well. It is vital that that is considered because it speaks to the good governance of this country. No Minister of the Crown should ever be given false information by their Department, so yes, those questions will be looked at in detail. On compensation, I remember this issue arising when I established the Hillsborough independent panel many years ago, and it is natural to ask that question.
