I said at that time, and I say again now, let us not rush too far ahead too quickly. The bishop said then, and I am sure he would say the same now, that the truth will have its own power. Once the truth is established, the full power of it will open doors and make things change in a way that it is hard to imagine right now. Of course we should go wherever the truth takes us, and we should make whatever recompense is needed as a result, but those are questions that will come in the next phase. It will be a straightforward process. Bishop James is extremely experienced in these matters. He will know where to go and he will know the information to ask for, but, as I said, he will have the ability to speak directly to the First Secretary of State or to me to ensure that he does not have any barriers put in his way. The right hon. Lady asks about the records. They exist but sadly many veterans and their families have spent years fighting to see those records. We should bear it in mind that these records relate to some very significant personal medical information for those families. It is simply indefensible that those records have been withheld from people. It is a non-statutory inquiry, but I believe experience shows that such inquiries can work to get to the truth more quickly. That is particularly the case when there is a Government Department involved, with papers held at a national level. In many ways, this inquiry will not present the same challenges as infected blood or Hillsborough because the subject is more contained. James will be able to come to us, as I said, if there are any problems. The right hon. Lady is right to say that this matter goes to the heart of how the country treats veterans. We cannot be selective—it cannot be right that one group of veterans is treated in a second-class way compared with others. That is why what we are doing today is so important. I think that the debate about the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill may be for another occasion, but I have heard what the right hon. Lady said. We will always listen to any concerns that any veteran has about their treatment, but on that difficult issue we have to get the balance right and honour the Good Friday agreement. To finish, the right hon. Lady’s support today is important. I know that it will be appreciated by the test veteran community, and it gives us everything we need to build on and make this process a success.

Having raised this issue on numerous occasions over the years, including in our Defence Committee deliberations, I welcome, thank and commend the Prime Minister on fulfilling his promise about this long-awaited independent inquiry for the long-suffering nuclear test veterans. The courageous campaigning that has been happening behind the scenes to obtain complete medical records and clear answers must also be commended. After decades of delay, we need this non-statutory process to lead to resolution. Will the Prime Minister commit today to a clear timetable for considering and implementing the panel’s recommendations next year?

I will do precisely as the Chair of the Defence Committee says because we owe it to the community to work differently in this regard. As I said, time is not on their side and we should have that in our minds at all stages. We need to compress timescales, avoid consultations and be in action-oriented mode to make things happen quickly. That is the spirit in which I go into this whole process.

I thank the Prime Minister for advance sight of his statement and, above all, for his personal action on this issue. He deserves thanks from across the House, as well as from the veterans and their families. This has been a shameful Government scandal and, as the examples that the Prime Minister read out show, a heartbreaking human tragedy for so many. Veterans who stepped up to serve our country were left exposed to dangerous radiation, and when they developed serious health conditions, they were not helped. They were lied to again and again. When they told their story and said that they remembered having blood tests taken, they were told that they did not have blood tests taken. When they asked for medical records, they were denied access to those medical records. Officials, Ministers, whether misled or not, and courts denied them justice, so this really is a stain on our country and on our institutions. Just as we learned from Hillsborough and so many other scandals, we need to change the law to ensure that people who are affected get justice, by strengthening whistleblowing and many other aspects of how we treat the individual citizen when the state abuses them. The Prime Minister is right to say that the families of the veterans and the veterans themselves deserve so much better. Does he agree that they deserve an explicit apology from the Government today? I join the Prime Minister in paying tribute to all those veterans, widows and children who have campaigned for so long to get justice. He was right to mention a number of them. Last year, I was privileged to meet Alan Owen, the founder of LABRATS, with John Morris and Steve Purse. I was particularly impressed by their dedication, as well as that of Susie Boniface, the journalist who has done so much over such a long period to expose the scandal and has never let up. It is also right to credit and pay thanks to Members from all parties across the House. I give particular credit to my hon. Friend the Member for Epsom and Ewell (Helen Maguire), who has done a lot of work on the issue. It is critical that the investigation delivers justice quickly, while some of the veterans are still with us, as the Prime Minister has said. Will he assure us that neither national security nor legal privilege will be used to stop the panel getting to the truth? As a non-statutory inquiry, will the panel have the power to compel witnesses to give evidence, even if they are not in government? Will he commit today that any compensation the panel recommends will be paid at the earliest moment, ideally by the end of next year, the 75th anniversary of the first nuclear test? At its core, this scandal is about power: the veterans and their families made to feel powerless in the face of abuse by the state, and the Ministry of Defence abusing its power by covering it all up to avoid being held to account. We welcome the Prime Minister’s action today and I hope that we can finally start putting all that right.

I thank the right hon. Gentleman for his kind words and his very thoughtful contribution. It is good to know that we are all aligned on this issue. I completely agree with everything he says. Something has been seriously awry in the way that the state treats people, given that they have been left in this seriously harmed position. We have seen that repeat over time, so it is right that the Hillsborough law will be on the statute book shortly to rebalance the relationship between state and individual. The right hon. Gentleman is right to point to the fact that it was denied for years that medical records and blood tests existed, and that issue needs to be looked into. The right hon. Gentleman asked about an explicit apology, and I have thought about that. I could have made such an apology today, but I would prefer it to be a full, meaningful apology for the full extent of what is revealed, so that it does not appear glib or unserious. I worked with David Cameron, who made the apology from the Government Dispatch Box on the publication of the Hillsborough independent panel, and it feels to me that that is the right time to do it. I am absolutely certain that on or around 3 October next year, I will be standing here doing just that, but I want to talk to the families and others affected to ensure that it is meaningful and right. The right hon. Gentleman asked whether national security and legal privilege will be used in an appropriate way, and we will be like hawks watching the process. We will not allow some of the things that are done in these circumstances to throw up barriers. I am not in any way walking away from the question of compensation, but let us take each step in its time, and once the full truth is known we can answer those questions in a meaningful way. The right hon. Gentleman is right about the power imbalances that still exist in our country, and we in this House should be relentless. We have to ask—I asked this 20 years ago about Hillsborough—how this country could have allowed such an injustice to stand for so long. I am afraid that this time I find myself asking that with even greater emphasis and force. Veterans who served our country overseas, and who were called up for national service, have been fighting their own country for basic answers—how has this Parliament left them in that position for decades? It says something not particularly easy about our democracy and the failure of this place to give people truth. We must ask some hard questions of ourselves in this place, because we have not yet answered them fully.

I thank you, Mr Speaker, for your resolute support for this cause over the years, and I thank the Prime Minister from the bottom of my heart. He has long supported this campaign because, like me, when he heard the harrowing truth all those years ago about what these men and their families suffered, he found that it changes you; it creates a burning anger inside that the truth has been buried and justice has been denied to veterans, their widows and their children for more than 70 years. We must remember that these men were repeatedly told by officials that there was no evidence to explain the radiation exposure, suffering and pain that they and their families had experienced, when all along, blood and urine test results and key documents were being withheld not only from the veterans, but even from the courts and serving Ministers. This inquiry finally promises to uncover the full unredacted truth about the scandal, and it must do so with rigour, and without reservation or caveat. Ultimately, the Government must deliver the long-awaited justice that these men and their families deserve. Today is the veterans’ day. They did this, and if you will indulge me for a few moments, Mr Speaker, I am sure that the Prime Minister will join me in thanking the whole campaign team: Laura Morris, her grandad John Morris, Steve Purse, Alan Owen and the LABRATS team. The support of the right hon. Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes) for the veterans has been unwavering over the years; he has been my partner in crime. There have been so many other supportive Members across the House, including my hon. Friend the Member for South Shields (Emma Lewell) and, of course, the Defence Secretary. Finally, I thank one woman whose sheer tenacity for over a decade to expose the truth has undoubtedly brought us to this point: Susie Boniface.

My hon. Friend puts it better than I ever could, and that was a fantastic contribution. She was right to name all those people, but I will turn the compliment around. I was first asked to help in late 2021, when the Mayor of the Liverpool City Region, Steve Rotheram, and I were asked to apply our Hillsborough experience. I remember going to a meeting in January 2022 in a windswept Manchester very early in the new year, and my hon. Friend was there. The care that she had for the veterans and the confidence they had in her were clear, and she made a massive difference. I thank her from this Dispatch Box. She has played a huge role in bringing about this day, and she should be very proud.

It is a particular delight to follow the hon. Member for Salford (Rebecca Long Bailey). This is probably breaching a parliamentary convention, but Becky and I became friends because of this issue. We met through our shared determination to get justice and to right this wrong. All that the Prime Minister has said today is immensely welcome. It follows the commitment made by Lord Cameron, and the ex gratia payment that he made to veterans; and, as has been said, Boris Johnson gave them a long-denied service medal, which they now wear with pride. This inquiry is a landmark day for the campaign, and I thank the Prime Minister warmly for it, and for his kind words about me and other hon. Members, but the real thanks goes to the veterans, who have been mentioned by name, for they have done extraordinary things. One of them is no longer with us: the man who first inspired me, my constituent Douglas Hern. He, his wife Sandie and I became friends when he persuaded me, as a good—I hope—constituency MP, to take up this issue and make it a national campaign. I think we could all recount similar stories. I simply ask the Prime Minister this, and in a sense, it echoes what has been said. The critical things are the timetable, and the character of the action taken. This has to be definitive. It cannot be the beginning of a new process, and it has to bring this matter to a conclusion. That will require, if necessary, further steps by the Prime Minister to ensure that information is provided by all concerned in an appropriate fashion, and then acted on quickly and decisively. I hope the Prime Minister can affirm that commitment, and bring this sorry matter to a happy conclusion.

The right hon. Member made a little breach of convention, as I did earlier by calling him my right hon. Friend. Indeed, I will call him that again, because we have worked together on many things, including this issue, and he deserves huge credit. He was with us in Downing Street yesterday when we heard one of the family members say that his parents submitted a petition to Downing Street on this in the early ’90s. A lot of people are not here to see this day; I think we all need to pause and remember that today, because this will be very poignant for many people watching these proceedings around the country. I answer the question by saying this: I hesitate to overplay my hand, but I am giving a warning to the system. If I hear of any obfuscation, resistance or wilful failure to co-operate, I will not take kindly to that, and I will come down on it extremely heavily. It cannot be justified, when people are struggling with health issues and waiting for the truth. All the material that needs to be released must be released. The panel must be able to do its job without any let or hindrance, and we will ensure that that happens.

I thank the Prime Minister. My constituent and dear friend Jack Taylor is a nuclear veteran who I have fought alongside for recognition, truth and justice, together with LABRATS, Susie Boniface, my hon. Friend the Member for Salford (Rebecca Long Bailey), my right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes), and so many others. They never thought this day would come. I sat with Jack and read the countless letters that he sent to Parliament, and the disappointing responses he received. There is nothing worse than knowing the truth, but hearing the state, which he and others so proudly served, deny that truth time and again. So many veterans have passed away during the fight for truth and justice; so many have suffered deep anguish when door after door has been closed to them. Today that ends. Today belongs to all those veterans and families who have campaigned so relentlessly. Jack’s letters span the tenure of 10 Prime Ministers, but he has just one question for this Prime Minister today: please can you ensure that every single nuclear veteran and their families are part of this inquiry? Jack also wanted to say, “Thank you, Prime Minister, for fulfilling your duty towards those who served.”

Jack is very kind, and that shows what kind of a person he is, but we should all be thanking him for never giving up the campaign. He makes such an important point about our obligation to involve everyone in the community, and to involve and consult those who are perhaps not as active as others. I will ask the First Secretary of State to take that on board as part of the “families first” principle that I set out in my statement.

The Prime Minister has done a good deed today, and we all thank him for it. In recognising the contribution of many people to this campaign, I am delighted that he singled out the splendid investigative journalist Susie Boniface and my right hon. Friend the Member for South Holland and The Deepings (Sir John Hayes). I would like to add one further name—that of our former colleague, the former Member for Basildon and Billericay, John Baron, who campaigned relentlessly for this excellent cause for at least 15 years, up until he left Parliament in 2024. Operation Relentless is the name of our continuous at-sea deterrent; it could equally be applied to the people, including the Prime Minister, who have promoted this admirable campaign. My question to him relates to the fact that so many veterans were told that their medical records were no longer available, could not be found or had been permanently lost. Will he undertake to warn anyone who is tempted to withhold or even destroy medical records that still exist that such misconduct will be met by condign punishment?

I am glad that the right hon. Gentleman mentioned John Baron, whom I knew well and worked very closely with in this House. I am conscious that other former Members and other people have helped this cause over the years; I cannot name them all today, but I know that this has been a joint effort by many people across the House. I absolutely agree with the right hon. Gentleman’s specific point. I mentioned the Hillsborough law and the criminal sanctions in it. That will take a while to commence, but it will commence while this panel is doing its work. I ask every civil servant involved in this work and responding to the panel’s request to be mindful of it at all times. That is not to threaten anybody; it is simply to say: do the humane, right and decent thing. Those should be the values with which all Government Departments work, all the time.

I commend the Prime Minister on following through on this, and being true to his word, as he has been consistently on this issue. It is easy to be a supporter of a campaign like this, but I really do commend him on following through in the way that he has done today, when he holds the highest office in the land. We have had contaminated blood, the Horizon Post Office scandal, LGBT service people, Grenfell—I could go on. Those are all situations in which the state became the enemy of the people it is there to serve. Inquiries and independent panels make recommendations and act on behalf of victims, but we need a process for carrying forward those recommendations, and for holding the Government to account for how they respond. It is time that we had an independent body, or a part of Parliament, that holds the Government to account and does that work. At the moment, no one has responsibility for seeing how the Government respond to reports and inquiries. We should sort that out.

I thank my hon. Friend for his very kind words, and I agree with him strongly. That was part of my reason for leaving this House 10 years ago; I could not understand the way that Parliament, rather than being a check on the Executive, is often just a rubber stamp on long-held departmental positions. That says something about the need to change our democracy. On the specific question, the First Secretary of State is looking at a national oversight mechanism, which is precisely the kind of body that my hon. Friend suggests, and we will involve him in that discussion. Let me come back to the point that the pattern is too entrenched here; we have had too many injustices going on for too long, and so many people have been left in the wilderness and traumatised by that. We cannot keep seeing that and not act to fundamentally change the balance of the relationship between citizen and state.

Since being elected in 2024, I have been working closely with Alan Owen, John Morris and Steve Purse from LABRATS, as well as Susie Boniface and Members from across the House, to support our nuclear test veterans. Justice for our veterans is important, and I pay full tribute to all those who have campaigned on their behalf. I very much welcome the independent panel, because it is long overdue. The average age of a nuclear test veteran is 88, and around two of them pass away every single week. However, the panel will be effective only if it has real power; the truth must not be hidden behind national security. Will the Prime Minister commit to providing the panel with access to all national security data, and give a commitment that nothing will be withheld, whether it is from Porton Down, the Atomic Weapons Establishment or Five Eyes?

I thank the hon. Lady for her work on this matter. Let me say again that Bishop James Jones is exactly the right person to carry out this work, because he is known in the Whitehall world and can be trusted to see all material. We accept that some material will not be able to be put into the public domain, given the nature of the issue that we are discussing, but I do not want to see information withheld. Where necessary, I will intervene, with the clearance that I have, to look at it myself and see whether it is justifiable for that information to be withheld. Sometimes in government, the phrase “national security” is thrown around and used perhaps at times when it should not be used, and we must not have a situation like that here. I will never compromise national security—nothing that I would ever do would do that—but at the same time, it cannot be used as an excuse to hide the truth.

Order. To help the Chamber along, let me say that I want to get everybody in, but you are going to have to work with me. The intention is to finish this statement at around 2 o’clock, but I am sure that we can achieve that between us all. Let us start with a good example. I call Becky Gittins.

I welcome the announcement from the Prime Minister, which comes after years of campaigning from my constituent Steve Purse. Steve’s father was a nuclear test victim, and Steve was born with disabilities and health conditions that he believes are a direct result of his father being exposed to radiation while serving in the RAF. It has been an absolute privilege and really heart-warming to hear Steve’s name spoken so many times in this Chamber today, and to have seen him sat with the Prime Minister, talking about this experience. As well as paying tribute to the tireless work of Steve, his family and the formidable nuclear test veteran community, will the Prime Minister confirm that this work will begin straightaway? My constituent and many others have already had to wait too long for the truth.

My hon. Friend has a constituent to be proud of. I have found it wonderful to work with Steve; he is an incredible person, and his family are behind him. They have done so much to make today happen, and I am sure that he can very much say to his dad that he did everything that he could. For certain, we will ensure the quickest possible timeframe; I have mentioned an interim report by 3 October. I hope that my hon. Friend will understand that that is as challenging as a process like this gets, but Bishop James has taken on that challenge, to his great credit, and we will give him every possible support to meet it.

I commend the Prime Minister on taking this decision and making it very clear to Whitehall that the usual obfuscations and ways of hiding information cannot and shall not operate. He is right about Bishop Jones, who is exactly the right person to run this work. However, in order to ensure that this work goes through at the pace that the Prime Minister wishes, I wonder why he does not put a Minister of State right alongside Bishop Jones. They could hunt ahead of him for any delays heading towards them, would know how to work the system, and could report straight back to the Prime Minister. Finally, as an ex-serviceman who served in Northern Ireland, may I support my right hon. Friend the Leader of the Opposition, and ask the Prime Minister to have a look at the problems confronting veterans who face not just prosecution, but constant delays?

I have asked the First Secretary of State to oversee this from her position at the very top of Government, so she will do exactly the job that the right hon. Gentleman asks for. We will do that together. On the wider issue, I also heard what the Leader of the Opposition said. We are working hard to balance the issues in relation to Northern Ireland, but I know there are inquiries related to Afghanistan and Iraq, and that people feel like they are under a constant cloud and find it hard to move on with their lives. As I committed to meet the right hon. Member for Goole and Pocklington (David Davis), I also make the commitment to the right hon. Member for Chingford and Woodford Green (Sir Iain Duncan Smith) that I will meet members of the special forces community.

Once again, a Prime Minister must explain and apologise for a state cover-up. If anyone in this House or the other place does not now recognise the need for a full Hillsborough law, I genuinely despair. I am absolutely delighted by the Prime Minister’s announcement of an independent panel that will be chaired by Bishop James Jones, who is the right choice. I commend the Prime Minister both for his support and for delivering what he promised. This is a fantastic achievement. From my own experience of Hillsborough and the Hillsborough independent panel, I recognise how much this will mean to those families, if it is done correctly. However, as we both know from Hillsborough, acting merely in the spirit of the Hillsborough law will not be enough; families will need its full legal duties and powers. I listened intently to the points that the Prime Minister made about speed. Although I agree, he will forgive my deep suspicion: when we are dealing with the state, speed must sometimes be tempered by the need to get this right, and to get the truth that has been sought for so long. Will the Prime Minister assure me, the families and the many others who fought for the Hillsborough law that a non-statutory inquiry will not go through until we have the Hillsborough law in statutory legislation? A non-statutory inquiry alone will not be enough.

I thank my hon. Friend and all members of the Hillsborough Law Now campaign. They have given the nuclear test veteran community incredible support, and we would not be here without the work that he and others have done. The Hillsborough campaign has helped other campaigns move forward. It is a real movement for change, and it is one that is changing the country for the better. I understand what my hon. Friend says. I am very conscious of this issue, and I am not a person who does half a job; I would never forgive myself. The reason for the interim report in October next year is to give at least some truth to people while they can see it. There will be a further period of work beyond that to ensure the full job is done. I think it is right to construct the inquiry in this way, but I encourage him and other hon. Members to watch it at every stage to ensure this is the right process.
Order. We need the questions to be shorter, and the answers too please, Prime Minister.

Last night, I saw a very moving “Newsnight” programme, on which the Defence Secretary appeared. There was one veteran who had fought to get his medical records and was told he would get them in 2069, by which time he will most probably have passed. Those medical records exist today, so will the Prime Minister commit to giving the nuclear test veterans and their families access to those records now rather than having to wait until way down the line in October 2027? That would go a long way towards helping our veterans.

I find myself agreeing with the hon. Gentleman. I have never been persuaded how national security could be a reason that somebody cannot see their personal medical records. I am sure this is an issue that Bishop James will pick up very quickly, and the hon. Gentleman is right to raise it on the Floor of the House.

I, too, saw “Newsnight” last night, and I would recommend it to all hon. Members who have not had the chance to see it. I was pleased to hear the Prime Minister pay tribute to the journalists, and to Victoria Derbyshire for her coverage of this issue. Does he agree that we must pay tribute to the entire “Newsnight” team, and the BBC in general, for this represents the very best of public service broadcasting?

This is a difficult position I am in, with a member of the “Newsnight” team looking down on me from the Press Gallery. I pay tribute to them all, because they have provided magnificent coverage. I have to say that, even before “Newsnight”, the Daily Mirror was relentless in changing people’s impression of this whole thing, and people have mentioned Susie Boniface. My hon. Friend is right that this is what public service broadcasting does at its best, and it is why we should cherish it.

I thank the Prime Minister for bringing this issue to the fore, and I thank Members on both sides of the House for their dogged determination in raising it and driving us to this point. As a veteran, I recognise that the Ministry of Defence does not have an unblemished record in how it has treated its service personnel in the past. Has the Prime Minister made an initial estimation of the scale of this investigation, such as the number of nuclear test veterans it affects, all the way through to their children, grandchildren and likely great-grandchildren? Has he also made an assessment of where any potential compensation pot would be paid from? Would it come from the Ministry of Defence or the Treasury?

It is a sad thing to say, but I think there are 1,000 to 2,000 veterans still with us. I may have got that number wrong, but I think the figure is somewhere in that space. The descendants are many more, and as I said in my statement, health complications have carried on down the years. To me, it is not a question at this stage of who pays; we just have to do the right thing from here. It is important that we put those figures into the public domain as soon as we can, so that everyone can see the scale of what is involved here.

I thank the Prime Minister for his statement. I also thank the late Ken McGinley, who was a co-founder of the British Nuclear Test Veterans Association. Can the Prime Minister confirm that the inquiry will also look at the situation of those merchant mariners who were in the vicinity of the tests? They clearly recall being exposed to what seems, in retrospect, to have been radiation, yet their deployment records suggest that this was not the case. For many years, many of them have tried to get this information clarified, but they have come up against a brick wall. It would be very helpful if they could find out one way or another.
It is important that the work of the panel includes the concerns of everybody who believes that they were affected by what happened. I, too, want to pay tribute to Ken and recognise his role.

I thank the Prime Minister for the sincerity with which he has detailed the panel for the House today. This is one of the most heinous betrayals of the UK state against its own people. Servicemen and women, both then and now, are the best among us. They willingly put on that uniform and put themselves in harm’s way, never once thinking that the harm would come deliberately from the state that they were seeking to defend. Can the Prime Minister advise on the rigour and candour with which individual discussions between officials and Ministers throughout the decades of this scandal will be brought into the public domain? When does he think the panel might have a chance of reporting in that window?

I do believe that, like the Hillsborough panel, this should be a disclosure process, so that documents that have been held in secret can finally be brought into the public domain, when it is acceptable to do so. I think it is important for people to see how this was handled, and why we are in a position where, only today, we are setting a course towards the truth being known. In relation to the hon. Gentleman’s other point, there will be an interim report by 3 October. That is a challenging timetable, but I think it is an important one to set.

I am really proud to be on the Prime Minister’s Back Benches today for this announcement. I hope he will allow me to raise another historic injustice. My constituent Ghanendra Limbu is a Gurkha veteran who served during the Falklands conflict. Despite losing an eye and sustaining life-changing injuries, he received no pension and no compensation from the MOD. More than 40 years on, he lives in poverty in my community. He gets £50 a month from the Government of Nepal as a pension, yet he wears his medals with immense pride. This issue is urgent, because the Gurkha veterans have been in negotiations with the MOD for five years, and they are about to go back on hunger strike in Whitehall if we do not make progress with the talks that will take place in December. We still want to recruit Gurkhas to serve in our Army, yet we are not doing the right thing. If we cannot recruit the soldiers we need, that is a huge risk to our national security, so will the Prime Minister meet me to discuss how we can finally right that historic wrong, close the door on it and secure the future of Gurkhas in our armed forces?

My hon. Friend has done her constituent an incredible service, which is exactly what a good MP should do. It is often the case that these cases come before us on Remembrance Sunday, and we need to act when we see them. The Defence Secretary has just said to me that he is willing to meet my hon. Friend to discuss all the issues she has raised, because he recognises their importance.

Like others in the House today, I welcome the Prime Minister’s statement. I know that it will be particularly welcomed by my constituent, as three generations of her family have suffered as a result of her father being a nuclear test veteran. One difficulty they have in establishing the root cause of the medical implications referred to, is the fact that not only are her father’s records missing, but so are her own medical records for the first 20 years of her life. Can the Prime Minister ensure that not only veterans, but their families, get access to their missing records through this inquiry?

These are precisely the questions that I would like the panel to answer. How can that be justified under any provision of the Ministry of Defence? I cannot think of one. How can someone be denied access to their medical records—what possible reason could there be? The hon. Lady is right to put that question on the record, and it needs an answer.

I congratulate the Prime Minister and thank him for this independent review for nuclear test veterans, and I applaud those veterans’ bravery and tenacity. I need to raise other groups affected by their military service. Simon Kirkham, known as Pup to his naval colleagues, was a Fleet Air Arm pilot. He flew Sea Kings for search and rescue in the early 2000s, but three years ago at 54, he died of multiple myeloma. He was not alone—a startlingly large number of his colleagues who were air or ground crew on Sea Kings have died of blood cancer. The MOD has paid compensation to some, but not to others; it says that the link between exhaust emissions and blood cancer is not proven. Thanks to this Government, we now have the military cancer epidemiology study with independent advocate Gareth Collett, who has also done a huge amount of work on bomb disposal unit members and bladder cancer. However, that study could take two years. Over that time, other personnel and veterans will not be aware of those potential links, and their symptoms will go undiagnosed. Will the Prime Minister please meet me and veterans to discuss what we can do to warn them and make them aware?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising that case, and I am sure the Defence Secretary will ensure she gets a full answer. I know that there are other campaigns, including the Chinook campaign, which is now part of the Hillsborough law. However inconvenient it is, where wrong has happened, it is always right to face up to all of it.

I thank the Prime Minister for his statement, and commend him for establishing this panel. As he rightly said, far too many nuclear test veterans are no longer with us, which is why I am so pleased to hear that that panel will be undertaking a listening exercise with the families of the deceased as well. Will the Prime Minister give particular consideration to how we ensure that that listening process is as accessible as possible, so that all those who wish to contribute can do so, irrespective of where in the UK they live?

The hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. Within the time strictures, it may be difficult, but we are going to have to get the balance right. I want this process to be as inclusive as possible, and I am sure Bishop James wants the same thing.

I join others in thanking the Prime Minister, particularly for his clarification that the duty of candour applies and for the appointment of Bishop James Jones. He was absolutely right about “the patronising disposition of unaccountable power”, and I thank him for his support for the Grenfell families, too. It is so important that people have confidence that these panels, inquests, investigations and inquiries will lead to change. As such, I join my hon. Friend the Member for Eltham and Chislehurst (Clive Efford) in encouraging the set-up of a national oversight mechanism, so that we have something long-lasting that gives the campaigners reassurance that they will not have to be the ones who track all these things for years to come.

I absolutely agree with my hon. Friend. The Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee is going to be looking at that very issue—the national oversight mechanism—and I encourage all Members of the House, including my hon. Friend, to be involved in that work.

My constituent was a member of 543 Squadron, who flew through the nuclear test clouds of foreign states to take samples. They have long been left out of the conversation about nuclear test veterans. My constituent is also worried about the ground crews, particularly those who were required to clean the returning aircraft. Can the Prime Minister give us an assurance that these people, who were clearly involved, will be part of the scope and will be made to feel welcome, part of this conversation, and part of the panel’s terms of reference?
That is a really good question. There is no intention to limit the scope to leave people outside the inquiry, and we will take that point into consideration when finalising the terms of reference.

I thank the Prime Minister for his commitment to truth and justice for our nuclear test veterans. My constituent Edward Luther was stationed on Christmas Island in 1957. Aged just 20, he was told on the way over that he would not make it to 50. At 89 years old, he is still waiting for answers to medical issues that both he and his family have suffered. He told me that he feels abandoned and dismissed. Today, I hope that he feels heard. Edward received his medal through the post. Can the Prime Minister ensure that surviving veterans such as Edward are invited to next year’s national memorial day, so that they can be properly seen and honoured?

Can I say a heartfelt sorry to Edward, who has been left in a completely unacceptable position by the country he served so well? I can give my hon. Friend that assurance, because the national memorial service I mentioned in my statement is entirely intended for that purpose—that we get a moment to put things right as best we can, and give people the recognition that they rightly deserve.

I really welcome the Prime Minister’s statement today, and I know the families and the LABRATS will as well. I have to mention another case on behalf of my constituents—families in my constituency of Lagan Valley. Chinook Zulu Delta 576 crashed on 2 June 1994. There were no survivors. It took 31 years for those families to have a meeting with Defence Ministers. That meeting took place last year, but nothing came from it. Today, I am again asking the Prime Minister to meet the Chinook families and ensure that they—as well as the LABRATS and everyone else failed by the state—get justice.
I make a commitment today to the hon. Member that I will meet the families with her.

I welcome today’s statement, and congratulate the campaigners on campaigning for so long when they suffer from ill health themselves—that is so hard. I would like to raise the issue of the Poly Implant Prothèse breast implant scandal, which the Prime Minister has mentioned in this place before. Those campaigners are also looking for answers, and next week, they will be coming to Parliament to lobby. Will the Prime Minister meet Jan and Louise, two of the 47,000 women affected by toxic implants? So many of them suffer ill health, but doctors said to them, “It’s all in your heads.” They are looking for truth and justice, so will the Prime Minister talk to them about the possibility of setting up a panel for them, similar to this one?

I thank my hon. Friend for raising their case—it is one I have also supported in the past. I may struggle, but I will see if another Minister is available to meet them. I think we need to have a different day to discuss a range of health campaigns that are still unresolved, and that is one of them.

I welcome the Prime Minister’s response to the question from my hon. Friend the Member for North Norfolk (Steff Aquarone) about the scope of the inquiry. My constituent, Colin, served with RAF Wyton squadrons that flew through French and Chinese nuclear test clouds. The ground crews who decontaminated those aircraft without protective clothing are still denied the nuclear test medal and access to their records. Many have since died of cancer. Will the Prime Minister commit to righting those wrongs?
I will ask the Defence Secretary to look into that issue. I cannot make the full commitment today, but we can at least look into that question.

The memorial stone to British nuclear test veterans in Portsmouth cathedral bears a simple, but powerful inscription: “All we seek is justice.” I sincerely thank the Prime Minister for launching today’s long-awaited inquiry into the truth. First, will he join me in recognising the extraordinary efforts of veterans and campaigners who brought us to this point? Will he honour those who sadly did not live to see this day? Secondly, given Portsmouth’s proud naval heritage, will he ensure that, through medical record retrieval, we establish how many local veterans in my city took part in the tests and the lasting impact on them and their families, so that we can finally deliver the justice that they all seek?

I think my hon. Friend’s city and her constituency has probably been impacted more than any other in the country as a result of this issue, hence the stone in the cathedral. We will work with her to ensure that as much information as she needs to help local people is provided, so that we live up to what is written on that stone.

I thank the Prime Minister for his response to my hon. Friend the Member for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood). The Prime Minister will recall that he made that commitment in our very first exchange in this Chamber after his return. When my hon. Friends the Members for Lagan Valley and for Wells and Mendip Hills (Tessa Munt) and I wrote to the Prime Minister’s Office, it was passed over to the Ministry of Defence, but the families have no trust in the Ministry of Defence. Can the Prime Minister repeat that he will personally meet the families, rather than passing it to a Minister, however wonderful they may be?

The hon. Lady will understand that sometimes letters go around the system like that, but I am making a personal commitment to the hon. Lady and the hon. Member for Lagan Valley (Sorcha Eastwood) at this Dispatch Box that I will meet the families with you both, and any other Members who want to be part of that meeting. We will do that this side of the break.
Order. I always appreciate a meeting with the Prime Minister, but by “you” he means the hon. Members opposite, not me. I thank him for the offer.

First of all, after decades of no progress, today we have small steps in the right direction. I personally thank the Prime Minister and our Government for the initiative that they have taken today. Across the United Kingdom, it does not go unnoticed among all of us who look for guidance and progress. Our nuclear test veterans across the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland served Queen and country in the 1950s and 1960s. They have waited for too long for justice, with too many of them sadly passing away before seeing accountability. Alongside the welcome announcement of Bishop James Jones’s panel, what immediate steps are the Government taking to ensure timely recognition and fair compensation for the 2,000 remaining veterans and their bereaved families before the 75th anniversary?

The hon. Gentleman asks an important question. To answer it, the best thing I can say is that we need to have some tracks moving concurrently through this process. I will have to wait for the interim report before we can make those decisions, but I do not think we should delay all the work. With the First Secretary of State, I will look at every possible way to move things forward together. I thank the hon. Gentleman for his comments, as indeed I thank all Members for their comments in relation to this statement. I want the whole of Whitehall to see the complete unanimity across both sides of this House and from all parties. It sends the strongest of messages that we need to get on. We have got to do this. We have to treat people properly at all times, not only in this instance, but in every instance in relation to how the state works with people who have suffered injustice, bereavement or any other form of injury. That is unfinished business in this House, and we need to be focused on fixing it.

title: International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women

items.txt: These last few weeks have seen our national conversation dominated by accounts of, and finally some accountability for, some of the most grotesque and horrific abuses of male power, not merely to limit the lives of women but, through coercion, control and violence, to seek to scar them and to wreck them. I pay tribute to those survivors who came forward, often in great fear and despite immense pressure. They spoke to the police and spoke in public, and their bravery and moral purpose is a beacon to us all. The stories of what was done to women and what men have got away with have dominated our media and our discussions in a way that is rare, important and incredibly powerful. As we mark the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, I am proud that, working with ministerial colleagues right across Government, we are bringing action to go further and faster to bring change in our country. I am sure I speak for women everywhere when I say that we have had enough of hoping that reflections on stories like those we have heard again in recent weeks will alone prompt the wider cultural and social change we so desperately need to protect women. There has been much welcome change, but we know that there has not been enough, and we have to meet the moment. We must step up the pace of change to build the country that we all deserve, and that change must come in every corner of our country and in every part of our society. It must also come from this House, through the law and through the courts and the police. Nearly a year ago, we launched our landmark cross-Government strategy to tackle violence against women and girls and to provide freedom from violence and abuse. I pay tribute to amazing colleagues across these Benches who crafted it, steered it and fought for its progress. Today, they push us to go further, as we must and as we will. For the first time, our Government are focused squarely on prevention, on what more we must do to change our culture, to improve healthy relationships education and to crack down on toxic content online that harms women. Our misogyny prevention fund will back those interventions, too, with £15 million of new funding to step in before harmful attitudes turn to hateful action. We will work day and night to disrupt the attitudes, dissuade the behaviours and end the consequences that make women’s lives smaller. That is informed by the voices of experts and those who have lived experience through our cross-Government national taskforce for tackling misogyny. Misogyny and the further evils that flow from it are a whole society problem that we must address in every space where they arise. Therefore, I am setting out three new areas of action today, working together with colleagues from across Government. First, we are taking action to provide the police and the courts with stronger tools to protect victims from domestic abuse, enabling them to intervene earlier and to crack down on perpetrators. We are rolling out domestic abuse protection notices and domestic abuse protection orders across England and Wales. These powers have already protected more than 3,000 victims in two years across a wide range of pilot areas. Courts will be able to impose any requirement they think is necessary to protect victims of abuse. That action can be robust, to meet the fear that we see and hear far too often with real safeguards, including forcing abusers out of homes they share with their victims, or preventing perpetrators from using social media to continue campaigns of abuse, intimidation and control. Courts will also be able to force abusers to take action to address their behaviour, and the orders cover all forms of domestic abuse, including controlling or coercive behaviour, stalking and economic abuse. These changes are urgent. An estimated 4.7 million people experienced domestic abuse in the past year, and it is the mission of this Labour Government to halve violence against women and girls in a

It is a pleasure to respond to the Minister to mark White Ribbon Day. I thank her for advance sight of her statement. I pay tribute today to all the domestic abuse survivors who have come forward, who have spoken out and who have made their voices known through Members of Parliament. May I praise the cross-party work over the years of the many Members, both Back Benchers and Front Benchers, who have put this issue at the forefront of a policy that they wanted to take through the House? I thank everyone here for their excellent work in raising and highlighting it—and I thank Mr Speaker and you, Madam Deputy Speaker, for recognising White Ribbon Day ahead of today. I am grateful for that leadership and for the invitation to us all to come to Speaker’s House to discuss how we can tackle violence against women and girls on a cross-party basis. Mr Speaker led from the front on behalf of the House. Leadership matters, but it feels as though it is absent from this Government. The announcement today shows a Government who are seeking to hide from their own failures, announcing domestic abuse prevention orders while simultaneously releasing domestic abusers early from prison. Releasing domestic abusers and stalkers early while wanting to put more in prison seems slightly counterproductive. The Minister is promoting a discussion on a staggered age of consent, while this morning she was unable to say herself that sex with a 14 or 15-year-old was rape. The statement that we have just heard was from a parallel universe. The right hon. Lady has commented on the failures of others to stop crime, believing that it is a basis for excusing the inaction of her Government. White Ribbon Day is about leadership and action to stop violence against women and girls. From the Prime Minister to the Minister for Women and Equalities to the Minister for Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls, we have seen a failure to show leadership and take action. When the Prime Minister allows the grotesque sight of a so-called influencer parroting disgusting, anti-women lyrics from the door of Downing Street, something has gone badly wrong. When the Minister for Safeguarding and Violence Against Women and Girls goes on television and her first thought is to defend the Prime Minister from embarrassment rather than to protect women and girls, something has gone badly wrong. When the Minister for Women and Equalities goes on television and cannot say unambiguously that sex by an adult with a 14 or 15-year-old girl is rape, something has gone badly wrong. When the Government take a year and then fail to implement the recommendations of the Casey review into grooming gangs and ignore the powerful campaign of Maggie Oliver, something has gone badly wrong. When the Minister for Women and Equalities refuses to work cross-party with me and listen to women in Piddington, Linton-on-Ouse and Barnham about their concerns about the safety of women and girls, something has gone badly wrong. When the Government fight the Information Commission to avoid publishing data on crimes by illegal migrant men against women and girls, something has gone badly wrong. When the Government release domestic abusers, stalkers and men committing violent assaults early, something has gone badly wrong. Does the Minister condemn the decision to allow an influencer to degrade women and girls on the steps of Downing Street? Will the Minister confirm when the Government will implement the grooming gang recommendations? Will the Minister confirm to this House that she will seek to stop the fight against the Information Commissioner’s Office and release the migrant crime data? Will the Minister confirm that she will stop the early release of criminals who have committed violence against women and girls? Finally, will the Minister show courage and meet the women who are concerned about the thousands of illegal migrant men this Government are placing in their communities? Will she meet the women of

I hardly know where to begin with what was genuinely quite a disappointing contribution from the hon. Lady. I will respond to the points that she raises, and I welcome robust debate in this place, but I also think that she might have taken a moment to reflect on some of the important measures that the Government are taking. She talked about the importance of cross-party working and then embarked on one of the most nakedly partisan speeches that I think I have heard in this place. It failed to grasp the challenge that we are seeing, and it did a disservice to this important debate that is taking place on White Ribbon Day. My right hon. Friend the Lord Chancellor had little option other than to bring forward the early release scheme, given the shocking failure that the hon. Lady’s party left behind. We take our responsibilities to protect victims incredibly seriously, but let me be absolutely clear with this House: the former Prime Minister and Conservative Members knew exactly what was going on and were not prepared to confront the challenges that they faced. They called a general election. They ran away from the difficult decisions, and they left it to this Labour Government to tackle the enormous scandal around prison capacity, which would have seen new men arrested for fresh crimes today with nowhere to go had we not acted as my right hon. Friend has done. An ounce of humility in understanding what took us to this place would really advance the debate in this House. I take extremely seriously the concerns of all women when it comes to violence. No matter someone’s background, no matter how rich, popular or famous they are, no matter who they are and where they are, if they commit crimes against women they should face the full force of the law. I take seriously the hon. Lady’s contribution about Piddington, but I think it would be both wrong and dangerous to suggest that violence against women is only committed by some men from some kinds of background. We have a responsibility to root it out, wherever it happens and whoever carries it out. The reality is that the vast majority of abuse against women in this country is committed by those who know them well, who are meant to love them and who usually live in the same home. As soon as the Conservative party gets to grips with that reality and stops weaponising violence against women and girls, we will be in a much stronger position to change things. Women will—
We passed the Domestic Abuse Act, which had cross-party consensus!

As long as the Conservatives go on making this a question of ethnic background rather than appalling male violence, they will do women a disservice. I am absolutely clear that we will tackle violence against women and girls, and we will make our country safer for every young woman growing up today. That is why we have our commitment to halve violence against women and girls, while we are going further on tackling misogyny. I will welcome efforts from any Member of this House who is genuinely serious about doing that rather than point scoring.

I would like to start by saying a massive thank you to Zelda Perkins, a woman who for nine years campaigned and begged the previous Government to get rid of non- disclosure agreements that kept rape victims like the women she worked with, who were raped by Harvey Weinstein, from being able to speak out. I pay credit to her today. When will we see the changes to non-disclosure agreements move beyond the employment sphere? For example, the 18-year-old girl listed by ITV in the Walliams case, who was not an employee, should be covered. Can the Minister also assure me and the House that when the Government’s 10-year plan comes forward in the coming weeks, violence against women and girls will be a large part of it?

I can give my hon. Friend that assurance. I commend her, alongside Zelda, for the amazing campaigning work that she has done to bring this issue to the fore and to demonstrate that this Government are serious about tackling violence against women and girls. She is right to say that today we have gone further on NDAs, but there remain gaps and loopholes. We are keen to look as quickly as we can at how much further we can go to make sure that everyone, including freelancers and fans alike, are protected from abuse and from harm. We really have seen some shocking examples. In certain industries, we have seen young women—often those who are very young—put at significant risk of harm when the culture should have done better by them.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I am grateful to the Minister for Women and Equalities for bringing this important statement to the House today. I was the Minister who proudly took through the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, which outlawed non-fatal strangulation and outlawed the rough sex defence. As the Minister for Women, I also looked very closely at the issue of non-disclosure agreements. We in this House are all in agreement that no one who is subject to sexual harassment should be constrained by NDAs, but the right hon. Lady has—I think inadvertently—misdescribed the work that I did as the Minister for Women from 2018, when the officials who are advising the current Minister advised me that the law was clear that NDAs could not be used in that way. How can the Minister help to ensure that the message—

Order. The right hon. Member is very well aware of what is and is not a point of order. This debate will continue as it is. It is not for the Chair to define exactly what Members are saying or what those on the Government Front Bench are saying. I am going to let this debate continue—we cannot have another debate on top of this one. There are lots of ways in which Back-Bench MPs can pursue this issue if they wish to do so.

I thank the Minister for advance sight of her statement, and for marking White Ribbon Day in the House. As we all know, online misogyny is rife, and it is lucrative. Court backlogs are spiralling, and just 3% of rapes recorded last year led to a charge, so rapists know that they are likely to get away with it. Our laws on stalking, domestic abuse and harassment have failed to keep pace with technology. Victim and campaigner Hannah Parkin says that despite planting a tracker on her car, her ex-partner could not be prosecuted because police could only prove that it happened once and stalking law requires multiple instances. Why is once not enough, and if it is, will the Minister change the law without delay? I welcome the measures announced today, including the one on NDAs for victims of crime and workplace harassment, although that is long overdue and I note that it will not apply to NDAs signed before January next year. Victims are still vulnerable to lawfare that is designed to threaten and silence them, so tackling NDAs alone is sadly not enough. It certainly is not enough to end the shocking and despicable violence that women and girls face every day in this country. I look forward to shortly meeting the Safeguarding Minister about the impunity of rich and powerful men who try to buy victims’ silence. In the meantime, will the Minister commit to working with colleagues on comprehensive anti-SLAPP—strategic lawsuit against public participation—legislation so that lawfare cannot be used to silence victims? Almost a year on from the publication of the Government’s VAWG strategy, will she return to the House to set out what progress has been made?

I am grateful to the Lib Dem spokesperson for her contribution and for making some important points. When it comes to the prosecution and conviction rates for rape charges, I am pleased to see that things are moving in the right direction, but there is much more to do, given that we saw a near collapse in the prosecution rate and significant pressures on the courts. We are making significant progress on specialist courts and making sure that all victims get the support they need, given the sensitivity of their experiences. I note the hon. Lady’s point about stalking. She asks whether areas are under consideration and says that she will shortly meet the Safeguarding Minister. I will work with the hon. Lady and Members from across the House to make sure that we have the right legislation in place to protect women. The hon. Lady’s point about the fast-changing nature of technology is an important one. It is imperative that the Government seek to keep pace with that change as we work to keep women safe, and I look forward to discussing that further with her.

On the UN International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women and Girls, may I congratulate you, Madam Deputy Speaker, as well as Mr Speaker and the Clerk of the House, on achieving White Ribbon accreditation for the House of Commons Administration? Although that is great for the House, it does not cover MPs or our staff because of the ancient and really odd rules that we have here. Will the Minister join me in calling on each and every MP to make the White Ribbon pledge that they will never use, excuse or remain silent about men’s violence against women and girls? May I also raise another issue? Together with my hon. Friends the Members for Buckingham and Bletchley (Callum Anderson) and for Milton Keynes North (Chris Curtis), I have been working very closely with the Croucher family following Leah Croucher’s murder. She was murdered by a repeat sex offender who had not served a jail sentence. Had he served a jail sentence for his last sexual offence, he would not have been free to murder Leah. Leah’s case was devastating to all of us in Milton Keynes, as for three years we looked for her in every nook and cranny. Every child knew her name, and every lamp post had her picture on it. I pay tribute to her family for the work they are now doing to pass Leah’s law, which would put sexual offences in line with burglary and repeat drug offences by ensuring that there is a mandatory prison sentence following someone’s third offence. Will the Minister join me and my colleagues from Milton Keynes in making sure that we secure justice for Leah?

On White Ribbon Day, I think it is important that all of us back that campaign as much as we can. I am also grateful to Mr Speaker and to you, Madam Deputy Speaker, for the support that you have both given to this important cause. I also send my condolences to Leah’s family. I pay tribute to my Parliamentary Private Secretary—my hon. Friend the Member for Buckingham and Bletchley (Callum Anderson), who is sitting behind me—and other Members for the work they have been doing to support Leah’s family, and to make the case for change. I am sure that Justice Ministers would be more than happy to meet my hon. Friend the Member for Milton Keynes Central (Emily Darlington) and other Milton Keynes Members to discuss what more can be done to make sure that no family experiences the appalling tragedy of Leah’s.

I welcome the statement’s commitment to taking action on using non-disclosure agreements to cover up sexual offences. I think those on both sides of the House support the Labour Government’s objective of halving violence against women and girls. Could the Minister clarify what baseline figure she is using when assessing progress on that manifesto commitment, and what is the latest position today?

We are approaching a year on from the publication of our violence against women and girls strategy, and we will provide an update to the House on that shortly. Given that we know reporting is often not as we would like it—there is significant under-reporting when it comes to domestic abuse and sexual violence—we follow the work of the British crime survey to understand the real rates we are seeing. That is in part because it would obviously be perverse if we encouraged reporting and areas felt disproportionately affected for having done a good job in raising awareness and encouraging victims to come forward. In parallel, we intend to set out further steps on a metric to track attitudes, because we know that violence against women seen in the experiences of women follow from attitudes that often start young and develop over time. That is why our focus on prevention is also important.

I am incredibly proud that White Ribbon UK was founded in my Calder Valley constituency, and I am proud to wear a white ribbon every day, not just on White Ribbon Day. I recently re-read the Casey review of group-based child sexual exploitation, and it struck me that many of the older teenage victims were not considered victims of child sexual exploitation, just by dint of being over 16. While grooming is not a specific offence, if teenagers are over 16, there is very little that grooming gangs can be prosecuted for. Could we undertake to look at the idea of grooming as a specific offence, but also to look at what more we can do to change the consent laws, so there is a recognition that younger girls should not be targeted and preyed on by older men?

In the cases my hon. Friend describes and in many cases over the years, we have seen a consistent failure to listen to and believe young women when they come forward and share their experiences—whether that involves what we tend to refer to as group-based sexual exploitation, or abuse that takes place in the family home, which is also significantly under-reported. Intrafamilial sexual abuse still scars too many lives, and we know there is a significant challenge in encouraging victims to come forward and seek the support they need. In part, that comes down to a failure to believe, and to listen to, those who report it. There are questions about consent in the current legislation for those in positions of trust, and that is precisely what we want to consider as part of the national conversation we are launching. We will set out more details in the new year. I encourage my hon. Friend to look out for that, and to encourage groups, organisations and young people in his area to share their views to inform this conversation in what is a complex area, but one where I believe progress is needed.

I think it is very telling that, while some in this House profess to care about reducing violence against women and girls, not one Reform or Restore Member of Parliament is in this Chamber today. I pay tribute to the hon. Member for Milton Keynes Central (Emily Darlington) for her work—working with you, Madam Deputy Speaker, and Mr Speaker—in driving this Parliament to become the first White Ribbon Parliament in the country. In her question, the hon. Member spoke about how it is important that MPs and their staff sign up to the pledge, but does the Minister agree that peers should also sign up to this pledge, including all the peers in my own party?

The hon. Gentleman makes a compelling case. We all have a responsibility to tackle violence against women and girls, wherever it occurs and whoever is responsible. We see a consistent pattern of men putting themselves into positions of trust and authority in order to abuse and exploit women. That happens in politics, sadly; it happens in the creative industries; it happens in business; and it happens in the Church. It happens right across society. The sooner and the more quickly we confront that reality and talk openly about it, the better the place we will be in to support women to come forward, share their experiences and not feel that there should be any stigma or shame in seeking support.

Bedfordshire police has made important progress in protecting women and girls, including through increased use of domestic violence protection orders and Clare’s law disclosures. However, the latest PEEL—police effectiveness, efficiency and legitimacy—assessment highlights concerns about victim support. Given that Bedfordshire is one of the lowest funded forces, despite demand increasing by about 50%, will the Minister make the case with Home Office Ministers for sustainable funding to ensure that the force can deliver the improvements set out in the report and help to achieve our ambition to halve violence against women and girls?

I will of course make sure that my hon. Friend’s views on what is needed for his constituents in Bedford and across his area are known and understood by Home Office colleagues. I am pleased to hear that the police are making progress with domestic abuse protection orders, and doing everything they can to encourage women to come forward to report crimes and get the support they need.

On behalf of the Women and Equalities Committee, I welcome the statement, which reflects much of the work we have done on NDAs. As far back as 2024, we produced a report on misogyny in the music industry, which unfortunately was ignored by the Government at that time. However, the new Labour Government took on board the recommendations of our second report on misogyny in the music industry in 2025, and much of that was in the Employment Rights Act 2025, which we welcome. Today goes much further, but we are still concerned about the women who are outwith standard employment arrangements, like freelancers and fans in certain situations, so can the Minister tell us when we might see the NDA ban extended to those areas?

I am grateful to the Select Committee, the hon. Lady, and the Chair of the Committee, my hon. Friend the Member for Reading West and Mid Berkshire (Olivia Bailey), for the important work they are doing in this area. I am also grateful to the previous Chair, my hon. Friend the Member for Luton North (Sarah Owen), who also campaigned tirelessly for change. I look forward to being in front of the Committee, before too long I hope, when we can discuss this in more detail. I can give the House the assurance that we are looking very carefully at how we can address gaps and loopholes, particularly when it comes to certain industries in which freelancers tend to predominate or where we see the more shocking examples of failure in industry practice. For example, allowing young women who are 16 or potentially under 16 to be with older men without supervision or oversight strikes me as a clear breach of safeguarding responsibilities. I know the Culture Secretary is working with the sector to see further action more rapidly ahead of any wider change in the legislation that we may need to make.

Today is about taking decisive action to end violence against women and girls. Does my right hon. Friend agree we cannot tackle violence against women and girls comprehensively while the abuse of older women remains largely hidden from view? As I set out in my Westminster Hall debate yesterday, too many older victims are not identified or are failed by the current system and are trapped in relationships for decades. Will she therefore commit to strengthening data collection, identification and services for older women, so that we can uncover the true scale of domestic abuse in later life?

My hon. Friend makes an important point. Those who have survived domestic abuse or are still experiencing it can come from any background and walk of life, including older women. I know from my own personal experience of running a women’s refuge that older women often feel limited in coming forward. They have often been in a relationship for a very long time, and wonder whether there is any support available and whether they could really make such a change. My message to anyone living today with domestic abuse is that there is support available, and the police will take it seriously. I will of course look carefully at my hon. Friend’s suggestions about ensuring that we have a full picture of what is going on across the country.

My right hon. Friend the Member for North East Cambridgeshire (Steve Barclay) made a really important point earlier when he asked the Minister to provide the baseline metric and the progress to date on the Government’s much-vaunted pledge to halve violence against women and girls. In her answer, she provided not one single number, so I ask again: will she please provide us with the baseline metric she is measuring from and what the number is to date so that we can look at what progress there has been?

I can only repeat what I said to the right hon. Gentleman, which is that we will be providing a full update a year on, in response to our violence against women and girls strategy. We intend to use British crime survey data to understand the full picture on domestic abuse and sexual violence, given the under-reporting that we know is often represented in the police crime data. Alongside that, we intend to publish a metric to better understand attitudes towards women. That work is under way and is connected very closely to the tackling misogyny taskforce, which will ensure that we do not just deal with the consequences of male violence, but address its root causes.

My right hon. Friend has gone a long way on non-disclosure agreements today and that is certainly very welcome. She acknowledges that many have been signed under fear or some degree of duress. That is absolutely true, and it begs the question why we would continue to allow historical NDAs to stand. [ Interruption. ] If the right hon. Member for Louth and Horncastle (Victoria Atkins) would please let me finish. The important thing is that settlement agreements should continue to bind in general, but women should be able to speak about what has happened to them. Similarly, no matter what we do with NDAs, if injunctions continue to be used in defamation law to stop women from speaking out, as they currently are, banning NDAs will unfortunately be of limited effect. What is really important is that we take away the threat of costs under injunctions and look to reduce the burden of proof in injunction proceedings where there are allegations of sexual misconduct.

My hon. Friend raises important points, including on making sure that victims are not silenced and further action that the Government should consider taking. She brings real experience to this House, having long campaigned on these areas. I would be more than happy to discuss this matter further, because I think we share a commitment to making sure that the rich and powerful cannot silence victims and cannot prevent them from seeking the support they need.

I am pleased to hear the Minister acknowledge that we all need to meet the moment on tackling violence against women and girls in all areas on this White Ribbon Day. My hon. Friend the Member for Chelmsford (Marie Goldman) asked about strategic lawsuits against public participation. It is not only NDAs that are being weaponised by rich and powerful men, but SLAPPs and the threat of legal action. The amount of time, energy and money that individuals must expend to fight SLAPPs is immensely prohibitive and keeps instances of abuse against women and girls in the dark for years—if they ever come to light. Will the Government therefore commit to bringing forward universal anti-SLAPP legislation that will enable such things to be dismissed at an early stage of proceedings and fully compensate targeted defendants, so that the truth can come out and justice can be served?

We are looking very carefully at the areas the hon. Lady identifies. I would be more than happy to ensure that she has a meeting with a Minister to discuss the area she has identified for further action and what more we can do.

I have a fantastic charity in Nottinghamshire called Equation, which runs excellent programmes in schools about healthy relationships. In 2024-25, the programme reached 35,000 pupils across 70 schools through over 200 projects. It also acts as a safeguarding referral channel. Given the Government’s commitment in the violence against women and girls strategy on mandatory relationships education, would the Minister be willing to meet Equation so that we can talk about the fantastic work it is doing?

I pay tribute to Equation and to my hon. Friend for drawing attention to its brilliant work. I would be more than happy to meet and have a conversation about what more we can do. I was proud to introduce new relationships, sex and health education guidance in September that will allow all young people to better understand the issues of healthy relationships, consent and misogyny. That is especially important in a world where we know so many young people have seen and been exposed to certain attitudes and behaviours, and inappropriate material— [ Interruption. ] If the right hon. Member for Louth and Horncastle (Victoria Atkins) has something to say on this important topic I would be pleased to hear it, but she just keeps chuntering, Madam Deputy Speaking, in a way that I think demeans her role. This is an important area, and we are discussing how we keep our children safe from harm. I am pleased that young people will, from this year, have a much better understanding of those important areas, but there is scope to go further and the work of organisations such as Equation will be very important.

I was a director of Moray Women’s Aid during my time as a councillor, and it was a privilege to work closely with and support such an important organisation that provides refuge, support and advocacy for women and children whose lives have been devastated by the impacts of abuse, predominantly by men.
