Does the Minister agree that it is deeply disturbing that we have such a level of need for services such as Moray Women’s Aid, that eradicating violence against women and girls fundamentally requires men to change their behaviour, and that men challenging men on misogynistic and abusive behaviour is one of the most powerful ways to tackle the root causes of domestic abuse?

I am very glad that the hon. Gentleman makes that point, because it has long fallen to female campaigners, advocates and others to make the case for the change we need to see across society. Of course, it is very important that men stand up and make it absolutely clear that there is no place for violence against women in our society. I am pleased to hear about the work that he was involved in to ensure that women have access to timely support, including refuge support, when they need it. There is more to do, but there is a lot that is positive in the work the Government are doing around masculinity and through our men and boys strategy to make sure that we do not just talk about male violence and the negatives, but allow men the opportunity to talk, particularly about the challenges they experience. That is important, given that suicide is one of the biggest killers of men in our country.

I thank the Minister for her really welcome announcements today and for the tone she has brought to this discussion. We know, as the hon. Member for Moray West, Nairn and Strathspey (Graham Leadbitter) just pointed out, that if we are to drive out violence against women and girls, we need more men to step up and be active bystanders in driving the behavioural and cultural changes we need to see. It was fantastic recently to meet six cracking lads at Hitchin boys’ school who, after some recent programmes there, had stepped up to become leaders in their school community and to think about how they can drive out misogyny and challenge harmful stereotypes. If we are seeking to empower more young men to take on the active role that we know they want to play in their school communities, how can we use the curriculum review to give them the space to talk about these issues, step up and be the active bystanders and allies they would love to be?

My hon. Friend has done so much to raise the profile of this important work. I am really glad to hear about the work of Hitchin boys’ school. It demonstrates very powerfully that young men can be role models in their community and support one another in a positive way. We must not see boys and young men as a problem to be solved, but as part of the solution. I am pleased that from this year, young people will have a better understanding through the school curriculum of healthy relationships, consent and much more besides. We need to see more of exactly the kind of exercise that my hon. Friend describes. He consistently champions such issues, including with his important private Member’s Bill, which will ensure that we consider how those over the age of 16 can have access to the right kind of information, too.

May I begin by associating myself with the Minister’s response to the Conservative shadow Minister’s sadly partisan contribution? On White Ribbon Day, we commit ourselves to tackling misogyny and violence against women and girls, of which I am all too well aware as the father of four daughters. That is why it was so disappointing that the Fairfield review found that misogyny, along with racism and homophobia, still exists in the Metropolitan police. According to Dr Fairfield, none of those behaviours have changed sufficiently since Baroness Casey’s review three years ago. Clearly the Met is not within the Minister’s immediate responsibilities, but what conversations is she having with the Home Secretary in her role as Minister for Women and Equalities about finally ridding the Met of these behaviours?

I welcome Dr Fairfield’s review. It makes clear that progress has been made since Baroness Casey’s report, but that there is much more the Met needs to undertake, including on serious sexual offences where further improvement is needed. It is right that the Met has accepted all the recommendations. The Home Secretary will be working closely with the Metropolitan Police Commissioner to make sure that further progress is made, so that all those living in London can have confidence when they come forward.

On my way here, I stopped by the guide dog stand in Westminster Hall. I was talking to one of the women who came along with her guide dog and was shocked to hear that on the way to collect her guide dog, she was attacked by a group of men because they saw that she was vulnerable. It really opened my eyes to the challenges that we still face, so I thank the Minister for her work in this area. I pay tribute to Safer Places and other charities in Harlow that help to support victims of domestic violence. I worked for a homelessness charity, and the Minister will know from her background in working for a domestic violence charity that the pinch point for people who are victims of domestic violence comes when they choose to leave. Often, the support is not there for those victims to escape the perpetrator. Will she reiterate what the Government are going to do to protect victims of domestic violence so that they are able to escape the perpetrator?

I am pleased to hear about the work that Safer Places is doing in Harlow to ensure that women can access timely support when they are experiencing abuse. My hon. Friend is right that it is often at the point of choosing to leave that women are at gravest risk. That is why it is important that we provide routes and avenues for women to seek help, including through universal services such as health provision, whether it is at the midwife or the GP, because those are often the only places where women can be seen. Such routes and avenues mean that we do not just have to wait for women to come forward. I am really pleased that the Health Secretary is leading further work in this area to ensure that health services can identify where women are experiencing abuse, rather than leaving it to the women to find that help for themselves.

Misogyny on social media normalises violence against women and girls in our communities. This is a direct threat to the safety of women and girls, and as a mum and an auntie to young girls, I refuse to allow it to impact their futures. Does the Minister agree that all of us across the House have a role to play in challenging misogyny at source and preventing real-life consequences? And that means all of us!

I absolutely agree with the hon. Lady. This is about tackling the attitudes that we see as well as dealing with the consequences that arise and lead to male violence. She is also right that we need to continue to take action on what we see online, which all too often poisons the minds of young people and leads to harm. That is why we are taking firm action on online abuse, and why we have launched a national taskforce on tackling misogyny to address the root causes that give rise to women losing their lives to male violence.

I welcome the Minister’s statement and her personal commitment to these issues. I am proud to stand today as a White Ribbon ambassador, because it is incredibly important that men stand up against misogyny, sexism, violence and abuse against women. The Minister said that the police will have stronger powers. My constituent, Debbie, reported harassment and stalking in May. It took a month for her to first be contacted by the police, and fully five months for her statement to be taken. In light of the statement today, will the Minister reassure Debbie and other women facing this kind of abuse that in future they will be responded to faster and given more protection, more quickly?

I am very sorry to hear about Debbie’s experience, because it is clearly completely unacceptable. No woman should have to wait so long to report and then progress her case. If the hon. Gentleman is willing to share more information about Debbie’s case, I can ensure that it is looked into in more detail, so that women like Debbie get much better treatment when they come forward. It is difficult enough for women to report such crimes; we should not be making it harder with long waits.

Emotional, physical and sexual violence against women and girls is abhorrent, and must be condemned by all, regardless of the ethnicity of the perpetrators or victims. All those who are politicising the pain and trauma of the victims and survivors by focusing on perpetrators from selected ethnicities, are harming not helping the survivors, and should be ashamed. Such despicable crimes against women and girls are widely prevalent across our country and must be a top priority for Government. In my constituency, the most common crimes are violence and sexual offences. What additional funding and resources have been offered to local police forces in places like Dewsbury and Batley, and what more can we do to ensure that victims who come forward, as well as those who are too afraid to do so, are supported after these horrific crimes are committed?

We are investing in more support for police forces and more support around accommodation and other services for victims. The hon. Member is right to draw attention to the importance of that area. This Government are clear that whoever perpetrates violence against women and girls should face the full force of the law, no matter how rich, no matter how powerful and no matter their background.

Earlier this year, I visited Torbay Ladies Lounge, a group of women who have survived domestic violence. They shared with me how some of them had been failed by Devon and Cornwall police. Only last month, nine women received compensation from Devon and Cornwall police due to failings around domestic violence and abuse investigations. While Devon and Cornwall police made some assurances to myself and the community within its region, what assurances can the Minister give that she will be driving cultural change throughout the police services in the United Kingdom, so that these crimes can be investigated in a timely and appropriate way?

The hon. Gentleman is right about the wider cultural change that we need to see. We know that it is very difficult for women to come forward and report crimes that are often highly personal around relationships, domestic abuse and sexual violence. We need to make it as easy as possible and ensure that they have experienced support when they do so. I have seen some pioneering work that has gone on in other police forces, such as my own in Northumbria, which is using technology to make it easier for women to report crimes and further explore what action will be taken. There are lessons that can be taken forward from that. I will ensure that my colleagues in the Home Office consider the wider point that the hon. Gentleman raises and respond to him in detail.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. Can you advise me whether it is acceptable for what happened on the steps of Downing Street—the degrading language—not to be addressed and roundly called out in this statement on White Ribbon Day— [ Interruption. ] Don’t tell me to sit down.

Order. It is not a matter for the Chair to be responsible for the content of statements or any responses that the Front Bench wishes to give. We cannot continue the debate; the statement is now done. We have to move on to the next business, but no doubt the Member has got her point of view on the record.

On a point of order, Madam Deputy Speaker. I wish to correct the record about two references I have made about my constituent’s daughter, Amanda Walker, on 15 September 2025 and 27 October 2026. In those remarks, I stated that Amanda took her own life. While it is correct to say that the cladding crisis consumed Amanda towards the end of her life, following the inquest into her death, the coroner recorded a conclusion of misadventure. It is important that the official record reflects that, so I make this contribution to correct the record. I also look forward to continuing to work with the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to ensure that Amanda’s legacy is reflected in forthcoming legislation. —[ Official Report, First Delegated Legislation Committee Delegated Legislation Committee, 25 September 2025; c. 6.] and [ Official Report , 27 October 2026; Vol. 792, c. 219.]

I beg to move, That leave be given to bring in a Bill to create offences in relation to the sale of certain electric personal vehicles; to create penalties in relation to those offences; and for connected purposes. The laws on licensing and selling battery powered two-wheel vehicles are being abused by those who do not share our values. They are being abused by those who are exploiting them to further criminal behaviour, and in doing so, these people are not only committing crimes but endangering and taking the lives of innocent people, making our communities feel unsafe and draining the resources of our police, fire brigades and NHS hospitals. The laws must be tightened, and new offences brought in and enforced, and this Bill is another attempt by Members of this House who stand against this behaviour to do just that. The Bill proposes a new offence for companies that fail to prevent their products from being used illegally, and, where it can be proven that they have not taken reasonable steps to mitigate against this misuse, penalties and cases can be brought against them. The Bill also proposes that the Secretary of State be given powers to publish what is expected of the battery vehicle market and what is needed to demonstrate that sellers have met all reasonable steps. A long time ago, when I was a journalism student, my lecturer took me aside and said, “If in doubt, follow the money.” That is sage advice. The Bill does not, of course, place full responsibility on the sellers for the prevalence of dangerous and intimidating behaviour in the people using their vehicles or associated products. These people are using those vehicles to evade the police or pursue criminal activity such as drug dealing, as has been proven many times in my constituency. Responsibility belongs to those committing the crimes and injuring themselves and others—sometimes even fatally—and they will continue to be brought to justice by our valiant police forces. However, even with more resources, as campaigned for by myself and my colleagues in Durham and Cleveland, the police cannot tackle this alone. That is why my Bill proposes that if a company’s business model relies on criminals using its products, or those hosted on its e-marketplace rely on the illegal misuse of those products, and it does not help to mitigate against that, it will find itself on the wrong side of the law. For the avoidance of doubt, I will provide the House with some real examples of this. Currently, the law states that if I buy a car, the seller must verify my identity and contact the Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency to transfer ownership of that vehicle to me. The DVLA would then send out a V5C, and I could either apply for a statutory off road notification or tax, insure and drive my car in line with local traffic laws. I would face penalties for breaking speed limits regardless of the maximum speed that my new car could reach, and I must adhere to the speed set by the law. That law is enforceable because of this registration, and because speed cameras can detect my plates. If I buy a new motorbike, the same rules apply. The seller must verify my identity and contact the DVLA to transfer ownership of my new motorbike to me. I would then follow the same process as for other legal road vehicles. Even if my new motorbike could reach a maximum speed that is more than double the speed limit set by law, I must adhere to the legal speed limit or face penalties for breaking it. Again, that law is enforceable because of this registration, and because speed cameras can detect my licence plates. However, if I buy a dirt bike or a motocross bike, the law is different. Dirt bikes and motocross bikes are sold as off-road vehicles for use on so-called private land—it is illegal to ride them on the road. The seller does not need to register the ownership of the vehicle with the DVLA, and the owner does not need to register their ownership unless they want to ride their vehicle on the r

title: Restoration and Renewal of the  Palace of Westminster

items.txt: I inform the House that Mr Speaker has selected the amendment in the name of the Prime Minister. I call the shadow Leader of the House.

I beg to move, That this House expresses grave concern at the enormous projected costs of the Restoration and Renewal Programme, estimated at between £11.1 billion and £39.2 billion; believes that the scale of expenditure contemplated is particularly difficult to justify given the severe pressure on public finances; recognises the urgent need to address serious deficiencies in the Palace of Westminster’s fabric, infrastructure and fire safety, while expressing concern at the absence of an agreed budget or affordable scope of works to do so and the continuing failure to establish effective governance, financial control and accountability; and questions the assumptions underlying the proposals for the extensive decant of Parliament, the resulting disruption to parliamentary proceedings and the substantial additional costs involved. This, as the House will be aware, is nominally an Opposition day debate. However, the motion stands first in my name, and, on the Opposition Benches, it is subject to a free vote. It is, it must be said, a rather unusual procedure, but we have been forced to it by the Government’s unwillingness to act over the past nine months on the restoration and renewal of the Palace of Westminster. The R and R client board published its costed proposals document on 5 February. Since then, the Government, who control the business of the House, have done nothing about it. That is nine whole months. You will be pleased to know, Madam Deputy Speaker, that I have just seen that we have been successful: the Government have at last published their motion, just a few minutes ago. I am delighted by that fact. [ Interruption. ] The Leader of the House, who is grumbling somewhat from a sedentary position, may try to decry this debate as an attempt to make this piece of House business party political— [ Interruption. ] Thank you. He may criticise our call to do the necessary work at a far lower cost as a needless further delay, but the opposite is true. My colleagues can vote as they wish on this motion. I hope that all Members of this House will be allowed to do so by their Whips at the end of this debate. I ask the Leader of the House to confirm that Labour will not be whipping its own Members on this House business and that all Members will be able to speak when the motion comes before the House. The truth is that this delay has been caused by the Government’s absolute unwillingness to act. I have asked time and again from the Dispatch Box for them to publish a motion, but far from approaching this issue in a cross-party way, they have done the exact opposite. They have offered no debate, no engagement, no attempt to bring colleagues together. If there is any urgent safety work to be done now, the Government have had two-and-a-half years in which to amend the legislation and get it done, so I ask the Leader of the House again what the reason has been for this delay. It seems that the Government’s goal is to leave this business to a quiet day long after the Budget, perhaps on a one-line Whip, and push through this House a £3 billion spend—that is just the initial spend—after a single, short debate and the thinnest possible scrutiny by this Chamber. Now they offer the weakest of amendments in response to our motion today.

I remember debating this when I was in the House in 2017—obviously there were a number of Conservative Governments in that subsequent period who did not bring forward a resolution. The right hon. Gentleman’s motion sets out the things he disagrees with and what he thinks the cost will be. At what point will he publish his alternative measure so that if we do support this motion today, we know what we are likely to back?

I am grateful to the hon. Gentleman for his intervention, but he is very sadly misinformed. He seems to have forgotten that the Government brought a motion forward in 2019 on restoration and renewal. As regards my own views, they have been extensively published, but I will come to them in due course. As I was saying, the amendment that the Government have offered is, I am afraid, astoundingly weak. The cost of the Government’s nine-month delay this year has been estimated by the Public Accounts Committee to be between £220 million and £290 million. The Government own this cost and those nine months. It would be disingenuous in the extreme for them to now push ahead on this wildly expensive project with no serious scrutiny, no genuine accountability and no political consensus, either in this House or between the Houses. Indeed, as experience has shown time and again, it would be an act of extreme folly. No one disputes that the Palace of Westminster needs restoration; the question is at what cost.

Isn’t the problem that nobody can justify spending somewhere between £10 billion and £40 billion on repairing this great place? The issue is that the brief is wrong, because there is not one, not two, not three but four boards of governance. That is one of the first problems.

I thank the hon. Gentleman for his remarks. Knowing that he will have closely scrutinised the costed proposals report, I am sure he will have seen that the proposal is now to add another board in relation to the client board and the programme board following passage of the motion. That would be a further catastrophic downgrading of the very little accountability that presently exists.

If I may, I will make a bit more progress. If a Department proposed to spend up to £40 billion on restoring a single building without an agreed budget, settled scope, clear political leadership or accountability to Ministers, Parliament would vigorously object, but this is precisely the situation that Parliament now finds itself in. The costed proposals report, as has been mentioned, gives a range of £11 billion to £39 billion in projected cost. These figures are estimates, I would emphasise. There is no budget as such here. These are not contractual commitments or guaranteed upper limits, and they are eye-watering sums. Moreover, they are being proposed without the normal disciplines of ministerial responsibility, Treasury oversight and departmental accountability applied to major governmental infrastructure projects. Given the history of British infrastructure mega-projects, it is not hard to foresee scope for massive further cost inflation.

As a member of the Public Accounts Committee, which has scrutinised the proposals in some detail, along with many other historical infrastructure projects, I am surprised that the right hon. Gentleman and his party seem to be ignoring the Committee’s recommendations that Members now have plenty of information to make a decision and that it is vital that we get on and start with this project as soon as possible.

I am afraid to say that I did not think that the Public Accounts Committee showed itself at its best in that report. We did not see, for example, anything like the detailed scrutiny of individual costs that I would have expected. I will come on in a second to the costings, then the hon. Lady can decide whether the PAC has done its job in relation to those. It is easy to get lost in such enormous numbers, but what do they mean in real terms? By way of comparison, the cost of the restoration of Notre-Dame was about £600 million. Yes, it has just a quarter of the footprint of the Palace of Westminster and was not occupied during its restoration, but as one commentator remarked, we could restore a Notre-Dame every single week over a year for the cost of one R and R and still have enough cash left over for a nuclear-powered aircraft carrier.

I wonder whether the right hon. Gentleman would like to check his figures. He just said that Notre-Dame has a quarter of the footprint of the Palace of Westminster. I believe Notre-Dame to have a floorspace of 5% of the Palace of Westminster, making it one twentieth of the size. Would he like to correct the record?

Of course, it has never been known for the Liberal Democrats to indulge in equivocation. The hon. Lady has shifted the argument from the footprint to the floorspace. The footprint is a quarter of the size, and that is what I described. What else could £40 billion pay for? We could have 40 major new hospitals up and down the country, 50 new Wembley stadiums, and new Elizabeth lines in two large cities, perhaps in and around Birmingham or linking Manchester and Liverpool. We could pay for the standing military aid of this country to Ukraine for 13 more years to defend the security of Europe. It would amount to £1,400 for every household in this country, and if one were to spend one pound every second on R and R, it would take nearly 1,270 years to spend £40 billion. That is how large that number is. Let us be clear: spending this gigantic sum on a single building would be the utmost folly, but still more when the national debt is hovering near 100% of GDP and the public finances are so tight. The cost is so high that the Office for Budget Responsibility will need to include in its forecasts. Every Member of this House will have to account at the next election for their vote on this matter today. When their constituents ask where the money is for potholes, social housing or defence, they will have to explain why so much was overspent on a single building. We might feel more confidence if the parliamentary authorities had a good track record of managing infrastructure projects, but I am afraid that the reverse is true. The new security fence outside St Stephen’s gate has been widely criticised for its ugliness and cost. The Lord Speaker rightly described the new £10 million entrance to the House of Lords as “a complete white elephant and a disaster”. The procurement to restore the Victoria Tower failed and had to be redone. The doors in Portcullis House were not disability-friendly even when it was built. Today the atrium roof leaks and is swathed in unsightly protective wrapping and needs replacing just 25 years after it was installed. These are not reassuring precedents.

One thing I think we need to get clear is what is the primary purpose of this restoration. Is it fundamentally just to make the building safe or is it to try and in some way transform the building? According to the National Audit Office’s June 2026 update report, it is the former. It says: “The Palace requires extensive restoration to address serious risks and priority improvements, including deteriorating mechanical and electrical systems, fire safety issues, the presence of asbestos and the condition of the historic fabric.” Why should it take £40 billion just to do repairs?

I thank my right hon. Friend for his question. Of course, it should not. My whole point has been that we should focus on restoration and the vital safety, security and wellbeing work that is required and mentioned by the NAO, but not on other aspects of the project that push up its costs as much as they are doing.

No. If I may, I will keep pushing on. The recent precedents from construction around the House of Commons and the House of Lords are not reassuring. Instead, let us look at the restoration of Buckingham Palace. The NAO has praised its disciplined management, risk controls and willingness to make practical trade-offs. The palace has remained operational throughout, with Her late Majesty the Queen in residence there in her final years. That project has a budget of £389 million, which is less than 1% of the potential cost of R and R. Can any sane person think R and R makes sense in the face of that comparison? Buckingham Palace also shows us a better way. Successful restoration requires a good client, clear accountability, tightly defined objectives and competent execution. R and R presently lacks the political consensus it needs both within this House and in the two Houses as a whole. When it fails, as it surely must, Parliament will need a fall-back. Here is my suggestion. Parliament should immediately commission a rapid, independent red team review of the entire proposition. That 90-day exercise should bring together existing engineering assessments, cost estimates, procurement plans and safety requirements and subject them to rigorous challenge. It should be run by a small team under the joint leadership of the two Speakers, with explicit cross-party support in both Houses and a clear mandate to distinguish essential health and safety works—the point made by my right hon. Friend the Member for New Forest East (Sir Julian Lewis)—from discretionary enhancements. Its objective should be to put before Parliament a clear budget, scope and schedule for a scaled-back programme, focusing on the primary job of restoration. Some temporary decanting may be unavoidable, but only as justified by engineering necessity.

I thank the shadow Leader of the House for taking an intervention—I promise that it is a friendly one. He is a good friend of my predecessor in this place. Does he recognise that, as well as the health and safety aspects he mentioned, we should think about enhancements to make the place more accessible for people with disabilities?

I very much agree with that. We have already done good work, led by the Leader of the House, on the Modernisation Committee in relation to disability improvements across the Palace. Before I close, let me address the Government’s amendment. It is remarkably weak. Nobody disputes the responsibility to protect the Palace of Westminster; the questions are how, at what cost, over what period and under whose supervision? R and R has always been a parliamentary programme, not a Government programme. In that spirit, the previous Conservative Government passed the Parliamentary Buildings (Restoration and Renewal) Act 2019. The motion before us is not a partisan one. It does not blame the Labour party for what has always been House business, but it presses the Government on the delay and lack of scrutiny. Only the Government can remedy that failure. At last, they have done so by publishing their motion. The Government’s amendment implies that the Opposition are seeking to delay essential safety works; that is not true. Every Member of the House believes that remediation should continue. The Government have had 2.5 years to make it so. The Government’s amendment presents no evidence that a more focused programme could not deliver safety improvements still more rapidly than is being contemplated. It contains no recognition of the pressure on the public finances of the national debt or the cost of servicing it. As for its claim about jobs, any infrastructure project of tens of billions of pounds would support thousands of jobs—that is not a test of value for money. In comparison, High Speed 2 is expected to support 34,000 construction jobs and no one thinks that HS2 will be good value for money. Many more jobs and much more growth would be created if that money were better spent. Finally, the amendment makes the extraordinary claim that “the phase one works will deliver value for money for the taxpayer by capping initial costs”. That is economically illiterate. Capping initial costs is not the same as capping final costs. A spending cap is not evidence of value for money, and the amendment offers no comfort on that issue, on scope, on schedule or on accountability; nor does it offer any justification for why Parliament should exempt itself from the financial disciplines that it seeks to apply to other public bodies. The Government’s amendment is an insult to the Commons. It would be folly to proceed with R and R on that basis, especially when better models exist. I commend the motion to the House.

I beg to move an amendment, to leave out from “House” to the end of the Question and add: “recognises that it has a responsibility to repair, secure and protect the Palace of Westminster, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site of global historic and symbolic significance, for future generations; notes the previous Government’s failure to support Parliament in implementing a credible Restoration and Renewal Programme in 14 years; further notes that this indecision has added significant costs to the remediation required and that further delay would only increase costs and risk catastrophic failure of the buildings, putting the safety of those who work on and visit the parliamentary estate at risk; also notes the National Audit Office Report, Restoration and Renewal of the Palace of Westminster: 2026 Update, HC 32, and the 19th Report of the Committee of Public Accounts, Restoration and Renewal of Parliament: Costing and governance, HC 90, which recommended proceeding immediately with works; notes that the Restoration and Renewal Programme will support thousands of jobs across the country; further notes that the phase one works will deliver value for money for the taxpayer by capping initial costs; and supports the Government’s commitment to table a motion for debate so that individual hon. Members can take a decision in a proper and informed way before the end of the year.” It is entirely a matter for the Opposition what they choose to debate on their Opposition day, but I have to say that their choice today is both disappointing and, frankly, odd. It is disappointing because the Opposition knew full well that the Government intended to provide time for a debate on restoration and renewal before Christmas. The shadow Leader of the House had seen a draft motion.
It is true. [ Interruption. ] That is absolutely true . I gave it to you some weeks ago.
Order. The Leader of the House is very experienced. There should be no “you” or “yours”, and no secondary debates when a debate is already taking place here in the Chamber.

Thank you, Madam Deputy Speaker. What has happened with that motion is that I tried—we tried—to build consensus around the approach on this matter. As the right hon. Gentleman has said, it is not a Government project; it is a parliamentary project, and in my view any progress needs to be sustainable.

I thank the Leader of the House for being so generous in giving way. Last year, along with probably most of the MPs in the Chamber, I went on an R and R tour of Parliament. At that time, we were presented with three choices, and there was a middle ground, which to me seemed extremely sensible. I have yet to hear a good answer as to why that middle ground has been removed from the final options. We are being given a binary choice between something that is incredibly expensive and—well, actually both are incredibly expensive.

I will get to that point in a moment, as I want to say something about costs and about choices, but this is a matter not just of choices but of when those choices will be exercised. My intention was to give the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman) and the House the courtesy of announcing the debate in the business statement tomorrow, but instead it seems that he has preferred to jump the gun. It is odd, because most Opposition parties would make the case to the Government of the day that they have so much to say and so little time in this place to say it, with just 17 Opposition days. This Opposition seem to have the opposite problem: they have got too much time and nothing much to say. The Opposition’s motion is sadly predictable. It sums up Conservative party policy over the last 14 years in a nutshell: identify a problem, say how bad it is and then run away from making a decision. We saw that in its approach to health, defence, education and all other matters, and that approach is reflected in the motion before us. In 2017, the then Deputy Leader of the House, Sir Michael Ellis—a man I hugely admired, who is missed in this place—said: “We have reached a point where make-do-and-mend is simply not an option.” He also said that “we cannot pass the buck any longer.” —[ Official Report, 25 January 2017; Vol. 620, c. 117WH-118WH.] Yet here we are, nearly 10 years later, with a motion that seeks to pass the buck. In 2020, the then Leader of the House, Sir Jacob Rees-Mogg, said, rightly, that “if we fail to act, the building risks being lost to history forever.” —[ Official Report , 16 July 2020; Vol. 678, c. 1736.] A year later, he said: “The work needs to be done, and it needs to be done as soon as is practicable.” —[ Official Report , 20 May 2021; Vol. 695, c. 958.] But he then went on to warn against hurrying along in an over-hasty fashion. In 2022, the then Leader of the House Sir Mark Spencer said: “The building needs to be repaired”, but he then asked, “why are we here again?” —[ Official Report , 12 July 2022; Vol. 718, c. 272-272.] That is a very good question.

My right hon. Friend is clearly setting out the dither and delay from the Conservative party. Does he recognise that it has been seven years since the passing of the 2019 Act, which the shadow Leader of the House mentioned, and that in that time the building has become even more unsafe? We do not want a Notre-Dame. We do not want to wait for the building to burn down. Does my right hon. Friend agree that the time for reviews and further diagnosis is over? Does he agree with the Public Accounts Committee that we need to get on and make the decision?

I absolutely agree. One problem with the speech of the shadow Leader of the House was that it suggested not a single solution apart from applying the brakes. I listened carefully to what he said today. I have heard on the airwaves and have read in the newspapers over recent weeks his calls for the programme to be paused and reviewed. He even likened it to a runaway train. It is the only runaway train that has yet to leave the station. I fully appreciate the real anxieties caused by the costs associated with the programme. However, the reality is that the hope for a cheaper, less disruptive solution and a delay until we find one is a message that we have heard over and over again. The only thing we know is that it gets us no further and only increases cost and risk. We are approaching a fundamental question that has loomed over this House for more than a decade. We are the current custodians of the seat of British democracy. We need to fulfil our duty to preserve and restore the Palace of Westminster. As the shadow Leader of the House’s predecessors have said, and as I have quoted, we cannot allow this iconic building to fall victim to catastrophic failure on our watch because we are too hesitant to put into action the advice and the expertise of every independent review that this House has ever sought.

The Leader of the House talks a lot about our democratic duty, but he fails to mention our duty as legislators and parliamentarians to take account of the public purse. Does he agree that, at the end of the day, it is taxpayers’ money that he seeks to spend?

We are the custodians of the public purse. I am not arguing that there should be any amount of money available. There are ways in which we can look at what needs to be spent and make sure that we get value for money. However, when the right hon. Lady is next on the radio, having been sent out by her Front Benchers to do the 8.10 am slot on Radio 4, and she wants to talk about some foreign affairs issue of the day, I can guarantee that at some point, if she is not careful, she will not get that question about foreign affairs, because for the first 20 minutes she will be asked, “How did you allow the House to burn to the ground?” That is the risk we run.
No, no. The right hon. Lady has had her go. As all the shadow Leader’s predecessors have said, and as I have quoted, we cannot allow this building to fall victim to catastrophe.

Let me start with an admission: the Leader of the House knows far more than I do about this issue and the detail. What I cannot understand, however, is how the PAC report can come up with figures like this: “each year of delay adds up to £420 million to the potential lifetime cost of delivering the Programme.” We are all agreed that we do not want a catastrophic event, but how can it cost billions and billions to stop the place burning down? It is just nonsense.

Because the right hon. Gentleman takes an interest in these matters, he may well have been in the debate at which the then Leader of the House Andrea Leadsom addressed that point. She talked about the cost of delay in terms of the sticking-plaster approach, which we still have. She also talked about the billion pounds of neglect that is not being addressed by a sticking-plaster. That bill is only going up. The right hon. Gentleman knows, from his constituency and from every constituency, that the cost of repair and restoration will not come down over the years. It will go up.

Members need to take into account the fact that this is a workplace. There are 3,000 workers who work here. They have had to endure asbestos. Some have to have their health monitored for the rest of their life. There have been floods, electrical faults and, to be frank, working conditions that are just unacceptable in the 21st century. We have a responsibility to those workers, and every single trade union representing them has made it clear that they do not wish any further delay in the refurbishment and restoration of this building.

I am grateful to my right hon. Friend, who speaks a great deal of sense on these matters. On these occasions, we tend to think about the 650 Members of Parliament whose right it is to turn up at this building, but what about the thousands of people who work here, along with the hundreds of thousands of visitors who come into this place?

I should like to report that in the summer, the second floor of 53 Parliament Street had a complete failure of air conditioning and my staff were overheated, working illegally. There is now a complete failure of central heating, so my staff are completely freezing. I echo what my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell) says about the conditions for our workers.

As ever, my hon. Friend makes a sensible case. What he describes is far too typical, not just in that building but in this one. The shadow Leader of the House wishes to criticise me and the Government for a lack of progress on the costed proposals before now. I remind the House that the report was published in February this year, following years of engagement and analysis. The National Audit Office considered costings and governance in its June report, which was followed by a report from the Public Accounts Committee earlier this month. The Public Accounts Committee report builds on the NAO report and two public evidence sessions. Any delay was to ensure that Members had enough time to consider the reports and the expert opinions of the NAO and the PAC. To me, that seems entirely sensible. I thank everyone who was involved in the preparation of those reports, including the hon. Member for North Cotswolds (Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown). The NAO report warned: “There is no way forward that does not incur cost and risk, with inaction itself being a choice with serious consequences.” I agree. As the NAO sets out: “The costed options provide enough information for a decision on the way forward”. The Public Accounts Committee said: “Having scrutinised the costed proposals, we consider there is enough information to inform a debate and a vote.” I agree with that, too—but it seems that, as ever, the Opposition think they know better. We have been around this track before. We debated, re-debated, picked and unpicked options for more than 10 years while the Conservatives were in government. We do not need another review. We need resolve. The House needs to decide whether or not to tackle this issue.

One of the key reasons why the costs are so exorbitant is the enormous contingency increases, ranging from the lowest at 32% to the highest, which goes up to 135% of the core base price. The primary reason, in addition to the fact that this is an old building, is that, collectively, we are terrible clients: we do not know what we want, we have not decided what the scope is, we change our minds the whole time and we have labyrinthine governance that includes both Houses, the Commons Commission, the Lords Commission, the client board, the programme board and its sub-board, the Commons Clerk, the Lords Clerk, the client team, Strategic Estates and the delivery authority. No one is in charge. If the Leader of the House is serious about our progressing this, he first has to get simple, accountable governance that we can all believe in.

I will come to that point in a minute, but the hon. Gentleman hits the nail on the head about the cost of contingency, which is in some of the numbers. I will tell him why they are so high: because any company that comes along here will look at how much the job will cost and then build in risk. The reason it builds in risk is that this House has never made up its mind. Anybody looking from the outside, and any company, will question whether we will ever be serious about this and whether we will continue with the plan that we have. Let me just say this and be somewhat controversial, I suspect, to people on both sides here. It is my considered view that one of the reasons it has become so elongated and things have chopped and changed is not because politicians have not been in charge; it is because politicians have stuck their finger into, messed about with and changed almost every decision. We have had an Act. We have had review after review. It is not that businesses come in and seek to take us for a ride; it is the fact that politicians cannot make their mind up and then stick to it. We have to be honest about the state of this building, and that is something the Opposition motion fails to acknowledge. One of the reasons that the pause and review approach is so troubling is that the building that we occupy is in managed decline. It is a decline that pause will not change; it will simply make it worse. Since 2016 and the publication of the costed proposals, there have been 36 fires, 12 asbestos incidents and 19 stonemasonry incidents. The House authorities have assessed that while current mitigations would protect human life in a major fire, they cannot prevent the loss of the building itself. Every week, £1.5 million of public money is spent on patching up decaying systems, and that figure is set to rise to £2 million a week. Only 12% of the Palace is step-free and accessible. That is entirely unacceptable for a modern legislature.

The right hon. Gentleman seems somewhat rattled this afternoon—certainly towards me, anyway—but putting that aside, can he not understand that those of us on the Conservative Benches are simply seeking more detailed information? I will speak later, but an example would be the information that I have failed to get in response to my written parliamentary questions.

I think “frustrated” would be a better description than “rattled”. There will be ample opportunity to get information. The right hon. Lady might even get information from this debate, but she will certainly get information over the next two weeks as we approach a decision moment. Since my appointment as Leader of the House, I have sought to find a pragmatic, financially responsible way forward that carries as great a consensus as possible among Members across the House, and I intend to announce during the business statement tomorrow a full day of debate to allow the House to decide on 8 December. If the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire, thinks that a Tuesday is a quiet day in the House, he probably needs to get out more. That motion has been tabled today, in good time before the debate. I want to ask the right hon. Gentleman a question. Do the Opposition intend to whip their MPs on that day? If he says no, that is funny, because until yesterday that is exactly what they intended to do. I understand that they are not whipped to vote on the motion today, but I suspect that yesterday afternoon they were whipped to vote on it. I sense that an element of realism is coming into the Opposition’s whipping. Whipping on that side of the House is a matter for the Opposition. Whipping on this side of the House is a matter for us. But this is not a debate on House matters called in Government time. This is an Opposition day debate. The Government are perfectly entitled to get their MPs here and, if necessary, vote down an Opposition motion.

I have been an advocate of the “kicking the can down the road” strategy, because this proposal has not made sense financially and it is still not proven. However, as the motion says, the Opposition also accept that the situation is not sustainable. It is quite clear that all this motion is asking for is further analysis. We have heard that from the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) and from the Opposition Front Bench. There is no risk in taking a few more weeks before the Leader of the House’s motion is put in front of Parliament, so as to have as much consensus building as possible, because the challenges are quite legitimate.

I do not like disagreeing with the right hon. Gentleman, but I think on this he is just wrong. The reality is that if it goes into next year, the costs will continue to go up every week in that time. Every week costs between £1.5 million and £2 million. We have been through this process for long enough. What we need to do is make a decision. I will put before the House exactly the plan that the House would be asked to agree or not agree on 8 December. I believe that is a responsible way of bringing forward an important matter. The shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire, has asked for notice of the debate and he will be getting notice of the debate. In fact, he has already got it. I have also written to all Members with an offer to speak to any and all of them ahead of the debate to discuss the motion. If the right hon. Member for Aldridge-Brownhills (Wendy Morton) has questions, I look forward to speaking to her. In contrast, the Opposition have chosen to offer the House, at minimal notice today, a motion that offers no solutions, ignores the mounting risks and simply kicks the can further down the road.
I will not take interventions, as I am going to make some progress.

I am grateful to the Leader of the House for giving way. I had not really intended to intervene, but I have been listening carefully to the debate, much of which I agree with: I think the costs are too high, the governance is far too complicated, and too much about the whole matter has been discussed behind closed doors, in secret. I would like to get one concession from the Leader of the House today. I have looked at his motion very carefully. One of the key recommendations of the PAC, which I have the privilege to chair, was that this Parliament, although it cannot bind its successor, recommend to the next Parliament to have an early vote, in 2030, which would give the authorities plenty of time to see if they could get the costs down, and sort out the governance and a way forward. Would he give serious consideration to that before he puts his motion before the House?

It may not be a decision for me, but that will become self-evident when we get into the initial programme of seven years. There is initial work that needs to be done when that option is put before the House in mid-2030. One of the issues to look at will be governance and another will be financial costs. We will have an annual debate, every year. The hon. Gentleman knows that because we have talked about the role that the PAC might want to play in all this. Although I would be very surprised if I was in the job that I am doing now when we get to that time, I would find it extraordinary if, when the House had a view on the costed proposals or anything else, there would not be an opportunity to have a debate on those matters. It is not about shutting MPs out of this process; it is about getting on with it and making sure that the right people are there to drive it.

I will take the Leader of the House up on the offer to meet him. He is correct: of course we want to ensure that the fire and safety measures are updated and appropriate for this place, but the truth is that the scope of this restoration and renewal is far broader than that in order to make the building net zero compliant. Here is the flaw. There are 50 lifts in this building, and after this programme of restoration and renewal, there will still be 50 lifts in the building, but not a single one will be in the same place.

That is a bit rich coming from the hon. Gentleman. When he was asked about accessibility at the time of the Modernisation Committee’s report on the subject, I remember him saying, “Nobody is coming to this House to complain about accessibility to the building.” Well, that is because they could not get in. During the process that I am quickly going to outline, there is a process for all these considerations to be dealt with. It is not closing off something at this point—it is a fixed term, not a fixed plan. It will adapt over a period of time, but the key question is: are we going to get on with it? On 8 December, we will be putting before the House an initial package of phase 1 works lasting seven years, capped at a maximum of £3 billion. This is for essential groundwork, and investment in resilience and enabling works, which must happen no matter which final route we take. It caps our immediate investment and keeps long-term options open. Let me also say—in response, I think, to an intervention taken by the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire—that the package also takes into account best practice for major programmes. It reflects advice from the Government’s Office for Value for Money by ensuring that delivery plans are sufficiently mature before final decisions are made, to avoid unrealistic expectations about cost and schedule. The NAO has described phase 1 preparatory works while progressing the programme as “sensible”. We narrow two paths. We get the programme moving. We save on unnecessary, wasteful expenditure. The client board will provide updated costs by no later than 2029, enabling a final, informed decision on whether or not to decant by the middle of 2030.

I understand the frustration of the Leader of the House. I recognise that getting leaner governance will be like herding cats. My right hon. Friend the Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman) challenged him on this. There is a real role for the Leader of the House to bang heads together and make sure that, whatever we decide going forward, we do not have this ludicrously complex set of intertwined governance. Does he agree and does he accept his personal role in trying—however challenging that may be—to bang heads together and get a leaner set of governance arrangements?

Yes, I do. One of the first jobs in phase 1, if we agree to go down that path, is to get the governance right within six months. I agree with whoever read out the list of all the bodies involved in governance: it is madness! It is like spaghetti, and I find it incredibly difficult to understand. We need to get a better, leaner system. It needs to be clear and people need to be accountable. But we cannot really start that process, I am sorry to say, unless we get on with phase 1—because it costs. I understand the costs issue, but delay is not a saving. A 90-day review, supported by the shadow Leader of the House, would cost £100 million and would not guarantee progress at the end. All we get is the warm bath of endless review from the Opposition, but at what stage will they accept the stark warnings of the National Audit Office, the Public Accounts Committee, and every independent assessment the House has ever commissioned? Let me turn briefly to an issue that the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire was a bit sniffy about, actually: the benefit to the country. This building does not belong to us; it belongs to the nation, and we have a responsibility to restore it. This programme will bring not just costs but benefits. It will invest billions of pounds into supply chains reaching into constituencies right across the country. We will draw on the industrial expertise and craftsmanship of the whole nation. We will back up 4,000 jobs and 1,000 apprentices. I know that the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire, cares passionately about this building and the work we do in it, but I have to say to him and to others: passion alone is not enough to put out a fire, and another review will not make the project move forward in any way. We have an opportunity to halt the cycle of delay and cut wasteful expenditure. The Opposition propose a pause without a plan, a recipe for continued decline, a guarantee of hundreds of millions of pounds wasted in delay, and an acceptance of the increased risk of catastrophic failure. We cannot accept that approach, and we cannot accept this motion. I therefore commend the Government amendment to the House.
Order. Before I call the Liberal Democrat spokesperson, let me say that this is a time-limited three-hour debate, so I hope colleagues will manage the length of their speeches.

Since the beginning of this week I now sit on the House of Commons Commission, which, together with the House of Lords Commission, makes up the client board for this programme—there has been some quick reading and quick learning! I thank the Opposition for tabling this motion. I say that with some affection, because it is not every day that a party turns up to complain about its own homework. Nobody in this House should be relaxed about spending tens of billions of pounds of public money, and the Liberal Democrats share that concern. But let us remind the House whose idea this was. A Conservative Leader of the House, Dame Andrea Leadsom, tabled the motions in 2018 that sent this House on its way out of the Palace. A Conservative Government introduced and passed the Parliamentary Buildings (Restoration and Renewal) Act 2019, and when Notre-Dame burned down that year, a Conservative Leader of the House told us all to “get on with it”. Now, a Conservative Opposition table a motion expressing “grave concern.” Grave concern about what exactly—their own signature?

The grave concern is the truly eye-watering sums that are being debated. My constituents, and I suspect those of the hon. Gentleman, will be appalled that we should be spending that sort of money on ourselves—and that is how it will be presented, rightly or wrong. Does he not share those concerns?

I absolutely share those concerns, but the motion in the name of the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman), would involve the largest possible range of options being available. I would not support that; I would support the cheapest option on the table.

No, the coming motion would take our choice down to two options. Concern is fair, but concern is not a plan and the motion does not offer one. The Lord Speaker, who chairs the client board, wrote last week: “This is not a party political matter and a decision is best reached by consensus.” I would argue that an Opposition day motion is not the way we reach such a consensus. Let us look at the figures in the motion. The range of £11.1 billion to £39.2 billion is not one project but two options stapled together. The National Audit Office puts the cost of full decant at £15.6 billion over 19 to 24 years and the cost of enhanced maintenance and improvement-plus, or EMI+,—at £19.5 billion to £39.2 billion over 38 to 61 years. The figure that so alarms the Opposition belongs to the option in which Members stay in the building, but the cheaper, quicker option involves us leaving. Their motion complains that staying put is too expensive, but, in the same breath, it questions the plan to leave. That is not a policy; it is the Conservative party having a tantrum. Notre-Dame has about 5% of the floor space of this Palace and cost in the region of €700 million. If we multiply that figure by 20, we land close to the bottom of the full decant range. Buckingham Palace has lessons for us to learn on phasing and asbestos, but it is half the size of this Palace and has one sixth of the users, and its costs left out stonework restoration and fire safety. It is not a like-for-like comparison.

Given the fact that the motion before us is unnecessarily confused, jams together different options and does not lay things out clearly, any confusion that our constituents may have today is actually because of the Opposition making them confused and angry about potential spending that is significantly above the range that we should, in reality, be discussing. Does my hon. Friend agree?

I agree. This is the Conservatives trying to cause an argument for the sake of publicity, rather than because of the real detail. There is no quick or cheap method waiting to be revealed, and delaying until one turns up is hope, not a plan. The cost of postponing this debate alone is more than £200 million. Some £500 million has gone on design consultancy and the delivery authority, which costs more than £1 million a week and will soon have nothing to do without a decision. That is the real waste.

I assume that the hon. Member will get further into the detail of the length of time that this work will take. We are focusing quite significantly on the cost, but ultimately this will potentially mean decades of time in which our constituents will not be able to access this mother of all democracies—the Palace of Westminster. Is it the position of the Liberal Democrats that the public should be kept out of here for a significantly long period of time? Do they not want to minimise the distress caused to them?

The interesting thing about that intervention is that the greater number of years and the higher cost relate to the Palace being in constant use. If we went for the cheaper option of decant, Members and the public would be back in the place sooner. What the Conservatives propose is not restoration; it is dithering. Uncertainty is not free. The Lord Speaker points out that where the scope is unclear and decisions are delayed, contractors put a risk premium on their prices. The Leader of the House also noted that. Every month without a decision adds to the bill. The 2019 Act set clear tests: good value for money, consultation with Members and staff, and a prompt return to the Palace. That legislation was passed by a Conservative Government. They said that there would be no blank cheques, and they wrote those tests. We are simply asking that some of them are met. What is actually being proposed is more measured than the motion pretends. The first phase is capped at £3 billion—about £429 million a year over seven years, excluding inflation. Around 85% of the Palace’s construction costs are priority works, such as power, water, heating, fire safety, asbestos and stonework.

As a former Government accommodation Whip, I absolutely accept that we have to do something about the fire risk to the Palace. The hon. Gentleman has said that we should try to proceed by consensus, and I think everyone agrees that whatever we do, we must do something about that. However, does he accept that whether it is £10 billion or £40 billion for the overall solution, at a time when people’s gas prices are about to go up and they are feeling the cost of living challenge, the problem is that we would be perceived—rightly or wrongly—as spending that money on ourselves? That is the fundamental nub of the problem.

I do not accept that we are spending money on ourselves; Members are, in effect, one of the smallest groups of employees in this Palace. It is about protecting the 3,000 people who work here, and ensuring that we have a safe and welcoming environment for our constituents. As I said, more than 3,000 parliamentary employees work here, and the motion forgets to mention them. Asbestos has been found and, in several cases, released during general maintenance, meaning that the workers affected now face lifelong health monitoring. Legionella has been found in the water supply. Fire, leaks and flooding are daily risks. Last night, we had a sewage tanker brought in to drain the toilets, and I know that the toilets downstairs were not in use this morning either. It is often those who are paid the least—the cleaners and the catering staff—who carry that risk. No other employer would ask people to carry on like this. The building is too hard for disabled staff and visitors to use. Having been on crutches, and now a stick, over the last few months, I have come to realise how awkward it can be to get around this building. The plans would increase the step-free floor space from 12%, where it currently stands, to 60%, and up to 90% in the areas most used by Members and visitors. Most of that comes straight from essential fire safety work. Fire evacuation lifts, for example, are needed to get people out safely, and they open up step-free access as a result. The Leader of the Opposition has called the plans a “net zero Dubai hotel”, but the returned Palace will not be net zero. The Education Centre and the visitor entrance account for just 0.8% and 2.7% of the construction costs. What this programme is really about is having a safe workplace, a building that everyone can use, and jobs and apprenticeships across the United Kingdom. The Lord Speaker, who co-chairs the client board, has asked whether that board of around 25 members, as well as the programme board of 15 members, provides clear leadership and accountability. That is a question that I also have. Since the client board is made up of the two Commissions, and I now sit on one of them, I will not pretend that it is for somebody else to answer. Before the letter from the Leaders of both Houses arrived in our inboxes earlier today, I was planning to push for a clear timescale for the decisions; the cost and risk information that Members need; answers about who is accountable for cost control; a commitment that Members will see the whole-life cost, including the cost of delay, before any vote; and regular reports on the £3 billion cap and on progress on access for disabled staff and visitors. I welcome the fact that the Leader of the House outlining that in his letter. Let me conclude with a word about the Conservative party.
Order. It is not my Opposition day. I remind the hon. Gentleman that he is speaking through the Chair.

It is the Conservatives’ Opposition day, Madam Deputy Speaker, and I think it is right that we address them, in particular. The Conservatives had a Prime Minister who campaigned to remain in the European Union, they had a Prime Minister who legislated for net zero by 2050, and they proposed a sensible approach to restoration and renewal, which we are now debating today. They were right then, but now they just look like a populist party. They could have tabled a motion about provision for special educational needs and disabilities, which is failing families in every constituency, or they could have tabled a motion on the state of the water industry or the defence of the country. Instead, they have brought us a press release in the form of a motion about a programme that they started, and it offers no alternative. That is why the Liberal Democrats will abstain this evening. The motion deserves neither our support nor our opposition. The issue deserves a decision, and this motion does not make one. We cannot back a motion that questions the decant by keeping the price of delay off the page, but neither will we vote against a call for proper financial control and accountability, because a programme of this size needs that. We will keep pressing for value for money, transparency and a clear timetable, and we will hold the Government to account—and I will hold myself to account, as a member of the Commission—on all three.
About 20 colleagues are trying to catch my eye, and this debate has to conclude before 6 pm. Can Members please keep their speeches short?

I rise to speak in favour of the Government’s amendment. I support a restoration and renewal programme that happens at the right pace, and that ensures good value for money. Dame Andrea Leadsom, the former Conservative Leader of the House, when introducing the R and R programme in 2018, said: “We do need to get on and take a decision”. —[ Official Report , 31 January 2018; Vol. 635, c. 887.] I agreed with her then, and I still agree with her. It is up to us to move this forward. We are the custodians of this brilliant place. Now is the time to invest in, and improve, our democratic home. It will take more time than we want, because it is such a vast estate with so many aspects to protect. It will cost more money than we want to spend, but the fine stone, the beautiful windows, the great works of art and, of course, this wonderful Chamber all need to be properly looked after. In the end, I believe the effort will be worth it, but we must help bring the works in at a good price. There are other benefits; our economy will receive a much-needed boost from skilled people across our country carrying out these necessary works. Many parts of our country will benefit, whether it is the slate coming from Wales or the textiles coming from the west midlands. If we do not move forward with the restoration and renewal programme now, there will be serious consequences. We face critical risks, including fire, asbestos and falling masonry. Anybody who has been down to the basement of the Palace and seen the archaic muddle of pipes and wiring there will understand what I mean. While the Palace is a UNESCO world heritage site and the Elizabeth Tower is a global icon, most of all, the people of this country know that it is this Chamber—where we raise and work through the difficult challenges facing our world—that we must protect. That is why this place is worth investing in, and why it is priceless. It is our duty to invest in it, and when the work is done, we should return to this democratic crucible. The works cannot be done on the cheap, and we should have strong financial controls and oversight of them. Of course, as the Leader of the House has said, doing nothing also costs a lot. We presently spend £1.5 million a week on maintenance and repair; if we delay, those costs will go up and up, again and again.
Order. Before the hon. Member makes his intervention, I note that it is customary to be in the Chamber for a while before an intervention is made. Can he confirm that he has been here for a while?
I cannot, Madam Deputy Speaker. I was late, and I apologise.

This work cannot be done on the hoof. There are around 1,100 rooms in this Palace, and many different buildings from across the ages. France rebuilt Notre-Dame in five years and eight months at an estimated cost of £600 million; however, as has been said, we must remember that Notre-Dame has only 5% of the floor area of the Palace of Westminster. Sadly, I think that the approach taken by the official Opposition today has not been constructive at all. I hope that as we get nearer to the vote on costs, a degree of consensus will emerge across the House. The initial £3 billion-capped phased programme ahead of us focuses on investment in underground construction, wiring and plumbing, building temporary Chambers, and restoration of the wonderful medieval cloister court. A “make do and mend” approach is not going to get us anywhere, and a 90-day red team review—a rabbit out of a hat—is not a serious proposal. Let us get on with it.

I first got involved in this issue over 10 years ago. Our colleague Jacob Rees-Mogg, who has been mentioned, served on the original Committee that 10 years ago recommended a full decant to Richmond House. It did not fill us with great enthusiasm that that Committee got its measurements wrong—the IKEA-style chamber could not fit into that part of Richmond House, and of course there would have been enormous expense. I have been working on this issue all this time, and it was apparent to me 10 years ago that we were constantly proposing gold-plating and decanting instead of getting on with the work. The delivery authority—all this period, and certainly from 2019—has been spending vast amounts of taxpayers’ money endlessly developing plans and not repairing the building. It has proposed endless gold-plating works, and it has devised completely unnecessary new ideas, such as a new underground visitors’ entrance. I agree that it is very hard to make things happen in politics, but if you are relentless, you can stop things from happening. I know that I have been a deep disappointment to the right hon. Member for Alyn and Deeside (Sir Mark Tami).

I served with him on these boards for many years, and I did my best to constantly argue, “Please just get on with it.” Eventually, I could not take it any more, and I had to resign from them because of the endless delays. I agree that this is a world heritage building that we love, but at the end of the day it is just a building. All this work has accumulated in a Byzantine structure of layered bureaucracy and committees, officials and consultants. Fractured responsibility and an inevitable lack of accountability is leading year after year to a ballooning bill, with potentially billions wasted on unnecessary works. That is fertile ground for contractors seeking to take advantage to charge what they like for unnecessary works. I have constantly questioned that on these boards, saying, “Why are we not just repairing this building?” We are proposing to spend £40 billion, but we do not yet know the agreed budget. It has not been finalised, and there is no settled scope and no clear accountability to Ministers and the House. Costs are merely estimates. We have £11 billion to £39 billion—for a building! There is a huge amount of uncertainty on which to make decisions. This building was built superbly by the Victorians. Of course it needs maintenance, like all historic buildings, but it is fundamentally sound. The electrical services are complex and in places they are in a mess. We have all been down into the cellar again and again to look at them, but we do not need 15 years of full decant to deal with them. In my view, the problem started when we created the September sitting. Previous Conservative Leaders of the House have been mentioned again and again, and there has been talk of delays, but I hope that people accept that I have at least tried to be consistent on this point about the September sitting. I have made it again and again and been ignored. The problem started when we created it. Years ago, this building was effectively closed from 20 July when we went into recess until 12 October. Everywhere there were workmen working, but we have just bled the building dry. We have even had the public coming in so that they can have lunch in the Members’ Dining Room—very nice, too—but the building is more important. The September sitting is where many of these maintenance problems started. I know that Governments are wary of changing it, because the September sitting is The Daily Mail sitting. The paper might say, “Oh, these MPs are lazy,” and all that, but there is a perfect excuse: this building has to be worked on—it is an old building—for three months or even four months every year without interruption.

I thank my right hon. Friend for making that point, which I was hoping to make myself. Does he agree that 2010, when the September sitting was fully introduced, to 2026 is 16 years, and that six weeks times 16 years is 1.8 years of time that could have been spent working on this place? That is a huge missed opportunity. The renovation work that he speaks of so eloquently could have been happening, and we would now be looking to restore a different Parliament.

That is a very good point. I have argued again and again—and been ignored—that we should repeal the 2019 Act. That is the real problem that has been delaying everything. We cannot do proper works because we are bound by the delivery authority and by the Act. We should abolish the delivery authority. We should get on with it. Some may say, “These people are just selfish. They never want to decant.” There may come a time when we have to decant for a brief period—maybe a month, a year or two years—but we should get on with the work, such as on asbestos in the Chamber. The best way to deal with asbestos, by the way, is to leave it alone, but I put that to one side. We are not ideologues on this. We are prepared to decant for six months, a year or two years if those who advise us say that it is necessary, but we cannot decide all these things in a vacuum. We have to start the work and prepare it. A full decant would be extremely costly, and, according to some estimates, would involve as much as 19 to 24 years away from the Palace. Some people think there is a risk that we would never come back, although actually I do not think that is true: I think that we would come back, and would then be amazed that the thing was exactly the same, with the same pictures in the same places, after 24 years. A whole generation of MPs would be deprived of participating in this historic building. I am not selfish about this. I am quite happy for us to decant, because by the time we decant I shall be in my grave, so I do not care for myself. However, I do care for this building and for future generations. Most important, this is a symbol of the nation. When people across the world think of the United Kingdom, what is the photograph that flashes into their minds? It is the Palace of Westminster. This is not just a building. It is a working building. It is not just a monument. It is not just a museum, although some people want to create it as one. This is about the “mother of parliaments”. It has to be occupied. By the way, I have worked with Prime Ministers and Leaders of the House all along the line on this issue, and they all pay lip service to moving out, but when it comes to it, no Prime Minister ever allows the decant to happen. You do not become Prime Minister after all those years and then end up in Church House or Richmond House. Let us be completely honest about this: they have been kicking it into the long grass because they do not want to decant, and they have got a point, because this building is the symbol of the nation.

I am slightly surprised that the Father of the House is so optimistic that he thinks that after years away from this building, we would come back—I really doubt that—but given that the proposal is to reduce the four available options to two, would it not be sensible to remove the full decant option and choose between two of the other three options that offer a variety of different ways in which we could stay in this House?

I do not know about that. It may be a fair point, and it does reveal part of the problem.
