When it comes to this building there are so many different opinions, so I have some sympathy for the Leader of the House, which is why I have consistently argued—I hope—that we just have to get on with the work. As we all know, the real risk is fire. I have argued again and again that we need fire doors in corridors that are 100 yards long, but apparently we cannot put them in because English Heritage will not let us do it. I have argued for sprinklers for years, and they were installed in the basement, but then the “blob”—the authorities—said, “You cannot turn them on because the firemen might get Legionnaires’ disease.” But the building might burn down! I have asked for sprinklers in every room, and the establishment has said, “You cannot have sprinklers, because English Heritage said that the pictures might be damaged.” But if there is a fire in the building, the place will burn down. Notre-Dame has, of course, been mentioned, and the cause of that fire was the ongoing works. That is the real danger: workers with blowtorches and so forth. The recent record for this sort of work, as we know, has been disastrous. The atrium roof in Portcullis House was replaced after only a quarter of a century, and a massively expensive door has been provided for the House of Lords. It cost £10 million, and it does not work. I sincerely believe that the last thing we should do is to vote through either of these options, which would mean more years of delay, more planning for gold-plating, and more costing that cannot be evaluated. We should all read the excellent letter from the Lord Speaker. It is all there. It says: “The Costed Proposals report recommends authorising up to £3 billion of preparatory expenditure over the next seven years”. That alone is extortionate, in my view, and illustrative of the fact that this will be a very long-winded, expensive, ultimately dissatisfying and potentially disastrous process if pursued in the wrong way. We have been addressing these issues in the most expensive way at a time when the public purse is strained. What would the public make of these figures when there is so much pressure on our hospitals and schools, for instance, and when we are spending so much money on ourselves? They pay for all this. They would be astonished, and they deserve better. Let us pause on what we are talking about. A full decant of the building would cost £11.5 billion, excluding inflation, or £15.6 billion with inflation, and it would take up to 26 years. EMI+, which we have not heard a lot about, could cost up to £39 billion and take 61 years. This is not sensible. I agree with the Lord Speaker that we need “a clear and agreed specification of essential works”. There should be no gold-plating, but we must make the building safe and restore it.

The right hon. Gentleman has mentioned gold-plating a few times, but he has also said that this building is the jewel in the crown for the United Kingdom. He mentioned the underground visitors’ centre, which I want to ask him about. I do not know if he has been to the current visitors’ entrance recently, but I have, and I do not think it is befitting of a grade I listed building. What would he do differently in this situation? What is he actually proposing?

I would repair the building! I would make it safe, which is what we should have done 10 years ago, and make sure that it does not burn down. That is what I would do. We do not need a new visitors’ entrance, a Nelson Mandela room or anything else. The building works. Let us just get on with it. I have served on the R&R boards, and it is staggering. There are 25 members on the client board, and 15 members on the programme board. The delivery authority has been working on this since 2019, and has been endlessly developing plans but not doing anything. My final words: just get on with it.

Madam Deputy Speaker, “Without action, at best the Palace will be in a process of managed decline. At worst, a catastrophic event could occur that endangers lives and interrupts the functioning of democracy in the UK…A failure to act would have serious consequences for taxpayers and future generations.” These are not my words, but those of the Public Accounts Committee—which is chaired by the hon. Member for North Cotswolds (Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown), who is not here today—in its report, “Restoration and Renewal of Parliament: Costing and governance”, and the devil is in the detail. That is a fair assessment by a cross-party group of 16 MPs. The Committee set out a number of conclusions and recommendations. There were eight in total, including engagement with parliamentarians, a timetable of work from the client team, and the question of a “competitive dialogue” procurement approach in relation to gaining clarity on the scope and the cost band schedule. In addition, the Committee set out the remaining cost estimates for phase 1 and suggested a detailed delivery schedule. The Committee also recommended the production of an integrated plan across a number of themes and a temporary accommodation proposal, as well as setting out the risks associated with divided responsibilities. Then there was the recommendation about the simplification of the phase 1 governance process, which will be reviewed ahead of the start of phase 2. That covers a number of the issues that Members have raised today. The final two recommendations relate to a potential restoration and renewal Select Committee, based on the Canadian model—I make no comment about that, but the Public Accounts Committee put that in its recommendations—and to an annual update on the programme’s progress, with an independent annual examination of the programme. Those recommendations are set out in the context of a full decant of both Houses, which would cost £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion over the best part of two decades—I suspect that some of our younger colleagues will still be Members of Parliament at that stage—and a continued presence for up to 45 years, which would cost £22 billion. Then there is the enhanced maintenance and improvement proposal, which would cost £56.3 billion and take between 52 and 84 years. Finally, EMI+ would cost up to £39 billion—and so it goes on. However, the latter options are less developed and more uncertain. At this stage, I would say that I have always been able, notwithstanding the complexity of the issues and the cost programme, to get information from the appropriate teams, including regular information sessions in Portcullis House about the programme. I have managed to get lots of information; if other Members have not got the information, it is not because it is not available. It is there, and if Members choose not to look for it or to do a bit of research, that is a matter for them.

My hon. Friend is making a very good point. Does he recognise that the independent advice and assurance panel itself recommended the scale of works proposed by the restoration and renewal programme, that the R and R client board’s assessment at the end of last year checked and benchmarked the proposals against comparable projects, including Manchester town hall, and that delivery costs per square metre are similar to those for the Canadian Parliament when judged by volume?

My hon. Friend makes a really important point. There is a lot of ultracrepidarianism going on here. People who think that they are, or may even be, experts in one field seem to think they can make judgments in an expert fashion about things that frankly they do not know very much about. It is also called epistemic trespass. I suggest that Members go and have a look at what that means, if they are not an expert on it. In July 2022, both Houses—the Commons on 12 July and the Lords on 13 July—agreed a mandate, unamended and without a vote, that in effect the vision for the restoration and renewal programme would be “preserving the Palace of Westminster for future generations and ensuring the safety of all those who work in and visit the Palace, now and in the future”. It is now the job of this House to put that intention into practice. I fully appreciate that Members across the House have differing views about the timetable and the costs. Having decided on phase 1, for example, is it not time to just move on? I think the time has passed for continuing the debate about whether we want to do it, because it is time to move on. We really need to act. We need to stick to a timetable for making decisions without further prevarication, because that is all I have heard today. Have we not prevaricated enough over this? At what point do we stop asking for more information, more facts, more projections, more reassessments, more surveys and more re-evaluations? The longer we delay, for whatever reason, the more money we will be asking the taxpayer for.

Madam Deputy Speaker, I look in your direction with trepidation, but I apologise abjectly for my tardiness. I may be about to ruin my career in this place, but if Members do not know, I served on the small committee that oversaw the building of the Scottish Parliament. [Hon. Members: “Ooh!”] Members may well say “Ooh!” What I know from the experience—I speak bearing the scars—is that every time there was a delay, for whatever reason, the price went up. To that, I would add two things. First, the building was completed in 2004, and today people say, “It won the Stirling prize. What was the fuss all about?” Secondly, there is a cautionary tale here for my friends sitting to my right: the Conservatives, led by my old friend the late David McLetchie, refused to have anything to do with the building of the Parliament, which meant that they were not involved in some crucial decisions that affected the way the offices were laid out. The hon. Member for Berwickshire, Roxburgh and Selkirk (John Lamont) will remember that. I would argue, and I think the Conservatives would now argue, that it was a mistake not to get fully involved and work on a consensual and cross-party basis.

Kicking the can down the road, as it has been referred to today, is not going to sort out the problem. We are facing this problem now—not tomorrow, next week or the week after, but now. It is the problem set out at the very beginning of my speech, and it is the undeniable concern that many people have about the safety of this building. In just eight years’ time, it will be the 200th anniversary of the fire that consumed this Palace in 1832. I acknowledge that in these debates we do not want to present selective and out-of-context quotes from various associated documents, for example from members of the restoration and renewal client board, as a blunt instrument. Having said that, when those documents are there, we do have to look at them and put them into context. We do not have to take them at face value, but we do have to acknowledge that they are not manufactured. The people advising us are not just sitting there making things up as they go along. In paragraph 114 of “Delivering restoration and renewal of the Palace of Westminster: the costed proposals”, the board states: “The independent health, safety and fire panel concluded that all delivery options could be delivered safely, including both EMI variants.” Those are the one that will go on till the cows come home. But the panel did note that “concurrent construction sites, continued occupation of the Palace of Westminster and longer programme duration for the EMI variants increased the risks arising in a number of areas” and therefore increased the costs that people are talking about. I repeat that I do not want to take those observations out of context, but it is important to note that there are increased risk factors in delays to implementing the longer term plans that phase 1 wishes to put in train. What about the concerns expressed by staff about the conditions they work in, to which my right hon. Friend the Member for Hayes and Harlington (John McDonnell) referred? Only today, we received a letter—hon. Members may have read it—from representative bodies expressing their concern about the further delays that the Opposition motion may produce. The report sets out the cost of delay. We have heard various figures: £250 million to £350 million a year in inflationary construction costs across the Parliament. That is a huge amount. If we accept the figure cited by the shadow Leader of the House, then, as the Leader of the House says, that is another £100 million to put it off for three months. Are they being serious? We all acknowledge the importance of this world heritage site. We have to move on. I have heard comparisons with Notre-Dame, but I think that is a spurious argument. On the Hansard Society podcast, Ruth Fox and Mark D’Arcy interviewed the shadow Leader of the House—I am sorry he is not here to hear this point—and said, in effect, that it was a spurious comparison. As Members have said, this area is 14 times the size of Notre-Dame. Actually, the figures for fixing and refurbishing the building are not far off. We should not prevaricate much longer. The taxpayer is used in all sorts of forums to justify this or that expenditure on the grounds of “the interest of the taxpayer”. I do not want to rehearse those examples again; we just have to try to move the debate on. I will finish shortly. The shadow Leader of the House—it is a shame that he is not here for this—is a Burkean scholar, so I hope he will appreciate my quoting Edmund Burke: “It is a general error to suppose the loudest complainers for the public to be the most anxious for its welfare.” The right hon. Gentleman, when he reads that, will forgive me, but that is what I am seeing today. I do not trust the loudest voices of the complainers, and neither did Edmund Burke. I am not suggesting that anyone is telling lies today, but I will quote the French philosopher Alexis de Tocqueville: “It is easier for the world to accept a simple lie than a complex truth.” This is the complex truth, and we really do hav

The restoration and renewal programme is best characterised as one clouded in denial. We can see that from the costs that have already been cited in this debate. Understandably, the hon. Member for Boston and Skegness (Richard Tice) quoted from the National Audit Office report. Figure 1, on page 20, sets out the cost of decant: £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion. Those NAO costs came from the fully costed proposals from the delivery authority, but Members are kidding themselves if they think that they are the true costs. The intervention from the hon. Member for Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket (Dr Prinsley) was a good illustration of that point. He said that we need to get on with restoration and renewal because of the work in his office on Parliament Street. That is outside the scope; it is actually covered by a different programme. It is £5.3 billion that is being spent and kept off the books. It is off the restoration and renewal books, but £3 billion of it is presented as essential to enable decant to happen. It is presented as integral to the R and R programme, but it is kept off the books. Of that £5.3 billion, a further £1.7 billion is actually work on the Palace: bridging work over the next 10 to 15 years, much of which will be ripped out because of the delay. This is work that we are going to commit to but then remove, none of which is on the restoration and renewal books.

The right hon. Member referred to the National Audit Office, which said in its update earlier this year that carrying out phase 1 preparatory works while progressing the programme is “a sensible approach”. Does the right hon. Member agree with the NAO on that point?

The hon. Member is talking about the £3 billion that the NAO has said is for phase 1. We have taken seven years to go from one option in the original legislation to four options. Now, those in the House today who are saying that we must get on with it are actually saying, “Let’s go, over the next seven years, from four options to two.” That is the proposal. Interestingly, most of the £3 billion that the hon. Member is talking about is not work on restoration and renewal. It is things like a temporary jetty, the QEII centre, temporary accommodation for the House of Lords and a temporary Chamber of the House of Commons. Most of that is not work on things like asbestos or work on the House, but facilitation for the future restoration. It is not dealing with the immediate fire risk that many Members have cited. That £3 billion is just preparatory work for after 2042, when the full decant actually happens. Let me go back to the figures, because it is not just £5.3 billion that is being kept off the books. We start with £15.6 billion in the NAO report. We have £5.3 billion of work on our estate—work that our constituents will say is for MPs’ offices. We have £5.3 billion off the books, but we know that because of delays that have arisen since February, the delivery authority now says that decant is going to take three years longer, from 2039 to 2042. The Lord Speaker says that that will cost an additional £800 million. That is not in the figures given in figure 1. There is also a further £612 million, which relates to work that the delivery authority has already spent. That is not in the figures. There is other work, too, such as the £100 million or so that is to be spent on streetscape to pedestrianise Parliament Square. That is not in these figures either. My point is that the figures are huge: we are talking about north of £22 billion. To put that in context, the Government’s defence investment plan is only £15 billion—half of which, incidentally, was unfunded, and when I challenged the Defence Secretary on the £3 billion of capital reprioritisation, he did not have a clue where it was coming from. The Treasury Committee, which has a majority of Labour MPs, has said that it is a “moral imperative” to address the freeze on student loans. That will cost about £255 million to £355 million over this Parliament. For R and R, we are talking about north of £22 billion, which does not even include inconvenient things like inflation. The figures were based on inflation as of December last year, and we already know that inflation is now higher. That is before we get on to highly predictable cost overruns. It is great to hear the Scottish Parliament mentioned as an example: that was a programme that massively overran. The Elizabeth Tower started at below £30 million and ended up at just under £80 million. The Lords gate, which has also been mentioned, started at £3 million, ended up at £9 million and then did not properly work. We know that there is a high likelihood of cost overruns, and yet these sums are absolutely huge in the context of wider Government pressure. The second issue is that we are ignoring advice from the people who actually know what they are talking about on these issues. Let me give an example: Lord Morse, the former Comptroller and Auditor General, was a figure respected across the House. He said that due to the constraints of the site, capacity-wise there is a limit on what can be done in any one year, using the phrase, “There is only so much you can force through the tube.” I have not heard anyone mention the run rate. We are going from a run rate of £200 million to a run rate of £600 million by 2030—a threefold increase. Let us look at whether we are managing our existing flow effectively. Has anyone walked over to College Green car park? We took it back from Westminster council, but it is now mired in legal dispute, as my right hon. Friend the Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison) knows, because it has been

The right hon. Gentleman has clearly studied the figures, and I know that he has a great reverence for the building that we are in. Given that he has looked at the figures and has quite a good understanding, what is the top figure he would put on spending to do the work? What I am hearing from the Opposition is all the things that are wrong, but no proposals for what could go right, other than more time.

That is an absolutely fair challenge. To be fair, I grappled with it for a while, because it is not enough just to say what we are against; we have to come forward with solutions. I will close with exactly that point, because it is a fair challenge and people need to get off the fence. I have a very clear answer. However, I want to say first that I think people are having the wool pulled over their eyes on the total cost, and I think Members will have other priorities in their constituencies where that money could be spent. Secondly, there are capacity issues. People need only to look at some of the existing programmes to see that. For example, the streetscape project will require changing the New Palace Yard programme, which was finished just this year. There are interplays between these programmes that we also need to consider. I have huge respect for the Leader of the House. I do not know what the dispute is between the Front Benches, but he is someone I hold in the highest regard. However, I would just say to Labour MPs that although those on their Front Bench are saying that this is just a parliamentary matter and that it is nothing to do with the Government, we are in fact talking about taxes raised by a Labour Government, to a Labour Treasury, to fund something in a House, the majority which is made up of Labour MPs. It will be quite hard for the Minister on the morning media round to say that this is nothing to do with a Labour Government. The Government may say that emotions come in. I spoke in the Sir David Amess debate, pointing out that we have had the full cost since February and asking where the debate was. If anyone thinks I was coming to it late, I also spoke in the same debate the year before. The Leader of the House knows that I wrote a detailed five-page letter to the previous Leader of the House, to which I got a cursory couple of paragraphs in response; I sent him that in his first week in office. That letter flagged things like the complete shambles of the governance, which is highlighted in the NAO report. These are not new issues. We have known about the governance issue. Turning back to the figure of £3 billion, people are being asked to sign that off before fixing the known governance issue. The point I have repeatedly tried to make to colleagues is that more than half of this House is new, and yet, two and a half years in, we have still not tested its opinion. It has taken an Opposition day to float these issues, which some of us have been trying to flag as a national scandal that is going to fall before us. The Government will be responsible for this, because, ultimately, the Government have control. The Leader of the House was a Chief Whip. He knows that when there is a free vote, colleagues will often turn to those on their Front Bench and ask for a steer. I do not think it is credible for the Prime Minister to say that he does not have a view on the spending of £20-odd billion. I will close by addressing exactly what I feel we should do. I think we should decant for a very fixed period of four years: within one Parliament, addressing the concerns of the Father of the House—equivalent to a world war in terms of time. We should have very clear accountability and reform the governance process. More than half of this House is new; we should agree as a House what the budget is. We should do as much as we can on the key risks—fire, flood and asbestos—within that time. We can do a lot of work in four years. Covid showed that when there is a will, people can work differently and work can be done quickly. We also need to be clear about the trade-offs. There will be a difference of views. If we go from having 12% to 60% stair-free access, disability rights campaigners may say that this is money well spent, whereas others may have concerns. Reducing the energy bill by 40% may be what some people want to do, while some may feel that there are other things that can be done instead. I will put this in context

I declare an interest as co-chair of the disability parliamentary Labour party group and chair of the cross-party Members’ accessibility group. I rise to speak against the Opposition motion, and to support the points in the Government’s motion that Parliament is an important heritage asset and a large employer and that delay in making the necessary changes will lead to soaring costs for the British public. I make this case in support of the Government on the basis of 20 years working in disability law and policy, and over two decades driving access audits, physical adaptations and infrastructure improvements to public buildings from university institutions to civic town halls. Consequently, I firmly disagree with the Opposition that the scale of changes to Parliament as part of restoration and renewal are particularly difficult to justify. Indeed, I think the reverse. It is a great travesty that the Conservatives spent 14 years failing to implement the Equality Act 2010 in the fabric of the building that makes the laws of our country, thus driving up the cost of restoration and renewal through their dither and delay. Making this case is especially important as we are in the middle of Disability History Month, the theme of which is “Disability, Politics and Democracy”. The accessibility of our democratic institution increases the inclusion in our politics of disabled people. When I was growing up in my constituency and deciding what I wanted to do for my degree, I understood then, as I do now, that law is power. Just as we need our courts to include representation of a wide range of protected characteristics, so too do we need to ensure that this House has the widest possible representation as the place of our nations’ legislators. I am proud to be the first ever Member of Parliament with a congenital limb difference. Disabled people make up 20% of the voting-age population in the UK, yet at the last count only eight of the 650 of us elected to this Chamber have a disability. That is just not good enough. “Nothing about us without us” is a central tenet of the disability rights movement. This Chamber passed the Equality Act 2010, which requires public sector providers and organisations to make reasonable adjustments to their buildings, processes and services to enable disabled people to be included. It is urgent to make those changes for the representation of our democracy. Centenary Action’s 2025 report cites the “lack of reasonable adjustments by political institutions and…parties” as a “major barrier” to disabled women standing for election. Indeed, article 29 of the UN convention on the rights of persons with disabilities, which the UK ratified in 2009, requires state parties “To ensure that persons with disabilities can effectively and fully participate in political and public life on an equal basis with others…including the right and opportunity…to…be elected” and the active promotion of an environment in which persons with disabilities can effectively and fully participate. Yet when I was elected to Parliament in 2024, there was no disabled toilet near the Chamber, there were no accessible door handles in Portcullis House—the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman), referred to that—and there was no specific means of reserving a seat on these green Benches for any of us who have mobility impairments without using a prayer or Select Committee card.
My hon. Friend is making a powerful speech. Would she describe the measures she is outlining as gold-plating?

No, I would describe them as a gateway to an inclusive democracy. This building, in which laws are made and where we ensure power is fully exercised in a way that reflects the vibrance and diversity of our proud British democracy, should be accessible and inclusive to our citizens. This Parliament is a House where all British people should feel at home: it belongs to them, too. Thanks to the state education I had in Penistone, which helped me catch up on three years of surgeries that I needed, I was able to go on to study at the University of Oxford, where I did a law degree to understand how disabled people could have a greater role in making and changing the law. It is the honour of my life to sit on these green Benches and speak in this Chamber as the voice for the place where I grew up.

The hon. Member is making a really passionate speech about something incredibly important: the accessibility of this building, along with attracting people from all walks of life—with all disabilities and none—to take part in democracy. Would she say something about the importance of getting people with disabilities to work here? This is also a workplace; it is not just about parliamentarians.

The hon. Lady will be pleased to hear that I am about to come to that. When I was at Oxford, I spent nearly a decade working to make the places and spaces of that other great British institution and globally renowned university more inclusive. That means that I am well versed in what inclusive design looks like in beautiful heritage assets. If that is possible in one of the world’s global universities, it is possible to do such work empathetically and inclusively in the mother of all Parliaments. That matters: it ensures that disabled people up and down the country know that they can access the space that holds the seat at the country’s decision-making table. There are 2 million visitors to this place every year; it is likely that at least 20% of those people will be disabled. People contributing evidence to Select Committees, all-party parliamentary groups and Bill Committees need access to this place, too. While they are here, they should be treated with the dignity and respect they deserve. It is not only that; Parliament provides jobs for thousands of people. In the last two weeks, this Chamber has seen statements on the biggest overhaul of how we increase the employment of disabled people in nearly a generation. We must therefore ensure that the restoration and renewal of this building plays its own part in increasing the representation of disabled people in this workplace and in closing the disability employment gap. Our parliamentary procedures, research and constituency offices all serve our constituents better when it is easier to employ disabled staff members and when this workplace is more accessible to them—and that is not to mention the need to make sure that they are all protected from accident and injury in this workplace.

Does my hon. Friend not find it incredible that 88% of this building is not wheelchair-accessible? In the case of a fire, what would happen to people who were here in wheelchairs? Again, that is not gold-plating.

I agree. That is the result of 14 years of Conservative dither and delay. I task colleagues on the Conservative Benches with spending a day going around this Parliament sat in a wheelchair so that they can really understand the barriers that many of us face.

Specifically on that point, I was at an event in the Churchill Room and there was a young man in a wheelchair. I decided to accompany him out of the building and it was quite an assault course to get out. I wholeheartedly agree with my hon. Friend. She is making a powerful and important speech. We need to put in investment in order to enable disabled people. They are disabled by institutions such as this House, unfortunately, and those elsewhere in the country. We need to end that and to enable them.

I completely agree. My experience of forging adaptations to heritage assets in other public institutions has taught me that making accessibility changes in spaces such as this one is not the Gordian knot that those on the Conservative Benches seem to fear. Perhaps they do not know that because, when in government, they avoided any action to try to unravel that knot. Over the last two years since being elected, I have set up the first disability parliamentary Labour party grouping, along with other colleagues on the Labour Benches. That has enabled us to feed in our concerns about the accessibility of this Palace to the Government. Thanks to the hard work of the Leader of the House and the Secretary of State for Education in her previous role, a number of disabled MPs were able to contribute to the Modernisation Committee. Further to that, I have been pleased to work with House officials to establish Parliament’s first ever Members’ Accessibility Group, so that we can work cross-party to identify the changes that we need to make in this place to ensure that it is more accessible. So far, that has led to changes such as the first accessible toilet near the Chamber, accessible door handles across the estate—though that is still a work in progress—and reasonable adjustment cards to reserve spaces on these green Benches. My thanks go to Mr Speaker and the Serjeant at Arms in particular for their support in making that happen. It is the first centralised system for Members to communicate about reasonable adjustments in the House’s history. As the mother of all Parliaments, it is paramount that this space is accessible and inclusive so that it attracts and enables a greater group of disabled people to be represented in the Chamber, because democracy is an order of equality and non-discrimination. It is an enormous irony that this place, where laws are made, is not sufficiently accessible to millions of people to whom those laws apply. The inclusiveness of the law and the power that it has over people’s lives is further legitimised when more disabled people have a voice, whether it is in the recent reforms to employment, the forthcoming reforms to SEND legislation or anything from the access to inclusive maternity care for disabled women to inclusive action on climate change. Embedding inclusion into this House has a filter-down effect on the inclusiveness of the laws of this land and sets the very highest bar of leadership for organisations up and down this country, including public services, which must make their workplaces more accessible. You can only be what you can see, so we must remove physical barriers to disabled participation in this place to ensure that every disabled person who wants to make a change and be the difference can do that. I want them to hear this from us today: they deserve to be in the room and, more than that, they deserve to sit at those decision-making tables wherever they find them. Their ideas matter, their questions matter and their solutions matter. We must always put down the ladders and the ramps to enable other disabled people to rise with us into this House. For too long, our presence has not adorned the places and spaces of public life; our mark has gone unrecorded. Let us change that together today by making this place more accessible through restoration and renewal.
Order. I will impose a five-minute time limit after the next speaker.

I want to put on record my thanks to all the House officials who, over the last 10 years, have had the deeply unenviable task of trying to come up with recommendations, solutions, ideas and briefings for MPs of this Parliament and previous ones. It has not been easy for them. I agree with the Leader of the House that far too many confusing signals have been sent to House staff about what this House and the other place want. I have always argued, since I first became the MP for South Leicestershire over 10 years ago, that this building is large enough to zone off, repair and get on with it, as the Father of the House, my right hon. Friend the Member for Gainsborough (Sir Edward Leigh), has rightly reminded colleagues. We sit in a Chamber that many, even some MPs, think is a Victorian Chamber, but of course it is a 1951 edifice. In May 1941, the Luftwaffe struck a direct hit on what was the Victorian Chamber, blowing it to smithereens. We have passed the portrait of Winston Churchill on the back stairs at the north end hundreds of times, in which he is standing in the ruins of the Victorian Chamber. Within the space of weeks, the House of Commons was relocated to the House of Lords, and the House of Lords was relocated to the Robing Room. Notwithstanding all the Victorian pipework, the asbestos and all the other infrastructure and plant that continues to work to this day, they seemingly managed to do it. People often say, “Oh, but the health and safety laws were different back then.” Yes, they were, but not so different that people were unable to work around the building and construction work. What other buildings have commonalities with this Chamber? The Chair of the Administration Committee, the hon. Member for Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney (Nick Smith), rightly referred to Notre-Dame, but I encourage him, and indeed the whole Committee, to visit the University of Glasgow. That is another Gothic revival edifice, and it is about a quarter of the size of this building. Incidentally, the architect of the University of Glasgow was the grandfather of the architect of this Chamber that we are seated in today. We visited the University of Glasgow to learn how it was done. Over the last three decades, the main building was renovated without having to decant the main headquarters. It can be done. I would go further. Most Members are probably utterly unaware that a few metres behind the Government Benches, a five-storey building was built in the early 1970s. The House was not decanted, the work did not create subsidence problems for Westminster Hall and we now have a car park that was built with minimal fuss in four years. That was only in the 1970s. When I first visited this place back in 1984, at the young age of 13, the entire building was covered with scaffolding. Over a five-year period, stonemasonry and sandblasting work was undertaken quickly, efficiently and at reasonable cost, and the House of Commons and the House of Lords continued to meet in this locus. There was no need to decant. Those of us who were in the last Parliament, as many Labour Members were, had the personal experience of seeing the part of the building that we call the Elizabeth Tower being zoned off. The clock tower was repaired with minimal fuss. Yes, the repairs were completed a few years after the original timeline that had been set out, but it was repaired without causing any blockage between the Palace and the rest of the northern estate. The House agreed to the renewal of the Victoria Tower, an even larger edifice. The parliamentary archives were shipped off to Kew and the building stands empty. It could easily be zoned off and refurbished. There is no need to do a full decant of this building—this building is so large that it can be zoned off over a period of years, and necessary urgent repair and remedial work can be undertaken. The hon. Member for Caithness, Sutherland and Easter Ross (Jamie Stone) rightly referred to Holyrood and his own involvement in t

Lord Fraser conducted the Holyrood inquiry and I gave evidence to it. I did not say, “It wisnae me.” I am proud of what Lord Fraser said in his concluding remarks, because he said that I gave surprisingly honest evidence. I rest my case.

I welcome the hon. Member’s intervention and I am glad to hear him confirm that, indeed, “It wisnae me.” The point remains that this country has had a problem with public sector building work. The Scottish Parliament building is a prime example and HS2 is another. I am not blaming MPs, Lords or House officials, but businesses out there are licking their lips about what will be the biggest building project in recent British history if we decide to do a full decant.

In around 2009, I hand-delivered a pre-qualification questionnaire to Parliament as the company I was working for at the time wanted to be a part of that bonanza. Many years later, as the hon. Gentleman’s colleagues are talking about these huge contingency plans, does he not recognise that the delay has made many contractors not want to work with us, and that they will probably be building a hell of a lot of risk into what they put in their estimates?

That may well be the case. However, 10 years ago, I and many colleagues were arguing, as the Father of the House said, just to get on with it and repair the building. It is sad to see that after 10 years we have simply not done that. I still do not understand why the Victoria Tower stands empty when that particular part of the building could be repaired. I am mindful that others want to speak, but a couple of hon. Members have referred to this building representing the mother of all Parliaments. My concern is not so much that we remind colleagues that this is the mother of all Parliaments; my concern is that if we squander taxpayers’ money and we do a full decant, it will become the mother of all white elephants in British public building work.

Given that the Opposition have, peculiarly, chosen this issue for an Opposition-day debate, I will start with the Conservative party. I thought its raison d’être was to conserve, but apparently not when it comes to conserving this place, the UK Parliament. The Leader of the Opposition called it akin to bankrolling billions to create a “net-zero Dubai hotel”, mocking efforts to restore this very place. I have been with the Public Accounts Committee to Buckingham Palace to see how the decisions that gripped the timeline and project management led to a successful restoration programme there. I have been underneath this building, metres below, and I thank the R and R team who do a wonderful job in explaining why Parliament needs restoring. This issue was ducked by the Conservative party for years and years. In 2018, the Labour party backed a timely decant to allow essential restoration. Who voted against that? The Leader of the Opposition. Now, more than five years after that, Conservative Members come crowing about the cost of their own decision. This is just a wider problem of a failure to deliver infrastructure projects such as High Speed 2. We saw that with Crossrail, the completion of which was delayed, and even with a garden bridge. Now Conservative Members come here pointing the finger at everyone but themselves. I have heard many contributions from Conservative Members, but what has not been mentioned? An apology. Conservative Members have a pattern: destroy public services, let large projects spiral in cost, get obliterated in a general election, and never show even a modicum of humility. They really have learned nothing. I am the son of a surveyor and joiner, and a fire safety officer—my mum. The safety of buildings is perhaps in my DNA, which is why I believe that the safety of the staff who work here—the Doorkeepers, cleaners, cooks and so on—should be central to our decision. I encourage hon. Members to go to the ticket office in Central Lobby, where a plaque commemorates the contributions of those who made this place. The safety of those who work in this place should never be debated and traded off. I wish to touch on something important. In 1984, York Minster had a fire. I am proud that my dad was an apprentice joiner in the restoration work. We learned that timely decisions on decant were integral to that. I also want to touch on heritage skills, because my York Outer constituency will play a huge role in the restoration of this place. There is a centre of excellence for heritage skills in the grounds of York Minster, and there has been a revival of the 800-year-old tradition of apprentices living and working on the site. Up the road at York College in my constituency, stone masons learn their craft. It is one of the few places in the country to do that, and the pride of a stone mason is always seeing their mark left in the stone—a signature that will outlast them for centuries. That is a metaphor, if ever we needed one, for the generational impact of investing in vocational skills.

Green MPs think the motion is incredibly irresponsible, and I have heard some unusual and, quite honestly, dangerous suggestions from people who, with respect, I suspect have never picked up a screwdriver, yet who are apparently now experts in construction. Does the hon. Gentleman agree that we need more people from ordinary backgrounds and with those skills in this place? When I was working as a plumber, there is no way I would have advised a customer to keep spending eye-watering sums of money rather than just getting on with the job. We need to make these Benches more accessible for everyone.

I hope the hon. Lady will therefore encourage her party to back the Milburn report, which will be transformative in bringing those vocational skills and opportunities to young people. I will let other Members contribute, but I just wanted to touch on some recent visitors. Club Wilber, a local group of visually impaired children, visited Parliament just the other week. Their curiosity and fascination with this building was humbling. They saw things where they could, and asked questions where they could not. I will always remember when the children walked through the corridors just behind the Chamber. They were reaching for the MPs’ lockers and using their sense of touch to explore the immense history of this place.

I will not just because of the other Members wanting to speak. We must remember the visitor experience of those disabled children from my constituency, and the thousands who visit here every month—that is the point that my hon. Friend the Member for Penistone and Stocksbridge (Dr Tidball) made so well. There is no price too high when it comes to accessibility for some incredibly inspirational children to this place. Let me end by praising the Prime Minister, who took the decision to lift part of the Executive branch to No. 10 North. That really fosters a conversation with the public about how we can share debate across the country. As we look to the R and R of this place, I encourage conversations so that we can have further debates closer to communities such as mine. That is precisely our ambition with rewiring the state. This is the home of our democracy, and we must look after it.

I disagree with some of the things that the hon. Member for York Outer (Mr Charters) just said, but I agree vehemently with his points about heritage skills. I will not repeat his points, but I agree with them completely. It is clear that there is broad agreement across the House that the Palace of Westminster must be restored. The question before us is not whether that work should take place, but how we deliver it in a way that protects a historic building while providing value for money for the British taxpayer. As a former Heritage Minister, I have a particular passion for protecting our historic built environment. Parliament is one of the most recognised symbols of our democracy. It is a UNESCO world heritage site and a building entrusted to us by previous generations to be preserved for those who come after us. For centuries, it has been at the heart of our national life, witnessing some of the most significant moments in British history. It is precisely because this institution matters so much that we must get its restoration right. It is therefore worrying that no one appears to be truly in charge. Cost estimates continue to rise and timelines continue to slip, yet accountability remains fragmented across committees, boards and delivery bodies—I think we have had five boards and counting. If everyone is responsible, we know that no one is responsible, so governance is key. Especially at a time when we are asking families to make difficult financial decisions, Parliament cannot except itself from the standards that it expects of every Department and every household budget. Every pound spent here is a pound that cannot be spent elsewhere. We must therefore ensure that the process is streamlined wherever possible, that unnecessary costs are eliminated and that savings are secured without compromising safety. The Notre-Dame restoration has been commented on several times already today. It cannot be directly referenced—it is not directly the same thing—but there are many lessons to be learned from its restoration, particularly in how the French had a sense of urgency, a clear scope, decisive delivery and clear governance. After the 2019 fire, they were able to restore Notre-Dame and reopen it in just over five years, at a cost of about £846 million. It did not seem to have layers of billions of pounds of contingency funding and management costs, as our plans do. That is an important point. What is it that others are able to do overseas that we are getting wrong here? We need to genuinely look at where we can learn. The costs are truly astronomical, ranging from £11 billion to £39 billion. Why is so much of the money being allocated to contingency, planning and project management? Why is so little of the total proportion going to actual, physical labour on construction and actual building materials? We must carefully consider those things. Several hon. Members have said today, “Oh, these big infrastructure projects and big Government projects overrun all the time.” No, they do not. I am very proud that I led the delivery of the Commonwealth games. That was a different project, but it was a major project of £750 million involving construction and the building of a stadium and a new aquatics stadium. The reason why I reference that is that not only did we deliver on time, despite construction happening during the pandemic, but we delivered under budget. The lessons from that are important, because we had clear governance and accountability, a sense of focus, a fantastic team and, really importantly, rigorous discipline in the oversight of contractors. We can deliver projects on time and on budget. This debate is not about whether we restore the Palace of Westminster—of course we must. It is not about whether we preserve one of the great democratic institutions—of course we should. The question is about how we do so with the discipline, accountability and value for money that the British public expect from us all. Let us ensure
Order. With a four-minute time limit, I call Dr Jeevun Sandher.

This place is not merely a place in which we live or represent others; it is the physical manifestation of what makes this country great—indeed, the greatest country that has ever been. This place is where we expanded voice, and it is where different people were represented in the making of powerful decisions that not only ensured they had political representation, which they did, but set the stage for the industrial revolution, and therefore the greatest expansion in human dignity and welfare there has ever been. We also know that in this place—in this building—we must not only preserve the values that we hold dear for future generations, but ensure that the building physically remains. As we all accept on both sides of the House, the building is not physically where it needs to be. When I say this place is a physical manifestation of what makes this country great, I refer to the fact that it was first built by one of the sons of William I, and it was where we saw the Earl of Leicester call his first Parliament in Westminster. It is where we then saw a king who tried to implement his absolutist monarchy be not only rejected by MPs, but sadly sentenced to death. It is where we saw the passage of reform Acts that ensured the representation of people and their voices in the making of decisions. This place does not just represent those events; it is where they happened. This place—and this country— was the first on Earth to see sustained economic growth, precisely because of the ways in which power spread from this area and ensured that policy was made in the interests of people outside a very narrow and select few. We also know that this place is falling apart. We know about the fire risks, and we know about the risks to the electrics and the leaks, because we see and experience them. We also know about falling masonry. I heard of one colleague who had some masonry fall on their staff member’s desk. Of course, had it fallen somewhere different, that may have had a rather more tragic outcome. That is what we are here to fix. I believe that everyone across the House acts in good faith in seeking to not only preserve the physical institution, but ensure that our values are preserved for future generations. Others may say that the Conservatives are cynical, having not dealt with this issue during 14 years in office. Some say they are now cynical in knowing that delays will cost us money. Some may say they are cynical in trying to undermine the good faith of those who are trying to renew this place for future generations, by making that look short-sighted. Some would say that the Conservatives are cynical, but I would not—I will leave that to other hon. Members. I remember how I felt when I entered this place for the first time—it was not actually when I became an MP, but when I was 20 years old. I did not have a beard back then, so a lot has changed, but my reverence for this place never has. I know this is a special place that represents so much more than the building. It represents the values we hold dear, and the values that we have given to not just our people but the entire globe.

There is no doubt in my mind that, right across the House, we all recognise the historic and democratic importance of this building, as well as the need to ensure that it is safe for everyone who works here, and for everyone who visits. We have a duty to preserve this place for future generations. We also have a duty and responsibility to our constituents—the people whose taxes will pay for this work. For people in Aldridge-Brownhills, the sums being discussed today, which range between £11.1 billion and £39.2 billion, are absolutely eye-watering. They rightly expect us to ask questions about how their hard-earned money will be spent. That is why over recent months, not just today, I have tabled a series of written questions to the restoration and renewal client board. I want to focus on three issues arising from those answers: the scope of the programme, the initial expenditure and the accountability for delivery. My first concern is whether we have properly examined a more affordable approach. I asked the client board whether a reduced programme focused on only the essential safety and resilience changes had been fully costed. The answer confirmed that no alternative scope had been costed to the same level of detail as the preferred scheme. How can that be the case? Surely that estimate matters. If we are to be able to make informed choices and comparisons before committing billions of pounds, we need to understand what is essential, what improvements are proposed alongside it, and what each approach would cost. I recognise that the Leader of the House is not in his place at the minute, but I would be grateful if he could explain to me how Members are expected to make an informed decision on value for money without that information. Secondly, there is the proposed £3 billion initial works package. I specifically asked how much of that expenditure could become sunken costs if Parliament subsequently changed its plans. The answer did not give me a figure. The Public Accounts Committee has since warned that once the initial package is approved, it will be extremely difficult and costly not to proceed with the entire project. That is a significant warning, so we need to understand how far the first decision will, in practice, commit us to the next. What expenditure would be recoverable, what would be lost, and what choices would remain open to a future Parliament? Thirdly, there must be accountability. When I asked about individual enhancements such as new visitor facilities, the proposed visitor plaza, relocating the Education Centre and so on, the client board confirmed that “there are no standalone business cases for individual scope elements within the Palace”. When I asked about construction risks, it acknowledged that “some…are not yet fully reflected in the quantitative modelling”. Those answers reinforce the need for scrutiny before further commitments are made. Who will take responsibility if costs increase, how will Members scrutinise changes, and what action will follow if delivery falls behind? I recognise that delay has a cost. I also recognise the work undertaken by staff to keep this building safe and operational, but the answer must be a restoration project with clear priorities, a credible timetable and proper financial control. When we are spending money on Parliament itself, we should be setting that example.

In this debate, we have heard many wise words from Conservative Members. It is just a shame that they did not voice those wise words when they were in power. The decision to decant and get on with the works was taken on 31 January 2018. A similar resolution was passed in the House of Lords. I and other Members who were in Parliament then voted; it was a cross-party vote, not a whipped vote, because it was a matter for the House. In that debate, the then Leader of the House, Dame Andrea Leadsom, spoke about the urgent need for restoration and renewal works to begin because of, among other things, the “hotch-potch of pipework and wiring” —[ Official Report , 31 January 2018; Vol. 635, c. 880.] in the basement of the Palace, the risk of fire and the need for asbestos removal. A number of Members who are on the Opposition Benches today took part in that Division and voted in the way they wanted to vote. At the time, the cost of doing the works was around £3.5 billion. Since then, there has been a 36% increase in the consumer price index—that is inflation alone. Dame Andrea Leadsom said at the time that the debate we were having, on 31 January 2018, should have taken place 40 years earlier. Following the two votes that we had, in the Commons and in the other place, an Act was passed: the Parliamentary Buildings (Restoration and Renewal) Act, which set up a Sponsor Body to get on with the works. Unfortunately, the Sponsor Body did not do its job, and its powers were then subsumed back into Parliament. The restoration works have a chequered past, and it is incumbent on all of us to make sure that we start those works as soon as possible, progress them and get things done. Other Parliaments seem able to do this: Canada has decanted its Parliament, which is still undergoing restoration and renewal works; the Dutch Parliament has been decanted, and works are under way; the Austrian Parliament has already done its works. The Public Accounts Committee’s report on the cost of these restoration works says that the cost of delaying would be about £420 million each year. Kicking the can down the road is not an option. That will cost £1.5 million a week, and that is unacceptable. We need to get a move on, and we need to get the works done as soon as possible. As to what those works will be, I do not know whether it was by fortune or design, but there is a stall in Portcullis House that lists all the information. If people want to know what the £3 billion will go to, there is a phase 1 sheet that lists all the works, and I encourage people to have a look at it. The Father of the House, the right hon. Member for Gainsborough (Sir Edward Leigh) said that we need to get a move on, and we do, but we will only be able to do so if we start phase 1 of the works as soon as possible. There will be a vote in this House on 8 December, as the Leader of the House has said. I encourage everybody to take part in that and to vote the way they want to. It should not be a whipped vote; we should all have our say in how we want the future of Parliament to progress.

Although he is no longer in his place, I put it on the record that I certainly did not put my name to this motion with any inclination to embarrass the Leader of the House. I think he is very good in his role, and I am sure he is pursuing this matter with his customary energy and vigour. What I am concerned about, as I have said in a number of interventions, is the sheer scale of expenditure envisaged and the lack of clear direction, both in the control of the project and in understanding what the objectives are, namely whether it is primarily and almost exclusively to make the building safe or whether it is to turn it into something else. If we do not know where we are going, we cannot chart an economically viable path to our destination. I detected one area of agreement, however, when the Leader of the House described the network of committees and bodies that have been involved hitherto as “spaghetti”. I entirely agree, and we heard that point from my hon. Friend the Member for Droitwich and Evesham (Nigel Huddleston). I think W. S. Gilbert put it very well in “The Gondoliers”: “When everyone is somebody, then no one’s anybody.” The truth of the matter is that when everyone is in charge, no one is in charge. We need to bring into this process a single directing unit with the power to see it through—if not an individual, a very small number of individuals. If we carry on as we are, with these large bodies in some sort of kaleidoscopic combination of pretty patterns that leads to no discernible progress other than an ever-increasing bill potentially running into the billions, we will not only expose the House to physical danger, but expose Parliament to public contempt. There is a real risk in spending billions on ourselves in this way, no matter how worthy the cause, that the public will not tolerate something that is grossly uneconomic.

I just want to ask the right hon. Gentleman a quick question. He talks about spending money on ourselves. Does he recognise that it would be spending money not only on democracy, but on the people who work here, who deserve a safe environment to work in?

Yes, I do recognise that, but I point out to the hon. Lady that having a good cause—a vital project, such as stopping this building burning down—is not a justification for spending possibly two, three, four or five times as much on prevention as could be spent to achieve the same objective. The worthiness of a cause is not a justification for spending 200%, 300% or 400% of what competent professionals should be able to budget for to carry out a project efficiently. In the short time that remains to me, I want to revert briefly to the question of the options and the question of decanting. I am in the same position as the Father of the House: I am unlikely to be affected personally by whatever arrangements are made for decanting. However, if the Houses of Parliament are emptied of MPs for 20 years—although it will probably not be 20 years, but 30 or even more—two, three or four generations of MPs will be out of here. They will be put in modern facilities, and when the time comes for them to return, they will not want to do it. If this building is indeed the heart of our parliamentary democracy, and if we wish to preserve it and prevent it from becoming nothing more than an over-expensive museum to the sort of political system that we used to have, we must ensure that MPs remain in at least partial occupation of the building, whichever option we finally choose.

I support the Government’s approach. I speak as someone who approaches major public spending programmes with a healthy degree of scepticism and who spent much of his pre-political career planning and delivering electrical installation works in period buildings across central London. I have looked at the evidence, and it is clear to me that the greatest risk to the taxpayer is not action, but delay. We know the condition of the Palace. We have heard that since 2016 there have been 12 asbestos incidents, 19 stonemasonry incidents and, importantly, 36 fire incidents. We know that key services fail regularly. We know that the current patch-and-mend approach is costing about £1.5 million every week and that the figure is forecast to rise to £2 million a week. Most importantly, we know that every year for which we defer a decision costs money. Continued delay adds about £70 million in direct maintenance and option planning costs, alongside between £250 million and £350 million in construction inflation. That is not caution; it is a very expensive form of procrastination. The Opposition seem to believe that these concerns are an argument for slowing down decision making yet again. We have seen that approach from them before, including in new nuclear capacity, when years of hesitation left us needing to import more energy at a higher cost. The “do nothing” brigade invariably presents delay as the cautious option, but in reality it is often just storing up bigger bills for the future. We have been debating variations of this issue for years. During that time, the condition of the building has not improved, the bills have not become smaller and the risks have not diminished. That is why I think that the Government are taking a sensible approach. What is being suggested is cracking on with a capped first phase, stronger financial controls, greater parliamentary oversight, annual scrutiny and further reporting before future decisions are taken. There is another aspect that should not be overlooked, which is that this should not be seen simply as a project for Westminster. The restoration of the Elizabeth Tower involved specialist skills drawn from across the United Kingdom. Indeed, a company from my own county, the Cumbria Clock Company of Dacre, near Penrith, played a central role in the conservation and restoration of the Great Clock mechanism itself, painstakingly restoring more than 1,000 components of what is arguably the most famous clock in the world. That is a reminder that projects such as these support highly specialist skills and expertise far beyond London. This programme has the potential to support thousands of jobs, apprenticeships and traditional crafts in every nation and region of the country.

The point is extremely well made. I am sorry to talk again about the building of the Scottish Parliament, but a decision was taken to use suppliers of all sorts of building materials from all parts of Scotland, and that was extremely well received by the people of Scotland. Secondly, one should always remember that—as I think the hon. Member is saying—all the money that is spent boosts the economies of various parts of the UK, so let us hope that the money is spent all over the UK.

The hon. Member makes a very good point. I can envisage a different debate in the future, when Members will come to the House and ask, “How do the businesses in our constituencies benefit from a project of this scale?” The National Audit Office says there is sufficient information to move forward, as does the Public Accounts Committee. At some point, prudence stops being prudence and starts becoming procrastination, and I believe that point has now been reached. For that reason, I support the Government’s approach and oppose the Opposition’s motion, which reminds me of a grumpy old man telling his long-suffering wife that their 1990s MFI kitchen is fine and just needs a lick of paint and some new knobs. I met a few of them during my career, and I have seen a few of them in the Chamber today.

I sympathise with the frustration of the Leader of the House, which was evident in everything he said. This is not an easy matter—if it was, we would have dealt with it by now. I loved his term “spaghetti governance”, because that lies at the heart of where we are. The situation has been a disgrace over many years, and my plea is to have a single accountable officer who is responsible for what is going on at the moment, for phase 1, on which we will be voting shortly, and for the definitive project in due course. We cannot demand of other Government Departments and agencies the financial discipline that we are not prepared to apply to ourselves. The Leader of the House said that we are the custodians of the seat of democracy, and he is absolutely right. But the exercise of democracy is a darn sight more than simply a stack of limestone, however exquisite; it is the functioning of democracy. It is what we do here, and what we must not interrupt in the course of the refurbishments. Unfortunately, confidence in democracy is low and confidence in ourselves is low, and I fear that the public simply will not understand why we are contemplating spending the spectacular sums that have been cited on ourselves. That is how it will be seen, regardless of whether that is fair or not. I have two tests, which I think are reconcilable. First, we must keep this place open for business. It is more than a pile of a bricks; it is the living, vibrant cockpit of our democracy. If it closes or decants, I genuinely fear that we will never return, and we will be spending all this money on what will amount to a museum—a white elephant. We can plan essential works around parliamentary business, not the other way around. We can do that with reasonable adjustments, such as canning September sittings and shifting the revising Chamber elsewhere, if we really must. In my view, a full decant is out. The EMI+ option is not great, but it is preferable. However, I am tempted by the suggestion from my right hon. Friend the Member for North East Cambridgeshire (Steve Barclay) that we could have the midway option of a temporary and time-bounded decant. Secondly, we have to keep this affordable. The public sector has a tradition of gilding the lily, and I fear that may be the case here. We must fix the basics, and we must do so quickly. Let us get on with it and make a decision beyond phase 1 now, not in 2030. That is where the cost of delay lies, not in the reasonable acquisition of details on the proposed spend, as has been suggested today. Let Notre-Dame and Buckingham Palace, which were delivered on time and on budget, be the guide, not the Elizabeth Tower and the disastrous Peers’ Entrance. We need to take a view on some of the proposals being made on net zero and exquisite energy-efficiency in an ancient building, coffee shops, educational facilities and visitors’ centres. We must not make the excellent the enemy of the good.

I appreciate the opportunity to speak, having listened to this very important debate, particularly as I am one of the 2024 Conservative intake. I am a historian by nature, and I came here as an 18-year-old and fell in love with the place. On the point made by the hon. Member for York Outer (Mr Charters), if we cannot bring young people into this building for the entire length of time of the proposed decant, we will be wrecking the opportunity for entire generations of young people to be inspired by the Palace of Westminster and the Parliament that sits within it. We Conservatives are not saying that restoration should not happen—far from it. This building is something we value, and we recognise that it needs to be improved and fixed, but we are against the renewal process, which will effectively introduce to the building architectural features that we will not get to use for 30 or 40 years, by which point they will be out of date. We will be setting up future Members of Parliament to be embarrassed by what we decided to go forward with. I want to say, as one of the 2024 intake, that it still remains the case that I value the heritage of this place and want to maintain it as much as possible, but I also want to keep access to it. I also want to make a point about the Christian heritage of this building. The Chapel of St Mary Undercroft is not mentioned once in the 125-page report, and there are some artist’s impressions that call into question what will actually happen to that unique and important part of the building. Worship takes place there several times a week, and it is an important part of the life of the Palace of Westminster. Would the Leader of the House reassure Members, when we come back on 8 December, where that worship will take place, and what will happen to the chapel and, indeed, to the Christian heritage of the building as a whole? Mr Speaker has said that “Parliament is a veritable trove of our Christian heritage”, and it is up to us to ensure that we maintain that. Furthermore, there are questions about the ceremonial and remembrance work that we do. Ultimately, the State Opening of Parliament is grand because it is here. I would be interested to know what will happen to that. I was with Baroness Fookes from the other place yesterday, talking about the importance of remembrance, and she highlighted the turning of the page of the remembrance books that takes place in the Royal Gallery, and we know the turning of the page takes place here every week as well. Where will that sort of remembrance and commemoration take place if we are decanted into Richmond House or the Queen Elizabeth II centre? We are Parliament, and it is up to us to maintain the heritage of our country. If we cannot do that because we are, in effect, sitting in a conference centre for decades, I would love to know how we can ensure that we continue to play that role.

I thank the shadow Leader of the House for opening this debate and Members from across the House for their thoughtful and considered contributions. We have heard almost 20 speeches. The restoration and renewal of this place—the home of British democracy, the mother of Parliaments—was never going to be easy.

I am going to make some progress, if I may. Anyone who has ever embarked on a renovation of their own home could have told us that this was never going to be easy. The scale of the works is clearly different, but the emotions of a home renovation are similar. The excitement and enthusiasm soon give way to the frustration of delays, the irritation of cost overruns and the mounting desire just to get it over with. Most home owners get through it, because they see progress and know that the end is in sight. We do not have that advantage. The renovation of Westminster has achieved little to date, with many billions and decades to go, so we must get this right from now—from this moment. We cannot allow this project to become a symbol of the failure of the political class to get things done, which it will if it continues on this path.

Much has been made of the first phase of works, and the hon. Member talks about how difficult it is for home owners to do projects in their own home. Does he agree that a lot of the work that goes into someone redecorating their own home comes from the preparatory work? We need to get that right, so does he also agree that the £3 billion for the first phase of works is really about getting some of the prep work right?

The hon. Lady makes a fair point, but the problem is that we do not know what the project is yet. It is not clearly defined, there is no clear timescale, and the cost is not clearly capped. If I am renovating my home, I know how much I can afford. We have responsibility for how much this project is going to cost on behalf of all British taxpayers.

For the record, I have consistently voted for a full decant, because I believe we need to sort this out and grip it. Would my hon. Friend agree with me that the test is not just whether we can get the maintenance right, but whether we, as custodians of this building, can work as a Parliament with clear governance and clear direction, not changing our mind and scoring points, and get this part right? I fear at the moment that the public will see what has gone on and worry that we are going to kick this down the road, spending money and wasting money. We need to get it right once, properly—not by designing the most expensive building in the world, but by making it safe and workable for the next generation.

My hon. Friend makes an important point. Of course, accountability is the key, and I will come to that a bit later. As the Father of the House, my right hon. Friend the Member for Gainsborough (Sir Edward Leigh), highlighted in his speech, the lack of clarity is concerning. When a hospital needs a new wing, we expect a clear budget. When a school needs rebuilding, we expect a timetable. Yet so far, when Parliament has needed restoring, it has been a struggle to get either. Of the options outlined to date, some will be more palatable to the public than others, but we surely cannot agree to an open-ended programme of works that could cost £39 billion and last 61 years. That point was by made a large number of right hon. and hon. Members, including my right hon. Friends the Members for Gainsborough and for North East Cambridgeshire (Steve Barclay), my hon. Friends the Members for South Leicestershire (Alberto Costa) and for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith), my right hon. Friend the Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison), my hon. Friend the Member for Droitwich and Evesham (Nigel Huddleston) and my right hon. Friend the Member for Aldridge-Brownhills (Wendy Morton). I recently met a group of high school students from the Borders who were here on a tour of Westminster. They would be long retired by the time this project finished, and that £39 billion cost would cover their local council’s budget for all the years in between. We have an obligation to ensure that these buildings stand for future generations, but we should not be passing them a bill of this size for that privilege. Despite what the Leader of the House claimed, we all understand that there must be investment to make the estate safe, but the spending must be made with restraint. If we agreed to that £39 billion budget and a 61-year project, tourists would add Westminster scaffolding to the list of famous sites to visit. The scaffolding itself may even get listed status! No, the renewal works must not drag on for decades at ever-escalating costs, otherwise the public will understandably ask why we can find tens of billions of pounds for improvements to the place where politicians work, while telling communities across the country that money is too tight to improve necessary services in the places where they live. While recognising the need to make buildings safe and accessible—a point made by the hon. Member for Penistone and Stocksbridge (Dr Tidball)—the project must demonstrate the fiscal responsibility that we seek of others. The restoration of Westminster should meet the same financial standards that any home renovation seeks. It must stick to its budget, provide good value for money, deliver a functioning building and preserve this home of democracy for future generations. The excellent Public Accounts Committee report published this month laid out in great, excruciating detail the scale of the problems. None of us can say we were not warned of what is going wrong with this programme. We do not yet know the true cost, the duration, the scope or who leads it. As the shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman), succinctly put it: “No single entity is empowered to make the difficult trade-offs needed between cost, scope and timetable. Ask who is in charge, and the correct answer is: no one.” All the boards and committees set up to manage the programme are simply, as the Leader of the House highlighted, the spaghetti junction of accountability. That is not acceptable. The Public Accounts Committee also makes it clear that MPs have not been properly engaged on the scope and purpose of the programme. By June, fewer than half of sitting MPs had engaged with the project team, and the Committee questioned the quality of that engagement. If I may say so, the intervention by the hon. Member for Bury St Edmunds and Stowmarket (Dr Prinsley) highlighted that perfectly. He rightly highlighted some of the failures of
