It is a pleasure to close this debate on behalf of the Government. I am delighted to see so many Members on the Labour Benches who are interested in R and R. It is hard to believe, but it has been six and a half years since I was last at the Dispatch Box. I was in opposition, and it was on this very subject—good things come to all who wait. At that time, I accused one Jacob Rees-Mogg, late of this parish, of wanting to kick the can down the road, as many Members have said today. As a former Prime Minister once said, “Nothing has changed.” Nothing has changed because we are here again with the Conservatives making exactly the same points. The shadow Leader of the House, the right hon. Member for Hereford and South Herefordshire (Jesse Norman), wants us to rip everything up and start all over again, in pursuit of a mythical option that will somehow take far less time and cost far less money, without any explanation from the Opposition of how that is going to happen. I am going to praise the right hon. Gentleman. He is famed for his works on Edmund Burke and Adam Smith, but I was drawn to one of his earlier works, entitled “Breaking the Habits of a Lifetime”—something I am afraid he has not followed today by once again failing to tackle the hard decisions. I will be honest: I thought I had hit comedy gold when I discovered another work entitled “Stand Up Straight and Sing!”, only to find out that it was actually by an American opera singer of the same name. I am sure that one day the right hon. Gentleman will get his wish, and Vogue will come calling. We have had a lively debate today, and I hope that the Opposition have found that this was a good use of their Opposition day, ahead of the main debate. I am not sure whether Opposition Members actually thought this was a good idea. At its heart, restoration and renewal is a House matter. The Government have done the responsible thing and waited for the reports of the National Audit Office and the Public Accounts Committee, which agree that the House now has all the evidence it needs to move forward. That is why we have tabled a motion and will allow time for a full and informed debate on the matter on 8 December. For the avoidance of any doubt, that is a Tuesday—the shadow Leader of the House obviously thought otherwise. There have been many contributions today. I would like first to mention the Liberal Democrat spokesman, the hon. Member for Newbury (Mr Dillon), on what is, I think, his first outing. I agreed with almost everything he said. He was very good. My hon. Friend the Member for Blaenau Gwent and Rhymney (Nick Smith) pointed out the dangers of make do and mend, and said that that was not an answer. As the Father of the House pointed out, we have sparred on a number of occasions. He is very clear in his view. I remember him telling the Sponsor Body that because it had come up with a decision that certain people would not like, it would be abolished—and he was right. That is part of the problem: the fact that we have had this constant chop and change all the time. My hon. Friend the Member for Bootle (Peter Dowd) made some very important points and said that it is clearly time for us to actually take the decision. The right hon. Member for North East Cambridgeshire (Steve Barclay), the Chair of the Finance Committee, whom I do not see in his place at the moment, gave us a lot of figures. He said that we should decant for four years—based on what, I don’t quite know. Again, he did not actually come up with a solution. In a powerful contribution, my hon. Friend the Member for Penistone and Stocksbridge (Dr Tidball) talked about disability access to this House and, indeed, the importance of staff benefiting from that. As someone who looks after office accommodation for Government Members, I am sure that Members will say—

I want to thank my right hon. Friend for setting an example to this House when I was first elected and ensuring that I got an accessible office that was close to the Chamber as soon as I possibly could. It made a great difference to my ability to settle into this House and do my job for my constituents.

I thank my hon. Friend very much for that intervention. She identified problems that many of us probably did not think about, such as where the lights and door handles are fitted. It took me a year and a half to get a door changed in Portcullis House, which is ridiculous. The hon. Member for South Leicestershire (Alberto Costa) wanted no decant whatsoever. My hon. Friend the Member for York Outer (Mr Charters) again pointed out the cost of delays, and the great opportunity for apprenticeships that this programme will deliver. The hon. Member for Droitwich and Evesham (Nigel Huddleston) talked about the importance of heritage; my hon. Friend the Member for Loughborough (Dr Sandher) spoke about the importance of heritage, too, as well as the risks around the project. The right hon. Member for Aldridge-Brownhills (Wendy Morton) talked about the cost of the project. My hon. Friend the Member for Southgate and Wood Green (Bambos Charalambous) reminded us all of the vote in 2018. We are now in 2026—it is a bit like “Groundhog Day”, isn’t it? Here we are again, rather than actually getting on with it. The right hon. Member for New Forest East (Sir Julian Lewis) spoke about the importance of keeping the building safe and the importance of a good governance structure, which I accept is a point a lot of Members have brought up today. It is certainly something that we need to get right. My hon. Friend the Member for Penrith and Solway (Markus Campbell-Savours) talked about his own experience in major construction projects and, again, spoke of the dangers of delay. The right hon. Member for South West Wiltshire (Dr Murrison) also talked about the governance structure, and said that we could somehow do everything without the September sittings, which, if I am brutally honest, I am not convinced about. The hon. Member for South West Devon (Rebecca Smith) also spoke about the importance of heritage. We should never forget that we are the custodians of this building, and we will pass it on to the next generation. We have heard the usual rhetoric from the Opposition Benches today. However, we cannot live with another decade of delay and another review. If we are honest, we actually knew about these problems 70 years ago— I did not, because I am not quite that old, but a lot of these problems were known about—and we did nothing about them. Pausing this programme is not the frugal choice. The act of merely propping up the estate costs the taxpayer £1.5 million every week, and that figure will rise to £2 million, which is a point a number of Members made. Every year of dithering adds up to £420 million to the lifetime costs of the programme. We have been around this track before. We have debated it, redebated it, picked and unpicked options for over 10 years. I seem to recall that the Conservatives were in government at the time. Meanwhile, the risk to this building will not wait for another review cycle. Members of this House are entirely right to demand tighter governance and a relentless approach to cost control, but there is nothing stopping us making progress while we continue to improve the way that the programme is run and seek cost reductions ahead of the 2030 decision point. The motion that the Government have tabled for debate next month will build on the momentum of the programme through an initial package of works with a capped spending profile, narrow the options under development to refocus the programme and bring immediate cost savings. It will require a thorough reassessment of the programme’s governance ahead of a final decision by the Houses in 2030. I urge the House to reject the Opposition’s motion and support the Government’s amendment. Question put (Standing Order No. 31(2)), That the original words stand part of the Question.

I am here for my constituents residing in the 500 units of the Collective, a co-living block in NW10, who face a potentially illegal bout of evictions—I have checked this—in this cold, by an absentee overseas landlord who claims that they have zero tenancy rights because they are members, not tenants. This has been in The Times and in the Metro . The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to ensure that The Collective Old Oak, in matters relating to the management of their homes, engage meaningfully with residents over concerns raised by residents about the building, and that decisions are made in a fair and transparent manner, providing sufficient support to residents and avoiding evicting them over the Christmas period. Following is the full text of the petition: [The petition of the residents of the constituency of Ealing Central and Acton, Declares that those living in The Collective Old Oak are very strongly concerned with the level of service they have been provided; further declares that residents are unsatisfied with The Collective ’ s inadequate communication with the community; and further declares that residents are frustrated with the buildings owner’s apparent lack of compassion having served notice on hundreds of residents, requiring them to leave their home before Christmas. The petitioners therefore request that the House of Commons urge the Government to ensure that The Collective Old Oak, in matters relating to the management of the building, engage meaningful with residents’, and that concerns raised by residents about decisions affecting their homes are listened to, and that The Collective Old Oak manage such situations in a fair and transparent manner, providing sufficient support to residents and avoiding evictions across the Christmas period. And the petitioners remain, etc.]

title: Medomsley Detention Centre:  Youth Custody Safeguarding

items.txt: I thank Mr Speaker for granting today’s debate on the work of the Medomsley detention centre survivors and their fight to ensure that the youth custody system is fit for future generations. I do not claim to be the representative for all the men who were subjected to horrific abuse at Medomsley, and over the next few minutes I know that I will not fully capture all the pain and disappointment that they have carried with them throughout their lives. All I can do is set out to this House how their courage, determination and resilience materially changed our system—a system that they have pushed against for decades and which has finally opened its eyes to the seriousness of what happened in County Durham. Between 1961 and 1987, hundreds if not thousands of young men were physically and sexually abused at Medomsley detention centre. The perpetrators of this abuse were the very people responsible for their care. They knew that many of those young men were already extremely vulnerable because of their childhoods. Victims were told not to speak up, and when they did they were not believed. Prison staff were aware of the abuse that was taking place, but often did nothing. That meant that Neville Husband and others acted for years with impunity. The Prisons and Probation Ombudsman report, which I will come to later, lays bare what took place in harrowing detail. Above all else, tonight is about the victims and what their determination means. Many are no longer with us to see the changes that would eventually be made. We know of at least two young men who died in custody, Ian Shackleton and David Caldwell. There is compelling evidence to suggest that their deaths were avoidable and caused by neglect. It is unbelievable that their deaths did not trigger any meaningful review by the Prison Service or the Home Office. Sadly, there were others who also did not survive. Some victims took their own lives because of what they had endured at Medomsley and the shame they carried with them. Richard Hall, or Richie as he is known, is one of the Medomsley survivors. I have had the honour of getting to know him, and tonight he is in the Gallery—thank you for allowing me to say that, Madam Deputy Speaker. I first spoke with Richie not long after the general election in 2024. If someone had told him then that two years later he would walk into the Deputy Prime Minister’s office to make a powerful case about these issues, he would not have believed them, yet earlier this year he did just that. I give special thanks to the Minister for his part in making that meeting possible, for his continued support for Richie and for dedicating so much time to this critical issue. Richie spent his entire childhood in the care system. He was moved 32 times, during which he suffered frequent physical and sexual abuse. Like Richie, many of the children and young men who arrived at Medomsley already carried with them unimaginable trauma. A while ago, Richie sent me a local authority document outlining his placements in care, telling me that that was his life in a few pieces of paper. Richie’s interactions with the state over the decades made him feel invisible. He told me about his experience of bringing a claim against the Home Office and attending a hearing in the judge’s chambers, where the local authority told him that there was no trace of a Richard Hall. He later found out that his files had been destroyed. It was devastating for Richie to learn that any potential trace of what he lived through was erased as if it had never happened. I want Richie to know his worth. It is more than what is written on the pieces of paper he sent me. Richie is a remarkable and resilient man. His bravery, and that of other victims, has truly moved the dial. Their courage led to the conviction of Neville Husband, who was described by the PPO as “possibly the most prolific sex offender in British history.” It is a moral scar on previous Governments that Husband was released before thes

I am really grateful to my hon. Friend for securing this debate. Kevin Young was a constituent of mine, and he retold to me the horrific abuse that he experienced at Medomsley in 1977. That trauma stayed with him until his premature death in 2021, and he never received the apology that he was due. One of the things he told me was that when he left the gates of Medomsley, he went and reported the crimes to Durham police; they told him to go home because he should not report on prison officers. The injustices in Durham police need investigating. Does my hon. Friend agree?

Kevin was one of the survivors, and he was a testament to what people like him can be, even though they have to overcome the most severe and horrible traumas. It is so sad that he did not live to see any apology to him. The fact that he was told to go home, as my hon. Friend says, must hit all our hearts really hard. What happened with the Law Lords is just a snapshot of the survivors’ fight. It has been a year since the PPO published its report on what the authorities knew about the abuse that took place at Medomsley, the opportunities to have intervened at the time and the lack of action taken. Before the special investigation was commissioned in 2023, victims had fought long and hard for a detailed examination of the abuse that took place and how it was allowed to go on for so long. The independent inquiry into child sexual abuse initially included Medomsley in its scope. However, in 2019, a determination was made by the chair that the inquiry would not proceed to investigate what happened at Medomsley, because of the ongoing police investigations and because many of the survivors were over 18 when they were abused. Countless letters to the Government, meetings with Ministers, a judicial review and inspiring persistence pushed the previous Government to commission the independent review in 2023. The report that was produced is absolutely sickening. It sets out the systematic nature of the abuse that took place and the litany of failures from authorities that enabled the culture to embed itself. A severe deficit of governance, leadership and oversight meant that violence could be, and was, a part of everyday life at Medomsley. The Prison Service, the police, the Home Office and other organisations in authority ignored and dismissed the abuse. What was happening at Medomsley became an open secret in the local community. One of the crucial outcomes of the report is that it underlines what is needed to improve safeguarding in today’s youth custody estate. Adrian Usher, the ombudsman, asked that particular consideration be given to the complaints process. He also highlighted the absence of a requirement for children to be asked proactively by an independent party about their experience in custody. In response, the Government announced a rapid review of safeguarding arrangements in youth custody, led by Isabelle Trowler, which reported in July. I would be grateful if the Minister could respond to a series of questions that I have about the implementation of its recommendations. First, will the Minister confirm whether appropriate procedures have now been put in place to ensure that heads of safeguarding inform the local authority designated officer of all corruption allegations involving children? Secondly, the routine involvement of heads of safeguarding in counter-corruption case management meetings has the potential to inject safeguarding expertise into the early stages of investigations—something that the Medomsley victims deserved but were not afforded. I would be grateful if the Minister could outline to victims how the Government will monitor the implementation of that recommendation to ensure that it improves decision making and the planning of investigations involving harm to a child. Thirdly, will the Minister update the House on the Government’s progress in implementing recommendation 4, which concerns the independent inspection of HM Prison and Probation Service’s counter-corruption practices? The Trowler review highlighted that, although HM inspectorate of prisons tests whether staff know how to make referrals to counter-corruption, and a senior leader has responsibility for this, it does not test decision making or the quality of investigations. Has HMPPS concluded the review of its counter-corruption, fraud and bribery functions? When will it implement strengthened independent assurance and scrutiny processes? Fourthly, Isabelle Trowler recommended that the complaints process be changed to permit trusted adults to

I thank my hon. Friend for her passionate speech. She will know that the former Medomsley detention centre was located in my current constituency of Blaydon and Consett. As she says, the Usher report, which was published last year, sets out the horrific events and offences that took place there. It sets out and how people like Neville Husband managed to abuse hundreds of young men and boys—so much so that he has been labelled one of British history’s worst sex offenders. Does my hon. Friend agree, as I know she will, that we must make sure that this cannot happen in future and that the Government are taking the steps needed to prevent situations like this?

My hon. Friend is right. What I am trying to say today is that we are thankful to the victims, that hopefully things will change and that our Government are doing everything they can to ensure that this does not happen again, so the victims who are still here can feel vindicated to some degree. I will end by paying tribute to the survivors. Throughout my engagement on the issue, I have been deeply moved by the experiences of those who were at Medomsley: people like Richie, who have kept going despite what they have been through. There are others who did not wish to be named today. They should always be proud, because the work that they have done will protect countless children. On behalf of this House, I say thank you.

Let me start by thanking my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne East and Wallsend (Mary Glindon) for securing a debate on such an important issue, as well as the Members around here who have raised this critical issue in Parliament over many years. I should mention the right hon. Member for Basildon and Billericay (Mr Holden), who sits on the Opposition Benches. When he was a representative of the north-east in the last Parliament, he also raised this issue consistently, and I think he deserves great credit for doing so. As my hon. Friend set out, between 1961 and 1987, thousands of young men sent to Medomsley detention centre were subjected to the most horrific systematic sexual and physical abuse. Those young men should have been safe in the care of the state. Instead, they were subjected to appalling acts of physical, sexual and psychological abuse at the hands of the very people who were supposed to protect them. Two of those young men tragically died, and countless others have lived with the consequences of what happened for the rest of their lives.

I thank the Minister for giving way, and congratulate my hon. Friend the Member for Newcastle upon Tyne East and Wallsend (Mary Glindon) on bringing such an important issue to the Chamber. My patch is in Northumberland. A significant number of individuals—young lads—were sentenced to Medomsley, yet very few have come forward with cases of abuse. These people are hiding some of the worst possible abuse by some vile individuals. Does the Minister have any idea why on earth lots of these young individuals are not prepared to come forward with their case of abuse?

My hon. Friend raises a really important point. I came into this job in September 2025, and the ombudsman’s report we have heard about was published in November. I went to Newcastle to meet some of the victims, and I will talk later about the meeting I had with Richie and others, but I was shocked and concerned that more victims did not want to meet me. That is not because I thought they especially wanted to meet me, but I am concerned that thousands of victims—across the country, but perhaps mainly in the north-east—do not want to talk about it, perhaps for good reason. Now, that is perfectly acceptable. No one is suggesting that that is wrong, but I hope those victims are getting the support they need, and we in government have a role to try as much as we can to reach them and make sure they know support is available. I hope that this debate will raise awareness—even in a small way—among those victims who may be watching that support is available, and they can talk about these issues and play a part in making sure what happened at Medomsley never happens again, as Richie and others have. As I said, in November last year, the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman published the findings of the investigation into Medomsley. That report lays bare systematic failures by the authorities and a litany of failures by Governments. Through inaction, the abuse was allowed to continue for decades, with devastating consequences for many thousands of young men. Anyone who reads that report—I have read it twice now—cannot but be shocked and ashamed of the country during that period.

One of the things that Kevin Young always asked, and that I have always asked, is how it was that people in leadership said that they did not know what was happening or the scale of abuse that was occurring, but everybody else did. Should there not be a liability on those individuals to make it their business to know what is happening within their institution, but also to ensure they do not sign off promotions for people such as Neville Husband, who then went on to other institutions and continued the abuse?

My hon. Friend is absolutely right that structures need to be in place to make sure that that kind of culture, where things are overlooked and heads are in the sand, does not develop. I hope that in the rest of this debate, I will be able to set out some of the measures we have taken to ensure such structures are in place and that any mistreatment of children in the care of the state is clamped down on immediately. I will come on to some of the action we have taken since the ombudsman’s report. No apology can undo what happened or make amends—far from it—but I want to say in this place in the strongest terms that the abuses at Medomsley should never have happened. The state failed these young men. Last year, the Deputy Prime Minister apologised on behalf of the Government, and I do so again today. On behalf of this Government, we are sorry, and today I am thinking of every man who survived Medomsley and the families who have lived with the consequences alongside them. As I mentioned in response to an intervention, earlier this year I had the privilege of meeting several men who are survivors of Medomsley, including Richie, who is in the Gallery today. Their stories—the hours I spent speaking to those who came forward to meet me—have weighed on me more heavily and moved me more significantly than any other issue I have encountered, whether as a Minister or over the best part of a decade working at the Bar, mainly in child public protection work. Simply put, I came away from those meetings completely in awe of those men’s courage, not just to have gone through what they did but then to come forward to meet me and relive it, which I know was a difficult experience. They have shown remarkable and ongoing bravery, and it is thanks to their persistence and determination that we are taking action—which I will come on to discuss—to make sure that what happened at Medomsley is never repeated and others do not have to suffer as they did. The PPO’s report has been the catalyst for that action, but that report would not have happened if not for the brave advocacy of those survivors. It has triggered a whole programme of work to strengthen safeguards for everyone in the state’s care, and I thank Adrian Usher and his team for their work to uncover the full extent of these failures. Their report made it clear that the complaints process at Medomsley was deeply flawed. When young men found the courage to speak out, their complaints were denied or dismissed, as we have heard from my hon. Friend and her constituent, Mr Young. They were left with no one independent to turn to and nobody to trust. While the youth estate today bears little resemblance to the detention centre back then, the report rightly challenged us to consider whether we are doing enough to make sure that every child has someone to turn to. The report recommended that we strengthen access to trusted, independent adults across the young estate, ensuring that there is always someone who children can raise concerns with, and that is why I commissioned Isabelle Trowler, the chief social worker for children and families for England, to carry out a rapid review of safeguarding arrangements. Again, I am extremely grateful to Isabelle for her careful and diligent work. The review made 34 far-reaching recommendations and set a clear direction for the system. What I know, and what the review made clear, is that safeguarding must underpin everything we do in youth custody, and that responsibility is shared by everyone across the system. The review set out the need for stronger oversight and accountability in safeguarding investigations, so that when concerns are raised, they are taken seriously, properly investigated and acted upon. It made recommendations for building a stronger, safer workforce with strengthened recruitment, vetting and better training. Importantly, it made recommendations for giving children a stronger voice through advocacy services and more accessible complaints proc

title: Strategically Important Industries: Private Sector Investment

items.txt: 1. What steps he is taking to support private sector investment in strategically important industries.

Good morning Mr Speaker. We are backing strategically important industries through our industrial strategy, with growth-driving sectors and frontier technologies underpinned by the strength of our foundational industries to deliver growth in every postcode. Through the Office for Investment we work directly with domestic and international investors to enable major projects to crowd in private capital. We are also tackling barriers to investment, from planning and energy costs to access to finance. Since the industrial strategy was launched, more than £390 billion of private investment commitments have been secured across those key sectors.

The INEOS Inovyn saltworks in my constituency is one of only two producers of evaporated salts in the United Kingdom, and its salts are used in food production and water treatment. Will the Minister meet me and INEOS Inovyn to discuss whether the critical chemicals resilience fund could be used to back private investment and keep the Runcorn plant going?

The Government place a high priority on our critical industries through procurement, investment through access to capital with the British Business Bank and, as the hon. Lady mentioned, schemes such as the critical chemicals resilience fund and our £2.5 billion support for the steel industry. I am familiar with the situation with the Inovyn saltworks, which she raised with me last year when I was the Minister for industry. We had a productive meeting then, and I confirm that the Under-Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (Blair McDougall) agrees with the opportunity for an additional meeting, and would be happy to meet the hon. Lady and INEOS.

To speed up investment in strategically important industries in Grangemouth, Government intervention must be used to accelerate investment decisions. With ground remediation identified as the biggest barrier at Grangemouth, will the Minister lobby Treasury colleagues to use the new energy wealth fund to invest in ground remediation quickly in strategically important sites such as Grangemouth? Will he update the House on conversations that the Department is having with the Scottish Government, whose agency Scottish Enterprise is primarily responsible for ground remediation at Grangemouth?

My hon. Friend is right: ground remediation is a significant barrier to investment in Grangemouth, just as we have seen at other large brownfield sites around the country. I am happy to take forward his suggestions, and we are pushing the Scottish Government hard to move faster on this.

I know that the sympathies of the House will be with the nearly 11,000 employees of Poundland who, as Christmas approaches, face an uncertain future. We do not think the solution to Poundland’s collapse is public sector investment into a business that, for all its importance to our high street, would not meet the threshold as strategically important. Nationalisation in this instance is a political sideshow and a trade in false hope, and I believe that the Government agree. Poundland employees need practical help, and industry—strategic or otherwise—needs a climate in which it can survive. What will the Government be doing to support the protection of employee pensions? When it comes to the future of town centres, and any industry, will the Government address the economic policies that are making it hard to survive and operate a viable business?

There is clearly a lot more than the economic environment when we look at the issues around Poundland, and it is important to be slightly cautious about how we talk about things. I understand what the hon. Lady says when she talks about Poundland not being a strategic industry, but Poundland stores are strategic stores in towns in my constituency—I am sure she would acknowledge that—and they are strategically important to the employees who work there and who are currently our greatest concern. Poundland is part of the fabric of high streets up and down the country and this will be a very worrying time, particularly for employees who are very much in the front of our mind. The Secretary of State has been in close contact with Gordon Brothers about Poundland, as well as with USDAW, the shopworkers union, which is working hard on this. We want all parties to make every effort to secure the best possible deal to retain trading in as many stores as possible, and to protect as many jobs as possible.

As official statistics show, despite considerable pressure arising from international events, British businesses continue to be resilient, and growth to the end of the year in September was back to over 2%. Small and medium-sized enterprises represent 99% of businesses in the UK, and they are the backbone of that resilience and success. The Department supports them in a number of ways, including increased access to finance, cutting regulation, increasing small business rates relief thresholds, and tackling late payments with the Commercial Payments Bill.

I thank the Secretary of State for that answer. As he said, the UK Government are taking action to support our small businesses, from cutting business rates for high-street hospitality businesses in England, to ensuring that employers pay no national insurance on young employees under 21 and apprentices under 25. Many of our fantastic small businesses in Wrexham and across Wales want to play their part in tackling the NEET crisis and giving young people a route into good, local work. Does my right hon. Friend agree that the Welsh Government must match that ambition by ensuring that employers have the support and incentives they need to create those opportunities, so that, whenever we can, we make it easier for businesses to take a chance on young people and invest in their future?

I agree wholeheartedly with my hon. Friend about the role that small business plays in Wrexham, and in every constituency, in providing opportunities for young people. The Government’s work across a number of policy areas recognises that. He is right to mention the tax system, and the Milburn report suggested a further tilting of apprenticeship funding towards opportunities for young people. As he says, business rates and high street regeneration are devolved in Wales, and we would encourage the Welsh Government to use those powers alongside UK-wide measures to help businesses invest in young people and give them those opportunities.

My constituent, Paul Dyson, runs a small independent business that provides specialist motorcycle cleaning products and professional ceramic protection services. Paul’s ambition is to maintain strong customer relationships, generate a sustainable profit and remain financially secure, but he tells me that has become increasingly difficult in recent years because of regulatory and cost pressures. Will the Minister set out what steps he is taking to support small business owners like Paul, whose goal is not necessarily to expand and employ more staff, but to remain commercially viable?

Paul sounds to me like exactly the sort of person who is playing a major role in his local community; a business like that is a pillar of so many local economies up and down the UK. I say to my hon. Friend and to Paul that our small business plan is about supporting firms with the everyday pressures they face, through measures such as tackling late payments, improving access to finance and greater business support, all of which have come out of engagement with small business representative organisations and small businesses themselves. I direct Paul towards the business growth service, available at business.gov.uk, which provides a full list of interventions that might support him in his mission.

One thing that would make a significant difference to small businesses in rural constituencies like mine, is having a reliable mobile service. Unfortunately, my constituency is rated as one of the worst in the whole UK for mobile service. That has an impact on small businesses, as I heard at my surgery last week. Will the Minister work with his colleagues in the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport to ensure we can finally resolve this issue and get everyone access to adequate mobile service?

Many of us will recognise the problems that the right hon. Gentleman cites. He mentions his constituency, but I have to say that I find the mobile signal quite poor here in London at times, when I am going to and from the House of Commons. As he says, the issues he raises are the responsibility of DCMS, but he is right that they have a direct relationship to business productivity. I will continue to seek to work with colleagues to rectify the problems for his area, and for all our constituencies.

This week, households were informed about significant increases to the energy price cap, but small and medium-sized businesses in my Chichester constituency are petrified about continued rises in energy costs, as they have been offered no protection from the market. At a time when this Government are talking about economic growth, employing more young people and easing the cost of living, businesses will be struggling, potentially having to cut staff hours and increase prices, as a result of rising energy costs. Will the Minister outline what protections the Government are providing to such businesses against those costs, particularly over the winter months?

The hon. Lady has probably heard me talk many times about my personal obsession with the record high industrial energy prices we inherited from the Conservative party, and the need to take action in that regard. A difference between businesses and households is that businesses tend to be on fixed-rate arrangements, but as she says they will be concerned about going into next year, when those arrangements may expire. For manufacturers, who are the most exposed to those pressures, the British industrial competitiveness scheme is open and will reduce energy bills for eligible businesses by a quarter. The deadline for that scheme is on Monday, so hon. Members should ensure businesses in their constituencies get their applications in. All of this is part of the need for a much more resilient energy system that is less exposed to fluctuations in the price of gas.
I call the Chair of the Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee.

Hundreds of small businesses in our country are Poundland creditors, so this will be a moment of real anxiety to them, as it will be to the 12,000 staff who work at Poundland. I thank the Secretary of State for everything he has done so far, but will he give the House an assurance that he will use every means at his disposal to work with the administration so that we can get a solution that keeps Poundland as whole as possible, keeps as many staff in work as possible, and keeps as many stores open as possible?

I am grateful to the Chair of the Business and Trade Committee for his question, and I thank him and his Committee for the work that they have done in this area. I echo the comments of the Science Minister about the concerns that we all have for the employees of Poundland and the position that they are in. This is a commercial process, but we have been closely involved because of the impact on so many of our fellow citizens and on the public policy issues involved. This is a deeply worrying time, but there is still the prospect of a substantial package in terms of the number of bidders for Poundland stores, and ensuring that we get the best possible outcome for each of our constituencies and constituents is our priority. I will not say too much more at this stage, but I will endeavour to update the House as soon as I can next week on further developments in this area.

Following up on that, I have dozens of Poundland staff in two stores in Boston and Skegness who are deeply concerned about their futures. Can the Secretary of State reassure the House that the Government will ensure that the administration process is conducted properly, transparently and fairly to avoid any concerns about favouritism towards Gordon Brothers?

I can give the hon. Gentleman that assurance. The administration process will be run in the proper fashion, according to established rules. At the same time, in case they are unfamiliar with this process, I reassure the people who work for Poundland that they will get paid. While the stores continue to trade, payroll will be met. There are many different and contesting parts to this story, and I think he is hinting at part of that. He is right; the administrators will produce a report on the circumstances that have led to this set of events, including the directors and the process that has got us to this stage, but at the minute we should all try to reassure as many of our constituents as possible. There is still hope that we get a significant part of the business being purchased by a new owner out of this process.
4. What steps his Department is taking to help increase economic growth.

Economic growth is a top priority for this Government. Despite the international pressures that I mentioned in my last answer, the performance and resilience of the UK economy has been strong. Whether it is our industrial strategy, unlocking key markets with our trade deals, our reform of the planning system, our record commitment to science and innovation or the big increase in public investment that comes from the new fiscal rules, the statistics are unequivocal that the economy is stronger today than when this Government came to power.

Real economic growth should be not just seen in statistics, but felt on our high streets. It needs to go hand-in-hand with this Government’s devolution plan, and people and the communities that they live in need to really see and feel the results. What steps are being taken to ensure that local authorities benefit from the growth generated in their communities and will be able to reinvest it straight back into their local areas?

I agree wholeheartedly with what my hon. Friend puts forward. I believe that all economic growth is felt by our constituents, but at times in our history we have had differential performance in different parts of the UK, and people have not always felt that they have had the benefits of a high-performing economy. Her question hints at something that I believe is fundamental to the Government’s agenda: the devolution agenda, particularly fiscal devolution. For the first time, many parts of the country will have economic incentives to back growth, development and businesses in their area, and they will retain a share of the proceeds of that success. We have had some embryonic steps towards that in the last few years, but what this Government are doing is a major change in that regard. The fact that more areas will have not only the opportunity, but the power to lead themselves and say what is right for them is a significant innovation.

The education sector is often overlooked as a potential driver for economic growth. As the Secretary of State will know, his Department is in charge of education exports. While the Government have been particularly focused over the last couple of weeks on education imports, may I encourage them to refocus, at least within the Secretary of State’s Department? Will he look at how his Department can support leading universities to export education with an international presence in overseas markets? While he is here, may I invite him and perhaps the Minister for Artificial Intelligence to Harper Adams University in my constituency to look at the world-leading agritech university campus that we have there?

I strongly agree with the right hon. Gentleman’s statement. University exports and our ability to put the British higher education product in overseas markets are a key part of our work around trade deals—for instance, look at the progress in recent years in India with the presence of British universities abroad. That has always seemed to me to be a significant opportunity. To be frank, I want to change our conception of what an overseas student is. I would love for people to access British higher education in their own country—perhaps some of their modules—and for their overall experience to be a much more shared one between the UK and the place that they are from. The opportunity to have a different offer as well as export success is pretty exciting. I cannot promise to make that visit, because of my diary, but we will certainly do our best. The AI Minister is coming—[Interruption.] I think the Science Minister is also coming. I do not know how many of us the right hon. Member for The Wrekin (Mark Pritchard) can accommodate. If anyone else wants to come, it sounds like we are having a day out; he has united the House in this export opportunity.

The last time I questioned the Secretary of State on economic growth, he said with a great deal of sincerity that he is ambitious and wants more economic growth. He also said that he would be speaking to the Chancellor of the Exchequer about further work on the growth agenda. Two weeks later, the Chancellor announced in the Budget that next year, growth will be downgraded to just 1%. Did the Secretary of State forget to speak to the Chancellor, and does he want to distance himself from the lack of ambition shown by both the Chancellor and the Prime Minister?

Perhaps I will not thank the shadow Minister for that question. If we are frank about the 14 years of Conservative Government, the economy was basically stagnant over that period, despite the fact that there was record immigration—it is actually quite hard to underperform that badly and for the economy to not develop when so many people are coming to the UK. Since the election, we have seen not only stronger economic growth, but stronger economic growth per capita, so people are really feeling the benefits. Going back to the debates we had on the Budget, look at the environment the Chancellor faced going into that Budget. Gas prices had tripled, oil prices were up by 60%, and I think our 10-year borrowing cost was up by at least 75 basis points. He presented a package that gave real, substantial help to households and commanded market confidence. It contained an offer to entrepreneurs in the form of founders’ relief, an offer to high streets on the small business rate relief threshold, and major reforms to the energy market for industry. Business investment and economic growth have accelerated this year because of this Government’s stewardship of the economy.

Labour pledged a £2.5 billion steel fund as part of its industrial strategy, which was meant to be used across the UK to help modernise the UK’s steel industry and boost economic growth. However, research commissioned by the Liberal Democrats shows that over a third of that fund has now been spent, and so far not a single penny has been spent in Wales, despite the fact that Port Talbot is the biggest steel producing plant in the UK. It is not just Port Talbot; other steel producers in the UK—7 Steel in Cardiff, Sheffield Forgemasters and Liberty Steel in Scotland—are all potentially losing out on funds that could help them grow if the funding was not all being concentrated elsewhere. Modernising our domestic steel industry would not only make British steel far more competitive but protect and create jobs in local communities, so will the Secretary of State provide a boost to local economies across the UK and commit to using the steel fund to modernise our steel industry in all parts of the country?

I am for more jobs in all parts of the UK, but I have to say, whoever conducted that research for the Liberal Democrats needs to be sacked. A little bit of research in Hansard would reveal that the £2.5 billion steel fund is in addition to the half a billion pounds already committed to Port Talbot for the transformation of that steelworks. By the way, despite the commitment, that steelworks would have closed on polling day had it not been for the Labour party intervening to keep it open, then taking the money that was nominally allocated by the Conservative party and increasing the output—the terms and conditions for the staff, the money that was going to them, and the terms on which the transformation was to be completed. If you were to take that £3 billion envelope and allocate it on a per capita basis, Wales would get less than it has got. Of course Wales stands to gain more from our steel fund, but to say that it has not got the money, Mr Speaker—
Order. Secretary of State, you are meant to be going through the Chair, not having a personal conversation. You are getting far too excited!
5. What steps he is taking to support access to finance for women.

Hopefully we can be just as excited about access to finance for women in business. [Hon. Members: “Hear, hear!”] Currently, women only receive about 2% of equity investment for their businesses, which is why at the Budget, we announced that the British Business Bank would commit a further £100 million to back women-led businesses and funds on top of its £400 million investor pathways capital and diverse angel syndicate programmes, widening participation in venture investing. The Government also back the Invest in Women Taskforce, which has raised £635 million, including £130 million from the British Business Bank. We lead the Investing in Women Code, which is driving industry action on access to finance and has over 300 signatories.
